title: Acceleration bound
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.3 Timeline and the acceleration bound
text:
Acceleration bound. An upper bound on events averted if approval had moved earlier by the Bayesian saving for a whole treated population, which the book says is a bound and not a forecast.

## What it is
The calculation supposes approval moved earlier by the all-trial median saving and that N patients received the treatment during that window, at the trial's placebo event rate of about 2.4 percent a year and its relative reduction of 20 percent.
The events averted are N times that rate times that reduction times the years saved.

## Why it matters
Two orders of magnitude separate it from the in-trial figures.
That asymmetry is the real economics of trial design: the value of a trial is overwhelmingly in the decision it enables for the population outside it.

## In the book
The post-trial population size is the $M$ of the loss function in the working paper.
For REWIND the all-trial median decision is the end of the trial, so there is no median calendar saving.
The summary table ranks the population QALYs row last and defends it only as a bound.

## Pitfalls
The calculation assumes approval, reimbursement, manufacturing and clinical uptake would all move forward by the full years, and none of those would.
Manufacturing capacity for these agents was the binding constraint on access, so the realistic acceleration is a fraction of the statistical one.

## Check yourself
- Q: Is the acceleration bound a forecast? A: No, it is an upper bound under assumptions that did not hold.
- Q: Which assumption would you relax first? A: The book names approval, reimbursement, manufacturing and uptake as all moving forward by the full time.
R functions (bayestrials): select_month_of_events

title: ACE reporting guideline
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.3 Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
text:
ACE reporting guideline. Also called: ACE, Adaptive designs CONSORT Extension. The CONSORT 2010 extension for reporting adaptive trials, which adds items on the prespecified adaptations.

## What it is
The CONSORT 2010 adaptive-designs extension (ACE) is the reporting counterpart for adaptive trials.
It extends CONSORT 2010, predates CONSORT 2025, and adds items on the prespecified adaptations.

## Why it matters
A Bayesian adaptive design is reported in two layers: the generic randomized-trial items and the adaptation items ACE supplies.
The guideline is not a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial.

## In the book
The book lists ACE beside SPIRIT 2013, CONSORT 2025, a guideline on the content of statistical analysis plans, and the Bayesian checklists.
The Bayesian items that these lists do not name are the prior, calibrated success criterion, interim schedule, simulation report, software with seeds, and prior sensitivity.
Placing each where the generic checklist asks for its traditional counterpart satisfies the intent of all the lists.

## Pitfalls
None of the reporting guidelines around the protocol is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does ACE add to CONSORT 2010? A: Items on the prespecified adaptations.
- Q: Is ACE required by regulators for a Bayesian trial? A: No.

title: Adaptive enrichment
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.5 Adaptive enrichment and subgroup-specific doses
text:
Adaptive enrichment. A design that starts with broad enrollment and restricts to responsive biomarker subgroups as interim data accumulate.

## What it is
When benefit or the best dose differs by a biomarker-defined subgroup, broad enrollment can dilute estimates, and one dose may be wrong for part of the population. An enrichment design starts broad and restricts to responsive subgroups as data accumulate. At each interim, the subgroup posterior probability of benefit $\Pr(\theta_g > 0 \mid \text{data})$ maps to one of three actions: continue broadly, restrict enrollment to promising subgroups, or stop.

## Why it matters
The thresholds are calibrated by simulation, which is what the FDA draft Bayesian guidance asks for.

## Pitfalls
The multiplicity cost is real: subgroup-by-interim looks multiply chances of a chance finding. Hierarchical models that borrow across subgroups are the Bayesian answer. For dose-finding, dose-selection and enrichment decisions are usually treated separately unless the trial is built for both.

## Check yourself
- Q: Name the three interim actions. A: Continue broadly, restrict to promising subgroups, or stop.

title: adaptr
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text:
adaptr. An R package that simulates Bayesian adaptive multi-arm trials with response-adaptive randomization, early stopping and calibrated stopping rules.

## What it is
adaptr is an R package for simulating Bayesian adaptive multi-arm trials. It handles response-adaptive randomization, early stopping and calibration of the stopping rules, summarized as operating characteristics.

## Why it matters
The book calls it the closest open R counterpart to the simulation part of `bayestrials` for multi-arm designs.

## In the book
The book lists it among the R packages on CRAN.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does adaptr summarize its simulations as? A: Operating characteristics.
- Q: Which part of bayestrials is it closest to? A: The simulation part, for multi-arm designs.

title: Adequate and well-controlled investigation
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.3 The regulation: what "adequate and well-controlled" means
text:
Adequate and well-controlled investigation. Also called: adequate and well controlled. The study type defined in 21 CFR 314.126 that the statute requires: a clear objective, a valid control comparison, bias minimized, and an adequate analysis.

## What it is
The statute leaves the phrase undefined, and FDA's regulation at 21 CFR 314.126 defines it. Its purpose is to distinguish the effect of the drug from other influences, such as spontaneous change in the disease course, placebo effect, or biased observation.

The book paraphrases seven characteristics.
- A clear statement of objectives and of the method of analysis.
- A design that permits a valid comparison with a control.
- Subjects selected by an adequate method.
- Assignment that minimizes bias and assures comparability at baseline, usually by randomization.
- Measures against bias by subjects, observers and analysts, usually blinding.
- Well-defined and reliable methods of assessing response.
- An adequate analysis of the results.

## Why it matters
The book calls this the most useful list for a trialist to carry. The regulation expects the protocol to state the proposed analysis methods, which is the regulatory root of pre-specification, for Bayesian analyses as for frequentist ones.

## In the book
The regulation names placebo concurrent control, dose-comparison, no treatment, active treatment and historical control as recognized control types. The 2026 draft cautions that external controls differ from the treated group "because of the lack of randomized treatment assignment".

## Check yourself
- Q: Which item of the list is the root of pre-specification? A: Item 7, an adequate analysis, with methods stated in the protocol.
- Q: Is historical control an admitted control type? A: Yes, but the 2026 draft warns about its weakness.

title: Adverse event hierarchy
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.5 Aggregate safety assessment
text:
Adverse event hierarchy. Also called: hierarchical adverse event model. A hierarchical model across adverse event terms that shrinks many rare events toward a common distribution before flagging.

## What it is

A hierarchical model across adverse event terms, as in Xia, Ma and Carlin, shrinks the many rare events toward a common distribution before flagging. It works in the same way as the gamma-Poisson shrinker does for spontaneous reports.

## Why it matters

A trial reports many adverse event terms, so unadjusted flags multiply by chance. Berry and Berry borrow strength across adverse event categories within a trial, the within-trial version of the same remedy for multiplicity.

## In the book

After shrinkage a false discovery rate flag, such as the double FDR of Mehrotra and Adewale, limits the expected false-discovery proportion among flagged terms. Their procedure groups adverse events by body system.

## Pitfalls

- Shrinkage protects against noise in rare cells, not against bias.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the hierarchy borrow across? A: Adverse event terms, shrinking rare ones toward a common distribution.

title: Aggregate safety assessment
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.5 Aggregate safety assessment
text:
Aggregate safety assessment. A sponsor safety review built from four layers: blinded pooled review, unblinded committee review, hierarchical models across terms, and a false discovery rate flag.

## What it is

A sponsor's safety review is not one statistic. Four layers sit side by side, and each answers a different question.

- Blinded pooled review asks whether the overall event rate is higher than expected, without revealing the arms.
- The unblinded DMC review compares arms, with the boundaries and posterior rules of the monitoring and toxicity sections.
- A hierarchical model across adverse event terms shrinks many rare events toward a common distribution before flagging. See Adverse event hierarchy.
- A false discovery rate flag, such as the double FDR of Mehrotra and Adewale, limits the expected false-discovery proportion among flagged terms.

## Why it matters

Which layer is a trigger for action and which only a hypothesis for review is a decision for the safety plan to state, and the regulator will ask for it. The FDA guidance recommends reviewing accumulating events in aggregate and not one report at a time.

## In the book

Outside the trial, surveillance of marketed products uses MaxSPRT. 21 CFR 312.32 lists an aggregate analysis showing more frequent events on drug than on control among the evidence that triggers an IND safety report.

## Pitfalls

- No monitoring rule shortens or lengthens the reporting clocks.

## Check yourself

- Q: How many layers does the book list, and which one reveals no arm labels? A: Four. The blinded pooled review.

title: Allocation concealment
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.4 Allocation concealment
text:
Allocation concealment. Also called: concealment. Keeping the randomization list hidden from those who decide whether a patient enters, until the patient is irreversibly enrolled.

## What it is
Sequence generation produces the unpredictable list. Allocation concealment keeps that list hidden from the people who decide whether, and when, a patient enters the trial, until the patient is irreversibly enrolled.

## Why it matters
Concealment is about the time before the assignment. Blinding is about the time after it. A trial can be concealed and open label, which prevents selection bias but not bias in treatment and assessment. A trial cannot be properly blinded without concealment.

## In the book
The practical means are central randomization by an interactive response system, sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes and pharmacy-controlled coded packs. Central telephone or web randomization is the strongest and the usual choice in pivotal trials.

Schulz and colleagues examined 250 controlled trials. Inadequately concealed allocation went with odds ratios exaggerated by about 41 percent, and unclear concealment by about 30 percent. These are averages over one body of trials, an association and not a randomized comparison. Another paper describes clinicians holding envelopes up to bright lights and opening several at once.

The site sees only the kit number, returned after the patient is irreversibly enrolled. The protocol should say how concealment was done, and the book gives a model paragraph.

## Pitfalls
Even a perfectly random list is useless if the enrolling clinician can read it.

## Check yourself
- Q: Can a trial be concealed but open label? A: Yes. Investigator selection bias is prevented, but bias in treatment and assessment is not.
- Q: Which method is strongest? A: Central telephone or web randomization, because it cannot be opened in advance.

title: ANCOVA
al: change from baseline; analysis of covariance
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.10.1 Continuous outcomes: ANCOVA
text:
ANCOVA. Also called: change from baseline, analysis of covariance. Regress the follow-up outcome on treatment and the baseline value, which multiplies the variance of the effect by about one minus R squared.

## What it is
For a continuous outcome with a prognostic baseline covariate, the standard adjusted analysis is analysis of covariance: regress the outcome on treatment and the covariate, and read the treatment coefficient.

If the covariate explains a fraction $R^2$ of the outcome variance within arms, the variance of the effect and the sample size for a given power are multiplied by about $1 - R^2$.

## Why it matters
With a baseline-to-follow-up correlation $\rho$, the variance relative to the final-value analysis is 1 for the final value, $2(1 - \rho)$ for the change score and $1 - \rho^2$ for ANCOVA. The change score beats the final value only when $\rho > 0.5$, and ANCOVA is better than both at every $\rho$.

## In the book
For 90 percent power at a two-sided 5 percent level and a difference of 0.4 standard deviations, the example has the baseline explaining 30 percent of the variance. The book uses `covadj_ancova_gain` for this calculation.

FDA says power and sample size can be based on adjusted or unadjusted methods, and that the unadjusted choice is often more conservative.

For a linear model, the treatment effect is identical whether the outcome is the raw follow-up value or the change, so reporting on the change scale is a separate question from estimation.

## Pitfalls
The gain applies to a planned adjusted analysis: the covariate must be committed to in the protocol. The change-score analysis is unbiased in a randomized trial, but it spends precision.

## Check yourself
- Q: When does the change score beat the final value? A: Only when the baseline correlation exceeds 0.5.
- Q: By what factor does ANCOVA scale the variance? A: About $1 - R^2$.
R functions (bayestrials): covadj_ancova_gain, covadj_variance_factors

title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.4 ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: the same pattern with a hazard ratio
text:
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK. Also called: ANDROMEDA SHOCK. A septic shock trial comparing capillary refill and lactate targeting, reanalyzed on the hazard ratio scale under five priors to show the EOLIA pattern again.

## What it is
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK randomized 424 adults with septic shock in 28 intensive care units to an 8-hour resuscitation targeting capillary refill time or serum lactate.
Twenty-eight-day mortality was 34.9 percent (74 of 212) in the capillary refill arm and 43.4 percent (92 of 212) in the lactate arm, hazard ratio 0.75 with 95 percent interval 0.55 to 1.02 and $p = 0.06$.

## Why it matters
It shows the same pattern as EOLIA: the primary test did not reject the null, yet sizeable benefits stayed compatible with the data.
A cheaper, faster strategy that is probably better need not clear $p < 0.05$ to be adopted.

## In the book
Zampieri and colleagues used four priors on the odds ratio and found a posterior probability of benefit above 90 percent under all of them.
The book works on the hazard ratio scale with five normal priors: flat, neutral (standard deviation 0.35), skeptical (0.15), pessimistic (mean log 1.1, standard deviation 0.15) and optimistic (mean log 0.8, standard deviation 0.20).
Its pessimistic row gives a lower probability of benefit than Zampieri's, which is not a contradiction because priors, scale and model differ.
Capillary refill needs a finger and a stopwatch, and lactate needs a laboratory.

## Pitfalls
Our hazard ratio rows are not a replication of Zampieri's odds-ratio table.
A hazard ratio of 1.1 is a ten percent higher instantaneous hazard, not a ten percent higher probability of death.
Whether to adopt the strategy needs a utility function, a measured cost difference and a mapping to absolute mortality, which the posterior probabilities do not supply.

title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.4 ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: the same pattern with a hazard ratio
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: How much prior skepticism does the result tolerate? A: The table of five priors shows it; a sufficiently concentrated prior at no effect also lowers the probability of benefit.
- Q: Why is the choice of strategy not settled by the posterior alone? A: It also needs costs and utilities.
R functions (bayestrials): reanalysis_andromeda

title: Anytime-valid inference
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12 Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
text:
Anytime-valid inference. Also called: always valid p-value, optional stopping. Inference whose error guarantee holds at every stopping time, however the looks were chosen, built from e-values and test martingales.

## What it is

A group sequential design is a promise made in advance: the number of looks, their timing and the boundary at each are fixed in the protocol. Anytime-valid methods give a guarantee that does not depend on the schedule. The central object is the E-value.

## Why it matters

Four situations leave the plan behind: an unplanned look, an external publication, continuous review, and extending the trial. A guarantee that is a property of the data path covers all of them. If the schedule is known and will be kept, a group sequential design is the more powerful choice.

## In the book

A naive z test at the 0.025 level applied at every look inflates the false positive rate as looks increase. The e-value rule, monitored after every observation, stays within its bound by Ville's inequality.

The always-valid p-value is $p_n = \min(1, 1/\max_{m\le n} E_m)$. It is nonincreasing in $n$. The validity costs the Surcharge for anytime validity.

No FDA or ICH guidance names e-values, test martingales or anytime-valid inference as of November 2026. A sponsor proposing one is proposing a method and should expect to justify it in a CID paired meeting. No trial has yet been run on an e-process as its primary analysis.

## Pitfalls

- The protection is against optional stopping only. It does not repair bias from unblinding, selective data collection or invalid model changes.
- A posterior is coherent under any stopping rule, but a decision rule calibrated to type I error under a stated monitoring scheme is not.

title: Anytime-valid inference
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12 Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: A DMC adds a fifth, unscheduled look after the trial's own interim signal. Does a classical boundary schedule cover it? A: No. A look triggered by an interim signal in the trial's own data is outside the guarantee.
- Q: When should a sponsor not pay for anytime validity? A: When the monitoring schedule is under its control and will be kept.
R functions (bayestrials): ev_naive_false_alarm, select_simulate

title: Armitage recursion
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.3 The Armitage recursion
text:
Armitage recursion. Also called: Armitage-McPherson-Rowe recursion. An exact numerical recursion for the density of the accumulated score at each look, which gives crossing probabilities for any boundary.

## What it is

Armitage, McPherson and Rowe observed that the accumulated score is a Markov process. Given the score at look $k$ the next score is a normal increment, so the density of the score at look $k+1$ among trials that have not stopped is an integral of the density at look $k$ against a normal kernel, truncated at the boundary.

With $S(t)$ Brownian motion with drift $\xi$ and $f_k(s)$ the density on the event of no stop through look $k$, the recursion is as follows.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_1(s) &= \phi_{t_1}(s - \xi t_1)\,\mathbf 1\{s < b_1\sqrt{t_1}\}, \\
f_{k+1}(s) &= \int_{-\infty}^{b_k\sqrt{t_k}} f_k(u)\,\phi_{\Delta_{k+1}}\bigl(s - u - \xi \Delta_{k+1}\bigr)\,du, \qquad s < b_{k+1}\sqrt{t_{k+1}},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\Delta_{k+1} = t_{k+1} - t_k$.

## Why it matters

The type I error of the design is $\sum_k p_k$ at $\xi = 0$, and power is the same sum at the alternative's $\xi$. A futility boundary enters by truncating the integral in the other direction.

## In the book

The package computes it with `gs_crossing_prob`, using Gauss-Legendre nodes, accurate to many digits. Four unadjusted looks at 1.96 give 0.0631.

The recursion is exact except for numerical integration, because it uses only independent normal increments and the fact that the standardized statistic is a function of the score.

## Pitfalls

- Real trials depart from the Brownian model. Jennison and Turnbull show the canonical joint distribution holds asymptotically for a wide class of endpoints, and the simulation report is where departures are checked.

## Check yourself

- Q: What makes (look index, score) a Markov chain? A: Independent normal increments and a standardized statistic that is a function of the score.
- Q: How do you get power from the recursion? A: Sum the crossing probabilities at the drift of the alternative.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_crossing_prob, gs_naive_inflation

title: Arnold's measure of randomness
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.6.2 Arnold's measure of randomness
text:
Arnold's measure of randomness. Also called: stochasticity parameter, Arnold's stochasticity parameter. A geometric diagnostic that sums squared gaps between points on a circle to flag sequences that are too regular or too clumped to be random.

## What it is
V. I. Arnold proposed a geometric way to judge how random a set of points on a circle looks. His measure asks whether the points are spread the way independent draws would be: evenly spaced points are too regular, and clumped points are too attracted to one another.

Take $T$ points on a circle of length $L$. Let $x_1,\dots,x_T$ be the gaps between neighbors, so $\sum x_i = L$. The stochasticity parameter is the normalized sum of squared gaps:

$$
s \;=\; T \sum_{i=1}^{T} \left(\frac{x_i}{L}\right)^{2}, \qquad 1 \le s \le T .
$$

## Why it matters
Evenly spaced points give $s = 1$, strong repulsion. All points in one place give $s = T$, strong attraction. For independent uniform points the expected value is $s_1 = 2T/(T+1)$, close to 2 for large $T$.

A schedule from a linear congruential generator with a short period or poor lattice structure fails such tests. That is a reason to use a modern generator such as the Mersenne Twister, the R default, or PCG64, and not to write one's own.

## In the book
With $T = 15$ points modulo 100, the sequence $37i$ sits at about 1.19, near the floor of 1, and is unmistakably too regular. The sequence $3^i$ is at about 1.55, inside the central 95% interval of random sets, so the measure does not reject it.

## Pitfalls
The measure is a diagnostic and not a theorem. With $T = 15$ the random distribution is wide, and a single sequence inside the interval proves nothing. Such diagnostics detect pattern but do not certify an allocation mechanism.

title: Arnold's measure of randomness
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.6.2 Arnold's measure of randomness
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: What does $s = 1$ mean? A: The points are evenly spaced, strong repulsion, too regular to be random.
- Q: What is the expected $s$ for independent uniform points? A: $2T/(T+1)$, close to 2 for large $T$.
R functions (bayestrials): arnold_stochasticity

title: ASA statement on p-values
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.1.1 The ASA statement and the dirty dozen
text:
ASA statement on p-values. Also called: ASA statement, dirty dozen. The American Statistical Association's 2016 consensus on what a p-value can and cannot show, read together with Goodman's list of twelve common misreadings.

## What it is

The ASA statement (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016) is the consensus statement of the profession on what a p-value can bear, and regulators and journals cite it. Goodman's "dirty dozen" lists twelve misreadings of the p-value. A p-value is the probability of a test statistic at least as large as the observed one if the null hypothesis were true.

## Why it matters

Three misreadings recur in every trial team. The fix the statement suggests is to surround the p-value, not to abolish it: a pre-specified primary analysis, an effect estimate with an interval, and an account of everything that was looked at.

## In the book

- "p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null is true" is false. The p-value is a probability of data given the null, and the probability of the null needs a prior.
- "A non-significant result means there is no effect" is false. EOLIA reported p = 0.09, and a later Bayesian reanalysis put the probability that ECMO lowers mortality between 88% and 99%, depending on the prior.
- "p = 0.05 in one trial and p = 0.001 in another means the second effect is bigger" is false, because the p-value mixes effect size with trial size.

## Pitfalls

The p-value is not a bad tool. It underlies the type I error control that regulators require. Trouble starts when it is asked a question it was not built for.

title: ASA statement on p-values
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.1.1 The ASA statement and the dirty dozen
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: A trial reports p = 0.03. Is there a 3% chance the drug does nothing? A: No. The p-value is about the data given the null, not the null given the data.
- Q: A trial has p = 0.09. Does the drug do nothing? A: Not necessarily. The trial only failed to clear the bar.

title: Assurance
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2 A conventional power calculation is assurance under a point-mass prior
text:
Assurance. Also called: Bayesian power, expected power. The average of the power curve over a prior on the effect, the unconditional chance that the trial succeeds given what the sponsor believes.

## What it is

With a prior $\pi(\theta)$ on the effect, the probability that the trial succeeds is the average of the power curve:

$$
\text{Assurance} = \int \text{Power}(\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta .
$$

This is eq-assurance. O'Hagan, Stevens and Campbell named it; earlier versions are predictive power and expected power. For a normal prior $N(m, s^2)$ and a z test with standard error se,

$$
\text{Assurance} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{m - z_\alpha\,\mathrm{se}}{\sqrt{s^2 + \mathrm{se}^2}}\right).
$$

This is eq-assurance-normal.

## Why it matters

A conventional power calculation is assurance under a point-mass prior. Uncertainty lowers assurance even when symmetric, because the power curve flattens near one.

## In the book

For a trial sized for 0.20 at 90% power, a prior mean of 0.20 with standard deviation 0.10 gives assurance 0.75, and standard deviation 0.20 gives 0.65. Near a point-mass prior it is about 0.89. For phase 3 sized on a phase 2 estimate, assurance is often 50% to 70%.

## Pitfalls

Assurance is a forecast, not a measure of evidence and not an error rate. It does not replace the scenario table of operating characteristics. Type I error is computed under the null, whatever the sponsor believes. Keep the design prior (to forecast) apart from the analysis prior (to be defended).

## Check yourself

- Q: Does more uncertainty about the effect raise or lower assurance? A: It lowers it, for a prior centered on the design value.
- Q: Is assurance the Type I error under the design prior? A: No, type I error is computed under the null.
R functions (bayestrials): assurance, n_fixed

title: ASTIN
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.6 ASTIN: a Bayesian adaptive dose-response trial in stroke
text:
ASTIN. Also called: ASTIN trial. A Bayesian adaptive dose-response trial of a neutrophil inhibitor in acute ischemic stroke that stopped for futility at an interim.

## What it is
The Acute Stroke Therapy by Inhibition of Neutrophils (ASTIN) trial was a Bayesian adaptive dose-response study of a neutrophil inhibitor in acute ischemic stroke.

## In the book
Rather than a few fixed doses, it modeled the dose-response curve over a wide range with a smoothing model, so each dose borrowed strength from its neighbors. The accumulating posterior chose later patients' doses, targeted the dose near maximum effect, and drove early stopping for efficacy or futility under prespecified rules. The trial stopped for futility at an interim analysis.

## Why it matters
The dose-finding model, allocation rule and stopping rule were all specified in advance and evaluated by simulation, as the 2026 FDA draft expects for a Bayesian design.

## Pitfalls
The book keeps the description general. The exact dynamic linear model and allocation criterion should be taken from the original papers.

## Check yourself
- Q: How did ASTIN share information across doses? A: A smoothing model of the dose-response curve.
- Q: How did it end? A: Stopped for futility at an interim.

title: AWARD-5
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.4 Dulaglutide (AWARD-5): seamless dose finding
text:
AWARD-5. Also called: AWARD 5, dulaglutide seamless dose finding. A Bayesian seamless dose-finding trial of dulaglutide in type 2 diabetes, the best-documented precedent for the design.

## What it is
AWARD-5 tested dulaglutide in type 2 diabetes. It started in 2008 with seven doses and two controls.

## In the book
Stage 1 used response-adaptive randomization with interim analyses every two weeks, scored by a composite clinical utility index of HbA1c, weight, heart rate and blood pressure. Longitudinal modeling predicted the 12-month outcome from early data. The algorithm selected two non-adjacent doses, 0.75 and 1.50 mg, at the earliest permitted time, and stage 2 used fixed randomization against controls. In April 2009 randomization to 3.0 mg was stopped on the monitoring board's recommendation after heart rate increases and pancreatic safety concerns. Both doses were approved by FDA in 2014. By Berry's estimate the design saved at least a year.

## Why it matters
It needs a prespecified algorithm, an agreed role for the data monitoring committee, which could depart from the algorithm only on safety, and a simulated operating-characteristics report.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which two doses advanced to stage 2? A: 0.75 and 1.50 mg.
- Q: Why was the 3.0 mg dose stopped? A: Increases in heart rate and pancreatic safety concerns.

title: Backward induction
al: optimal stopping; dynamic programming; Bellman equation
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6 Backward induction: the Bayes-optimal stopping rule
text:
Backward induction. Also called: optimal stopping, dynamic programming, Bellman equation. Finding the Bayes-optimal stopping rule for a stated loss and cost by working backward from the end of the trial over the sufficient-statistic lattice.

## What it is

For a sequential decision problem with a finite horizon, a best rule exists for a stated loss and can be found by working backward from the end. After $k$ pairs the trial stops and declares a winner, or pays a cost $\kappa$ for one more pair. With $V_k(s_1,s_0)$ the minimum expected loss, the Bellman equation is

$$
V_k(s_1,s_0) = \min\Big\{ h_k(s_1,s_0),\ \kappa + \sum_{y_1,y_0\in\{0,1\}} \Pr(y_1,y_0 \mid s_1,s_0,k)\, V_{k+1}(s_1+y_1,\, s_0+y_0) \Big\},
$$

with $V_T = h_T$ at the horizon.

## Why it matters

The sufficient-statistic reduction collapses the exponential decision tree to a lattice with $(k+1)^2$ states at stage $k$, so the recursion is exact and costs $O(T^3)$ states. It prices stopping explicitly through the cost per patient and the loss per error.

## In the book

A loss ratio of 39:1 gives $\gamma = 0.975$, the Bayesian reading of one-sided 0.025. In the book's example a classification-loss policy gives power 0.903 with an expected sample size of 54.3 pairs against 100 for the fixed design. A utility-only rule declares treatment better with probability 0.513 under the null, so it is no confirmatory rule.

## Pitfalls

The rule is optimal only for the stated loss and prior, and the loss function is the design. The lattice assumes outcomes are seen before the next decision and balanced allocation; delays and response-adaptive allocation make it harder. No guidance mentions backward induction, so submit it as a pre-specified table.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a 39:1 loss ratio correspond to? A: $\gamma = 0.975$, one-sided 0.025.
- Q: Why can the policy be computed exactly? A: The posterior depends on the history only through $(s_1, s_0, k)$.
R functions (bayestrials): backward_induction, forward_oc, fixed_oc, decide_stop_single_arm

title: Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.3 Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
text:
Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines. Also called: BARG. Author guidelines for reporting Bayesian analyses, one of the few reporting checklists written for Bayesian work and not a regulatory requirement.

## What it is
The Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines (BARG) are one of the few guidelines written for Bayesian analyses, and they are author guidelines.
The other Bayesian lists are the seven-item ROBUST checklist and a consensus checklist for clinicians who read a trial analyzed by Bayesian methods.

## Why it matters
Generic protocol and reporting checklists have no named place for a prior, a calibrated threshold or a simulation report.
BARG helps an author report them.

## In the book
A report that gives the prior and its source, the success criterion with its threshold and calibration, the interim schedule and the simulation report, the software and seeds, and the prior sensitivity analyses, each where the generic checklist asks for its counterpart, satisfies the intent of all these lists.
The sponsor checklist turns the same content into numbered items.

## Pitfalls
None of the reporting guidelines around the protocol is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial.
The reviewer checklist asks more than a reporting guideline does, for example whether the simulated design is the design that was run.

## Check yourself
- Q: Is BARG a regulatory requirement? A: No.
- Q: Who is the clinicians' consensus checklist for? A: Clinicians who read a trial analyzed by Bayesian methods.

title: Basket trial
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.13 Borrowing across subgroups: basket trials
text:
Basket trial. Also called: basket design, tissue-agnostic basket. A trial of one therapy in several tumor types or biomarker subgroups, where a hierarchical model lets small baskets borrow from one another.

## What it is

A basket trial tests one therapy in several tumor types or biomarker-defined subgroups that share a molecular target. Each basket is small, and the question is which baskets respond. The traditional design runs a separate single-arm test in each basket with a multiplicity adjustment. The Bayesian design puts the baskets in a hierarchical model, for $K$ baskets with response rates $p_1,\ldots,p_K$:

$$
y_k \mid p_k \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_k,p_k),\qquad \mathrm{logit}\,p_k \mid \mu,\tau_b \sim N(\mu,\tau_b^2),\qquad (\mu,\tau_b)\sim \pi(\mu,\tau_b).
$$
This is eq-hier.

## Why it matters

Berry and colleagues applied the hierarchical model to oncology subpopulations and reported designs needing fewer patients per subgroup than independent analyses at the same type I error, under their own scenarios. The quoted figure is 4 to 7 fewer patients per group, and shows what the method can achieve, not what it will.

## In the book

In a mechanism example with ten baskets of 30 patients, nine baskets have 12 responders (40%) and one has 3 (10%). The outlier raises $\tau_b$, the nine typical baskets are pulled down from 40%, and the outlier is pulled up from 10%. If all ten have 12, the estimate stays at 40% and intervals narrow. Variants include the calibrated hierarchical model (CBHM), BLAST and EXNEX. FDA lists basket trials under borrowing and asks for justified exchangeability and explicit effect modifiers.

## Pitfalls

A basket that does not respond has its response overestimated, by almost three-fold in the example, and may be rejected more often than under independent analyses. The remedy is calibration by simulation with some baskets not responding.

title: Basket trial
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.13 Borrowing across subgroups: basket trials
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to a 10% outlier among nine 40% baskets? A: It is pulled up toward the others, a response overstatement.
- Q: Which error should be reported? A: The false positive rate for non-responding baskets.
R functions (bayestrials): borrow_basket_posterior

title: BATTLE
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.9.3 BATTLE
text:
BATTLE. Also called: BATTLE trial. A biopsy-mandated trial in pretreated advanced non-small cell lung cancer that moved allocation toward treatments performing better within biomarker groups.

## What it is

BATTLE was a biopsy-mandated trial of pretreated advanced non-small cell lung cancer with about 255 patients and four treatments: erlotinib, vandetanib, erlotinib plus bexarotene, and sorafenib. After an initial period of equal randomization, a Bayesian probit model moved allocation toward the treatments performing better within biomarker groups.

## Why it matters

It is described as the first completed biomarker-based, adaptively randomized trial in this disease. It shows RAR used among several arms within biomarker strata.

## In the book

The book also cites an earlier Bayesian adaptive randomization design for recurrent glioblastoma, evaluated retrospectively on four phase 2 trials. The lesson drawn is the caution of the multi-arm and time-trend sections: allocation inside small biomarker strata moves on little data.

## Pitfalls

Because allocation moves on little data in small strata, the burn-in, the cap and an analysis that respects calendar time matter more, not less. The book's guidance for such designs is a fixed control share, a burn-in, capped probabilities and concurrent controls.

## Check yourself

- Q: What preceded the adaptive allocation in BATTLE? A: An initial period of equal randomization.
- Q: Why is RAR in small biomarker strata risky? A: Allocation moves on little data.

title: Bayes factor
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3 The exact p-value and the Bayes factor
text:
Bayes factor. Also called: BF. The ratio of the probabilities that the alternative and the null assigned to the observed data, which turns prior odds into posterior odds.

## What it is

The Bayes factor measures the evidence in the data for one hypothesis against another. For a null $H_0:\theta = 0$ and an alternative with prior $\pi(\theta)$:

$$
\mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid H_1)}{p(y \mid H_0)} \;=\; \frac{\int p(y \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}{p(y \mid \theta = 0)},
$$

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\Pr(H_1 \mid y)}{\Pr(H_0 \mid y)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} \;=\; \mathrm{BF}_{10} \times \underbrace{\frac{\pi_a}{\pi_0}}_{\text{prior odds}},
$$

the second being eq-bf-odds. It weighs the data against both hypotheses and averages the likelihood over the prior, which is where its penalty for vague alternatives comes from.

## Why it matters

The p-value says nothing about how well an alternative explains the data. The Bayes factor does, but it needs a prior under the alternative. With a normal alternative $N(0,\tau^2)$ and $k = I_n\tau^2$ the integral is closed form:

$$
\mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; (1 + k)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left\{\tfrac12 Z_n^2 \,\frac{k}{1+k}\right\}, \qquad 2 \log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; Z_n^2 \,\frac{k}{1+k} \;-\; \log(1+k).
$$

This is eq-bf-gauss, the finite-sample version of the Schwarz criterion.

## In the book

With $\tau = 0.25$ and $I_n = 400$ the penalty is 3.26, so the Bayes factor reaches 1 only near $|Z_n| \approx 1.8$, where the one-sided p-value is 0.036. See Ockham penalty and Lindley's paradox.

## Pitfalls

The answer depends on the prior scale $\tau$. Choosing $\tau$ after seeing the data is as open to abuse as choosing the test statistic afterward, so pre-specify it. Sources sometimes write the ratio the other way up as $\mathrm{BF}_{01}$, its reciprocal.

## Check yourself

- Q: What turns prior odds into posterior odds? A: Multiplication by the Bayes factor.
- Q: Why does a vague alternative lower the Bayes factor? A: It spends prior mass on effects the data rule out.
R functions (bayestrials): bf10_normal, posterior_null

title: Bayes risk
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.1 The Bayes risk of a test
text:
Bayes risk. Also called: Bayes risk of a test. The expected loss of a test over both the parameter and the data, weighing each error by its prior probability and cost.

## What it is

Let $D(y) = 1$ declare the treatment effective, $\pi_0 = \Pr(H_0)$, and let the loss be $\ell_1$ for approving a useless drug and $\ell_0$ for withholding a useful one. The Bayes risk is:

$$
r(D) \;=\; \pi_0\,\ell_1\,\alpha(D) \;+\; (1-\pi_0)\,\ell_0 \int \beta_\theta(D)\, g(\theta)\, d\theta .
$$

This is eq-bayes-risk. A frequentist who reports $\alpha$ and $\beta$ reports its ingredients, but not the weights.

## Why it matters

The rule that minimizes $r(D)$ is found one data set at a time:

$$
D^{B}(y) = \mathbf 1\{\mathrm{BF}_{10}(y) > b\}, \qquad b = \frac{\pi_0}{1-\pi_0}\cdot\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_0},
$$

which is eq-bayes-rule.

## In the book

With equal odds and loss, the exact bar on $|Z_n|$ is $\sqrt{(1 + 1/q)\log(1+q)}$. The type I error of the Bayes rule exceeds 5% for small trials, passes 5% at the crossing, and then falls roughly like $(q \log q)^{-1/2}$. The fixed-level test has Bayes risk at least $\pi_0\ell_1\alpha$ at every $n$. For the Bayes rule both error rates tend to zero. A fixed bar spends a constant error forever.

## Pitfalls

The alternative $N(0,\tau^2)$ puts mass on harmful effects, so $\Pr(H_1\mid y)$ is not the benefit probability $\Pr(\theta>a\mid y)$. Restricting the rule to $Z_n>0$ does not preserve optimality.

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the fixed 5% test have Bayes risk that goes to zero as n grows? A: No, because its type I error stays at alpha.
- Q: What does the Bayes rule threshold b contain? A: The prior odds times the loss ratio.
R functions (bayestrials): decide_bayes_risk, decide_bayes_type1_table

title: Bayes' rule
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.1 Bayes' rule with a diagnostic test
text:
Bayes' rule. Also called: Bayes theorem, Bayes's rule. The rule that reverses a conditional probability: the posterior is proportional to the prior times the likelihood.

## What it is
Bayes' rule reverses a conditional probability. A screening test has sensitivity 90%, specificity 95% and the disease has prevalence 2%. Sensitivity is a probability about the test given the disease, but the patient wants the probability of disease given a positive test.

Writing the joint probability of disease and positive in two ways gives the answer. The prior $\mathbb{P}(D)$ is the belief before the result, the likelihood is $\mathbb{P}(+ \mid D)$ viewed as a function of the unknown state, and the posterior $\mathbb{P}(D \mid +)$ is the belief after.

For a parameter $\theta$ and data $y$:

$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta')\, \pi(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta),
$$

## Why it matters
In a trial the unknown is no longer disease or not but a continuous quantity such as the response rate or the log hazard ratio, and the prior is a distribution over its values. The Bayesian adds the prior and the multiplication. What is given up is practical: the answer depends on a prior that must be chosen, defended and written into the protocol.

## In the book
A patient with a positive test has a 27% chance of having the disease, not 90%, because the disease is rare and most positives come from the large healthy group.

ICH E9 permits Bayesian approaches when the reasons are clear and the conclusions sufficiently robust. It does not forbid them.

## Pitfalls
The denominator does not depend on $\theta$. It only rescales the product to integrate to one.

title: Bayes' rule
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.1 Bayes' rule with a diagnostic test
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: A test is 90% sensitive and 95% specific, prevalence 2%. Is a positive result 90% likely to mean disease? A: No, about 27%.
- Q: What is the shape of the posterior? A: The prior times the likelihood.

title: Bayes sequential decision problem
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.8.3 The Bayes sequential decision problem
text:
Bayes sequential decision problem. Also called: Bayesian sequential decision. Choosing a stopping time and terminal decision to minimize expected loss plus sampling cost, solved by backward induction on a sufficient statistic.

## What it is

A design is a pair $(T, d)$: a stopping time $T \le N_{\max}$ adapted to the data and a terminal decision $d$. Let $\ell(\theta, d)$ be the terminal loss and $\kappa(\theta)$ the cost per enrolled patient. The Bayes rule minimizes expected total loss $\ell(\theta, d) + \kappa(\theta)\,T$ under the prior.

With $V(n,S)$ the minimal expected future loss in state $(n, S)$:

$$
V(n,S) = \min\Bigl\{\min_d \mathbb{E}[\ell(\theta,d) \mid n, S],\;\; \mathbb{E}[\kappa(\theta) \mid n, S] + \mathbb{E}_{\text{pred}}\bigl[V(n+1, S+X_{n+1})\bigr]\Bigr\}.
$$

## Why it matters

The traditional design chooses the boundary to control a type I error and then asks what it costs. The Bayes design chooses the boundary to minimize expected loss and then asks what error rates it has. For error-calibrated use the second must be turned into the first by simulation.

## In the book

A decision tree over $N_{\max}$ steps has exponentially many branches. Indexed by the sufficient statistic it becomes a table over states, filled by backward induction. For a single-arm binary endpoint the lattice has order $N_{\max}^2$ entries.

The set of states where stopping is optimal is the stopping region, and its boundary is the Bayes boundary. The continuation region narrows toward the horizon because the option value of another observation shrinks. Early in the trial the boundary is wide, since a premature decision is expensive.

## Pitfalls

- The exact shape of the continuation region depends on the loss and sampling cost, and it need not be triangular.

## Check yourself

- Q: What makes the problem computable? A: The posterior depends on the data only through a sufficient statistic, so the state is $(n, S_n)$.
- Q: Why does the continuation region narrow near the horizon? A: The option value of another observation shrinks with fewer remaining observations.

title: Bayesian adaptive design
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.7 Preview: the thesis and four mechanisms
text:
Bayesian adaptive design. Also called: Bayesian adaptive trial. A trial design that can meet the legal standard of evidence sooner and with fewer patients on inferior arms, through monitoring, joint handling of arms and prior information.

## What it is
The book's thesis has two sentences. A regulator approves a drug on evidence that meets a legal standard, and a Bayesian adaptive design can meet it sooner and with fewer patients exposed to inferior arms. The saving comes from monitoring, from handling multiple arms jointly and from prior information, not from a lower bar.

## Why it matters
Four mechanisms are usually run together and the book keeps them apart. M1 is the deviation scale. M2 is one calibrated threshold for monitoring plus shrinkage for estimation. M3 is informative priors. M4 is optimal stopping under a sampling cost. M2 and M4 rest on structure a regulator can verify by simulation, M3 on a judgment that must be defended, and M1 is a mathematical fact with a trade-off.

## In the book
Saville and Berry simulated 5,000 programs in which one in ten treatments works. A traditional sequence needed 1,966 patients and 12.0 years; an adaptive platform needed 640 patients and 3.2 years. This is a simulation, not an empirical result. REMAP-CAP reported tocilizumab meeting its efficacy criterion with posterior probability 99.75 percent.

## Pitfalls
The book does not claim that a Bayesian design dominates. In the REWIND reconstruction the scheduled design acts more often, though the Bayes rule decides earlier when it decides. Every gain has a price: a prior to defend, simulations to run and a design that is more work to specify.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the saving come from a lower bar? A: No, it does not.
- Q: Where is a Bayesian design judged by the regulator? A: In simulated operating characteristics under a pre-specified design.

title: Bayesian borrowing
al: borrowing information; dynamic borrowing; static borrowing
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.3 Bayesian borrowing: the idea
text:
Bayesian borrowing. Also called: borrowing information, dynamic borrowing, static borrowing. Using external or earlier data in the analysis of a trial through a prior, with the amount of borrowing fixed in advance or adjusted by the data.

## What it is

Bayesian borrowing puts earlier data into the prior for the current trial's parameter. Borrowing a whole historical control arm of $n_h$ patients is a prior with effective sample size $n_h$ (effective sample size).

The methods differ in what they assume about the current control rate $p_c$ and the historical rate $p_h$: they are equal (full pooling), close with a fixed discount (power prior), draws from a common distribution (hierarchical model, MAP prior), either like $p_h$ or unrelated (mixture priors), or tied by a parameter the data update (commensurate priors, normalized power priors). The first two are static and the last three are dynamic, and FDA uses the same split.

## Why it matters

Every patient who need not be randomized to control can be treated, or the trial can finish sooner. Done well, borrowing recovers precision a small trial cannot supply, and done badly it can introduce substantial bias that the small trial cannot reveal.

## In the book

A traditional trial uses prior data only before it starts, to choose the alternative, the control rate and the sample size, and then ignores it in the analysis. The Bayesian design lets prior data enter the analysis through a prior on the control parameter. REBYOTA and OPTIMIZER Smart are the two regulatory cases of dynamic and static borrowing.
In the book's simulation, 60 treated and 30 control patients borrow a historical arm of 100 patients with 30 responders: full pooling raises power from 0.43 to 0.79, and matching that without borrowing would take roughly 170 control patients instead of 30.

title: Bayesian borrowing
al: borrowing information; dynamic borrowing; static borrowing
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.3 Bayesian borrowing: the idea
text:
## Pitfalls

Borrowing is not free: the price is measurable by simulation, and the regulator will ask to see it before agreeing to the design. The methods decide how much to rely on external data once it is admissible, and do not make inadmissible data admissible.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which of the five relationships between $p_c$ and $p_h$ are static? A: Full pooling and a power prior with a fixed discount.
- Q: What is the effective sample size of borrowing a whole historical arm of $n_h$ patients? A: $n_h$.
R functions (bayestrials): borrow_priors, borrow_reject_prob, borrow_ess_robust

title: Bayesian logistic regression model
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.6 A worked escalation decision with the logistic model
text:
Bayesian logistic regression model. Also called: BLRM. A two-parameter logistic dose-toxicity model with informative priors, used with interval probabilities and an overdose bound.

## What it is
The BLRM of Neuenschwander and colleagues uses a two-parameter logistic model with informative priors. It estimates the slope too, and needs informative priors to behave. It applies the overdose-control idea to interval probabilities of the DLT rate.

## Why it matters
It shows what the posterior looks like at a decision point and how one early DLT is weighed against all the other data, which the 3+3 rule forgoes.

## In the book
Doses are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 mg with reference dose 8 mg, and $\mathrm{logit}\,p(d) = \log\alpha + \beta \log(d/8)$. The priors are $\log\alpha \sim N(\mathrm{logit}\,0.25, 2^2)$ and $\log\beta \sim N(0, 1)$. Four cohorts: 0 of 3 at 1 mg, 0 of 3 at 2 mg, 1 of 3 at 4 mg and 1 of 6 at 8 mg. Underdosing is below 0.16, target 0.16 to 0.33, overdosing 0.33 or above. The 16 mg dose is excluded because its overdose probability exceeds 0.25, and the next cohort gets 8 mg.

## Pitfalls
The result depends on the prior. Rerun the table with a different `prior_sd` before trusting it.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why was 16 mg excluded? A: Its probability of overdosing was above the bound of 0.25.
- Q: Did the single DLT at 4 mg stop escalation? A: No, the model weighed it against the other data.
R functions (bayestrials): dose_blrm_table

title: History of Bayesian monitoring
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.8.2 A short history of Bayesian monitoring
text:
History of Bayesian monitoring. The lineage of Bayesian stopping rules from Freedman and Spiegelhalter in the 1980s and 1990s to the calibrated posterior rules of this book.

## What it is

The Bayesian monitoring rule of the chapter has a lineage.

## Why it matters

The rule of the chapter keeps the posterior of these earlier proposals and adds the calibration of operating characteristics by simulation that a regulator asks for.

## In the book

- Freedman, Lowe and Macaskill proposed stopping rules that incorporate clinical opinion as a prior.
- Freedman and Spiegelhalter compared Bayesian monitoring with group sequential methods.
- Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar proposed skeptical and enthusiastic reference priors and a range of equivalence, with a rule that stops when the posterior probability of benefit, or of exceeding that range, passes a threshold.
- Grossman and colleagues gave a unified method for monitoring and analyzing controlled trials, and Fayers, Ashby and Parmar wrote the tutorial.
- Berry argued from the likelihood principle that interim analyses should not be penalized, and Rosner and Berry gave a Bayesian group sequential design for a multiple-arm trial.

The wider history of Bayesian trial design is in the book's decision chapter.

## Pitfalls

- Armitage held the other view: the logic of repeated significance tests applies to the trial, and a conclusion must account for how often the data were examined.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does this book add to the earlier Bayesian monitoring rules? A: Calibration of operating characteristics by simulation.
- Q: Which argument did Berry make? A: From the likelihood principle, that interim analyses should not be penalized.

title: Bayesian protocol
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23 Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators
text:
Bayesian protocol. A confirmatory protocol that keeps the traditional skeleton and changes the sections that depend on how evidence is summarized: prior, success criterion, interim rules and operating characteristics.

## What it is
A Bayesian protocol shares most sections with a group sequential protocol and differs in a handful, and the handful is where reviewers will spend their time.
A traditional protocol states a null hypothesis, a one-sided type I error of 0.025, a fixed sample size or event count, scheduled interim looks and a stated multiplicity procedure.

## Why it matters
Four things stay the same: the estimand, the default randomization, the calibration bar of one-sided familywise error 0.025, and the need to prespecify.
The sponsor owes the reviewer a simulation rather than a formula in each moved row.

## In the book
The prior is stated in full, with its effective sample size, the source of any informative component and a prespecified sensitivity analysis.
The success criterion is $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$, where $a$ is the minimum benefit and $c$ the minimum probability, both to be justified.
The sample size becomes a maximum, and the looks are prescheduled with decision rules at each one.
Adaptive randomization, if used, belongs in the protocol with its limits: burn-in, floors, caps and analysis stratified by allocation period.
Safety can be stated as a posterior probability whose false-stop rate is simulated, and it sits outside the efficacy error budget.
Nothing about the estimand is different, and the common error is to describe a convenient model in estimand language afterwards.
Three rows carry most of the difference: interim looks, multiple arms and operating characteristics.

## Pitfalls
The protocol should not say "continuous monitoring": operating characteristics depend on when and how often the rule is evaluated.
Calibration is this book's default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, not FDA's universal requirement.

title: Bayesian protocol
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23 Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Which section has no traditional counterpart? A: The prior.
- Q: What replaces the closed-form power calculation? A: The simulation report.
R functions (bayestrials): select_simulate

title: Bayesian reading of the phases
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.9 A Bayesian reading of the phases
text:
Bayesian reading of the phases. Each phase updates a posterior and hands it to the next, so one probability model spans the whole development program.

## What it is
Each phase updates a posterior and hands it to the next. Phase I produces a posterior over the dose-toxicity curve that becomes the prior for dose selection in Phase II. Phase II produces a posterior over the dose-response curve, and its predictive distribution gives the probability that Phase III will succeed. Phase III produces the evidence for approval, and Phase IV keeps updating.

## Why it matters
The distinction is not that the traditional path passes verdicts and the Bayesian path passes distributions. A Bayesian program specifies one probability model across the phases, so what one phase learns propagates into the predictive probabilities of the next, whereas the traditional path links phases through estimates and judgment. The rest of the book is about the conditions (calibration, pre-specification, simulation) under which a regulator will accept the alternative.

## In the book
The phase map pairs each phase with its question, traditional design and Bayesian method.

- Phase I asks safe or not and which dose. The traditional design is 3+3 and the Bayesian method is model-based escalation.
- Phase II asks whether it works and at which dose. Traditional designs are fixed-dose arms or a single-arm response test; Bayesian methods are dose-response models, predictive probability and adaptive allocation.
- Phase III asks whether it is confirmed. The traditional design is fixed or group sequential at type I error 0.025; the Bayesian method is a posterior success criterion calibrated to error control, or borrowing.
- Phase IV asks about harm after approval. Traditional tools are spontaneous reports and observational studies; Bayesian methods are empirical Bayes shrinkage and sequential monitoring.

title: Bayesian reading of the phases
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.9 A Bayesian reading of the phases
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: What becomes the Phase II prior for dose selection? A: The Phase I posterior over the dose-toxicity curve.
- Q: Do traditional programs pass information forward? A: Yes, through estimates, models and safety findings.

title: Bayesian reanalysis
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22 Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials
text:
Bayesian reanalysis. Rereading a published trial from its reported estimates under a family of stated priors, to ask what we should now believe, not whether the trial crossed its threshold.

## What it is
A published trial gives a likelihood, not a conclusion.
The same three steps recur: reduce the report to an approximately normal likelihood for a log relative risk, a log hazard ratio or a risk difference; combine it with a small family of priors that represent defensible positions; and report posterior probabilities of effects large enough to matter.
The chapter applies this to GUSTO, EOLIA, ANDROMEDA-SHOCK and RECOVERY.

## Why it matters
Existence and magnitude of an effect are separate questions, and a posterior adds direct probability statements at chosen thresholds.
Each prior stands for a position someone held or could defend, so showing the posterior under each shows readers where they stand.
Decisions need utilities: the reanalyses supply probabilities and a utility turns them into choices.

## In the book
Each trial did its job: it answered the question its protocol asked.
In EOLIA and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK the primary test did not reject the null, and the intervals (0.55 to 1.04 and 0.55 to 1.02) already showed that sizeable benefits were compatible with the data. EOLIA stopped for futility at its fourth analysis, after 240 patients.
The book's numbers differ from published reanalyses because it uses normal approximations on the stated effect scale and simple stand-in priors.

title: Bayesian reanalysis
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22 Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials
text:
## Pitfalls
A reanalysis is done after the results are known, so the choice of priors, thresholds and scale is made in the light of the answer; it is exploratory in ICH E9's sense and should list every prior tried.
The FDA Bayesian draft is written for a trial designed to be Bayesian and says nothing that turns a post hoc reanalysis into evidence of effectiveness.
A reanalysis uses the data once more: it cannot add patients, repair a design flaw or change the probability that the trial would have rejected a null effect.
A strongly positive posterior after a negative trial is a reason to run a confirmatory trial with priors written in the protocol.

## Check yourself
- Q: A trial misses $p < 0.05$ and a reanalysis gives a high probability of benefit. Is the trial now positive? A: No, the primary analysis missed its threshold and a reanalysis cannot change that.
- Q: What should an honest report list? A: Every prior tried, not only the favorable ones.
R functions (bayestrials): reanalysis_normal, reanalysis_gusto, reanalysis_eolia, reanalysis_andromeda, reanalysis_recovery

title: Bayesian sample size criteria
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5 Bayesian sample size criteria
text:
Bayesian sample size criteria. Rules that turn a design prior and an analysis prior into a sample size: average length, average coverage, worst outcome and posterior probability criteria.

## What it is

Inoue, Berry and Parmigiani separate the Bayesian rules into families. Most involve two priors: the design prior that predicts the data and the analysis prior that turns data into a posterior. The criteria are the average length criterion (ALC), the average coverage criterion (ACC), the worst outcome criterion (WOC) and the posterior probability criterion.

## Why it matters

Read by the question each answers, the length and coverage criteria size an estimate, the posterior probability criterion and assurance size a decision, and expected-utility criteria size a decision together with its cost. The power calculation is the posterior probability criterion with a point-mass design prior and a flat analysis prior.

## In the book

With design prior $N(0.3, 0.1^2)$ and a flat analysis prior, 90% power needs 234 per arm. With a flat analysis prior the ALC reduces to $n \ge 2(3.92\sigma/\ell)^2$. If the informative prior is also the analysis prior, the prior alone gives $\Pr(\theta > 0) = \Phi(3) = 0.9987$, so the trial is unnecessary for an analyst holding it. In the lupus example, 50% on control and a hoped-for 25% on treatment needs 77 per arm by power. An estimation-based width of 0.3 gives 75 per arm.

## Pitfalls

The criteria take their inputs from the design prior, so a sensitivity analysis applies. A smaller trial buys feasibility and costs the guarantee of a decision. For a confirmatory trial the regulator still asks for the operating characteristics of the final analysis.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which criterion needs no design prior when the variance is known? A: The average length criterion.
- Q: How does a power calculation appear among these criteria? A: As the posterior probability criterion with a point-mass design prior and a flat analysis prior.
R functions (bayestrials): decide_ss_acc_woc, decide_ss_alc, decide_ss_min_n, decide_ss_posterior_prob

title: Bayesian time machine
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.5.3 The Bayesian time machine
text:
Bayesian time machine. Also called: time machine, control smoothing. A model that lets the control rate drift across calendar periods and borrows from neighboring periods with a smoothing parameter to use non-concurrent controls.

## What it is

The time machine lets the control rate drift as a random walk across calendar periods and estimates the current control rate by borrowing from neighboring periods, with a smoothing parameter $\sigma_s$ controlling how fast the rate may change. Small $\sigma_s$ pools almost everything and large $\sigma_s$ is nearly the concurrent-only estimate. It is the idea of Saville and colleagues, used in I-SPY 2, proposed for GBM AGILE and Precision Promise, and cited in FDA's Bayesian draft.

## Why it matters

When nothing changes, borrowing is nearly free. Under a step of 8 points in the last period, pooling is worse than the current period alone.

## In the book

The book's code is an illustrative first-order Gaussian smoother over four periods of 100 control patients, not the published second-order model. Three histories were simulated: constant, linear drift of 2 points per period, and an 8 point step in the last period. The learned smoother, which must infer a break from four periods, is worse than the current period alone under the step. Only the loosest fixed smoothing improved on concurrent-only data, and that value was fixed with knowledge of the scenarios.

## Pitfalls

Borrowing gains precision when history is stable and gives it back when history breaks. Three scenarios do not establish that it is better for other histories. The simulation report must include a step change.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does large $\sigma_s$ approximate? A: The concurrent-only estimate.
- Q: Which history hurts pooling most? A: The step change in the last period.
R functions (bayestrials): platform_time_machine

title: Pediatric belimumab in lupus
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17.2 Belimumab in pediatric lupus: a robust mixture and a tipping point
text:
Pediatric belimumab in lupus. Also called: belimumab, belimumab in children, PLUTO. A pediatric lupus trial whose wide interval was supported by a post hoc Bayesian robust mixture analysis borrowing from two adult trials, with a tipping point at weight 0.55.

## What it is

The pediatric trial of intravenous belimumab in systemic lupus erythematosus (C1109, PLUTO) randomized 93 children, 92 in the analysis below. At week 52 the SRI-4 response was 28 of 53 (52.8%) on belimumab and 17 of 39 (43.6%) on placebo, a difference of 9.2 points with an odds ratio of 1.5 (95% CI 0.6 to 3.5).

## Why it matters

That interval is far too wide to stand alone. FDA recommended a post hoc Bayesian analysis borrowing from two adult trials (C1056 and C1057) with the same SRI-4 endpoint and the same 10 mg/kg dose.

## In the book

The prior was a robust mixture with an informative component built from the adult placebo and 10 mg/kg arms and a minimally informative component, with borrowing weight $w$. The analysis was a tipping-point analysis over $w$. The posterior probability of efficacy reached at least 97.5% whenever $w$ was 0.55 or more, and the review division judged such a weight reasonable given a similar disease course, similar pharmacokinetics and similar baseline characteristics. The tipping point reports the smallest borrowing that supports the conclusion and leaves its plausibility to the clinical and pharmacological evidence.

## Pitfalls

The analysis was post hoc. The case study stresses that future programs should pre-specify it, with the discussion starting before the IND.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why was borrowing needed? A: The pediatric odds ratio of 1.5 had a 95% CI of 0.6 to 3.5.
- Q: What did the tipping point show? A: Posterior probability of efficacy of at least 97.5% for $w$ of 0.55 or more.

title: Beta prior
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.3 The coin and the Beta family
text:
Beta prior. Also called: Beta distribution, Beta family. The convenient family of priors for a probability, Beta(a, b), with mean a/(a+b); Beta(1,1) is flat.

## What it is
The convenient family of priors for a probability is the Beta distribution, $\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$, with density proportional to $\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}$ on $[0,1]$ and mean $a/(a+b)$.

Beta(1,1) is flat: every value of $\theta$ is equally believable. Beta(2,2) is a gentle bell centered at one half. Larger $a$ and $b$ give narrower bells.

## Why it matters
The binomial likelihood has the same algebraic form as the Beta density, so the update is addition:

$$
\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b), \quad h \text{ heads}, \; t \text{ tails} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + h,\; b + t).
$$

The prior is worth $a + b$ patients, so the flat Beta(1,1) is worth two and Beta(30,70) is worth one hundred.

## In the book
With 7 heads in 10 tosses, the Beta(2,2) prior gives Beta(9,5) with mean $9/14 = 0.643$. The flat prior gives Beta(8,4) with mean $0.667$. The traditional estimate is 0.70.

In Bartlett's 1985 ECMO trial all 11 newborns assigned to ECMO survived. With a flat prior the posterior is Beta(12, 1).

The BNT162b2 trial used the prior Beta(0.700102, 1), a prior of real shape and almost no weight.

## Pitfalls
Two descriptions are in use: Beta(a,b) as $a-1$ prior responders, or as $a+b$ pseudo-observations. They differ by the two pseudo-observations of the flat prior.

## Check yourself
- Q: Prior Beta(2,2), then 7 heads and 3 tails. What is the posterior? A: Beta(9,5).
- Q: What is the mean of Beta(a,b)? A: $a/(a+b)$.
R functions (bayestrials): beta_post, grid_update

title: Bioequivalence
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.7 Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
text:
Bioequivalence. The finding that a generic or reformulated drug delivers the same exposure as the reference, declared when the geometric mean ratio lies in (0.80, 1.25).

## What it is
A generic or reformulated drug must deliver the same exposure as the reference product, measured by the area under the concentration-time curve. The parameter is the ratio $\rho = \mu_T/\mu_R$ of geometric means. Bioequivalence is declared when $\rho$ lies in the interval $(0.80, 1.25)$.

## Why it matters
The classical analysis is the TOST procedure, equivalent to checking that the 90 percent confidence interval lies inside $(\log 0.80, \log 1.25)$. A Bayesian version asks directly for the posterior probability of equivalence. In a simplified normal model with a reference prior,

$$
\Pr\bigl(\log 0.80 < \eta < \log 1.25 \mid d\bigr) = F_{t_{n-1}}\!\left(\frac{\log 1.25 - \bar d}{s/\sqrt n}\right) - F_{t_{n-1}}\!\left(\frac{\log 0.80 - \bar d}{s/\sqrt n}\right).
$$

This is equation eq-lifecycle-be.

## In the book
Under the reference prior each one-sided posterior tail probability equals the corresponding one-sided TOST p-value, so the posterior probability of equivalence is $1 - p_L - p_U$. TOST at 0.05 implies a posterior probability above 0.90, but not the reverse. In an illustrative scenario a data set passes the 0.90 posterior rule with probability 0.9291 and fails TOST with p-value 0.0709.

## Pitfalls
TOST is the standard in FDA's final guidance of May 2026, so a posterior-probability rule would need agreement with the regulator and an evaluation of its operating characteristics. The model is a simplification, not the regulatory crossover analysis, and some highly variable drugs use reference-scaled approaches.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which implication holds, TOST success to posterior above 0.90, or the reverse? A: TOST success at 0.05 implies a posterior probability above 0.90, not the reverse.

title: Blinded pooled review
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.5 Aggregate safety assessment
text:
Blinded pooled review. Review of the pooled event rate of the whole trial, without revealing arms, to see whether it exceeds what comparable untreated patients would show.

## What it is

Blinded pooled review of the whole trial asks whether the overall event rate is higher than expected, without revealing the arms.

## Why it matters

It lets a sponsor watch safety while the trial stays blinded. The FDA guidance recommends keeping individual treatment assignments blinded where the trial is blinded, with unblinded aggregate review by a group independent of the sponsor's study team.

## In the book

Given credible external information about adverse event rates in comparable untreated patients, Gould and Wang describe Bayesian monitoring for potential excess risk using pooled blinded data. Their title calls it the canary in the coal mine. It sits beside the unblinded DMC review, which compares arms.

## Pitfalls

- It needs credible external rates for the comparison to mean anything.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the pooled blinded review compare the overall rate with? A: The expected rate from external information on comparable untreated patients.

title: Blinding
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.7 Blinding
text:
Blinding. Also called: masking. Keeping participants, investigators or analysts unaware of the assigned treatment after allocation, to protect against bias in reporting, care and judging outcomes.

## What it is
Randomization protects the comparison against bias in who receives each treatment. Blinding, also called masking, protects it against bias in what happens afterward: how patients report symptoms, how investigators care for them and how outcomes are judged.

ICH E9 defines a double-blind trial as one in which neither the subject nor any of the investigator or sponsor staff involved in treatment or evaluation are aware of the treatment received.

## Why it matters
The book lists open label, single blind, double blind, triple blind (also the data analysts) and blinded outcome assessment. Blinding matters most when outcomes are subjective, such as pain, depression or symptom scores.

## In the book
RECOVERY compared dexamethasone with usual care without blinding. The primary outcome was death within 28 days, an objective endpoint that limits assessment bias. When masking is impossible, as with surgery or devices, the protocol should use blinded outcome assessment and objective endpoints.

Maintaining the blind takes work: matching placebos, a double-dummy design when comparators differ in form, independent unblinded staff and a prespecified emergency unblinding procedure.

## Pitfalls
Side effects can unblind, such as nausea, a rash or a visible lab change. The DMC and its statistician see unblinded data and the sponsor does not, so the charter should state who sees what and when.

## Check yourself
- Q: When is an open-label trial still informative? A: When the outcome is objective, as with death within 28 days in RECOVERY.
- Q: Can a trial be properly blinded without concealment? A: No. An investigator who knows the next assignment already knows the arm.

title: BNT162b2 trial
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.12.1 Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, phase 3 (C4591001)
text:
BNT162b2 trial. Also called: BNT162b2, Pfizer-BioNTech phase 3, C4591001. The phase 2/3 vaccine trial whose success rule was a posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 percent, with a weak Beta prior.

## What it is
The phase 2/3 trial of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine is the book's cleanest large example of a Bayesian success rule. Its statistical analysis plan used a beta-binomial model, conditional on the total number of first COVID-19 cases $s$, of whom $s_1$ occur in the vaccine arm.

## Why it matters
With equal allocation and follow-up, a case falls in the vaccine arm with probability $p = (1 - \mathrm{VE})/(2 - \mathrm{VE})$. The prior is $p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)$, with mean 0.4118, the value of $p$ at VE $= 30\%$. The plan calls it minimally informative. Its effective sample size is 1.7 cases.

## In the book
- Design feature: efficacy was declared if $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\% \mid \text{data}) > 0.986$ at the final analysis, and above 0.995 at an interim. The thresholds were calibrated to a one-sided type I error of 2.5%.
- Plan: final analysis at 164 cases, with interim looks at 62, 92 and 120 cases.
- Result: 8 cases in the vaccine group against 162 in the placebo group, so $s = 170$ and $s_1 = 8$. The posterior is Beta(0.700102 + 8, 1 + 162).
- The posterior probability that VE exceeds 30% is $1 - 2 \times 10^{-28}$. The 95% credible interval for VE is about (90.4%, 97.6%), with a point estimate of 95.1% (plug-in) or 94.9% (posterior median). The paper reports 95.0% with interval 90.3 to 97.6.
- FDA authorized the vaccine for individuals 16 years and older on 11 December 2020, and approved the biologics license on 23 August 2021.

title: BNT162b2 trial
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.12.1 Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, phase 3 (C4591001)
text:
## Pitfalls
With ESS 1.7 and 170 cases the prior is irrelevant to the conclusion, and a flat prior would shift the interval by well under a point. The statistical analysis plan cited is version 10 dated 7 October 2022, not an archived 2020 version.

## Check yourself
- Q: What posterior probability did the final analysis need? A: $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\% \mid \text{data}) > 0.986$.
- Q: Does the prior carry the result? A: No. It was chosen to be defensible, not to carry the result.
