and the expected number of pairs to reach $1/\alpha$ is roughly $\log(1/\alpha)/g(\lambda)$, which is Wald's identity.

## Why it matters

The bet is chosen in advance from the effect one hopes to detect. An unrealistic choice costs power, not validity, and validity holds for every $\lambda$. This is the e-value analogue of choosing a design effect size.

## In the book

In the 45 versus 30 percent design the best fraction is $\lambda^\ast = 0.312$ with $g = 0.0238$ nats per pair, giving an expected crossing near 155 pairs. In simulations a fraction of 0.10 gives power 0.119, 0.31 gives 0.723 and 0.50 gives 0.589 at 200 pairs.

## Pitfalls

- A fraction that is too small or too large loses power, as the 0.10 and 0.50 results show.

## Check yourself

- Q: If you pick a poor betting fraction, what is damaged, validity or power? A: Power. Validity holds for every fraction.
- Q: Which of 0.10, 0.31 and 0.50 gave the highest power at 200 pairs? A: 0.31, with power 0.723.
R functions (bayestrials): ev_betting_paths

title: E-value safety monitoring
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.2 Monitoring continuously: posterior probability and e-value
text:
E-value safety monitoring. Also called: e-value monitoring, continuous monitoring. Continuous safety monitoring with a harm-only Bayes factor read as an e-value, so that acting at 20 keeps false alarms below 5 percent at any look schedule.

## What it is

Two statistics survive continuous looking. The posterior probability is coherent under any stopping rule, but its false alarm rate is not controlled. The Bayes factor read as an e-value is a nonnegative martingale under the null, so Ville's inequality gives

$$
\Pr\left(\sup_t \mathrm{BF}_t \geq 1/\alpha \mid RR = 1\right) \leq \alpha.
$$

This is eq-safety-ville.

## Why it matters

Safety asks about harm, so the null is $RR \leq 1$. The alternative is $\log RR \sim N(0, 0.5^2)$ restricted to positive values, and acting when this harm-only Bayes factor first reaches twenty gives a false alarm probability below 5 percent however often one looks. A two-sided factor also alarms for protective risk, so its bound is for the wrong null.

## In the book

For rofecoxib at the end of 2000 the harm-only factor was substantial but short of the threshold of 20. The posterior probability answers how probable harm is given a prior. The e-value rule answers whether the evidence is strong enough to act with a guaranteed bound on false alarms.

Over 60 monthly looks at a drug with no effect, the simulation compares a posterior rule at 0.95 with the e-value rule, whose Ville bound is 0.05. A posterior probability can rank signals while a charter threshold on the e-value sets the level for a stop or restrict recommendation.

An e-value version of the toxicity boundary would be valid at any look, including an unscheduled one.

## Pitfalls

- The price is a larger sample to reach the same alarm when harm is present.
- Whether a sequential monitor would have alarmed earlier for rofecoxib needs data the book does not supply.

title: E-value safety monitoring
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.2 Monitoring continuously: posterior probability and e-value
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Why use a harm-only alternative? A: The null is $RR \leq 1$, and a two-sided factor would alarm for protection too.
- Q: What is the false alarm bound at a Bayes factor threshold of 20? A: 0.05.
R functions (bayestrials): safety_bf_monitor

title: E-value
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2 E-values as bets
text:
E-value. Also called: e value, betting score. A nonnegative statistic whose expectation under the null is at most one, read as the payoff of a fair bet against the null.

## What it is

An e-value for a null hypothesis $H_0$ is a nonnegative random variable $E$ whose expectation under every distribution in $H_0$ is at most one.

The name suggests a bet. A gambler stakes one dollar against the null, and if the null is true the expected wealth afterwards is at most one dollar. An observed e-value of 20 means the data multiplied by 20 an amount of evidence that is fair under the null.

## Why it matters

Markov's inequality turns an e-value into a test: reject $H_0$ when $E \ge 1/\alpha$. At $\alpha = 0.025$ the threshold is $E \ge 40$. For a single fixed sample this is only a new way of writing a test. The new thing is what happens when the data keep coming, because a sequence of e-values built as a Test martingale stays valid at every stopping time.

## In the book

A Bayes factor against a simple null is an e-value, because its expectation under the null is one. The same number, say 40, is "strong evidence" on a Jeffreys scale and "a level 0.025 test" on the e-value scale. The difference is one of calibration, not of statistic.

In the binary two-arm trial the e-value is a product of terms $1 + \lambda D_i$, a bet against no particular prior.

## Pitfalls

- A Bayes factor with a prior on a composite null parameter is not an e-value in general.
- Most e-values are not Bayes factors, so the e-value framework is wider than Bayes factors.
- A fixed-sample e-value converted by $p = \min(1, 1/E)$ is a valid but conservative p-value.

title: E-value
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2 E-values as bets
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: A trial ends with $E = 20$. What is the most you can say about the null probability of such an outcome? A: At most 1/20, by Markov's inequality.
- Q: Is a Bayes factor of 3 enough to reject at a low error rate? A: No. Rejecting at 3 has a frequentist type I error as high as 1/3.
R functions (bayestrials): ev_betting_paths, ev_first_cross

title: East Horizon
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text:
East Horizon. Commercial software from Cytel for the design, simulation and monitoring of fixed, group sequential and adaptive trials.

## What it is
East Horizon is commercial software from Cytel for the design, simulation and monitoring of fixed, group sequential and adaptive trials.

## Why it matters
It belongs to the same family as the East product line from the same company.

## In the book
It is listed with the other tools as in wide use, with only its purpose described.

## Pitfalls
The descriptions in the book cover only the purpose of each tool, so a reader should consult the documentation for current features and versions.

## Check yourself
- Q: Who makes East Horizon? A: Cytel.
- Q: Which trial types does it cover? A: Fixed, group sequential and adaptive.

title: ECMO trial
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3 ECMO: the case every trialist knows
text:
ECMO trial. Also called: ECMO, Harvard two-stage trial. The 1985 play-the-winner trial of ECMO in newborns that ended 11 of 11 on ECMO and 0 of 1 on conventional therapy, and the controversy and follow-up trials it started.

## What it is

Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a form of heart-lung bypass for newborns with persistent pulmonary hypertension. Bartlett and colleagues thought randomizing to conventional medical therapy was close to unethical, and used a randomized play-the-winner rule. The final tally was 11 of 11 on ECMO and 0 of 1 on conventional therapy.

## Why it matters

The conclusion that ECMO works rested on twelve infants, and the comparison with control on one death. The design meant to reconcile ethics with science had allocated the information away from the comparison.

## In the book

With uniform priors the posteriors are Beta(12,1) and Beta(1,2), and the posterior probability that ECMO is better is $90/91 \approx 0.989$. The Harvard two-stage trial had 9 of 9 ECMO infants survive against 6 of 10 on control in phase one, then 20 further ECMO infants with 19 survivors. The UK collaborative trial enrolled 185 infants; thirty of 93 allocated to ECMO died against 54 of 92, a relative risk of 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.77). By then the data swamp any of the priors tried.

## Pitfalls

Extreme early data and an informative prior can make a rule stop almost immediately, and a protocol must show by simulation that this is the behavior it wants. A posterior above 0.98 under two priors is a statement about extreme data, not about a good design.

## Check yourself

- Q: What was the allocation outcome of the Bartlett trial? A: 11 infants to ECMO and 1 to conventional therapy.
- Q: Which trial settled the question? A: The conventional randomized UK collaborative trial.
R functions (bayestrials): ecmo_data, ecmo_beta_comparison, ecmo_prior_sensitivity, rar_ecmo_urn

title: Economic futility threshold
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.4.2 The economic threshold $PP^*$
text:
Economic futility threshold. Also called: PP star, PP*. The predictive probability below which continuing a phase 2 trial no longer pays, derived from the cost of the remaining patients and the value of a true positive.

## What it is

The thresholds 0.05 and 0.95 of phase 2 monitoring are conventions, and a decision-theoretic reading ties the futility threshold to money. A false go costs $c_3$, the expected cost of a failed phase 3, a missed active drug forfeits $V$, and continuing costs the remaining patients $m c_2$. The myopic rule gives

$$
\mathrm{PP}^* = \frac{m c_2}{\rho V - (1-\rho) c_3},
$$

where $\rho$ is the probability that phase 3 succeeds given a phase 2 success.

## Why it matters

The threshold is small when the drug is valuable and the remaining phase 2 is cheap. The futility threshold should be derived from economics, then judged by operating characteristics like any other threshold.

## In the book

The book uses two invented drugs, in millions of dollars, "for teaching, not taken from a real program". For the valuable drug the conventional 0.05 is more aggressive than the economics justify. For the crowded indication the denominator is negative, so a phase 2 success does not justify going on to phase 3 and the trial should not be running at all.

## Pitfalls

The book's lesson is not that a particular number is right, only that the threshold follows from the economics. The inputs are invented, so do not quote them as program data.

## Check yourself

- Q: When is PP* small? A: When the drug is valuable and the remaining phase 2 is cheap.
- Q: What does a negative denominator mean? A: A phase 2 success leads to a phase 3 of negative expected value.
R functions (bayestrials): p2_pp_star

title: Effective sample size
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.6 How much does a prior weigh: effective sample size
text:
Effective sample size. Also called: ESS, prior effective sample size. The number of observations whose information about the parameter equals the prior's, turning an argument about the prior into one about patients.

## What it is

Morita, Thall and Müller defined the effective sample size of a prior as the number of observations whose information is equivalent to the prior's. For a Beta(a, b) prior,

$$
\mathrm{ESS} = a + b.
$$

For a normal prior $N(\mu_0, s_0^2)$ on the mean of observations with variance $\sigma^2$,

$$
\mathrm{ESS} = \frac{\sigma^2}{s_0^2}.
$$

These are eq-ess-beta and eq-ess-normal. For a log hazard ratio each event carries variance 4, so the ESS is $4/s_0^2$ events.

## Why it matters

"A prior worth five patients in a trial of five hundred is a modelling choice; a prior worth two hundred is an assumption that needs defending". Reviewers may disagree on the weight, but both sides can see what they disagree about.

## In the book

A skeptical prior with $s_0 = 0.175$ is worth 131 events, about 26 percent of the information in a 508-event trial. The BNT162b2 prior Beta(0.700102, 1) has an ESS of 1.7 cases, against a final analysis planned at 164 cases.

## Pitfalls

ESS summarizes a prior's variance, not its location. A prior can be small in ESS and still decisive at a decision boundary, so report ESS beside a sensitivity analysis. For a mixture prior the ESS moves with the data, so the FDA draft asks for it over the plausible range of outcomes. Under the Novick and Grizzle convention the ESS differs from $a+b$ by 2.

## Check yourself

- Q: What is the ESS of a Beta(3, 7) prior? A: 10.
- Q: What is the ESS in events of a normal prior with $s_0 = 0.175$ on the log hazard ratio? A: About 131 events.
R functions (bayestrials): ess_beta, ess_events

title: EffTox
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.4 EffTox and phase 1/2 designs
text:
EffTox. Also called: phase 1/2 design, phase 12 designs. A phase 1/2 design of Thall and Cook that models efficacy and toxicity by dose and picks the acceptable dose with the best trade-off.

## What it is
EffTox of Thall and Cook models efficacy and toxicity probabilities as functions of dose. Efficacy has a quadratic logistic form, so the curve can turn down. Toxicity has a monotone logistic form. A copula links the two outcomes in a patient. Instead of utilities for four outcomes, the original design elicits a trade-off contour in the plane of $(\pi_T, \pi_E)$ through pairs of equally desirable probabilities. The next cohort gets the acceptable dose with the highest desirability.

## Why it matters
The trial can state what it says about the dose-response, with a distribution of efficacy and toxicity at the chosen dose.

## In the book
Three things differ from toxicity-only designs. An efficacy endpoint must be observable fast enough to use during the trial. Samples are larger, usually 40 to a few hundred. The contour or utility elicitation must be defended.

## Pitfalls
Early efficacy readouts that are only surrogates bring a surrogacy question into the dose decision. The decisions need each cohort's outcome before the next is dosed, which is the late-onset problem.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does EffTox elicit instead of four utilities? A: A trade-off contour of equally desirable efficacy and toxicity pairs.
- Q: What typical sample size does it need? A: 40 to a few hundred.

title: EMA reflection paper on platform trials
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6.2 EMA
text:
EMA reflection paper on platform trials. Also called: EMA platform reflection paper, EMA/217509/2026. The EMA draft reflection paper on methodological aspects of confirmatory platform trials, in public consultation from 19 October 2026 to 31 January 2027.

## What it is
The EMA draft Reflection Paper on Methodological Aspects in Confirmatory Platform Trials (EMA/217509/2026) was in public consultation from 19 October 2026 to 31 January 2027. It covers pre-specification, randomization, controls including non-concurrent controls, type I error control and estimands for platform trials.

## Why it matters
The draft is more cautious than FDA about the shared control of a platform. It notes that a shared control makes errors correlated, and that the chance of at least one false positive may fall while the chance of several rises.

## In the book
Tightening each arm's level to hold down the chance of several false positives would need thresholds stricter than Bonferroni, so the draft offers alternatives such as larger control groups. It treats the choice of family as a design decision to be made in advance and argued. It puts more weight than FDA on arms that share a submission or a sponsor, and on the distribution of the number of errors.

## Pitfalls
For a program whose arms are all developed by one sponsor for one eventual label, a regulator in either jurisdiction may regard the arms as a single family, which needs a conversation.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does a shared control do to errors across arms, according to the draft? A: It makes them correlated.
- Q: Is the choice of family a post hoc matter? A: No, it is a design decision to be made in advance and argued.

title: EMA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.8 EMA and MHRA counterparts
text:
EMA. Also called: European Medicines Agency. The European regulator whose adaptive-design, complex-trial, Bayesian and platform-trial documents are generally more cautious than FDA drafts.

## What it is
EMA and the UK MHRA apply the same statistical principles as FDA, since both adopt ICH guidelines. Their documents on adaptive and complex designs differ in emphasis and date.

## Why it matters
A sponsor seeking approval in several regions needs to read them together. The EMA drafts are the more cautious on flexibility in the primary analysis of a confirmatory trial. A global program should plan European scientific advice in parallel with the US meetings.

## In the book
- The adaptive-design reflection paper of October 2007 (CHMP/EWP/2459/02) is more conservative than the 2019 FDA guidance and still current until E20 is final in the EU.
- The Q&A on complex clinical trials (EMA/298712/2022, May 2022) covers master protocols, platform designs and Bayesian methods.
- A concept paper on Bayesian methods (EMA/CHMP/1813/2026) was open for consultation from 30 January to 30 April 2026, with a draft reflection paper tentatively set for September 2027 and a final text for June 2028.
- The draft platform-trial reflection paper (EMA/217509/2026) is in consultation from 19 October 2026 to 31 January 2027.

## Pitfalls
The platform draft says "response adaptive randomisation (RAR) is not supported" and that non-concurrent controls are usually not acceptable for the primary analysis, so design to the stricter position until it is final.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the EMA platform draft discuss Bayesian methods? A: No.
- Q: Is a concept paper guidance? A: No, it proposes that a reflection paper be written.

title: Empirical Bayes
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.4.2 Stein, Efron and Morris, and the batting averages
text:
Empirical Bayes. Estimate the hierarchy's parameters from the data and plug them in, as in fitting the between-arm spread by marginal likelihood.

## What it is

In the ulcer illustration the between-arm standard deviation $\tau_g$ is estimated by marginal likelihood and then treated as known. The fit is `shrink_eb_fit()` in the package.

Efron and Morris made the shrinkage idea concrete with batting averages shrunk toward the league mean.

## Why it matters

It gives a usable hierarchical estimate without choosing a hyperprior.

## In the book

The fit gives a between-arm standard deviation on the log odds scale that shrinks each arm roughly half way to the common mean.

## Pitfalls

- The estimate of $\tau_g$ rests on four arms, which is thin. A plug-in estimate treats it as known.
- A fully Bayesian analysis would integrate uncertainty in the hierarchy's parameters. The sensitivity to the prior scale is the first thing a reviewer will ask.
- The Stein theorem does not establish that this fit improves every arm or a clinical decision.

## Check yourself

- Q: How is tau_g obtained in the ulcer fit? A: By marginal likelihood.
- Q: What does a plug-in estimate ignore? A: The uncertainty in tau_g.
R functions (bayestrials): shrink_eb_fit

title: Enthusiastic prior
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.3 Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors
text:
Enthusiastic prior. A prior centered at the design alternative with the same spread as the skeptical prior, standing for the investigator who designed the trial.

## What it is

The enthusiastic prior is centered at the design alternative with the same spread as the skeptical one, $\theta \sim N(\theta_a, s^2)$, so that the prior probability that the effect is zero or harmful is 0.05. It represents the investigator who designed the trial.

## Why it matters

It is a calibration device and not an analysis prior. If a trial is negative even under the enthusiastic prior, even the investigator must accept the drug is not delivering what it promised, which is the logic of a futility rule. As a stress test, a conclusion that holds under a skeptical-to-neutral analysis prior and is not overturned by the optimist is hard to attack.

## In the book

The multiplatform heparin trials pre-specified an enthusiastic prior as the sensitivity analysis, with a mean odds ratio of 1.75 (95% credible interval 0.74 to 4.15, prior probability of superiority 90%). In EOLIA the posterior probability of any mortality benefit ranged from 88% under a strongly skeptical prior to 99% under an enthusiastic or published-study prior. In the 508-event example the data carry about four times the weight of either reference prior, so the posterior ends close to the likelihood.

## Pitfalls

It expresses an informative position. Do not treat it as the primary analysis.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a negative trial under the enthusiastic prior tell you? A: Even the investigator must accept the drug is not delivering.
- Q: In EOLIA, how far apart were the skeptic and the enthusiast? A: 88% against 99% posterior probability of benefit.
R functions (bayestrials): normal_update, grid_update

title: EOLIA
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.3 EOLIA: probable benefit after a nonsignificant primary analysis
text:
EOLIA. Also called: EOLIA trial. A trial of early ECMO in severe ARDS whose nonsignificant primary result the book reanalyzes, finding probable benefit under all four priors examined.

## What it is
EOLIA randomized 249 patients with very severe acute respiratory distress syndrome to early venovenous ECMO or conventional ventilation.
Sixty-day mortality was 35 percent (44 of 124) with ECMO and 46 percent (57 of 125) in the control arm, relative risk 0.76 with 95 percent interval 0.55 to 1.04 and $p = 0.09$.
The design was group sequential with a two-triangle boundary and a maximum of 331 participants, and the trial stopped for futility at the fourth interim analysis.

## Why it matters
It was widely reported as negative, yet the reanalysis shows probable benefit after a nonsignificant primary analysis.
Of the 125 control patients, 35 (28 percent) crossed over to ECMO, which matters to a clinician reading the result.
A stopping rule can stop a trial despite a high probability of some benefit, because it asks whether the final criterion is likely to be met.

## In the book
Goligher and colleagues reported under a minimally informative prior a posterior relative risk of 0.78 (0.56 to 1.04) and a 96 percent probability of any mortality reduction.
The book's four priors on the log relative risk are flat, skeptical with $s_0 = 0.25$, skeptical with $s_0 = 0.15$ and enthusiastic, centered at 0.67 (the relative risk the design assumed).
Across the four priors Pr(RR<1) runs from 0.87 to 0.99, and Pr(RR<0.67) is 0.17 under the flat prior.
EOLIA did not rule out the effect it was designed to find, but made it less likely, and some benefit is probable under all four priors.
A probability of about 0.9 that the treatment helps is a strong argument for a hospital maintaining an ECMO program.

title: EOLIA
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.3 EOLIA: probable benefit after a nonsignificant primary analysis
text:
## Pitfalls
A nonsignificant result is nonrejection of the null, not evidence of no effect, and the interval already said as much.
The reanalysis does not make EOLIA a positive trial.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does the book's relative risk differ from the published 0.76? A: The counts give an unadjusted value and the published one is adjusted.
- Q: Can a futility boundary and a high probability of benefit coexist? A: Yes, they answer different questions.
R functions (bayestrials): reanalysis_eolia

title: EPAD
al: EPAD platform; European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.9 EPAD: a platform that never opened an arm
text:
EPAD. Also called: EPAD platform, European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia. An Alzheimer prevention platform with a 2,000-participant readiness cohort that never enrolled a treatment arm, a governance failure.

## What it is

The European Prevention of Alzheimer's Dementia program (EPAD) is the standard example of a platform that did not work. It was a 64-million-euro, five-year IMI-funded project that built a 2,000-participant readiness cohort with pre-characterization such as amyloid status, cognitive baselines and longitudinal follow-up.

## Why it matters

The cohort was meant to reduce the high screen-failure rates of Alzheimer's prevention trials. It never enrolled a single treatment arm. In the project's post-mortem, two obstacles were decisive: owners of candidate interventions were reluctant to hand sponsorship of a critical asset to a university-run platform, and stakeholders could not agree on a legal framework.

## In the book

When the five-year term ended in 2020 the treatment platform had never opened, and the pandemic had made funding harder. The cohort data and biobank outlived the project. The lesson is organizational and not statistical: nothing in the statistical design was at fault, and the sample-size, borrowing and decision rules were never tested.

## Pitfalls

Platforms need three things before a first arm: a legal framework arm sponsors will sign, a funding model that does not depend on the commercial pipeline, and governance that answers who decides. The Healey ALS platform is the contrast.

## Check yourself

- Q: Was EPAD's failure statistical? A: No, it was organizational.
- Q: Did EPAD enroll a treatment arm? A: No.

title: Equivalence trial
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9.2 Equivalence
text:
Equivalence trial. Also called: equivalence. A trial asking that the difference lie inside a two-sided margin, analyzed by two one-sided tests or by an interval inside the margin.

## What it is
An equivalence trial asks for the difference to lie inside a two-sided margin, $-\log M<\gamma<\log M$ on the log scale, so the hazard ratio lies between $1/M$ and $M$. The standard analysis is two one-sided tests, one against each end of the margin, and equivalence is declared only if both reject. This is the same as the confidence interval lying entirely inside $(-\log M, \log M)$.

## Why it matters
Putting the burden of proof on the claim of similarity, by reversing the roles of null and alternative, goes back to Dunnett and Gent for equivalence. Bioequivalence studies and some biosimilar comparisons use this form.

## In the book
Most clinical efficacy trials that say equivalence mean noninferiority, and the one-sided test is the more common. The upper bound of a two-sided 95% interval is the standard one-sided 0.025 noninferiority test, and noninferiority imposes no corresponding lower-bound requirement.

## Pitfalls
A sponsor who wants noninferiority should say so. Framing the trial as equivalence adds a lower-bound requirement that the question does not need.

## Check yourself
- Q: When is equivalence declared? A: Only if both one-sided tests reject.
- Q: How many bounds does noninferiority check? A: One, the upper bound.

title: Estimand
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.8.2 Estimands and intercurrent events
text:
Estimand. Also called: estimand framework. A precise description of the treatment effect that a trial is meant to measure, with five attributes including how intercurrent events are handled.

## What it is
The ICH E9(R1) addendum (Step 4, November 2019) asks the sponsor to define an estimand before the trial: "a precise description of the treatment effect reflecting the clinical question posed by a given clinical trial objective".

It has five attributes: the population, the treatment conditions compared, the variable (endpoint), the population-level summary and the way intercurrent events are handled.

## Why it matters
"The effect of the drug in patients who take it" differs from "the effect of prescribing it". A protocol that names the estimand tells the reviewer what the analysis can and cannot show. The strategy must match the label the sponsor hopes to obtain.

## In the book
The addendum names five strategies: treatment policy, hypothetical, composite variable, while on treatment and principal stratum. Treatment policy and composite fit the randomization directly. Hypothetical and principal stratum need a model or assumptions.

For nonlinear models the population-level summary is a choice between conditional and marginal effects, and the protocol should name it. A Bayesian posterior must be for the stated estimand. A probability computed for one estimand and quoted for another is the same error as quoting an ITT p-value for a per-protocol claim.

The protocol table asks for five attributes written down and one strategy per intercurrent event.

## Pitfalls
A trial with substantial discontinuation can give a valid answer to the treatment-policy question and a doubtful one to the hypothetical question.

## Check yourself
- Q: How many attributes does an estimand have? A: Five.
- Q: Is per-protocol one of the strategies? A: No.

title: Event-driven trial
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.2 Events are information
text:
Event-driven trial. Also called: events are information. A trial that ends when a target number of events has accrued, because the information on the log hazard ratio is proportional to events.

## What it is
The trial ends not at a fixed sample size but when a target number of events has accrued. The number of patients enters only through the events they produce, so the design fixes $D$ and lets accrual and follow-up deliver it. Inverting the variance gives
$$
D = \frac{4\,(z_{\alpha} + z_{\beta})^2}{(\log \mathrm{HR})^2}
$$
events (eq-sv-schoenfeld). The information per event is $I = 1/4$.

## Why it matters
With a flat prior, $\theta \mid \text{data} \sim N(\hat\theta, 4/D)$. A prior with standard deviation $s_0$ on the log hazard ratio is worth $4/s_0^2$ events, so $s_0 = 0.2$ is worth 100 events.

## In the book
SELECT used 1,225 planned events for a hazard ratio of 0.83 at 90 percent power. About 800 events are needed to be 95 percent sure that an observed 0.80 is below 0.90.

## Pitfalls
Events must be adjudicated and counted by agreed rules, interim timing prespecified, and an actual information fraction off target handled by a prespecified method.

## Check yourself
- Q: How many effective events is a prior of standard deviation 0.2 worth? A: 100.
R functions (bayestrials): surv_events_table

title: Evidence toll
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.9.2 The three tolls
text:
Evidence toll. Also called: three tolls, tolls. The three bars on the squared standardized score: a constant for a fixed level, log n for a Bayes rule, and log n plus 2 log(1/alpha) for an anytime-valid rule.

## What it is

With $L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2)$ and $q = I_n\tau^2$, the three calibrations act, for a one-sided claim with $Z_n > 0$, when the following holds.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{fixed level } \alpha: && Z_n \ge z_\alpha,\\
&\text{Bayes, threshold } b: && Z_n^2 \ge \Bigl(1 + \tfrac{1}{q}\Bigr)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log b\} \approx L_n + 2\log b,\\
&\text{anytime valid } \alpha: && Z_n^2 \ge \Bigl(1 + \tfrac{1}{q}\Bigr)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log(1/\alpha)\} \approx L_n + 2\log(1/\alpha).
\end{aligned}
$$

## Why it matters

The anytime-valid rule requires about $2\log(1/\alpha)(1 + 1/q)$ more than the Bayes rule at $b = 1$, approximately the constant 7.38 at large information.

## In the book

A fixed-level test asks for 1.96 however much information there is, so its squared bar is $z_\alpha^2 = 3.84$. The Bayes bar with $b = 1$ is below the unadjusted bar at small information but overtakes 1.96 once $L_n$ exceeds 3.84, asymptotically for $I_n \tau^2 > 46$. The exact bar of the stated mixture crosses 1.96 at $q \approx 41.6$.

The seventy percent result: the excess is $n_{\mathrm{LD}} - n_{\mathrm{MD}} \approx 2\log(1/\alpha)/\theta^2$, and relative to the fixed-sample requirement it is $7.38/10.51 \approx 0.70$ at $\alpha = 0.025$ and 90 percent power.

## Pitfalls

- The 70 percent figure compares boundary terms asymptotically and is not an exact sample-size identity. Calibration narrows the realized gap.
- The Bayesian saving is not a saving against a single unadjusted look once past the crossing point. The saving comes from monitoring and prior information.
- Because the ratio tends to one only as $1/\log n$, the additive excess never shrinks.

title: Evidence toll
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.9.2 The three tolls
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What is the constant surcharge at alpha 0.025? A: $2\log 40 = 7.38$ at large information.
- Q: Does a calibrated Bayes rule pay the whole 70 percent? A: No, it has already paid part of the surcharge.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_tolls

title: Exchangeability
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.2 Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally
text:
Exchangeability. The judgment that the probability of a set of outcomes does not depend on the order in which patients are listed.

## What it is
Exchangeability is a weaker symmetry than independence: the probability assigned to a set of outcomes does not depend on the order of the patients. Eight tosses with four point up are equally probable in the order 1,0,1,0,1,0,1,0 and in 0,1,1,0,1,0,0,1.

Independent and identically distributed outcomes are always exchangeable, but not conversely. Exchangeability makes no reference to a parameter. It is a statement about beliefs concerning data not yet seen.

## Why it matters
Given $\theta$, outcomes are independent. But a trial does not have $\theta$. After 500 tosses with 499 point up, nobody believes the next toss is as uncertain as the first.

For the trialist, a response model and a prior come as a package, and the response model assumes exchangeability within each arm or within covariate strata.

## In the book
Exchangeability is a judgment about the patients, and it can fail. If patients enrolled in the first year differ from later ones, or sites differ, the order matters. Time trends, site effects and covariates relax it to "exchangeable within strata".

Batch-wise updating is valid because $y_1$ and $y_2$ are conditionally independent given $\theta$, which exchangeability delivers.

## Pitfalls
The same judgment returns when information is borrowed from earlier studies.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does exchangeability imply independence? A: No. Independent outcomes are exchangeable but not the reverse.
- Q: Can it fail? A: Yes, with time trends or site effects.

title: Expected sample size
cx: Chapter 14: Operating Characteristics by Simulation > 14.5.3 Power, expected sample size, early stopping and bias
text:
Expected sample size. The average number of patients a design enrolls under a stated true effect, smaller than the maximum when the trial can stop early.

## What it is

The expected sample size E[N] is the average total enrollment under a stated truth. For a group sequential design, the differences between successive "not yet crossed" probabilities give the probability of stopping at each look, hence the expected sample size.

## Why it matters

It is the price side of stopping early. A fixed design uses all its patients, and a design that can stop uses fewer on average.

## In the book

For the four-look Bayesian design with flat priors and a maximum of 160 per arm, the expected sample size under the null is below the maximum of 320 because the only way to stop early is a false success. Under the null E[N] is 317 of 320. At an effect of 0.15 the design has power 0.713, stops early in 57 percent of trials and has E[N] of 232 against 320 for the fixed design, about 28 percent fewer; the cost is about 8 points of power against the fixed design's 0.794. Adding a futility rule at the first three looks cuts the null E[N] from 317 to 282. The analytic O'Brien-Fleming design has E[N] of 263.

## Pitfalls

Analytic expected sample size of a group sequential design counts completers, while a simulation that models accrual counts everyone enrolled, which is larger. A report should give expected and maximum $N$ for enrolled patients, not only completers.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is expected N under the null below the maximum when there is no futility rule? A: Because the only way to stop early is a false success.
- Q: Which count is larger, completers or enrolled patients? A: Enrolled patients, because those still in the pipeline count when the trial stops.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_crossing_prob, oc_simulate, oc_summarize, gs_power

title: FACTS
al: Fixed and Adaptive Clinical Trial Simulator
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text:
FACTS. Also called: Fixed and Adaptive Clinical Trial Simulator. Commercial software from Berry Consultants for designing and simulating Bayesian adaptive trials, including dose finding, response-adaptive randomization and platform designs.

## What it is
FACTS is commercial software from Berry Consultants for designing and simulating Bayesian adaptive trials. It covers dose finding, response-adaptive randomization and platform designs.

## Why it matters
Simulation output of this kind is what regulators ask for in a CID meeting.

## In the book
The book says its free studio in the companion lab is a free tool in the style of commercial design software such as FACTS.

## Pitfalls
The book did not check this tool's version.

## Check yourself
- Q: Who makes FACTS? A: Berry Consultants.
- Q: Why does its kind of output matter? A: Regulators ask for it in a CID meeting.

title: FAERS
al: spontaneous reports; FDA Adverse Event Reporting System
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.3 Signals in spontaneous reports
text:
FAERS. Also called: spontaneous reports, FDA Adverse Event Reporting System. The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System, a database of spontaneous reports in which the FDA screens for signals with disproportionality methods.

## What it is

FAERS and the WHO's VigiBase together hold tens of millions of reports. The data are a sparse table of counts $n_{ij}$ of reports that mention drug $i$ and event $j$.

## Why it matters

Most rare adverse effects are first noticed in spontaneous reports, not in trials. The FDA applies disproportionality screening there, with empirical Bayes methods in use since the late 1990s. A successor system, AEMS, was announced in March 2026.

## In the book

Reports come from voluntary submissions by clinicians and patients and mandatory reports from manufacturers. Neither gives exposure denominators and ascertainment is incomplete, so the table cannot give incidence. It can only say which pairs are reported more than the margins predict.

## Pitfalls

- Reporting is influenced by publicity, indication and the reporter.
- Bayesian machinery protects against noise in rare cells, not against bias in the reporting mechanism.

## Check yourself

- Q: Can a spontaneous report table give incidence? A: No, because it has no exposure denominators and ascertainment is incomplete.

title: False discovery rate
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.4.5 Where familywise control is not the target: false discovery rate and prior probabilities
text:
False discovery rate. Also called: FDR. The expected proportion of false rejections among the rejections, the target for screens and signal detection where no confirmatory claim is made.

## What it is

For hundreds of biomarkers, signatures or adverse event terms the aim is to find most of the real signals and tolerate a known share of false leads. Benjamini and Hochberg defined the false discovery rate as the expected proportion of false rejections among the rejections.

Their step-up procedure orders the $p$-values, finds the largest $j$ with $p_{(j)} \le jq/m$, and rejects the hypotheses with the $j$ smallest $p$-values. It controls the rate at $q$ for independent $p$-values and under positive dependence.

## Why it matters

False discovery rate control is used for screening, exploratory endpoints and signal detection. It is not used for a confirmatory claim, which stays under familywise control.

## In the book

In a simulated screen of 1000 hypotheses, 100 with a true effect (a $z$ statistic centered at 3), all at level 0.025 and averaged over 1000 replications, the book compares the unadjusted test, Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg.

The Bayesian reading is Efron's two-groups model: each statistic comes from the null with probability $\pi_0$ and from an alternative otherwise. The local false discovery rate is the posterior probability of the null given the statistic.

Scott and Berger show that if the prior probability of a true effect is learned from all hypotheses, the posterior imposes a penalty that grows with the number of hypotheses when few signals are present among many. The penalty relaxes as more signals appear.

## Pitfalls

- Benjamini-Hochberg thresholds an estimate of the tail-area false discovery rate with the null proportion set to one.
- Using it for a confirmatory claim would drop the familywise guarantee that guidance expects.

title: False discovery rate
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.4.5 Where familywise control is not the target: false discovery rate and prior probabilities
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: When is false discovery rate control the right target? A: For screens, exploratory endpoints and signal detection, not confirmatory claims.
- Q: What is the local false discovery rate? A: The posterior probability of the null given the statistic in the two-groups model.

title: False positive risk
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.2 The false positive risk
text:
False positive risk. Also called: FPR. The probability that a drug does not work given that its trial was significant, which depends on the prior probability that such drugs work.

## What it is

The false positive risk is the fraction of significant trials in which the drug does not work. It is the screening-test calculation: sensitivity is the power $1-\beta$, the false alarm rate is the type I error $\alpha$, and prevalence is the prior probability $\pi_a$ that the drug works.

$$
\text{FPR} \;=\; \Pr(\text{no effect} \mid \text{significant}) \;=\; \frac{\alpha\,(1-\pi_a)}{\alpha\,(1-\pi_a) + (1-\beta)\,\pi_a}.
$$

This is equation eq-fpr. Colquhoun later called it the false positive risk.

## Why it matters

The type I error is $\Pr(\text{significant} \mid \text{no effect})$ and is what a design controls. The false positive risk is $\Pr(\text{no effect} \mid \text{significant})$ and is what a decision-maker wants. The prior probability connects them. Power also protects against false positives, because $(1-\beta)\pi_a$ is in the denominator.

## In the book

At one-sided alpha 0.025 and 90% power, if half of drugs work the false positive risk is about 2.7%. If one in ten works it is 20%, and if one in a hundred works it is 73%. In a review of phase III oncology trials that repeated a regimen already positive in phase II, only 28% were positive.

## Pitfalls

The equation conditions on the trial being significant at level $\alpha$, not on the exact p-value. It is not an alternative to the type I error rate.

## Check yourself

- Q: With 90% power, if one in ten such drugs works, is a significant result mostly right? A: Mostly, but about one in five (20%) is a false positive.
- Q: Why does an underpowered trial that crosses the line deserve more suspicion? A: Low power shrinks the true-positive term in the denominator, so chance explains more of the significant results.
R functions (bayestrials): false_positive_risk

title: Familywise error rate
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.1 The problem: many chances for luck
text:
Familywise error rate. Also called: FWER. The chance of at least one false positive among a family of hypotheses, which regulators expect to be controlled in the strong sense for claims.

## What it is

Suppose a drug does nothing and we test it on $k$ independent endpoints, each at one-sided level $\alpha = 0.025$. The chance that at least one test crosses the bar is one minus the chance that none does.

$$
\Pr(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1-\alpha)^k .
$$

This probability is the familywise error rate when all $k$ null hypotheses are true. For $k=1$ it is 0.025 by design.

## Why it matters

With twenty independent tests of a useless drug the chance of at least one "significant" result is about 0.40. The FDA multiple endpoints guidance expects strong control of the familywise error rate for the endpoints that support a claim.

## In the book

Independence is neither the best nor the worst case. With a shared control group or positively correlated endpoints the probability is typically smaller, but false positives come in clumps.

The formula is about a drug that does nothing. What a regulator wants to prevent is a false claim, so the family is the set of hypotheses whose rejection would be presented as evidence supporting approval or labeling.

## Pitfalls

- The global null alone is not enough when checking strong control: simulation must cover mixed configurations where some hypotheses are true and others false.
- Shrinkage does not give a familywise guarantee. A rule with shrinkage must be calibrated by simulation if a regulator requires one.

## Check yourself

- Q: What is the chance of at least one false positive for twenty tests at 0.025? A: About 0.40.
- Q: Do interim looks on the same endpoint belong to the cross-endpoint family procedures? A: They are handled by a group sequential boundary and then combined with the cross-endpoint procedures.
R functions (bayestrials): mult_simulate

title: FDA adaptive design guidance 2019
al: adaptive design guidance; Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.1 Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics (final, November 2019)
text:
FDA adaptive design guidance 2019. Also called: adaptive design guidance, Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics. The final November 2019 FDA guidance with four principles for adaptive designs: error control, reliable estimation, full prespecification and trial integrity.

## What it is
The founding FDA document for the book, and it is final. It defines an adaptive design as "a clinical trial design that allows for prospectively planned modifications to one or more aspects of the design based on accumulating data".

## Why it matters
Its four principles are that the chance of erroneous conclusions be adequately controlled, estimation be sufficiently reliable, design details be completely prespecified, and trial integrity be maintained. It says adaptive features can inflate the type I error probability, with repeated looks as the simplest example.

## In the book
- It names simulation for operating characteristics and limited access to comparative interim data.
- It gives an example of effectiveness rules based on a Bayesian posterior probability.
- It works through a single interim look at 50 percent of the information.
- It says simulation is a major use for estimating operating characteristics.

## Pitfalls
The Bayesian draft of 2026 builds on this document, so the 2019 text stays the baseline for both frequentist and Bayesian designs.

## Check yourself
- Q: Name the four principles. A: Controlled error, reliable estimation, complete prespecification, maintained integrity.
- Q: Is it a draft? A: No, it is final (November 2019).

title: FDA Bayesian draft guidance 2026
al: Bayesian draft guidance; Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.3 Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026)
text:
FDA Bayesian draft guidance 2026. Also called: Bayesian draft guidance, Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products. The January 2026 FDA draft on Bayesian methods for drugs and biologics, covering success criteria, priors, borrowing, simulation and documentation.

## What it is
A draft guidance for industry from CDER and CBER, issued in January 2026 under docket FDA-2025-D-3217 and marked as nonbinding. Its scope is INDs, NDAs, BLAs and supplements, with a primary focus on Bayesian support for primary inference, and it does not apply to devices. Success is stated as $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$.

## Why it matters
It describes three routes: calibration to a type I error rate, direct interpretation of posterior probabilities, and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria. For trials with an overall frequentist plan, the familywise type I error rate is almost always required to be no greater than 0.025 one-sided. It requires nothing by itself, since it is a draft.

## In the book
- Priors: "It is always critical for Bayesian analyses to have a prespecified prior."
- Borrowing needs strong justification and is judged by effective sample size, not type I error inflation.
- Simulations "should comprehensively cover the plausible range of assumptions".
- Reports should give software versions, code and MCMC seed numbers, and FDA requires no specific software.

## Pitfalls
Calibration is this book's default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, not the draft's. Never call a draft a requirement.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the draft require calibration to 0.025? A: No, calibration is one of three routes.
- Q: Which measure does the draft prefer for borrowing? A: Effective sample size and similar influence metrics.

title: FDA fit-for-purpose determination
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.2 BOIN and FDA's fit-for-purpose determination
text:
FDA fit-for-purpose determination. An FDA Drug Development Tools initiative listing dose-finding methods reviewed for a stated context of use, including BOIN and MCP-Mod.

## What it is
The FDA Drug Development Tools Fit-for-Purpose Initiative lists dose-finding methods FDA has reviewed for a stated context of use. The list as printed, current as of 10 January 2025, includes BOIN (determination issued 10 December 2021) and MCP-Mod (26 May 2016).

## Why it matters
BOIN is the one model-assisted design with an FDA determination. What was reviewed was the method for a stated context of use, phase 1 dose finding with a toxicity endpoint.

## Pitfalls
The regulator's acceptance attaches to a method and a context of use. A sponsor still has to supply its own simulations and a protocol-specific justification.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does a fit-for-purpose determination exempt a sponsor from simulations? A: No.
- Q: Which determination is older, BOIN or MCP-Mod? A: MCP-Mod, 26 May 2016, against 10 December 2021.

title: FDA master protocols guidance 2026
al: master protocol guidance; Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.5 Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development (revised draft, June 2026)
text:
FDA master protocols guidance 2026. Also called: master protocol guidance, Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development. The June 2026 revised FDA draft on umbrella, basket and platform protocols, favoring concurrent controls and no multiplicity adjustment across different drugs.

## What it is
A first draft appeared in December 2023, and a revised draft that "revises and replaces" it was announced in the Federal Register on 24 June 2026 (91 FR 37991), with comments closing on 24 August 2026. It is issued under the Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022. It defines a master protocol as a protocol with multiple substudies, which may have different objectives.

## Why it matters
- The primary comparison should use "only concurrently eligible control participants".
- Nonconcurrent controls are allowed only in rare circumstances agreed with FDA in advance, with concurrent-only sensitivity analyses.
- FDA generally does not recommend multiplicity adjustment across different drugs, but expects adjustment across doses or formulations of the same drug.
- A master protocol pre-IND meeting is requested as Type B.

## In the book
The EMA draft on platform trials is stricter on controls and allocation, so a global platform should treat the stricter position as the design constraint. The guidance complements the March 2022 oncology master protocols guidance.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does FDA recommend adjusting across drugs in a master protocol? A: Generally not, because the expected number of type I errors is the same as in independent trials.
- Q: Which meeting type fits a master protocol pre-IND? A: Type B.

title: FDA meetings
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7 Interacting with FDA
text:
FDA meetings. Also called: interacting with FDA, formal meetings. The ways a sponsor learns whether FDA agrees with a design: formal PDUFA meetings, the CID and MIDD programs, CPIM and DDT qualification.

## What it is
FDA's meeting types and programs differ in what they can promise, and the differences matter. The formal types are Type A, B, B (EOP), C, D and INTERACT. The programs are the CID and MIDD paired meeting programs, CPIM and DDT qualification.

## Why it matters
Permissions that matter for Bayesian adaptive designs are all of the form "if FDA agrees", so the agreements are sought in writing, early and on the record. A novel design should go to FDA early, with simulations in hand.

## In the book
- A narrow question with one or two issues goes to Type D.
- A stalled program or a safety issue goes to Type A.
- A Bayesian, complex adaptive or simulation-driven design goes to the CID program, or Type C otherwise.
- A dose that depends on a model goes to the MIDD program.
- A general method goes to CPIM, and a biomarker for many sponsors to DDT qualification.
- A master protocol goes to Type B pre-IND.

## Pitfalls
Minutes are not a binding contract, but a sponsor that departs from documented agreements should expect a question.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which meeting fits "Is the phase 3 plan acceptable?" A: Type B (end of phase 2).
- Q: Which meeting requires no product? A: CPIM.

title: FDA multiple endpoints guidance 2022
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.6 Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials (final, October 2022)
text:
FDA multiple endpoints guidance 2022. Also called: Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials. The final October 2022 FDA guidance on handling several endpoints, doses or comparisons with strong control of the familywise error rate.

## What it is
A final guidance that describes the multiplicity problem and the strategies for handling it when a trial has several endpoints, doses or comparisons. It covers procedures for strong control of the familywise error rate: Bonferroni, Holm, fixed-sequence and gatekeeping procedures, and graphical methods.

## Why it matters
It is the regulatory partner of ICH E9 section 5.6. It sets the expectation that a claim supported by several endpoints comes with a stated multiplicity strategy. The statistical analysis plan states that strategy.

## In the book
The Bayesian draft echoes the guidance by recommending that the familywise error rate be controlled "across all primary and secondary estimands". The guidance also leaves room for hierarchical modeling as a complement to, not a replacement for, the confirmatory strategy. Its status is final, October 2022.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which procedures does it cover? A: Bonferroni, Holm, fixed-sequence, gatekeeping and graphical methods.
- Q: Can hierarchical modeling replace the confirmatory strategy? A: No, only complement it.

title: FDA substantial-evidence draft guidance 2026
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.4 The 2026 substantial-evidence draft
text:
FDA substantial-evidence draft guidance 2026. Also called: 2026 substantial-evidence draft. The June 2026 revised draft guidance on how FDA reads the substantial-evidence standard, including a single-trial route that needs a highly persuasive trial or strong confirmatory evidence.

## What it is
*Demonstrating Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness for Human Drug and Biological Products* is a revised draft guidance of June 2026. It revises the draft issued in December 2019, and as a draft it is not for implementation. The revision was announced in the Federal Register on 24 June 2026 under docket FDA-2019-D-4964. When finalized it will replace the 1998 guidance.

## Why it matters
It describes the conventional two-trial route and a single-trial route, which "will involve a highly persuasive trial or a source of strong confirmatory evidence". It lists the factors FDA weighs: the seriousness of the disease and unmet need, the strength of the single trial, the strength and source of the confirmatory evidence, and whether it is ethical and practicable to conduct more than one trial.

## In the book
- Confirmatory evidence may be of types that are not trials, such as mechanistic evidence.
- The plan for one trial should be discussed with FDA before it starts.
- The draft explicitly recognizes Bayesian analyses.

## Pitfalls
Check the date on the document itself: the address of the 2019 draft now serves the June 2026 revision. A draft is nonbinding and subject to change.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which earlier document will it replace once final? A: The 1998 guidance on clinical evidence of effectiveness.
- Q: Is this draft a requirement? A: No, it is a nonbinding draft.

title: FDA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5 FDA design guidances
text:
FDA. Also called: Food and Drug Administration. The US regulator whose statute, regulations and guidances set the evidence standard the book designs trials to meet.

## What it is
FDA issues guidance documents that "contain nonbinding recommendations". In its convention "should" means suggested or recommended, but not required. The statute it applies is section 505(d), and the regulation is 21 CFR 314.126.

## Why it matters
A sponsor may depart from a guidance but must show that the alternative meets the statute and regulations. A departure without prior discussion with the agency is a risk to the program, which is why meetings exist. A guidance first appears as a draft, comments follow (60 days after the Federal Register notice is usual), and then a final, a revision or a withdrawal.

## In the book
- The adaptive design guidance of November 2019 is final.
- The Bayesian methodology draft of January 2026 comes from CDER and CBER.
- The master protocols revised draft is dated June 2026.
- FDA offers formal meetings and programs for asking whether it agrees.
- Expedited programs change the speed and intensity of FDA's interaction, not the standard.

## Pitfalls
A draft is labeled not for implementation, though sponsors often follow it. The review division that examines an application has the last word on what is adequate for that product.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does "should" in an FDA guidance mean required? A: No, it means suggested or recommended.
- Q: Is a faster expedited review a lower bar? A: No.

title: Fixed allocation
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.1 The traditional default: fixed allocation
text:
Fixed allocation. Also called: 1:1 allocation. Setting the allocation ratio in the protocol, almost always 1:1, and keeping it for the whole study; the default that response-adaptive randomization must beat.

## What it is

A traditional two-arm trial fixes the allocation ratio in the protocol and keeps it for the whole study. Almost always the ratio is 1:1, implemented by permuted blocks, perhaps stratified.

## Why it matters

For equal variances the standard error of the difference is proportional to $\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_0}$, smallest when $n_0 = n_1$ for a fixed total. Permuted blocks also balance calendar time, so any change in patient mix hits both arms equally. Allocation independent of outcomes keeps the randomization distribution exactly known.

## In the book

A 2:1 ratio costs 12.5 percent more patients, 3:1 costs a third more, and 9:1 costs almost three times as many. For a control response of 0.30 and a treatment response of 0.45 the optimal share on treatment is only 52 percent. Unequal ratios are justified when stated in advance, for example for safety exposure or a shared control. With $k$ experimental arms, Dunnett's result is that the control arm should be about $\sqrt{k}$ times as large as each treatment arm; with three arms equal allocation puts 25 percent on control and Dunnett's rule 36.6 percent.

## Pitfalls

A fixed control share protects control accrual but does not establish acceptability of adaptive allocation among experimental arms. For a confirmatory two-arm trial, use fixed allocation.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does 2:1 allocation cost in sample size for the same power? A: 12.5 percent more patients.
- Q: Why does blocking make time trends harmless? A: Each arm receives the same number of patients within a block, so changes in patient mix hit both arms equally.

title: Fixed-sequence testing
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.2.5 Fixed-sequence (hierarchical) testing
text:
Fixed-sequence testing. Also called: hierarchical testing, fixed sequence. Order hypotheses in advance and test each at the full alpha, stopping at the first failure.

## What it is

Order the hypotheses in advance by clinical importance: $H_1, H_2, \dots, H_k$. Test $H_1$ at the full $\alpha$. If it is rejected, test $H_2$ at the full $\alpha$, and so on. Stop at the first failure and do not test the rest.

## Why it matters

The familywise error rate is controlled at $\alpha$ with no division of the level, because at most one hypothesis can be the first true null, and it is tested at $\alpha$.

This is the most common strategy for a primary endpoint followed by key secondaries. It is what "primary/secondary hierarchy" means in a protocol.

## In the book

The price is that the order is final. A failure on the primary, or on an early secondary, makes all later results exploratory regardless of how impressive they look. This surprises clinical teams that have seen a large effect on endpoint 4.

Two consequences for writing the hierarchy: put first the endpoint with the best chance of success and the most important claim, since a failure ends the chain. And the sequence can be a tree and not a line, which is a graphical procedure.

## Pitfalls

- Testing four secondaries at alpha/4 regardless of the primary may be worse for the claims the sponsor cares about than a fixed-sequence or graphical procedure.

## Check yourself

- Q: A primary endpoint fails. May the key secondaries be tested at full level? A: No, later results become exploratory.
- Q: Why is no division of alpha needed? A: At most one hypothesis can be the first true null, and it is tested at alpha.

title: Forking paths
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.3.1 Why a Bayesian must also ask how the result was chosen
text:
Forking paths. Also called: garden of forking paths. Multiplicity hidden in analyst choices: even one test is many if which test was run depended on the data.

## What it is

The analyst who sees a promising subgroup usually chose how to cut: age above or below 65, 60 or 70, tertiles or a threshold. Gelman and Loken called this the garden of forking paths. Even if the analyst ran only one test, the choice of which test depended on the data.

The effective number of comparisons is the number of tests that would have been run had the data looked different. The multiplicity is hidden in decisions, not in the number of $p$-values.

## Why it matters

A Bayesian analysis conditions on the data it is shown. The regulator sees a message $M = \varsigma(X)$, where the reporting rule $\varsigma$ is chosen by the sponsor. The protocol is the specification of $\varsigma$.

## In the book

If the sponsor reports the largest of $K$ independent components, the likelihood of the reported value $m$ is given below.

$$
\mathcal{L}_\varsigma(\theta; m) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p(m \mid \theta_k) \prod_{j \ne k} F(m \mid \theta_j),
$$

with $F$ the distribution function of a component. For exchangeable components the ratio to the naive likelihood approaches $K$ in the upper tail.

With a common effect $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$ and only the maximum reported, the correct likelihood carries an extra factor $\Phi(m - \theta)^{K-1}$, which pulls the posterior down.

## Pitfalls

- The retort that optional stopping does not affect the posterior is correct only when the full sample path is reported. It is beside the point when the report is a summary chosen after the fact.
- The regulator cannot compute the correct posterior without knowing the reporting rule.

title: Forking paths
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.3.1 Why a Bayesian must also ask how the result was chosen
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Where does the multiplicity hide when only one test was run? A: In the choice of which test, which depended on the data.
- Q: What fixes the reporting rule for a regulator? A: The protocol.

title: Four-operation ulcer trial
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.5 An illustration motivated by the four-operation ulcer trial
text:
Four-operation ulcer trial. Also called: ulcer trial. A 1965 duodenal ulcer trial of four operations that Novick and Grizzle used to argue for Bayesian analysis, and the book's worked multiplicity example.

## What it is

Novick and Grizzle made one of the first cases for Bayesian analysis of trial data using an experiment then in progress that compared four operative treatments for duodenal ulcer. It has four arms, six pairwise contrasts, repeated analysis and a modest effect on a binary endpoint.

The counts in the book are illustrative, set at the scale of that trial and not transcribed from the 1965 paper. They ship with the package as the dataset `ulcer`.

## Why it matters

It is the structure on which the traditional apparatus does worst, so it shows both ways to pay for looking.

## In the book

The best against worst contrast, drainage and vagotomy against 75 percent resection, is a difference of 12.4 percentage points in the recurrence rate, with $Z=2.45$. With six contrasts the Bonferroni-adjusted $p$ is 0.0855, not reportable, and Holm does not rescue it.

A group sequential design with four interim analyses at the corrected level would put the first boundary at 5.34.

The hierarchical model pays in the estimate instead. The best against worst contrast is shrunk from 1.053 to 0.464 on the log-odds scale, and the posterior probability that drainage and vagotomy is worse than 75 percent resection is 0.952, a number a clinician can use. It is not a claim of significance under strong familywise control.

The four operations are ordered by extent of resection, so a single prespecified linear trend contrast carries no multiplicity burden (trend $p = 0.0043$).

## Pitfalls

- The companion lab's module 05 uses a different table for this trial, so its numbers differ from the chapter's.
- The estimate of the between-arm spread rests on four arms and is the sensitive part.

title: Four-operation ulcer trial
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.5 An illustration motivated by the four-operation ulcer trial
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Why does the best against worst contrast overstate the effect? A: It was chosen because it is the largest of six.
- Q: What single contrast avoids a multiplicity burden here? A: A prespecified linear trend over the ordered extent of resection.
R functions (bayestrials): shrink_logodds, shrink_eb_fit, shrink_post_prob

title: Futility boundary
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.6 Futility boundaries: binding and non-binding
text:
Futility boundary. Also called: futility rule, futility, binding futility. The lower edge of the continuation region: stop if the interim statistic is below it. Binding rules enter the type I error, non-binding ones do not.

## What it is

An efficacy boundary is the upper edge of the continuation region. A futility boundary is the lower edge: if the interim statistic is below it, the trial stops because the treatment is unlikely to show benefit.

- A binding boundary is part of the design. If crossed the trial stops, and the type I error assumes it does. The reduction can lower the efficacy boundaries a little.
- A non-binding boundary is a guideline. The type I error is computed as though it did not exist, so it is at most $\alpha$ whether the committee follows it or not.

## Why it matters

Futility stops shorten trials of useless drugs and reduce false positives. The traditional position, encouraged by regulators, is the non-binding rule, because a DMC's decision to continue should never invalidate the type I error.

## In the book

On a four-look O'Brien-Fleming design the book stops for futility at looks 1, 2, 3 if the standardized statistic is below zero. Under the null this stops the trial early about 69 percent of the time, and 50 percent at the first look alone.

The rule costs some power under the alternative, because trials with a true benefit sometimes have a negative interim statistic by chance. A binding rule recovers a little of it, but if overridden the type I error is no longer controlled.

EOLIA stopped for futility under a two-sided triangular test, with relative risk 0.76 (95% confidence interval 0.55 to 1.04).

## Pitfalls

- Power must be computed as if the futility rule were followed.
- A threshold of Z below 0 is crude. In practice the criterion is usually conditional power or predictive probability.

title: Futility boundary
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.6 Futility boundaries: binding and non-binding
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: If a DMC overrides a binding futility rule, what happens to the type I error? A: It is no longer controlled.
- Q: Why is a non-binding rule safe for the type I error? A: Ignoring it can only increase the chance of crossing the efficacy boundary, and that is already at most alpha.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_boundary, gs_expected_information, gs_power, gs_power_drift

title: Gamma-Poisson shrinker
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.3.2 The gamma-Poisson shrinker
text:
Gamma-Poisson shrinker. Also called: GPS, MGPS. An empirical Bayes method that shrinks noisy reporting ratios with a two-component gamma mixture and ranks signals by their geometric mean and fifth percentile.

## What it is

Each pair has a true reporting ratio $\lambda_{ij}$, with $n_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{ij} E_{ij})$. The ratios come from a mixture of two gamma distributions:

$$
\lambda \sim P\, \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_1, \beta_1) + (1 - P)\, \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_2, \beta_2),
$$

eq-safety-gps, with five parameters estimated from the whole table by maximum marginal likelihood. The posterior is again a two-component gamma mixture, with component $k$ becoming $\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_k + n, \beta_k + E)$.

Signals are ranked by $\mathrm{EBGM} = \exp(\mathbb{E}[\log \lambda \mid n])$ and screened on its fifth percentile, EB05.

## Why it matters

DuMouchel proposed it as the empirical Bayes method behind the FDA's data mining of its reports database. It ranks signals by evidence as well as by size.

## In the book

With illustrative hyperparameters, the single report with a raw ratio of twenty is shrunk and its lower bound is well below one, so it is not a signal. Two pairs with the same raw ratio of four are treated differently: the pair with 40 reports has a high EB05 and is flagged, the pair with 12 less so. A screening rule of EB05 above 2 flags the pairs with $n = 12$ and $n = 40$ and nothing else.

## Pitfalls

- The illustrative values only show the mechanics. In a real analysis they are fitted to the whole table, because shrinkage is only as good as the estimated mixture.
- A high EB05 is a hypothesis, not evidence of causation. It does not correct for bias in the reporting mechanism.

title: Gamma-Poisson shrinker
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.3.2 The gamma-Poisson shrinker
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Does a raw ratio of 20 on one report survive shrinkage? A: No, its EB05 is well below one.
- Q: Two pairs share a raw ratio of 4, with 12 and 40 reports. Which has the higher EB05? A: The one with 40 reports.
R functions (bayestrials): safety_gps, safety_gps_fit

title: Gamma posterior for a hazard
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.3 The gamma posterior for a hazard
text:
Gamma posterior for a hazard. Also called: gamma posterior. For a constant hazard, a Gamma(a, b) prior and d events in exposure T give a Gamma(a + d, b + T) posterior.

## What it is
For a single arm with constant hazard $\lambda$, $d$ events in total follow-up $T$ give likelihood $\lambda^d e^{-\lambda T}$ whatever the censoring pattern, if censoring is noninformative. With a $\mathrm{Gamma}(a, b)$ prior the posterior is $\mathrm{Gamma}(a + d, b + T)$. The prior is worth $a$ events and $b$ years of exposure.

## Why it matters
Dividing time into intervals with constant hazards gives independent gamma terms per interval. A random walk on $\log\lambda_k$ smooths the hazard and lets sparse late intervals borrow from earlier ones. This piecewise exponential model underlies most Bayesian time-to-event analyses.

## In the book
A control arm has 60 events in 400 patient-years, with a vague Gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior. Median survival under the exponential model is $\log 2/\lambda$. Its posterior mean is not the plug-in $\log 2/0.15$, because the median is a reciprocal of the hazard, and its interval is asymmetric. The posterior is transformed directly, with no delta method. The posterior mean hazard is 0.150 (95% interval 0.114 to 0.190), and the posterior mean median is 4.7 years against the plug-in 4.62, with interval 3.6 to 6.1.

## Pitfalls
A constant hazard is rarely realistic over years of follow-up.

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the posterior after d events in T years of exposure with a Gamma(a, b) prior? A: Gamma(a + d, b + T).
R functions (bayestrials): surv_gamma_hazard

title: GBM AGILE
al: GBM AGILE trial; Adaptive Global Innovative Learning Environment
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.2 GBM AGILE: a registration platform
text:
GBM AGILE. Also called: GBM AGILE trial, Adaptive Global Innovative Learning Environment. A Bayesian response-adaptive glioblastoma platform designed for registration, with a seamless phase 2/3 structure and a shared control.

## What it is

GBM AGILE (NCT03970447) is a Bayesian response-adaptive platform in glioblastoma designed with registration in mind, which I-SPY 2 was not. It uses a seamless phase 2/3 structure. In stage 1 each arm is randomized adaptively against a shared control (temozolomide in newly diagnosed disease, lomustine in recurrent), with allocation proportional to the posterior probability of a hazard ratio below a benchmark and arms evaluated monthly. An arm that clears the bar graduates to stage 2 with fixed randomization to confirm the finding.

## Why it matters

Patients are classified into signatures by newly diagnosed versus recurrent disease and MGMT methylation status, and 20% of each subtype's patients are assigned to control. FDA's Bayesian draft names the platform as its example for the time machine, since the shared control must be used carefully when standard of care changes.

## In the book

For regorafenib, efficacy required a Bayesian probability of benefit (hazard ratio below 1) of at least 98%, and enrollment stopped for limited efficacy when predictive power fell below 25% in all signatures. The report has since been corrected by an erratum. The 98% is set by simulation so that the false positive rate is acceptable, not by a view about the prior. The registry lists 17 arm entries, several running dose-finding and enhanced safety management phases first, which is a pattern worth copying.

## Pitfalls

Thresholds like 98% are calibrated per design, so they cannot be carried over to another platform without a new simulation report.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a stage 1 graduate do next? A: Moves to stage 2 with fixed randomization.
- Q: What share of each subtype is on control? A: 20%.

title: Gittins index
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.4 The Gittins index
text:
Gittins index. The exact solution to the discounted infinite-horizon bandit problem: give each patient the arm with the highest index, which depends only on that arm's own history.

## What it is

Each arm has a state, which for a binary outcome is its counts of successes and failures, and future rewards are discounted by a factor $\gamma < 1$ per patient. The index of an arm in state $s$ is the highest achievable ratio of expected discounted reward to expected discounted time, over the stopping times $\tau$ at which one might abandon the arm:

$$
G(s) = \sup_{\tau > 0} \frac{\mathrm{E}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \gamma^t r_t \mid s\bigr]}{\mathrm{E}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \gamma^t \mid s\bigr]}.
$$

## Why it matters

Equivalently it is the constant payoff per patient at which a decision maker is indifferent between continuing with the arm and retiring to a sure thing. The optimal policy gives each patient the arm with the highest index, and each arm's index depends only on its own history, so many arms are solved by tabulating one-arm indices.

## In the book

The index exceeds the posterior mean when the arm is uncertain, and the excess is the value of learning. This premium makes an optimal policy try a new arm even when its estimate is mediocre, and a longer horizon raises it. Gittins showed the result for geometric discounting.

## Pitfalls

It is exact for an infinite, discounted horizon, whereas a trial has a fixed number of patients and a finite-horizon problem has no index solution. The objective is the reward to patients in the trial, not that of a confirmatory comparison. Practical designs use approximations, with Thompson sampling the most common.

title: Gittins index
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.4 The Gittins index
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Does an untried arm's index sit above or at its posterior mean? A: Above, because uncertainty carries a premium for learning.
- Q: Why is the index not a design for a fixed-size trial? A: It solves the infinite discounted horizon; a finite horizon has no index solution.
R functions (bayestrials): gittins_table, gittins_index, rar_gittins_index

title: Goldilocks design
cx: Chapter 14: Operating Characteristics by Simulation > 14.7 The Goldilocks design
text:
Goldilocks design. A trial that lets accrual run until two predictive probabilities say the sample is not too big and not too small, with thresholds calibrated by simulation.

## What it is

The Goldilocks sample size design of Broglio, Connor and Berry does not fix its sample size. At each look it computes $\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}$, success if enrollment stops now and pending outcomes complete, and $\mathrm{PP}_{\max}$, success at the maximum sample size. It stops enrolling for expected success when the first is high and stops for futility when the second is low.

## Why it matters

The sample size is an output, bounded by $N_{\max}$, and the thresholds are calibrated by simulating type I error, not derived. The design replaces an interim efficacy boundary, a futility boundary and sample size re-estimation with one pre-specified rule. Its price is a random sample size, so budgets must be planned for the maximum.

## In the book
