With immediate outcomes $\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}$ collapses to an indicator and only the $\mathrm{PP}_{\max}$ futility rule remains. In the chapter 14 sketch, futility at $F = 0.05$ cuts the expected sample size under the null by more than half, at a cost in power largest at the design alternative 0.15. In the chapter 15 example, 30 of 50 against 15 of 50 stops enrollment, and equal rates of 18 of 50 stop for futility. DAWN's plan is a trial-sized version.

## Pitfalls

Stopping enrollment when the predictive probability is high is an efficacy decision and spends type I error. The look frequency and the delay length change the calibration.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which predictive probability triggers futility? A: $\mathrm{PP}_{\max}$, when it is low.
- Q: Does the design fix the sample size? A: No, it is an output bounded by $N_{\max}$.
R functions (bayestrials): oc_calibrate, oc_predictive_matrix, oc_with_futility, prob_superior

title: Governance and firewalls
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.4 The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
text:
Governance and firewalls. Also called: firewall. Who sees unblinded comparative data in an adaptive trial: an independent statistical center and a DMC see it, and the sponsor does not.

## What it is
Adaptive trials need someone to see unblinded comparative data during the trial in order to apply the adaptation rules, and the sponsor must not.
The integrity concern is that knowledge of interim results, or even of what decision was made, can change the behavior of investigators, patients and sponsor staff.

## Why it matters
The FDA DMC guidance of 2006 remains the starting document, with a draft revision issued in February 2024.
Nothing about the Bayesian rule changes the firewall; what changes is the number the committee reads.

## In the book
A workable arrangement has four parties.
The independent statistical center holds the randomization code, runs the interim analyses and computes posterior and predictive probabilities.
The DMC applies or overrides the rules, and the charter states that the prespecified rules are guides so the committee keeps its judgment on safety.
The sponsor's blinded team receives only what the charter allows, and regulators may see more than the sponsor.
The DMC should receive the simulation report or a summary, so its members know what the rules were designed to do.

## Pitfalls
For response-adaptive randomization the allocation ratios themselves can reveal results. The usual safeguard is a burn-in period of equal allocation before adaptation begins, with the statistical center and not the sponsor holding the algorithm.
Firewalls in a platform trial are more complex since arms enter and leave, and a sponsor of one arm should not see data of competing arms.
A DMC asked to apply a rule it does not understand will either follow it blindly or ignore it.

## Check yourself
- Q: Who computes the decision quantities? A: The independent statistical center.
- Q: Does a Bayesian design change the firewall? A: No, it changes what the DMC reads.

title: Graphical procedure
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.2.6 Graphical procedures
text:
Graphical procedure. Also called: graphical multiple testing. A multiple testing framework where hypotheses are nodes with weights and edges pass a rejected hypothesis's level to others, so the graph is the protocol.

## What it is

Bretz, Maurer, Brannath and Posch gave a framework that unifies Bonferroni, Holm, fixed sequence, fallback and gatekeeping procedures in one picture. Each hypothesis is a node with a weight $w_i$, its share of $\alpha$, with $\sum w_i \le 1$. Directed edges carry weights $g_{ij}$, the fraction of $H_i$'s level that passes to $H_j$ if $H_i$ is rejected.

The algorithm rejects any $H_i$ with $p_i \le w_i\alpha$, removes it, passes its weight along the edges, updates the edge weights, and repeats. It controls the familywise error rate strongly because each step is a closed-test shortcut.

## Why it matters

The graph is the protocol. A statistician can draw it for the clinical team, the team can see which results unlock which, and the same picture goes into the statistical analysis plan.

## In the book

The example has two primary endpoints and two secondaries. Each primary gets half the level. A rejected primary passes its level to the secondary that clinically follows it, and a rejected secondary passes its level to the other primary.

In the second scenario P1 at 0.020 fails alone, but P2 is rejected and passes to S2. S2 is rejected and returns its level to P1, which then clears 0.025, and S1 follows. A single common marginal $p$-value of 0.015 is not enough when each primary has only half of the level, 0.0125.

For an outcomes trial with a group sequential design, the protocol needs three statements: the spending function for each hypothesis, the rule that a transferred weight is spent from the look at which the transfer happens, and the graph with its weights printed.

## Pitfalls

- A design that says only "alpha is spent by O'Brien-Fleming" has left the key secondary undefined.

title: Graphical procedure
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.2.6 Graphical procedures
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What does an edge weight g_ij mean? A: The fraction of H_i's level passed to H_j when H_i is rejected.
- Q: Why can two primaries at p=0.015 each fail when alpha is 0.025? A: Each has only half of the level, 0.0125, and nothing unlocks.
R functions (bayestrials): mult_graph

title: Group sequential design
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11 Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales
text:
Group sequential design. Also called: interim looks. A design with planned interim looks at fractions of the information, where boundaries keep the total type I error at its nominal level.

## What it is

A trial that looks at accumulating data needs a rule for stopping that keeps the type I error at its nominal level. In a group sequential trial the interim analyses are written at information fractions $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_K = 1$, and that is the whole of the design language the chapter needs.

ICH E9 calls group sequential designs the usual vehicle, because assessing grouped outcomes at periodic intervals is more practicable than continuous review.

## Why it matters

Every look is another chance for chance to produce a convincing-looking result. Every sequential method is a response to that inflation, and methods differ only in what they charge for the right to look.

## In the book

Boundaries come from the Wang-Tsiatis family $b_k = c\, t_k^{\Delta - 1/2}$, with Pocock at $\Delta = 1/2$ and O'Brien-Fleming at $\Delta = 0$. The constant $c$ is found so that the crossing probabilities sum to 0.025 under the null. The trade-off: Pocock inflates the sample size by about 18 percent and stops on average at 0.59 of the information, O'Brien-Fleming inflates it by about 2 percent and stops at 0.75.

Other families include Armitage's plans, Whitehead's triangular test, futility boundaries added by Pampallona and Tsiatis, and the unified family of Kittelson and Emerson. A design is chosen by weighing maximum sample size, expected sample size and stopping probabilities, not by ranking families.

The final bar for four O'Brien-Fleming looks is 2.02 and the sample-size inflation is about 2 percent.

## Pitfalls

- The number and timing of looks must be written down before the data are seen.
- Where only a few looks at fixed fractions are planned and no prior information is used, the traditional design is hard to improve on.

title: Group sequential design
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11 Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What does a group sequential design fix in advance? A: The boundaries, or a spending function, at planned information fractions.
- Q: Why is a fixed 1.96 cutoff at every look not a test? A: Looks are correlated but not identical, so the chance of at least one crossing exceeds 0.025 and grows with the number of looks.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_power, gs_boundary, gs_spending_boundary, gs_expected_information, gs_power_drift

title: gsDesign
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text:
gsDesign. An R package for group sequential design, including spending functions, boundaries, power and sample size calculation.

## What it is
gsDesign is an R package for group sequential design. It includes spending functions and boundaries, and power and sample size calculation.

## Why it matters
A reader can use it to check the book's own boundary code.

## In the book
The book suggests comparing its boundaries with `gs_boundary` and `gs_spending_boundary`. The build machine had gsDesign 3.11.0. The book's own boundary code can be checked against it, which makes gsDesign an independent reference for a calculation the reader would otherwise have to trust. Its listed alternative, rpact 4.4.0 on the build machine, covers confirmatory adaptive design: group sequential designs, sample size reassessment and combination tests, with simulation.

## Pitfalls
The description covers only purpose, so check the documentation for current features.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which bayestrials functions does the book suggest comparing against gsDesign? A: gs_boundary and gs_spending_boundary.
- Q: Which version was installed? A: 3.11.0.

title: GUSTO
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.2 GUSTO: when prior trials disagree with the new one
text:
GUSTO. Also called: GUSTO trial. A myocardial infarction trial of accelerated tPA against streptokinase that the book reanalyzes with priors built from two earlier megatrials at several weights.

## What it is
GUSTO randomized 41,021 patients with acute myocardial infarction to four strategies, including accelerated tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and two streptokinase arms.
Thirty-day mortality was 6.3 percent on accelerated tPA and 7.2 and 7.4 percent on the two streptokinase-only arms.
The prespecified comparison gave a 14 percent relative reduction in mortality (95 percent interval 5.9 to 21.3 percent), $p = 0.001$, an absolute benefit of one percentage point at a substantially higher drug cost.

## Why it matters
Brophy and Joseph asked what a cardiologist should have believed given the earlier megatrials GISSI-2 and ISIS-3.
They weighted the earlier trials at 100, 50 and 10 percent and concluded that the clinical superiority of tPA "remains uncertain".

## In the book
With GUSTO alone the probability that tPA lowers mortality was 0.9995, and 0.17, 0.44 and 0.98 at the three weights in Brophy and Joseph's arm model.
The book puts the prior on the risk difference, with the earlier trials at weight $w$, and `reanalysis_gusto()` reproduces both models.
That tPA lowers mortality at all is very probable under every weight, but that it lowers it by a full percentage point is unlikely once the earlier trials count at half weight or more.
The models part company because pooling each arm's rate across trials absorbs the difference between trials into the difference between agents, the mechanism of Simpson's paradox.

## Pitfalls
Borrowing within-trial treatment contrasts avoids pooling dissimilar baseline mortality rates; an arm-level model needs trial-specific baseline risks and justified borrowing.
The decision to pay for tPA turns on whether the benefit is large enough to matter, and on the price of a life year.

title: GUSTO
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.2 GUSTO: when prior trials disagree with the new one
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Does the book's difference model agree with the arm model on GUSTO alone? A: Yes, they part company as the earlier trials gain weight.
- Q: What question does the one-point threshold address? A: Whether the benefit is large enough to justify the price.
R functions (bayestrials): reanalysis_gusto

title: Hazard ratio
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.1 The traditional analysis
text:
Hazard ratio. Also called: HR. The ratio of event hazards between arms, a clean summary only when hazards are proportional.

## What it is
The hazard ratio compares the instantaneous event rates of two arms. The book's convention is benefit-positive: $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$ is positive when treatment reduces the hazard.

## Why it matters
Sample size in event units depends on it. SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 percent power and 1,225 events. A hazard ratio of 0.90 needs far more events, so tens of thousands of patients followed for years.

## In the book
Under non-proportional hazards one hazard ratio misdescribes both phases of an effect. In the book's scenarios the cumulative hazard ratio at five years is not constant, "which is the point". Across 54 oncology trials, the hazard ratio gave on average a larger effect than the ratio of restricted mean survival times (average ratio 1.11). The label summary is still usually a hazard ratio.

## Pitfalls
A hazard ratio is one summary measure among others, such as the RMST difference. The choice is made before the trial.

## Check yourself
- Q: Is a hazard ratio of 0.8 a 20 percent hazard reduction? A: Yes.

title: HEALEY ALS platform trial
al: HEALEY ALS; Healey ALS Platform Trial
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20 Master Protocols and Platform Trials
text:
HEALEY ALS platform trial. Also called: HEALEY ALS, Healey ALS Platform Trial. A platform trial the book uses as the contrast to EPAD, with a funding model that does not depend on the commercial pipeline it serves.

## What it is

The Healey ALS Platform Trial is named in the book only as a contrast to EPAD. It appears in the chapter on master protocols and platform trials, where platforms are described as machinery that keeps site contracts, database, randomization system, monitoring board and regulatory file standing.

## Why it matters

The book lists three needs before a platform's first arm: a legal framework that arm sponsors will sign, a governance structure that answers who decides, and a funding model that does not depend on the commercial pipeline the platform is meant to serve. The Healey platform is the contrast on the funding point.

## In the book

A platform survives its first arm only if governance is built for arms that are not yet known. Typically a single data monitoring committee oversees all arms, an independent statistical center runs the unblinded interim analyses, and a separate committee approves applications for new arms. The book's discussion question asks the reader to list what EPAD lacked that Healey ALS had, and which of those a statistician could have fixed.

## Pitfalls

The book gives no design numbers or results for the Healey platform, so nothing about its operating characteristics should be inferred from this entry.

## Check yourself

- Q: What role does the Healey platform play in the book? A: It is the contrast to EPAD on funding.
- Q: Which of the three pre-arm needs is organizational rather than statistical? A: All three, as EPAD's lesson is organizational.

title: Hierarchical model
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.3.1 Exchangeability and hierarchical models
text:
Hierarchical model. Also called: Bayesian hierarchical model, partial pooling. A model in which group parameters are draws from a common distribution with estimated spread, so that groups borrow strength from one another.

## What it is

Two groups are exchangeable if nothing we know distinguishes the rate of one from that of the other. That does not make the rates equal. It makes their joint prior symmetric. The hierarchical model treats the group rates as conditionally independent draws from a common distribution with unknown parameters. For binary data from $K$ groups:

$$
y_k \mid p_k \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_k,p_k),\qquad \mathrm{logit}\,p_k \mid \mu,\tau_b \sim N(\mu,\tau_b^2),\qquad (\mu,\tau_b)\sim \pi(\mu,\tau_b).
$$

This is eq-hier. The spread $\tau_b$ controls borrowing: near zero the groups are nearly identical, and large $\tau_b$ leaves them nearly independent.

## Why it matters

Because $\tau_b$ is estimated, borrowing falls when the groups disagree. For a normal outcome the posterior mean is approximately a weighted average (eq-shrink), $\mathbb{E}[\theta_k \mid y] \approx \lambda_k \bar\theta + (1-\lambda_k)\hat\theta_k$ with $\lambda_k = \sigma_k^2/(\sigma_k^2+\tau_b^2)$, so a small group with a large $\sigma_k^2$ is shrunk more.

## In the book

The model is used in multicenter trials, where the groups are centers. In the eight-center topical-cream trial, centers had 5 to 37 patients per arm. It is also the basket trial model, and REBYOTA used it with dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study.

## Pitfalls

Shrinkage lowers total error only under conditions, and an individual group can be estimated worse. With few groups $\tau_b$ is poorly estimated and the answer depends on its prior: with four historical trials, half-normal priors with scale 0.5 and 1.0 can give quite different borrowing.

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to borrowing if the groups disagree? A: The posterior for $\tau_b$ moves up and borrowing falls.
- Q: Which groups are shrunk more? A: Small groups, which have large sampling variance.
R functions (bayestrials): borrow_basket_posterior, borrow_map_prior

title: Historical control
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.2 External and historical controls: the traditional objections
text:
Historical control. Also called: external control, externally controlled trial. A control group taken from outside the current randomized comparison, such as an earlier trial or registry, whose use ICH E10 and regulators treat with caution.

## What it is

In a single-arm trial the effect is judged against what is expected without treatment, and that expectation comes from a published control arm, a registry, earlier trials or routine care. ICH E10 calls this the externally controlled trial and lists it among five kinds of control group. Assignment is not randomized and the controls may be nonconcurrent, so the design is regarded as suitable only when the effect is large relative to the variability of the natural course.

## Why it matters

In a small or pediatric rare-disease trial the number of eligible patients may not support a conventional-size randomized control arm at all.

## In the book

Three mechanisms make an external control misleading: selection, time and measurement. Each gives a bias and not a variance, so a larger external sample does not help. Pocock (1976) listed conditions for combining historical and randomized controls: same treatment, same protocol, same institutions where possible, same prognostic factors and no unexplained outcome differences. FDA issued a draft guidance on externally controlled trials in February 2023, and the MHRA and EMA followed in 2025 with a draft guideline and a concept paper. Both stress pre-specification and fitness for purpose. Propensity-score methods decide how much external data enters, but cannot repair covariates that were not measured.

## Pitfalls

Matching on measured covariates removes only the measured bias, as the NSCLC case study shows. The FDA rare-diseases guidance reserves external controls for specific circumstances.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does a larger external sample not fix an external control? A: The three mechanisms produce bias, not variance.
- Q: Which source gave the classic list of conditions for historical controls? A: Pocock (1976).

title: History of Bayesian trials
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.9 A short history
text:
History of Bayesian trials. Also called: short history. The decision-theoretic view of trials is as old as the randomized trial, running from Thompson in 1933 to the FDA draft guidance of January 2026.

## What it is
The decision-theoretic view of trials is as old as the randomized trial. The book gives a short chain of episodes.

## In the book
- Thompson asked in 1933 for the probability that one treatment is better than another and proposed allocating patients accordingly.
- Wald's sequential analysis came from the wartime problem of sampling only as much as needed.
- Grundy, Healy and Rees posed the economic choice of the amount of experimentation in 1956, and Raiffa and Schlaifer's 1961 decision theory supplied the preposterior analysis.
- Anscombe and Colton observed in 1963 that a trial informs the treatment of a much larger population of future patients.
- Novick and Grizzle gave a Bayesian analysis of a four-arm surgical trial in 1965.
- Cornfield gave a Bayesian sequential test in 1966 and set out the Bayesian outlook in 1969.
- Berry restated the case for Bayesian interim analysis in 1985, and Lewis and Berry evaluated Bayesian designs by their classical operating characteristics.
- In January 2026 the FDA issued draft guidance on Bayesian methodology for drugs and biologics, and the EMA released a concept paper for consultation.

## Pitfalls
The objections deserve their strongest form. The prior can decide the answer, the type I error rate of a Bayesian rule is not controlled by the Bayes calculation itself, interim peeking can bias a trial, and a Bayesian design is harder to review. Whitehead's "case for frequentism" is the standard statement of the opposing view.

## Check yourself
- Q: Who asked in 1933 for the probability that one treatment is better than another? A: Thompson.
- Q: What did Lewis and Berry do? A: They evaluated Bayesian decision-theoretic designs by their classical operating characteristics.

title: Hochberg procedure
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.2.3 Hochberg
text:
Hochberg procedure. Also called: Hochberg. A step-up version of Holm that rejects at least as many hypotheses but needs independent or suitably positively dependent test statistics.

## What it is

Hochberg runs the order in the other direction from Holm. Start from the largest $p$-value and compare it with $\alpha$, the next largest with $\alpha/2$, and so on. At the first $p_{(j)} \le \alpha/(k-j+1)$, reject that hypothesis and all with smaller $p$-values.

It is a step-up version of Holm's step-down test and rejects at least as many hypotheses.

## Why it matters

It is more powerful than Holm, which matters when several endpoints are moderately significant.

## In the book

The price is an assumption. The guarantee holds when the statistics are independent or positively dependent, such as nonnegative correlation among one-sided normal statistics, which covers comparisons with a shared control.

Its step-up logic rests on the Simes inequality, and Hommel gave a more powerful procedure under the same conditions. The Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure is likewise controlled under positive dependence of this kind, which is why the book links the two.

In Table 10.3 Bonferroni, Holm and Hochberg all reject only E1 ($p = 0.004 < 0.025/6 = 0.0042$); the procedures separate only when several $p$-values are small. The key points of the chapter state it plainly: Holm uniformly beats Bonferroni with the same dependence-free guarantee, and Hochberg is more powerful but needs positive dependence.

## Pitfalls

- FDA's multiple endpoints guidance states the dependence conditions and does not treat Hochberg as assumption-free.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which direction does Hochberg order the p-values? A: From the largest, as a step-up procedure.
- Q: What does Hochberg assume that Holm does not? A: Independence or a specific positive dependence of the test statistics.
R functions (bayestrials): mult_hochberg

title: Holm procedure
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.2.2 Holm
text:
Holm procedure. Also called: Holm. A step-down version of Bonferroni that rejects everything Bonferroni rejects and sometimes more, with the same dependence-free guarantee.

## What it is

Order the $p$-values $p_{(1)}\le\dots\le p_{(k)}$. Compare $p_{(1)}$ to $\alpha/k$. If it is rejected, compare $p_{(2)}$ to $\alpha/(k-1)$, and continue until a $p$-value fails. Then stop and retain that hypothesis and all remaining ones.

Holm controls the familywise error rate in the strong sense with no assumption on dependence. It rejects everything Bonferroni rejects and sometimes more.

## Why it matters

Holm is a uniform improvement over Bonferroni at no extra assumption. It is the closed test that uses Bonferroni for each intersection hypothesis.

## In the book

In the six-endpoint example all three adjusted procedures reject only E1, with $p=0.004$ just under $0.025/6 = 0.0042$. Holm's next threshold is $0.025/5 = 0.005$, which 0.011 misses, so it stops.

The procedures separate when several $p$-values are small, for example 0.004, 0.005, 0.006 and the rest large.

In the ulcer illustration Holm and Bonferroni agree on the smallest $p$-value, and none of the other contrasts is stronger, so Holm does not rescue the finding.

## Pitfalls

- Plain Bonferroni may still be written into a protocol because its simplicity helps when many people must read it.
- Holm does not use the ordering of arms, such as recurrence falling as more stomach is removed.

## Check yourself

- Q: With six hypotheses, what is Holm's second threshold if the smallest is rejected? A: alpha divided by 5.
- Q: Can Holm reject fewer hypotheses than Bonferroni? A: No, it rejects everything Bonferroni rejects.
R functions (bayestrials): mult_holm

title: I-SPY 2
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.1 I-SPY 2: graduation by predictive probability
text:
I-SPY 2. Also called: I-SPY 2 trial, I-SPY2. A Bayesian platform for neoadjuvant breast cancer that graduates arms by predictive probability of success in a hypothetical phase 3 trial.

## What it is

I-SPY 2 is a platform for neoadjuvant breast cancer that has enrolled since 2010 and was later reconfigured as I-SPY 2.2. The primary endpoint of each arm was pathologic complete response (pCR) at surgery, with MRI tumor volume used to predict pCR for patients still in follow-up. Each therapy was evaluated in each of up to ten *signatures*, the subtype combinations that might become a regulatory indication.

## Why it matters

An arm graduated in a signature when its Bayesian predictive probability of success in a hypothetical 300-patient, equally randomized phase 3 trial reached 85%. It was dropped if that probability fell below 10% in all ten signatures, and no arm took more than 120 patients. This ties the decision to the confirmatory trial the platform feeds, which a posterior probability of benefit does not.

## In the book

A simulation with 50 patients per arm and a phase 3 of 150 per arm tested at one-sided 0.025 compares predictive and posterior probability for four phase 2 results. Randomization was response adaptive within a signature, with 20% held on control, and a time machine smoothed the control response over time. The platform also tested combination regimens against the shared control.

## Pitfalls

It is a phase 2 screening platform: a graduation is a decision to run a phase 3, not an approval, and its false positive rate was calibrated for a screening stage. Because allocation adapts toward responsive subtypes, the raw difference should not be read as the treatment effect.

## Check yourself

- Q: What predictive probability graduates an arm? A: 85%.
- Q: Why use the predictive scale rather than posterior probability? A: It accounts for the size and power of the phase 3 that follows.
R functions (bayestrials): platform_predictive_graduation

title: ICH E11A
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.10 Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
text:
ICH E11A. Also called: E11A, pediatric extrapolation guideline. ICH guideline on pediatric extrapolation, adopted at Step 4 in August 2024, requiring a plan that assesses similarity between adult and pediatric populations.

## What it is

ICH E11A is the guideline on pediatric extrapolation, adopted at Step 4 in August 2024. It is a framework for deciding how much pediatric efficacy can be inferred from adult or other source data, with a place for Bayesian methods in the quantitative part.

## Why it matters

The guideline asks for a *pediatric extrapolation plan* with three parts. The first assesses how similar the disease, the drug's pharmacology and the response to treatment are in source (adult) and target (pediatric) populations. The second describes gaps and uncertainties. The third plans the data to be generated in children, from PK and safety only (full extrapolation of efficacy) to a reduced efficacy trial to a full one. The more similar the populations, the less pediatric data are needed.

## In the book

Bayesian borrowing is one of the quantitative tools for the middle case, in which adult data inform the pediatric efficacy analysis. The guideline emphasizes that the evidence-based judgment of similarity comes first and the statistics second. The book's decision guide says to begin with the E11A plan and write the similarity judgment as a number ($\omega$, $a_0$ or $w$).

## Pitfalls

The guideline does not make the statistics the starting point. The similarity judgment should be defended with the pharmacology and the case in which it is wrong should be simulated.

## Check yourself

- Q: What range of pediatric data does the plan allow? A: From PK and safety only to a reduced efficacy trial to a full one.
- Q: When was E11A adopted? A: At Step 4 in August 2024.

title: ICH E9(R1)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.4 ICH: the harmonized principles
text:
ICH E9(R1). Also called: E9(R1) addendum. The ICH addendum on estimands and sensitivity analysis, Step 4, 20 November 2019, which defines the estimand and five strategies for intercurrent events.

## What it is
E9(R1) is the Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis, Step 4, 20 November 2019. FDA labels its own publication of the document May 2021. It defines an estimand as "a precise description of the treatment effect reflecting the clinical question posed by a given clinical trial objective".

## Why it matters
It requires that "the targets of estimation are to be defined in advance of a clinical trial". It introduces intercurrent events, events after treatment initiation that affect the interpretation or existence of the measurements. A posterior probability is only as interpretable as the estimand it is posterior about.

## In the book
The pivotal protocol fixes the primary endpoint, the estimand with a strategy for intercurrent events such as rescue medication or discontinuation, and the primary analysis. The five strategies are treatment policy, hypothetical, composite variable, while on treatment and principal stratum.

## Check yourself
- Q: How many strategies does E9(R1) name for intercurrent events? A: Five.
- Q: When must estimation targets be defined? A: In advance of the trial.

title: ICH E9
al: E9; Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.4 ICH: the harmonized principles
text:
ICH E9. Also called: E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials. The ICH guideline on statistical principles for clinical trials, Step 4, 5 February 1998, still the foundation for randomization, blinding, analysis populations and multiplicity.

## What it is
E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials, reached Step 4 on 5 February 1998. It describes randomization, blinding, the analysis populations, the primary variable, interim analysis and multiplicity.

## Why it matters
After more than 25 years E9 remains the foundation. It says that all interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol, and that group sequential designs are the usual way to look repeatedly. On multiplicity it says the usual frequentist approach may necessitate an adjustment to the type I error.

## In the book
E9 mentions Bayesian approaches only briefly, in Section 1.2 and the Glossary, and does not elaborate them, so it neither prohibits nor privileges them. The document list gives it as Final (Step 4), 5 February 1998, covering randomization, blinding, the intention-to-treat principle, multiplicity and interim analysis.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does E9 forbid Bayesian analysis? A: No, it neither prohibits nor privileges Bayesian approaches.

title: ICH M11
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.3 Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
text:
ICH M11. Also called: M11, structured protocol. The harmonized structured protocol template and technical specification (CeSHarP), Step 4 in November 2025, into which a Bayesian design must be mapped.

## What it is
ICH M11, the Clinical Electronic Structured Harmonised Protocol (CeSHarP), reached Step 4 in November 2025.
It comes with a harmonized template and a technical specification, so protocols present the same information in the same place and can be exchanged in a format acceptable to regulators.

## Why it matters
Neither M11 nor SPIRIT 2025 is specific to Bayesian designs, so the practical consequence is a mapping problem.
The structured format is harmonized across regulators, which helps.

## In the book
M11 has sections where design and statistics go, and a Bayesian design has components the template does not name: the prior, simulation-based calibration and predictive probability rules.
The book places the prior with the statistical hypotheses and analysis methods, the decision rules with the interim analysis section, the operating characteristics with the sample size justification, and the detailed model and computation in the SAP.
The sponsor checklist asks that the protocol be mapped into the M11 template and SPIRIT items with the Bayesian components where a reviewer would look.

## Pitfalls
The test of a good mapping is that a reviewer who has read only the protocol knows the design is Bayesian, what the success criterion is and where the simulation report is.
A protocol that mentions Bayesian methods only in an appendix invites the first review question to be where the prior is.

## Check yourself
- Q: Where does the book put the operating characteristics in an M11 protocol? A: With the sample size justification.
- Q: Does M11 name the prior? A: No, the template does not name Bayesian components.

title: ICH
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.4 ICH: the harmonized principles
text:
ICH. Also called: International Council for Harmonisation. The body that brings regulators and industry together to agree guidelines, such as E8(R1), E9, E9(R1), E20 and M15, that member regulators then adopt.

## What it is
The International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use brings regulators and industry together to agree guidelines. A guideline reaches Step 4 when the ICH Assembly adopts the final text, and regional regulators then implement it. Step 2 is a draft out for consultation.

## Why it matters
FDA publishes an ICH guideline as guidance and EMA as a scientific guideline. Six documents shape the book: E8(R1), E9, E9(R1), E20, E11A and M15.

## In the book
- E8(R1), Step 4, 6 October 2021, brings in quality by design.
- E9, Step 4, 5 February 1998, is the foundation, and it neither prohibits nor privileges Bayesian approaches.
- E20 is a draft at Step 2, endorsed 25 June 2025, and the work plan targets sign-off in February 2027.
- E11A, Step 4, August 2024, covers pediatric extrapolation.
- M15, Step 4, January 2026, covers model-informed drug development.

## Pitfalls
Until E20 is final it binds no region.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does Step 4 mean? A: The ICH Assembly adopts the final text.
- Q: Does E9 elaborate Bayesian approaches? A: No, it mentions them only briefly.

title: Ignorability of assignment
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.9.1 Ignorability of the assignment mechanism
text:
Ignorability of assignment. Also called: ignorability, ignorable assignment mechanism. When assignment depends only on recorded data, the posterior for the effect can be computed from the outcome model alone, and randomization guarantees it.

## What it is
Let $d_i$ be the arm, $x_i$ the recorded covariates and $y_i$ the outcome. Rubin showed that the posterior for $\theta$ can be computed from the outcome model alone if the assignment depends only on recorded data. Strictly, $\theta$ and the assignment parameters $\phi$ must also be independent a priori. Then the likelihood factorizes:

$$
p(d, y \mid x, \theta, \phi) \;=\; \underbrace{p(d \mid x, \phi)}_{\text{assignment}} \;\times\; p(y \mid d, x, \theta),
$$

and the first factor drops out of the posterior of $\theta$.

## Why it matters
If assignment depends on something unrecorded, such as a doctor's impression, the factorization fails and the posterior can be badly biased whatever the prior. Randomization makes the first factor a known constant.

The book gives three Bayesian arguments for randomizing: Rubin's ignorability, the robustness argument of Kadane and Seidenfeld, and Berry's practical position. The Bayesian randomizes for credibility and robustness.

## In the book
Response-adaptive randomization needs one more step, since assignment depends on earlier outcomes. If the assignment probabilities are known and depend on $\theta$ only through the recorded history, they can be omitted from the posterior.

## Pitfalls
The Bayesian does not use the permutation distribution. What randomization buys is the factorization with a known assignment factor. Under confounding, more data concentrate the posterior around the wrong value.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does randomization do to the assignment factor? A: It makes it a known constant, because the coin ignores everything.
- Q: Why does the Kadane and Seidenfeld argument favor randomizing? A: It yields an analysis whose validity does not depend on one person's beliefs about unmeasured determinants.

title: Implied loss
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6 A test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss
text:
Implied loss. Also called: test as a Bayes rule. Every fixed-level test is a Bayes rule for some prior odds and loss ratio, which a trialist who fixes alpha has chosen without saying so.

## What it is

A test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss. The Bayesian ledger holds one number, the Bayes risk, which weighs the two errors by how likely each state is and how much each mistake hurts. The optimal rule rejects when $\mathrm{BF}_{10} > b$ with $b = \frac{\pi_0}{1-\pi_0}\cdot\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_0}$. A Neyman-Pearson most powerful test is a Bayes rule for some prior odds and loss ratio.

The implied Bayes factor threshold shrinks as information grows:

$$
2\log b_n \;=\; z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\frac{q}{1+q} - \log(1+q), \qquad\text{so}\qquad b_n \approx \frac{e^{z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2/2}}{\sqrt{q}} \to 0 .
$$

This is equation eq-implied-c.

## Why it matters

A fixed $\alpha$ hides the loss ratio. As trials grow, a fixed level behaves as if the prior odds on the null or the harm of a false approval were shrinking toward zero. In normal model the implied threshold satisfies $2\log b_n = z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\frac{q}{1+q} - \log(1+q)$.

## In the book

A posterior threshold of 0.975, 0.99 or 0.995 says approving a useless drug is 39, 99 or 199 times worse than withholding a useful one. The ratio is not statistical. It depends on the disease, and Isakov, Lo and Montazerhodjat find the best threshold differs by disease.

## Pitfalls

This is the point-null, two-sided calculation. It is not the benefit probability of the FDA criterion, and the two 0.975 thresholds are not interchangeable. The one-sided confirmatory rule is a different decision problem.

## Check yourself

- Q: What loss ratio does a posterior threshold of 0.99 imply? A: A false approval is about 99 times worse than a false rejection.
- Q: What does a regulator holding alpha fixed behave like as trials grow? A: As if the prior odds on the null were shrinking toward zero.
R functions (bayestrials): decide_lindley_table, decide_loss_ratio

title: IND safety report
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.5 Aggregate safety assessment
text:
IND safety report. The expedited report under 21 CFR 312.32 of a serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction, due within 15 calendar days, or 7 for fatal or life-threatening cases.

## What it is

Under 21 CFR 312.32 the sponsor must notify FDA and all participating investigators in an IND safety report of a suspected adverse reaction that is both serious and unexpected. The deadline is as soon as possible and no later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines the information qualifies.

An unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction is due no later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt.

## Why it matters

The regulation lists the evidence that suggests a causal relationship, among it an aggregate analysis of specific events that occur more frequently in the drug group than in a control group. It is a requirement and prescribes no statistical method for that analysis.

## In the book

The FDA guidance of December 2025 recommends a safety surveillance plan, aggregate review, and blinded individual assignments with unblinded aggregate review by a group independent of the sponsor's study team. Guidance recommends and does not require. ICH E2A supplies the definitions of serious, unexpected and related events.

The 7-day limit runs from initial receipt for a single interpretable case, whereas the 15-day limit runs from the date the sponsor determines the information qualifies. For events needing an aggregate analysis, the sponsor makes the determination once the analysis meets the criterion and then reports as soon as possible.

## Pitfalls

- No monitoring rule shortens or lengthens these limits.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which clock is shorter, and for what? A: Seven days, for an unexpected fatal or life-threatening reaction, from initial receipt.

title: Indirect comparison
al: tirzepatide chain; chained comparison; imputed placebo
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.12 Indirect comparison through a common comparator: the tirzepatide chain
text:
Indirect comparison. Also called: tirzepatide chain, chained comparison, imputed placebo. Estimating an effect against a common comparator by adding log effects from two trials, with a power-prior weight to discount the second.

## What it is

No trial compared tirzepatide with placebo. SURPASS-CVOT compared tirzepatide with dulaglutide and REWIND compared dulaglutide with placebo. On the log scale the effects add:

$$
\log\mathrm{HR}_{T:P}=\log\mathrm{HR}_{T:D}+\log\mathrm{HR}_{D:P},
$$

with variances adding if the estimates are independent (eq-chain).

## Why it matters

A guideline committee asks how much tirzepatide lowers cardiovascular risk against no incretin therapy. The chain assembles an answer no trial gives.

## In the book

SURPASS-CVOT gave a hazard ratio of 0.92 (95.3% CI 0.83 to 1.01) and REWIND 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.99). At $a_0=1$ the chain gives 0.81 with interval 0.70 to 0.94. Dividing the REWIND variance by $a_0$ widens the interval to 0.67 to 0.98 at $a_0=0.5$ and 0.63 to 1.04 at $a_0=0.25$, so the benefit survives halving the weight but not quartering it. A published analysis used propensity-score adjustment to select 2055 of 9901 REWIND participants and found a hazard ratio of 0.72 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.94).

## Pitfalls

The chain assumes the dulaglutide effect in REWIND holds in the SURPASS-CVOT population, and the populations differ. The discount widens the interval and leaves the center, so it is the wrong correction if the effect differs. Neither analysis is a randomized comparison with placebo, and it supports a label discussion, not a primary efficacy claim.

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict the chained hazard ratio from 0.92 and 0.88. A: About 0.81.
- Q: What does lowering $a_0$ do to the estimate? A: Nothing, it only widens the interval.

title: Information fraction
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.5 Spending functions and the information fraction
text:
Information fraction. Also called: information time. The share of the planned total information that has accrued at an interim look, such as events observed over events planned.

## What it is

The information fraction is $t = n I / (N_{\max} I)$, the share of the planned total information that has accrued.

For a time-to-event endpoint, $t$ is the number of events observed divided by the number planned. For a binary endpoint with equal arms it is the fraction of the planned patients with outcome data. The final analysis is at $t = 1$.

## Why it matters

Real trials do not look at exact multiples of one quarter. A DMC meeting scheduled for the first Tuesday of a quarter may find 47 percent of the planned events, not 50, and a boundary computed for a $t$ that did not occur is wrong.

## In the book

Lan-DeMets spending computes the boundary at each look from the realized information fraction. Four looks planned at $t = 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1$ have an O'Brien-Fleming-type boundary of 2.68 at the second look. If the second look takes place at $t = 0.55$, that boundary becomes 2.82 and the later ones move slightly.

## Pitfalls

- The timing of looks must not depend on the observed treatment effect.
- A trial that stops short of its planned size must decide in the protocol whether the remaining alpha is spent at the last look held.

## Check yourself

- Q: What is $t$ for an event-driven trial when half of the planned events have been observed? A: One half, events observed over events planned.
- Q: May the look be moved because the interim effect looks good? A: No, timing must not depend on the observed effect.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_power, gs_spending_boundary

title: Intention to treat
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.8.1 The ITT principle
text:
Intention to treat. Also called: ITT, ITT principle. Analyze every randomized patient in the arm they were assigned to, whatever happened afterward, so the groups remain the ones the coin created.

## What it is
The intention-to-treat (ITT) principle says to analyze every patient in the arm they were randomized to, whatever happened afterward. ICH E9 section 5.2.1 says the primary analysis should include all randomized subjects, and that preserving the initial randomization in analysis is important in preventing bias.

A patient assigned to the drug who never took a pill is still analyzed as a drug patient.

## Why it matters
After randomization, patients stop the drug, take rescue medication, move away or die of something else. Dropping or moving them means the arms are no longer the groups the coin created.

## In the book
The drug adds 10 percentage points to recovery for anyone who takes it. About 15 percent of the drug arm stops early, more often the sicker patients. Three analyses were compared on 4,000 patients in each of 300 trials: ITT, per-protocol and as-treated.

ITT is diluted: it estimates the effect of assigning the drug. The per-protocol and as-treated analyses remove or reshuffle exactly the patients who differ in prognosis, and exceed what the drug does.

ITT corresponds in spirit to the treatment-policy strategy of the Estimand framework.

## Pitfalls
Neither bias can be seen in the data of a single trial. A per-protocol analysis is not among the five ICH E9(R1) strategies, because it drops patients on a post-randomization event.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is the ITT estimate smaller than the drug's effect in those who take it? A: About one in seven did not take it, so ITT estimates the effect of assignment.
- Q: Does a per-protocol analysis err toward or away from the truth in the book's simulation? A: Above the truth, since the stoppers differ in prognosis.

title: Intercurrent event
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.8.2 Estimands and intercurrent events
text:
Intercurrent event. An event after treatment starts, such as stopping the drug, rescue medication, switching or death, that affects the interpretation or existence of the measurements.

## What it is
Intercurrent events are events after treatment initiation that affect either the interpretation or the existence of the measurements. Examples are stopping the drug, taking rescue medication, switching treatment and death before the endpoint.

## Why it matters
Each one needs an explicit strategy, written into the Estimand. The addendum names five.

- Treatment policy: effect of being assigned the drug, with whatever follows.
- Hypothetical: effect if the event had not happened.
- Composite variable: effect on a combined outcome.
- While on treatment: effect up to the event.
- Principal stratum: effect in patients who would not have the event.

## In the book
The drug-discontinuation event of the ITT simulation illustrates the strategies. Treatment policy uses the outcome regardless of the event. The composite strategy counts stopping as failure.

For a Bayesian analysis under treatment policy, the model is fit to all randomized patients by arm. This requires the outcome to remain defined after the event, and terminal events such as death may need another strategy.

## Pitfalls
The hypothetical strategy needs a submodel for the unobserved outcome, with priors on the unidentifiable part, and this deserves a sensitivity analysis because the data cannot correct it.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which two strategies compare the groups the coin made? A: Treatment policy and composite variable.
- Q: Why does the hypothetical strategy need sensitivity analysis? A: It rests on a model for what would have happened, and the data cannot correct its prior.

title: Interim analysis
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.2 Why repeated testing at a fixed level fails
text:
Interim analysis. Also called: repeated testing, interim look. Any analysis comparing arms on efficacy or safety before formal completion, which inflates the type I error if each look uses a fixed level.

## What it is

ICH E9 defines an interim analysis as any analysis intended to compare arms on efficacy or safety before formal completion. Interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol.

## Why it matters

Suppose a committee reviews the data $K$ times and declares success each time $Z > 1.96$. The chance that at least one statistic exceeds 1.96 is larger than 0.025, and it increases with $K$. Armitage and colleagues quantified this.

Two equally spaced looks take the false positive rate from 2.5% to about 4.2%. Four unadjusted looks at 1.96 give a type I error of 0.0631, more than two and a half times the nominal 0.025.

## In the book

The inflation does not come from a flaw in the data. "Was $Z$ large at any of the looks" is a different event from "was $Z$ large at the end", and the null distribution computed for the second is the wrong one for the first.

A committee that reviewed the data continuously at a fixed level would eventually see $Z$ exceed 1.96 with probability one, by the law of the iterated logarithm. The rule that turns the data into a decision is part of the experiment, and the error rate belongs to the rule.

## Pitfalls

- Looking is not free for the posterior, but it is for the error rate: a Bayesian rule perfectly calibrated under the prior can still reject a true null far above 2.5%.
- A DMC that reviews safety without an efficacy comparison does not touch alpha at all.

title: Interim analysis
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.2 Why repeated testing at a fixed level fails
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to the false positive rate with two equally spaced looks at 1.96? A: It rises from 2.5% to about 4.2%.
- Q: Does continuous monitoring at a fixed cutoff ever stop being a problem? A: No, the cutoff is eventually crossed with probability one.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_power, gs_naive_inflation

title: Jeffreys scale
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.5 The Jeffreys table, in terms of $q$
text:
Jeffreys scale. Also called: Jeffreys table. Jeffreys' criterion that the evidence bar for a normal mean grows with the sample size, restated in terms of the prior information q.

## What it is

Jeffreys derived the growth of the bar for a normal mean with the Cauchy prior he recommended on invariance grounds. To leading order in $n$ the Bayes factor in favor of the null is $K = \sqrt{\pi n/2}\,\exp(-t^2/2)$, which falls through one at $t_{\mathrm{crit}} = \sqrt{\log(\pi n/2)}$. Kass and Raftery give the scale on which Bayes factors are usually read.

## Why it matters

The table restates the criterion in terms of $q$ and sets it beside the exact bar of the normal-mixture rule, which the rest of the chapter uses.

## In the book

This is a large-information approximation, not an identity. Evaluated exactly, the Cauchy Bayes factor at $t_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is not one at small $n$. At $q = 10$ the two bars in the table are approximately 1.66 and 1.62.

## Pitfalls

Two cautions. The bar is a function of the prior scale through $q$, not of $n$ alone. With $\tau = 0.25$ the rows read at $q = n/16$ and the crossing with 1.96 arrives at the thousands of events. The statement that the fixed level is too lenient beyond a phase I cohort holds only for a unit-information prior. Second, the calculation prices a point null, and against an interval null the bar depends on the interval and priors chosen.

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the Jeffreys bar depend on n alone? A: No, it depends on the prior scale through $q$.
- Q: Is $t_{\mathrm{crit}} = \sqrt{\log(\pi n/2)}$ exact? A: No, it is a large-information approximation.
R functions (bayestrials): decide_jeffreys_table

title: Kaplan-Meier estimator
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.1 The traditional analysis
text:
Kaplan-Meier estimator. Also called: Kaplan and Meier. A model-free estimate of the survival function that handles censoring, and the curve every trial report draws.

## What it is
The Kaplan-Meier estimate of $S(t)$ handles censoring without a model. It is the curve every trial report draws.

## Why it matters
It displays the data before any treatment comparison. The comparison itself uses the log-rank test or the Cox model.

## In the book
The Fleming-Harrington weights use the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate: each event time is weighted by $S(t)^\rho\{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma$. Survival curves in the book's scenarios overlap or cross early and separate late under a delayed effect.

## Pitfalls
Censoring must be noninformative for the likelihood results the book gives. A single curve difference may hide a changing hazard ratio.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the estimator need a parametric model? A: No.
- Q: What happens to patients still event-free at cutoff? A: They are censored.
R functions (bayestrials): surv_pwexp_S

title: Keyboard design
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.3 The other interval designs: mTPI, mTPI-2 and Keyboard
text:
Keyboard design. A model-assisted phase 1 design that lays equal-width keys over the DLT-rate axis and moves toward the key with the highest posterior probability.

## What it is
The Keyboard design of Yan and colleagues lays equal-width keys, each as wide as the target interval, over the DLT-rate axis. It recommends the move toward the key with the highest posterior probability.

## Why it matters
Like BOIN and mTPI, its decisions are printed as a table by number of DLTs and number treated, so the logic can be checked by hand.

## In the book
The book mentions Keyboard alongside mTPI and mTPI-2 and does not simulate it. Which design to choose is an empirical question, and the evidence is simulation. Published comparisons looked at accuracy, safety and reliability of several newer phase 1 designs.

## Pitfalls
Those comparisons are in stated scenarios at stated sample sizes. The protocol should report the chosen design's own operating characteristics in scenarios that include a badly placed target.

## Check yourself
- Q: How wide is each key? A: As wide as the target interval.

title: Kolmogorov complexity
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.6.1 Randomness as incompressibility
text:
Kolmogorov complexity. Also called: randomness as incompressibility. The length of the shortest program that outputs a string; a string is random if it cannot be described by anything much shorter than itself.

## What it is
Compare 0101010101... with a string from coin tosses. The first can be described in a few words, "repeat 01". The second cannot be described more briefly than by writing it out. Kolmogorov turned this into a definition: a string is random if it cannot be described by anything much shorter than itself.

Formally, the complexity of a string is the length of the shortest computer program that outputs it.

## Why it matters
Randomness in this sense belongs to a sequence, not a procedure, and no finite sequence can be certified random because Kolmogorov complexity cannot be computed. A trialist can only apply tests.

A sequence from a pseudo-random generator and a seed has low complexity by definition. That is not a flaw: what matters is that nobody can predict it without the seed. This is why the seed belongs in the sealed randomization specification.

## In the book
A compression experiment used an everyday compressor in place of the shortest program. The alternation compressed to about 1 percent. The coin sequence compressed to about 0.18 of its size, with a floor of 0.125.

The bits of a one-line multiplicative generator, $x_{k+1} = 75\,x_k \bmod 65537$, were not compressed either. The compressor could not tell them from a physically random quantum source.

## Pitfalls
Passing a compression test is not a proof of randomness. The equivalence between randomness and incompressibility holds for infinite sequences whose prefixes all have high prefix-free complexity, not for the finite-string definition.

## Check yourself
- Q: Can a trialist certify a given schedule as Kolmogorov-random? A: No, the complexity cannot be computed.
- Q: What does a clinical trial need from its generator instead? A: Documented statistical quality, a recorded seed, and a schedule the enrolling staff cannot see.
R functions (bayestrials): rand_bits_lcg

title: Label revenue brought forward
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.4 Label revenue brought forward
text:
Label revenue brought forward. A modeled estimate of the sales an earlier cardiovascular label would add, because patent expiry is fixed; the book treats it as an upper bound on revenue, not profit.

## What it is
Patent expiry is fixed, so a cardiovascular indication reached earlier adds the same number of years of protected, label-driven sales.
The estimate multiplies sales by an assumed label share and by the years brought forward.

## Why it matters
It is the largest sum in the accounting and rests on the least.

## In the book
Novo Nordisk reported global Wegovy sales of DKK 58.2 billion for 2024.
The label share is not public, so the book assumes 10 to 25 percent, and converts at an assumed 6.9 DKK per dollar.
For REWIND, Trulicity revenue in 2019 and the FDA approval of its cardiovascular indication on 21 February 2020 anchor the analogue, with an assumed 10 to 20 percent label share.
The REWIND analogue assumes 24 months of linear enrollment and 85 months between registered start and primary completion.
In REWIND the all-trial median saving is zero, because fewer than half of the simulated trials cross, so the revenue figures hold only conditionally on the rule acting.
For the SELECT reconstruction, 2024 sales of about $8.4 billion, brought forward by the all-trial median saving of 2.2 years, give $1.8 to $4.6 billion.
For REWIND, conditional on the rule acting, the decision comes at 680 of 1,257 events (month 51, 2.8 years early), giving $1.2 to $2.3 billion.
The key points call the SELECT figure of order a few billion dollars of Wegovy revenue, an upper bound and not profit.

## Pitfalls
Approval, reimbursement and uptake would not all have moved forward by the full statistical acceleration.
The sales level, the label share and the exchange rate are assumptions.
Multiplying a crossing probability by a conditional median would not give an expected revenue.

title: Label revenue brought forward
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.4 Label revenue brought forward
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Is the figure profit? A: No, it is revenue, and an upper bound.
- Q: Why is the REWIND saving only conditional? A: The Bayesian rule acts in fewer than half the simulated trials.
R functions (bayestrials): label_revenue_forward, select_month_of_events

title: Large deviation scale
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.8.4 Wald's test and the large deviation ledger
text:
Large deviation scale. Also called: large deviation, large deviation ledger. The scale where ruling out a null at error alpha needs a fixed quantity of evidence, log(1/alpha), accruing at the Kullback-Leibler rate.

## What it is

Wald's expected sample size formula has three features that the book calls the large deviation ledger. The numerator, such as $\log\{(1-\beta)/\alpha\}$, is a fixed quantity of evidence in nats, set by the error levels alone. The denominator is a Kullback-Leibler divergence, the rate at which evidence accrues, linearly in $n$. The governing relation is $n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \log(1/\alpha)$, the Chernoff-Stein relation.

$$
\mathbb{E}_1[T] \approx \frac{(1-\beta)\log\{(1-\beta)/\alpha\} + \beta \log\{\beta/(1-\alpha)\}}{\mathrm{KL}(P_1 \| P_0)}
$$

## Why it matters

To rule out a null with error probability $\alpha$ requires evidence $\log(1/\alpha)$, and evidence comes at rate KL. It is a statement at exponential speed.

## In the book

Ville's inequality is Markov's inequality at a stopping time. For the exponential martingale, the first passage to $1/\alpha$ is the first time the cumulative log likelihood ratio reaches $\log(1/\alpha)$. Wald's identity then gives $\mathbb{E}[T_\alpha] = \{\log(1/\alpha)/\mathrm{KL}\}(1 + o(1))$.

The surcharge of the normal-mixture rule is this Chernoff toll: the bar $\log(1/\alpha)$ is fixed and evidence accrues at rate KL.

## Pitfalls

- The surcharge is a cost of this construction and comparison, not a lower bound for all anytime-valid procedures. Realizable boundaries with iterated-logarithm rates exist and behave differently.

## Check yourself

- Q: What is the governing relation of the ledger? A: $n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \log(1/\alpha)$.
- Q: What unit measures the fixed quantity of evidence? A: Nats.

title: Lecanemab phase 2b dose finding
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.5 Lecanemab: Bayesian dose finding in phase 2b
text:
Lecanemab phase 2b dose finding. Also called: lecanemab. A Bayesian phase 2b trial in early Alzheimer disease that missed its primary criterion yet identified the dose carried into phase 3.

## What it is
Study 201 of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease was a Bayesian phase 2b trial with five dose regimens and placebo, response-adaptive allocation, and interim analyses starting after 196 patients and then every 50.

## In the book
It identified 10 mg/kg biweekly as the estimated 90 percent effective dose, the dose achieving 90 percent of the modeled maximum effect. The trial did not meet its prespecified 12-month primary criterion: the posterior probability of at least a 25 percent reduction in decline was 0.64, short of the required 0.80. The selected regimen was carried into the phase 3 program.

## Why it matters
A design can fail its primary criterion and still produce the right dose, so the protocol should say in advance how dose-selection evidence will be read in that event. A prespecified Bayesian criterion that is not met is a result, to be reported as one.

## Check yourself
- Q: What was the posterior probability against the required threshold? A: 0.64 against 0.80.
- Q: What does ED90 mean? A: The dose achieving 90 percent of the modeled maximum effect.

title: Likelihood ratio
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.3.1 Likelihood ratios
text:
Likelihood ratio. The ratio of the density under an alternative to the density under the null, multiplied across observations, which is a test martingale when both are single distributions.

## What it is

When the null and the alternative are each a single distribution, the likelihood ratio $\prod_i q(Y_i)/p_0(Y_i)$ is a test martingale. Under $p_0$ the expected ratio of densities is $\int (q/p_0)p_0 = 1$.

## Why it matters

This is Wald's SPRT statistic. For a simple alternative it is the best possible bet in the sense of growth.

## In the book

The limitation is that it requires committing to one alternative. A bet on a hazard ratio of 0.70 pays badly if the truth is 0.90. The remedy is to average over alternatives, which gives the Mixture method.

## Pitfalls

- Committing to one alternative makes the bet fragile when the true effect differs.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is the likelihood ratio a test martingale under the null? A: Its expected value under the null density is the integral of $(q/p_0)p_0$, which is 1.
- Q: What is its main limitation? A: It commits to a single alternative.

title: Likelihood
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6 Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
text:
Likelihood. Also called: likelihood function. The probability of the observed data viewed as a function of the unknown parameter; the Bayesian and traditional analyses share it.

## What it is
The likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$ is the probability of the observed result under each possible value of the unknown parameter. In the diagnostic example, $\mathbb{P}(+ \mid D)$ viewed as a function of the unknown state is the likelihood.

The likelihood enters Bayes rule as the factor that multiplies the prior:

$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta')\, \pi(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta),
$$

This is equation eq-bayes.

## Why it matters
The traditional analysis uses the same likelihood. The maximum likelihood estimate is the value of $\theta$ at which $p(y \mid \theta)$ peaks, and a z test is a calculation on its sampling distribution. The Bayesian adds only the prior and the multiplication.

The likelihood principle says that, given the data, the evidence about $\theta$ depends on the data only through the likelihood function, not on the stopping rule or on results that might have been observed but were not.

## In the book
For a time-to-event trial with $d$ total events, the book uses the approximate likelihood $\hat\theta \mid \theta \sim N(\theta, 4/d)$ for $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$. It is an approximation to the Cox partial likelihood in large samples.

For a binary endpoint, the likelihood of $h$ heads and $t$ tails is $\theta^{h}(1-\theta)^{t}$, which has the algebraic form of a Beta density.

A protocol that specifies a likelihood without a prior has specified half of a Bayesian model.

## Pitfalls
Because the posterior depends on the data only through the likelihood, it is unchanged by the decision to look. The type I error of a stopping rule is a different matter, since it is a property of the procedure over repeated trials.

title: Likelihood
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6 Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Where does the likelihood peak for the traditional estimate? A: At the maximum likelihood estimate.
- Q: Does the likelihood depend on the stopping rule? A: No, by the likelihood principle the evidence depends on the data only through it.

title: Lindley's paradox
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3.2 Lindley's paradox
text:
Lindley's paradox. Also called: Lindley paradox. A fixed p-value does not mean a fixed amount of evidence: holding p constant while the trial grows turns a rejection of the null into evidence for it.

## What it is

Lindley, following Jeffreys, noticed that the Ockham penalty can turn a rejection of the null into evidence for the null. Take trials of increasing size that all end with a two-sided p-value of exactly 0.01, so $|Z_n| = 2.576$. The frequentist reading is the same each time. The Bayes factor is not, because the penalty keeps growing while $Z_n^2$ stays at 6.63.

## Why it matters

A fixed p-value threshold cannot mean a fixed amount of evidence as a trial grows. This is why very large trials sometimes find significant effects that are clinically trivial. The Bayesian remedy is to ask whether $\theta$ exceeds a clinically relevant $a$, not whether it is exactly zero.

## In the book

With prior $N(0, 0.25^2)$ and prior probability 0.5 on the null, at $n = 100$ the Bayes factor is 6.5 and the posterior probability of the null is 13%. By $n = 10{,}000$ the Bayes factor is 1.1 and that probability is 48%. At $n = 10^6$ it is 90%.

## Pitfalls

The paradox lives at sample sizes far larger than those of most confirmatory trials of a large effect, and with a vague prior on a point null. It also depends on the prior scale. Picking $\tau$ after seeing the data is the dishonest reaction.

## Check yourself

- Q: Two trials both give p = 0.01, one with 100 patients and one with a million. Which has stronger evidence against the null? A: The smaller one. At $n = 10^6$ the posterior probability of the null is 90%.
- Q: What does the Bayes factor do as n grows with p fixed? A: It first rises, then falls below one.
R functions (bayestrials): bf10_normal, posterior_null

title: Log hazard ratio
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.9 Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio
text:
Log hazard ratio. Also called: negative log hazard ratio. The scale on which a hazard ratio is modeled, with estimate standard error about 2 over the square root of the total events under 1:1 randomization.

## What it is
In trials with a time-to-event endpoint, the treatment effect is a hazard ratio and the Beta-binomial model does not apply. The normal-normal model works on the log scale.

For 1:1 randomization with $d$ total events, the log hazard ratio estimate has standard error about $2/\sqrt{d}$. Each arm contributes about $d/2$ events, and the variance is about $1/d_1 + 1/d_0 = 4/d$.

With $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$, so a positive $\theta$ means benefit:

$$
\hat\theta \mid \theta \;\sim\; N\!\left(\theta,\; \frac{4}{d}\right).
$$

## Why it matters
The logrank test is, to a good approximation, the z test $z = \hat\theta \sqrt{d} / 2$, and the number of events, not patients, is the sample size in both frameworks.

## In the book
With $d = 200$ events and $\widehat{\mathrm{HR}} = 0.74$, $\hat\theta = 0.30$ and the standard error is 0.141. The approximation is the standard route of Bayesian design in survival studies.

## Pitfalls
The Cox partial likelihood is only close to normal in large samples. The approximation is a modeling choice, and a final analysis that wants the exact likelihood can use a piecewise exponential model.

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the standard error of the log hazard ratio with 200 events? A: $2/\sqrt{200} = 0.141$.
- Q: Why use $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$? A: So that a positive value means benefit.
R functions (bayestrials): normal_update

title: Log-rank test
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.1 The traditional analysis
text:
Log-rank test. Also called: log rank test. The standard comparison of two survival curves: observed minus expected events in the treated arm, summed over event times.

## What it is
At each event time the log-rank test compares the observed number of events in the treated arm with the number expected if both arms shared one hazard, and sums the differences. It is the score test of a proportional hazards model.

## Why it matters
Most event-driven trials analyze with a log-rank test or a Cox model. When randomization was stratified, the test should be stratified on the same factors.

## In the book
Under a delayed effect the log-rank test loses power, because the early events it weights are uninformative about treatment. A simulation with 300 patients per arm and treated survival at 5 years of 0.57 in both scenarios compares a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 with a two-year delay then 0.583. Fleming-Harrington weights with $\rho = \gamma = 0$ give the ordinary log-rank test.

## Pitfalls
The Schoenfeld calculation assumes a single hazard ratio and would not warn about the loss of power.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does it lose power under a delayed effect? A: Early events carry weight but say nothing about the treatment.
R functions (bayestrials): fh_z

title: Margin synthesis
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.11.1 Margin synthesis
text:
Margin synthesis. Also called: synthesis method, retention of effect. A noninferiority analysis that asks for the posterior probability that the new drug keeps a stated fraction of the control effect, carrying the full historical uncertainty.

## What it is

Regulatory practice preserves a fraction $f$ of the control's effect against placebo, $\delta_{CP}$, estimated from historical trials as $N(d,s_{CP}^2)$. The fixed-margin approach multiplies the lower 95% limit of $\delta_{CP}$ by $1-f$ to get the margin. The synthesis alternative asks for

$$
\Pr\bigl(\theta_{NC}<(1-f)\,\delta_{CP}\mid\text{data}\bigr),
$$

the posterior probability that the new drug retains at least the fraction $f$ (eq-ni-synth).

## Why it matters

The fixed margin reduces the historical estimate to one conservative number, while the synthesis carries the full uncertainty. Both rest on the constancy assumption, and the synthesis makes it visible.

## In the book

With a hypothetical 10-point historical event reduction with standard error 0.02 and half preserved, the trial with estimate 0.01 and standard error 0.015 (upper limit 0.039) does not meet the fixed margin. The two answers differ because the fixed margin stacks two conservative operations. The synthesis is not automatically more lenient: for an estimate of 0.04 the retention probability is low. In the simple margin case with margin 0.04, a skeptical prior centered at the margin is the natural regulatory prior.

## Pitfalls

If care has improved and the control effect shrank, a power prior with $a_0<1$ only widens $\delta_{CP}$ and leaves its center. A shrunken effect must be modeled directly with an attenuation parameter and checked over plausible downward shifts.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the synthesis estimate? A: The posterior probability of keeping at least fraction $f$ of the control effect.
- Q: Does discounting by $a_0$ fix a shrunken control effect? A: No, it leaves the center where it was.
R functions (bayestrials): ni_synthesis, ni_posterior_table

title: Master protocol
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.2 Definitions: master protocol, basket, umbrella, platform
text:
Master protocol. Also called: master protocols, substudy structure. One protocol with several substudies that keeps trial infrastructure standing and lets questions pass through it, as basket, umbrella or platform designs.

## What it is

A conventional program builds a trial, answers one question and takes it down. A master protocol keeps the site contracts, database, randomization system, monitoring board and regulatory file standing and lets questions pass through. FDA's June 2026 draft defines it as "a protocol designed with multiple substudies, which may have different objectives and involve coordinated efforts to evaluate one or more drugs".

## Why it matters

The idea is not Bayesian. The frequentist STAMPEDE opened in 2005 and shows that a shared control and a standing infrastructure pay for themselves. The master protocol holds what is common: eligibility, endpoints, schedule of assessments, randomization system, statistical framework and governance.

## In the book

The treatment-specific part sits in a module, called an intervention-specific appendix, sub-protocol, substudy appendix or, in REMAP-CAP, a domain-specific appendix. It holds the dose, safety monitoring, exclusions and decision thresholds. The terms and taxonomy were set out by Woodcock and LaVange (2017). The three kinds are umbrella, basket and platform.

## Pitfalls

A master protocol supports a marketing application for each drug on the evidence of that drug's comparison, and the legal standard of substantial evidence is not lowered. The FDA 2026 document is a draft that recommends and does not bind.

## Check yourself

- Q: What belongs in the master document and what in the module? A: Common items in the master, drug-specific dose, safety and thresholds in the module.
- Q: Is a master protocol necessarily Bayesian? A: No.

title: Maximum tolerated dose
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.1 Why the MTD is a poor target for modern agents
text:
Maximum tolerated dose. Also called: MTD. The highest dose whose probability of a dose-limiting toxicity is acceptable, the target of classical phase 1 oncology trials.

## What it is
The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) is the highest dose whose probability of a dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) is acceptable. The acceptable level is a target toxicity rate, commonly 0.20 to 0.33, and the chapter uses 0.25. The true MTD in the book's scenarios is the highest dose with DLT probability at most 0.25.

## Why it matters
For cytotoxic drugs, both efficacy and toxicity were expected to rise with dose, so the highest tolerable dose was expected to be the most active one. The toxicity-only designs of the chapter all aim at this dose.

## Pitfalls
The MTD paradigm assumes that more is better until it hurts. That is a poor assumption for targeted therapies, immunotherapies and antibody-drug conjugates, where efficacy may plateau well below the MTD. A drug may be taken for months or years, and chronic low-grade toxicity can cause dose reductions that a short DLT window cannot show. A dose chosen as the MTD can then be both more toxic and no more effective than a lower one. The FDA's stated concern is that patients may be left on doses with more toxicity and no more benefit.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which dose is the true MTD in the book's scenario A? A: Dose 3.
- Q: Why can the MTD be the wrong target for an antibody-drug conjugate? A: Efficacy may plateau below it, and chronic toxicity may force dose reductions.
R functions (bayestrials): dose_true_mtd

title: MaxSPRT
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.5 Aggregate safety assessment
text:
MaxSPRT. Also called: maximized sequential probability ratio test. A sequential Poisson test for drug and vaccine surveillance whose log likelihood ratio is maximized over relative risks above one.

## What it is

Kulldorff and colleagues proposed a maximized sequential probability ratio test for drug and vaccine safety surveillance. With a Poisson count $c$ against an expected count $\mu_0$ under no excess risk, the statistic is the log likelihood ratio maximized over relative risks above one, $c\log(c/\mu_0) - (c-\mu_0)$ when $c > \mu_0$.

## Why it matters

It is the likelihood-ratio machinery of the e-value chapter with a fixed alternative replaced by its maximum. A signal is declared when it crosses a critical value calibrated for the planned surveillance.

## In the book
