Because the alternative is maximized, it needs a critical value from calibration rather than the $1/\alpha$ of an e-value. Surveillance of marketed products and vaccines is sequential in the Wald sense.

## Pitfalls

- A signal is a trigger or a hypothesis for review depending on what the safety plan states.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does MaxSPRT not use the threshold $1/\alpha$? A: It maximizes over alternatives, so its critical value needs calibration.

title: MCP-Mod
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.4 Dose-response estimation outside oncology: MCP-Mod
text:
MCP-Mod. Also called: MCP Mod, dose response estimation. A two-step dose-response method: a multiple contrast test over prespecified shapes, then model fitting and target-dose estimation.

## What it is
MCP-Mod combines a multiple comparison step with a modeling step. Before the data, the protocol names candidate shapes (linear, Emax, exponential, umbrella) with guessed parameters. Each gives an optimal contrast of dose means. The test of no dose-response is the maximum contrast statistic, with its critical value from their joint distribution, holding familywise type I error at one-sided 0.025. If a signal appears, the passing models are fitted and a target dose is estimated by selection or averaging.

## Why it matters
It is on FDA's fit-for-purpose list with a determination of 26 May 2016, the frequentist dose-finding method there.

## In the book
With five doses, 40 per dose and standard deviation 1, the critical value is below the Bonferroni value for four comparisons because the monotone contrasts are positively correlated. When the top dose returns to the placebo mean, the top-dose test has only its type I error rate, while the contrast test with an umbrella candidate keeps power.

## Pitfalls
The candidate set is prespecified, and a truth outside it loses power, the counterpart of the CRM skeleton choice. The test detects a non-flat dose-response, not benefit at some dose.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why use an umbrella among the candidates? A: A top-dose-only comparison fails when the top dose returns to placebo.
R functions (bayestrials): mcp_contrasts, mcp_power

title: Meta-analytic-predictive prior
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.6 Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures
text:
Meta-analytic-predictive prior. Also called: MAP prior, MAP. A prior for a new trial control parameter, taken as the predictive distribution from a random-effects meta-analysis of several historical control arms.

## What it is

The meta-analytic-predictive (MAP) prior of Neuenschwander and colleagues (2010) runs a random-effects meta-analysis of the historical control rates, using the hierarchical model (eq-hier), and takes the predictive distribution of the control parameter in a new trial as the prior. The predictive distribution is wider than the meta-analytic mean because it includes the between-trial variation $\tau_b$. The hierarchical model for $K$ groups is:

$$
y_k \mid p_k \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_k,p_k),\qquad \mathrm{logit}\,p_k \mid \mu,\tau_b \sim N(\mu,\tau_b^2),\qquad (\mu,\tau_b)\sim \pi(\mu,\tau_b).
$$

This is eq-hier.

## Why it matters

A MAP prior does not become more informative than the heterogeneity warrants, however many historical patients there are.

## In the book

Four illustrative historical control arms of 80, 100, 70 and 150 patients (400 in total) give a normal-normal model on the logit scale with a half-normal prior with scale 0.5 on $\tau_b$. The predictive distribution is converted to a Beta prior by matching mean and variance. The pooled analysis that ignores between-trial variation would claim an effective sample size of 402, while the MAP prior is worth far fewer patients. That difference is the number a regulator can ask for. The R package RBesT fits MAP priors by MCMC and approximates them by mixtures of conjugate distributions, while the chapter uses a simpler approximation from `bayestrials`.

## Pitfalls

A MAP prior is still an exchangeability assumption. If standard of care changed or the population is different, it is confidently wrong. The robust MAP prior adds a vague component for protection.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is a MAP prior worth less than the pooled count of patients? A: It includes between-trial variation.
- Q: When is a MAP prior confidently wrong? A: When the new trial differs systematically from the historical ones.
R functions (bayestrials): borrow_map_prior

title: MHRA
al: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.8 EMA and MHRA counterparts
text:
MHRA. Also called: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency. The UK regulator, which consulted in 2025 on a draft guideline for external control arms built from real-world data.

## What it is
The MHRA is the UK medicines regulator. It applies the same statistical principles as EMA, since both adopt ICH guidelines. Its document in the book is the draft guideline on the use of external control arms based on real-world data to support regulatory decisions.

## Why it matters
External controls are a form of borrowing. The draft parallels FDA's February 2023 draft guidance on externally controlled trials. The three regulators share pre-specification, control of false positive conclusions, simulation and integrity.

## In the book
The MHRA consulted on the draft in 2025. The document table lists it as Draft, 2025, relied on in the borrowing chapter.

## Pitfalls
It is a draft, so its status can change, and the book gives the status as of November 2026.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which year did the MHRA consult on external control arms? A: 2025.
- Q: Which FDA document does it parallel? A: The February 2023 draft on externally controlled trials.

title: MIDD paired meeting program
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.3 The MIDD paired meeting program
text:
MIDD paired meeting program. Also called: MIDD. An FDA program of paired meetings on modeling and simulation approaches for a specific development program, the procedural counterpart of ICH M15.

## What it is
The model-informed drug development paired meeting program offers paired meetings with FDA on modeling and simulation in a specific development program. Examples are dose selection, trial design simulation, and an exposure-response model supporting a labeling claim.

## Why it matters
It is the procedural counterpart of ICH M15. M15 sets principles for assessing model credibility, and the program is where a sponsor tests a particular modeling plan against FDA's reading. M15 defines model-informed drug development as the use of computational modeling and simulation that can integrate nonclinical data, clinical data and prior information.

## In the book
A Bayesian adaptive design with a model-based dose-response component can fall under both the CID and MIDD programs. The book's advice is to ask which fits the question. A dose that depends on a model points to the MIDD program.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which program handles the models that feed a design's decision rules? A: The MIDD paired meeting program.
- Q: Is the outcome binding? A: No.

title: Minimization
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.3.4 Minimization
text:
Minimization. Also called: minimisation, Pocock-Simon minimization. Each new patient is assigned to the arm that makes the total imbalance across several factors smaller, usually with probability 0.8, for small trials.

## What it is
Minimization is the method for small trials with many prognostic factors. Taves, and independently Pocock and Simon, proposed assigning each new patient in a way that depends on what has happened so far. Look at the patient's level of each factor, count earlier patients with those levels in each arm, and assign to the arm that makes the total imbalance smaller.

## Why it matters
It balances the margins of each factor, for example the number of women in each arm, but not necessarily the combinations. In the simulation it cut the imbalance in a known trait to a fraction of that under simple randomization.

## In the book
In its deterministic form it is not random at all, and anyone who knows the current counts can predict the next assignment. Pocock and Simon therefore assign to the preferred arm with probability $p$ above one half, 0.8 being common, and use a fair coin on ties. The function `assign_minimization` implements this.

The analysis should include the minimization factors as covariates, because the assignment is not independent of them. A Bayesian trial can use covariate-dependent assignments such as minimization without changing the likelihood.

## Pitfalls
Minimization does nothing for a hidden trait. The deterministic version is predictable.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does minimization use a probability such as 0.8? A: Deterministic assignment can be predicted from the current counts.
- Q: Does it balance combinations of factors? A: Not necessarily. It balances the margin of each factor.
R functions (bayestrials): assign_minimization

title: Minimum Bayes factor
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.4 How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value
text:
Minimum Bayes factor. Also called: calibrating the p-value, p-value calibration. A bound on how strongly any prior in a stated class can make the data favor the alternative, used to calibrate a p-value.

## What it is

Sellke, Bayarri and Berger showed that for $p < 1/e$ and a stated class of alternatives, the Bayes factor in favor of the null is at least:

$$
\mathrm{BF}_{01} \;\ge\; -e\, p \log p.
$$

This is eq-sbb. The class has a non-increasing hazard for $-\log p$ under the alternative. The bound is not a statement about every prior.

## Why it matters

It says something that does not depend on a particular prior, at the cost of being generous to the alternative. With even prior odds it gives a lower bound on the posterior probability of the null.

## In the book

A two-sided p-value of 0.05 corresponds at best to a Bayes factor of about 2.5 and a posterior probability of the null of at least 29%. So "95% sure" is at best "71% sure". At p = 0.01 the Bayes factor is at most 8 and the null keeps at least 11%. Only at p = 0.001 does it reach 53. In a worked trial with Z = 2.8 the bound allows at most 13.6 for $\mathrm{BF}_{10}$.

## Pitfalls

The bound does not replace a design-specific calculation, and it understates what a reasonable analysis would find. It should be quoted with its class. The proposal to tighten thresholds for discovery is controversial and does not apply to regulatory trials.

## Check yourself

- Q: What posterior probability of the null does p = 0.05 allow at the very least, from even odds? A: About 29%.
- Q: Why is the bound generous to the alternative? A: It asks which alternative in the class would make the data look best for $H_1$.
R functions (bayestrials): min_bf

title: Mixture method
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.3.2 Mixtures
text:
Mixture method. Also called: mixture e-value. Averaging likelihood-ratio martingales over a distribution of alternatives to get an e-value that does not commit to one effect size.

## What it is

If $L_n(\theta)$ is a likelihood-ratio martingale for each $\theta$ in the alternative, then for any mixing distribution $H$,

$$
E_n = \int L_n(\theta)\,dH(\theta)
$$

is again a test martingale, because an average of martingales with unit start is a martingale with unit start.

For a Gaussian trial with $X_i \sim N(\theta, 1)$, $S_n = \sum_{i\le n} X_i$ and $H_0:\theta \le 0$, mixing over a half-normal distribution with scale $\rho$ gives, with $A_n = n + \rho^{-2}$,

$$
E_n^{+} = \frac{2}{\rho\sqrt{A_n}}\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{S_n^2}{2A_n}\Bigr)\,\Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{A_n}}\Bigr).
$$

This is eq-evalues-mix.

## Why it matters

Mixing removes the need to commit to one alternative. The scale $\rho$ plays the role of a prior standard deviation on the effect and is a design parameter. Ville's inequality holds for the whole composite null.

## In the book

The mixture e-value is a Bayes factor: the ratio of the marginal likelihood under a half-normal prior to the likelihood at the null value. In the authors' sweep the integrated Bayes risk changes by only a few percent across $\rho$ from 0.10 to 0.32, so the threshold matters more than $\rho$.

An equal-weight mixture over $K$ prespecified subgroup analyses is a valid fixed-look e-value for the global null, but it loses to the Sidak maximum when the statistics are correlated.

## Pitfalls

- The fixed-look mixture has no time index, so applying its constant threshold repeatedly would eventually cross under the null with probability one.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is an average of test martingales a test martingale? A: An average of martingales with unit start is a martingale with unit start.
- Q: Which matters more for cost, $\rho$ or the threshold? A: The threshold.
R functions (bayestrials): ev_mixture, ev_log_mixture

title: Moderate deviation sample size
al: moderate deviation; moderate deviation sample size equation
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3 The moderate deviation sample size
text:
Moderate deviation sample size. Also called: moderate deviation, moderate deviation sample size equation. A sample size equation from the Bayes decision rule that replaces the fixed critical value by a boundary growing like the square root of log n, giving larger fixed designs.

## What it is

The Bayes-optimal boundary on the standardized scale is

$$
t_{\text{crit}} = \sqrt{\log n + C}\,\bigl(1 + o(1)\bigr), \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0/\pi_a}{\pi(\theta_0)\sqrt{2\pi/I(\theta_0)}},
$$

which is eq-md-boundary. Replacing $z_\alpha$ by it gives the sample size equation

$$
n\,I\,\theta^2 = \left(\sqrt{\log n + C} + z_\beta\right)^2 .
$$

This is eq-md-ss, solved by fixed-point iteration. The matching power function (eq-md-power) is

$$
\text{Power}_n(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\sqrt{nI}\,\theta - \sqrt{\log n + C}\right) + o(1), \qquad \theta > 0 \text{ for the one-sided benefit rule}.
$$ For a unit-information prior with equal prior odds $C = 0$ and the boundary is $\sqrt{\log n}$.

## Why it matters

With $C = 0$ the boundary exceeds 1.96 for every $n$ above 46. It is 2.63 at $n = 1000$ and 3.03 at $n = 10{,}000$. The result runs against the book's thesis: the fixed design is larger, not smaller.

## In the book

At $\theta = 0.20$ the ratio to the textbook size is 1.30, about 30% larger. It is 1.52 at $\theta = 0.10$ and 1.73 at $\theta = 0.05$. The extra patients buy a type I error that falls with $n$. For $d$ parameters the boundary is $\sqrt{d\log n}$, which is 2.63, 3.72 and 4.55 for one to three at $n = 1000$. The saving comes from monitoring, not from the fixed design.

## Pitfalls

Calibrated to 0.025, the fixed-sample Bayesian design needs the same sample size as the traditional one. Any stated $C$ must name its unit, events or information. The expression is asymptotic.

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the moderate deviation design need fewer patients than the textbook design? A: No, about 30% more at $\theta = 0.20$.
- Q: Where does the Bayesian saving lie? A: In monitoring.
R functions (bayestrials): n_md, events_md, n_fixed

title: Monte Carlo error in calibration
al: calibration noise; Monte Carlo standard error
cx: Chapter 14: Operating Characteristics by Simulation > 14.5.4 Where the calibration noise comes from
text:
Monte Carlo error in calibration. Also called: calibration noise, Monte Carlo standard error. The binomial sampling noise in a simulated rate, which also makes the calibrated threshold an estimate that needs enough trials and a fresh-seed check.

## What it is

The Monte Carlo standard error of a simulated rejection probability is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}$ for $B$ trials. The calibrated $c$ is itself a quantile of a simulated distribution, so it inherits this noise.

## Why it matters

A design calibrated on a small simulation can be miscalibrated on the fresh data that will decide the trial. A reported "0.0252 against a target of 0.025" with no standard error invites the question of whether it is a violation.

## In the book

At $p = 0.025$, $B = 10{,}000$ gives 0.0016, which is 6 percent of the target. With $B = 100{,}000$ it is 0.0005, and showing an error of 0.0250 within $\pm 0.0005$ needs about 380{,}000 trials. The experiment calibrates $c$ on $B$ trials with 30 seeds and evaluates each on 400,000 fresh null trials. In the null grid, an excess of a fraction of a point at the worst grid point was under two standard errors, so probably noise.

## Pitfalls

The validation estimate is unbiased, but the calibration estimate is not, because it was chosen to hit the target.

## Check yourself

- Q: How many calibration trials at minimum? A: At least $10^5$, and more near a boundary one must defend.
- Q: Why validate on a different seed? A: The calibration estimate was chosen to hit the target, so only fresh data give an unbiased error estimate.
R functions (bayestrials): oc_calibrate, oc_max_pp, oc_simulate

title: MRC streptomycin trial
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.12.1 The MRC streptomycin trial (1948): concealment before the word existed
text:
MRC streptomycin trial. Also called: streptomycin trial, MRC 1948 streptomycin trial. The 1948 Medical Research Council trial in pulmonary tuberculosis whose contribution was concealed random allocation in sealed envelopes, not the coin itself.

## What it is
The 1948 Medical Research Council trial compared streptomycin with bed rest against bed rest alone in acute pulmonary tuberculosis. It is the book's first example of the distinction between sequence generation and concealment.

## Why it matters
Hill, who designed the trial, used random allocation, as Fisher had in agricultural experiments. His chief aim was to prevent selection bias in the choice of patients for each arm. He paired it with concealment.

## In the book
- What was tested: streptomycin with bed rest against bed rest alone.
- Design feature: the allocation was determined from a series of random numbers and kept in sealed envelopes, so the admitting physician decided eligibility before knowing the treatment.
- Yoshioka documents how the random numbers and envelopes were actually used.

The lesson is that the contribution of the trial was not the coin but the concealment. A list the admitting doctor could see would have recreated the doctor-chosen arm of the confounding simulation. See Confounding by indication.

The regulatory descendant is 21 CFR 314.126(b)(4), which requires a method of assignment that minimizes bias.

## Pitfalls
The book reports the design, not an outcome comparison, for this trial. The point it draws is about process, which is a property of assignment and not of the mathematics of randomness.

## Check yourself
- Q: What was the real contribution of the trial, the coin or the concealment? A: The concealment.
- Q: Why did the envelopes matter? A: The admitting physician decided eligibility before knowing which treatment the patient would get.

title: mTPI design
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.3 The other interval designs: mTPI, mTPI-2 and Keyboard
text:
mTPI design. Also called: mTPI, mTPI-2. Toxicity probability interval designs that pick the next dose by the posterior mass of underdosing, equivalence and overdosing intervals.

## What it is
The toxicity probability interval designs divide the DLT-rate axis into an underdosing interval, an equivalence interval around the target and an overdosing interval. The first version is Ji and colleagues (2007). The modified form, mTPI, computes the posterior mass of each interval divided by its width and moves toward the interval with the largest value. The mTPI-2 design changes how the intervals are formed, in response to a weakness of mTPI that its authors frame as an Ockham's razor problem.

## Why it matters
As with BOIN, the protocol carries a table of decisions by DLTs and number treated, and the logic can be checked by hand.

## In the book
Which design to choose is an empirical question answered by simulation. One study compared CRM, mTPI and BOIN on correct selection, allocation near the MTD and an accuracy index.

## Pitfalls
Such comparisons hold only in stated scenarios at stated sample sizes. The protocol should report the chosen design's own operating characteristics, including a badly placed target.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does mTPI divide by the interval width? A: The posterior probability mass of each interval.

title: Multi-arm multi-stage design
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.3 The frequentist platform: multi-arm multi-stage designs
text:
Multi-arm multi-stage design. Also called: MAMS, MAMS trial. A group sequential platform design in which every research arm is compared with a shared control at each interim look, and arms that fail a pre-specified bar are dropped.

## What it is

The multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) design follows the logic of a group sequential trial with one change: at each interim look every research arm is compared with the control, and arms that fail a pre-specified bar are dropped while the others continue. The MAMS design for time-to-event outcomes, with stopping for lack of benefit on an intermediate outcome, was introduced by Royston and colleagues in 2003.

## Why it matters

Three features carry over to every platform: an intermediate outcome first, concurrent controls only, and new arms by amendment. Early stages use a lenient hazard-ratio cutoff that tightens, so arms with no sign of benefit leave at a fraction of the cost. The intermediate outcome need not be a validated surrogate.

## In the book

General MAMS methods calibrate boundaries through the joint distribution of test statistics across stages and arms to control a chosen error rate such as the pairwise or familywise rate. The cutoffs were derived under proportional hazards, and non-proportional hazards need an appropriate summary measure and delayed-effect simulations. Online error-rate control methods exist for hypotheses that arrive over time. STAMPEDE is the standing example.

## Pitfalls

A MAMS error calculation for a fixed family assumes the family is known, so for added arms the family must be chosen and justified.

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens at each interim look? A: Each arm is compared with control, and arms that fail the bar are dropped.
- Q: Is the Bayesian machinery required for a platform? A: No, STAMPEDE shows it is optional.

title: Multi-armed bandit
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2 Allocation as a bandit problem
text:
Multi-armed bandit. Also called: bandit problem. The problem of assigning patients one at a time among arms with unknown success rates, balancing treating the patient now against learning for later patients.

## What it is

Suppose two treatments have unknown success probabilities $p_0$ and $p_1$ and patients arrive one at a time. Each assignment treats the patient, which is the reward, and teaches us about the arm. Assigning the arm that looks better exploits what is known, and assigning the other arm explores. The problem is named for a row of slot machines with unknown payout rates.

## Why it matters

A trial that explores too little may lock onto the wrong arm, and one that explores too much wastes patients on the arm it already suspects is worse.

## In the book

The best policy solves a Bellman equation on the posterior state with $m$ patients still to treat:

$$
V(\pi_t, m) = \max\Bigl\{ \underbrace{m \max_k \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k]}_{\text{stop and treat}},\; \max_k \Bigl( \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k] + \mathrm{E}\bigl[ V(\pi_{t+1}, m-1) \mid \pi_t, \text{arm } k \bigr] \Bigr) \Bigr\}.
$$

It is solvable exactly only for small problems, so the book looks at two approximations: the Gittins index for the discounted infinite horizon and Thompson sampling. Robbins formulated the sequential allocation problem, and Gittins showed that with geometric discounting the optimal policy is an index policy.

## Pitfalls

The bandit objective is the reward to patients in the trial, which is not the objective of a confirmatory comparison. Villar, Bowden and Wason review these models in trial design and are frank about the obstacles.

## Check yourself

- Q: What are the two things an assignment does? A: It treats the patient and teaches us about the arm.
- Q: Why are approximations needed? A: The Bellman equation is solvable exactly only for small problems.
R functions (bayestrials): rar_alloc_probs

title: Multiplicity across arms
al: master protocol multiplicity; family of hypotheses
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6 Multiplicity across arms
text:
Multiplicity across arms. Also called: master protocol multiplicity, family of hypotheses. The question of which comparisons in a platform form one family for error control, with FDA not recommending adjustment across unrelated drugs.

## What it is

A traditional trial with several arms and one control usually controls the familywise error rate at 0.025 by Bonferroni, Holm or Dunnett's step-down procedure. A platform raises the question of what the family is. Five unrelated drugs sharing a control would never be put in a common family in separate trials.

## Why it matters

FDA "generally does not recommend the use of multiplicity adjustments to strongly control the probability of making at least one type I error across the multiple comparisons of different drugs". The expected total number of type I errors is the same in independent trials or one trial. The draft keeps the adjustment for several doses of one drug, combination components or several endpoints, with the family defined before the data.

## In the book

EMA notes that errors are correlated, that the chance of at least one false positive may fall while several rise, and that tightening each level would need thresholds stricter than Bonferroni, so it offers larger control groups. A Bayesian platform moves the question: each arm has a criterion $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$, calibrated by simulation. With exchangeable arms, shrinkage multiplies information by $1/w$, as in the table where each posterior standard deviation falls from 0.30 to 0.20. The multiple $1/w$ is an upper bound that treats the common mean as known, and an arm far from its neighbors is shrunk toward them.

## Pitfalls

Shrinkage across arms is most defensible for one drug class, doses or related subgroups, and is not a substitute for the multiplicity decision across unrelated drugs.

title: Multiplicity across arms
al: master protocol multiplicity; family of hypotheses
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6 Multiplicity across arms
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Which comparisons does FDA still adjust? A: Doses, combination components and endpoints of one drug.
- Q: What does the shared control do to the error count? A: Same mean, but errors correlate.

title: Multiplicity
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10 Multiplicity and Shrinkage
text:
Multiplicity. Also called: multiple comparisons. Multiplicity is the problem that every extra question a trial asks is another chance for luck to look like a discovery.

## What it is

Most trials have a primary endpoint, several secondary ones, a few doses, some prespecified subgroups and an interim analysis or two. Each added question is another chance for luck to produce a result that looks like a discovery. Multiplicity is the name for this problem; the procedures that control it are among the most settled parts of trial statistics.

The family is defined by the claims the sponsor may make, not by the number of tests the statistician runs. A statistician who runs forty tests but whose protocol rests the claim on one prespecified comparison has a family of one.

## Why it matters

A sponsor who reports the best of twenty results as though it were the only one asked has not told the reader how the result was found. A regulator who approves on it has accepted a risk that nobody measured.

## In the book

ICH E9 lists three sources: multiple primary variables, multiple treatment comparisons, and repeated evaluation over time or interim analyses. Keeping K analyses open and guaranteeing 0.025 for the best of them makes the trial grow by the factor $((z_K + z_\beta)/(z_1 + z_\beta))^2$.

With twenty independent tests of a useless drug the chance of at least one significant result is about 0.40.

Exploratory endpoints, safety endpoints and descriptive subgroup displays are outside the family because no claim is made on them, and the protocol should say so.

## Pitfalls

- Dividing alpha among co-primary endpoints is unnecessary and costs power, because success on all of them is tested at the full level.
- Reviewers will ask for the family, the procedure, the interim spending and the status of secondaries if the primary fails, all before unblinding.

title: Multiplicity
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10 Multiplicity and Shrinkage
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: A protocol says the claim rests on one prespecified comparison, but the analyst runs forty tests. How big is the family? A: One, because the family is defined by the claims.
- Q: Does keeping many analyses open cost patients? A: Yes, by the factor $((z_K + z_\beta)/(z_1 + z_\beta))^2$, about 1.48 for five analyses and 2.38 for a hundred.
R functions (bayestrials): decide_subset_cost, mult_simulate

title: Non-proportional hazards
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5 Non-proportional hazards
text:
Non-proportional hazards. Also called: NPH. A hazard ratio that changes over time, as with delayed or cure-type effects, which breaks the single hazard ratio summary.

## What it is
Hazards are non-proportional when the hazard ratio changes over time, so no single hazard ratio summarizes the treatment effect. Immunotherapy trials have taught oncologists that hazards need not be proportional. A treatment may do nothing for months and then produce durable responses in a minority. Curves overlap or cross early and separate late. One response is to change the estimand to the restricted mean survival time up to a horizon $\tau$ (eq-sv-rmst):

$$
\mathrm{RMST}(\tau) = \int_0^\tau S(t)\,dt.
$$

## Why it matters
The log-rank test loses power, and the Cox hazard ratio depends on how long the trial runs. No FDA or ICH document, to the authors' knowledge, sets a required method. A cross-pharma straw-man guidance treats the choice of test and the plausible scenarios as a design-stage matter settled by simulation.

## In the book
Three Bayesian responses: a piecewise treatment effect with a hierarchical prior, a mixture cure model, and the RMST estimand. With 300 patients per arm, a control hazard of 0.15 per year and the same treated survival of 0.57 at five years, power is 0.68 under a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 and 0.55 under a two-year delay, with 287 events in both.
FDA practice is to accept prespecified alternatives to the log-rank test as sensitivity analyses and to scrutinize post hoc ones.

## Pitfalls
Choosing weights or a horizon after seeing the curves invalidates the type I error. Agreement with the agency at a pre-submission meeting matters more than the method.

## Check yourself
- Q: Name three Bayesian responses. A: Piecewise effect, mixture cure model, RMST.
R functions (bayestrials): surv_nph_example, surv_pwexp_S

title: Noninferiority margin
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9.1 Where the margin comes from
text:
Noninferiority margin. Also called: margin. The largest loss to the active control that is acceptable, built from the control's historical effect over placebo and fixed before unblinding.

## What it is
A noninferiority trial with no placebo arm cannot show by itself that the new drug works. The comparison is informative only if the control's effect is known from earlier placebo-controlled trials and is assumed to hold now. The FDA guidance builds the margin in two steps. $M_1$ is the whole effect of the active control over placebo that can be assumed in the present trial, conventionally the conservative limit of a meta-analytic interval. $M_2$ is the margin actually used, preserving a clinically meaningful fraction of that effect, so $M_2\le M_1$.

## Why it matters
How much to preserve is a clinical judgment, and the margin should be justified for the setting and not read from a convention. The margin must be fixed in the protocol and justified before unblinding.

## In the book
Two ways to use the historical estimate are described. The fixed-margin approach sets the margin from the historical confidence limit and runs an ordinary test. The synthesis approach combines the historical and current estimates and carries both uncertainties into one test. In SURPASS-CVOT the margin of 1.05 did the work, and a margin of 1.00 would have been a superiority trial.

## Pitfalls
The scheme rests on the constancy assumption: the control's historical effect is the effect it would have in this trial. It cannot be checked within the trial. Assay sensitivity, the ability to tell an effective from an ineffective treatment, therefore matters, and poor adherence or crossover helps the sponsor.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which is larger, $M_1$ or $M_2$? A: $M_1$, since $M_2\le M_1$.
- Q: Does sloppiness hurt or help a noninferiority sponsor? A: It helps, by pulling the arms together.

title: Noninferiority trial
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9 Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin
text:
Noninferiority trial. Also called: noninferiority. A trial against an active control with the null hypothesis moved: the claim is that the new drug is not worse than a margin allows.

## What it is
When an effective treatment exists, withholding it for placebo is often unethical, so the new drug is compared with an active control. Let $\gamma = \log \mathrm{HR}$. For margin $M>1$ on the hazard ratio scale the hypotheses are

$$
H_0:\ \gamma \ge \log M \qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1:\ \gamma < \log M.
$$

This is equation eq-ni-hyp. The test is one-sided at 0.025, equivalent to checking that the upper limit of the two-sided 95% interval is below $\log M$. Blackwelder put the burden of proof on the claim of similarity for noninferiority.

## Why it matters
The answer depends entirely on $M$, a number the data do not supply. A sloppy trial pulls the arms together and makes any drug look noninferior.

## In the book
SURPASS-CVOT compared tirzepatide with dulaglutide 1.5 mg, with a pre-specified noninferiority margin of 1.05 for the upper limit of the 95.3% interval. The primary outcome occurred in 801 patients (12.2%) on tirzepatide and 862 (13.1%) on dulaglutide, hazard ratio 0.92 (95.3% CI 0.83 to 1.01). Noninferiority was established, since 1.01 is below 1.05, and superiority was not, since 1.01 is above 1.00.

## Pitfalls
A margin changed after the data are seen is not a margin. The traditional report does not give the probability that the hazard ratio lies below a given value.

## Check yourself
- Q: Can a trial win noninferiority and lose superiority? A: Yes, the two nulls differ.
- Q: Why was dulaglutide a legitimate control? A: REWIND had shown it reduces cardiovascular events against placebo.

title: Noninformative prior
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.3 Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors
text:
Noninformative prior. Also called: default prior, flat prior. A prior with a very large variance that adds essentially no information on its own scale, but is vague only on one parameterization.

## What it is

A noninformative or reference prior, such as a normal with a very large variance, adds essentially no information. For a normal likelihood the posterior is the likelihood, and the posterior probability that $\theta > 0$ equals one minus the one-sided p-value. In the 508-event example, a very large variance gives 0.994, which is one minus the p-value of 0.006.

## Why it matters

"Noninformative" is a statement about one parameterization. A prior vague on a parameter is generally informative about every nonlinear function of it. The FDA draft says no single approach is universally preferred, and that such priors are not invariant to transformation.

## In the book

Independent Jeffreys Beta(1/2, 1/2) or uniform Beta(1, 1) priors on two arms put 49 to 56 percent prior probability on a risk difference larger than 30 points. A prior that says "no opinion" about each rate says the drug is very likely dramatically effective or harmful. A vague $N(0, 10^2)$ on logistic coefficients pushes mass to the boundaries because the inverse logit saturates. A weakly informative default such as a half-normal on a between-trial standard deviation is common for nuisance parameters.

## Pitfalls

A flat prior is a choice with implicit commitments on every other scale. Compute what it implies about the estimand before calling it neutral. In a large trial with a normal likelihood the issue disappears.

## Check yourself

- Q: Under a flat prior and a normal likelihood, what is the posterior probability of benefit? A: One minus the one-sided p-value.
- Q: Why can independent uniform priors on two response rates be a problem? A: They imply a prior on the risk difference that favors extreme differences.
R functions (bayestrials): cmp_samples

title: Normal approximation to the posterior
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.1 The normal approximation and its posterior
text:
Normal approximation to the posterior. Also called: normal approximation. Turn a reported estimate and 95 percent interval into a normal likelihood on the log scale, combine it with a normal prior and read posterior probabilities at chosen thresholds.

## What it is
Let $\hat\theta$ be the estimate on the log scale and $s$ its standard error.
A reported 95 percent interval $(\ell, u)$ gives
$$
s = \frac{\log u - \log \ell}{2 \times 1.96}.
$$
With a normal prior $\theta \sim N(m_0, s_0^2)$, the posterior is normal with precision equal to the sum of the precisions and mean equal to the precision-weighted average.
$$
\frac{1}{s_1^2} = \frac{1}{s^2} + \frac{1}{s_0^2},
\qquad
m_1 = s_1^2\left(\frac{\hat\theta}{s^2} + \frac{m_0}{s_0^2}\right).
$$

## Why it matters
Write $\theta = -\log RR$ so that positive means benefit; then for a threshold $\theta^\ast$, $\Pr(\theta > \theta^\ast \mid \text{data}) = \Phi((m_1 - \theta^\ast)/s_1)$.
The prior is worth $s^2/s_0^2$ trials of the present size, so a prior with $s_0 = s$ counts as much as the trial itself.

## In the book
A skeptical prior is centered at no effect with enough spread that a large benefit is unlikely a priori, an enthusiastic prior is centered at the effect the trial was designed to detect, and a reference prior is flat.
The family follows Spiegelhalter and colleagues, and elicited skeptical priors have an earlier statement in Freedman and Spiegelhalter, with the CHART trials as the worked example.
A positive trial is convincing when it persuades the skeptic, and a negative trial when it discourages the enthusiast.
For ANDROMEDA-SHOCK the interval 0.55 to 1.02 gives the log hazard ratio and its standard error.
The book reduces SURPASS-CVOT and REWIND the same way, from published intervals.

## Pitfalls
The approximation is on the stated effect scale and the book's numbers are not replications of published odds-ratio analyses.
Ratios are reported back on their natural scale.

title: Normal approximation to the posterior
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.1 The normal approximation and its posterior
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: A prior has $s_0 = s$. How much is it worth? A: As much as the trial itself.
- Q: How do you get $s$ from a 95 percent interval? A: Divide the difference of the log limits by $2 \times 1.96$.
R functions (bayestrials): reanalysis_normal, normal_update

title: Normal-normal model
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.9 Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio
text:
Normal-normal model. Also called: normal normal model, normal-normal conjugacy. A normal prior and a normal likelihood on the log hazard ratio give a normal posterior whose precision is the sum of the two precisions.

## What it is
With prior $\theta \sim N(m_0, \tau^2)$ and the likelihood $\hat\theta \mid \theta \sim N(\theta, 4/d)$, the posterior is normal:

$$
\theta \mid \hat\theta \;\sim\; N\!\left(m_1, s_1^2\right), \quad
\frac{1}{s_1^2} = \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{d}{4}, \quad
m_1 = \frac{m_0/\tau^2 + \hat\theta\, d/4}{1/\tau^2 + d/4}.
$$

## Why it matters
This is the weighted average of the Beta-binomial case with weights given by precision. The data have precision $d/4$, a prior has $1/\tau^2$, and the prior's effective sample size in events is $4/\tau^2$. A $N(0, 0.2^2)$ prior is worth 100 events and $N(0, 0.35^2)$ about 33.

## In the book
A trial observes $d = 200$ events and $\widehat{\mathrm{HR}} = 0.74$, so $\hat\theta = 0.30$ with standard error $0.141$, $z = 2.12$ and one-sided p-value $0.017$.

With a flat prior, $\Pr(\theta > 0) = 0.983$, exactly one minus the p-value. With the skeptical prior of 33 events the posterior mean is 0.258 (HR 0.77) and the probability is 0.975. With the strong prior of 100 events it is 0.958.

## Pitfalls
The likelihood is an approximation, a modeling choice and not an exact result. It treats $\hat\theta$ as sufficient, which holds only approximately for a Cox model, and ignores the discreteness of event times.

At a threshold of 0.975 the first prior passes, the second only in the fourth decimal, and the third fails, so the prior must be specified before the data.

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the ESS in events of a $N(0, 0.2^2)$ prior? A: $4/\tau^2 = 100$ events.
- Q: With a flat prior, how does $\Pr(\theta > 0)$ relate to the one-sided p-value? A: It equals one minus the p-value exactly.
R functions (bayestrials): normal_update

title: NSCLC borrowing failure
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.14 When borrowing failed: the NSCLC case study
text:
NSCLC borrowing failure. Also called: NSCLC case study. A study in which a matched real-world control augmented with a fixed-weight power prior did not reproduce the randomized result in first-line lung cancer.

## What it is

Struebing and colleagues (2024) built a matched real-world external control arm in first-line non-small cell lung cancer and augmented it with historical-trial data through a fixed-weight power prior. They compared the result with the survival result of the randomized trial whose control arm it replaced. The augmented external control did not reproduce the randomized result.

## Why it matters

A power prior with a fixed discount lowers the weight of the historical data but does not change their center. Discounting does not remove differences between sources.

## In the book

If real-world patients differ from trial patients in prognostic factors that matching did not capture, the augmented control stays biased. Matching on measured covariates removes only the measured bias. The book uses it as the example to show a team that proposes replacing a concurrent control with a matched external one. The decision guide says to expect the lesson to apply when the only sources are non-randomized.

## Pitfalls

It is one case and should not be generalized beyond what it shows.

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict: does a fixed discount repair prognostic differences? A: No, it changes weight and not center.
- Q: What bias does matching remove? A: Only the measured bias.

title: O'Brien-Fleming boundary
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.4 O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock, and the family between them
text:
O'Brien-Fleming boundary. Also called: O'Brien-Fleming. An efficacy boundary proportional to one over the square root of the information fraction: early looks are almost impossible to cross and the final bar stays near 1.96.

## What it is

O'Brien-Fleming uses a critical value proportional to $1/\sqrt{t_k}$, which is $\Delta = 0$ in the Wang-Tsiatis family $b_k = c\, t_k^{\Delta - 1/2}$. Early looks are nearly impossible to cross, and the final critical value is close to the single-test value. As a spending function it is the first half of the book's equation (eq-spending, the second half is Pocock's):

$$
\alpha^*_{\text{OBF}}(t) = 2\{1 - \Phi(z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{t})\}, \qquad
\alpha^*_{\text{Pocock}}(t) = \alpha \log\{1 + (e - 1)\,t\}.
$$

## Why it matters

For a cardiovascular outcomes trial with an event-driven analysis and a durable commercial case, the final result should carry the weight of a fixed trial, so O'Brien-Fleming is almost universal.

## In the book

For four equally spaced looks the boundaries are 4.05, 2.86, 2.34, 2.02 (exact solution of the recursion, $c = 2.024$). Polson and Sokolov print 4.05, 2.87, 2.34, 2.03 from the rounded constant 2.026, and the third decimal is not something a protocol should hinge on.

The first look requires $Z > 4.05$, a one-sided $p$ of about $2.6 \times 10^{-5}$. The final look requires $Z > 2.02$, a $p$ of about 0.021. The unadjusted 0.025 at the end becomes 0.021.

The cost is about 2 percent more patients for 90 percent power if the trial runs to the end. When the treatment works the design stops on average at about 75 percent of the planned information.

As a spending function, $\alpha^*_{\text{OBF}}(t) = 2\{1 - \Phi(z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{t})\}$ spends about 0.0015 of the 0.025 by $t = 0.5$.

## Pitfalls

- A boundary does not fix the point estimate at stopping, and a design with an O'Brien-Fleming boundary is not immune to early-stop bias.

title: O'Brien-Fleming boundary
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.4 O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock, and the family between them
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What bar does the final look of a four-look O'Brien-Fleming design ask for? A: About 2.02.
- Q: What does it cost in sample size? A: About 2 percent.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_boundary, gs_expected_information, gs_power_drift, gs_spending_boundary

title: OCEAN(a)-Outcomes
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.8.2 What a Lp(a)HORIZON result does to OCEAN(a)
text:
OCEAN(a)-Outcomes. Also called: Lp(a)HORIZON. A running olpasiran outcomes trial used to show how a sibling trial, Lp(a)HORIZON, moves its probability of success, read as an implicit Bayes factor.

## What it is
OCEAN(a)-Outcomes (olpasiran, Amgen) is a randomized, double-masked phase 3 trial with 7,297 participants and a primary endpoint of time to coronary heart disease death, myocardial infarction or urgent coronary revascularization.
Its primary completion is estimated for March 2028.

## Why it matters
When an analyst moves the probability that a related trial succeeds from $p_0$ to $p_1$ after a sibling reads out, the analyst has implicitly applied a Bayes factor, the ratio of posterior odds to prior odds.
The formula is
$$B = \frac{p_1/(1 - p_1)}{p_0/(1 - p_0)}.$$

## In the book
Lp(a)HORIZON (pelacarsen, Novartis) enrolled 8,323 participants.
Novartis announced on 4 September 2026 that its primary endpoint was not met, and full results followed on 7 November 2026.
The full results reported a hazard ratio of 1.02 (95 percent interval 0.90 to 1.15) overall and 1.00 (0.87 to 1.15) among patients with Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL.
On a flat-prior normal approximation, a 10 percent or larger benefit is largely ruled out for pelacarsen at its depth of lowering.
The book could not confirm a published analyst estimate, so it uses an illustrative move from 50 to 20 percent, which is not a finding about any analyst.

## Pitfalls
HORIZON informs OCEAN(a) only to the extent that olpasiran's benefit is expected to track pelacarsen's.
A hierarchical model with the depth of lowering as a covariate makes that assumption explicit, which one revised probability does not.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does a drop from 50 to 20 percent imply about the evidence? A: An implicit Bayes factor, here an illustration only.
- Q: Does the HORIZON result decide OCEAN(a)? A: No, it helps only if the two drugs share how benefit scales with Lp(a) lowering.

title: Ockham penalty
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3.1 A Gaussian example with closed form
text:
Ockham penalty. Also called: Lindley information. The automatic charge a Bayes factor makes for a flexible alternative, growing like the logarithm of the information in the trial.

## What it is

The Ockham penalty is the charge a Bayes factor makes for an alternative that is flexible. Take the alternative $\theta \sim N(0,\tau^2)$, centered at no effect. For large $k = I_n\tau^2$ the Bayes factor reads:

$$
2 \log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;\approx\; \underbrace{Z_n^2}_{\text{fit}} \;-\; \underbrace{\log(1+I_n\tau^2)}_{L_n,\ \text{Ockham penalty}}.
$$

This is eq-ockham. The first term is how well the best-fitting alternative explains the data. The second is a charge for flexibility.

## Why it matters

An alternative that spreads its prior over a wide range gives most of it to effects the data rule out, so it predicts the data worse than a sharp alternative. The more information, the larger the wasted share, and the penalty grows like $\log I_n$.

## In the book

With $\tau = 0.25$ and $I_n = 400$ the penalty is $L_n = \log(26) = 3.26$. The Bayes factor reaches 1 only at $|Z_n| \approx 1.8$, a one-sided p-value of 0.036. Lindley defined the information in an experiment as the mutual information between $\theta$ and the data. For a normal mean it is $\tfrac12\log(1 + q)$, half the penalty. Each quadrupling of the trial adds about one bit.

## Pitfalls

The penalty belongs to a point null with a diffuse alternative. Against an interval null the penalties can cancel, and no general growth rate is claimed.

## Check yourself

- Q: If the trial quadruples in size, what happens to the information it delivers about $\theta$? A: It grows by about one bit.
- Q: What does the penalty do to the Bayes factor as $I_n$ grows? A: It lowers it, and the amount grows like $\log I_n$.

title: One-sided test
al: one sided test; 0.025; one sided alpha
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.8 One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
text:
One-sided test. Also called: one sided test, 0.025, one sided alpha. A test that counts only departures in the direction of benefit; regulators prefer a one-sided level of 0.025, half the conventional two-sided 0.05.

## What it is
A two-sided test counts departures from the null in either direction. A one-sided test counts only departures toward benefit. In the shuffle picture the one-sided p-value is the right tail and the two-sided is that tail plus its mirror image.

## Why it matters
ICH E9 section 5.5 asks the sponsor to "justify prospectively the use of one-sided tests" and prefers one-sided type I errors at half the two-sided level. With the conventional 0.05, half is 0.025. A one-sided 0.025 is the same bar as a two-sided 0.05, since both reject when the 95% interval excludes zero on the favorable side. The FDA draft Bayesian guidance of January 2026 uses this language.

## In the book
A paper reporting "p = 0.04, two-sided" for a helpful drug has a one-sided p-value of 0.02 and meets the bar; "one-sided p = 0.04" does not. The binary trial gives one-sided p-values of 0.014 (normal), 0.020 (Fisher) and 0.021 (randomization). The sample size formula uses $z_{0.025} = 1.96$ either way.

## Pitfalls
If the sponsor sees the drug ahead and then declares a one-sided test at 0.05, the type I error rate has doubled to 5%. A one-sided test gives no weight to harm, and a strongly negative difference can give a one-sided p-value near 1. Safety review handles harm.

## Check yourself
- Q: A two-sided p of 0.04 corresponds to what one-sided p? A: 0.02.
- Q: Where is harm handled? A: In the safety analyses and interim monitoring, not the efficacy test.

title: One trial with confirmatory evidence
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.2 The 1997 amendment: one trial and confirmatory evidence
text:
One trial with confirmatory evidence. Also called: one trial, 1997 amendment. A 1997 amendment letting FDA treat one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence as substantial evidence, at its discretion.

## What it is
The Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 1997 added a sentence to section 505(d). If the Secretary determines, based on relevant science, that data from one adequate and well-controlled clinical investigation and confirmatory evidence are sufficient, those data may be treated as substantial evidence. The confirmatory evidence may come from before or after the trial.

## Why it matters
The power is discretionary: it is FDA's determination, not a right of the sponsor. It has been used more often over time, especially in oncology, rare diseases and pediatric settings where a second trial is impractical or unethical. The permission is of the form "if FDA agrees", so the route goes through a meeting.

## In the book
Plans for one trial should be discussed with FDA before the trial starts. REBYOTA was approved on one phase 3 trial plus a Bayesian model that borrowed from a phase 2b study. Its observed posterior probability of superiority was 0.991, which clears the 0.9750338 threshold for one adequate and well-controlled trial and misses the 0.9993275 bar for one trial standing in for two, so the evidence counts as one adequate and well-controlled trial, not two, and approval rested on the totality of evidence.

The arithmetic behind the standard: two independent trials each at one-sided 0.025 pass a useless drug with probability $0.025 \times 0.025 = 1/1600$, while a single trial at 0.025 passes it 1 time in 40.

## Pitfalls
The thresholds in REBYOTA were case-specific evidentiary criteria agreed with FDA, not numerical standards set by the 1997 amendment. An informative Bayesian prior is a close cousin of "one trial plus confirmatory evidence", but FDA still evaluates its relevance, weight and contribution.

title: One trial with confirmatory evidence
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.2 The 1997 amendment: one trial and confirmatory evidence
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Who decides that one trial plus confirmatory evidence suffices? A: FDA, as a determination based on relevant science.
- Q: When should a sponsor raise the plan? A: Before initiating the single trial.

title: Operating characteristics
cx: Chapter 14: Operating Characteristics by Simulation > 14 Operating Characteristics by Simulation
text:
Operating characteristics. How often a trial design declares success or stops under assumed true effects: type I error, power, expected sample size, early stopping and bias.

## What it is

A regulator who is asked to accept a design wants to know how often it will go wrong and how often it will go right. The answers are the design's operating characteristics. For a fixed-sample trial a formula gives them in a line, and for a group sequential trial a short numerical integration does.

## Why it matters

For designs with response-adaptive allocation, arm dropping, borrowing or predictive stopping, a closed formula is usually unavailable. The operating characteristics then come from running the design many times against assumed truths, and the written result is the Simulation report.

## In the book

For a two-arm binary trial with control rate 0.30 and treatment rate 0.45, the fixed design needs 160 per arm. Its exact type I error is 0.0252 and exact power is 0.794. Adding looks at 40, 80 and 120 per arm with an O'Brien-Fleming boundary is still analytic, with no random numbers drawn.

For the four-look Bayesian design the book reports power, expected total sample size, probability of stopping early for success or futility, and the bias of the estimate at stopping.

## Pitfalls

Reporting only the type I error at the design null reports the easy half. The error must hold over the whole null space. A bias table is needed because the final estimate is taken at a favorable moment when a trial stops on good data.

## Check yourself

- Q: When can operating characteristics be computed without random numbers? A: For fixed and group sequential designs, where the answer is analytic.
- Q: Why does a Bayesian adaptive design usually need simulation? A: Because adaptations leave the standard normal setting and no closed formula exists.
R functions (bayestrials): n_binary, gs_boundary, gs_crossing_prob, gs_power, oc_simulate, oc_summarize

title: OPTIMIZER Smart
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17.3 OPTIMIZER Smart: what a fixed 30% weight buys
text:
OPTIMIZER Smart. Also called: OPTIMIZER Smart device trial, FIX-HF-5C. A heart failure device trial analyzed with a fixed 30% Bayesian borrowing weight from an earlier study, without which the success criterion was missed.

## What it is

The OPTIMIZER Smart System (cardiac contractility modulation, Impulse Dynamics, PMA P180036) was reviewed by an FDA device panel on 4 December 2018 and approved on 21 March 2019 for heart failure patients in NYHA class III with ejection fraction 25 to 45%.

## Why it matters

The pivotal trial FIX-HF-5C randomized 160 patients 1:1 and used a Bayesian model with 30% fixed borrowing from 229 patients with ejection fraction above 25% in the earlier FIX-HF-5 study. The endpoint was the change in peak VO2 at 24 weeks, with success at posterior probability above 0.975.

## In the book

With borrowing the posterior probability was between 0.977 and 0.989 under four ways of handling missing data. FIX-HF-5C alone gave 0.957 and 0.960 under two imputation models, 0.916 for the complete-case analysis and 0.911 with last observation carried forward, below 0.975 in each. The success of the device therefore depended on the borrowed 30%.

## Pitfalls

If the earlier study overstated the effect, the conclusion rests on that overstatement. The FDA device guidance expects simulated operating characteristics under such discrepancies. The fixed weight is the device analogue of a power prior with $a_0=0.3$.

## Check yourself

- Q: Would the trial have met 0.975 without borrowing? A: No, the posterior probabilities were 0.911 to 0.960.
- Q: What kind of borrowing is a fixed 30% weight? A: Static.

title: Escalation with overdose control
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.5 Escalation with overdose control
text:
Escalation with overdose control. Also called: overdose control, EWOC. A dose-escalation rule that picks the highest dose whose posterior probability of overdosing stays within a feasibility bound.

## What it is
Escalation with overdose control (EWOC) changes the criterion for the next dose. Instead of the dose whose estimated DLT rate is closest to the target, it chooses the highest dose for which the posterior probability of overdosing does not exceed a feasibility bound $\eta$. The bound often starts at 0.25 and is raised as the trial proceeds.

## Why it matters
A dose with some chance of being too toxic is not the one most likely to be chosen. This builds a patient-safety constraint into the decision and was an early attempt to give ethical control a formal expression.

## In the book
The Bayesian logistic regression model applies the same idea to interval probabilities of the DLT rate. In the worked example the admissible-dose bound is 0.25 on the probability of overdosing.

## Pitfalls
With either design the decisions rest on a posterior that depends strongly on the prior. The FDA draft on Bayesian methodology says the prior should be justified and subjected to sensitivity analysis.

## Check yourself
- Q: How does EWOC differ from CRM in choosing a dose? A: It bounds the posterior probability of overdose instead of picking the dose closest to target.

title: P-value
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.5 The p-value, defined carefully
text:
P-value. Also called: p value. The probability, under the null and over repetitions of the trial, of a result at least as favorable to the drug as the one observed.

## What it is
The ingredients are a null hypothesis $H_0$ (a zero average effect), a test statistic that is large when the data favor the drug, and the data. Then

$$
p \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{test statistic at least as favorable to the drug as the one observed} \;\bigm|\; H_0 \text{ true}\bigr) ,
$$

equation eq-testing-pvalue, with the probability taken over repetition of the trial. It answers: if nothing is going on, how often would luck look this good?

## Why it matters
Sloppy definitions drive misuse. A p-value of 0.014 does not mean a 1.4% chance that the drug does not work. It depends on the plan: the same 9 heads and 3 tails have different p-values under different stopping rules. It depends on how many questions were asked, and ICH E9 section 5.6 says multiplicity may necessitate an adjustment.

## In the book
In the simulated trial, about 1.0% of null reruns reach a difference of 0.15 or larger, and the p-values from the three methods range from 0.014 to 0.021. The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial gave P = .06 with a hazard ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.02), which is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect.

## Pitfalls
It mixes the effect size with the trial size. A large p-value is not evidence of no effect. The ASA statement collects these points and Goodman lists twelve misreadings.

## Check yourself
- Q: Is a p-value the probability the null is true? A: No, it is about the data given the hypothesis.
- Q: Why must interim looks be pre-specified? A: The p-value depends on the stopping rule and the number of analyses.

title: PANORAMIC
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.5 Pragmatic pandemic platforms: RECOVERY and PANORAMIC
text:
PANORAMIC. Also called: PANORAMIC platform. A pragmatic UK primary care COVID platform with a Bayesian logistic analysis whose molnupiravir comparison was a clear negative result.

## What it is

PANORAMIC took the pragmatic platform approach into UK primary care. It analyzed its primary outcome with Bayesian logistic regression using weakly informative Cauchy priors.

## Why it matters

Not every pandemic platform was an elaborate Bayesian adaptive design. RECOVERY was a large, pragmatic, open-label platform analyzed with frequentist methods, and PANORAMIC shows that simplicity and volume can do the work of a more elaborate adaptive design.

## In the book

The molnupiravir comparison randomized 25,783 participants between December 2021 and April 2022 to molnupiravir plus usual care or usual care alone. The platform's total of 26,411 includes other comparisons. Hospitalization or death within 28 days was about 1% in each group (adjusted odds ratio 1.06), a clear negative result. A platform that can enroll that many community patients in under five months shows that its value comes first from infrastructure and speed. The book contrasts it with RECOVERY, whose first major result was a dexamethasone rate ratio of 0.83 for 28-day mortality.

## Pitfalls

The book groups it with RECOVERY as evidence that a platform's value comes first from infrastructure and speed, not from adaptive machinery.

## Check yourself

- Q: What prior did PANORAMIC use? A: Weakly informative Cauchy priors in Bayesian logistic regression.
- Q: What did molnupiravir show? A: Hospitalization or death in about 1% of each group, adjusted odds ratio 1.06.

title: PDUFA
al: Prescription Drug User Fee Act; formal meetings under PDUFA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.1 Formal meetings under PDUFA
text:
PDUFA. Also called: Prescription Drug User Fee Act, formal meetings under PDUFA. The user fee law under which FDA commits to review goals and meeting timelines, and the August 2026 guidance defining six formal meeting types.

## What it is
PDUFA, the Prescription Drug User Fee Act, is the law, periodically reauthorized, under which sponsors pay fees and FDA commits to review goals and meeting timelines. The current commitments are in the PDUFA VII goals letter for fiscal years 2023 through 2027. The guidance *Formal Meetings Between the FDA and Sponsors or Applicants of PDUFA Products* (August 2026) withdraws the December 2017 guidance.

## Why it matters
It defines six meeting types: Type A, Type B, Type B (EOP), Type C, Type D and INTERACT. Type C is the usual route for design questions between milestones, such as a Bayesian analysis plan.

## In the book
- FDA responds to a request within 14 calendar days for Type A, Type B (EOP) and Type D, and within 21 for Type B and Type C.
- The meeting is scheduled within 30 days for Type A, 60 for Type B, 70 for Type B (EOP), 75 for Type C and 50 for Type D.
- A Type C meeting on a novel design takes roughly three months from request to answer.

## Pitfalls
Minutes are not a binding contract, but an agreement documented in minutes is persuasive.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which meeting suits a stalled program? A: Type A.
- Q: How soon is a Type C meeting scheduled? A: Within 75 days of receipt.

title: Pediatric extrapolation
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.10 Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
text:
Pediatric extrapolation. Also called: extrapolating adult data to children. Inferring pediatric efficacy from adult or other source data, with Bayesian borrowing as one quantitative tool after a judgment of similarity.

## What it is

Pediatric extrapolation uses source data, usually from adults, to infer efficacy in children. ICH E11A (Step 4, August 2024) asks for a plan with three parts: a similarity assessment, the gaps and uncertainties, and a pediatric data plan that ranges from pharmacokinetics and safety only to a full efficacy trial.
Pediatric trials are where borrowing is most often justified, because enrollment is small and withholding treatment from children is ethically difficult. The FDA Bayesian draft names pediatric extrapolation as a core use of an informative prior, with empagliflozin and linagliptin in pediatric type 2 diabetes as examples where Bayesian analyses were supportive.

## Why it matters

Undiscounted adult data would often overwhelm a small pediatric sample, so a prior centered on the adult effect with inflated variance is often more reasonable than pooling. Adult and pediatric sources can be related as equally relevant, exchangeable, linked by a bias parameter, or linked by a pharmacometric model.

## In the book

In the bias-parameter form the pediatric effect is $\theta_p=\theta_a+b$ with $b\sim N(0,\omega^2)$, and the sponsor's similarity judgment is the number $\omega$. A worked example takes an adult log odds ratio of $-0.5$ with standard error 0.08 and a pediatric estimate of $-0.35$ with standard error 0.30, under the mixture

$$
\theta_P\sim w\,N(\hat\theta_A,\,0.08^2+\omega^2)+(1-w)\,N(0,1).
$$

This is eq-ped-mix. With $w=0.7$ and $\omega=0.15$ the posterior weight on the adult component rises to 0.87 and Pr(benefit) is 0.98, against 0.88 for the trial alone. If the pediatric estimate were $-0.05$, the weight falls only to 0.75 and Pr(benefit) is 0.89, against 0.57 alone.

title: Pediatric extrapolation
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.10 Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
text:
## Pitfalls

The mixture is a weak safeguard in a trial this small: with a standard error of 0.30 the data cannot tell the components apart, so the answer is mostly the prior. Drift here means the pediatric effect is not the adult effect, and its range is a clinical judgment about physiology. Simulations should include scenarios where children respond less well.

## Check yourself

- Q: What is $\omega$? A: The allowed adult-pediatric difference, the sponsor's similarity judgment.
- Q: Which comes first in E11A, similarity or statistics? A: The evidence-based judgment of similarity.
R functions (bayestrials): borrow_pediatric_mixture

title: Permuted block randomization
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.3.2 Permuted block randomization
text:
Permuted block randomization. Also called: permuted blocks, blocked randomization. Patients are grouped in blocks, and each block contains an equal number of each treatment in random order, which keeps arm sizes balanced.

## What it is
Permuted block randomization fixes the arm sizes at intervals. Patients are grouped in consecutive blocks of, say, four. In each block two get the drug and two get control, in random order, and there are six possible orders.

## Why it matters
After every block the arms are exactly balanced in size, and at any moment the imbalance cannot exceed half a block. Both arms also have patients from each period, which protects against a slow time trend.

## In the book
Block length fixed at four is predictable. If the first three patients were drug, drug, control, the fourth must be control. A clinician who can see past assignments can use that to select patients. The standard remedy is to vary block length at random, for example blocks of 4 and 6, and to keep block sizes out of the protocol text.

Blocks do nothing for covariate imbalance: a block makes the number of patients per arm equal and says nothing about which patients. The "block" boxplots match the "simple" ones.

For permutation tests, the shuffle should respect the blocks. Ignoring them made the test conservative under a time trend: the empirical type I error was 0.011 for the unrestricted shuffle and 0.022 within blocks, against a nominal 0.025.

## Pitfalls
The price is predictability, especially in open-label trials or trials with unmasked packaging. Blocks help with arm size and time trends. For covariates, stratification inside blocks or Minimization is needed.

## Check yourself
- Q: With blocks of four, the first three assignments were drug, drug, control. What is the fourth? A: Control, which is why fixed block length is predictable.
- Q: Do blocks reduce imbalance in a known covariate? A: No. The block boxplots match simple randomization.
R functions (bayestrials): assign_block

title: Phase I trial
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.2 Phase I: is it safe, and at what dose?
text:
Phase I trial. Also called: phase I. The first exposure of humans to a drug, asking about tolerability, pharmacokinetics and, in oncology, the maximum tolerated dose.

## What it is
Phase I is the first exposure of humans to the drug. In most therapeutic areas it enrolls 20 to 100 healthy volunteers; in oncology it enrolls patients for whom standard therapy has failed. The questions are tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and, in oncology, the maximum tolerated dose.

The traditional oncology design is the 3+3 rule: treat three patients at a dose, escalate if none has a dose-limiting toxicity, add three more if one does, and stop if two or more do. It fits no dose-toxicity curve and so identifies a dose with little precision. Model-based designs replace it, for example the Bayesian logistic regression model. After each cohort the posterior is updated and the next dose is chosen subject to a cap on the posterior probability of overdosing.

## Why it matters
Phase I is a safety problem first. Phase I produces a posterior over the dose-toxicity curve that becomes the prior for dose selection in Phase II.

## In the book
In March 2006 six healthy volunteers in London received the first human doses of TGN1412 and two received placebo. Within hours all six who got the drug developed a cytokine storm with multiple organ failure. The doses were given within minutes of one another, so the first reaction could not inform the others. Staggered dosing is now standard.

## Pitfalls
A sequential design is a safety device before it is an efficiency device.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does the 3+3 rule use? A: Only toxicity counts at the current dose.
- Q: What did TGN1412 show? A: A design that cannot update between patients can be dangerous.
R functions (bayestrials): dose_three_plus_three

title: Phase 2 to phase 3 optimism
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.6.3 Phase II to phase III: why the design alternative is too large
text:
Phase 2 to phase 3 optimism. Also called: phase 2 selection problem. A phase 2 estimate that justified moving on is biased upward, so a phase 3 trial sized on it is underpowered and succeeds less often than its nominal power suggests.

## What it is

A drug is taken into phase III because phase II looked good. A design alternative equal to the phase II estimate is therefore biased upward, a trial sized on it is underpowered at the true effect, and the chance it succeeds is the assurance, not the 90% in the protocol. In a simulation the same selection inflates a prior centered on the phase 2 estimate.

## Why it matters

Planning on a shrunk estimate reports the probability of success the program will face, and the time to learn it is before the trial is funded. For a phase 2 estimate of 0.14 with standard deviation 0.10, a 90% power trial has assurance well below that.

## In the book

Zia and colleagues examined 181 phase III studies in advanced solid tumors. Of these, 43 used regimens identical to those in 49 preceding phase II studies. Twelve of the 43 (28%) were positive, 81% had lower response rates than phase II, and the mean difference was 12.9 percentage points. In a synthetic example, a flat posterior $N(0.30, 0.141^2)$ and a skeptical one $N(0.20, 0.115^2)$ give different optimal pivotal sizes, with the expected net present value flat from 400 to 800 per arm. The costs, US\$20 million fixed plus US\$0.1 million per patient, and a US\$1 billion value are invented.

## Pitfalls

The study concerns chemotherapy in solid tumors, and other areas differ. The 28% does not identify the fraction of ineffective treatments.

## Check yourself

- Q: What fraction of phase III trials repeating phase II regimens were positive? A: 28% (12 of 43).
- Q: Which direction is the bias in a phase 2 estimate that justified a phase 3? A: Upward.
R functions (bayestrials): decide_pivotal_optimum, decide_pivotal_table

title: Phase II trial
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.3 Phase II: does it work, and at what dose?
text:
Phase II trial. Also called: phase II. The phase where most drugs fail, asking whether the drug moves an endpoint at all and which dose to carry into Phase III.

## What it is
Phase II is where most drugs fail and where most of the value of a development program is created or destroyed. Phase IIa is proof of concept, a small study asking whether the drug moves a clinical or biomarker endpoint. Phase IIb is dose ranging against placebo, to choose the dose for Phase III.

## Why it matters
Bayesian methods have their strongest claim here, because the purpose is learning rather than confirming. The natural output is a posterior over the dose-response curve and a predictive probability that Phase III will succeed, not a p-value. The traditional design uses fixed-dose arms or a single-arm response test.

## In the book
ASTIN tested a neutrophil inhibitory factor in acute ischemic stroke. Patients were allocated adaptively among many doses and placebo with a Bayesian dose-response model, and the design had rules to stop for futility or efficacy. It found no effect and stopped early for futility at 966 patients according to the published report. A conventional group sequential design with a futility rule could also have stopped early.

## Pitfalls
A Phase III designed around the Phase II point estimate is usually underpowered.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does Phase II ideally output? A: A posterior over the dose-response curve and a predictive probability of Phase III success.
- Q: What was ASTIN's most valuable output? A: A fast, well-founded negative result.

title: Phase III trial
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.4 Phase III: confirming, and the regulatory decision
text:
Phase III trial. Also called: phase III. Large randomized, usually blinded trials that confirm efficacy and characterize safety, on which the regulatory decision rests.

## What it is
Phase III trials are large, randomized and usually blinded, designed to confirm efficacy and characterize safety in the population for which the drug will be licensed. They enroll hundreds to tens of thousands of patients and cost from tens to hundreds of millions of dollars. The traditional FDA standard is two adequate and well-controlled trials, or one large trial with confirmatory evidence.

## Why it matters
This is the stage at which the type I error rate is the contract with the regulator and at which interim analyses are governed by the strictest rules. A Bayesian criterion here is judged by its operating characteristics under a pre-specified design.

## In the book
In December 2006 Pfizer stopped ILLUMINATE, a Phase III outcomes trial of torcetrapib, after the data monitoring committee found an excess of deaths on the drug. Torcetrapib had been associated with higher blood pressure in earlier studies. The episode shows that off-target information from earlier phases belongs in the prior for Phase III, and that an interim analysis is as valuable for stopping for harm as for benefit.

## Pitfalls
The type I error rate is the contract with the regulator, so a Bayesian Phase III design must keep it through calibration or borrowing rules. The traditional design is fixed or group sequential at type I error 0.025.

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the traditional FDA evidentiary standard? A: Two adequate and well-controlled trials, or one large trial with confirmatory evidence.
- Q: What earlier information belonged in the Phase III prior for torcetrapib? A: Higher blood pressure seen in earlier studies.

title: Phase IV study
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.5 Phase IV: after approval
text:
Phase IV study. Also called: phase IV, postmarketing. Studies after approval: required postmarketing trials, surveillance of adverse events and confirmatory trials, where rare harms become visible.

## What it is
Approval is not the end of learning. Phase IV comprises postmarketing studies required or agreed at approval, observational surveillance of adverse events, and confirmatory trials for drugs given accelerated approval on a surrogate endpoint. Premarketing trials are often too small or too short to characterize rare harms.

## Why it matters
Postmarketing surveillance is a sequential decision problem in which the action is to warn, restrict or withdraw, and the cost of waiting is counted in patients harmed.

## In the book
Rofecoxib was approved in 1999 and withdrawn on 30 September 2004 after the APPROVe trial. In 2,586 patients with a history of colorectal adenoma it showed 46 confirmed thrombotic events on the drug against 26, rate ratio 1.92 (95% CI 1.19 to 3.11). VIGOR had earlier shown fewer gastrointestinal events than naproxen but more myocardial infarctions. A cumulative meta-analysis found a clear excess of myocardial infarction at the end of 2000.

Spontaneous reporting systems compare the observed count for a drug and event pair with the count expected under independence. The gamma-Poisson shrinker reports a posterior estimate, so an estimate from three reports is shrunk heavily toward the common distribution and one from three hundred is not.

## Pitfalls
Evidence of harm can be in hand years before action.

## Check yourself
- Q: How were the rofecoxib thrombotic events split in APPROVe? A: 46 on the drug against 26.
