- Q: Why shrink crude reporting ratios? A: They are unstable when counts are small.

title: Phase transition probability
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.9 A Bayesian reading of the phases
text:
Phase transition probability. The probability that a program moves from one phase to the next, or from Phase III to approval, which drives the cost of each approved drug.

## What it is
The book writes $p_{12}$, $p_{23}$ and $p_{3A}$ for the probabilities of moving from Phase I to II, from II to III, and from III to approval.

## Why it matters
Each transition probability enters the cost per approved drug. Programs that use biomarkers to select patients have higher success probabilities. A Phase II predictive distribution gives the probability that Phase III will succeed.

## In the book
Wong, Siah and Lo used over 400,000 trial records for more than 21,000 compounds and estimated that about 13.8 percent of programs entering Phase I eventually reach approval, and 3.4 percent in oncology. Over 2011 to 2020 the likelihood that a drug entering phase I was approved was 7.9 percent, and only 28.9 percent of candidates cleared phase II. Of 43 phase III studies that repeated the regimen of a preceding phase II study, only 12 (28 percent) were positive.

## Pitfalls
Raising a transition probability by advancing more compounds is not better selection. The case for predictive methods is that they advance the right ones.

## Check yourself
- Q: Do the published approval rates agree to the decimal? A: No. The book quotes 13.8 percent from one source and 7.9 percent from another, for different data and periods.
- Q: What did the 43 repeated Phase III studies show? A: Only 12 were positive.

title: Platform trial
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20 Master Protocols and Platform Trials
text:
Platform trial. Also called: adaptive platform trial. A master protocol that fixes the disease and infrastructure and lets drugs enter and leave over time under pre-specified decision rules.

## What it is

FDA's June 2026 draft describes a platform as a trial to "evaluate multiple drugs for one or more diseases, conditions, or disease subtypes in an ongoing manner, with drugs entering or leaving the platform". A platform fixes the disease and the infrastructure and lets the drugs change. The EC, EMA and HMA question-and-answer document defines it as a shared framework in which investigational products enter and leave at different times under pre-specified decision rules.

## Why it matters

A platform answers $k$ questions with one control group, enrolling $(k+1)m$ patients rather than $2km$. Saville and Berry simulated whole programs and found platforms found beneficial treatments with fewer patients and less time than a traditional strategy, under stated assumptions.

## In the book

Both frequentist and Bayesian platforms can accommodate new arms and share information, and both need a justified hypothesis family and demonstrated operating characteristics. The Bayesian platforms use a decision rule per arm calibrated by simulation, with optional hierarchical sharing. Governance typically has a single monitoring committee, an independent statistical center and an arm-approval committee.

## Pitfalls

Arms added later create the non-concurrent control problem. A platform survives its first arm only if governance is built for arms not yet known, and EPAD never opened an arm.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a platform fix and what does it vary? A: It fixes disease and infrastructure and varies the drugs.
- Q: How many patients does a platform of five drugs at 80 per arm need? A: 480, against 800 for separate trials.
R functions (bayestrials): platform_shared_control_table

title: Play the winner
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3 ECMO: the case every trialist knows
text:
Play the winner. An urn allocation rule that adds a ball for the treatment that succeeded, so allocation drifts toward the apparent winner; used in the ECMO trial.

## What it is

Zelen proposed the play-the-winner rule, and randomized versions followed. In its simplest urn form, start with one ball for each treatment and draw a ball to assign each patient. After each outcome, add a ball for the treatment that succeeded, or for the other treatment after a failure.

## Why it matters

The ECMO trial of Bartlett and colleagues used a randomized play-the-winner rule. As the urn drifted toward ECMO, one infant was assigned to conventional therapy and the other eleven to ECMO.

## In the book

The book simulates the urn with 12 infants and true survival 0.80 on ECMO and 0.20 on conventional therapy, against a fixed 6:6 trial analyzed by a one-sided Fisher exact test at level 0.025. Play-the-winner puts few infants on the control arm, and in a sizable share of trials at most one, which makes a comparison essentially impossible. The rule gave more infants the treatment investigators believed in, at the cost of the information the trial was meant to produce.

## Pitfalls

A rule that reacts to a few early outcomes can move allocation sharply on very little evidence, and an urn that has drifted toward a treatment that only looked best early takes a long time to correct. The pattern of every RAR design is in-trial reward against terminal information.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the urn do after a failure? A: It adds a ball for the other treatment.
- Q: What did play-the-winner cost the ECMO comparison? A: Information, because almost no infants were left on the control arm.
R functions (bayestrials): rar_ecmo_urn

title: Pocock boundary
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.4 O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock, and the family between them
text:
Pocock boundary. Also called: Pocock. An efficacy boundary with the same critical value at every look, which stops early more easily but sets a final bar well above 1.96.

## What it is

Pocock uses the same critical value at every look, which is $\Delta = 1/2$ in the Wang-Tsiatis family. Early stopping is easy, but the final critical value is well above 1.96. As a spending function it is the second half of the book's equation (eq-spending, the first half is O'Brien-Fleming's):

$$
\alpha^*_{\text{OBF}}(t) = 2\{1 - \Phi(z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{t})\}, \qquad
\alpha^*_{\text{Pocock}}(t) = \alpha \log\{1 + (e - 1)\,t\}.
$$

## Why it matters

A trial in which an early answer is worth much more than a marginally larger sample, such as one in a serious acute illness, may choose a boundary closer to Pocock.

## In the book

For four equally spaced looks the Pocock row has the same value, 2.36, at every look. A one-sided $p$ of 0.009 at the first look is enough to stop.

To have 90 percent power the Pocock design needs about 18 percent more patients than the fixed design if the trial runs to the end, against about 2 percent for O'Brien-Fleming. When the treatment works it stops on average at about 59 percent of the planned information, against about 75 percent for O'Brien-Fleming.

The spending-function form is $\alpha^*_{\text{Pocock}}(t) = \alpha \log\{1 + (e - 1)\,t\}$, which spends steadily.

A third, informal rule uses a very small fixed nominal level at every interim look, for example two-sided $|Z| > 3$, and the unadjusted level at the end.

## Pitfalls

- Under the null both designs run almost to the end when there is no futility rule, so Pocock's early-stop advantage appears only when the drug works.

title: Pocock boundary
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.4 O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock, and the family between them
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What does the Pocock design charge for earlier stops? A: A final bar of about 2.36 and about 18 percent more patients if it runs to the end.
- Q: When the treatment works, which stops earlier, Pocock or O'Brien-Fleming? A: Pocock, at about 59 percent against about 75 percent of the information.
R functions (bayestrials): gs_boundary, gs_expected_information, gs_power_drift, gs_spending_boundary

title: Posterior distribution
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6 Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
text:
Posterior distribution. Also called: posterior. The distribution of the unknown parameter after seeing the data, obtained by multiplying the prior by the likelihood and rescaling.

## What it is
The posterior is what is believed about the parameter after the data, $\pi(\theta \mid y)$. It is the prior times the likelihood, rescaled to integrate to one.

Bayes rule gives the posterior:

$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta')\, \pi(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta),
$$

This is equation eq-bayes.

## Why it matters
The traditional analysis answers whether the difference could be produced by chance alone. A trialist usually wants to know how likely it is that the new treatment is better and by how much. The posterior answers this directly.

Its statements are probabilities about the parameter given these data. A confidence interval is a statement about a procedure over repeated trials.

## In the book
Put a flat Beta(1,1) prior on each arm of the running trial, 30 of 100 control and 45 of 100 treatment responders. The posteriors are Beta(31, 71) and Beta(46, 56).

There is no neat formula for the difference, so many samples are drawn from each posterior (Monte Carlo). The probability $\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid y)$ is 0.9855, against $1 - p = 0.9858$.

The posterior also answers questions a p-value cannot: the probability that the effect exceeds a margin such as 5 or 10 percentage points.

## Pitfalls
With a flat prior and a nearly normal likelihood the posterior probability and one minus the one-sided p-value nearly coincide. The match is not a theorem of the model. It fails with an informative prior, a small sample or rates near 0 or 1.

The same data under three normal priors gave 0.983, 0.975 and 0.958, so the prior must be specified before the data.

title: Posterior distribution
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6 Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: After 45 of 100 responders and a flat prior, what is the posterior? A: Beta(46, 56).
- Q: Does a flat prior always make $1-p$ equal the posterior probability? A: No, only approximately, in nearly normal settings.
R functions (bayestrials): beta_post, grid_update, prob_superior

title: Posterior predictive distribution
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.8 The posterior predictive distribution
text:
Posterior predictive distribution. Also called: predictive distribution. The distribution of future data after averaging over the uncertainty about the parameter, wider than a plug-in prediction.

## What it is
Decisions depend on what will happen next, such as how many of the next 50 patients will respond. The posterior predictive distribution averages the model for future data over the posterior:

$$
p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta .
$$

## Why it matters
For a Beta$(a', b')$ posterior and $m$ future patients, the number of future responders follows a beta-binomial distribution with mean $m a' / (a' + b')$.

The traditional analogue is a plug-in calculation: assume $p = \hat p$ and compute a binomial. It ignores the uncertainty in $\hat p$ and is too narrow.

Futility rules and Goldilocks-type sample-size choices are built on it. The same two-stage logic, draw the parameter from its posterior and then the future data from the model, gives the probability that a trial in progress will succeed at its final analysis.

## In the book
After 45 of 100 and a flat prior, the treatment-arm posterior is Beta(46, 56). The next 50 patients are predicted with the beta-binomial function `dbetabinom`. A prediction made as if $\hat p = 0.45$ were the truth would be overconfident by about 20 percent. In Table 6.8 the predictive standard deviation is 4.27 against 3.52 for the plug-in binomial, and the 95% predictive interval is 14 to 31 responders.

## Pitfalls
The predictive is for future data and the posterior is for the parameter.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which is wider, the posterior predictive or the plug-in binomial? A: The posterior predictive, because it includes the uncertainty about $p$.
- Q: What distribution gives the number of future responders from a Beta posterior? A: Beta-binomial.
R functions (bayestrials): dbetabinom

title: Posterior probability of benefit
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7 From p-values to posterior probabilities of benefit
text:
Posterior probability of benefit. Also called: probability of benefit. The posterior probability that the treatment effect exceeds a threshold a, the quantity in the FDA draft's Bayesian success criterion.

## What it is

The January 2026 FDA draft describes the standard Bayesian success criterion:

$$
\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) \;>\; c,
$$

which is eq-fda. The threshold $a$ says how big an effect counts, and $c$ says how sure one must be.

## Why it matters

With a flat prior and $a = 0$, the posterior probability is one minus the one-sided p-value, so $c = 0.975$ succeeds exactly when $Z_n > 1.96$. With a flat prior the type I error at no effect is $\alpha(a, c) = 1 - \Phi(a/s + z_c)$. A skeptical prior raises the bar on the estimate.

## In the book

With s = 0.10 and $a = 0.10$, the rule $c = 0.975$ has type I error 0.0015, and the calibrating $c$ falls to 0.83. With skeptical priors of 0.2 and 0.1, the type I error at $c = 0.975$ falls to 0.014 and 0.003 and power falls to 0.79 and 0.59 from 0.85. In a worked trial with estimate 0.28 and s = 0.10, the probability of benefit is 0.9974. The probability the effect exceeds 0.10 is 0.964, which clears $c = 0.95$ but not 0.975.

## Pitfalls

The pair $(a, c)$ means nothing until attached to a sample size and a model. Calibrating at $\theta = 0$ establishes superiority over zero, not benefit exceeding $a$.

## Check yourself

- Q: With a flat prior and a = 0, what c matches one-sided alpha 0.025? A: c = 0.975.
- Q: Does a calibrated criterion with a skeptical prior beat the z test at a single look? A: No, it has the same type I error and about the same power.
R functions (bayestrials): calibrate_c_flat, type1_posterior_flat, calibrate_c_normal, power_posterior_normal, type1_posterior_normal, prob_superior

title: Posterior probability success criterion
al: success criterion; FDA success criterion; success threshold; posterior probability threshold
cx: Chapter 14: Operating Characteristics by Simulation > 14.2 The Bayesian success rule and why it has no error rate until calibrated
text:
Posterior probability success criterion. Also called: success criterion, FDA success criterion, success threshold, posterior probability threshold. A rule that declares success when the posterior probability that the treatment effect exceeds a threshold a is larger than a level c.

## What it is

The FDA Bayesian draft guidance describes a success criterion of the form $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$. The treatment effect $\delta$ must exceed a threshold $a$ with posterior probability larger than a level $c$. For two response rates, $\delta = p_1 - p_0$.

With independent Beta(1,1) priors the posterior in each arm is Beta$(1 + x_j, 1 + n_j - x_j)$, and the probability is a one-dimensional integral.

## Why it matters

The rule has no type I error until $a$, $c$, the prior and the schedule of looks are all fixed, because the error rate belongs to the whole procedure, not to the posterior. With one look and a flat prior, $c = 0.975$ is roughly the familiar one-sided 2.5 percent test. Add a second look and the same $c$ is no longer a 2.5 percent test.

## In the book

The threshold $a$ is a clinical quantity, the smallest effect worth having, and $c$ is a statistical quantity set by Calibration of the success threshold. The pivotal BNT162b2 trial used 0.995 at the interim analyses and 0.986 at the final one to keep the overall type I error at 2.5 percent.

## Pitfalls

Reusing 0.975 at every look inflates the error. In the book's example the rule applied at any of four looks needs $c = 0.991$ to be a 2.5 percent test. Examples with $a > 0$ depart from the draft's $a = 0$ calibrated superiority form; they show mechanics and are not a form the draft prescribes.

title: Posterior probability success criterion
al: success criterion; FDA success criterion; success threshold; posterior probability threshold
cx: Chapter 14: Operating Characteristics by Simulation > 14.2 The Bayesian success rule and why it has no error rate until calibrated
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Is $c = 0.975$ a 2.5 percent test when the trial looks four times? A: No. The book finds $c = 0.991$ gives 2.5 percent at four looks.
- Q: Which two quantities does the rule depend on besides the data? A: The effect threshold $a$ and the level $c$, plus the prior and the looks, which together fix the error rate.
R functions (bayestrials): oc_post_table, oc_simulate

title: Power curve
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.4 The power curve
text:
Power curve. The plot of power against the true effect for a fixed sample size, showing the threshold effect below which a trial is more likely to miss than find a benefit.

## What it is

The power curve plots $\text{Power}(\theta)$ for fixed $n$ and $\alpha$ over the whole range of effects.

$$
\text{Power}(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\theta\sqrt{nI} - z_\alpha\right).
$$

(eq-power-z) It equals $\alpha$ at $\theta = 0$, rises through 50% at $\theta = z_\alpha/\sqrt{nI}$, and passes the design value $\theta_d$ at $1-\beta$.

## Why it matters

A single power number hides the shape. The trial has a threshold effect at which power is 50%, and below it effects are more likely missed than found. For a design with 90% power, that threshold is 60.5% of the design effect. The curve is also flat near the design point: going from 90% to 95% power needs 24% more information.

## In the book

If the trial is sized for $\theta_d$ and the truth is $\rho\,\theta_d$, power is $\Phi(\rho(z_\alpha+z_\beta) - z_\alpha)$, which depends only on $\rho$. A trial sized for 90% power has 83% power at 90% of the design effect, 62% at 70%, and 37% at half. A trial with 90% power at hazard ratio 0.80 is, for an effect smaller than about a 13% hazard reduction, more likely than not to fail.

## Pitfalls

At the left end of the curve the probability of a positive result for a drug that does nothing is $\alpha$, independent of $n$. If the drug is better than assumed, the trial is overpowered and ends later than needed.

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict the power if the true effect is half the design effect at 90% design power. A: About 37%.
- Q: What fraction of the design effect has 50% power? A: 60.5%.
R functions (bayestrials): power_z

title: Power prior
al: normalized power prior; NPP; Ibrahim-Chen power prior
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.4 Power priors and their normalized version
text:
Power prior. Also called: normalized power prior, NPP, Ibrahim-Chen power prior. A prior that raises the historical likelihood to a power a0 between 0 and 1, so that a0 sets the fraction of historical patients that count.

## What it is

The power prior of Ibrahim and Chen (2000) down-weights historical data $D_h$ with a single parameter $a_0$:

$$
\pi(\theta \mid D_h, a_0) \propto L(\theta \mid D_h)^{a_0}\,\pi_0(\theta),\qquad 0\le a_0\le 1.
$$

Setting $a_0=0$ discards the historical data and $a_0=1$ pools them fully (eq-power). If $a_0$ is fixed in advance the method is static. With a Beta$(1,1)$ initial prior the power prior is Beta$(1+a_0y_h,\,1+a_0(n_h-y_h))$, so its effective sample size is $a_0 n_h+2$. With $n_h=100$ and $a_0=0.3$ the historical arm counts as about 30 patients.

## Why it matters

The regulator sees the borrowing in one number, the effective sample size, and FDA's distinction between static and dynamic borrowing is the distinction between a fixed and a learned $a_0$.

## In the book

If $a_0$ is given its own prior, the data can choose it. The *normalized power prior* divides by the $a_0$-dependent constant (eq-npp), and the marginal posterior of $a_0$ rises when the current data resemble the historical data. In the rare-disease example, 12 responders in 40 historical controls are borrowed for a trial with 6 of 15 on control, and the marginal likelihood of the current controls guides $a_0$ (eq-borrow-marg). Pr(pT>pC) is 0.83 without borrowing and 0.95 at $a_0=0.5$, and the marginal likelihood is maximized at $a_0=1$ with m(1)/m(0)=2.3. The tirzepatide chain divides the REWIND variance by $a_0$.

## Pitfalls

The power prior discounts the precision of the historical data but does not move their center. With $a_0=0.3$ the prior is Beta$(10,22)$, centered at 0.3125, and nothing in the method notices a conflict if the truth is 40%. In the NSCLC case study a fixed-weight power prior did not reproduce the randomized result.

title: Power prior
al: normalized power prior; NPP; Ibrahim-Chen power prior
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.4 Power priors and their normalized version
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: What does $a_0=0.3$ mean for a historical arm of 100? A: It counts as about 30 patients.
- Q: Does discounting fix a biased center? A: No, it only widens the prior.
R functions (bayestrials): grid_update, borrow_power_prior, borrow_marginal_a0, borrow_rare_table

title: Statistical power
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9 Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size
text:
Statistical power. Also called: power, power calculation. The probability that a trial declares success when the true effect equals a stated value, a conditional probability and not a chance of success.

## What it is

A one-sided trial can declare a useless drug effective (type I error, fixed at $\alpha$, conventionally 0.025) or miss an effective drug (type II error, $\beta$). The complement $1-\beta$ is the power. With $Z = \hat\theta\sqrt{nI}$ and a true effect $\theta$,

$$
\text{Power}(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\theta\sqrt{nI} - z_\alpha\right).
$$

This is eq-power-z.

## Why it matters

Type I error control is a central regulatory design criterion. Type II error is a business and ethical quantity that the sponsor chooses, usually at 0.10 or 0.20. At 90% power $(z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2 = 10.51$, and at 80% it is 7.85, so 90% power needs a third more patients.

## In the book

Power is a conditional probability: the chance of a significant result given that the true effect equals $\theta_d$. A statement such as "90% power" is regularly heard as "90% chance of success", which would be true only if the sponsor were certain of the effect. A conventional power calculation can be represented as Assurance under a point-mass prior. The power curve shows how power changes with the effect.

## Pitfalls

Raising the sample size buys power and nothing else, since the type I error stays at 0.025. Power is not a condition of approval in the way that error control is.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does 90% power need about a third more patients than 80%? A: 10.51 over 7.85 is 1.34, whatever the effect.
- Q: Is 90% power a 90% chance of success? A: No, it is conditional on one effect value.
R functions (bayestrials): power_z

title: Predictive probability monitoring
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.4 Predictive probability monitoring for phase 2
text:
Predictive probability monitoring. Also called: Lee-Liu design, phase 2 monitoring. A phase 2 design that stops for futility or efficacy when the predictive probability of final success crosses a lower or upper threshold, with a printed stopping table.

## What it is

Lee and Liu turned the predictive probability of success into a two-threshold monitoring design for phase 2 with a printed stopping table. After each cohort compute the predictive probability that the trial ends in success; stop for futility if it is below $\eta_L$, stop for efficacy if above $\eta_U$, otherwise continue. At the maximum sample size success needs $\Pr(p > p_0 \mid \text{data}) > \eta$. The predictive probability is approximated by

$$
\mathrm{PP} \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(q_n) - \Phi^{-1}(\eta)\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{1-r}}\right),
$$

## Why it matters

The rule depends only on $(n, s)$, so the decision for every interim outcome can be tabulated before the trial and printed in the protocol. It computes a boundary in a Bayesian way and judges it in a frequentist way.

## In the book

With $N = 40$, $p_0 = 0.20$, thresholds 0.05 and 0.95 and looks after 10, 20 and 30 patients, futility stops are at 0 responders after 10, 3 or fewer after 20, and 7 or fewer after 30. Efficacy stops are at 6 or more after 10, 9 or more after 20, and twelve or more after 30. Operating characteristics follow from exact enumeration, power is essentially unchanged and the sample size falls by roughly a third.

## Pitfalls

Once efficacy stopping is allowed, the type I error is not guaranteed to stay at the fixed-design value, so thresholds need recalibration. The thresholds 0.05 and 0.95 are conventions; an economic reading gives (eq-ppstar)

$$
\mathrm{PP}^* = \frac{m c_2}{\rho V - (1-\rho) c_3},
$$

## Check yourself

- Q: How many responders out of 10 stop the trial for futility in the example? A: None, that is zero responders.
- Q: Is the type I error guaranteed after adding efficacy looks? A: No, recalibrate by enumeration or simulation.
R functions (bayestrials): lee_liu_table, lee_liu_oc, p2_pp_star

title: Predictive probability of success
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.2 Predictive probability of success
text:
Predictive probability of success. Also called: predictive probability, PPoS, predictive power. The chance that the trial will meet its final success criterion if it continues, averaging over what the remaining patients might show.

## What it is

Conditional power fixes the effect $\xi$. The Bayesian replaces it by the posterior distribution of $\xi$ and averages:

$$
\mathrm{PP} = \int \mathrm{CP}(\xi)\, \pi(\xi \mid y_{1:n})\, d\xi = \Pr(\text{final success criterion met} \mid y_{1:n}).
$$

For a binary endpoint with $m$ future patients the future responders are beta-binomial (eq-betabinom) and the predictive probability is the exact sum (eq-pp-binary):

$$
\Pr(X = x \mid s, n) = \binom{m}{x}\frac{B(a_0+s+x,\; b_0+n-s+m-x)}{B(a_0+s,\; b_0+n-s)}, \qquad x = 0,\dots,m,
$$

$$
\mathrm{PP}(s, n) = \sum_{x=0}^{m} \Pr(X=x \mid s,n)\; \mathbf{1}\{\Pr(p > p_0 \mid s+x,\, N) > \eta\}.
$$

Marion's approximation (eq-marion) is

$$
\mathrm{PP} \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(q_n) - \Phi^{-1}(\eta)\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{1-r}}\right),
$$

## Why it matters

It accounts for uncertainty in the effect, which conditional power does not. The final success criterion must be named when the number is reported, because it can be a frequentist test or a Bayesian rule.

## In the book

With a normal prior and the normal-drift model the integral has a closed form, computed by `pp_normal`. For a binary endpoint no approximation is needed: the future responders follow a beta-binomial distribution, and the predictive probability is an exact sum. In a single-arm example with $N = 40$ and $p_0 = 0.20$, twenty patients with six responders give 0.457, with 5 responders 0.219, and with 7 responders 0.713. The approximation of Marion needs only the current posterior probability and the information fraction.

## Pitfalls

Neither a flat-prior value nor a design-alternative-prior value is the right one; they answer under different priors, so the prior must be pre-specified. The approximation is a design component to validate, not an identity.

title: Predictive probability of success
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.2 Predictive probability of success
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: How does PP relate to conditional power? A: It is conditional power averaged over the posterior of the effect.
- Q: Does the binary case need simulation? A: No, it is an exact beta-binomial sum.
R functions (bayestrials): pp_normal, cond_power, pp_one_arm, pp_two_arm

title: Prespecification
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.1 Prespecification
text:
Prespecification. Fixing the prior, thresholds, schedule and analysis before the data are seen, which separates a designed Bayesian trial from a post hoc reanalysis.

## What it is
A trial's prespecified analysis is the one the protocol and statistical analysis plan fixed before the data were seen.
For GUSTO, EOLIA and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK that analysis was frequentist and fixed in advance.

## Why it matters
A Bayesian reanalysis is done after the results are known, by people who know them, so it is exploratory in ICH E9's sense.
The same discipline applies to a prospective Bayesian design: the FDA draft asks that the prior be stated and justified and that sensitivity be shown across a range.
E9 says interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol.

## In the book
The honest report lists every prior tried, and the book's tables show each row, including the pessimistic prior that gives the weakest result.
The recommended practice is to state each prior's mean and standard deviation, show the posterior across a range of them and say which readers each represents.
The success criterion, the schedule, the prior and the stopping rule all go into the protocol and the statistical analysis plan, prospectively.
A Bayesian SAP that defers the prior or the success threshold to a later version has not prespecified the design.
The success criterion's a and c are justified, with calibration evidence or the agreed alternative route, before the data are seen.

## Pitfalls
A reanalysis that reports one prior, chosen after the data, does not meet the standard.
A look added after an external publication is a deviation from the simulated design.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why can a Bayesian reanalysis not be prespecified? A: Priors, thresholds and scale are chosen in the light of the answer.
- Q: What does a deferred success threshold do to a SAP? A: It means the design was not prespecified.

title: Prior-data conflict
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.7 Prior-data conflict and robust priors
text:
Prior-data conflict. Also called: prior data conflict. The case where the data disagree with an informative prior, which a single normal prior handles badly and a robust mixture prior handles by shifting weight.

## What it is

A prior-data conflict is a disagreement between an informative prior and the observed data. The effect scale here is $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$, so benefit is positive. Suppose the prior is informative and well justified, and the data disagree. A single normal prior compromises by precision however far apart they are. The FDA draft recommends that sponsors examine prior-data conflict and not assume it away.

## Why it matters

The standard defense is a robust mixture prior, an informative component combined with a weakly informative one. For example, $0.8\, N(0.29, 0.10^2) + 0.2\, N(0, 1)$ is an 80 percent chance that the effect looks like the phase 2 estimate and a 20 percent chance that nothing is known. After the data the weights update, and the component that predicted better gains weight. Schmidli and colleagues developed this construction for historical controls.

## In the book

When the observed effect is $\hat\theta = -0.20$ on the $-\log$ HR scale (a hazard ratio of 1.22, harm), the pure informative prior still reports a positive posterior mean, while the mixture moves weight to the vague component and follows the data. The FDA applied the construction in the pediatric belimumab trial in lupus.

## Pitfalls

The weight 0.2 on the vague component is itself a prior judgment. Type I error when the informative prior is wrong, and the extra patients needed, must be simulated. The mixture's ESS depends on what the data do.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a mixture prior do when data contradict its informative part? A: Its posterior weight moves to the vague component and the posterior follows the data.
- Q: Does a single normal prior notice conflict? A: No, it compromises by precision however far apart they are.
R functions (bayestrials): mixture_posterior, normal_update

title: Prior distribution
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8 Choosing and Defending Priors
text:
Prior distribution. Also called: prior. The distribution a sponsor states for the treatment effect before the trial, which the traditional design hides inside its design alternative.

## What it is

A prior is something a sponsor can state, justify, quantify and defend. The Bayesian analysis is distinguished mainly by writing one of its assumptions down. The traditional design has a prior of its own that rarely gets the name. Its protocol states alpha, power and a design alternative, and the prior column reads "Not stated".

For example, the traditional design fixes the number of events for a hazard ratio design alternative $\theta_a$:

$$
d = \frac{4(z_{\alpha} + z_{\beta})^2}{\theta_a^2}
$$

This is equation eq-events.

## Why it matters

For time-to-event data with 1:1 allocation the design needs $d = \frac{4(z_{\alpha} + z_{\beta})^2}{\theta_a^2}$ events (eq-events). A hazard ratio of 0.75 gives $\theta_a = 0.288$ and 508 events. The design alternative is a planning assumption that treats one value as known, and nobody believes it. Averaging power over a stated prior gives assurance.

## In the book

Four sources recur: phase 2 data from the same program, the published literature and earlier programs, expert elicitation, and mechanistic models. Phase 2 is the most natural and the most misleading, because programs advance when phase 2 looks good. In a simulation, about a third of drugs advance, and a prior centered on their phase 2 estimate would be centered on more than twice the true effect on the log scale. In the illustration, advanced programs had a phase 2 hazard ratio of 0.71 and a true one of 0.86.

## Pitfalls

The traditional analysis is not a bad choice for this reason. When a single test is run in a trial large enough that any reasonable prior is overwhelmed, it is simple and sufficient. The numbers of the simulation are illustrative and not from any program.

title: Prior distribution
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8 Choosing and Defending Priors
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Does the traditional design assume anything about the effect? A: It assigns no prior probability to any effect, but the power calculation treats one value as if it were known.
- Q: Why is a phase 2 estimate a risky prior center? A: Programs advance when it looks good, so it is biased upward.
R functions (bayestrials): events_schoenfeld, prob_success

title: Prior elicitation
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.2 Where priors come from in a sponsor's program
text:
Prior elicitation. Also called: sources of priors. The provenance of a prior in a sponsor's program, from phase 2 data, literature, structured expert judgment and mechanistic models, with its documented weaknesses.

## What it is

A prior has an identifiable provenance that the guidance asks the sponsor to document. Four sources recur: phase 2 data from the same program, the published literature and earlier programs, expert elicitation, and mechanistic or pharmacometric models.

## Why it matters

Each source has a failure mode. Phase 2 programs advance when results look good. A literature search is a sampling mechanism, so the prior should come from a pre-specified search guarding against "preferential selection of favorable studies". Experts are overconfident: intervals stated as 90 percent contain the truth far less often.

## In the book

The Sheffield Elicitation Framework has experts give individual judgments, share evidence, and agree on one distribution. Three rules protect the clinician and the sponsor: elicit observables, not parameters; elicit tails as well as the middle; and document the dissenters. A simulator's mean $\hat\mu$ and variance $\hat v$ can be converted to a beta prior by matching moments, with $a + b = \hat\mu(1 - \hat\mu)/\hat v - 1$. The remedies for selected phase 2 estimates are to discount them, to center on the distribution of true effects in the class, or to use them only through a skeptical prior.

## Pitfalls

A single consensus can hide a bimodal opinion that a mixture prior would represent honestly. A prior is not a mood.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why elicit a response rate and not a log odds ratio? A: Observables are what clinicians can judge.
- Q: What are three ways to handle a selected phase 2 estimate? A: Discount it, center on the class distribution, or use it only through a skeptical prior.

title: Prior odds in the sample size constant
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.4 The prior odds in the constant
text:
Prior odds in the sample size constant. Also called: prior odds. The constant C in the moderate deviation boundary, which makes the price of prior skepticism explicit in patients.

## What it is

The constant $C$ collects the prior odds and the prior density at the null. For a unit-information prior $C = 2\log(\pi_0/\pi_a)$, and with equal odds $C = 0$. Moving from even odds to two-to-one and four-to-one against the alternative raises $C$ from 0 to 1.39 and 2.77.

The moderate-deviation boundary for the critical $t$ value is:

$$
t_{\text{crit}} = \sqrt{\log n + C}\,\bigl(1 + o(1)\bigr), \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0/\pi_a}{\pi(\theta_0)\sqrt{2\pi/I(\theta_0)}},
$$

This is equation eq-md-boundary.

## Why it matters

Skepticism is paid for in patients, at a rate the formula makes explicit. The sponsor who says the drug is a long shot is told how many more patients it takes, and the sponsor who claims equal odds is told what that claim is worth. The requirement rises and the induced one-sided error falls as the odds worsen.

## In the book

The unit matters. The package function `events_md()` uses the information convention ($n = d/4$, $I = 1$), where $C = 0$ is the unit-information prior at equal odds. In the events convention, $C_{\text{info}} = C_{\text{events}} + \log 4$, so the same numerical $C = 0$ means $C_{\text{info}} = \log 4 = 1.39$. For a standard Cauchy prior on a unit-variance Gaussian mean, $C = \log(\pi/2) = 0.452$.

## Pitfalls

This is not a way out of a regulatory error-rate expectation. Where the sponsor calibrates to a one-sided 0.025 by simulation, that target stays. Keeping $C = 0$ while switching units changes the implied prior.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does C equal at 4:1 odds against the alternative? A: $2\log 4 = 2.77$.
- Q: Does the required sample size go up or down as odds against the alternative worsen? A: Up.
R functions (bayestrials): n_md, events_md

title: Prior specification in the protocol
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.11 Writing the prior into the protocol
text:
Prior specification in the protocol. Also called: prior in the protocol. What a protocol or analysis plan must state about the prior: its form, provenance, weight, comparison priors, sensitivity, robustness and success criterion.

## What it is

A prior section of a protocol should contain seven items: the analysis prior with its implied distribution for the estimand, its provenance, its effective sample size, comparison priors, the sensitivity analysis with a tipping-point report, a robustness provision, and the success criterion with its calibration.

## Why it matters

The FDA draft says "It is always critical for Bayesian analyses to have a prespecified prior". It distinguishes the analysis prior from design priors used only in simulation. It describes three routes for the success criterion: calibration, direct reading of the posterior, and benefit-risk criteria. Informative priors need greater justification. The draft leaves open how large an ESS is acceptable.

## In the book

Four failures recur: a prior chosen after the data, a single published estimate treated as a prior, a flat prior mistaken for no prior, and a prior that matters presented as one that does not. The 2010 device guidance is the final precedent: agree the prior with the Agency beforehand, and it allows type I error control at a less stringent level when prior information is used. ICH E20 treats the prior in the same spirit in Section 5.3.

## Pitfalls

The draft is not binding, and a sponsor relying on it should say so in the briefing document. What stays the same is the standard of evidence: a calibrated confirmatory design uses the same one-sided 0.025.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which prior enters the inference, the design prior or the analysis prior? A: The analysis prior.
- Q: When may a sponsor read the posterior probability directly? A: Where the prior accurately reflects external data, by agreement with the Agency.

title: Prognostic covariate adjustment
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.15 Prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins
text:
Prognostic covariate adjustment. Also called: PROCOVA, digital twin. A method that builds a prognostic score from external data and uses it as a baseline covariate in a randomized analysis, cutting variance without borrowing outcomes.

## What it is

Prognostic covariate adjustment (PROCOVA) builds a prognostic model of the control-arm outcome from external data, such as historical trial data. Each participant's predicted outcome, the "digital twin" prediction under control, is then a baseline covariate in the randomized analysis.

## Why it matters

The treatment effect is still estimated by comparing randomized arms, so the analysis stays valid, and the covariate absorbs outcome variation, so variance falls. No assumption about the stability of the control arm over time is made. The method is often the first to propose to a regulator wary of external controls.

## In the book

The EMA's CHMP adopted a qualification opinion in September 2022 for phase 2 and 3 trials with continuous outcomes. The model is fixed before the trial, and with an independently developed, pre-specified score PROCOVA can preserve asymptotic type I error control despite poor prediction. The contrast is that PROCOVA uses external data to sharpen a randomized comparison, whereas borrowing uses them to replace part of it. It is a special case of covariate adjustment with a single prognostic score.

## Pitfalls

Precision gains depend on prognostic performance, and small trials need suitable finite-sample inference. It gives up less and so buys less than a full borrowing design.

## Check yourself

- Q: Does PROCOVA borrow control outcomes? A: No, it uses external data only to build a score.
- Q: What does the sponsor gain? A: Variance reduction, which can become a smaller sample size.

title: Project Optimus
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.2 What the FDA guidance asks
text:
Project Optimus. Also called: dose optimization. FDA initiative, launched in 2021, behind the August 2024 oncology dosage guidance that asks sponsors to compare dosages rather than default to the MTD.

## What it is
The final guidance of August 2024 (docket FDA-2022-D-2827, Oncology Center of Excellence with CDER and CBER) was developed through Project Optimus, launched in 2021. It recommends that oncology sponsors compare multiple dosages, using pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, safety and efficacy information, rather than default to the MTD. It is a guidance: it states current thinking and does not bind.

## Why it matters
In paraphrase, it asks that doses taken to registrational trials be chosen on more than the MTD, including late and low-grade toxicities. Dose-ranging should compare several dosages, where feasible with randomization, to characterize dose-response and dose-toxicity, not to prove superiority. Model-based and Bayesian methods are expected to be useful, and the guidance neither requires a specific design nor excludes the 3+3.

## Pitfalls
The guidance does not address first-in-human starting-dose selection. It does not specifically address radiopharmaceuticals, cellular and gene therapies, oncolytic viruses, microbiota, cancer vaccines or pediatric development. ICH E4 had already set these principles in 1994. Exposure-response models fall under ICH M15.

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the guidance require a model-based design? A: No, and it does not exclude the 3+3.
- Q: What would a reviewer ask about a dose that does not maximize efficacy? A: The probability of choosing a dose that is too low or too toxic under each scenario.

title: Proportional hazards
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5 Non-proportional hazards
text:
Proportional hazards. Also called: proportional hazards assumption. The assumption that the hazard ratio is constant over time, which makes a single hazard ratio a clean summary.

## What it is
Under proportional hazards the hazard ratio does not change over time, so a single hazard ratio is a clean summary. The log-rank test is the score test of such a model.

## Why it matters
Non-proportional hazards break the shortcut that information about a log hazard ratio is proportional to the number of events. The Schoenfeld calculation assumes a single hazard ratio.

## In the book
The proportional scenario cuts a control hazard of 0.15 per year by 40 percent from the start. In a power simulation, a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 serves as the comparison for a delayed effect: the power is 0.68 under proportional hazards against 0.55 under the delayed effect, with the same number of events. Under proportional hazards the log-rank test beats the MaxCombo test, which beats the late-weighted test.

## Pitfalls
When the hazard ratio changes, the Cox estimate becomes a censoring-dependent weighted average.

## Check yourself
- Q: What breaks when hazards are not proportional? A: A single hazard ratio misdescribes the effect and the events-as-information shortcut fails.

title: Proportional reporting ratio
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.3.1 The traditional measure
text:
Proportional reporting ratio. Also called: PRR. A simple disproportionality statistic that flags a drug and event pair with a ratio of at least 2, chi-square at least 4 and three or more reports.

## What it is

The proportional reporting ratio, with the reporting odds ratio, is a cousin of the relative reporting ratio $n_{ij}/E_{ij}$, used with a confidence interval and a screening rule.

Evans and colleagues flagged a pair when the ratio is at least 2, the chi-square statistic at least 4 and there are at least three reports. A common variant asks for a lower confidence bound above 1 with at least three reports.

## Why it matters

The statistics are simple, transparent and still used, and the EMA guideline names them.

## In the book

The weakness is at the sparse end. For a rare pair the ratio is dominated by noise: one report against an expected count of 0.05 gives a ratio of twenty. A table with millions of cells will contain many such pairs by chance alone. The Gamma-Poisson shrinker was built to handle this.

## Pitfalls

- A statistical signal is only a hypothesis to be assessed clinically, so a flag is not evidence of causation.

## Check yourself

- Q: What three conditions did Evans and colleagues require for a flag? A: A ratio of at least 2, chi-square at least 4 and at least three reports.
- Q: Where does the ratio fail? A: For rare pairs, where it is dominated by noise.

title: Randomization test
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.5 Randomization inference: the test the design justifies
text:
Randomization test. Also called: randomization inference, permutation test. A test that shuffles treatment labels under the same procedure used to randomize, giving the exact distribution of the statistic over possible assignments.

## What it is
Take the observed outcomes, shuffle the group labels many times, and ask how often a shuffled difference is as large as the observed one. The test is justified by the design.

Under the sharp null, $Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)$ for every patient, each outcome would be the same whatever the arm, and only the assignment varied. The permutation distribution is then the exact distribution of the statistic over possible assignments.

## Why it matters
It requires no model for the outcome, and type I error is controlled by construction. Fisher put it forward in 1935, and the normal-theory z and t tests approximate it.

It also needs no random sample: it asks only about the patients actually enrolled. Generalizing to future patients is a separate step resting on clinical judgment.

## In the book
The shuffle must follow the design. A null trial of 40 patients with an upward drift of two standard deviations was analyzed with a one-sided permutation test at nominal level 0.025. With block assignment the unrestricted shuffle was conservative, and the shuffle within blocks was close to nominal. In Table 5.1 the empirical type I error is 0.011 for the unrestricted shuffle with block assignment and 0.022 within blocks, against 0.025 under simple randomization.

## Pitfalls
A test that ignores the blocks treats as possible many assignments the design excluded. It gives away power. The analysis should mirror the randomization, and stratification factors belong in the model.

## Check yourself
- Q: If assignment used permuted blocks of four, which shuffles are allowed? A: Only those with two drug and two control in each block.
- Q: What population does the p-value refer to? A: The patients actually enrolled, not a sample from anything.
R functions (bayestrials): perm_test_arm

title: Randomization
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5 Randomization From the Ground Up
text:
Randomization. Also called: random allocation. Assigning each patient to a treatment by chance, so that the groups differ only by luck of the draw and by the treatment.

## What it is
Randomization assigns a patient to a treatment by chance. The p-values, posteriors and interim looks of the book all assume that the two groups differ only because of the treatment and by luck of the draw.

ICH E9 says randomization introduces a deliberate element of chance into the assignment, and tends to make the distributions of prognostic factors, known and unknown, similar across groups.

## Why it matters
If a coin ignores everything about the patient, the selection term is zero on average and the difference in observed means estimates the average effect of the drug. R. A. Fisher made this argument central to experimental design.

The failures without it come in four forms: historical controls, predictable schemes such as alternation, unconcealed allocation and self-selection by patients.

## In the book
Sacks, Chalmers and Smith reviewed six therapies studied with both randomized and historical controls. The historically controlled studies were much more likely to report the new therapy as better. Schulz and colleagues examined 250 controlled trials and found that inadequately concealed allocation went with odds ratios exaggerated by about 41 percent.

The book covers Simple randomization, Permuted block randomization, Stratified randomization and Minimization. Stratified blocks and minimization cut the imbalance in a known trait. Nothing helps a hidden trait.

## Pitfalls
Randomization does not guarantee balance in any single trial. It guarantees that the imbalance is due to chance, with a known distribution that the confidence interval and p-value account for.

A random list the investigator can see is a way of choosing patients with extra steps, so randomization is only as good as its Allocation concealment.

title: Randomization
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5 Randomization From the Ground Up
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Does randomization balance a hidden trait in one trial? A: No. Its imbalance is the same under all four methods, as large as under simple randomization.
- Q: What did Schulz and colleagues find about weak concealment? A: Odds ratios exaggerated on average by about 41 percent, an association and not a randomized comparison.
R functions (bayestrials): covariate_imbalance

title: Critiques of response-adaptive randomization
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.4 The critiques of response-adaptive randomization
text:
Critiques of response-adaptive randomization. Also called: critiques of adaptive randomization. The published case that outcome-adaptive randomization offers little over equal allocation in two arms, with its costs in power and variability, and the replies.

## What it is

By the 2010s experience with Bayesian adaptive randomization in oncology produced criticisms that practitioners now regard as a fair statement of its costs. Korn and Freidlin argued that in two-arm trials it offers little over equal allocation. Thall, Fox and Wathen collected objections including lower power, highly variable arm sizes, a chance of more patients on the inferior arm, and sensitivity to time trends.

## Why it matters

The replies matter too. Berry analyzed adaptive assignment as a decision problem and found randomization satisfactory when the disease is at least moderately common. On the book's reading the case is weakest in a two-arm confirmatory trial with a large outside population and strongest with several arms and a small population, and this is not a point of agreement.

## In the book

The book reproduces the critique with a 400-patient trial at 0.30 against 0.45 under equal, Thompson and capped Thompson rules. Thompson adds responders but power falls, and the number on the better arm varies much more. The claim that RAR often puts more patients on the inferior arm is weaker in this scenario, where the effect is large and the outcome immediate. The balanced review of Robertson and coauthors advises a burn-in, restricted extreme allocation, modeled time trends and an explicit ethical justification.

## Pitfalls

The summaries follow the papers' main arguments and are not exhaustive. The loss of power is not a trade a sponsor should accept in a confirmatory setting.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which costs does the critique name for two arms? A: Lower power, variable arm sizes, and sensitivity to time trends.
- Q: Which setting does the book find strongest for RAR? A: Several arms and a small population.
R functions (bayestrials): rar_two_arm, rar_simulate

title: RBesT
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text:
RBesT. An R package for Bayesian evidence synthesis: meta-analytic-predictive priors, robustification and operating characteristics for designs with historical data.

## What it is
RBesT is an R package of Bayesian evidence synthesis tools. It builds meta-analytic-predictive priors, robustifies them, and gives operating characteristics for designs that use historical data.

## Why it matters
The book marks it as relevant to the borrowing chapter.

## In the book
Of the tools listed, only rpact, gsDesign, BOIN, brms and rstan were version-checked on the build machine, so RBesT was not checked.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does RBesT construct? A: Meta-analytic-predictive priors, with robustification.
- Q: Which chapter topic is it relevant to? A: Borrowing.

title: Phases as a sequence of options
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.6 The phases as a sequence of options
text:
Phases as a sequence of options. Also called: phases as options. Each phase is paid for only if all earlier ones succeed, so the cost per approved drug is driven by attrition.

## What it is
Let $p_{12}$, $p_{23}$ and $p_{3A}$ be the probabilities of moving from Phase I to II, II to III and III to approval, and $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$ the phase costs. Phase $k$ is paid for only if all earlier phases succeed, so the long-run cost per approval is the ratio of expected cost per start to expected approvals per start.

$$
C_{\mathrm{approved}} = \frac{c_1 + p_{12}c_2 + p_{12}p_{23}c_3}{p_{12}\,p_{23}\,p_{3A}}.
$$

This is equation eq-lifecycle-cost.

## Why it matters
The formula explains why attrition dominates the economics. Wong, Siah and Lo estimated that about 13.8 percent of programs entering Phase I reach approval, and 3.4 percent in oncology. Cost per approval falls as each transition probability rises or each phase cost falls.

## In the book
The stylized baseline has $p_{12} = 0.5$, $p_{23} = 0.3$, $p_{3A} = 0.6$ and phase costs of 25, 60 and 250 million dollars, illustrative values and not data. The rows change one input at a time, such as a Phase II success rise from 0.30 to 0.40 or a Phase III cost cut by a fifth. The baseline cost per approval is 1028 million dollars; the Phase II rise cuts it by 14.9 percent and the cheaper Phase III by 8.1 percent.

## Pitfalls
The ranking of two savings depends on the perturbations chosen, so it is not a general ranking of inputs. Advancing more compounds is not in itself better selection.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is Phase III cost multiplied by $p_{12}p_{23}$? A: It is paid only if Phases I and II both succeed.
- Q: Is the baseline in the table data? A: No, the values are illustrative.

title: Critiques of Bayesian reanalysis
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.5 What critics say
text:
Critiques of Bayesian reanalysis. Also called: critics of reanalysis. The literature for and against reanalyzing a trial after its result is known, including de Grooth and Cremer's argument that many priors do not build consensus.

## What it is
Reanalyzing a trial after the result is known has a literature of its own, with supporters and critics.
An early instance is the debate over ECMO in newborns, in which Ware described the trials and Kass and Greenhouse commented from a Bayesian perspective.
Wijeysundera and colleagues reanalyzed 88 randomized trials from four general medical journals and concluded that Bayesian and frequentist analyses complement each other.

## Why it matters
The case for reanalysis is that it states probabilities at clinically meaningful thresholds and that the posterior under several priors makes dependence on the prior visible.

## In the book
The criticism the book cites is de Grooth and Cremer's commentary that reanalyzing trials using many priors does not contribute to consensus.
It recommends testing whether a result would persuade a reasonable adversary and assessing bias and generalizability separately, which connects to the skeptical prior standing in for the adversary.
In the book's own words, a table of many priors invites each reader to pick the row that agrees with prior belief.
Two further objections follow from the structure: priors are chosen after the result is known, and which trials are reanalyzed is itself an unprespecified choice.
Brophy's EXCEL reanalysis shows both: adding three other trials found by a stated search lowered the probability of any excess mortality with stenting from 99 to 85 percent.

## Pitfalls
The book's reading is that each side is right about something different: a reanalysis shows what the data can support, and is weak as evidence when priors and trials were chosen after the fact.
The rule that follows is to write the reanalysis down before looking, with fixed priors and trials chosen by a stated rule, and to report every prior tried.

title: Critiques of Bayesian reanalysis
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.5 What critics say
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: What makes the choice of trials in a reanalysis auditable? A: A stated search rule.
- Q: What does the book treat the result of a reanalysis as? A: Input to the next trial, not a verdict on the last one.

title: REBYOTA
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17.1 REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study
text:
REBYOTA. Also called: REBYOTA trial, RBX2660, PUNCH CD3. A phase 3 trial of a fecal microbiota product that used a Bayesian hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study.

## What it is

REBYOTA (RBX2660) prevents recurrence of *Clostridioides difficile* infection after antibiotics and was approved on 30 November 2022. The sponsor first planned two phase 3 trials of about 300 patients each. After FDA's July 2013 enforcement discretion on fecal microbiota transplantation made enrollment difficult, it proposed a single phase 3 trial (study 2017-01, PUNCH CD3) plus a Bayesian integration of phase 2b study 2014-01.

## Why it matters

FDA wrote that the studies are generally exchangeable but not identical, and accepted a hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing, in which borrowing depends on how similar the effect is in both arms. The January 2026 FDA draft guidance cites it as its example of borrowing from a previous trial of the same drug.

## In the book

Two success thresholds on the posterior probability of superiority were analogues of one-sided type I errors of 0.025 (one trial) and 0.00125 (two trials), and after adjustment they were 0.9750338 and 0.9993275. The result was a success rate of 0.71 on RBX2660 against 0.57 on placebo (95% credible interval 0.02 to 0.24 for the difference), with posterior probability of superiority 0.991, meeting the one-trial threshold and missing the two-trial threshold. FDA requested a refined analysis aligning the success definition, the assessment period (9 weeks against 8 weeks) and the analysis populations. Both analyses reached the same conclusion.

## Pitfalls

The briefing document gives no borrowing weight or effective sample size, so the amount borrowed cannot be read from it.

## Check yourself

- Q: Did 0.991 meet the one-trial or the two-trial threshold? A: The one-trial threshold only.
- Q: What was the lesson? A: Data alignment, not the model.

title: RECOVERY
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.5 RECOVERY: subgroups and shrinkage
text:
RECOVERY. Also called: RECOVERY trial. The dexamethasone comparison in RECOVERY, reanalyzed by respiratory-support subgroup with hierarchical shrinkage that leaves strongly supported effects nearly unchanged.

## What it is
The dexamethasone comparison randomized hospitalized patients with Covid-19 to dexamethasone 6 mg once daily for up to ten days or usual care.
Twenty-eight-day mortality was 22.9 percent (482 of 2104) on dexamethasone and 25.7 percent (1110 of 4321) on usual care, an age-adjusted rate ratio of 0.83 with 95 percent interval 0.75 to 0.93.
The subgroup results by respiratory support at randomization were as important as the overall result.

## Why it matters
Subgroup analyses are a familiar source of false findings, and the Bayesian instinct is to shrink them toward a common mean by an amount the data choose.
Shrinkage is not a rule that every subgroup be pulled to the mean.

## In the book
With $\theta_j = -\log RR_j$ in stratum $j$ and $\theta_j \sim N(\mu, \tau_b^2)$, the marginal likelihood of $\tau_b$ is
$$
p(\tau_b \mid \hat\theta) \propto p(\tau_b)\, V_\mu(\tau_b)^{1/2} \prod_j (s_j^2 + \tau_b^2)^{-1/2} \exp\left\{-\frac{(\hat\theta_j - \hat\mu(\tau_b))^2}{2(s_j^2+\tau_b^2)}\right\},
$$
The conditional posterior mean of each $\theta_j$ is $(1 - B_j)\hat\theta_j + B_j \hat\mu$ with $B_j = s_j^2/(s_j^2 + \tau_b^2)$.
With only three strata the data say little about $\tau_b$, and the book uses a uniform prior over $(0, 1]$.
The shrinkage factors are small, and the shrunk estimates barely move; the pattern of benefit rising with severity is large and biologically expected.
The clinicians' conclusion was to treat patients on oxygen or ventilation and not those without oxygen.

## Pitfalls
The posterior of $\tau_b$ is sensitive to its prior, and moving the upper bound from 1 to 3 changes the median and mean, so the book reports the median.
The probability of harm in the no-oxygen stratum comes from the book's model, not from RECOVERY.
A trial so large that its prespecified analysis was decisive shows shrinkage changing the numbers but not the practice.

title: RECOVERY
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.5 RECOVERY: subgroups and shrinkage
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Do the data decide how much to shrink? A: Yes, through the posterior of $\tau_b$, though with three strata it depends on its prior.
- Q: Which subgroup motivated the advice not to treat? A: Patients without oxygen.
R functions (bayestrials): reanalysis_hier, reanalysis_recovery

title: Recruitment and the value of speed
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.8 Recruitment and the value of speed
text:
Recruitment and the value of speed. Also called: value of speed, recruitment. Trials are slow because of accrual, and a gamma-Poisson posterior turns an enrollment count into a rate, while a recruit is worth the evidence it adds.

## What it is
Most trials are slow because of accrual, not analysis, and the recruitment rate is the quantity a sponsor can least control. The book models enrollment of eligible families as a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ per week. With the reference prior $\mathrm{Gamma}(1/2, 0)$ and $n$ families seen in $t$ weeks, the posterior is $\mathrm{Gamma}(n + 1/2, t)$.

## Why it matters
The same calculation, with a prior borrowed from earlier sites, turns a protocol's accrual assumption into a predictive distribution of the end date. A rate is not the whole story, because a recruit is worth the evidence it contributes: count the information a patient contributes, not the patients.

## In the book
In November 1995 Michael Milken asked on CNN's Larry King Live for families with several men affected by prostate cancer to volunteer. More than 3,000 people called. Within three weeks about 300 qualified families were in hand, where Johns Hopkins had recruited 90 families over ten years. A LOD score is a log likelihood ratio, and log likelihood ratios add across independent families.

## Pitfalls
The comparisons are conditional on assumed conventional rates, since the conventional pace is not known. The value of the acceleration rests on labeled assumptions. A maximized LOD of 3 does not automatically imply a Bayes factor of 1000.

## Check yourself
- Q: What posterior follows $n$ families in $t$ weeks under the reference prior? A: $\mathrm{Gamma}(n + 1/2, t)$.
- Q: Why can broader recruitment lower information per family? A: A broad appeal brings in phenocopies and families not linked to the locus, which dilute the expected LOD.

title: Regret
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.5 Regret and the Lai-Robbins bound
text:
Regret. Also called: Lai-Robbins bound. The loss against an oracle that knows the best arm; the Lai-Robbins bound says the best possible policy still puts a log-order number of patients on the inferior arm.

## What it is

Regret measures how much a policy loses against an oracle that knows the best arm. For two arms the regret after $T$ patients is the expected number of patients on the inferior arm times the gap in response probabilities. Equal randomization puts half the patients on the inferior arm, so its regret grows linearly in $T$.

## Why it matters

Lai and Robbins showed that for a uniformly good policy the expected number of patients on an inferior arm $i$ satisfies

$$
\liminf_{T\to\infty} \frac{\mathbb{E}[N_i(T)]}{\log T} \;\ge\; \frac{1}{\mathrm{KL}(p_i, p^\ast)},
$$

where KL is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the two arms' response distributions. The regret of the best possible policy is logarithmic, not linear.

## In the book

A simulation compares equal allocation, Thompson sampling and the UCB1 rule, which adds a bonus $\sqrt{2\log t / N_i(t)}$ to each arm's mean. Polson and Sokolov observe that this logarithm matches the scale of the Bayes sequential boundary: for small effects $\mathrm{KL} \approx \theta^2/2$ and $n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \tfrac12 \log n$. The analogy is exact for the deviation scale and misleading for the objective.

## Pitfalls

The bound is asymptotic, so finite-horizon counts can sit below the plotted slope. Regret is a loss in the trial, power is a property of the final decision, and optimizing the first damages the second.

## Check yourself

- Q: How does regret of equal allocation grow? A: Linearly in $T$.
- Q: Can any good policy avoid putting patients on the inferior arm? A: No, the number grows like $\log T$ with constant $1/\mathrm{KL}$.
R functions (bayestrials): rar_regret_sim

title: REMAP-CAP
al: REMAP-CAP trial; Randomized, Embedded, Multifactorial Adaptive Platform trial for Community-Acquired Pneumonia
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.3 REMAP-CAP: domains, response-adaptive randomization, and an embedded design
text:
REMAP-CAP. Also called: REMAP-CAP trial, Randomized, Embedded, Multifactorial Adaptive Platform trial for Community-Acquired Pneumonia. A multifactorial, embedded Bayesian platform for pneumonia with response-adaptive randomization that declared IL-6 receptor antagonists beneficial in COVID-19.

## What it is

REMAP-CAP is a platform designed before the pandemic it became known for. After the 2009 H1N1 pandemic an EU-funded network built the infrastructure, which began enrolling in April 2016 (NCT02735707) with a dormant pandemic stratum later activated for COVID-19.

## Why it matters

Its design has four features. It is *multifactorial*: domains are sets of alternative interventions for one aspect of care, and a patient is randomized in every domain for which he or she is eligible. It is *embedded* in routine care. Its pandemic primary endpoint was organ-support-free days to day 21, analyzed with a Bayesian proportional-odds model. And allocation within a domain is updated to favor arms with higher posterior probability of being best.

## In the book

In the IL-6 domain the triggers were superiority at posterior probability of being best above 99%, efficacy at odds ratio above 1 with probability above 99%, futility if the probability of an odds ratio above 1.2 fell below 5%, and equivalence of non-control arms if the probability of an odds ratio between 0.83 and 1.2 exceeded 90%. The platform declared that tocilizumab and sarilumab improved outcomes, including survival, in critically ill COVID-19 patients. A domain can be declared complete without waiting for the others. The domains may be pooled in a hierarchical sense across strata, which is borrowing under the same conditions.

## Pitfalls

For confirmatory platforms the October 2026 EMA draft does not support response-adaptive randomization, a point to settle with the regulator.

## Check yourself

- Q: What is a domain? A: A set of alternative interventions for one aspect of care.
- Q: Can a patient join several domains? A: Yes, in every domain for which eligible.

title: Reproducibility
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.4 Reproducibility
text:
Reproducibility. Also called: simulation seed. The practice that every simulation shows its seed beside the result, that Monte Carlo error is reported, and that stored output is regenerated deliberately.

## What it is
Every simulation either calls `set.seed()` in the chunk or passes `seed =` to the package function, so the seed is visible next to the result. Functions draw from R's global generator after the seed is set.

## Why it matters
A chunk is repeatable, but its results depend on the order of the random calls inside it. Monte Carlo results are reported with their Monte Carlo error. A different seed gives values that differ in the third decimal place.

## In the book
- Quarto's freeze mechanism (`freeze: auto` in `_quarto.yml`) stores each chapter's output, so a rebuild reuses it unless the chapter source changed.
- Slow chunks are knitr-cached, keyed to a checksum of the installed package.
- To regenerate after a package change, reinstall it, delete the chapter's directory under `_freeze/` and its knitr cache, and render again.
- The authors recommend recording `sessionInfo()` for exact reproduction.
- The worked example uses 20,000 simulated trials per run with seeds 1, 3 and 2.

## Pitfalls
The calibration run's rejection proportion is the calibration target, not an error assessment, so a fresh null run with another seed is needed.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why check the type I error on a fresh run with another seed? A: The calibration run's rejection rate is the target, not an assessment.
- Q: What does FDA's Bayesian draft say to report about computing? A: Software versions, code and MCMC seed numbers.
R functions (bayestrials): oc_simulate, oc_calibrate

title: Requires, recommends, permits
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.6 Requires, recommends, permits
text:
Requires, recommends, permits. A sorting of regulatory sources by force: statutes and regulations bind, guidances recommend, and permissions depend on FDA agreeing.

## What it is
The force of a document varies, so the book sorts sources into categories. A statute binds, a regulation binds, and a guidance "contains nonbinding recommendations".

## Why it matters
A sponsor should never describe a draft as "FDA requirements" in a protocol or meeting package. A permission is not an entitlement. The permissions that matter most to Bayesian adaptive designs are all of the form "if FDA agrees".

## In the book
- Requires: FD&C Act 505(d), the FDAMA 1997 single-trial provision, FDORA 2022, and 21 CFR 314.126.
- Recommends: final guidances such as Adaptive Designs 2019, draft guidances such as Bayesian Methodology (January 2026), and ICH Step 2 and Step 4 documents.
- Permits: one trial plus confirmatory evidence, non-calibrated Bayesian success criteria with FDA agreement, and nonconcurrent controls in rare circumstances.
- Process: formal meetings and the CID and MIDD programs define how to ask, not the evidentiary standard.

## Pitfalls
A guidance is nonbinding, but a departure without prior discussion is a risk to the program.

## Check yourself
- Q: "FDA requires a simulation report for any Bayesian design." Accurate? A: No, the Bayesian draft recommends it and is only a draft.
- Q: Is a permission an entitlement? A: No, it is available only if the agency concurs.

title: Response-adaptive randomization
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16 Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits
text:
Response-adaptive randomization. Also called: RAR, adaptive randomization. Allocation that shifts toward the arm that is looking better as outcomes accrue, trading some information for benefit to patients inside the trial.

## What it is

Response-adaptive randomization (RAR) lets the odds shift toward the treatment that is looking better. Thompson's motive in 1933 was ethical: to spare patients from being "sacrificed" to the inferior treatment. In operations research it is a multi-armed bandit problem.

## Why it matters

It asks a randomized trial to do two jobs. The comparison is cleanest when allocation is fixed and balanced, while a bandit maximizes benefit inside the study by abandoning the losing arm.

## In the book

In a two-arm trial of 400 patients (0.30 against 0.45), Thompson sampling put 87 percent on the better arm but cut power from 88 percent to 61 percent. In a four-arm trial with a fixed control share of one quarter, a burn-in and a cap, the adaptive design put about half of 600 patients on the best arm and had higher power for the best arm against control than equal allocation. The book's conditions for a case for RAR: several experimental arms, a fast endpoint, a trial large enough to converge but small in population, a fixed control share with concurrent controls, and an exploratory or seamless role.

## Pitfalls

For a confirmatory two-arm trial, use fixed allocation. The EMA draft of October 2026 concludes that RAR is not supported in confirmatory platform trials. A fixed control share alone does not establish regulatory acceptability. Drift in calendar time is the failure that matters most (Time trend bias).

## Check yourself

- Q: In which setting does the book find the best case for RAR? A: Several experimental arms with a shared control held at a fixed share.
- Q: What does a two-arm confirmatory trial call for? A: Fixed allocation.
R functions (bayestrials): rar_simulate, rar_two_arm, rar_four_arm, rar_alloc_probs

title: Restricted mean survival time
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5 Non-proportional hazards
text:
Restricted mean survival time. Also called: RMST. The area under the survival curve up to a horizon, whose difference is the average event-free time gained and needs no proportional hazards.

## What it is
$$
\mathrm{RMST}(\tau) = \int_0^\tau S(t)\,dt,
$$
the area under the survival curve up to horizon $\tau$ (eq-sv-rmst). Its posterior is computed from draws of the survival curve.

## Why it matters
The RMST difference is the average event-free time gained within $\tau$, in months or years, the unit patients and payers think in, and it does not require proportional hazards.

## In the book
The control arm, with hazard 0.15 per year, has RMST 3.52 years over five years. In 54 oncology trials with reconstructed patient data, the hazard ratio gave on average a larger effect than the RMST ratio (average ratio 1.11, with substantial variation), and the authors recommend routine RMST reporting.

## Pitfalls
It requires a horizon. The choice of $\tau$ is part of the estimand and must be fixed in the protocol. A supportive RMST analysis chosen after a blinded look at the pooled curve would draw a regulatory objection.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does the RMST difference measure? A: Average event-free time gained within $\tau$.
R functions (bayestrials): surv_rmst, surv_nph_example

title: TRIUMPH-3
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.8.1 Retatrutide in TRIUMPH-3
text:
TRIUMPH-3. Also called: retatrutide. A retatrutide trial in obesity with cardiovascular disease whose imprecise cardiovascular interval the book turns into posteriors under flat, discounted SELECT and skeptical priors.

## What it is
TRIUMPH-3 is an 80-week randomized phase 3 trial in obesity with established cardiovascular disease, with 1,946 participants in the registry and a registered primary outcome of percent change in body weight.
Lilly announced topline results on 23 July 2026.

## Why it matters
A class prior turns an imprecise cardiovascular interval into a posterior.

## In the book
The announcement reports 44 five-component events on pooled retatrutide against 52 on placebo, hazard ratio 0.82 with interval 0.55 to 1.22.
The three-component hazard ratio in the same announcement was 1.12 (0.64 to 1.96).
The class prior is SELECT, hazard ratio 0.80 (0.72 to 0.90), discounted by inflating its variance: doubling for half weight, quadrupling for quarter weight.
For contrast the book uses a skeptical normal prior with standard deviation 0.15 and a flat prior.
The disagreement among the rows is the scientific question: whether a class effect measured with a three-component outcome in semaglutide carries over to a triple agonist and a five-component outcome.

## Pitfalls
With 96 events in all, none of the rows is a confirmatory result.
The three-component hazard ratio above 1 is a reason to give the class prior a low weight, not to hide it.

## Check yourself
- Q: How is half weight for the SELECT prior implemented? A: By doubling its variance.
