It is easy to explain to a team and an ethics committee, needs no software, and never escalates after two DLTs in a cohort.

## In the book
Across the three scenarios the 3+3 finds the true MTD in only about half or fewer of trials, and in roughly half it recommends a dose below the MTD (47 percent in scenario A, 53 percent in B). Its mean sample size is between about 10 and 19 patients, and about three or fewer patients are treated at toxic doses on average. One DLT in six with a Beta(0.25, 0.75) prior gives a Beta(1.25, 5.75) posterior.

## Pitfalls
The rule states no target toxicity rate, and the 3+3 forgets all previous doses when it moves. Little information is gathered at the recommended dose. It may still be reasonable for a well-understood toxicity profile and few doses.

## Check yourself
- Q: What happens after one DLT among the first three patients? A: Three more are treated at the same dose.
- Q: Why is the 3+3 called safe? A: Few patients are exposed at toxic doses, at the price of a low chance of finding the MTD.
R functions (bayestrials): dose_three_plus_three, dose_simulate

title: Time-to-event endpoint
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18 Time-to-Event Endpoints
text:
Time-to-event endpoint. Also called: survival analysis, time to event. An endpoint measured as the time to death, progression or another event, with patients censored if the event has not happened by last contact.

## What it is
Let $T$ be the event time and $S(t) = \Pr(T > t)$ the survival function. The hazard is $h(t) = \lim_{\delta \to 0}\Pr(t \le T < t + \delta \mid T \ge t)/\delta$, the cumulative hazard is $H(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,du$, and $S(t) = e^{-H(t)}$. Patients event-free at the data cutoff, or lost to follow-up, are censored: their event time is only known to exceed the last contact.

## Why it matters
Most confirmatory trials in cardiology and oncology are event driven. The endpoint is the time to death, progression or a major adverse cardiovascular event. The estimand must name the population, the variable, the handling of intercurrent events and the summary measure, chosen before the trial.

## In the book
SELECT planned 1,225 events and observed 1,270, and REWIND observed 1,257. A trial of 17,604 patients is, statistically, a trial of about 1,270 events.

## Pitfalls
The information is the number of events of the primary endpoint as defined, so any change to the definition or its intercurrent-event handling changes the information.

## Check yourself
- Q: What does a censored patient's record tell you? A: The event time exceeds the last contact.
- Q: What does a time-to-event trial wait for? A: A target number of events, not a fixed sample size.

title: Time trend bias
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.5 Time trends: the failure that matters most
text:
Time trend bias. Also called: temporal drift, time trends. Confounding of arm with calendar time when response drifts during enrollment, which inflates the type I error of response-adaptive randomization but not of blocked equal allocation.

## What it is

Suppose the background response rate rises during enrollment because the standard of care improves or the site mix changes. An arm that benefited from early luck receives more of the later, healthier patients and looks better still. Nothing about the treatment has changed, and the comparison is confounded with calendar time.

## Why it matters

This is the central practical objection to RAR in confirmatory trials, and the property that fixed allocation with permuted blocks was designed to defeat.

## In the book

In a null trial of 400 patients with response 0.30 in both arms, the response rises linearly across enrollment by a drift $d$. Under equal allocation, drift is harmless even for a 30-point drift. Under Thompson sampling the naive test's type I error climbs with the drift, and capped Thompson reduces but does not remove the problem. Three fixes should be pre-specified as a package: stratify the analysis by enrollment period, use burn-in and a cap, and keep control allocation fixed. A fourth route models the trend, as in the Bayesian time machine.

## Pitfalls

Stratifying costs power. Plain Thompson stays near 0.05 even when stratified until the critical value is calibrated by simulation. A Bayesian analysis does not by itself solve the confounding, because the model must contain the drift.

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is equal allocation immune to drift? A: Allocation does not depend on the outcomes, so each period contributes equally to both arms.
- Q: What does stratifying by enrollment period require? A: Allocation fixed within each period and arms compared only within a period.
R functions (bayestrials): rar_drift_sweep, rar_simulate

title: Tipping-point analysis
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.8.1 The tipping-point prior
text:
Tipping-point analysis. Also called: tipping point, tipping-point prior. Reporting the least extreme prior in a stated family for which the success criterion is no longer met, instead of the conclusion under one prior.

## What it is

A tipping-point prior is the least extreme prior in a stated family for which the success criterion is no longer met. The idea is borrowed from the handling of missing data. One family varies the prior standard deviation, another varies the prior mean at a fixed spread.

## Why it matters

It replaces a debate about the right prior with a statement about which priors the regulator would have to hold to disagree. A tipping point in an incredible region, such as a skeptic who thought the drug harmful or a prior worth two thirds of the trial, supports the claim that the data drive the conclusion. One close to the sponsor's own prior is a warning that the prior drives the answer.

## In the book

For the 508-event trial, holding the skeptical spread of 0.175, benefit drops below 0.975 only if the prior mean expects harm on average. For pediatric belimumab in lupus, FDA requested a post hoc analysis borrowing from adult trials with weight $w$. The posterior probability of efficacy was at least 97.5 percent whenever $w$ was 0.55 or more.

## Pitfalls

The family and criterion belong in the statistical analysis plan before unblinding. A family chosen after seeing the data would be a way of looking for a prior that works.

## Check yourself

- Q: What is a tipping-point prior? A: The least extreme prior in a family that reverses the success decision.
- Q: What did the belimumab analysis report? A: Efficacy of at least 97.5 percent once the borrowing weight was 0.55 or more.

title: TITE-BOIN
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.5 Late-onset toxicity and utility-based interval designs
text:
TITE-BOIN. Also called: late-onset toxicity. An interval design that assigns doses in real time while some enrolled patients still have pending toxicity data.

## What it is
Late-onset toxicity means the outcome of each cohort is not known before the next is dosed. The time-to-event CRM of Cheung and Chappell uses the fraction of the observation window completed for patients without a DLT, while observed DLTs contribute full information, so enrollment need not pause. TITE-BOIN builds the same idea into the interval design.

## Why it matters
TITE-BOIN allows real-time dose assignment while some toxicity data are pending. It addresses late-onset toxicity, which is common for targeted agents and immunotherapy, and rapid accrual.

## In the book
BOIN12 is a related design for the efficacy-toxicity trade-off. It targets the optimal biologic dose and is simple enough that its decision rules can be tabulated in the protocol as BOIN's are. A review covers design strategies for dose-optimization trials, including the randomized comparison the FDA guidance recommends.

## Pitfalls
The reviewer will ask how late toxicities and dose reductions after cycle 1 are handled in the dose decision.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why can enrollment continue under TITE-BOIN? A: Pending patients contribute partial information, so no pause is needed.

title: Toxicity monitoring
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.4 Toxicity monitoring inside a trial
text:
Toxicity monitoring. Also called: toxicity monitoring inside a trial. A prespecified stopping table that pauses a single-arm study when the posterior probability of exceeding the acceptable toxicity rate is high, with exact operating characteristics.

## What it is

Inside a trial the question is prospective: given a toxicity the protocol defines, when should enrollment pause?

The traditional counterpart is a repeated exact binomial test of $H_0: q \le \bar q$ after every five patients, up to 40, with $\bar q = 0.2$. A Pocock-type version uses the same nominal level at every look.

The Bayesian rule takes a Beta(0.5, 2.5) prior and, after every five patients, pauses if

$$
\Pr(q > \bar q \mid x, n) > \kappa, \qquad \kappa = 0.75.
$$

This is eq-safety-toxrule. It reduces to a table of counts, which is how it goes into a protocol and a DMC charter.

## Why it matters

The type I error of a safety boundary is a design choice stated with its consequences, set by the asymmetric loss between exposing patients and delaying a good drug.

## In the book

The Bayesian rule stops at 3 of the first 5 patients and 11 of 40. The Pocock-type rule at overall level 0.05 requires 4 of the first 5, and 14 of 40. The Bayesian rule is a constant-nominal-level repeated test at these looks. It does not escape repeated-testing arithmetic and chooses a point on it.

Operating characteristics are exact, from a dynamic program with no simulation. At the acceptable rate 0.2 the Bayesian rule pauses with probability 0.384. At a true rate of 0.3 expected enrollment is 19.7 of 40.

## Pitfalls

- A DMC would not follow either table mechanically. The boundary is a flag that triggers a review.
- The false alarm probability is guaranteed only for the stated schedule, not for looks off it.

title: Toxicity monitoring
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.4 Toxicity monitoring inside a trial
text:
## Check yourself

- Q: Is the Bayesian toxicity rule outside the family of repeated tests? A: No. It matches a Pocock-type test with a constant nominal level.
R functions (bayestrials): tox_bayes_boundary, tox_oc, tox_pocock_boundary

title: TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.4 TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2: a prespecified biomarker strategy and baseline tau strata
text:
TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2. A donanemab trial in early Alzheimer's disease with a biomarker-guided treatment duration and baseline tau strata, used to show how a Bayesian analysis could handle prespecified features.

## What it is
TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 randomized 1,736 participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease to donanemab or placebo, with efficacy measured at 18 months (76 weeks).
It reported a 35 percent slowing of decline on the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale in the prespecified low and medium tau population of 1,182 participants, and 22 percent in the combined population of 1,736.

## Why it matters
It is a different kind of case from SELECT: the traditional apparatus handled two prespecified features, and regulators accept them when specified in advance.

## In the book
The first feature is treatment duration guided by a biomarker: participants completed donanemab once they reached a prespecified level of amyloid plaque clearance, and 52 percent of the low and medium tau participants had reached it by one year.
The trial therefore estimates the effect of the strategy "stop when cleared" against placebo, and the estimand has to say so.
The second is baseline tau stratification, which does not change with accumulating results and is not an adaptive feature.
A prespecified hierarchical model could estimate effects in both strata, 1,182 in the low and medium tau stratum and 552 in the high tau stratum, with borrowing.
The weight on a stratum's own estimate is $\tau_b^2/(\tau_b^2 + s^2)$, so smaller strata and smaller between-stratum variance mean more shrinkage; the table in the book is illustrative, not the trial's estimates.

## Pitfalls
A hierarchical model that shrinks a null stratum toward a positive pooled effect raises the false-positive rate for that stratum.
Such a model needs a prespecified model, a rationale for exchangeability and a simulation of type I error where the effect is in one stratum only.

title: TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.4 TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2: a prespecified biomarker strategy and baseline tau strata
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Is the tau stratification an adaptation? A: No, tau is measured at baseline and the strata do not change with results.
- Q: What does a regulator worry about for the biomarker-guided duration? A: The estimand and the integrity of blinding.

title: Trial cost
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.2 Trial cost
text:
Trial cost. Also called: cost of a trial. The money a trial spends, split in the book into variable cost that scales with person-time and fixed cost that does not, so that early stopping saves only part of the budget.

## What it is
Moore and colleagues reviewed the pivotal trials of 59 novel agents approved by the FDA in 2015 and 2016.
The median estimated cost of a pivotal trial was 19.0 million dollars, the costliest single trial was about 347 million, and the mean for the five cardiovascular pivotal trials was 157.2 million.

## Why it matters
Cost is one of the currencies in which the book prices the SELECT saving.
The saving is not proportional to the whole budget: variable costs such as site payments, visits, monitoring, laboratory work and drug supply scale with person-time, while fixed costs such as protocol development, startup, regulatory work and the final analysis do not.

## In the book
The book has no published cost for SELECT, which is far larger than the typical trial in that review.
It takes the cardiovascular mean of 157 million dollars as the base case and 350 million and 600 million as scenarios for a larger trial, not as estimates for any particular trial.
The modeled saving is the avoided share of person-time times the variable share, and the variable share is an assumption because the split is proprietary.
For a trial of SELECT's size the order of magnitude is tens to a couple of hundred million dollars.

## Pitfalls
The figure leaves out the cost of longer exposure that a regulator might require to build the safety database, which would reduce the saving.
The book ranks the cost row as an order of magnitude, a weaker basis than the events and patient-years rows.

title: Trial cost
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.2 Trial cost
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: Why is the saving smaller than the avoided share of the budget? A: Only variable cost scales with person-time, and fixed cost does not.
- Q: Is 157 million dollars the cost of SELECT? A: No, it is the cardiovascular mean from the review, used as a base case.

title: trialr
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text:
trialr. An R package for Bayesian clinical trial designs fitted with Stan, including dose finding and phase II designs.

## What it is
trialr is an R package for Bayesian clinical trial designs fitted with Stan. It includes dose-finding and phase II designs.

## Why it matters
It is one of the established tools listed for readers who want existing implementations.

## In the book
The book lists it among the R packages on CRAN, and did not check its version.

## Pitfalls
The descriptions in the book cover only the purpose of each tool, so a reader should consult the documentation for current features and versions.

## Check yourself
- Q: Which engine does trialr use to fit designs? A: Stan.
- Q: Which kinds of designs does it include? A: Dose-finding and phase II designs.

title: Truncated trial bias
al: early stopping bias; truncated trials overestimate
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.12.1 Truncated trials overestimate: Bassler and colleagues (2010)
text:
Truncated trial bias. Also called: early stopping bias, truncated trials overestimate. A trial stopped early because the observed effect was large overstates the true effect, and a boundary does nothing for the estimate at stopping.

## What it is

A trial that stops at an early look because it crossed a boundary stopped because the observed effect was large, and a large observed effect is more likely to be a positive deviation from the truth. The estimate is biased away from the null. The bias is bigger the smaller the trial and the earlier the stop.

## Why it matters

A boundary controls the type I error but does nothing for the point estimate at stopping. Even an O'Brien-Fleming design is not immune. A trial stopped early should report its estimate with the information fraction and the interval in view.

## In the book

Bassler and colleagues matched 91 randomized trials stopped early for benefit, asking 63 distinct questions, to 424 nontruncated trials. The pooled ratio of relative risks was 0.71 (95% confidence interval 0.65 to 0.77), so truncated trials gave on average a 29 percent lower relative risk.

The difference was independent of whether a statistical stopping rule was present and of methodological quality, and it was greatest in smaller studies.

The frequentist remedy is a bias-adjusted estimator, and a shrinkage prior is the Bayesian answer.

## Pitfalls

- The size of the problem is debated. Freidlin and Korn argue the bias is smaller when boundaries are conservative.
- Bayesian shrinkage can reduce upward selection bias, but its bias and coverage depend on the prior and should be evaluated under the stopping rule.

## Check yourself

- Q: What ratio of relative risks did Bassler and colleagues find? A: 0.71, truncated over nontruncated.
- Q: Does a conservative boundary remove the bias? A: No, it controls type I error but not the estimate at stopping.

title: The two bars
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.5.1 The two bars
text:
The two bars. Also called: Bayes factor bar, level bar. A fixed-level test passes a constant bar on Z squared, while a Bayes rule passes a bar that grows with the logarithm of the information, and the two cross.

## What it is

A fixed-level one-sided test acts when $Z_n^2$ passes a constant bar, 3.84 at one-sided alpha 0.025, whatever the sample size. A Bayes rule that acts when the alternative is at least as probable as the null passes a bar that grows with the log of the information:

$$
Z_n^2 \;\ge\; L_n + C, \qquad L_n \sim \log n, \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_a}.
$$

This is eq-bayes-toll. The constant $C$ is zero at equal prior odds and positive when the null is favored.

## Why it matters

At small samples the Bayes bar is lower, at large samples higher. They cross where, with $C = 0$,

$$
n^\ast \;=\; e^{z_\alpha^2} \;=\; e^{3.84} \;\approx\; 46.
$$

This is eq-crossing. The exact Gaussian expression puts the crossing at $I_n\tau^2 = 41.6$. So the claim that Bayesian trials need less evidence fails against a single unadjusted look.

## In the book

For $\tau = 0.25$ on the log hazard ratio, the crossing corresponds to $I_n > 730$ and about 2,900 events (exactly 666 and about 2,660), the size of a large cardiovascular outcome trial. A third toll for monitoring raises the bar by about 7.38 at alpha 0.025.

## Pitfalls

The comparison is for the uncalibrated point-null rule with a symmetric normal alternative. A Bayesian bar calibrated to the same type I error is never lower at a single look without an informative prior.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which bar is higher for a very large trial, the fixed-level test or the uncalibrated Bayes rule? A: The Bayes rule.
- Q: Where do the bars cross for a unit-information prior? A: At about 46 observations, exactly 41.6.
R functions (bayestrials): bayes_bar, crossing_n

title: Two-group comparison
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.1 One trial, two endpoints
text:
Two-group comparison. Also called: two group comparison. The basic trial question of whether two arms differ, built in the book from one simulated trial with a binary and a continuous endpoint.

## What it is
A trial ends with two rows of numbers, one per arm, and the question: are they different? The book uses one trial with 100 patients per arm, allocated by a fair coin. The binary version has a control response rate of 30% and a true drug rate of 45%. The continuous version has a true extra fall of 4 mmHg in systolic blood pressure and a patient standard deviation of 12 mmHg.

## Why it matters
Patients differ, so a difference in averages comes with a question attached: would a gap like this appear anyway, from the luck of which patients landed where? A test is a procedure for answering it honestly. Notation: $p_j$ is the response probability in arm $j$, with $j = 0$ for control, and $\theta$ is the treatment effect, $p_1 - p_0$ or $\mu_1 - \mu_0$.

## In the book
In the simulated binary trial 30 of 100 respond on control and 45 of 100 on the drug. RECOVERY's dexamethasone comparison is statistically the same kind of trial: 482 of 2104 (22.9%) died on dexamethasone against 1110 of 4321 (25.7%) on usual care, an age-adjusted rate ratio of 0.83 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.93). The analysis is frequentist: only a p-value and an interval. The same 2.8 point gap in a trial of 100 per arm would be buried in a standard error of about 0.06.

## Pitfalls
Each patient has two potential outcomes and only one is seen. Randomization lets the observed gap stand in for the unobservable average difference.

title: Two-group comparison
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.1 One trial, two endpoints
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: What is the true effect in the binary version? A: 15 percentage points, 45% against 30%.
- Q: Why did the 2.8 point RECOVERY gap decide the question? A: The trial had thousands of patients, not 100 per arm.
R functions (bayestrials): sim_two_arm_binary

title: Two one-sided tests
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.7 Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
text:
Two one-sided tests. Also called: TOST. A test of equivalence that rejects two one-sided nulls, one at each end of the equivalence interval, and declares equivalence only if both reject.

## What it is
TOST runs one one-sided test against each end of the equivalence margin, and equivalence is declared only if both reject. This is the same as the confidence interval lying entirely inside the margin. For bioequivalence it is applied to $\eta = \log\rho$ and is equivalent to checking that the 90 percent confidence interval lies inside $(\log 0.80, \log 1.25)$.

## Why it matters
Schuirmann's procedure gives the confidence-interval criterion a test form. Westlake had proposed a symmetric confidence interval for the same purpose. TOST is the standard in FDA's final guidance of May 2026.

## In the book
Under a reference prior each one-sided posterior tail probability equals the corresponding one-sided TOST p-value. If both p-values are below 0.05, the posterior probability of equivalence exceeds 0.90. The TOST p-value is the larger of the two one-sided p-values.

## Pitfalls
Most clinical efficacy trials that say equivalence mean noninferiority, and the one-sided test is the more common. Framing a trial as equivalence adds a lower-bound requirement that a noninferiority question does not need.

## Check yourself
- Q: When is equivalence declared by TOST? A: Only when both one-sided tests reject.
- Q: What is the TOST p-value reported for a data set? A: The larger of the two one-sided p-values.

title: Type I error
al: type I error rate; alpha; false positive rate
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.7 Two kinds of error, and power
text:
Type I error. Also called: type I error rate, alpha, false positive rate. Rejecting the null when the drug has no effect, which means approving something useless; its probability is the level alpha of the test.

## What it is
A type I error is rejecting $H_0$ when the drug has no effect: approving something useless. Its probability is the level of the test, $\alpha$. The language of type I and type II errors comes from Neyman and Pearson. It is a probability computed under the null world.

## Why it matters
The rate is a promise about the procedure, made before any data exist: if the drug does nothing, at most a fraction $\alpha$ of trials run this way will declare success. It is the reason regulators trust the design. Regulators fix $\alpha$ by convention and leave $\beta$ to the sponsor.

## In the book
Run the binary trial many times with no effect and apply the rule "reject if $Z > 1.96$": the rejection rate is the type I error rate, close to the nominal 2.5%. A type I error falls mostly on future patients, who receive a drug that does not work, and on the regulator who approved it.

## Pitfalls
The promise survives repeated use only if the analysis plan is fixed in advance. At fixed information, lowering $\alpha$ generally increases $\beta$ and reduces power. If a sponsor sees the drug ahead and then declares a one-sided test at 0.05, the type I error doubles to 5%.

## Check yourself
- Q: In which world is $\alpha$ computed? A: The null world, where the drug does nothing.
- Q: What happens to the error rate if you test naively at 1.96 at each of four looks? A: The overall one-sided error is about 0.063, more than twice 0.025.
R functions (bayestrials): sim_two_arm_binary, z_test_binary

title: Type II error
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.7 Two kinds of error, and power
text:
Type II error. Also called: beta error. Failing to reject the null when the drug does work, which means abandoning something useful; its probability is beta and power is one minus beta.

## What it is
A type II error is failing to reject $H_0$ when the drug does work. Its probability is $\beta$, and the probability of avoiding it, $1 - \beta$, is the Statistical power. Unlike $\alpha$, $\beta$ is computed under a specific alternative. Power is a function of the true effect, so "90% power" invites the question: for what effect?

## Why it matters
A type II error falls on future patients, who will not receive a drug that would have helped, and on the sponsor who abandoned it. Sponsors pay for it, which is why they ask for more efficient designs.

## In the book
In the simulated trial with 100 patients per arm and a true rise from 30% to 45%, the power is 60%, so a drug that works would be missed four times in ten. Power is roughly 35% at 50 per arm, 78% at 150 and 97% at 300, and the customary 80% or 90% needs roughly 160 to 215 patients per arm. The continuous trial, with a 4 mmHg effect and standard deviation 12 mmHg, has power of about 65% at 100 per arm.

## Pitfalls
The two errors trade against each other. The only way to improve both at once is a smaller standard error, through more patients, a less noisy endpoint or better use of information. Success in one observed trial is not evidence that a 60% power design was good.

title: Type II error
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.7 Two kinds of error, and power
text:
## Check yourself
- Q: What does the book call the sample size proportional to at one-sided 0.025 and 90% power? A: $(z_{0.025} + z_{0.10})^2 = 10.51$ divided by the squared standardized effect.
- Q: Does a large p-value show no effect? A: No. In a trial of 50 per arm the 30% versus 45% drug has power near one in three.
R functions (bayestrials): sim_two_arm_binary, z_test_binary

title: Umbrella trial
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.2 Definitions: master protocol, basket, umbrella, platform
text:
Umbrella trial. Also called: umbrella design. A trial that evaluates multiple drugs concurrently for a single disease, often assigning patients to arms by biomarker.

## What it is

FDA's June 2026 draft defines an umbrella trial as "a trial designed to evaluate multiple drugs concurrently for a single disease or condition". An umbrella fixes the disease and varies the drug, often assigning patients to arms by biomarker.

## Why it matters

The three master protocol kinds differ in what is held fixed. A basket fixes the drug and varies the population, as in tissue-agnostic approvals built on a molecular marker. A platform fixes the disease and the infrastructure and lets the drugs change over time.

## In the book

In practice the terms overlap. I-SPY 2 is a platform with biomarker-defined signatures, and many baskets are platforms for one drug family. The taxonomy was set out by Woodcock and LaVange (2017), and early reviews of how often the three designs are used are cited. The FDA 2022 final guidance on oncology master protocols recommends a common standard-of-care control for multiple drugs in one disease.

## Pitfalls

The umbrella is not the same as a platform: an umbrella evaluates drugs concurrently, while a platform lets drugs enter and leave in an ongoing manner. The 2026 FDA text is a draft.

## Check yourself

- Q: What does an umbrella trial hold fixed? A: The disease.
- Q: Which master protocol fixes the drug instead? A: The basket trial.

title: Utility function
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.3 A Bayesian formulation: utility
text:
Utility function. Also called: utility. An elicited value for each joint efficacy and toxicity outcome, averaged under the posterior to score a dose.

## What it is
Let $\pi_E(x)$ be the probability of a favorable efficacy outcome at dose $x$ and $\pi_T(x)$ the probability of toxicity. Elicit a utility for each of the four joint outcomes: efficacy without toxicity is best, no efficacy with toxicity worst. The expected utility of a dose is the posterior average. A design picks the dose that maximizes it among acceptable doses, meeting a minimum efficacy and maximum toxicity bound at a stated posterior probability.

## Why it matters
It states the benefit-risk trade-off directly, so the chosen dose can sit below the MTD.

## In the book
In the illustrative curves, toxicity reaches 0.25 at dose 5, so the MTD is dose 5, but expected utility is highest at dose 4. The efficacy gain from 4 to 5 is small and the toxicity cost is not. The numbers 100, 40, 0 and -60 are illustrative, not clinical.

## Pitfalls
Utilities are elicited and subjective, and the winning dose depends on them. The protocol should record who elicited them, from whom, on what basis, and how the result changes if they change.

## Check yourself
- Q: In the book's example, which dose maximizes expected utility? A: Dose 4, one below the MTD.

title: Vaccine efficacy trial
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.5 BNT162b2: a Bayesian confirmatory trial that led to an authorization
text:
Vaccine efficacy trial. A trial that estimates vaccine efficacy from case counts in two arms; in the book BNT162b2 is a confirmatory trial whose Bayesian analysis led to an authorization.

## What it is
A vaccine efficacy trial splits cases between the vaccine and placebo arms, models the vaccine share of cases with a beta-binomial model, and transforms that share into vaccine efficacy (VE); VE of 30% corresponds to a vaccine share of 0.7/1.7. The success bar is set on VE above a clinical margin, not on zero.
As the example, the BNT162b2 phase 2/3 trial (Protocol C4591001, Pfizer and BioNTech) began in July 2020, and its statistical analysis plan makes the primary analysis Bayesian.
Unlike the SELECT and REWIND reconstructions, the Bayesian rule was the trial's own decision rule.

## Why it matters
It shows a regulatory path already traveled: a minimally informative prior, a margin, calibration to 0.025 one-sided, and thresholds fixed before the first case.

## In the book
The model is conjugate beta-binomial with prior Beta(0.700102, 1) on the vaccine share of cases.
The success criterion is $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} \ge 30\% \mid \text{data})$ above 0.995 at an interim analysis and 0.986 at the final analysis, calibrated so the overall one-sided type I error is 2.5 percent.
The final analysis was planned at 164 first primary cases, with a nonbinding futility rule at a predictive probability of success of 5 percent or less.
The bar is on vaccine efficacy of 30 percent and not on zero, so the criterion has $a$ different from zero.
The trial counted 8 cases in the vaccine group and 162 in the placebo group, an efficacy of 95.0 percent with a 95 percent credible interval of 90.3 to 97.6 percent.
FDA issued an emergency use authorization on 11 December 2020 for ages 16 and older and approved the biologics license application on 23 August 2021.

title: Vaccine efficacy trial
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.5 BNT162b2: a Bayesian confirmatory trial that led to an authorization
text:
## Pitfalls
The plan on ClinicalTrials.gov is a sponsor document with several amendments.
FDA's announcements contain no statement on the Bayesian criterion, so the lesson concerns the sponsor's side.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why are there two thresholds, 0.995 and 0.986? A: One applies at the interim analyses and one at the final, calibrated for 2.5 percent overall.
- Q: How does this case differ from SELECT? A: The Bayesian analysis was the actual analysis, not a counterfactual.

title: Ville's inequality
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2.2 Test martingales and Ville's inequality
text:
Ville's inequality. Also called: Ville inequality. For a test martingale, the probability that it ever reaches 1/alpha under the null is at most alpha, whatever the looks or the reason for stopping.

## What it is

For a test martingale $E_n$ with $E_0 = 1$, the bound holds for the whole path:

$$
\mathbb{P}_{H_0}\Bigl(\sup_{n} E_n \ge 1/\alpha\Bigr) \le \alpha .
$$ Markov's inequality gives the bound at one fixed time. Ville's inequality gives it for the supremum over all times, the probability that the wealth is ever above $1/\alpha$.

## Why it matters

The gambler may look after every patient, pause, resume, or stop for a reason the protocol never considered. The probability of ever declaring success under the null is still at most $\alpha$. This is what "anytime-valid" means.

## In the book

For likelihood ratios the bound is the one Wald used for the error rates of his sequential probability ratio test, and Ville's version covers any nonnegative martingale.

The proof takes the first time $T$ at which $E_n \ge 1/\alpha$. The stopped process is again a nonnegative martingale, so its expectation is one, and Markov's inequality at the stopping time gives $\mathbb{P}(T \le n) \le \alpha$. The argument does not use the distribution of the data, the number of looks, or the reason for stopping.

In safety monitoring the same bound applies to a Bayes factor computed with a fixed prior under the alternative.

## Pitfalls

- The bound is not tight. The wealth overshoots the boundary when it crosses, so the realized type I error is often below nominal.

## Check yourself

- Q: What changes between Markov's and Ville's inequality? A: Markov bounds the wealth at one fixed time. Ville bounds the supremum over all times.
- Q: Does Ville's inequality need the stopping rule to be prespecified? A: No. The proof does not use the number of looks or the reason for stopping.

title: Wald's sequential test
al: Wald SPRT; sequential probability ratio test
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.8.4 Wald's test and the large deviation ledger
text:
Wald's sequential test. Also called: Wald SPRT, sequential probability ratio test. Accumulate the log likelihood ratio and stop when it leaves an interval, giving the smallest expected sample size at fixed error rates but no maximum size.

## What it is

For simple hypotheses $H_0$ and $H_1$, accumulate the log likelihood ratio $\Lambda_n = \sum_{i\le n} \log\{p_1(X_i)/p_0(X_i)\}$. Stop when it leaves $(\log B, \log A)$ with $A = (1-\beta)/\alpha$ and $B = \beta/(1-\alpha)$, accepting $H_1$ at the upper edge and $H_0$ at the lower.

This is the posterior odds rule of a Bayesian with a two-point prior. Wald and Wolfowitz proved it has the smallest expected sample size under both hypotheses among tests with the same error probabilities.

## Why it matters

It is the reference point for everything in sequential monitoring.

## In the book

For a unit-variance normal mean, $H_0: \theta = 0$ against $H_1: \theta = 0.2$ with $\alpha = 0.025$ and $\beta = 0.10$, a fixed-sample test needs 263 patients. The Kullback-Leibler divergence is $\theta^2/2 = 0.02$ per patient, and Wald's approximation to the expected sample size under $H_1$ follows.
$$
\mathbb{E}_1[T] \approx \frac{(1-\beta)\log\{(1-\beta)/\alpha\} + \beta \log\{\beta/(1-\alpha)\}}{\mathrm{KL}(P_1 \| P_0)}.
$$

Whitehead's triangular test is a closed alternative whose boundaries converge at the maximum information, so the trial always ends with a decision.

## Pitfalls

- The sample size has no upper bound. The 95th percentile under $H_1$ is above the fixed-sample size, and a few trials run several times longer.
- It tests two simple hypotheses, whereas a trial's alternative is composite. The remedy is a prior on the effect and the mixture likelihood ratio.

## Check yourself

- Q: Which hypotheses does the SPRT assume? A: Two simple hypotheses.
- Q: Why do trials use group sequential designs instead? A: They have a hard end, a maximum sample size.

title: Weighted log-rank test
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5.2 Tests built for a delayed effect
text:
Weighted log-rank test. Also called: weighted log rank. A log-rank variant, with Fleming-Harrington weights or the MaxCombo maximum, that favors late events when an effect is delayed.

## What it is
The Fleming-Harrington test multiplies each event time's contribution by $S(t)^\rho\{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma$, with $S$ the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate. $\rho = \gamma = 0$ is the ordinary log-rank test. $(0, 1)$ weights late events. The MaxCombo test takes the largest of usually four standardized statistics with $\rho, \gamma \in \{0, 1\}$ and refers it to their multivariate normal distribution.

## Why it matters
Under a delayed effect the weighted and MaxCombo tests have more power than the log-rank test. Under proportional hazards the order reverses: MaxCombo gives up a little, the late-weighted test more. All three hold the level under identical curves.

## In the book
Under a 2-year delay followed by hazard ratio 0.583, the log-rank test has power 0.55, against 0.80 for FH(0,1) and 0.74 for MaxCombo. Under proportional hazards (HR 0.75) the figures are 0.67, 0.55 and 0.65. Under the null the levels are 0.024, 0.022 and 0.021.

## Pitfalls
These test identical curves, and can reject when early harm and late benefit cancel, so significance need not mean patients did better. Modestly weighted tests were proposed to control that risk. The primary test, weights and simulation go in the protocol before the curves are seen.

## Check yourself
- Q: What weights does FH(0,1) favor? A: Late events.
- Q: What does MaxCombo trade? A: A small power premium under proportional hazards for not knowing the shape.
R functions (bayestrials): fh_z

title: Winner's curse
cx: Chapter 10: Multiplicity and Shrinkage > 10.4.3 A numerical illustration: the winner's curse
text:
Winner's curse. The largest of several observed effects is on average too large because it was selected as the largest, and shrinkage corrects it.

## What it is

The largest of $k$ observed effects is on average too large, because it was selected as the largest. A hierarchical estimate pulls it back toward the mean by about the right amount.

## Why it matters

The correction for selection is an estimate that is smaller and more honest, not a harder test applied to an estimate that is still biased.

## In the book

Six arms have true effects drawn from $N(0, 0.2^2)$ on the log odds scale, each estimated with standard error 0.28. The trial reports the arm with the largest observed effect.

The raw estimate of the selected arm is too high on average, while the shrunken estimate has no average bias and a smaller root mean squared error.

The same logic applies to the RECOVERY subgroups: estimates move toward the overall effect in proportion to how little information each carries.

## Pitfalls

- In the simulation the true between-arm spread was known. In a real trial it is estimated, which adds uncertainty, and the model is only as good as its exchangeability assumption.
- A related effect appears at early stops: the estimate after an early stop is biased away from the null.

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the raw estimate of the best-looking arm tend to be too high or too low? A: Too high.
- Q: What does the book say fixes it? A: A smaller, shrunken estimate, not a harder test.

title: Women's Health Initiative
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.12.4 A stop for harm: the Women's Health Initiative (2002)
text:
Women's Health Initiative. Also called: WHI. The estrogen plus progestin trial in healthy postmenopausal women, stopped early for harm on the monitoring board's recommendation in 2002.

## What it is

The estrogen plus progestin trial of the Women's Health Initiative, in healthy postmenopausal women, was stopped early for harm on the recommendation of its data monitoring committee. The principal results were published in JAMA in July 2002.

## Why it matters

It shows a stop for harm as a decision under uncertainty, made with discretion by people who see unblinded data and are independent of the sponsor.

## In the book

At the board's recommendation on 31 May 2002, after a mean of 5.2 years of follow-up, the test statistic for invasive breast cancer had exceeded the stopping boundary for that adverse effect and the global index statistic supported risks exceeding benefits.

Hazard ratios with nominal 95% confidence intervals: 1.26 (1.00 to 1.59) for invasive breast cancer (290 cases), 1.29 (1.02 to 1.63) for coronary heart disease (286 cases), 1.41 (1.07 to 1.85) for stroke, and 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28) for the global index. Total mortality was not affected, at 0.98 (0.82 to 1.18).

## Pitfalls

- The nominal interval for breast cancer reaches 1.00. The stop rested on the crossing of a sequential boundary, not on that interval.
- Safety monitoring in such a trial is not a formal alpha-controlled test of a single endpoint. The committee weighs a pattern of outcomes.

## Check yourself

- Q: What triggered the stop? A: The statistic for invasive breast cancer exceeded its boundary, and the global index supported risks over benefits.
- Q: Was total mortality affected? A: No, the hazard ratio was 0.98.

title: z test
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.4 The normal approximation and the z test
text:
z test. Also called: normal approximation test. The randomization test with a bell curve in place of shuffling: the difference divided by its standard error, read against a standard normal.

## What it is
Under the null, the difference in response rates is approximately normal with mean zero. The statistic uses the pooled rate $\bar p = (x_0 + x_1)/(2n)$:

$$
Z = \frac{\hat p_1 - \hat p_0}{\sqrt{2\bar p(1-\bar p)/n}} .
$$

This is equation eq-testing-z. The reason is the central limit theorem: the observed difference is an average of many small independent contributions. $Z$ counts standard errors from zero, and $z_{0.025} = 1.96$.

## Why it matters
It replaces heavy shuffling with a formula. The z test is an approximation that is least reliable for binary outcomes at moderate $n$ close to the threshold.

## In the book
For the binary trial $\bar p = 0.375$, the standard error is 0.0685 and $Z = 2.19$. The one-sided p-value is 0.014 and the two-sided one is 0.029. For the continuous trial $Z = 4.69/1.83 = 2.56$. The randomization test gives one-sided 0.021 for the binary trial, because its tail includes the whole step at 0.15. A continuity correction moves the cutoff to 0.14, giving $Z = 2.04$ and a one-sided p-value near 0.021.

## Pitfalls
With a binary endpoint, moderate $n$ and a p-value near the threshold, the choice of statistic can change the verdict, so the analysis plan names the test exactly. The approximation fails when responses are rare, $n$ is small or extreme values dominate the mean.

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is the pooled rate used? A: The null says both arms have the same $p$.
- Q: Why do shuffling and the z test differ for the binary trial? A: Shuffled differences move in steps and the normal curve effectively counts only half of the step at 0.15.
R functions (bayestrials): z_test_binary

title: One trial, from the start
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.1 One trial, from the start
text: 1.1 One trial, from the start SELECT randomized 17,604 adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease, without diabetes, to weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, at 804 sites in 41 countries, enrolling from 2018 to 2021 ( Lincoff et al. 2023 ) . The primary endpoint, a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke, occurred in 569 of 8,803 patients on semaglutide and 701 of 8,801 on placebo: 1,270 events in all, a hazard ratio of 0.80 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.72 to 0.90. Mean follow-up was 39.8 months. A result of this kind changes practice, and it was earned honestly: the trial was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 percent power at one-sided 0.025, 1,225 planned events, and one superiority interim analysis at two thirds of them ( Ryan et al. 2020 ) . At that interim (831 events) the data monitoring committee recommended continuing (FDA clinical review), so the trial ran to its end. Important Regulatory anchor Section 505(d) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act ( United States Congress 1962 ) . The statutory standard: a drug is approved on “substantial evidence” of effectiveness, which the Act defines as evidence consisting of adequate and well-controlled investigations. Statute, binding. 21 CFR 314.126 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024 ) .

title: A ledger before the trial
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.2 A ledger before the trial
text: 1.2 A ledger before the trial The decision view of medical evidence is older than the randomized trial, and its first great practitioner was a nurse. Polson and Scott tell the story in AIQ as the beginning of the idea that the numbers a hospital already collects can change what the hospital does ( Polson and Scott 2018 ) . Florence Nightingale worked at the British army’s Barrack Hospital at Scutari, across the Bosphorus from Constantinople, from the winter of 1854 to 1855. Her figures are the founding data set of evidence based hospital care. The death rate among soldiers admitted was worst in February 1855, at 42.7 percent, and after sanitary reforms that began on 17 March 1855 it had fallen to 2.2 percent by June 1855 ( Neuhauser 2003 ; Nightingale 1858 ) . These are secondary-source figures: percentages of soldiers admitted who died in the month, as quoted by Neuhauser, and we have not rechecked them against the 1858 report. Suppose each of the two months had 1000 admissions, so that 427 and 22 deaths are recorded (illustrative counts, since the sources give percentages). With uniform priors on the two death rates, the posterior for the ratio of the June rate to the February rate has median 0.053 and 95 percent interval 0.034 to 0.078. With only 100 admissions a month (43 and 2 deaths, rounded to whole patients), the interval is 0.014 to 0.17. The size of the change is not in doubt at any plausible sample size, and no p-value is needed to see it. What is in doubt is the cause. title: A ledger before the trial
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.2 A ledger before the trial
text: What is in doubt is the cause. The comparison is before and after, not randomized: winter gave way to summer, and other things changed in the same months as the sewers were flushed. Historians dispute how much credit the sanitary reforms deserve, and Nightingale herself noted the arrival of the Sanitary Commission in explaining the decline. A Bayesian reading separates the two questions. The posterior for the change in mortality is concentrated. The posterior for the effect of sanitation on mortality depends on a model of what else changed, and the ledger alone cannot supply it. Why acting was defensible. The decision framework does not require a trial here. The intervention was cheap, the harm of trying it small, and the loss from inaction was measured in hundreds of deaths a month, so the expected utility of reform plausibly exceeded that of waiting under a wide range of priors, while a randomized comparison that left some wards unreformed would have been costly. This is a judgment about inputs (the size of the loss, the cost of acting, the strength of the prior, the value of further information), and the same inputs govern every decision in this book. The ledger is also a reminder that the first step is to count.

title: The price of a trial, of being wrong, and of waiting
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.3.1 The price of a trial, of being wrong, and of waiting
text: The price of a trial, of being wrong, and of waiting Developing one approved drug is estimated to cost between roughly one and two and a half billion dollars once failures and the cost of capital are included: $2,558 million (2013 dollars) in the survey-based estimate of DiMasi and colleagues ( DiMasi, Grabowski, and Hansen 2016 ) , and a median of $985 million (mean $1,336 million, 2018 dollars) for 63 products with public R&D data in Wouters and colleagues ( Wouters, McKee, and Luyten 2020 ) . The pivotal trials themselves are a smaller but still large share. For the 138 pivotal trials behind 59 novel agents approved by the FDA in 2015 and 2016, the median estimated cost was $19.0 million per trial ( Moore et al. 2018 ) . Counted per approved drug, a median of $48 million went on pivotal trials, at $41,413 per patient ( Moore et al. 2020 ) . Phase 3 studies in the United States averaged between $11.5 million (dermatology) and $52.9 million (pain and anesthesia) ( Sertkaya et al. 2016 ) . A patient enrolled is a cost of tens of thousands of dollars, so a design that needs fewer patients saves money in proportion. Most of the spending buys nothing that reaches a patient. Over 2011 to 2020 the likelihood that a drug entering phase

title: What efficiency looks like in real trials
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.3.2 What efficiency looks like in real trials
text: What efficiency looks like in real trials The numbers that follow come from five kinds of evidence, and they should not be mixed up. One is a simulation, three are trials or platforms (one of them frequentist) with their regulatory outcomes, and one is a reconstruction of a real trial. A simulated drug-development program. Saville and Berry simulated 5,000 development programs in which one in ten treatments works. A traditional sequence of two-arm trials needed 1,966 patients on average and 12.0 years to find an effective treatment, and found one with probability 0.78. An open adaptive platform with response-adaptive randomization (ten active treatments) needed 640 patients and 3.2 years, and found one with probability 0.87 ( Saville and Berry 2016 ) . That platform compares each arm with all control patients, including those enrolled before the arm entered; their concurrent-control response-adaptive design 3d, which also used five active treatments and a 100-patient cap per arm, needed 912 patients and 4.6 years, with probability 0.83. These designs differ in several respects, so the comparison does not isolate the contribution of nonconcurrent controls (the bias that non-concurrent controls can bring is discussed in Chapter 20 ). That is a 67 percent reduction in patients and a 73 percent reduction in time. It is a simulation under stated assumptions, not an empirical result, and Chapter 20 says which

title: The counterweight
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.3.4 The counterweight
text: The counterweight None of this says that a Bayesian design is automatically smaller or faster, and the book is built on saying where it is not. In the SELECT reconstruction the earlier decisions come from monitoring on the event grid at a bar that controls type I error, not from a lenient one. Against a single unadjusted look at a fixed level, the Bayesian bar is never lower without an informative prior, and the Bayes-factor bar is higher once \(I_n\tau^2\) exceeds about 42 (derived below; here \(I_n\) is the total information accumulated and \(\tau\) is the standard deviation of the prior on the effect under the alternative). And in a trial where the effect is modest, the scheduled design can win: in the REWIND reconstruction of Section 1.1 the Bayes rule decides earlier when it decides, but it decides less often. A sponsor should prefer a Bayesian design when the efficiency is real in that sponsor’s setting, and should be able to show it by simulation. The rest of the book is how.

title: A trial is a measurement and a decision
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.4 A trial is a measurement and a decision
text: 1.4 A trial is a measurement and a decision D. R. Cox, in Planning of Experiments ( Cox 1958 ) , described the setting of the clinical trial as one of “large uncontrolled variations.” In physics, once the apparatus is working, closely reproducible results emerge: the uncontrolled variation is small next to the effect being measured. A clinical trial lives in a different world. A patient’s outcome swings with the natural history of the disease, with the environment, with the psychological response to being treated, and with the supportive care received. The effect of a new drug, often only a modest improvement over existing therapy, has to be picked out from underneath all of that. Everything in this book follows from that sentence. Because the variation between patients is large and cannot be removed, a single trial can never prove anything. It can only change what we believe, and then someone has to act on the changed belief: approve or not, continue or stop, give the next patient drug A or drug B. A trial is therefore two things at once. It is a measurement, and it is a decision. The traditional apparatus that most readers use every day was built to make the measurement honest and to put a fixed ceiling on one kind of wrong decision. It does that well. This book asks what changes when the decision is put in the foreground, and what the regulator will want to see when it is.

title: The traditional trial, fairly stated
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.5 The traditional trial, fairly stated
text: 1.5 The traditional trial, fairly stated Most readers can recite the traditional design, and it deserves a careful statement before anything is set against it, because it is a coherent and successful answer to a real problem. The sponsor picks a primary endpoint and a treatment effect \(\theta\) that the trial should be able to detect. For a time-to-event endpoint, \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) , so that benefit is positive. The null hypothesis is that the new treatment is no better than control. The sponsor fixes a one-sided type I error rate \(\alpha\) , conventionally \(0.025\) , which is the same as the familiar two-sided \(0.05\) when only benefit counts. It also fixes power \(1-\beta\) , say ninety percent, against the design alternative \(\theta\) . A short calculation then gives the sample size, \[ I_n = \frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2}{\theta^2}, \qquad\text{which is}\qquad I_n = \frac{10.51}{\theta^2}\ \text{at } \alpha = 0.025,\ 1-\beta = 0.90, \] where \(I_n\) is the total information required (for a time-to-event endpoint with one-to-one randomization each event carries information \(1/4\) , so the number of events is \(4I_n\) , as Chapter 9 shows) and \(z_\alpha\) is the upper \(\alpha\) quantile of the standard normal distribution. Patients are randomized one to one, because equal arms minimize the variance of the comparison for a given total. The protocol states in advance when the data will

title: The traditional trial, fairly stated
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.5 The traditional trial, fairly stated
text: and \(z_\alpha\) is the upper \(\alpha\) quantile of the standard normal distribution. Patients are randomized one to one, because equal arms minimize the variance of the comparison for a given total. The protocol states in advance when the data will be analyzed, and the clinical study report (CSR) reports a point estimate, a confidence interval, and a p-value. The trial is “positive” if the p-value is below \(\alpha\) . Three features of this design are easy to underrate. First, the type I error rate is a promise about the procedure, made before any data exist. If the drug does nothing, then over many trials run this way, at most a fraction \(\alpha\) will declare success. That promise is checkable without anyone’s opinion about how likely the drug is to work, and it is the reason the design is trusted by regulators who must deal with sponsors who have every incentive to see a benefit. Second, the promise survives repeated use only if the analysis plan is fixed in advance. If the trial may be examined before it ends, the right to look is paid for. A group sequential design spends part of \(\alpha\) at each interim analysis according to a pre-specified function ( Lan and DeMets 1983 ) , and the boundaries of O’Brien and Fleming ( O’Brien and Fleming 1979 ) are very strict

title: The traditional trial, fairly stated

text: A group sequential design spends part of \(\alpha\) at each interim analysis according to a pre-specified function ( Lan and DeMets 1983 ) , and the boundaries of O’Brien and Fleming ( O’Brien and Fleming 1979 ) are very strict early and nearly the fixed-sample value at the end. If the trial has several arms, doses, endpoints or subgroups, the level is divided among the contrasts (Bonferroni, Holm) or passed along a pre-specified graph, so that the chance of any false claim stays at \(\alpha\) . The apparatus is complete and well understood, and ICH E9 describes it at length. Third, the regulatory machinery has grown around it. Statisticians at sponsors and at the regulator share a vocabulary, a set of software tools, and decades of precedent. A reviewer who sees “one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) , two interim looks with Lan-DeMets O’Brien-Fleming spending, graphical multiplicity procedure” knows what is meant without reading further. Nothing in this book is a reason to abandon that shared language. The question is which parts of the design can be improved, at what price, and in what terms a regulator will accept the improvement.

text: A sample size fixed in advance. The formula \(I_n = 10.51/\theta^2\) commits the trial to a guess \(\theta\) . If the true effect is larger than the guess, the trial runs longer than it needed to and patients stay on the inferior arm for no reason. If it is smaller, power is below target, although the estimate and confidence interval may remain informative. The cost of the guess is paid in one direction or the other, and the formula has no way to adjust. An error budget spent in advance. For four equally spaced analyses, the O’Brien-Fleming boundaries in Figure 1.2 run from about 4.05 at the first look down to about 2.02 at the last. A trial that stops at the first interim look must have produced a result four standard errors from zero. That is a very high bar for a treatment effect of the size a confirmatory trial usually studies. What the sponsor purchases is the right to stop early if the drug is spectacular , and the price is paid by every trial where the drug is merely good. Testing naively at 1.96 at each of four looks does not work either: the overall one-sided error is about 0.063, more than twice the nominal 0.025. That is the problem the spending function solves. A multiplicity correction applied at the end. With

title: From a test to a decision
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.6 From a test to a decision
text: 1.6 From a test to a decision At any moment in a trial, someone with authority to act (a sponsor, a data monitoring committee, a regulator) has a small set of options. Continue enrolling. Stop for futility. Stop because the drug has clearly worked. Take the drug to the regulator. Each option has consequences for patients inside the trial, for patients outside it who will or will not receive the drug later, and for the sponsor. A hypothesis test answers a narrower question, “is the data surprising if the drug does nothing?”, and leaves the rest to judgment outside the statistics. The decision framework tries to put that judgment inside the model, where it can be inspected. It needs three ingredients. A prior. A probability distribution \(\pi(\theta)\) for the treatment effect before the trial, summarizing what is known from earlier phases, from related drugs, from mechanism, and from the history of how often drugs entering a confirmatory trial turn out to work. A model for the data. The likelihood \(p(y \mid \theta)\) is the same as in the traditional analysis. Nothing about the Bayesian approach changes how the outcome data are modeled. After the data arrive, Bayes’ rule turns the prior into a posterior \(\pi(\theta \mid y)\) . A utility (or loss). A statement of what the possible outcomes are worth. Approving a drug that

A statement of what the possible outcomes are worth. Approving a drug that works gains something, approving one that does not harms the patients who take it and wastes resources, and failing to approve a good drug loses what those patients would have gained. Every additional month of the trial and every additional patient randomized to the inferior arm carries a cost. The decision rule follows. At a terminal analysis, suppose the only choices are to approve or to reject. Act when the posterior expected loss of approving is smaller than that of rejecting. Suppose that approving a drug that does not work costs \(L_{\mathrm{I}}\) , that failing to approve a drug that does work costs \(L_{\mathrm{II}}\) , and that correct decisions cost nothing. If \(p\) is the posterior probability that the drug works, the expected loss of approving is \((1-p)L_{\mathrm{I}}\) and the expected loss of not approving is \(p\,L_{\mathrm{II}}\) . Approval is better when \[ p > \frac{L_{\mathrm{I}}}{L_{\mathrm{I}} + L_{\mathrm{II}}}. \tag{1.1}\] The posterior probability must exceed a threshold that depends on the ratio of the two costs, and nothing else. title: The three things a protocol fixes
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.6.1 The three things a protocol fixes
text: The three things a protocol fixes Seen this way, every protocol, traditional or Bayesian, fixes three things before the first patient is randomized. What is known going in. In the traditional protocol this is implicit: the design alternative \(\theta\) and a variance. In a Bayesian protocol it is explicit, as a prior, and the protocol must justify it ( Chapter 8 ). What will count as success. In the traditional protocol, a p-value below \(\alpha\) with adjustments. In a Bayesian protocol, a posterior criterion such as \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , where \(\delta\) is the treatment effect, \(a\) is the smallest effect that matters, and \(c\) is the posterior probability threshold, the form that appears in the FDA draft guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . What the data-generating process allows the sponsor to do along the way. The sample size, the interim analyses, the permitted adaptations, the allocation ratio. These are the protocol’s operating rules, and they determine the operating characteristics: the probability of declaring success under each possible truth. The third item is where the regulator’s interest is concentrated, and it is why the book returns so often to simulation. A regulator does not need to share a sponsor’s prior or utility to evaluate a design. It can ask what the design does : under the null,

It can ask what the design does : under the null, how often does it declare success? Under a plausible alternative, how often does it succeed and how many patients does it use? A Bayesian design is judged, in practice, by the same standard as a traditional one, with the trial simulated many times under pre-specified truths ( Chapter 14 ). The Bayesian approach changes how the rule is built, not the court in which it is judged.

title: Two kinds of "decision maker"
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.6.2 Two kinds of "decision maker"
text: Two kinds of “decision maker” There is a second reason to put the decision in front. Two different people are deciding, and they are not asking the same question. In a study of the prostate cancer choices of two high-profile patients ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) , we found that the physician and the patient reasoned about different quantities. The physician, trained to think in terms of the population and the most likely disease state, reasons from the modal case: the cancer is probably low risk, the patient can probably be cured by something not too aggressive, so why be aggressive for a small gain in cure probability? The patient, who has one life and one decision, reasons about the whole posterior, including the thin tail in which the disease has spread. A colleague of the first patient wrote that this is exactly the distinction: “It’s different to think of things in population terms (and for other people) than to think about them as an individual patient with one life.” Both patients recognized that the published risk estimate was a point estimate with known calibration error, and that it should propagate into the decision rather than be treated as exact. The same asymmetry shows up in trial design. The regulator and the sponsor think at the level of the population: will the drug meet

title: Two kinds of "decision maker"
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.6.2 Two kinds of "decision maker"
text: calibration error, and that it should propagate into the decision rather than be treated as exact. The same asymmetry shows up in trial design. The regulator and the sponsor think at the level of the population: will the drug meet the standard? The patient in the trial, and the patient who will be prescribed the drug afterwards, bears the consequences one at a time. A design that lets the trial stop earlier when the posterior is decisive, or that allocates fewer patients to a losing arm, is a design that takes the second perspective seriously. Using the same decision-theoretic language for both is the attraction of the framework, and a utility function is where the disagreement between them can be written down and argued about instead of left implicit.

title: Preview: the thesis and four mechanisms
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.7 Preview: the thesis and four mechanisms
text: 1.7 Preview: the thesis and four mechanisms The thesis of this book can be stated in two sentences. A regulator approves a drug on evidence that meets a legal standard, and a Bayesian adaptive design can meet that standard sooner and with fewer patients exposed to inferior arms. The saving comes from monitoring, from handling multiple arms jointly, and from using prior information, and it does not come from a lower bar: against a single unadjusted analysis, the Bayesian bar is never lower without an informative prior, and the Bayes-factor bar is higher once \(I_n\tau^2\) exceeds about 42. That last claim is the one a skeptical reader should test first, so here is the arithmetic. A fixed-sample test at one-sided level \(0.025\) demands a standardized score of \(z_\alpha = 1.96\) whatever the amount of information. The Bayes-factor rule, which with even prior odds and equal costs acts when the posterior probability of the alternative exceeds that of the null, demands, approximately, a score whose square exceeds the logarithm of the accumulated information \(n\) . This logarithmic penalty is sometimes called the Ockham penalty: a hypothesis that could explain any data is rewarded less than one that made a sharp prediction, and the reward shrinks as the amount of data grows ( Chapter 7 ). For the stated mixture prior and \(b = 1\) the exact

cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.7 Preview: the thesis and four mechanisms
text: that could explain any data is rewarded less than one that made a sharp prediction, and the reward shrinks as the amount of data grows ( Chapter 7 ). For the stated mixture prior and \(b = 1\) the exact boundary is \(Z_n^2 \ge (1 + 1/q)\log(1+q)\) with \(Z_n > 0\) and \(q = I_n\tau^2\) (information times prior variance); on the score scale the logarithmic approximation of the bar is \(\sqrt{\log n}\) . The exact boundary crosses \(1.96^2\) at \(q \approx 41.6\) , and the approximation \(n = e^{1.96^2} \approx 46.6\) shown in the right-hand panel of Figure 1.2 overstates the crossing ( Chapter 11 ). Beyond the crossing the Bayes-factor bar is higher than the fixed-sample bar ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) . SELECT at the prior scale \(\tau = 0.25\) has \(q = 1270/64 \approx 19.8\) , below the crossing. Holding the Bayes-factor threshold fixed can increase the required information, whereas calibrating a single-analysis rule to the same type I error can instead reproduce the conventional test, and Chapter 9 does the calculation carefully. Three rules are called Bayesian in this book and they should not be confused: the flat-prior posterior threshold of equation Equation 1.1 (numerically a one-sided test), the Bayes-factor rule just described, and the continuously monitored rule calibrated to a type I error of 0.025 (a posterior probability threshold

The saving claimed in this book belongs to the third. So where does the saving come from? Claims that Bayesian designs need fewer patients draw on four mechanisms that are usually run together. They differ in how much they assume, and the book keeps them apart ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) . M1. The deviation scale. The deviation scale is the size of the standardized score that a rule must see before it acts, as a function of the amount of data. A decision rule that must be valid at every possible stopping time, as an anytime-valid e-value rule is (a rule whose false-positive guarantee holds however often and whenever the data are examined), pays a surcharge on top of the logarithmic term, which for the symmetric normal mixture is approximately \(2\log(1/\alpha)\) in squared standardized units when information is large (exactly \((1 + 1/q)\,2\log(1/\alpha)\) , with \(q = I_n\tau^2\) ). In plain terms the surcharge is the extra evidence demanded in return for the right to look at any time without

text: \(2\log(1/\alpha)\) in squared standardized units when information is large (exactly \((1 + 1/q)\,2\log(1/\alpha)\) , with \(q = I_n\tau^2\) ). In plain terms the surcharge is the extra evidence demanded in return for the right to look at any time without planning the looks. The uncalibrated Bayes-factor rule does not pay it. Asymptotically the surcharge is about seventy percent of the boundary term \(10.51\) of a conventional trial, a comparison of boundary terms and not an exact sample-size identity; calibration narrows the realized gap ( Chapter 11 and Chapter 12 ). The surcharge is a property of this normal-mixture construction, not a universal cost of anytime validity, and it is not free. M2. One calibrated threshold for monitoring, and shrinkage for estimation. A group sequential design pays for looking by raising the early boundaries, and Bonferroni pays for several contrasts by raising them again. A Bayesian analysis can monitor continuously with a single calibrated threshold (about 0.995 rather than 0.975 in SELECT), which is another monitoring boundary and not an escape from monitoring costs. For several arms it can shrink the estimates toward a common mean (pulling each arm’s estimate toward the average of all the arms, more strongly when the arm has little data). Shrinkage improves estimation, but it does not by itself control the familywise error rate, particularly under partial null configurations, so the

Shrinkage improves estimation, but it does not by itself control the familywise error rate, particularly under partial null configurations, so the complete confirmatory decision rule still needs its error evaluated and, where required, calibrated. Any saving must be shown between designs with comparable error and power ( Chapter 10 , Chapter 11 ). M3. Informative priors. If effects reaching a confirmatory trial are known to be small ( Sokolova, Sokolov, and Polson 2026 ) , a prior concentrated on small effects carries real information, formally equivalent to a number of pseudo-observations whose size can be reported as a prior effective sample size ( Morita, Thall, and Müller 2008 ) . It is genuine when the prior is right and a bias when it is wrong, so it must come with a sensitivity analysis ( Chapter 8 , Chapter 19 ). M4. Optimal stopping under a sampling cost. When each patient carries a cost, the best Bayes rule is found by working backward from the end of the trial (a dynamic program), and the continuation region (the set of interim results for which the trial keeps going) narrows as the horizon approaches, so its expected sample size is typically below that of a fixed design with comparable

Note Technical note: the arithmetic of M1 and M2 With \(q = I_n\tau^2\) , the exact symmetric normal-mixture bar is \(Z_n^2 \ge (1 + 1/q)(\log(1+q) + 2\log b)\) with \(Z_n > 0\) for a one-sided claim, and the e-value bar is the same with \(b = 1/\alpha\) . The exact surcharge over the Bayes-factor bar at \(b = 1\) is therefore exactly \((1 + 1/q)\,2\log(1/\alpha)\) , whose large-information approximation is \(2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38\) at \(\alpha = 0.025\) . The seventy percent quoted above compares \(7.38\) with \((z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2 = 10.51\) for a conventional trial at 90% power; it compares boundary terms asymptotically and is not a predicted sample-size reduction (subtracting the sample-size equations adds a positive \(\log\) term). We do not quote information ratios between the first O’Brien-Fleming boundary and the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar, because that compares a calibrated rule with an uncalibrated one. One (M1) is a mathematical fact, under stated approximations, that comes with a trade-off. Each is quantified in the chapters named, and the case studies of Chapter 21 apply them to real trials, among them SELECT, the semaglutide cardiovascular outcomes trial of 17,604 patients that read out on 1,270 primary events ( Lincoff et al. 2023 ) , and the four-arm ulcer-surgery trial in which Novick and Grizzle ( Novick and Grizzle 1965 ) made the original Bayesian case for treating several treatments together.
