title: What we claim and what we do not
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.7.1 What we claim and what we do not
text: What we claim and what we do not We claim that a Bayesian design can decide sooner when it is monitored, that the reason is the structure of the monitoring and of the multiple comparisons rather than a lenient threshold, and that the magnitude can matter in patient-years. We do not claim that it dominates. The surcharge a Bayesian rule declines to pay buys a real guarantee: a sponsor who cannot commit to a monitoring plan should pay it. A sponsor who runs a single well-powered look has no reason to pay an anytime-valid surcharge at all, and should use the fixed-sample test. The REWIND trial of dulaglutide is an example in which the scheduled design wins, and Chapter 21 says why. Equally, every Bayesian gain has a price (a prior that must be defended, simulations that must be run, a design that is more work to specify), and the price must be itemized in the currency the regulator accepts, which is simulated operating characteristics under a pre-specified design.

title: What the regulator needs, and what it does not
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.8 What the regulator needs, and what it does not
text: 1.8 What the regulator needs, and what it does not The regulatory standard is easy to misread in either direction. The statute says that a drug may be approved if there is substantial evidence that it has the effect claimed, and defines substantial evidence by reference to adequate and well-controlled investigations ( United States Congress 1962 ) . The regulation 21 CFR 314.126 lists what makes an investigation adequate and well-controlled (objectives, a valid control, bias-minimizing assignment and assessment, reliable response measures, and an adequate analysis; the full list is in Chapter 3 ) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024 ) . Nowhere does the statute or the regulation say “p-value” or “type I error.” A test of significance is the method that ICH E9 describes and that decades of practice have settled on, but the legal standard is evidence, not a procedure. This has two consequences that run through the book. First, a Bayesian design is not exotic in law. It is a different way of showing that the evidence is substantial, and the FDA’s 2026 draft says so by listing three routes to a success criterion: calibration to type I error, direct reading of the posterior, and a benefit-risk decision rule ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . Only the first is tied to type I error. Because the draft

title: What the regulator needs, and what it does not
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.8 What the regulator needs, and what it does not
text: to a success criterion: calibration to type I error, direct reading of the posterior, and a benefit-risk decision rule ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . Only the first is tied to type I error. Because the draft is a draft, it describes what the agency is prepared to discuss, not what it requires. Second, the standard is about the whole design : a valid comparison with a control, measures against bias, and a pre-specified analysis, usually achieved through randomization and blinding (the regulation also recognizes historical controls and settings where blinding is not feasible). A Bayesian posterior computed from a trial without a valid comparison and bias control does not meet 314.126 however sophisticated the model. Bayesian methods change the analysis and the adaptation rules, and they do not change the need for a fair comparison. Chapter 5 explains why a Bayesian still randomizes. ICH E8(R1) adds a point that fits this book’s emphasis on design. It asks sponsors to build quality into the trial from the start, by identifying the factors that are critical to the decision the trial will support and by concentrating effort on those ( International Council for Harmonisation 2021 ) . That is the decision framing in regulatory language: if you cannot say which decision the trial supports and which features of the trial bear on it,

title: What the regulator needs, and what it does not
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.8 What the regulator needs, and what it does not
text: and by concentrating effort on those ( International Council for Harmonisation 2021 ) . That is the decision framing in regulatory language: if you cannot say which decision the trial supports and which features of the trial bear on it, you cannot design it well. A Bayesian adaptive protocol makes those statements explicit, since the prior, the success criterion and the operating rules are all written down, and in that respect the Bayesian approach has an affinity with quality by design. ICH E9 and its addendum E9(R1) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 , 2019 ) remain the statistical baseline, and the FDA adaptive-design guidance of November 2019 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019 ) is the final guidance that allows pre-planned adaptations provided they preserve the integrity of the trial and control the chance of a false conclusion. All of these are described in Chapter 3 . The flat-prior equivalence of the Bayes rule and the one-sided p-value is derived for the normal model in Chapter 7 , where it is also contrasted with a point null.

title: A short history
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.9 A short history
text: 1.9 A short history The decision-theoretic view of trials is as old as the randomized trial. Thompson asked in 1933 for the probability that one treatment is better than another and proposed allocating patients accordingly ( Thompson 1933 ) . Wald’s sequential analysis came from the wartime problem of sampling only as much as needed ( Wald 1947 ) . Grundy, Healy and Rees posed the economic choice of the amount of experimentation in 1956 ( Grundy, Healy, and Rees 1956 ) , and Raiffa and Schlaifer’s 1961 decision theory supplied the preposterior analysis ( Raiffa and Schlaifer 1961 ) . Anscombe and Colton observed in 1963 that a trial is run to inform the treatment of a much larger population of future patients, and derived trial sizes from that population rather than from an error rate ( Anscombe 1963 ; Colton 1963 ) . Novick and Grizzle gave a Bayesian analysis of a four-arm surgical trial in 1965 ( Novick and Grizzle 1965 ) . Cornfield gave a Bayesian sequential test for clinical trials in 1966, and set out the Bayesian outlook for trials in 1969, with a prior probability on the null hypothesis and relative betting odds as the summary of the evidence ( Cornfield 1966 , 1969 ) , and with Halperin and Greenhouse an adaptive allocation procedure ( Cornfield, Halperin, and

title: A short history
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.9 A short history
text: in 1969, with a prior probability on the null hypothesis and relative betting odds as the summary of the evidence ( Cornfield 1966 , 1969 ) , and with Halperin and Greenhouse an adaptive allocation procedure ( Cornfield, Halperin, and Greenhouse 1969 ) ; Lindley’s decision theory ( Lindley 1985 ) gives the general framework. Berry restated the case for Bayesian interim analysis in 1985 and spent the following decades building Bayesian adaptive designs ( Berry 1985 ) , including decision-theoretic stopping boundaries with Ho ( Berry and Ho 1988 ) . Lewis and Berry evaluated Bayesian decision-theoretic designs by their classical operating characteristics ( Lewis and Berry 1994 ) , the idea behind the calibration route that the FDA draft describes ( Chapter 3 ). Whitehead’s “case for frequentism” is the standard statement of the opposing view ( Whitehead 1993 ) . Inside the pharmaceutical industry, the Basel group of Racine, Grieve, Flühler and Smith showed that Bayesian methods could be used routinely in drug development ( Racine et al. 1986 ) . In January 2026 the FDA issued draft guidance on Bayesian methodology for drugs and biologics ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) , and the EMA released a concept paper on Bayesian methods for consultation ( European Medicines Agency, Methodology Working Party 2026 ) ; the regulatory history and the

The objections deserve their strongest form. The prior can decide the answer. Prior choice can change the conclusion, and the FDA draft recommends prespecified sensitivity analyses across reasonable alternative priors, with the influence of the primary prior quantified and justified (answered by sensitivity analysis and the effective sample size of Chapter 8 ). The type I error rate of a Bayesian rule is not controlled by the Bayes calculation itself (answered by calibration through simulation, Chapter 14 ). Interim peeking at accumulating data can bias the trial and the people who run it (answered by firewalls and prespecification, Chapter 11 ). And a Bayesian design is harder to review than a fixed-sample trial (answered, so far as it can be, by the simulation report and by the protocol content of Chapter 23 ). Berry, a leading Bayesian designer, wrote of the promise and the caution of adaptive trials ( Berry 2011 ) , Bauer and colleagues reviewed the opportunities and pitfalls of confirmatory adaptive designs ( Bauer et al. 2016 ) ,

Chapter 2 follows a drug through phases I to IV and shows where each kind of evidence, and each kind of error, enters. Chapter 7 compares the evidence from p-values and Bayes factors and shows how the posterior probability criterion of the FDA draft reads. Chapter 8 is about choosing and defending a prior, which is where most regulatory discussion is concentrated. Part III, The Standard Apparatus Reconsidered. Each chapter takes one component of the traditional design and asks what the decision

Tip In the protocol Whatever the design, the protocol and statistical analysis plan should answer five questions in so many words. What decision does this trial support, and who makes it? What prior information is used, if any, and why? What is the success criterion, in a form that can be evaluated by computer? What are the permitted adaptations and the stopping rules? What are the operating characteristics (type I error, power or probability of success, expected sample size) under pre-specified scenarios, and how were they computed? A traditional protocol answers most of these implicitly. A Bayesian protocol must answer them aloud, and that is as much of a benefit as it is a burden. title: In practice
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > 1.11 In practice
text: 1.11 In practice Three regulatory episodes show the decision framing at work. The detailed accounts, with thresholds and sources, are in Section 3.11 , and the BNT162b2 calculation is worked in Section 6.12 . A Bayesian criterion and a frequentist guarantee are not alternatives. The BNT162b2 posterior bar was tuned by simulation to a one-sided type I error of 2.5 percent ( Chapter 14 ). The number of trials needed is itself a threshold. REBYOTA’s two posterior thresholds stood for one trial and for two, and the stricter one, for two trials, was not met ( Chapter 19 ). A decision rule on a predictive probability stops arms early. I-SPY 2 graduated neratinib on 115 evaluable patients (127 randomized), and the final predictive probability fell below the bar because the last outcomes arrive after the decision ( Chapter 15 ).

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 1: A Trial Is a Decision > Key points
text: Key points A clinical trial works against large uncontrolled variation between patients (Cox). It measures a treatment effect and, at the same time, supports a decision to approve, continue or stop. The traditional design (fixed \(I_n = 10.51/\theta^2\) for \(\alpha = 0.025\) and ninety percent power, one-to-one randomization, spending for looks, multiplicity correction, a p-value in the CSR) is coherent. Its central strength is a fixed ceiling on the false-positive rate, whatever the prior. A Bayesian trial adds a prior, a utility and a rule: at a terminal analysis, approve when the posterior expected loss of approving is smaller than that of rejecting (an interim decision must also weigh the value of continuing). With a flat prior and one look this is the same decision as a one-sided test, with a cost ratio of 39 to 1 at \(\alpha = 0.025\) . The law asks for substantial evidence from adequate and well-controlled investigations (FD&C Act 505(d), 21 CFR 314.126), not for a statistical philosophy. Bayesian methods change the analysis and the adaptation rules and leave the need for a fair, randomized, blinded comparison where it was. The saving from a Bayesian design comes from four mechanisms: the deviation scale, a single calibrated threshold for monitoring (with shrinkage for estimation, not a substitute for error control), informative priors, and optimal stopping. title: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2 The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV
text: A new medicine reaches patients through a sequence of experiments, each larger, longer and more expensive than the last, and each built to answer a different question. The conventional names, Phase I to Phase IV, describe this sequence, and every later chapter of this book sits inside one of them. This chapter is the map. It says what each phase is for, what can go wrong in it, how the traditional design handles it, and where a Bayesian decision maker would act differently. Throughout, a phase is treated as an experiment whose value lies in the decision it informs: whether to proceed to the next phase, at what dose, in which patients. Important Regulatory anchor The phases have regulatory definitions but need not form a rigid sequence. Chapter 3 describes each document in full and gives its status. Here only the roles matter. 21 CFR 312.21. Describes Phases 1 to 3 of an investigation under an IND and expressly allows them to overlap, so a program is not obliged to complete one phase before starting the next. ICH E8(R1), General Considerations for Clinical Studies (Step 4, October 2021). Classifies studies by objective (human pharmacology, exploratory, confirmatory, postmarketing) and says that the classic phase labels do not fit every program. A program is a set of studies, each with a stated question, organized by objective and

title: Before Phase I
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.1 Before Phase I
text: 2.1 Before Phase I A compound enters human testing after discovery, lead optimization, and preclinical studies in cells and animals that establish pharmacology and a safe starting dose. In the United States the sponsor then files an Investigational New Drug application. Some programs run a Phase 0 or microdosing study, giving subtherapeutic doses to a handful of volunteers to check that the drug reaches its target and behaves pharmacokinetically as predicted. The prior for everything that follows is built here, from animal data, from mechanistic models and from the history of similar compounds.

title: Phase I: is it safe, and at what dose?
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.2 Phase I: is it safe, and at what dose?
text: 2.2 Phase I: is it safe, and at what dose? Phase I is the first exposure of humans to the drug. In most therapeutic areas it enrolls 20 to 100 healthy volunteers. In oncology, where the drugs are toxic, it enrolls patients for whom standard therapy has failed. The questions are tolerability, pharmacokinetics (what the body does to the drug), pharmacodynamics (what the drug does to the body), and, in oncology, the maximum tolerated dose. The traditional oncology design is the 3+3 rule: treat three patients at a dose, escalate if none has a dose-limiting toxicity, add three more if one does, and stop if two or more do. The rule uses toxicity counts at the current dose, including any expansion cohort, without fitting a dose-toxicity curve, so it ignores the shape of that curve and identifies a dose with little precision. Model-based Bayesian designs replace it with a dose-toxicity model, for example \[ \mathrm{logit}\,\Pr(\text{toxicity}\mid d) = \log a + b\log(d/d^\star),\qquad a,b > 0, \] the Bayesian logistic regression model of Neuenschwander, Branson, and Gsponer ( 2008 ) . After each cohort the posterior over \((a,b)\) is updated, and the next dose is the one with the highest posterior probability of a toxicity rate in the target interval, subject to a cap on the posterior probability of overdosing. Section 17.1 simulates the 3+3 and sets it beside these designs on the same scenarios, and Chapter 17 develops them. Note TGN1412: a design that could not learn between patients In March 2006 six healthy volunteers in London received the first human doses of TGN1412, a monoclonal antibody against CD28, and two others received placebo ( Suntharalingam et al. 2006 ) . Within hours all six who received the drug developed a cytokine storm with multiple organ failure. The doses were given within minutes of one another, so the first volunteer’s reaction could not inform the decision to dose the others. In the language of this book, the design gave the first observation no chance to update the action for the rest of the cohort. Staggered dosing, in which the first participant is dosed alone and observed before the next, is now standard practice. title: Phase II: does it work, and at what dose?
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.3 Phase II: does it work, and at what dose?
text: 2.3 Phase II: does it work, and at what dose? Phase II is where most drugs fail, and where most of the value of a development program is created or destroyed. Phase IIa is proof of concept: a small randomized or single-arm study asking whether the drug moves a clinical or biomarker endpoint at all. Phase IIb is dose ranging: several doses against placebo, to estimate the dose-response curve and choose the dose for Phase III. Phase II is where Bayesian methods have the strongest claim, because its purpose is learning rather than confirming, a distinction made central to clinical pharmacology by Sheiner ( 1997 ) . The natural output of Phase II is not a p-value but a posterior over the dose-response curve and a predictive probability that Phase III will succeed. Chapter 15 builds that predictive probability, beginning from the traditional conditional power of Section 15.1 , and Section 9.6.3 shows why a Phase III designed around the Phase II point estimate is usually underpowered. Chapter 17 treats dose finding and dose optimization, and Chapter 16 the allocation rules that adaptive Phase II designs borrow from bandit theory. text: designs borrow from bandit theory. Note ASTIN: an early and well-founded no The ASTIN trial tested a neutrophil inhibitory factor (UK-279,276) in acute ischemic stroke ( Krams et al. 2003 ) . Patients were allocated adaptively among many doses and placebo, with a Bayesian dose-response model updated as outcomes accrued and allocation chosen to learn most about the dose giving 95 percent of the maximum effect. The design included rules to stop for futility or efficacy. The trial found no treatment effect and stopped early for futility, at 966 patients according to the published report. A fixed design without interim analyses would have run to completion before learning the same thing, although a conventional group sequential design with a futility rule could also have stopped early. ASTIN is the standard example of a Bayesian adaptive design delivering its most valuable output, a fast and well-founded negative result.

title: Phase III: confirming, and the regulatory decision
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.4 Phase III: confirming, and the regulatory decision
text: 2.4 Phase III: confirming, and the regulatory decision Phase III trials are large, randomized and usually blinded, designed to confirm efficacy and characterize safety in the population for which the drug will be licensed. They enroll hundreds to tens of thousands of patients and cost from tens to hundreds of millions of dollars. The FDA’s traditional evidentiary standard is two adequate and well-controlled trials, or one large trial with confirmatory evidence. This is the stage at which the type I error rate of Chapter 9 is the contract with the regulator, and at which interim analyses ( Chapter 11 , Chapter 15 ) are governed by the strictest rules. Chapter 3 describes the documents that apply. Note Torcetrapib: a signal that belonged in the prior In December 2006 Pfizer stopped ILLUMINATE, a Phase III outcomes trial of torcetrapib, a drug that raised HDL cholesterol, after the data monitoring committee found an excess of deaths on the drug ( Barter et al. 2007 ) . The program had cost hundreds of millions of dollars. Torcetrapib had been associated with higher blood pressure in earlier studies, a signal visible before the outcomes trial began. The episode illustrates two themes of this book: information from earlier phases about off-target effects belongs in the prior for Phase III, and the value of an interim analysis lies as much in stopping for harm as for benefit. Chapter 13 develops safety monitoring.

title: Phase IV: after approval
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.5 Phase IV: after approval
text: 2.5 Phase IV: after approval Approval is not the end of learning. Phase IV comprises postmarketing studies required or agreed at approval, observational surveillance of adverse events, and confirmatory trials for drugs granted accelerated approval on a surrogate endpoint. Premarketing trials are often too small or too short to characterize rare harms reliably, and such harms become clear only when many more patients are exposed. Note Rofecoxib: surveillance as a sequential decision Rofecoxib (Vioxx) was approved in 1999 and withdrawn on 30 September 2004, after the APPROVe trial, a randomized comparison with placebo in 2,586 patients with a history of colorectal adenoma, showed a higher rate of confirmed thrombotic events on the drug (46 events against 26, rate ratio 1.92, 95% CI 1.19 to 3.11) ( Bresalier et al. 2005 ) . Earlier, the VIGOR trial in rheumatoid arthritis had shown fewer gastrointestinal events than with naproxen but more myocardial infarctions ( Bombardier et al. 2000 ) . A cumulative meta-analysis found that a statistically clear excess of myocardial infarction was already present at the end of 2000, years before withdrawal ( Jüni et al. 2004 ) . Postmarketing surveillance is a sequential decision problem in which the action is to warn, restrict or withdraw, and the cost of waiting is counted in patients harmed. Chapter 13 returns to the case. Postmarketing surveillance is also

title: Phase IV: after approval
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.5 Phase IV: after approval
text: 2004 ) . Postmarketing surveillance is a sequential decision problem in which the action is to warn, restrict or withdraw, and the cost of waiting is counted in patients harmed. Chapter 13 returns to the case. Postmarketing surveillance is also where empirical Bayes has had its greatest regulatory success. Spontaneous reporting systems collect millions of reports of drug and adverse-event pairs. The observed count \(n_{ij}\) for drug \(i\) and event \(j\) is compared with the count \(E_{ij}\) expected under independence, and the crude ratio \(\hat\lambda_{ij} = n_{ij}/E_{ij}\) is unstable when counts are small. The gamma-Poisson shrinker of DuMouchel ( 1999 ) instead defines a latent relative reporting rate \(\lambda_{ij}\) through the model \(n_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{ij}E_{ij})\) , with a mixture of gammas for \(\lambda_{ij}\) , and reports its posterior estimate, so that an estimate based on three reports is shrunk heavily toward the common distribution and one based on three hundred is not. This is the same kind of partial pooling that Chapter 20 describes for platform trials, applied at the scale of a national database.

title: The phases as a sequence of options
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.6 The phases as a sequence of options
text: 2.6 The phases as a sequence of options Let \(p_{12}\) , \(p_{23}\) and \(p_{3A}\) denote the probabilities of moving from Phase I to II, from II to III, and from III to approval, and let \(c_1\) , \(c_2\) , \(c_3\) be the costs of the phases. Phase \(k\) is paid for only if all earlier phases succeed, so the expected cost per drug started is \(c_1 + p_{12}c_2 + p_{12}p_{23}c_3\) . The expected number of approvals per start is \(p_{12}p_{23}p_{3A}\) , and the ratio of the two expectations is the long-run cost per approval: \[ C_{\mathrm{approved}} = \frac{c_1 + p_{12}c_2 + p_{12}p_{23}c_3}{p_{12}\,p_{23}\,p_{3A}}. \tag{2.1}\] The formula explains why attrition dominates the economics of drug development. Wong, Siah, and Lo ( 2019 ) used over 400,000 trial records for more than 21,000 compounds, and estimated that about 13.8 percent of programs entering Phase I eventually reach approval, and 3.4 percent in oncology. Programs that use biomarkers to select patients have higher success probabilities. The sensitivity is easy to see with a stylized example. The probabilities and costs below are illustrative, not estimates from any source: they are chosen only so that the overall success probability is near the published range. Nor is advancing more compounds in itself better selection; the case for the predictive methods of Chapter 15 is that they advance the right ones.

title: Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.7 Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
text: 2.7 Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary A generic or reformulated drug must be shown to deliver the same exposure as the reference product. Exposure is measured by the area under the concentration-time curve, and the parameter of interest is the ratio \(\rho = \mu_T/\mu_R\) of geometric means for test and reference. Bioequivalence is declared when \(\rho\) lies in an equivalence interval, conventionally \((0.80, 1.25)\) . The classical analysis is the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure of Schuirmann ( 1987 ) , which gives the confidence-interval criterion a test form, on \(\eta = \log\rho\) , equivalent to checking that the 90 percent confidence interval lies inside \((\log 0.80, \log 1.25)\) ; Westlake had proposed a symmetric confidence interval for the same purpose ( Westlake 1976 ) , and Hauck and Anderson a different test of equivalence for two-group bioavailability trials ( Hauck and Anderson 1984 ) . The Bayesian version asks the question directly; it goes back to Rodda and Davis ( Rodda and Davis 1980 ) , Mandallaz and Mau ( Mandallaz and Mau 1981 ) and Selwyn, Dempster and Hall ( Selwyn, Dempster, and Hall 1981 ) , with the Basel worked example of Flühler et al. ( 1983 ) , a two-stage procedure by Racine-Poon and colleagues ( Racine-Poon et al. 1987 ) , and a decision-analytic treatment by Lindley ( Lindley

title: Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.7 Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
text: and Hall 1981 ) , with the Basel worked example of Flühler et al. ( 1983 ) , a two-stage procedure by Racine-Poon and colleagues ( Racine-Poon et al. 1987 ) , and a decision-analytic treatment by Lindley ( Lindley 1998 ) . Take a simplified model in which the \(n\) within-subject log differences \(d_i\) are independent and normal with mean \(\eta\) , sample mean \(\bar d\) and standard deviation \(s\) , and use a reference prior. (A standard two-sequence, two-period crossover analysis also models period and sequence effects and generally has different residual degrees of freedom, so this is a simplification, not the regulatory analysis.) Then the posterior of \(\eta\) is a scaled \(t\) distribution, \(\eta\mid d \sim \bar d + (s/\sqrt n)\,t_{n-1}\) , and the reported quantity is \[ \Pr\bigl(\log 0.80 < \eta < \log 1.25 \mid d\bigr) = F_{t_{n-1}}\!\left(\frac{\log 1.25 - \bar d}{s/\sqrt n}\right) - F_{t_{n-1}}\!\left(\frac{\log 0.80 - \bar d}{s/\sqrt n}\right). \tag{2.2}\] A rule that concludes bioequivalence when this probability exceeds a threshold such as 0.90 is an alternative to TOST, not the conventional criterion: TOST is the standard in FDA’s final guidance Statistical Approaches to Establishing Bioequivalence ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) (May 2026, Section II.C.1.a), and a posterior-probability rule would need agreement with the regulator and an evaluation of its operating characteristics. The relation to TOST is

title: Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.7 Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary
text: guidance Statistical Approaches to Establishing Bioequivalence ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) (May 2026, Section II.C.1.a), and a posterior-probability rule would need agreement with the regulator and an evaluation of its operating characteristics. The relation to TOST is exact under the reference prior. Each one-sided posterior tail probability equals the corresponding one-sided TOST p-value, so the posterior probability of equivalence is \(1 - p_L - p_U\) . If both p-values are below 0.05, the posterior probability exceeds 0.90. The two procedures can therefore disagree only in one direction: TOST at level 0.05 implies a posterior probability above 0.90, and a posterior probability above 0.90 does not imply TOST success. Choosing the threshold 0.95 (and, to match, TOST at 0.025 on each side) changes the comparison. The posterior probability is therefore a supplementary summary of the same data that is easy to read, and it is a weaker rule at 0.90: some data sets pass it and fail TOST (the third row of Table 2.2 , with posterior probability 0.9291 and TOST p-value 0.0709). Racine-Poon et al. ( 1987 ) made the procedure sequential, using the posterior and its predictive distribution after a first stage to decide whether to stop or how many further subjects to recruit, the template for the interim decision rules of Chapter 15 . Average bioequivalence is also not the

Average bioequivalence is also not the only approach regulators use: for highly variable drugs some product-specific recommendations use reference-scaled approaches, so the Bayesian rule is one design choice within a family and not a replacement for it. title: Recruitment and the value of speed
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.8 Recruitment and the value of speed
text: 2.8 Recruitment and the value of speed Most trials are slow because of accrual, not analysis, and the recruitment rate is the quantity a sponsor can least control. One episode shows both how to estimate a rate and what a recruit is worth. In November 1995 Michael Milken, who had founded CaP CURE (later the Prostate Cancer Foundation) after his own prostate cancer diagnosis, appeared on CNN’s Larry King Live with General Norman Schwarzkopf and the molecular biologist Leroy (Lee) Hood of the University of Washington, and asked families with several men affected by prostate cancer to volunteer for a genetic study ( Prostate Cancer Foundation 2025 ; Daniels 2004 ) . More than 3,000 people called. Within three weeks Hood’s group had a sample of about 300 qualified families, where Johns Hopkins had recruited 90 families over ten years ( Daniels 2004 ) ; a University of Washington release of 1999 reports 291 families enrolled in the resulting PROGRESS study, many of whom came after seeing the broadcast ( University of Washington 1999 ) . The coauthors’ working paper analyzes the episode ( Sokolova, Sokolov, and Polson 2026 ) , and the calculations below follow it. Model enrollment of eligible families as a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) per week. With the reference prior \(\mathrm{Gamma}(1/2, 0)\) and \(n\) families observed in \(t\) weeks, the

text: Sokolov, and Polson 2026 ) , and the calculations below follow it. Model enrollment of eligible families as a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) per week. With the reference prior \(\mathrm{Gamma}(1/2, 0)\) and \(n\) families observed in \(t\) weeks, the posterior is \(\mathrm{Gamma}(n + 1/2, t)\) , the conjugate update of Chapter 6 . The conventional pace is not known. “Several years” for 300 families is an assumption, and we bracket it at three to five years, which we treat as fixed scenario rates of \(300/156\) to \(300/260\) families a week, not as data. The posterior for the broadcast rate has mean 100 families a week and standard deviation 5.8, so the counting error is small. The ratio of the broadcast rate to an assumed fixed conventional rate is 52 (95 percent interval 46 to 58) if the conventional pace was three years, and 87 (77 to 97) if it was five. These are conditional comparisons against assumed conventional rates, rather than estimates from conventional recruitment data. The real uncertainty is the counterfactual pace, not the count. The reported three-week identification of eligible families was much faster than the assumed conventional scenarios, and completed enrollment and specimen-collection rates are not established by this account. This is the Bayesian answer to the planning question of how long accrual will take, and it is the same calculation

This is the Bayesian answer to the planning question of how long accrual will take, and it is the same calculation that, with a prior borrowed from earlier sites, turns a protocol’s accrual assumption into a predictive distribution of the end date. A rate is not the whole story, because a recruit is worth the evidence it contributes. Linkage studies report a LOD score, the base ten logarithm of the likelihood ratio for linkage against no linkage ( Morton 1955 ) . At a fixed recombination fraction and genetic model, a LOD score is a log likelihood ratio. A posterior probability of linkage requires a marginal Bayes factor \(B\) in the sense of Chapter 7 , integrating over uncertain linkage parameters, and with prior probability \(\pi\) that a disease gene lies in the region tested it equals \(\pi B / (\pi B + 1 - \pi)\) . A maximized LOD of 3 does not automatically imply \(B = 1000\) ( Génin, Martinez, and Clerget-Darpoux 1995 ) . If it did, with a prior of one in fifty the posterior probability would be 0.95. Because log likelihood ratios add across independent families, the value of a family is the expected LOD it contributes. A broad appeal brings

text: . If it did, with a prior of one in fifty the posterior probability would be 0.95. Because log likelihood ratios add across independent families, the value of a family is the expected LOD it contributes. A broad appeal brings in families whose clustering reflects screening rather than inheritance (phenocopies) and families whose disease is not linked to the locus under study, and both dilute that expectation. Under a crude working approximation, expected LOD per family is \(e_1 \alpha (1 - \phi)\) , with \(e_1\) the expected LOD of a fully informative linked family, \(\alpha\) the fraction of families linked to the locus and \(\phi\) the phenocopy dilution. These are illustrative inputs, not estimates: with \(e_1 = 0.3\) , \(\alpha = 0.2\) and \(\phi = 0.3\) , a family is worth 0.042 LOD, and under this toy assumption about expected information approximately 71 families would give an expected cumulative LOD of 3, against 29 if \(\alpha = 0.34\) and \(\phi = 0\) . These are mean-path calculations, not sample-size requirements: enrollment planning needs a specified probability of reaching the threshold and a model for family heterogeneity, and unlinked families need not contribute zero expected log likelihood ratio. Volume rose by a factor of fifty or more while quality per family may have fallen (a hypothesis, since comparative pedigree and informativeness data would be needed to establish it), so the sensible design takes the volume and then weights families by their posterior probability of carrying the signal, which is what a hierarchical model does automatically ( Chapter 19 ). The same logic applies to a trial: count the information a patient contributes, not the patients. The value of the acceleration is the part that depends on assumptions, and every one is labeled. Suppose the resulting family resource has probability \(p\) of leading to a clinically useful genetic test (assumed), that the test reduces mortality among hereditary cases by a fraction \(r\) (assumed), and that the broadcast brings that benefit forward by \(y\) years (assumed, and smaller than the years of accrual saved, because genotyping and replication take their own time). Take 37,000 United States prostate cancer deaths a year (late 1990s, as the working paper reports), a hereditary share of 9 percent (an assumption), ten life years lost per death (assumed) and $100,000 per life year (assumed). The expected value is \(V = 37{,}000 \times 0.09 \times r \times 10 \times \$100{,}000 \times y \times p\) , which is $67 million at \(p = 0.1\) , \(r = 0.1\) , \(y = 2\) and $500 million at \(p = 0.25\) , \(r = 0.2\) , \(y = 3\) . If the appeal replaced an assumed $2,000 to $5,000 of conventional outreach expenditure per family and had negligible marginal cost, the modeled gross saving would be $0.6 million to $1.5 million. Under the chosen assumptions, the larger modeled value comes from earlier clinical benefit. The range is wide because the inputs are, and it is an ex ante expectation: the first locus reported, HPC1 on 1q24-25 from 91 high-risk families ( Smith et al. 1996 ) , did not become a clinical test, and the actionable variant, HOXB13 G84E, was reported in 2012 ( Ewing et al. 2012 ) . An expectation can be the right basis for a decision even when one draw is disappointing. The full treatment of the value of information is in Volume II.

title: A Bayesian reading of the phases
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > 2.9 A Bayesian reading of the phases
text: 2.9 A Bayesian reading of the phases Each phase updates a posterior and hands it to the next. Phase I produces a posterior over the dose-toxicity curve and the pharmacokinetic parameters, which becomes the prior for dose selection in Phase II. Phase II produces a posterior over the dose-response curve, and its predictive distribution gives the probability that Phase III will succeed. Phase III produces the evidence on which approval is decided. Phase IV keeps updating after approval. Traditional development also passes information forward: estimates and their uncertainty, dose-response and pharmacokinetic models, and safety findings all inform the next phase, and the confirmatory phase is where formal hypothesis tests carry the decision. The distinction is not that the traditional path passes verdicts and the Bayesian path passes distributions. It is that a Bayesian development program specifies one probability model across the phases, so that what one phase learns propagates into the predictive probabilities and decisions of the next, whereas the traditional path links phases through estimates and judgment. The rest of the book is about what this buys, and about the conditions (calibration, pre-specification, simulation) under which a regulator will accept the alternative. title: Key points
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > Key points
text: Key points The phases are experiments in which each hands the next a decision. Traditional development passes estimates, models and safety findings forward; a Bayesian program additionally propagates one probability model into predictive decisions. Phase I is a safety problem first: TGN1412 shows the cost of a design that cannot update between patients. Model-based escalation fits a dose-toxicity curve to all accumulated toxicity data, where the 3+3 uses only the counts at the current dose. Phase II is where most programs fail and where Bayesian learning pays most: a posterior over the dose-response curve and a predictive probability of Phase III success replace a p-value. Phase III is confirmatory, and a Bayesian criterion there is judged by its operating characteristics under a pre-specified design. Phase IV is a sequential decision problem. The rofecoxib record shows that evidence of harm can be in hand years before action. Cost per approval, Equation 2.1 , falls with each transition probability and each phase cost. In the stylized example a one-third rise in Phase II success saves more than a one-fifth cut in Phase III cost, but that ranking depends on the perturbations chosen, and advancing more compounds is not itself better selection. Bayesian bioequivalence is a familiar posterior probability. Under a reference prior, TOST success at 0.05 implies a posterior probability above 0.90, but not conversely, so the

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 2: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV > Key points

Under a reference prior, TOST success at 0.05 implies a posterior probability above 0.90, but not conversely, so the posterior rule is a supplementary summary or an alternative needing regulatory agreement, while TOST remains the conventional criterion. Recruitment is usually the slowest step, and a recruit is worth the evidence it adds. A gamma-Poisson posterior turns an enrollment count into a rate with an interval, and a LOD score, a log likelihood ratio at a fixed model, shows why more participants can mean less information per participant when a broad appeal dilutes the signal. title: The Regulatory Framework
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3 The Regulatory Framework
text: A drug is approved or not approved on a legal finding, and everything in this book is aimed at that finding. A trial can be elegant, efficient and ethically admirable, and it still fails its sponsor if the evidence it produces does not meet the standard the law sets. The standard does not say how the evidence must be produced, and that gap is where design choices, including Bayesian and adaptive ones, live. This chapter is the map. It says what the law requires, what international and national guidance recommends on top of it, which meetings a sponsor can ask for, and where the European and British regulators agree or differ. Two cautions before starting. First, the regulatory text changes quickly. Several of the documents below were issued as drafts in 2025 and 2026, and a draft can be revised or withdrawn. The statuses in this chapter are as of November 2026, and the dates are those printed on the documents. Second, regulatory documents differ in force. A statute binds. A regulation binds. A guidance “contains nonbinding recommendations”. This chapter keeps those categories apart. Important Regulatory anchor This chapter is about the anchors themselves. The documents that carry the legal and procedural weight are: FD&C Act section 505(d) ( United States Congress 1962 ) , as amended in 1997 ( United States Congress 1997 )

title: What the statute says
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.1 What the statute says
text: What the statute says The central sentence of US drug regulation comes from the Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 1962, passed after the thalidomide tragedy, which for the first time required manufacturers to show that a drug works and not only that it is reasonably safe. Section 505(d) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act directs FDA to refuse approval of a new drug application if there is a lack of substantial evidence that the drug will have the effect it purports or is represented to have under the conditions of use in the labeling. The Act then defines substantial evidence as “evidence consisting of adequate and well-controlled investigations”, including clinical investigations, by experts qualified by training and experience, on the basis of which it could fairly and responsibly be concluded by such experts that the drug will have the claimed effect ( United States Congress 1962 ) . Two features of this definition matter for everything that follows. The first is the plural: the statute speaks of investigations, and for decades FDA read that as two independent adequate and well-controlled trials, each with a positive result. The second is that the standard is one of evidence and not of method: the statute names no test, level, sample size, prior or design, and asks only whether qualified experts could fairly and responsibly conclude that the drug

text: result. The second is that the standard is one of evidence and not of method: the statute names no test, level, sample size, prior or design, and asks only whether qualified experts could fairly and responsibly conclude that the drug works. Frequentist hypothesis testing at a one-sided 0.025 level became the customary way to show this, and the customary way hardened into expectation, but the law does not mention it. The Bayesian methodology draft says so in effect when it allows that its default calibration to 0.025 “may not be applicable or appropriate” in some circumstances ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) .

title: The 1997 amendment: one trial and confirmatory evidence
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.2 The 1997 amendment: one trial and confirmatory evidence
text: The 1997 amendment: one trial and confirmatory evidence The Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 1997 ( United States Congress 1997 ) added a sentence to section 505(d): if the Secretary determines, based on relevant science, that “data from one adequate and well-controlled clinical investigation and confirmatory evidence” are sufficient to establish effectiveness, the Secretary may consider those data to constitute substantial evidence. The confirmatory evidence may come from before or after the trial. The power is discretionary: it is FDA’s determination, based on relevant science, not a right of the sponsor. The amendment has been used more often over time, especially in oncology, rare diseases and pediatric settings where a second trial is impractical or unethical. FDA’s draft guidance on the topic was first issued in December 2019 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019b ) and was revised in June 2026 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ) , which, when finalized, will replace the 1998 guidance Providing Clinical Evidence of Effectiveness for Human Drug and Biological Products . The revision was announced in the Federal Register on 24 June 2026 under docket FDA-2019-D-4964.

title: The regulation: what "adequate and well-controlled" means
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.3 The regulation: what "adequate and well-controlled" means
text: The regulation: what “adequate and well-controlled” means The statute leaves “adequate and well-controlled” undefined. FDA’s regulation at 21 CFR 314.126 defines it, and it is the single most useful list for a trialist to carry in the head ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024a ) . The regulation says the purpose of conducting clinical investigations of a drug is to distinguish the effect of the drug from other influences, such as spontaneous change in the course of the disease, placebo effect, or biased observation. It then lists the characteristics of an adequate and well-controlled study. In paraphrase, the study: has a clear statement of its objectives and of the method of analysis to be used; uses a design that permits a valid comparison with a control, so that the effect of the drug can be quantified (the regulation names placebo concurrent control, dose-comparison, no treatment, active treatment and historical control as recognized types); selects subjects by an adequate method, with reasonable assurance that they have the disease or condition being studied; assigns subjects to treatment and control groups in a way that minimizes bias and assures comparability on baseline factors such as age, sex, severity and duration of disease (randomization is the usual way); takes adequate measures to minimize bias on the part of subjects, observers and analysts of the data (blinding is the

title: The regulation: what "adequate and well-controlled" means
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.3 The regulation: what "adequate and well-controlled" means
text: and assures comparability on baseline factors such as age, sex, severity and duration of disease (randomization is the usual way); takes adequate measures to minimize bias on the part of subjects, observers and analysts of the data (blinding is the usual way); uses well-defined and reliable methods of assessing response; analyses the results adequately to assess the effects of the drug. Two observations. Item 7 asks for an adequate analysis, and the regulation expects the protocol to state the proposed methods, and where it did not, the report to explain how the methods were chosen. This is the regulatory root of the pre-specification that every guidance in this chapter repeats, and it applies to Bayesian analyses as it applies to frequentist ones. Item 2 admits historical control as a recognized type, but the 2026 draft cautions that external controls have a weakness: differences between groups arise “because of the lack of randomized treatment assignment” ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ) . The hierarchy of controls will come back in Chapter 19 .

title: The 2026 substantial-evidence draft
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.4 The 2026 substantial-evidence draft
text: The 2026 substantial-evidence draft The June 2026 revised draft guidance, Demonstrating Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness for Human Drug and Biological Products ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ) , restates how FDA reads the statute. It is a draft, so it is not for implementation, and it revises the draft issued in December 2019 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019b ) . What it says that matters here, in the order the document gives it: It describes the conventional route (two trials) and a single-trial route. The single-trial route “will involve a highly persuasive trial or a source of strong confirmatory evidence” (Section IV.A of the draft). It lists the factors FDA weighs in deciding whether one trial and confirmatory evidence suffice: the seriousness of the disease and the unmet need, the strength of the single trial, the strength and source of the confirmatory evidence, and “whether it is ethical and practicable to conduct more than one adequate and well-controlled trial”. It allows confirmatory evidence of types that are not trials. For instance, “mechanistic evidence of the drug’s treatment effect in a particular disease may be appropriate to use as confirmatory evidence”, within the regulatory flexibility the draft describes in its Section V for serious disease and unmet need. It says that the plan for one trial “should be discussed with FDA prior

cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.4 The 2026 substantial-evidence draft
text: disease may be appropriate to use as confirmatory evidence”, within the regulatory flexibility the draft describes in its Section V for serious disease and unmet need. It says that the plan for one trial “should be discussed with FDA prior to initiating the single trial”. The draft explicitly recognizes Bayesian analyses, and it matters for them: a Bayesian analysis that uses an informative prior built from earlier data is a close cousin of “one trial plus confirmatory evidence”, and the borrowing discussion in Chapter 19 returns to the connection. Prespecified borrowing formalizes how earlier evidence enters the analysis, but FDA still evaluates its relevance, weight and contribution to substantial evidence, including in discussions before the trial. Tip Try it in the lab Open Module 11, What counts as proof ( https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/11-substantial-evidence.html ). Before you touch a control, predict: a first trial just clears the win line with p = 0.04 (two-sided, counting luck in both directions). If the drug’s true effect is exactly what that trial saw, what is the chance that a second trial of the same size also wins? Then run the repeats. The lab’s answer, about half, is the statistical reason a regulator may prefer replication; its second panel shows the other side, two independent wins at one-sided 0.025 by luck about once in 1,600 times.

title: What the standard implies for the numbers
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.1.5 What the standard implies for the numbers
text: What the standard implies for the numbers Two adequate and well-controlled trials, each tested at a two-sided 0.05 level (one-sided 0.025), independent and each required to succeed in the prespecified beneficial direction, imply that a useless drug passes both only with probability \(0.025 \times 0.025 = 1/1600\) . A single trial at 0.025 passes a useless drug 1 time in 40. A single trial at a stricter level (the book’s companion online lab, module 11, https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/11-substantial-evidence.html , uses 0.001) passes a useless drug 1 time in 1,000. In this sense, one very persuasive trial and two ordinary trials can offer comparable protection against a false positive, which is why FDA’s willingness to accept “a highly persuasive trial” is consistent with the statute. For trials with an overall frequentist statistical analysis plan, the Bayesian methodology draft says that the familywise type I error rate is almost always required to be no greater than 0.025 one-sided ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) . The draft also describes direct interpretation of posterior probabilities and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria, so calibration is one of its routes (the book’s default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing), not a universal requirement. FDA’s REBYOTA review used two posterior thresholds chosen as analogues of one-sided type I error rates of 0.00125 and 0.025 without borrowing ( Section 3.11 ). The notation of this book follows suit: one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) is the default, and we say so whenever we use two-sided.

title: What a traditional submission looks like
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.2 What a traditional submission looks like
text: 3.2 What a traditional submission looks like It is worth describing the traditional package accurately, because it is what a regulatory reviewer expects to see and what the Bayesian design is measured against. The development path. A sponsor begins with nonclinical work, then files an Investigational New Drug application (IND). FDA has 30 days to object; if it does not, the first human trials can begin. Phase 1 examines tolerability and pharmacokinetics, phase 2 looks for efficacy and chooses a dose, and phase 3 is the pivotal comparison, usually randomized, controlled and blinded. The sponsor then files a New Drug Application (NDA) or, for biologics, a Biologics License Application (BLA), which FDA reviews, checking completeness for 60 days first. At the major junctures FDA offers meetings: a pre-IND meeting, an end-of-phase 2 meeting to agree the phase 3 plan, and a pre-NDA or pre-BLA meeting to confirm the file is complete. Module 13 of the companion lab draws this road. The phases themselves, what each is designed to learn and how Bayesian methods enter each, are the subject of Chapter 2 , the chapter before this one. Bioequivalence studies, which establish that a generic or reformulated product delivers the same exposure as a reference product and so replace a new efficacy trial, follow a different pathway from the phase 1 to 3 efficacy sequence when

Bioequivalence studies, which establish that a generic or reformulated product delivers the same exposure as a reference product and so replace a new efficacy trial, follow a different pathway from the phase 1 to 3 efficacy sequence when they support a generic (ANDA) approval. They also occur inside an innovator program, for example to bridge formulations, and FDA’s final bioequivalence guidance covers INDs and NDAs as well as ANDAs. Chapter 2 treats the Bayesian version of the bioequivalence question. The pivotal trial protocol. The protocol fixes, before any patient is randomized, the primary endpoint and its definition, the estimand (the precise treatment effect the trial targets, with a stated strategy for intercurrent events such as rescue medication or treatment discontinuation, as set out in ICH E9(R1) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2019 ) ), the randomization scheme, blinding, the sample size computed from a power formula, the analysis populations, and the primary analysis. ICH E9 says the statistical methods must be described in the protocol and that “all interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol” ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 ) . The sample size is usually the number \(n\) that gives power \(1-\beta\) (often 80 or 90 percent) against a clinically relevant effect at one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) . Chapter 9 derives that formula. The statistical analysis plan (SAP). Written before database lock and typically before unblinding, the SAP states the primary analysis, the handling of missing data, the multiplicity strategy (a single primary endpoint, a gatekeeping hierarchy, a Bonferroni or graphical procedure; see the FDA multiple endpoints guidance of October 2022 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2022b ) and Chapter 10 ), the sensitivity analyses, and the timing and boundaries of any interim analyses, usually a group sequential design with alpha spending ( Chapter 11 ). An independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) sees the unblinded interim results under a charter, and the sponsor’s trial team does not. The evidence. For the standard route to approval, the package contains two adequate and well-controlled trials, each with a statistically significant result on its pre-specified primary endpoint, or one such trial plus confirmatory evidence in the circumstances discussed above. The primary result is a point estimate, a confidence interval and a p-value. FDA’s statistical reviewers re-run the analysis from the datasets the sponsor submits, in standardized formats, and check that what was done matches what the protocol and SAP said would

FDA’s statistical reviewers re-run the analysis from the datasets the sponsor submits, in standardized formats, and check that what was done matches what the protocol and SAP said would be done. What the regulator is really asking. The questions a statistical reviewer asks of a traditional trial are worth listing, because the same questions reappear in new form for Bayesian and adaptive designs. Was the primary analysis specified before the data were seen? Was the type I error rate controlled for the family of hypotheses that supports the claim? Is the effect estimate credible, free of selection bias, and clinically meaningful? Was the trial conducted with integrity: blinded, with limited access to comparative data, with deviations documented? The answers are almost entirely about pre-specification and error control, which the traditional package makes simple: the type I error rate is \(\alpha\) by construction and the power is a formula. Where the traditional design is the right choice. For a single-look trial with a well-understood endpoint and no usable prior information, the fixed-sample design is simple, transparent, and cheap to review. A sponsor with no meaningful prior information and no appetite for the added simulation work should not adopt a more elaborate design merely because it is available. title: What changes with a Bayesian adaptive design
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.3 What changes with a Bayesian adaptive design
text: 3.3 What changes with a Bayesian adaptive design The short answer is that the legal standard does not change, the evidentiary bar does not change, and the demands for pre-specification and error control do not change. What changes is how the operating characteristics are established, who has to be convinced, and what the sponsor must hand over. It is helpful to separate three kinds of change. The design becomes a rule set, and the rule set is the thing that is pre-specified. In a traditional trial the protocol pre-specifies a test and a sample size. In an adaptive trial it also pre-specifies decision rules that depend on accumulating data: when to stop for efficacy or futility, when to drop an arm, how to change allocation, and how to re-estimate the sample size. FDA’s 2019 guidance defines an adaptive design as “a clinical trial design that allows for prospectively planned modifications to one or more aspects of the design based on accumulating data” ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019a ) , and the draft ICH E20 sharpens the point: “prospectively planned means that the potential trial adaptations are pre-specified in the clinical trial protocol prior to initiation of the trial” ( International Council for Harmonisation 2025a ) . Operating characteristics are established by simulation, not by formula. A group sequential design has analytic boundaries. A

text: trial adaptations are pre-specified in the clinical trial protocol prior to initiation of the trial” ( International Council for Harmonisation 2025a ) . Operating characteristics are established by simulation, not by formula. A group sequential design has analytic boundaries. A Bayesian adaptive design with predictive probability stopping, response-adaptive allocation and borrowing generally does not. The 2019 guidance says “a major use of simulations in adaptive trial design is to estimate trial operating characteristics” ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019a ) , and the Bayesian draft recommends “comprehensive” simulation covering the plausible range of assumptions, with the simulation code available to FDA for verification ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) . Chapter 14 is devoted to this. This is the currency in which the book itemizes costs: each benefit of a Bayesian adaptive design is bought with a simulation burden, and the simulation report is how the sponsor pays. The success criterion is stated on the posterior and calibrated to error. The Bayesian draft gives the standard form: success is declared when the posterior probability that the true treatment effect exceeds a threshold is high enough, \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , where \(a\) is the minimum benefit and \(c\) the minimum probability ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) . Section IV.A describes three routes: calibration of the thresholds

Section IV.A describes three routes: calibration of the thresholds to a type I error rate (“typically 0.025 one-sided” for the overall familywise error rate), direct interpretation of posterior probabilities (for example with borrowing, by agreement with FDA), and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria. Calibration is this book’s default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, and the draft says it may be appropriate for complex adaptive designs; it is one route, not a requirement. Against a single unadjusted analysis the calibrated Bayesian bar is not lower without an informative prior. title: ICH: the harmonized principles
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.4 ICH: the harmonized principles
text: 3.4 ICH: the harmonized principles The International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) brings together regulators and industry to agree guidelines that member regulators then adopt. A guideline reaches Step 4 when the ICH Assembly adopts the final text, and regional regulators then implement it (FDA publishes it as guidance, EMA as a scientific guideline). Step 2 is a draft out for consultation. Six ICH documents shape this book. E8(R1), General Considerations for Clinical Studies (Step 4, 6 October 2021) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2021 ) . It replaces E8 of 17 July 1997. E8(R1) is the document where “quality by design” enters clinical research: it says quality should be “driven proactively by designing quality into the study protocol and processes” (Section 3.1). It states that “the major purpose of a control group is to separate the effect of the treatment(s) from the effects of other factors” (Section 5.3). Its critical-to-quality factors, for a Bayesian adaptive trial, include the prior, the calibration of the success criterion and the integrity of the interim data, though E8(R1) does not say so. E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (Step 4, 5 February 1998) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 ) . After more than 25 years E9 remains the foundation. It describes randomization, blinding, the analysis populations, the primary variable, interim

text: so. E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (Step 4, 5 February 1998) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 ) . After more than 25 years E9 remains the foundation. It describes randomization, blinding, the analysis populations, the primary variable, interim analysis, and multiplicity. On randomization it says that the deliberate element of chance “tends to produce treatment groups in which the distributions of prognostic factors, known and unknown, are similar” (Section 2.3.2), and on analysis populations that “Preservation of the initial randomisation in analysis is important in preventing bias” (Section 5.2.1). On multiplicity it says that “the usual frequentist approach to the analysis of clinical trial data may necessitate an adjustment to the type I error” (Section 5.6). On interim analyses it asks for pre-planning: “all interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol” (Section 4.5), and group sequential designs are “the usual way” to look repeatedly (Section 3.4). E9 mentions Bayesian approaches only briefly, in Section 1.2 and the Glossary, and does not elaborate them. Pre-specification applies to them as to any analysis; the point for this book is that E9 neither prohibits nor privileges them. E9(R1), Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis (Step 4, 20 November 2019) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2019 ) . FDA labels its own publication of this document May 2021. E9(R1) defines an

E9(R1) defines an estimand as “a precise description of the treatment effect reflecting the clinical question posed by a given clinical trial objective”, requires that “the targets of estimation are to be defined in advance of a clinical trial”, and introduces intercurrent events, events after treatment initiation that affect the interpretation or the existence of the measurements. It names five strategies for handling them: treatment policy, hypothetical, composite variable, while on treatment and principal stratum. A posterior probability is only as interpretable as the estimand it is posterior about. Estimands are developed in Chapter 5 . E20, Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials (draft, Step 2, endorsed 25 June 2025) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2025a ) . This is the first international guideline on adaptive designs. It remains a draft: the EMA consultation ran from 30 June to 30 November 2025, the EMA overview of comments was published on 16 February 2026, and the ICH work plan of July 2026 targets Step 3 and Step 4 sign-off in February 2027. Until final it binds no region, but it shows where regulators are heading. Its content: the definition quoted

Its content: the definition quoted above; the expectation that a “proposed adaptive design requires a clear and compelling justification”; the expectation that in confirmatory trials “the number and complexity of adaptations should generally be limited”; the statement that “controlling the chances of false positive efficacy conclusions” is “an essential element of regulatory decision-making”; the warning that naive analyses can raise the type I error probability to “more than double” its nominal value; and a section on simulation (5.2). E20 also has a Bayesian section (5.3), which says that Bayesian adaptive designs “can achieve targeted operating characteristics” while “maintaining Type I error probability control” and defines Bayesian methods as those that “combine a prior probability distribution with current trial data to obtain a posterior probability distribution”. Where E20 and the FDA Bayesian draft meet, the expectation is calibration to type I error for confirmatory trials. Chapter 14 uses E20 section 5 for the contents of a simulation report. E11A, Pediatric Extrapolation (Step 4, August 2024) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2024 ) . E11A sets out when and how evidence from an adult or other source population can be extrapolated to children, and it promotes quantitative approaches including Bayesian borrowing and modeling and simulation to do so. It matters for this book because pediatric extrapolation is the clearest case where a regulator has asked for, rather than tolerated, a quantitative statement of how much prior information counts. It is taken up in Chapter 19 , and belimumab in children is a worked case in Section 3.11 . The Bayesian draft itself uses “adult data for children” as an example of borrowing ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) . M15, General Principles for Model-Informed Drug Development (Step 4, January 2026) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2026 ) . FDA published this document in June 2026. M15 defines model-informed drug development (MIDD) as “the use of computational modeling and simulation (M&S) methods that can include and integrate nonclinical data, clinical data, prior information” to inform

text: Harmonisation 2026 ) . FDA published this document in June 2026. M15 defines model-informed drug development (MIDD) as “the use of computational modeling and simulation (M&S) methods that can include and integrate nonclinical data, clinical data, prior information” to inform decisions. Its structure is a credibility framework built on the question of interest, the context of use, model influence, the consequence of a wrong decision and model risk, where model risk is “derived by combining model influence and consequence of wrong decision” and “is essential for determining the requirements for model evaluation”. The more a decision rests on a model, and the worse a wrong decision would be, the more evidence the model needs. A Bayesian adaptive design is in part a model on which stopping decisions rest, and the simulation report is the evaluation, so the M15 vocabulary is a useful way to think about how much documentation FDA will want. Three older ICH documents round out the picture and are referenced elsewhere: E3 (Step 4, November 1995; the structure of the clinical study report) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1995 ) , M4 (M4(R4), Step 4, 2016; the common technical document format of the submission) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2016 ) , and E6(R3) on good clinical practice (Step 4, January 2025) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2025b ) . A sponsor

title: FDA design guidances
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5 FDA design guidances
text: 3.5 FDA design guidances FDA guidance documents “contain nonbinding recommendations”. The agency’s own convention is that the word “should” in a guidance means “suggested or recommended, but not required”. A sponsor may depart from a guidance, but must be prepared to show that the alternative approach meets the statute and regulations. In practice a departure without prior discussion with the agency is a risk to the program, and that is why the meetings of the next section exist. A guidance is first issued as a draft, comments are taken (60 days after the Federal Register notice is usual), and a final follows, or the draft is revised or withdrawn. A draft is labeled as not for implementation, but sponsors often follow it because it tells them what reviewers will look for.

title: Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics (final, November 2019)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.1 Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics (final, November 2019)
text: Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics (final, November 2019) This is the founding FDA document for the book ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019a ) . It is final. Its four principles for adaptive designs are the ones to remember: “the chance of erroneous conclusions should be adequately controlled, estimation of treatment effects should be sufficiently reliable, details of the design should be completely prespecified, and trial integrity should be appropriately maintained” (Section III). It says plainly that “adaptive features can inflate the Type I error probability of a trial”, with the simplest example a repeated look at accumulating data (Section III.A), and it works through the example of a single interim look at 50 percent of the information. It names simulation for operating characteristics (Section VI.A), limited access to comparative interim data (Sections III and VII), and an example of effectiveness rules based on a Bayesian posterior probability (Section V). It recommends that the four principles be addressed in the protocol and submission, and that complex designs be discussed with FDA beforehand. For frequentist and Bayesian adaptive designs alike, the 2019 document is the baseline, and the 2026 Bayesian draft builds on it.

title: Bayesian methods at the regulators before 2026
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.2 Bayesian methods at the regulators before 2026
text: Bayesian methods at the regulators before 2026 The January 2026 draft is not the first regulatory text on Bayesian trials. ICH E9 (1998) already allowed Bayesian approaches when the reasons for their use are clear and the conclusions are sufficiently robust ( Section 3.4 ), and the device side went first. CDRH issued a draft Bayesian guidance on 23 May 2006 and the final version on 5 February 2010 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2010 ) . The final text treats type I error as one operating characteristic among others and says that when prior information is used it may be appropriate to control it at a less stringent level, case by case (Section 4.8). The CDRH statisticians have written up the experience: Pennello and Thompson on reviewing Bayesian device trials ( Pennello and Thompson 2008 ) , Campbell on the Bayesian innovation the FDA sparked ( Campbell 2011 ) and on the similarities between Bayesian and adaptive designs ( Campbell 2013 ) , and Campbell, Irony, Pennello and Thompson on progress since 2010 ( Campbell et al. 2023 ) . On the drug side, the complex innovative trial design program gave Bayesian designs a forum for early dialogue ( Section 3.7 ), and Ruberg and colleagues argued in 2023 that wider use of Bayesian approaches in drug development could start a virtuous cycle of experience and acceptance ( Ruberg et al. 2023 ) . The practical lesson is the same on both sides of the Agency: agree the prior and the operating characteristics with the reviewers before the trial starts.

title: Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.3 Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026)
text: Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026) This is the document that most changes the conversation for a sponsor considering a Bayesian design ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) . It is a draft guidance for industry, marked “Contains Nonbinding Recommendations”, issued by CDER and CBER under docket FDA-2025-D-3217 in January 2026. It does not apply to devices, which have their own Bayesian guidance ( Section 3.5.2 ); two device approvals under it are in Section 3.11 . Its scope is INDs, NDAs, BLAs and supplements, with a “primary focus” on “the use of Bayesian methods to support primary inference”. Its main elements, in the order a sponsor will meet them: Success criteria. The criterion is “most often based on the posterior probability that the true treatment effect size exceeds some threshold”, \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) . For trials with an overall frequentist analysis plan, the thresholds \(a\) and \(c\) are almost always calibrated so that the familywise type I error rate across all primary and secondary estimands is no greater than 0.025 one-sided; the draft also describes posterior-probability and benefit-risk routes. Priors. “It is always critical for Bayesian analyses to have a prespecified prior.” The sponsor should “pre-specify and justify the full details of the proposed prior distribution in the protocol”.

title: Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.3 Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026)
text: 0.025 one-sided; the draft also describes posterior-probability and benefit-risk routes. Priors. “It is always critical for Bayesian analyses to have a prespecified prior.” The sponsor should “pre-specify and justify the full details of the proposed prior distribution in the protocol”. Skeptical priors “express skepticism about the presence of very large treatment effects”, and design priors that explore pessimistic assumptions should be considered. Where the data do not dominate the prior, “the accuracy of conclusions depends strongly on the choice of prior distribution”. Chapter 8 takes up these points. Borrowing. Static discounting fixes how much external information counts; dynamic methods “borrow less when the data are less similar and more when the data are more similar”. Borrowing needs “strong justification that considers feasibility … and the relevance of the available information”, information should typically come from patient-level data, and a prior that is too informative “risks overwhelming the data collected in the target population”. The draft says that type I error inflation is “not recommended” as the measure of borrowing, and prefers effective sample size and similar influence metrics. The draft’s named examples are summarized in Section 3.11 . Chapter 19 develops borrowing. Operating characteristics and simulation. “Simulations should comprehensively cover the plausible range of assumptions”, and the plan should compare complex designs with simpler alternatives and request an FDA meeting before the trial starts. Documentation.

title: Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026)
