text: Section 3.11 . Chapter 19 develops borrowing. Operating characteristics and simulation. “Simulations should comprehensively cover the plausible range of assumptions”, and the plan should compare complex designs with simpler alternatives and request an FDA meeting before the trial starts. Documentation. The sponsor should submit protocol, SAP and simulation report “as early as possible” and “during the design stage”. The report on the trial should state the estimates and credible intervals, the success criteria, the sensitivity analyses, the computational details (software versions, code, the MCMC seed numbers). On software the draft says that “FDA does not require use of any specific software for statistical analyses”. It requires nothing by itself, since it is a draft; it permits both the calibrated and the non-calibrated pathway, the latter with agreement. Chapter 23 turns the draft into a protocol and SAP checklist.

title: The response to the draft
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.4 The response to the draft
text: The response to the draft Three commentaries on the draft appeared together in JAMA on 19 May 2026 ( Lee et al. 2026 ; Evans et al. 2026 ; Gelman, Zwet, and Więcek 2026 ) . The routes the draft leaves open are described in Chapter 3 ; this book takes calibration as the default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, and direct posterior criteria with FDA agreement when prior information is borrowed, as the draft allows. The older cautions about prior dependence, type I error and operational bias are collected in Section 1.9 .

title: Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development (revised draft, June 2026)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.5 Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development (revised draft, June 2026)
text: Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development (revised draft, June 2026) A first draft appeared in December 2023; a revised draft that “revises and replaces” it was announced in the Federal Register on 24 June 2026 (91 FR 37991), with comments closing on 24 August 2026 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026d ) . FDA’s description of the changes is “additional recommendations on basket trials and minor changes for clarity on topics such as randomization, choice of control, and informed consent”. The document is issued under the Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022 ( U.S. Congress 2022 ) . It defines a master protocol as “a protocol designed with multiple substudies, which may have different objectives and involve coordinated efforts to evaluate one or more drugs”; an umbrella trial “evaluate[s] multiple drugs concurrently for a single disease or condition”, a basket trial “evaluate[s] a drug for multiple diseases, conditions, or disease subtypes”, and a platform trial evaluates multiple drugs “in an ongoing manner, with drugs entering or leaving the platform”. Its recommendations are specific. A shared control arm improves efficiency, and the draft discusses allocating more participants to the control arm than to each drug arm (the EMA platform-trials draft gives Dunnett’s square-root-of- \(k\) rule as one example). The primary comparison should use “only concurrently eligible control participants”; nonconcurrent controls are

title: Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development (revised draft, June 2026)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.5 Master Protocols for Drug and Biological Product Development (revised draft, June 2026)
text: the draft discusses allocating more participants to the control arm than to each drug arm (the EMA platform-trials draft gives Dunnett’s square-root-of- \(k\) rule as one example). The primary comparison should use “only concurrently eligible control participants”; nonconcurrent controls are allowed only in rare circumstances agreed with FDA in advance, with concurrent-only sensitivity analyses. On multiplicity, FDA “generally does not recommend the use of multiplicity adjustments to strongly control the probability of making at least one type I error across the multiple comparisons of different drugs”, because the expected number of type I errors is the same whether the comparisons are made in independent trials or in one master protocol. Adjustment is still expected across doses or formulations of the same drug. For a new master protocol the draft points sponsors to early discussion with FDA, and a master protocol pre-IND meeting is requested as Type B (see the meetings section below). It complements the March 2022 oncology master protocols guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2022a ) . Chapter 20 develops all of this.

title: Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials (final, October 2022)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.6 Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials (final, October 2022)
text: Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials (final, October 2022) This final guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2022b ) describes the multiplicity problem and the strategies for handling it when a trial has several endpoints, doses or comparisons, and the statistical procedures for strong control of the familywise error rate: Bonferroni, Holm, fixed-sequence and gatekeeping procedures, and graphical methods. It is the regulatory partner of ICH E9 section 5.6 and the basis of Chapter 10 . For the Bayesian reader the guidance matters in two ways. It sets the expectation that a claim supported by several endpoints must come with a stated multiplicity strategy, which the Bayesian draft echoes by recommending that the FWER be controlled “across all primary and secondary estimands”. And it leaves room for hierarchical modeling as a complement, not as a replacement, for the confirmatory strategy.

title: AI and new approach methodologies
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.7 AI and new approach methodologies
text: AI and new approach methodologies Two further FDA drafts share this book’s logic. Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence to Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2025) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025 ) sets a seven-step, risk-based credibility framework (question of interest, context of use, model risk, credibility plan, execution, documentation of results and deviations, adequacy determination), in which model risk combines “model influence” and “decision consequence”, the structure of M15. It covers AI that produces information supporting decisions on safety, effectiveness or quality, not AI used only for operational efficiency, so a machine-learned model that selects patients or imputes outcomes in a trial falls under it. General Considerations for the Use of New Approach Methodologies in Drug Development (draft, March 2026) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026c ) concerns nonclinical methods that replace or reduce animal testing. It says a NAM “does not necessarily need to be validated” and is judged in the weight of evidence.

title: Other FDA documents that recur
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.5.8 Other FDA documents that recur
text: Other FDA documents that recur Several other FDA documents recur and are listed in Table 3.4 : the final guidance Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases (August 2024, Project Optimus) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024b ) in Chapter 17 , the February 2023 draft guidance on externally controlled trials ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023 ) in Chapter 19 , the expedited programs guidance (final, May 2014) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2014 ) , and the guidance on data monitoring committees (final, March 2006; revised draft, February 2024) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2006 ) , the template for the DMC firewalls of Chapter 23 . Expedited programs change the speed and intensity of FDA’s interaction, not the substantial-evidence standard: a faster review is not a lower bar.

cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.6 Requires, recommends, permits
text: for comment E20 (June 2025) Not yet adopted in any region Recommends (ICH Step 4) ICH final, adopted regionally E11A (2024); M15 (January 2026) Adopted by FDA as guidance; see the issuer’s page for the regional status Permits Statute or guidance giving discretion One trial plus confirmatory evidence; non-calibrated Bayesian success criteria with FDA agreement; nonconcurrent controls in rare circumstances Available only if the agency concurs, so the route goes through a meeting Process Procedural guidance, PDUFA commitments Formal Meetings (August 2026); CID and MIDD paired meeting programs Defines how to ask. Not a source of evidentiary standards Two corollaries follow. A sponsor does not need a guidance to be final before using it; but a sponsor should never describe a draft as “FDA requirements” in a protocol or a meeting package. And a permission is not an entitlement. The permissions that matter most to Bayesian adaptive designs are all of the form “if FDA agrees”, and the practical meaning of “regulation as the spine” is that those agreements are sought in writing, early, and on the record.

title: Interacting with FDA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7 Interacting with FDA
text: 3.7 Interacting with FDA This section explains how a sponsor finds out whether FDA agrees. FDA’s meeting types and programs differ in what they can promise, and the differences matter.

title: Formal meetings under PDUFA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.1 Formal meetings under PDUFA
text: Formal meetings under PDUFA The procedural guidance Formal Meetings Between the FDA and Sponsors or Applicants of PDUFA Products (August 2026) is the current text; it states that it withdraws the December 2017 formal meetings guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) . PDUFA, the Prescription Drug User Fee Act, is the law, periodically reauthorized, under which sponsors pay fees and FDA commits to review goals and meeting timelines; the current commitments are in the PDUFA VII goals letter for fiscal years 2023 through 2027 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021b ) . The guidance defines six meeting types (Section III): “Type A, Type B, Type B (end of phase (EOP)), Type C, Type D, and Initial Targeted Engagement for Regulatory Advice on CDER and CBER ProducTs (INTERACT)”. In plain terms: Type A is “necessary for an otherwise stalled drug or biological product development program to proceed or to address an important safety issue”. It is for a program that is stuck, for instance after a disagreement with the review division. Type B covers the milestone meetings: pre-IND, and pre-NDA or pre-BLA meetings. Type B (end of phase) covers certain end-of-phase 1 meetings (for products to be considered under 21 CFR part 312 subpart E or part 314 subpart H, or similar products) and end-of-phase 2 meetings, where the sponsor shows the

title: Formal meetings under PDUFA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.1 Formal meetings under PDUFA
text: meetings. Type B (end of phase) covers certain end-of-phase 1 meetings (for products to be considered under 21 CFR part 312 subpart E or part 314 subpart H, or similar products) and end-of-phase 2 meetings, where the sponsor shows the phase 3 plan (Section III.C). A master protocol pre-IND meeting is requested as Type B. Type C is the residual category: any meeting other than A, B, B (EOP), D or INTERACT (Section III.D). It is the usual route for design questions between milestones, such as a novel endpoint or a Bayesian analysis plan. Type D is small and focused: “often one, but typically not more than two issues”. It is meant for a narrow question that does not need a multidisciplinary meeting. INTERACT is for very early engagement: it is “intended for novel drug and biological products and development programs that present unique challenges in early development”. It comes before the first IND. The timelines in the guidance (Tables 1 and 2) are how a trialist plans a calendar. FDA responds to a meeting request within 14 calendar days of receipt for Type A, Type B (EOP) and Type D, and within 21 for Type B and Type C. The meeting or written response is scheduled within 30 days of receipt for Type A, 60 for Type B, 70 for Type B (EOP), 75

title: Formal meetings under PDUFA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.1 Formal meetings under PDUFA
text: Type B (EOP) and Type D, and within 21 for Type B and Type C. The meeting or written response is scheduled within 30 days of receipt for Type A, 60 for Type B, 70 for Type B (EOP), 75 for Type C and 50 for Type D; the INTERACT clocks should be read from the guidance tables. Formats include face to face, video, teleconference and “written response only”, in which written answers replace a meeting (Section IV). Module 13 of the companion lab turns these tables into a clock, and the sensible planning conclusion is that a Type C meeting on a novel design takes roughly three months from request to answer, so it must be requested well before the protocol is final. Meeting minutes matter. FDA’s written responses and the sponsor’s record of agreements are the main evidence at the time of review that a design was discussed. They are not a binding contract: a review division can change its position if the science changes or if the data raise new concerns. But an agreement documented in minutes is persuasive, and a sponsor that departs from it should expect a question.

title: The Complex Innovative Trial Design (CID) paired meeting program
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.2 The Complex Innovative Trial Design (CID) paired meeting program
text: The Complex Innovative Trial Design (CID) paired meeting program The 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 ( United States Congress 2016 ) directed FDA to promote novel trial designs, including complex adaptive and Bayesian designs, through public meetings and guidance. FDA’s response, under its PDUFA commitments, was the CID paired meeting program ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.a ) , and the guidance Interacting with the FDA on Complex Innovative Trial Designs for Drugs and Biological Products (final, December 2020) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2020 ) describes how it works. The program is the main route for a sponsor proposing a Bayesian or otherwise complex adaptive design. In outline: a sponsor applies with a description of the proposed design, and accepted sponsors receive a pair of meetings with extra FDA attention, the second after the sponsor has developed the simulation work discussed in the first. Admission is selective, and the program page is the place to check current eligibility and application windows. Two features matter for the reader. The meetings do not replace the ordinary milestones, and the program asks the sponsor to bring the thing that matters most to a Bayesian design, the simulations: a CID package normally includes the proposed design, the scenarios, the operating characteristics, and the comparison with a simpler alternative.

title: The MIDD paired meeting program
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.3 The MIDD paired meeting program
text: The MIDD paired meeting program The model-informed drug development paired meeting program ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.d ) offers paired meetings with FDA on the use of modeling and simulation approaches in a specific development program, for instance dose selection, trial design simulation, or use of an exposure-response model to support a labeling claim. It is the procedural counterpart of ICH M15 ( International Council for Harmonisation 2026 ) : M15 sets the principles for assessing model credibility, and the program is where a sponsor tests a particular modeling plan against FDA’s reading. A Bayesian adaptive design with a model-based dose-response component (see Chapter 17 ) can fall naturally under both the CID and the MIDD programs, and a sponsor should ask which fits the question: the CID program for the trial’s decision rules, the MIDD program for the models that feed them.

title: Critical Path Innovation Meetings (CPIM)
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.4 Critical Path Innovation Meetings (CPIM)
text: Critical Path Innovation Meetings (CPIM) CPIM is a different kind of meeting ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.b ) . It is a nonbinding, informal discussion of methods or technologies that are not tied to a single product or an active application. FDA’s stated aim is to respond to a request for a CPIM within 14 days. For a group developing a general methodology, such as a class of Bayesian borrowing models, a CPIM is a low-cost way to get an informal view early.

title: Drug Development Tool (DDT) qualification
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.7.5 Drug Development Tool (DDT) qualification
text: Drug Development Tool (DDT) qualification DDT qualification ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.c ) is a formal process by which FDA qualifies a tool, such as a biomarker, a clinical outcome assessment or an animal model, for a stated context of use. Once qualified, the tool can be used by any sponsor within that context of use without FDA re-reviewing its suitability in each application. The context of use is the key idea: a tool is qualified for a purpose, not in the abstract. The 21st Century Cures Act ( United States Congress 2016 ) put the process on a statutory footing. For trial design the relevance is endpoints: a qualified tool is the kind of “well-defined and reliable method of assessing response” that 21 CFR 314.126 asks for, and using it in its context removes one reviewer question. DDT qualification is slow and is typically pursued by consortia.

title: EMA and MHRA counterparts
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.8 EMA and MHRA counterparts
text: 3.8 EMA and MHRA counterparts The European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) apply the same statistical principles, since both adopt ICH guidelines, but their documents on adaptive and complex designs differ in emphasis and date. A sponsor seeking approval in several regions needs to read them together. EMA adaptive-design reflection paper (2007) ( European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use 2007 ) . The reference paper on methodological issues in confirmatory trials planned with an adaptive design (CHMP/EWP/2459/02) was adopted in October 2007 and is still current until E20 reaches its final step in the EU. It is more conservative than the 2019 FDA guidance: adaptations need justification and seamless phase 2/3 designs are treated with caution. EC/EMA/HMA Questions and Answers on complex clinical trials (2022) ( European Commission and European Medicines Agency and Heads of Medicines Agencies 2022 ) . This final document (EMA/298712/2022, version of 23 May 2022, published in June 2022) is the first European text to deal with complex clinical trials as a class: master protocols, platform, basket and umbrella designs, and trials using Bayesian methods. It is practical rather than statistical, covering the clinical trial application under the EU Clinical Trials Regulation, sub-protocols, transparency, and use in marketing authorization applications. On Bayesian methods it asks sponsors to justify and

It is practical rather than statistical, covering the clinical trial application under the EU Clinical Trials Regulation, sub-protocols, transparency, and use in marketing authorization applications. On Bayesian methods it asks sponsors to justify and document the priors, to use prior-predictive simulation, and to engage in early dialogue. EMA concept paper on Bayesian methods (2026) ( European Medicines Agency, Methodology Working Party 2026 ) . The Methodology Working Party agreed a concept paper for a future reflection paper on Bayesian methods in clinical development in November 2025 (EMA/CHMP/1813/2026); the CHMP released it for consultation on 19 January 2026 and the consultation ran from 30 January to 30 April 2026. A concept paper is not guidance: it proposes that a reflection paper be written and lists the questions it should answer, among them what defines technical success for a Bayesian trial, how to assess error control for primary and secondary endpoints without frequentist inference, how much weight the prior carries relative to the data, and which sensitivity analyses are required. The tentative timetable puts a draft reflection paper out for consultation in September 2027 and the final text in June 2028; an EMA workshop on the topic was held in June 2025. Until then a sponsor should read the 2022 Q&A and ICH E9 together. EMA reflection paper on methodological aspects

EMA reflection paper on methodological aspects in confirmatory platform trials (draft, October 2026) ( European Medicines Agency 2026 ) . This is a draft (EMA/217509/2026) that follows the 2022 concept paper. The CHMP adopted it for consultation on 5 October 2026, and the consultation runs from 19 October 2026 to 31 January 2027. It concerns confirmatory platform trials only and deliberately avoids the broader term “master protocol”. It says that objectives, estimands and the overall testing strategy must be documented at the start “as far as possible”, warning that “lack of pre-specification could render a confirmatory platform trial as exploratory only”. It prefers concurrent controls, saying that “non-concurrent controls are usually not acceptable for the primary analysis of the primary endpoint”, and it holds the arm-to-control ratio for each comparison fixed, with the consequence stated plainly: “response adaptive randomisation (RAR) is not supported”. It does not discuss Bayesian methods. FDA’s June 2026 draft permits non-concurrent controls in rare cases by agreement, while the EMA draft is stricter on both controls and allocation, so a global platform should treat the stricter position as the design constraint until the paper is final. Chapter 20 and Chapter 16 discuss the consequences. MHRA draft guideline on external control arms (2025) ( Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency 2025 ) . The MHRA consulted in 2025 on a draft guideline on the use of external control arms based on real-world data to support regulatory decisions. It is relevant here because external controls are a form of borrowing. It parallels FDA’s February 2023 draft guidance on externally controlled trials ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023 ) and is taken up in Chapter 19 . The three regulators share the principles: pre-specification, control of false positive conclusions, simulation, integrity. They differ in how much flexibility they will accept in the primary analysis of a confirmatory trial, and the EMA drafts are the more cautious. A global program should plan European scientific advice in parallel with the US meetings.

title: Reading a regulatory document
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.10 Reading a regulatory document
text: 3.10 Reading a regulatory document Two habits prevent most misuse. Check the date and status on the document itself, and again before submission: FDA media URLs can serve a later revision, and the address of the 2019 substantial-evidence draft now serves the June 2026 revision. And read the context-of-use language of M15 and the AI draft as a rule of proportion: a design whose stopping rule decides approval is highly influential, so its simulation report should be proportionately thorough. None of this replaces the conversation: the review division that examines an application has the last word on what is adequate for that product, and the way to learn its view is to ask, with a concrete design and simulation report in hand.

title: In practice
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.11 In practice
text: 3.11 In practice The standard of this chapter has already been met with Bayesian arithmetic, in a vaccine, a biologic approved on one trial plus borrowing, a pediatric extension and two device approvals, and the January 2026 draft names further examples.

title: REBYOTA: one trial standing in for two
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.11.1 REBYOTA: one trial standing in for two
text: REBYOTA: one trial standing in for two Ferring’s RBX2660 (REBYOTA) for recurrent C. difficile infection was approved on 30 November 2022 ( US Food and Drug Administration, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research 2022 ) on one phase 3 trial (PUNCH CD3) plus a Bayesian hierarchical model that borrowed from a phase 2b study, an approach FDA called “acceptable” ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research 2022 ) . Success was a posterior probability of superiority with two thresholds chosen as analogues of one-sided type I error without borrowing: 0.9993275 (analogue 0.00125, a stricter bar for one trial standing in for two) and 0.9750338 (analogue 0.025, one adequate and well-controlled trial). The observed posterior probability of superiority was 0.991, which clears the second threshold and misses the first, so the evidence counts as one adequate and well-controlled trial, not two. Approval rested on FDA’s assessment of the totality of evidence, and the thresholds were case-specific evidentiary criteria agreed with FDA, not numerical standards set by the 1997 amendment ( Section 3.1 ). The 2026 draft cites it as its example of borrowing from an earlier trial of the same drug ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) . The planning history, the borrowing model and the data-alignment lesson are in Section 19.17.1 .

title: BNT162b2: a Bayesian criterion in an EUA and a BLA
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.11.2 BNT162b2: a Bayesian criterion in an EUA and a BLA
text: BNT162b2: a Bayesian criterion in an EUA and a BLA The pivotal efficacy trial of the Pfizer and BioNTech vaccine (C4591001) had a Bayesian primary criterion written in its statistical analysis plan ( Pfizer Inc. 2022 ) : success was a posterior \(\Pr(\mathrm{VE} \ge 30\% \mid \text{data}) > 0.995\) at an interim analysis or \(> 0.986\) at the final analysis, thresholds calibrated so that the overall one-sided type I error is 0.025. The trial observed 8 cases on vaccine against 162 on placebo, vaccine efficacy (VE) 95.0%, 95% credible interval 90.3 to 97.6 ( Polack et al. 2020 ) . FDA issued the emergency use authorization on 11 December 2020 for ages 16 and older ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021a ) and approved the BLA (Comirnaty) on 23 August 2021. The beta-binomial model and the prior are worked in Section 6.12 . The lesson is that a pivotal trial can use a posterior criterion calibrated to 0.025 (calibration is one of the three routes in the January 2026 draft, and this book’s default), and that both an EUA and a BLA accepted it.

title: Belimumab in children: a tipping point on the borrowing weight
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.11.3 Belimumab in children: a tipping point on the borrowing weight
text: Belimumab in children: a tipping point on the borrowing weight PLUTO (C1109), a small trial of belimumab in pediatric lupus, was not powered to stand alone ( Brunner et al. 2020 ) . At FDA’s request the sponsor borrowed from the adult trials through a robust mixture prior and reported a tipping point: the posterior probability of efficacy was at least 97.5% whenever the borrowing weight was 0.55 or more, a weight the review division judged reasonable, and FDA approved the pediatric indication ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research 2026 ; Pottackal et al. 2025 ) . The analysis was post hoc, and FDA’s case study recommends prespecifying such borrowing with the agency. The full case is in Section 19.17.2 .

title: Devices: Superion and OPTIMIZER Smart
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.11.4 Devices: Superion and OPTIMIZER Smart
text: Devices: Superion and OPTIMIZER Smart CDRH has accepted Bayesian primary analyses for years under its 2010 guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2010 ) . The Superion interspinous spacer (PMA P140004, approved 20 May 2015) was a randomized 1:1 non-inferiority trial against X-STOP with a Bayesian adaptive sample size, a 10% margin, independent Beta(1, 1) priors, and success declared if the posterior probability of non-inferiority was at least 0.958. The final analysis gave 0.9927 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, CDRH 2015 ) . The OPTIMIZER Smart system (P180036, approved 21 March 2019) analyzed FIX-HF-5C ( \(n = 160\) ) with a Bayesian model and 30% fixed borrowing from the earlier FIX-HF-5 study, with success if \(\Pr(\Delta > 0) > 0.975\) for the change in peak VO2. With borrowing the posterior probability was 0.977 to 0.989 across imputation models; the new trial alone gave 0.911 to 0.960 (the lower value when last-observation-carried-forward imputation is included), below the bar ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Devices and Radiological Health 2019 ) . The lesson is that the borrowing weight can decide the outcome, which is why the draft asks for justification and sensitivity analysis.

title: The other precedents in the draft
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > 3.11.5 The other precedents in the draft
text: The other precedents in the draft The draft names the GBM AGILE (NCT03970447) and Precision Promise (NCT04229004) platforms, which use Bayesian models for temporal drift when augmenting concurrent controls ( Saville et al. 2022 ) ; a pediatric multiple sclerosis non-inferiority study through the CID program, with a prespecified Bayesian analysis borrowing historical active-comparator data and modeling relapse rate by age ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, CDER, n.d.b ) ; supportive Bayesian analyses for empagliflozin and linagliptin in pediatric type 2 diabetes, accepted because the pediatric pathophysiology resembles the adult; an epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (EMAS) placebo-controlled study proposed through the CID program, with a hierarchical model borrowing from other epilepsy types ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, CDER, n.d.a ) ; and hierarchical subgroup borrowing in the LEADER trial of liraglutide and the Rinvoq Drug Trial Snapshot ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026e ) . For the last three we rely on the draft’s description.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > Key points
text: Key points The legal standard is substantial evidence of effectiveness: adequate and well-controlled investigations (FD&C Act 505(d)), characterized by 21 CFR 314.126. The statute is a standard of evidence, not of method; it names no test, level or prior. Since FDAMA 1997, one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence can suffice at FDA’s discretion. The June 2026 revised draft says this calls for a highly persuasive trial or strong confirmatory evidence, and that the plan should be discussed with FDA before the trial. A traditional submission rests on pre-specification and error control: a protocol with a fixed sample size, a SAP, a one-sided 0.025 level (two-sided 0.05), a stated multiplicity strategy, and a DMC for interim looks. Bayesian adaptive designs keep all of that and add a simulation report and a justified prior. For confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, this book uses calibration of the success criterion to one-sided 0.025; FDA’s draft also describes direct posterior interpretation and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria (Section IV.A). The Bayesian draft (January 2026) states success as \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) and describes three routes, by agreement with FDA: calibration to a familywise error rate (typically 0.025 one-sided), direct posterior interpretation, and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria. Calibration is this book’s default, not the draft’s. Against a single unadjusted analysis the calibrated bar is not lower without

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 3: The Regulatory Framework > Key points
text: agreement with FDA: calibration to a familywise error rate (typically 0.025 one-sided), direct posterior interpretation, and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria. Calibration is this book’s default, not the draft’s. Against a single unadjusted analysis the calibrated bar is not lower without an informative prior. Documents differ in force: statutes and regulations bind; guidances recommend; drafts are subject to change; permissions depend on FDA’s agreement. Never describe a draft as a requirement. The statuses that matter as of November 2026: Adaptive Designs final (2019); Bayesian, Master Protocols and Substantial Evidence drafts (2026); ICH E20 at Step 2; ICH M15 at Step 4; EMA platform draft in consultation to 31 January 2027. Real approvals already use the arithmetic: REBYOTA’s two posterior thresholds (0.9993275 for one trial standing in for two, 0.9750338 for one adequate and well-controlled trial; observed 0.991), BNT162b2’s calibrated posterior criterion, belimumab’s tipping-point analysis, and CDRH’s Superion and OPTIMIZER Smart approvals ( Section 3.11 ). FDA offers Type A, B, B (EOP), C, D and INTERACT meetings, the CID and MIDD paired meeting programs, CPIM, and DDT qualification. A novel design should go to FDA early, with simulations in hand. EMA’s drafts are more cautious than FDA’s on allocation and nonconcurrent controls; a global platform should design to the stricter position. Note Discussion questions The statute asks whether experts “could fairly and responsibly” conclude that the drug works, and does not mention a significance level. Why has 0.025 one-sided become so entrenched, and what would have to be true for a regulator to accept a different working standard in a given program? The June 2026 substantial-evidence draft allows one trial with confirmatory evidence. In what ways is an informative Bayesian prior similar to confirmatory evidence, and in what ways is it different? Who decides the weight, and when? Suppose your sponsor is considering a Bayesian adaptive phase 3 design with response-adaptive randomization across three arms, to be submitted in both the US and the EU. Using the FDA master protocol draft and the EMA platform draft, which design elements would you keep, and which would you change? A colleague says “FDA requires a simulation report for any Bayesian design”. Is that accurate? Classify the statement using the requires, recommends, permits distinction, and name the document you would cite. title: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4 Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up
text: A trial ends with two rows of numbers, one for each arm, and a question that sounds simple: are they different? Everything that follows in this book, the Bayesian machinery included, is an answer to a sharper version of that question: how much should the gap between the rows change what we do? This chapter rebuilds the traditional answer from nothing. We assume you have forgotten testing, or learned it as a set of recipes without the picture behind them. We use one trial, simulated many ways, so that every formula arrives after the thing it summarizes has been seen. The plan is short. First we look at how patients differ from one another, because that variation is the whole reason a trial needs statistics. Then we rerun the trial thousands of times on the computer and look at how the observed difference wobbles. That wobble is the sampling distribution, and every test and interval in the chapter is a way of reading it. The first test we build, the randomization test, needs nothing beyond shuffling labels. The z test is the same idea with a bell curve in place of the shuffling. Confidence intervals, error rates, power and the choice between one-sided and two-sided tests then follow, and we finish with what regulators write down about each. Important Regulatory anchor ICH E9, Statistical Principles

title: One trial, two endpoints
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.1 One trial, two endpoints
text: 4.1 One trial, two endpoints Throughout the chapter we use two versions of the same trial: an investigational drug against control, with 100 patients per arm, allocated by a fair coin. For these calculations, we condition on 100 patients in each arm. The first version has a binary endpoint, whether the patient responded. Suppose the control response rate is 30% and the drug’s true response rate is 45%, a difference of 15 percentage points. The second version has a continuous endpoint, the fall in systolic blood pressure in mmHg after twelve weeks. Suppose the true mean fall is 4 mmHg larger on the drug, and that patients vary around their arm’s mean with a standard deviation of 12 mmHg. These numbers are chosen to be plausible and round. They are the truth of the simulated world, which no real trial ever gets to see, and that is the point of simulating: we can compare what the analysis says with what we know is true. The notation follows the book. The response probability in arm \(j\) is \(p_j\) , with \(j = 0\) for control and \(j = 1\) for the drug. The treatment effect is \(\theta\) , here \(\theta = p_1 - p_0\) for the binary endpoint and \(\theta = \mu_1 - \mu_0\) for the continuous one. The number of patients in each arm is

The number of patients in each arm is \(n_0 = n_1 = n\) , so the total is \(2n\) ; this chapter writes \(n\) for the common arm size. The first thing to see is variation between patients. Figure 4.1 shows one simulated trial of each kind. In the binary version each square is a patient, filled if they responded. Nobody’s response is a fixed property of the drug: among 100 patients on control, about 30 respond, and which 30 is not something we can predict. In the continuous version each dot is a patient’s blood pressure fall. The two clouds overlap heavily. Many patients on the drug do worse than the average patient on control, and many on control do better than the average patient on the drug. Cox had in mind when he wrote about the comparison of treatments in the presence of what he called large uncontrolled variations between experimental units ( Cox 1958 ) . If every patient responded identically to a given treatment, one patient per arm would settle the matter. Because they do not, a single difference in averages comes with a question attached: would we have seen a gap like this anyway, from the luck of which patients landed where? A test is a procedure for answering that question honestly. A word on what the data cannot tell us. Each patient has, in principle, two potential outcomes, one under each treatment, and we see only one of them. The laboratory module that accompanies this chapter draws the unseen outcomes as faded cells for this reason. Randomization is what lets the observed gap stand in for the unobservable average difference between the two potential outcomes, and Chapter 5 takes that argument up properly. title: The same trial, rerun ten thousand times
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.2 The same trial, rerun ten thousand times
text: 4.2 The same trial, rerun ten thousand times Here is the experiment that makes the rest of the chapter easy. Take the binary trial and rerun it. Draw 100 new control patients with a 30% chance of responding, 100 new drug patients with a 45% chance, and compute the observed difference in response rates. Do it again. Do it ten thousand times. We cannot run a real trial ten thousand times, but a computer can, and the resulting histogram is the sampling distribution of the observed difference: the pattern of results the trial design produces, given a truth. It is a hill of about the same width centered on zero, and its upper tail is not empty: in roughly 1.0% of those reruns the observed difference is 0.15 or larger, which is the gap we saw. A drug that does nothing produces a result as good as ours about 1 time in 100. The p-values of the next sections (0.014 to 0.021, depending on the method) are the same idea computed from the data of one trial, and they differ from this 1.0% because a real trial does not know that both arms are at 30%. That last sentence is, in essence, a p-value, built from the picture and not from a formula. The same logic applied to RECOVERY’s 28-day mortality comparison is in Section 4.11 . To turn it into a method we must find a way to learn the right-hand histogram from the data of one trial, because in a real trial we do not know that both arms are 30%.

text: in Section 4.11 . To turn it into a method we must find a way to learn the right-hand histogram from the data of one trial, because in a real trial we do not know that both arms are 30%. The next two sections give two ways to do this. The width of the histogram has a formula worth knowing. The standard deviation of the observed difference, called the standard error, is \[ \mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n} + \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n}} , \tag{4.1}\] which for our numbers is \(\sqrt{0.3 \times 0.7/100 + 0.45 \times 0.55/100} = 0.0676\) , matching the simulation. For the continuous endpoint, with common standard deviation \(\sigma\) , it is \(\sigma\sqrt{2/n} = 12\sqrt{2/100} = 1.70\) mmHg. Two features matter for planning. The standard error shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{n}\) , so halving it requires quadrupling the trial. And it grows with the variability of the outcome: noisier patients mean wider histograms, which is why trials work so hard on reducing measurement noise.

title: The randomization test: shuffle the labels
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.3 The randomization test: shuffle the labels
text: 4.3 The randomization test: shuffle the labels The simplest honest test uses nothing but the randomization the trial already performed. Suppose the drug does nothing at all, a claim that Fisher called the null hypothesis ( Fisher 1935 ) . Then each patient’s outcome would have been what it was whatever arm they were assigned to (Fisher’s sharp null, which is stronger than a zero average effect, because opposing individual effects can average to zero; Chapter 5 gives the full definition), and the label “drug” or “control” on a patient is just the result of the coin. Under that hypothesis, a different toss of the coins would have produced the same 200 outcomes, dealt into the two arms differently. So we can imitate the coin: pool the 200 outcomes, shuffle the labels, deal 100 into a “drug” arm and 100 into a “control” arm, and compute the difference. Repeat many times. The histogram of those differences shows what chance alone does to this particular set of 200 patients. Figure 4.3 first shows the idea on a handful of shuffles, then the histogram from 20,000 of them, with the observed difference marked. The share of shuffles at least as large as the observed difference is the randomization p-value. Show the R code pt <- perm_test (y1, y0, nsim = 20000 , seed = 5 ) six

In real trials, with stratified randomization or a covariate-adjusted analysis, the shuffle must respect the randomization scheme, so only labels within a stratum are exchanged. title: The normal approximation and the z test
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.4 The normal approximation and the z test
text: 4.4 The normal approximation and the z test Shuffling is correct but heavy, and it was laborious before computers (exact enumeration and manual randomization tests existed long before them, but they were practical only for very small trials). The histograms we have drawn all look like bell curves. This is not an accident: the observed difference is an average of many small independent contributions, one from each patient, and the central limit theorem says that such sums settle into a normal distribution as \(n\) grows. This lets us replace the shuffling with a formula. Under the null hypothesis, where the drug does nothing, the difference in response rates is approximately normal with mean zero and standard error computed from the pooled response rate \(\bar p = (x_0 + x_1)/(2n)\) , where \(x_j\) is the number of responders in arm \(j\) : \[ Z = \frac{\hat p_1 - \hat p_0}{\sqrt{2\bar p(1-\bar p)/n}} . \tag{4.2}\] The pooling uses the null hypothesis that both arms have the same \(p\) . For the continuous endpoint the statistic is the difference in means divided by \(\sqrt{s_1^2/n + s_0^2/n}\) , with \(s_j\) the sample standard deviation in arm \(j\) . We then ask how far out in the tail of a standard normal curve \(Z\) falls. A value of \(Z\) means “this many standard errors from zero”, and the book’s notation

A value of \(Z\) means “this many standard errors from zero”, and the book’s notation \(z_\alpha\) is the upper \(\alpha\) quantile of the standard normal, so \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\) . For the binary trial, \(\bar p = 0.375\) , the standard error is 0.0685, and \(Z = 0.15/0.0685 = 2.19\) . text: Randomization (shuffle) 0.005 0.011 Continuous z test 0.005 0.010 Continuous t test 0.006 0.011 Note Technical note: why \(Z\) is approximately standard normal Write the difference in means as \(\bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0\) . Each mean is an average of \(n\) independent terms, so by the central limit theorem it is approximately normal with mean \(\mu_j\) and variance \(\sigma_j^2/n\) . The difference of independent normals is normal with variance \(\sigma_1^2/n + \sigma_0^2/n\) . Dividing by the standard error gives a statistic that is approximately \(N(0,1)\) under the null. For the binary endpoint the variance of a single response is \(p(1-p)\) , which is what Equation 4.1 uses. When the variance is estimated from the data and \(n\) is small, the reference distribution is a Student \(t\) with slightly heavier tails, but with 100 patients per arm the difference is in the third decimal (the 97.5th percentile is 1.972 on 198 degrees of freedom against 1.960). For the clinician: the approximation fails when responses are rare, when \(n\) is small, or when the outcome has extreme values that dominate the mean. In those situations use the exact or shuffle versions, and make the choice in the protocol.

title: The p-value, defined carefully
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.5 The p-value, defined carefully
text: 4.5 The p-value, defined carefully Both tests produced a number called the p-value. It is worth defining it once with care, because everything about misuse starts with sloppy definitions. The ingredients are three: a null hypothesis, a test statistic, and the data. The null hypothesis \(H_0\) is the claim that the treatment effect is zero, \(\theta = 0\) (or, for a one-sided test, \(\theta \le 0\) ), a statement about the average effect and weaker than the sharp null of the randomization test. The test statistic is a summary of the data that is large when the data favor the drug: here, the observed difference or the \(Z\) derived from it. The p-value is then \[ p \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{test statistic at least as favorable to the drug as the one observed} \;\bigm|\; H_0 \text{ true}\bigr) , \tag{4.3}\] where the probability is over the repetition of the trial, in the sampling sense of the previous sections. That is the share of the right-hand histogram of Figure 4.2 beyond the observed value. It is the answer to the question “if nothing is going on, how often would luck look this good?” The definition has several consequences that are easy to forget. The probability is about the data, given the hypothesis. It is not the probability of the hypothesis given the data. A p-value of 0.014 does not

title: The p-value, defined carefully
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.5 The p-value, defined carefully
text: luck look this good?” The definition has several consequences that are easy to forget. The probability is about the data, given the hypothesis. It is not the probability of the hypothesis given the data. A p-value of 0.014 does not mean a 1.4% chance that the drug does not work, and its complement is not the probability that the drug works. Getting from data to the probability of a hypothesis needs a prior, which is the subject of Chapter 6 . It depends on the plan, not only on the data. The same sequence of 9 heads and 3 tails has different p-values if the experimenter planned 12 flips or planned to stop at the third tail, because “as extreme or more” is evaluated over the trials one could have run. In trial language, a p-value depends on the stopping rule and on the number of analyses. This is the reason interim looks must be pre-specified, and it is the starting point of Chapter 11 . It depends on how many questions were asked. A p-value of 0.03 for the one endpoint the protocol named in advance and a p-value of 0.03 for the best of twenty endpoints are not the same evidence. ICH E9 section 5.6 states that multiplicity “may necessitate an adjustment to the type I error”, and Chapter 10 treats the methods.

title: The p-value, defined carefully
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.5 The p-value, defined carefully
text: in advance and a p-value of 0.03 for the best of twenty endpoints are not the same evidence. ICH E9 section 5.6 states that multiplicity “may necessitate an adjustment to the type I error”, and Chapter 10 treats the methods. It mixes the size of the effect with the size of the trial. A tiny and clinically irrelevant difference gives a tiny p-value in a huge trial, and a large and important difference can give an unimpressive p-value in a small one. The p-value says nothing about whether the effect is worth having. That is the job of the estimate and its interval. A large p-value is not evidence of no effect. It says the data were not surprising under the null. They may be even less surprising under a real and useful effect, and in a trial of 50 per arm the 30% versus 45% drug has a power near one in three (the next sections explain what that means). The American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values collects these points ( Wasserstein and Lazar 2016 ) , and Goodman’s “dirty dozen” lists twelve misreadings that survive in the clinical literature ( Goodman 2008 ) . We return to the evidential meaning of a p-value, and to what a Bayes factor or a posterior probability would say about the same data, in Chapter 7 .

text: that survive in the clinical literature ( Goodman 2008 ) . We return to the evidential meaning of a p-value, and to what a Bayes factor or a posterior probability would say about the same data, in Chapter 7 . To turn a p-value into a decision, we need a threshold. The protocol fixes a level \(\alpha\) in advance, and rejects \(H_0\) if \(p \le \alpha\) . That is a decision rule with a known long-run error rate, and the next sections look at what the rule does when the drug works and when it does not.

title: Confidence intervals
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.6 Confidence intervals
text: 4.6 Confidence intervals A p-value says whether the data are compatible with no effect. It does not say what effect is likely, and a decision about a drug needs both. A confidence interval reports the range of effect sizes that the data do not rule out. For a difference with an approximately normal estimator the 95% interval is the estimate plus and minus 1.96 standard errors: \[ \hat\theta \;\pm\; 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta) . \tag{4.4}\] For the binary trial the standard error with unpooled rates ( Equation 4.1 , estimated) is 0.0676, so the 95% interval for the risk difference is \(0.15 \pm 0.132\) , that is, 0.017 to 0.283. The data are compatible with a gain as small as 2 percentage points and as large as 28. For the continuous trial the interval is \(4.69 \pm 1.96 \times 1.83\) , that is, 1.10 to 8.28 mmHg. Neither interval contains zero, which agrees with the two-sided tests that gave p-values below 0.05. The interval is wide, and this is not a flaw of the method. It tells the truth about a trial of 100 per arm: a response-rate gain of 2 points and one of 28 points are both consistent with what we saw, and they would lead to different decisions about whether the drug is worth developing. ICH E9 section 5.5 asks that estimates of treatment effects “should be accompanied by confidence intervals, whenever possible”. The reason is that a bare p-value hides this width.

title: What the 95% refers to
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.6.1 What the 95% refers to
text: What the 95% refers to The correct reading of “95%” is about the procedure, not about one interval. If the same trial were rerun many times and an interval computed each time, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true effect. Figure 4.5 shows 50 reruns of the binary trial, with the true difference of 0.15 marked. The vertical line is the truth (0.15). Orange intervals miss it. In the long run about 5% of intervals miss; in 50 trials the count is itself random. Over 100,000 reruns the Wald interval covers the truth in 94.8% of reruns, close to the nominal 95%. That shortfall is a property of the normal approximation again, as with the p-values; better-behaved intervals for proportions exist, for example the score-based interval that Newcombe compared with ten other methods ( Newcombe 1998 ) . The practical rule is the one for tests: name the interval method in the analysis plan. Notice also what the interval is not. It is not a statement that there is a 95% chance that the true difference lies in 0.017 to 0.283. Once computed, the interval either contains the truth or does not, and the 95% describes the method’s long-run record. A statement of the form “given these data, the probability that the effect lies in this range is 95%” is a different object, a credible interval, and requires a

title: What the 95% refers to
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.6.1 What the 95% refers to
text: or does not, and the 95% describes the method’s long-run record. A statement of the form “given these data, the probability that the effect lies in this range is 95%” is a different object, a credible interval, and requires a prior. For a large trial with little prior information the two usually agree numerically, which is why the common misreading rarely does damage, but the distinction matters when the sample is small, the prior is informative, or when we want to evaluate a decision rule. Chapter 6 returns to it.

title: Tests and intervals are the same thing
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.6.2 Tests and intervals are the same thing
text: Tests and intervals are the same thing A confidence interval and a test are two views of one calculation. The 95% two-sided interval contains exactly the values \(\theta_0\) that a two-sided test at the 5% level would not reject: if you ask “can we reject that the true difference is \(\theta_0\) ?” for every \(\theta_0\) , the ones you cannot reject form the interval. This is the duality. It has a protocol consequence. A test of no effect asks only whether 0 is in the interval, but the same machinery also lets you test other hypotheses, such as “the benefit is at least 5 points”, by checking whether the relevant confidence bound (here the lower limit of a one-sided interval) is above 5, not merely whether 5 lies inside a two-sided interval. Non-inferiority testing rests on this: the null hypothesis is that the new treatment is worse than control by at least the margin, and the test is whether the lower end of a one-sided interval clears the margin. It also explains why ICH E9 links the two. The same section that calls for confidence intervals, section 5.5, says the one-sided type I error should be set at half of the two-sided one, and gives the reason: “This promotes consistency with the two-sided confidence intervals that are generally appropriate for estimating the possible size of

title: Tests and intervals are the same thing
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.6.2 Tests and intervals are the same thing
text: intervals, section 5.5, says the one-sided type I error should be set at half of the two-sided one, and gives the reason: “This promotes consistency with the two-sided confidence intervals that are generally appropriate for estimating the possible size of the difference between two treatments.” A one-sided test at 0.025 rejects essentially when the lower limit of the two-sided 95% interval is above zero, so the result in the CSR (a p-value) and the figure in the abstract (an interval) cannot disagree in any material way. (The equivalence is exact only when the test and the interval use the same standard error. Our binary trial uses 0.0685 in the pooled test and 0.0676 in the interval, so a result very close to the line could fall on different sides.) For the binary trial, the lower limit of the interval is 0.017, above zero, and the one-sided p-value from the normal test (0.014) is below 0.025. For the continuous trial the lower limit is 1.10 and the one-sided p-value is 0.005. Both trials “succeed” on the regulatory convention, though the binary one only just, and the width of its interval is a more honest summary than the verdict.

title: Two kinds of error, and power
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.7 Two kinds of error, and power
text: 4.7 Two kinds of error, and power So far we have asked what the data say about one trial. A regulator, a sponsor and a patient also want to know how often the decision rule, “reject \(H_0\) if \(p \le \alpha\) ”, gives the wrong answer. There are two ways to be wrong, and they are not symmetric. The language of type I and type II errors and of power is Neyman and Pearson’s ( Neyman and Pearson 1933 ) . Fisher’s p-value as a measure of evidence against a null hypothesis, and the 0.05 convention, come from his work ( Fisher 1935 , 1946 ) . A type I error is rejecting \(H_0\) when the drug has no effect: approving something useless. A type II error is failing to reject \(H_0\) when the drug does work: abandoning something useful. The probability of a type I error is the level of the test, \(\alpha\) . The probability of a type II error is \(\beta\) , and the probability of avoiding it, \(1 - \beta\) , is the power . Notice that \(\alpha\) is a probability computed under the null world and that \(\beta\) is computed under a specific alternative. Power is not a single number for a trial but a function of the true effect, and when someone quotes “90% power” the first question is:

title: Two kinds of error, and power
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.7 Two kinds of error, and power
text: computed under the null world and that \(\beta\) is computed under a specific alternative. Power is not a single number for a trial but a function of the true effect, and when someone quotes “90% power” the first question is: for what effect? We can read both off the simulation of Figure 4.2 . Run the same trial many times, apply the decision rule each time, and count rejections. In the world where the drug does nothing the rejection rate is the type I error rate, and it is close to the nominal 2.5% when we reject for \(Z > 1.96\) . In the world with the true 15-point effect the rejection rate is the power. Right: power of the one-sided 0.025 test against the number of patients per arm. The type I error is held at about 2.5%, because that is what the threshold 1.96 was chosen to do. The power at 100 patients per arm is 60%: if the drug truly lifts the response rate from 30% to 45%, this trial would detect it about six times in ten. The other four times, a drug that works would be missed. Our observed trial, with \(Z = 2.19\) , happens to be one of the six. It would be wrong to read that as evidence that the trial was well designed. The right-hand panel shows that power rises with the number of patients: roughly 35% at 50 per arm, 60% at 100, 78% at 150, 88% at 200, 94% at 250 and 97% at 300. The continuous trial, with a 4 mmHg effect and standard deviation of 12 mmHg, has power of about 65% at 100 per arm. The two errors trade against each other. Lower \(\alpha\) to reduce false positives and the rejection region shrinks, so power falls. Raise \(\alpha\) and power rises, along with the chance of approving something useless. The only way to improve both at once is to make the standard error smaller, with more patients, a less noisy endpoint, or better use of information, and this is where the later chapters of the book make their case. The size of a trial is dictated by the question “how many patients make both errors acceptably small?” and the answer is a formula in \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , the effect and the variance that Chapter 9 develops. A guide for the reader who wants the shape now: for a one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) and 90% power, the number of patients needed is proportional to \((z_{0.025} + z_{0.10})^2 = 10.51\) divided by the squared standardized effect. It is worth stating who bears each error. A type I error falls mostly on future

title: Two kinds of error, and power
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.7 Two kinds of error, and power
text: = 0.025\) and 90% power, the number of patients needed is proportional to \((z_{0.025} + z_{0.10})^2 = 10.51\) divided by the squared standardized effect. It is worth stating who bears each error. A type I error falls mostly on future patients, who receive a drug that does not work, and on the regulator who approved it. A type II error falls on future patients too, who will not receive a drug that would have helped, and on the sponsor who abandoned it. Regulators fix \(\alpha\) by convention and leave \(\beta\) to the sponsor’s judgment, which is why the traditional design is organized around the type I error and why sponsors, who pay for the type II error, ask for more efficient designs. Module 03 of the laboratory, errors and power ( https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/03-errors-power.html ), lets you move the slider and see the two areas trade off.

title: One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.8 One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
text: 4.8 One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025 We have used both kinds of p-value, so we must say which one counts. A two-sided test counts departures from the null in either direction as evidence: the drug might help or harm, and the test is alert to both. A one-sided test counts only departures in the direction of benefit. In the shuffle picture the one-sided p-value is the orange tail on the right, and the two-sided is that tail plus its mirror image on the left (twice as large, when the reference distribution is symmetric). The argument for the two-sided test is that a trial should be able to detect harm, and that a one-sided test with a generous level appears to lower the bar. The argument for the one-sided test is that the regulatory question for a new drug is asymmetric: approval depends on benefit being demonstrated, and a harmful drug is, for the purpose of the efficacy decision, not approved either way. Harm shows up in the safety analyses and in the interim monitoring by the data monitoring committee. The regulatory convention resolves the matter in a way that keeps both arguments. ICH E9 section 5.5 asks the sponsor to say in the protocol whether one- or two-sided tests will be used and to “justify prospectively the use of one-sided tests”. It then states

title: One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.8 One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
text: matter in a way that keeps both arguments. ICH E9 section 5.5 asks the sponsor to say in the protocol whether one- or two-sided tests will be used and to “justify prospectively the use of one-sided tests”. It then states the rule that decides the practical question: “The approach of setting type I errors for one-sided tests at half the conventional type I error used in two-sided tests is preferable in regulatory settings.” With the conventional two-sided level of 0.05, half is 0.025. That is the origin of the book’s default: a one-sided level of \(\alpha = 0.025\) is the same evidential bar as a two-sided level of 0.05, as the confidence interval duality of the previous section shows: both reject when the 95% interval excludes zero on the favorable side. The more recent FDA draft guidance on Bayesian methodology uses exactly this language, describing the usual standard as performing a statistical hypothesis test at a one-sided significance level of 0.025 (section IV.A, draft, January 2026, non-binding) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . Two practical consequences follow. First, when a paper reports “p = 0.04, two-sided” for a drug that helped, the one-sided equivalent is 0.02, and the trial meets the 0.025 bar. When a paper reports “one-sided p = 0.04”, it does not, and the usual regulatory reading would be that

title: One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.8 One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
text: “p = 0.04, two-sided” for a drug that helped, the one-sided equivalent is 0.02, and the trial meets the 0.025 bar. When a paper reports “one-sided p = 0.04”, it does not, and the usual regulatory reading would be that the trial missed. Always check which p-value is quoted. Our binary trial is a live example of this edge: the normal z test gives a one-sided p-value of 0.014, the Fisher exact test 0.020 and the randomization test 0.021. All three clear 0.025, but the last two with little room. The claim “the drug works” is the same in each, but the margin is slim. Second, the sample size formula contains \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\) for one-sided designs, which is the same number as the two-sided 5% critical value, so the trial size is the same under either label provided the conventions are matched. It is also possible to be tempted by the one-sided test in the wrong way. If the sponsor looks at the data, sees the drug is ahead, and then declares a one-sided test at 0.05, the type I error rate has doubled to 5% for a drug that does nothing, and the test is no longer prospectively justified. This is why E9 says what it says, and why the statistical analysis plan fixes the side, the level and the test before unblinding.

title: One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.8 One-sided or two-sided, and why 0.025
text: to 5% for a drug that does nothing, and the test is no longer prospectively justified. This is why E9 says what it says, and why the statistical analysis plan fixes the side, the level and the test before unblinding. The trap in the other direction is that a one-sided 0.025 test gives no formal weight to results in the harmful direction. A trial can end with a strongly negative difference and a one-sided p-value near 1, which is true but uninformative; the safety review and monitoring plan, and not the efficacy test, are where harm is handled.

title: Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9 Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin
text: 4.9 Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin Every test so far asked whether the drug beats a comparator. Many trials ask a different question. When an effective treatment already exists, withholding it in favor of placebo is often unethical, so the new drug is compared with the active control, and the claim is that it is not unacceptably worse, perhaps because it is safer, cheaper, easier to take, or because the trial is an outcomes trial in which the new drug is expected to help the heart as well as lower glucose. This is a noninferiority trial, and its logic is the logic of this chapter with the null hypothesis moved. Let \(\gamma = \log \mathrm{HR}\) be the raw log hazard ratio of the new drug against the active control, a separate symbol from the effect \(\theta\) of the book’s notation because here values above zero mean the new drug is worse. The superiority hypotheses are \(H_0:\gamma\ge 0\) against \(H_1:\gamma<0\) . For noninferiority with margin \(M>1\) on the hazard ratio scale, the hypotheses are \[ H_0:\ \gamma \ge \log M \qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1:\ \gamma < \log M. \tag{4.5}\] Rejecting \(H_0\) means the new drug is shown to be no worse than the margin allows. The test is one-sided at 0.025, exactly as in Section 4.8 , and it is equivalent to checking whether the upper

title: Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9 Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin
text: \log M. \tag{4.5}\] Rejecting \(H_0\) means the new drug is shown to be no worse than the margin allows. The test is one-sided at 0.025, exactly as in Section 4.8 , and it is equivalent to checking whether the upper limit of the two-sided 95% interval lies below \(\log M\) ( Section 4.6 ). Nothing about the machinery is new; what is new is that the answer depends entirely on \(M\) , a number the data do not supply. Putting the burden of proof on the claim of similarity, by reversing the roles of null and alternative, goes back to Dunnett and Gent for equivalence ( Dunnett and Gent 1977 ) and to Blackwelder for noninferiority ( Blackwelder 1982 ) .

title: Where the margin comes from
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9.1 Where the margin comes from
text: Where the margin comes from The FDA guidance on noninferiority trials (final, November 2016) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016 ) and ICH E10 ( International Council for Harmonisation 2000 ) give the reasoning. A noninferiority trial with no placebo arm cannot show by itself that the new drug works: if the new drug is “not much worse” than a control, and the control was never shown to work in this trial, the comparison is informative only if the control’s effect is known from earlier placebo-controlled trials and is assumed to hold now. The guidance builds the margin in two steps. The first, usually written \(M_1\) , is the whole effect of the active control over placebo that the sponsor can reasonably assume in the present trial, estimated from the historical trials (conventionally the conservative limit of a meta-analytic confidence interval, not the point estimate). The second, \(M_2\) , is the margin actually used, chosen to preserve a clinically meaningful fraction of that effect, so that \(M_2\le M_1\) . How much to preserve is a clinical judgment, and the guidance says the margin should be justified for the setting, not read from a convention. Two ways of using the historical estimate are described (Rothmann and colleagues set out both for noninferiority mortality trials in oncology ( Rothmann et al. 2003 ) ): the fixed-margin

title: Where the margin comes from
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9.1 Where the margin comes from
text: be justified for the setting, not read from a convention. Two ways of using the historical estimate are described (Rothmann and colleagues set out both for noninferiority mortality trials in oncology ( Rothmann et al. 2003 ) ): the fixed-margin approach, which sets the margin from the historical confidence limit and then runs an ordinary test, and the synthesis approach, which combines the historical and current estimates directly and carries the uncertainty of both into one test (the Bayesian version is in Section 19.11 ). The scheme rests on the constancy assumption : the effect of the active control against placebo, estimated years ago, is the effect it would have had in this trial’s population, with this background care and this endpoint definition. The assumption cannot be checked within the trial, which is why the guidance and ICH E10 attach so much weight to assay sensitivity , the ability of the trial to distinguish an effective treatment from an ineffective one. A noninferiority trial that is sloppy (poor adherence, crossover, loosely defined events) pulls the two arms together and makes any new drug look noninferior, so the usual protections against bias in a superiority trial work in the opposite direction here. Sloppiness helps the sponsor, which is the reason the analysis population also matters. The guidance stresses trial quality and conduct; it does not prescribe

title: Where the margin comes from
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9.1 Where the margin comes from
text: so the usual protections against bias in a superiority trial work in the opposite direction here. Sloppiness helps the sponsor, which is the reason the analysis population also matters. The guidance stresses trial quality and conduct; it does not prescribe a rule that intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses must agree, though reporting both and examining any discrepancy is common practice. The margin must be fixed in the protocol and justified before unblinding. A margin that is changed after the data are seen is not a margin.

title: Equivalence
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.9.2 Equivalence
text: Equivalence An equivalence trial asks for the difference to lie inside a two-sided margin, \(-\log M<\gamma<\log M\) on the log scale (the hazard ratio between \(1/M\) and \(M\) ). The standard analysis is two one-sided tests (TOST), each at the one-sided level, one against each end of the margin, and equivalence is declared only if both reject; this is the same as the confidence interval lying entirely inside \((-\log M, \log M)\) . Bioequivalence studies and some biosimilar comparisons use this form. Most clinical efficacy trials that say “equivalence” mean noninferiority, and the one-sided test is the more common. The upper bound of a two-sided 95% interval is the standard one-sided 0.025 noninferiority test, and noninferiority imposes no corresponding lower-bound requirement. A sponsor who wants noninferiority should say so, and should not frame the trial as equivalence, which adds a lower-bound requirement that the question does not need.

Dulaglutide was chosen as the control because REWIND had shown that it reduces cardiovascular events against placebo ( Gerstein et al. 2019 ) , which is what makes it a legitimate active comparator. The pre-specified noninferiority margin was 1.05 for the upper limit of the 95.3% confidence interval of the hazard ratio, and superiority would be claimed only if the upper limit were below 1.00. The trial randomized 13,299 patients; the modified intention-to-treat population was 13,165 (6586 on tirzepatide, 6579 on dulaglutide). Against the margin the one-sided p-value is 0.0037, in line with the reported 0.003 (the reported value comes from the trial’s own analysis, which can differ a little from a calculation on the rounded interval), so noninferiority is established. Against zero the one-sided p-value is 0.05, in line with the reported two-sided 0.09 for superiority, so superiority is not. Both statements come from the same interval. The two tests have two different nulls, and the trial can win the first and lose the second without contradiction. Notice also that the margin did the work: the upper limit 1.01 is above 1.00 and below 1.05, and a margin of 1.00 would have been a superiority trial. The traditional report stops here: noninferiority met, superiority not met. What it does not give is the probability that the hazard ratio lies below 1.05, below 1.00, or below 0.90, nor the effect against placebo that the dulaglutide comparison implies. The probability that the hazard ratio lies below a given value is a posterior probability, which is where the Bayesian distinction lies. The effect against placebo has frequentist treatments as well, such as the synthesis approach above. Both are taken up in Section 19.11 and Section 19.12 .

title: Where the traditional trial stands, and what changes next
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.10 Where the traditional trial stands, and what changes next
text: 4.10 Where the traditional trial stands, and what changes next Put the pieces together and you have the traditional single-look trial. The protocol states the endpoint, the effect to be detected, the one-sided level of 0.025 and the power. It fixes \(n\) from these. The trial runs to completion. The analysis computes a test statistic and a p-value from the pre-specified method, and an interval for the effect. The decision is “success” if the p-value is at most 0.025, one-sided, and the CSR reports the interval alongside. The method is transparent, its error rates are known by construction (type I by the choice of the level, power by calculation or simulation), and it has a regulatory history of decades. It is the benchmark against which every design later in the book is judged. When there is one look, a single primary endpoint and no useful prior information, it is also hard to improve on, and the book says so where it matters ( Chapter 21 ). What this design does not do is answer the questions a decision maker actually has. The p-value does not give the probability that the drug works, the interval’s 95% is a statement about the procedure, and the error rates describe a procedure that is run once at a fixed sample size, so they change when the trial is monitored,

Each of these is a place where the traditional answer needs repair, and where a Bayesian formulation offers another route at a price that the book will itemize. title: In practice
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.11 In practice
text: 4.11 In practice Two real trials show the machinery of this chapter at work. One demonstrated a mortality benefit; the other remained inconclusive despite an estimate compatible with substantial benefit.

title: RECOVERY: a two-group comparison, a rate ratio and an interval
cx: Chapter 4: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up > 4.11.1 RECOVERY: a two-group comparison, a rate ratio and an interval
text: RECOVERY: a two-group comparison, a rate ratio and an interval The RECOVERY platform trial randomized hospitalized patients with Covid-19 to usual care or to one of several treatments. Its dexamethasone comparison is, statistically, our trial: two groups, a binary outcome (death within 28 days) and a decision about whether the gap is more than chance ( RECOVERY Collaborative Group et al. 2021 ) . Of 2104 patients assigned to dexamethasone, 482 (22.9%) died, against 1110 of 4321 (25.7%) on usual care, a difference of 2.8 percentage points. The headline estimate was the age-adjusted rate ratio 0.83, with 95% confidence interval 0.75 to 0.93 and P < 0.001. The analysis was frequentist: no prior and no posterior probability, only a p-value and an interval computed from the repetition-of-the-trial logic of this chapter. Two features connect it to what we built. The interval is as informative as the p-value: the data are compatible with a relative reduction in mortality of 7% to 25%, which is the range a clinician needs. And the size of the trial, thousands of patients rather than our 100 per arm, is what makes a 2.8 point gap decisive; the same gap in a trial of 100 per arm would be buried in a standard error of about 0.06. The lesson for this chapter: a clean randomized two-group comparison with a pre-specified analysis
