title: The MRC streptomycin trial (1948): concealment before the word existed
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.12.1 The MRC streptomycin trial (1948): concealment before the word existed
text: The MRC streptomycin trial (1948): concealment before the word existed The Medical Research Council trial of streptomycin in acute pulmonary tuberculosis ( Medical Research Council Streptomycin in Tuberculosis Trials Committee 1948 ) is the chapter’s first example of the sequence-generation and concealment distinction. Hill, who designed the trial, used random allocation, as Fisher had in agricultural experiments ( Fisher 1935 ) , chiefly to prevent selection bias in the choice of patients for each arm, and paired it with concealment of the allocation ( A. B. Hill 1952 ) ; Yoshioka documents how the random numbers and envelopes were actually used ( Yoshioka 1998 ) . The allocation was determined from a series of random numbers and kept in sealed envelopes, so the admitting physician decided whether a patient was eligible before knowing which treatment the patient would receive. The comparison was streptomycin with bed rest against bed rest alone. The lesson for the chapter is that the contribution of the trial was not the coin but the concealment: a list that the admitting doctor could see would have recreated the doctor-chosen arm of Figure 5.1 . The regulatory descendant is the requirement of 21 CFR 314.126(b)(4) for a method of assignment that minimizes bias.

title: RECOVERY (2020): randomization at scale, open label, objective endpoint
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.12.2 RECOVERY (2020): randomization at scale, open label, objective endpoint
text: RECOVERY (2020): randomization at scale, open label, objective endpoint RECOVERY, a platform trial in UK hospitals, randomized patients with COVID-19 to usual care or to usual care plus dexamethasone, among other arms, without blinding ( RECOVERY Collaborative Group et al. 2021 ) . Of 11,303 patients randomized from 19 March to 8 June 2020, 2,104 were assigned to dexamethasone and 4,321 to usual care in the comparison reported. The mortality comparison itself, with its rate ratio and interval, is read as a two-group test in Section 4.11 . The preliminary results were announced on 16 June 2020, nearly 100 days after the protocol was first drafted, and were adopted into UK practice the same day. The analysis was frequentist, so this is not a Bayesian trial. It is the standard of this chapter at scale: central concealed randomization, an objective endpoint that limits assessment bias (open-label care can still introduce differences in co-interventions), and an intention-to-treat analysis of all randomized patients. The lesson is the one of the first row of Table 5.2 : when the endpoint is objective, open-label randomized evidence can be decisive, and the speed came from simple randomization with a small number of data items, not from any change in how assignment works.

title: The Women's Health Initiative (2002): randomization against observational evidence
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > 5.12.3 The Women's Health Initiative (2002): randomization against observational evidence
text: The Women’s Health Initiative (2002): randomization against observational evidence The Women’s Health Initiative randomized healthy postmenopausal women to estrogen plus progestin or placebo and reported its principal results in 2002 ( Rossouw et al. 2002 ) . Observational studies had suggested that hormone therapy protected against coronary heart disease, and the randomized trial did not confirm it: it found an increase in coronary events and in strokes, and the trial arm was stopped early because the risks outweighed the benefits. The paper reports the hazard ratios; what matters here is the direction of the result. The regulatory lesson is that the observational association was an instance of Equation 5.1 : women who chose hormone therapy differed from those who did not before any pill was taken, and the discrepancy illustrated the risks of confounding and of comparing different treatment histories. Subsequent analyses substantially reconciled the estimates after accounting for time since treatment initiation and confounding ( Prentice et al. 2005 ) . The trial’s answer was credible because assignment was by chance and because the analysis kept all randomized women in their assigned arm.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > Key points
text: Key points Randomization makes the selection term of Equation 5.1 zero on average, for factors measured or not. Bias from a doctor’s choice of patients does not shrink with sample size, and adjustment repairs it only for what was recorded. The standard methods are simple, permuted block (with random block sizes), stratified, and minimization (Pocock-Simon, with a probability of 0.8 or so of following the minimizing arm). They balance arm sizes and known factors, and they do nothing for hidden ones; chance does that, with a distribution that the inference accounts for. Concealment (the next assignment is hidden until the patient is enrolled) is a different protection from blinding (nobody knows the arm afterward). Inadequate concealment is empirically associated with exaggerated treatment effects. The permutation test is justified by the design and has the type I error of the randomization procedure. The analysis should mirror the design: shuffle within blocks, and adjust for stratification factors. Real trials show the same chain at work: concealed sealed-envelope allocation (MRC 1948), central randomization with an objective endpoint at scale (RECOVERY), and randomization overturning observational evidence (WHI). Randomization validity depends on the assignment process. Kolmogorov complexity concerns individual sequences and cannot be computed, and statistical diagnostics such as Arnold’s stochasticity parameter detect pattern but do not certify an allocation mechanism. Use a validated generator, record and seal the seed,

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 5: Randomization From the Ground Up > Key points
text: depends on the assignment process. Kolmogorov complexity concerns individual sequences and cannot be computed, and statistical diagnostics such as Arnold’s stochasticity parameter detect pattern but do not certify an allocation mechanism. Use a validated generator, record and seal the seed, and check the schedule. Analyze all randomized patients. ICH E9(R1) asks for an explicit estimand and a strategy per intercurrent event. A per-protocol analysis is not among the strategies and can be biased badly. A Bayesian randomizes so that the assignment mechanism is ignorable by construction and the result is persuasive to those who do not share the analyst’s model ( Rubin 1978 ; Kadane and Seidenfeld 1990 ) . Covariate adjustment for prespecified prognostic baseline covariates is the cheapest precision a trial can buy: ANCOVA multiplies the variance by about \(1 - R^2\) , and the stratification factors belong in the analysis. For binary and time-to-event outcomes name the estimand: the conditional odds ratio is not the marginal one even without confounding, and standardization gives the marginal effect with the adjusted precision. FDA (May 2023, final) and EMA (2015) recommend prespecified adjustment, and neither requires it. title: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6 Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
text: Chapter 4 asked one question of a two-group trial: could the difference we saw be produced by chance alone? The answer was a p-value, a number computed on the assumption that nothing is going on. A trialist usually wants the answer to a different question: given what we saw, how likely is it that the new treatment is better, and by how much? Bayesian inference answers that question directly. It does so by adding one ingredient the traditional analysis leaves out, a probability distribution describing what was known about the effect before the trial, and by combining it with the data through a single rule. This chapter introduces that rule and the vocabulary around it: prior, likelihood, posterior, credible interval, predictive distribution. We stay with the example of Chapter 4 , a control response rate of 30% and a treatment response rate of 45%, and we redo its analysis the Bayesian way. Each Bayesian quantity is introduced next to the traditional quantity it parallels, and we will see that with a flat prior the two give nearly the same numbers. The difference is in what the numbers are allowed to mean, and in what they let us do later: monitor, borrow, predict and decide. Important Regulatory anchor ICH E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (Step 4, February 1998) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 )

title: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6 Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
text: the numbers are allowed to mean, and in what they let us do later: monitor, borrow, predict and decide. Important Regulatory anchor ICH E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (Step 4, February 1998) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 ) . Section 1.2 observes that clinical-trial methodology has been based on frequentist methods, then states that this “should not be taken to imply that other approaches are not appropriate: the use of Bayesian (see Glossary) and other approaches may be considered when the reasons for their use are clear and when the resulting conclusions are sufficiently robust.” The Glossary defines Bayesian approaches as those that provide “a posterior probability distribution for some parameter (e.g. treatment effect), derived from the observed data and a prior probability distribution for the parameter.” Section 5.5 asks for estimates of treatment effect with confidence intervals in addition to tests. E9 permits Bayesian analysis and asks for reasons and robustness; it does not forbid it. ICH E20, Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials (Step 2 draft, June 2025) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2025 ) . Section 5.3 describes Bayesian methods as those that “combine a prior probability distribution with current trial data to obtain a posterior probability distribution,” and expects Bayesian adaptive designs to show targeted operating characteristics, including control of the type I error probability where that is the objective.

title: Bayes' rule with a diagnostic test
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.1 Bayes' rule with a diagnostic test
text: 6.1 Bayes’ rule with a diagnostic test The rule itself is old arithmetic, and a clinician has used it for years under another name. The rule is Bayes’s (1763) and Laplace’s, and it became a theory of decision with de Finetti and Savage ( Savage 1954 ) . Suppose a screening test for a disease has sensitivity 90% (it is positive in 90% of people who have the disease) and specificity 95% (it is negative in 95% of people who do not), and the disease has prevalence 2% in the population being screened. A patient tests positive. What is the probability the patient has the disease? The sensitivity is a probability about the test given the disease. The question asks for the reverse, a probability about the disease given the test. To reverse the conditioning, write the joint probability of “disease and positive” in two ways and equate them: \[ \mathbb{P}(D \mid +) \, \mathbb{P}(+) = \mathbb{P}(+ \mid D) \, \mathbb{P}(D), \qquad\text{so}\qquad \mathbb{P}(D \mid +) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(+ \mid D) \, \mathbb{P}(D)}{\mathbb{P}(+ \mid D) \, \mathbb{P}(D) + \mathbb{P}(+ \mid \bar D) \, \mathbb{P}(\bar D)}. \] This is Bayes’ rule. The three pieces have names that carry through the rest of the book. \(\mathbb{P}(D)\) is the prior , what was believed before the test result. \(\mathbb{P}(+ \mid D)\) , viewed as a function of the unknown state,

title: Bayes' rule with a diagnostic test
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.1 Bayes' rule with a diagnostic test
text: gives the numbers. A patient with a positive test has about a 27% chance of having the disease, not 90%. The test is good, but the disease is rare, so most positives come from the large healthy group. The only thing that changes in a trial is that the unknown is no longer “disease or not” but a continuous quantity, the response rate or the log hazard ratio, and the prior is a distribution over its possible values rather than a single prevalence. In symbols, for an unknown parameter \(\theta\) and data \(y\) , \[ \pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta')\, \pi(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta), \tag{6.1}\] where \(\pi(\theta)\) is the prior, \(p(y \mid \theta)\) the likelihood and \(\pi(\theta \mid y)\) the posterior. The denominator is the probability of the data averaged over the prior. It does not depend on \(\theta\) , so it only rescales the product to integrate to one; the shape of the posterior is the prior times the likelihood, “posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood.” The traditional analysis uses the same likelihood. A frequentist estimate, the maximum likelihood estimate, is the value of \(\theta\) at which \(p(y \mid \theta)\) peaks, and a z test is a calculation on its sampling distribution. What the Bayesian adds is the prior and the multiplication. What the

text: frequentist estimate, the maximum likelihood estimate, is the value of \(\theta\) at which \(p(y \mid \theta)\) peaks, and a z test is a calculation on its sampling distribution. What the Bayesian adds is the prior and the multiplication. What the Bayesian gives up is nothing mathematical, but something practical: the answer now depends on a choice, the prior, that has to be made, defended and written into the protocol. That is the subject of Chapter 8 and the reason the FDA draft is emphatic that the prior be prespecified.

title: Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.2 Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally
text: 6.2 Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally A trial analysis nearly always begins with the sentence “patients’ outcomes are independent and identically distributed with response probability \(p\) .” The sentence is a perfectly good model when \(\theta\) is treated as a fixed unknown constant: given \(\theta\) , outcomes are independent. The Bayesian view adds a distribution for \(\theta\) , and that addition changes what the model says about outcomes we have not yet seen, which is the cleanest route into it. Consider a thumbtack tossed repeatedly, with \(y_i = 1\) if it lands point up. If we knew the probability \(\theta\) of landing point up, the tosses would be independent: the first result would tell us nothing about the second. But we do not know \(\theta\) . After 500 tosses with 499 point up, nobody believes the next toss is as uncertain as the first one was. So, once \(\theta\) is given a distribution and integrated out, the predictive distribution of the tosses is not independent; they are independent only given \(\theta\) , and a given \(\theta\) is exactly what a trial does not have. The same applies to patients: ten consecutive responders in an arm tell us something about the next patient, because they tell us about the arm’s response rate. What is plausible in place of independence is a weaker symmetry, exchangeability : the

title: Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.2 Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally
text: same applies to patients: ten consecutive responders in an arm tell us something about the next patient, because they tell us about the arm’s response rate. What is plausible in place of independence is a weaker symmetry, exchangeability : the probability we assign to a set of outcomes does not depend on the order in which patients are listed. Eight tosses with four point up are equally probable in the order 1,0,1,0,1,0,1,0 and in the order 0,1,1,0,1,0,0,1. Independent and identically distributed outcomes are always exchangeable, but not conversely, and exchangeability makes no reference to a parameter at all. It is a statement about our beliefs concerning data not yet seen. de Finetti’s representation theorem ( de Finetti 1937 ) says what an exchangeable sequence of binary outcomes looks like. If any number of further outcomes could be added and the sequence stays exchangeable, then there exists a probability distribution \(\Pi\) on \([0,1]\) (the mixing distribution, which need not have a density) such that \[ \mathbb{P}(y_1, \ldots, y_n) = \int_0^1 \prod_{i=1}^n \theta^{y_i} (1-\theta)^{1-y_i} \, d\Pi(\theta) . \tag{6.2}\] Read it left to right: the joint probability of the data is a mixture, over the unknown response rate, of the independent-coin probabilities. The theorem does not assume a parameter and then a prior. It produces both from the single judgment of exchangeability. The parameter \(\theta\) is the limiting

title: Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.2 Exchangeability and de Finetti, informally
text: the data is a mixture, over the unknown response rate, of the independent-coin probabilities. The theorem does not assume a parameter and then a prior. It produces both from the single judgment of exchangeability. The parameter \(\theta\) is the limiting fraction of responders, and \(\Pi\) is our uncertainty about it (when it has a density we write \(\pi(\theta)\,d\theta\) , as in the Beta examples below). For the trialist the content is practical: The model “responses are Bernoulli( \(p\) ) given \(p\) ” and the prior on \(p\) come as a package. A protocol that specifies a likelihood without a prior has specified half of a Bayesian model; the traditional protocol specifies the likelihood half and handles the other half through the sampling distribution. Exchangeability is a judgment about the patients, and it can fail. If patients enrolled in the first year are systematically different from those enrolled later, or the sites differ, the order does matter. Time trends, site effects and covariates are ways of relaxing exchangeability to “exchangeable within strata,” and the same judgment returns when we borrow information in Chapter 19 . Randomization ( Chapter 5 ) makes treatment assignment independent of prognosis and potential outcomes. The response model separately assumes exchangeability within each arm, or within specified covariate strata. A full treatment, including the proof and the connection to subjective probability, is

title: The coin and the Beta family
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.3 The coin and the Beta family
text: 6.3 The coin and the Beta family The simplest trial has one arm and a binary outcome, and the simplest model for it is the coin. The prior-and-posterior module of the book’s companion online lab ( https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/01-prior-posterior.html , described in the Preface) uses a coin of unknown bias. After 10 tosses, 7 are heads. The traditional estimate of the heads probability is \(7/10 = 0.70\) , with a standard error of about \(\sqrt{0.7 \times 0.3 / 10} = 0.145\) . The Bayesian analysis starts with a prior distribution over the bias \(\theta\) , which Figure 6.1 shows at work on a coarse grid of values. (In this and the next two sections \(\theta\) is the success probability of a single arm, which the two-group sections call \(p_j\) .) The prior bar is the \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\) density there, \(6 \times 0.7 \times 0.3 = 1.26\) , rescaled so that the eleven bars sum to one: 0.127. The likelihood bar is the probability of 7 heads in 10 tosses at \(\theta = 0.7\) , 0.267, rescaled the same way: 0.293. Multiply the two bars at every grid value, then divide each product by the sum of the eleven products so that the posterior sums to one. At \(\theta = 0.7\) the result is 0.300. That is all Bayes’ rule does. In the top row the prior still counts: it pulls the posterior toward one half, and the bar at 0.6 is nearly as tall as the bar at 0.7. In the bottom row the likelihood is so narrow that any smooth prior is nearly constant across it, and the posterior is the likelihood. Make the grid finer and the bars become thin slivers along a smooth curve. With a Beta prior and a binomial likelihood those curves are Beta densities, which the rest of this section uses. title: The coin and the Beta family
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.3 The coin and the Beta family
text: likelihood those curves are Beta densities, which the rest of this section uses. The convenient family of priors for a probability is the Beta distribution , \(\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)\) , with density proportional to \(\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\) on \([0,1]\) . Its mean is \(a/(a+b)\) . \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) is the flat distribution on \([0,1]\) : every value of \(\theta\) is equally believable. \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\) is a gentle bell centered at one half. Larger \(a\) and \(b\) give narrower bells. The convenience is that the likelihood of \(h\) heads and \(t\) tails, \(\theta^{h}(1-\theta)^{t}\) , has the same algebraic form as the Beta density. Multiplying them as in Equation 6.1 gives \[ \theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b), \quad h \text{ heads}, \; t \text{ tails} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + h,\; b + t). \tag{6.3}\] A prior with this property, that the posterior belongs to the same family, is called conjugate to the likelihood. For the Beta prior and a binomial likelihood the update is addition: add the responders to \(a\) and the non-responders to \(b\) . One reads \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\) as “as if \(a-1\) responders and \(b-1\) non-responders had already been seen, starting from a flat prior” (with a convention that makes the rule exact, shown in the Technical note below). title: Posterior mean as a weighted average, and the prior's effective sample size
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.4 Posterior mean as a weighted average, and the prior's effective sample size
text: 6.4 Posterior mean as a weighted average, and the prior’s effective sample size The posterior mean of a Beta-binomial model has a form every trialist can read. Let \(n = h + t\) be the number of patients and \(\hat p = h / n\) the observed proportion. Then \[ \mathbb{E}[\theta \mid y] = \frac{a + h}{a + b + n} = \frac{a + b}{a + b + n} \cdot \frac{a}{a+b} + \frac{n}{a + b + n} \cdot \hat p . \tag{6.4}\] It is a weighted average of the prior mean \(a/(a+b)\) and the sample proportion \(\hat p\) , with weights proportional to \(a+b\) and \(n\) . The prior acts as if it were a sample of size \(a + b\) . This is the effective sample size (ESS) of a \(\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)\) prior: a flat \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) is worth two patients, a \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\) four, a \(\mathrm{Beta}(30,70)\) one hundred. More refined definitions exist, which match the prior to the amount of information in the data under different criteria ( Morita, Thall, and Müller 2008 ) , and Chapter 8 treats them; for the Beta-binomial, \(a + b\) is the answer all of them roughly agree on. The prior of the BNT162b2 vaccine trial in Section 6.12 , \(\mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)\) , has an ESS of 1.7 cases (the trial’s patients enter through the cases they produce): a prior

title: Posterior mean as a weighted average, and the prior's effective sample size
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.4 Posterior mean as a weighted average, and the prior's effective sample size
text: is the answer all of them roughly agree on. The prior of the BNT162b2 vaccine trial in Section 6.12 , \(\mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)\) , has an ESS of 1.7 cases (the trial’s patients enter through the cases they produce): a prior of real shape and almost no weight. A prior with an ESS of 10 in a trial of 200 contributes 5% of the weight; the same prior in a trial of 10 contributes half. As \(n\) grows, the data dominate and every reasonable prior gives the same posterior. This is why Bayesian analysis of a large trial with a weak prior looks like the traditional analysis, and why the debate over priors matters most in small trials, rare diseases, pediatric extrapolation and anywhere a prior of substantial ESS is deliberately used to borrow information. The FDA draft’s warning (Section IV.B.2) that conclusions can depend strongly on the prior is a statement about exactly this weight ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . title: The two-group comparison, redone
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.5 The two-group comparison, redone
text: 6.5 The two-group comparison, redone Return to the trial of Chapter 4 : a control arm with a true response probability \(p_0 = 0.30\) , a treatment arm with \(p_1 = 0.45\) , and suppose 100 patients per arm are randomized 1:1. For the worked numbers, let the trial come out at its design values: 30 of 100 control patients respond, and 45 of 100 treatment patients respond.

title: The traditional analysis
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.5.1 The traditional analysis
text: The traditional analysis The traditional analysis is the one Chapter 4 derived. The observed difference is \(\hat p_1 - \hat p_0 = 0.15\) . The pooled response is \(0.375\) , the standard error of the difference under the null is \(\sqrt{0.375 \times 0.625 \times (1/100 + 1/100)} = 0.0685\) , so \(z = 2.19\) and the one-sided p-value is \(0.014\) . Against the usual one-sided level of 0.025, this is a (modest) success. The 95% confidence interval for the difference, using the unpooled standard error 0.0676, runs from \(0.017\) to \(0.283\) . Fisher’s exact test gives a one-sided p of \(0.020\) .

title: The Bayesian analysis
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.5.2 The Bayesian analysis
text: The Bayesian analysis Put an independent flat \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) prior on each arm’s response rate. By Equation 6.3 the posteriors are \(p_0 \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(31, 71)\) and \(p_1 \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(46, 56)\) , independent. The quantity of interest is a function of both parameters, the difference \(p_1 - p_0\) or the event \(p_1 > p_0\) . There is no neat formula for its distribution, but there does not need to be: draw many samples from each posterior and compute the quantity of interest on the pairs. This is Monte Carlo and it is how almost every Bayesian trial quantity in this book is computed. title: Why the two nearly agree
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.6 Why the two nearly agree
text: 6.6 Why the two nearly agree With a flat prior, the posterior of \(p_1 - p_0\) is centered, approximately, at the observed difference \(\hat d\) with standard deviation approximately equal to its standard error \(s\) , and approximately normal (this is the Bernstein-von Mises phenomenon: with enough data the posterior looks like the normalized likelihood). So \[ \Pr(p_1 - p_0 > 0 \mid y) \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{\hat d}{s}\right) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(-\frac{\hat d}{s}\right). \] The one-sided p-value for testing \(H_0: p_1 \le p_0\) is \(1 - \Phi(\hat d / s_0)\) , with \(s_0\) the standard error under the null. If \(s \approx s_0\) the p-value is \(1 - \Phi(\hat d / s)\) , and so \(1 - p \approx \Phi(\hat d/s)\) . The two expressions are the same up to which standard error (pooled or unpooled) is used and the slight skewness of the Beta. The match is not a theorem of the model, it is a property of a flat prior and a nearly normal likelihood, and it fails when the prior is informative, when the sample is small or when the response rates are near 0 or 1. We check it numerically on many simulated trials. Across 500 simulated trials with 100 patients per arm and true rates 0.45 and 0.30, the largest gap between \(1 - p\) and the flat-prior posterior probability (computed

title: Why the two nearly agree
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.6 Why the two nearly agree
text: near 0 or 1. We check it numerically on many simulated trials. Across 500 simulated trials with 100 patients per arm and true rates 0.45 and 0.30, the largest gap between \(1 - p\) and the flat-prior posterior probability (computed exactly) is 0.002, and the average gap is 0.0005. Two cautions come with this near-equality. First, it is a numerical coincidence that has no logical force: the p-value is a statement about the data under the null, and \(\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid y)\) is a statement about the parameter given the data. A reader who says “ \(1-p\) is the probability that the drug works” is correct in this one setting only because the prior is flat, which is itself a strong choice (it gives a prior probability of one half to the claim that treatment is better, and puts substantial mass on differences nobody believes). Second, the near-equality is what makes the Bayesian bar not lower. A trial that declares success when \(\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid y) > 0.975\) with a flat prior is, to a good approximation, the trial that declares success when the one-sided p-value is below 0.025. The Bayesian design’s savings, to be shown in later chapters, come from monitoring, multiple arms and prior information, not from a lower threshold at a single final analysis. title: Credible intervals and confidence intervals
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.7 Credible intervals and confidence intervals
text: 6.7 Credible intervals and confidence intervals The 95% confidence interval for the difference is (0.017, 0.283). The 95% credible interval, the central 95% of the posterior of \(p_1 - p_0\) , is (0.015, 0.277). They are numerically close, and they mean different things. A confidence interval is a procedure. If the trial were repeated many times and the interval computed each time by the same recipe, 95% of the intervals would contain the true \(p_1 - p_0\) . The probability statement is about the procedure; for the one interval in the CSR, the true value is either inside or it is not, and the “95%” does not say how likely it is that this interval covers the truth. A credible interval is a statement about the parameter: given the data and the prior, the probability that \(p_1 - p_0\) lies in the interval is 95%. There is also a choice of which 95% region, and two are common: the equal-tailed interval, leaving 2.5% in each tail, and the highest posterior density (HPD) interval, the shortest region with 95% probability. For a skewed posterior they differ; for the symmetrical one above they nearly coincide. Many trialists read confidence intervals as if they were credible intervals, and in most large trials with weak priors they get away with it. The distinction matters in two places. One is

The distinction matters in two places. One is when the prior is informative: the credible interval shifts and narrows, which is the intention, and the confidence interval cannot. The other is near boundaries, where a confidence interval built from the normal approximation may stray outside \([0,1]\) or cover poorly, while a credible interval built from the Beta posterior stays inside by construction. title: The posterior predictive distribution
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.8 The posterior predictive distribution
text: 6.8 The posterior predictive distribution A trial is not only about the parameter. Decisions depend on what will happen next: how many of the next 50 patients will respond, how likely it is that the trial, if continued to its planned size, will end in success. The Bayesian answer is the posterior predictive distribution , the distribution of future data after averaging over the uncertainty about the parameter: \[ p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta . \tag{6.5}\] For a Beta posterior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a', b')\) and \(m\) future patients, the number of future responders follows a beta-binomial distribution, which has a closed form, and its mean is \(m a' / (a' + b')\) (the posterior mean times \(m\) ). The traditional analogue is a prediction interval, or more often a plug-in calculation: assume \(p = \hat p\) and compute a binomial. The plug-in ignores the uncertainty in \(\hat p\) and is therefore too narrow. title: Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.9 Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio
text: 6.9 Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio Many pivotal trials, in oncology, cardiovascular disease and neurology, do not have a binary endpoint but a time to event, and the treatment effect is a hazard ratio (HR). The Beta-binomial model does not apply. The normal-normal model, which does, rests on a standard approximation. For 1:1 randomization with \(d\) total events, the log hazard ratio estimate has standard error \(\approx 2/\sqrt{d}\) . (Each arm contributes about \(d/2\) events and the variance of a log hazard ratio is about \(1/d_1 + 1/d_0 = 4/d\) .) With \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) , so that a positive \(\theta\) means benefit, the data are summarized by \[ \hat\theta \mid \theta \;\sim\; N\!\left(\theta,\; \frac{4}{d}\right). \tag{6.6}\] This is the likelihood, an approximate one: the Cox partial likelihood in large samples is close to a normal in \(\theta\) , and the approximation is the standard route taken by Bayesian design in survival studies. In the traditional trial the logrank test is, to a good approximation, the z test \(z = \hat\theta \sqrt{d} / 2\) , and the one-sided p-value is \(1 - \Phi(z)\) . The number of events, not patients, is the sample size, in both frameworks; this chapter uses the same events-as-information language that Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 use. Take a trial that observes \(d = 200\) events and \(\widehat{\mathrm{HR}} = 0.74\)

title: Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.9 Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio
text: The number of events, not patients, is the sample size, in both frameworks; this chapter uses the same events-as-information language that Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 use. Take a trial that observes \(d = 200\) events and \(\widehat{\mathrm{HR}} = 0.74\) , so \(\hat\theta = -\log 0.74 = 0.30\) with standard error \(2/\sqrt{200} = 0.141\) . Then \(z = 2.12\) and the one-sided p-value is \(0.017\) , a success at the 0.025 level. For the prior take a normal distribution, \(\theta \sim N(m_0, \tau^2)\) . A normal prior and a normal likelihood give a normal posterior (normal-normal conjugacy), with precision (the reciprocal of the variance) equal to the sum of the precisions: \[ \theta \mid \hat\theta \;\sim\; N\!\left(m_1, s_1^2\right), \quad \frac{1}{s_1^2} = \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{d}{4}, \quad m_1 = \frac{m_0/\tau^2 + \hat\theta\, d/4}{1/\tau^2 + d/4}. \tag{6.7}\] This is the same weighted average of Equation 6.4 , now with weights given by precision. The data have precision \(d/4\) , so each event carries a quarter of a unit of precision, and a prior of variance \(\tau^2\) carries \(1/\tau^2\) . The effective sample size of the prior, in events, is therefore \(4/\tau^2\) : a prior \(N(0, 0.2^2)\) is worth 100 events, and \(N(0, 0.35^2)\) is worth about 33. title: Sequential updating: the posterior today is the prior tomorrow
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.10 Sequential updating: the posterior today is the prior tomorrow
text: 6.10 Sequential updating: the posterior today is the prior tomorrow A trial accrues over months or years. Suppose data arrive in batches, \(y_1\) and then \(y_2\) . Bayes’ rule can be applied twice: first to the prior and \(y_1\) , giving \(\pi(\theta \mid y_1)\) , then to \(\pi(\theta \mid y_1)\) taken as the prior and \(y_2\) : \[ \pi(\theta \mid y_1, y_2) \;\propto\; p(y_2 \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid y_1) \;\propto\; p(y_2 \mid \theta)\, p(y_1 \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta), \tag{6.8}\] provided \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are conditionally independent given \(\theta\) (which is what exchangeability delivers). The last expression is the posterior obtained from all data at once with the original prior. Updating in batches, one patient at a time or all at once, gives the same posterior: the posterior today is the prior tomorrow, and the path by which the data arrived does not matter. title: Looking does not change the posterior
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.10.1 Looking does not change the posterior
text: Looking does not change the posterior The traditional trialist’s reaction to the last paragraph is that something has been skipped. In a group sequential design (the subject of Chapter 11 ) every look at the data costs something: the nominal level at each look is reduced, because testing five times at 0.025 does not preserve a type I error of 0.025. Yet the Bayesian posterior at any interim analysis is computed with exactly the same formula as the posterior at the end, and it does not know how many looks preceded it. How can both statements be true? They are answers to different questions. The likelihood principle says that, given the data, the evidence about \(\theta\) in an experiment depends on the data only through the likelihood function, and not on the stopping rule or on what other results might have been observed but were not ( Berger and Wolpert 1988 ) . The posterior depends on the data through the likelihood only, so it is unchanged by the decision to look, or by the decision to stop because the posterior crossed a threshold. A p-value, by contrast, is a statement about all the data sets the procedure could have produced, and which data sets those are depends on the stopping rule: “stop at the first of five looks where \(z > 1.96\) ” is

title: Looking does not change the posterior
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.10.1 Looking does not change the posterior
text: p-value, by contrast, is a statement about all the data sets the procedure could have produced, and which data sets those are depends on the stopping rule: “stop at the first of five looks where \(z > 1.96\) ” is a different procedure from “analyze once at the end,” and has a different sampling distribution. The type I error rate is a property of the procedure over repeated trials under the null, so it is changed by looking. The posterior probability, a statement about this trial’s parameter given this trial’s data, is not. We can see both statements in one simulation of the trial of this chapter. Five looks at 50 patients per arm (cumulative n = 50, 100, 150, 200, 250 per arm). That is the reason group sequential designs adjust the thresholds, and the reason regulators insist that the monitoring plan be prespecified (ICH E9 Section 4.5 on interim analysis). The second is the Bayesian finding. When the true response rates are drawn from the prior that the analysis assumed, the trials that stop at a looked-at threshold of 0.975 have, on average, a posterior probability of 0.9969 at the moment they stop, and the fraction of those trials in which the treatment is truly better is 0.9955. The posterior is right on average among the trials that stopped, despite the five opportunities to stop. Two cautions keep this from being an overstatement. text: the treatment is truly better is 0.9955. The posterior is right on average among the trials that stopped, despite the five opportunities to stop. Two cautions keep this from being an overstatement. Stopping-rule invariance follows from the likelihood factorization: for an ignorable stopping mechanism and a fixed analysis prior, the stopping factor cancels. Calibration across trials additionally depends on the assumed prior and sampling model. The calibration in the second block was produced by drawing truth from the same prior the analysis used. If the true effects are not drawn from that prior, then the posterior at the moment of stopping is not calibrated to anything in the real world, and the frequentist inflation reappears as an operating characteristic: the fraction of null drug trials that stop for success is what the regulator cares about, and it is a property of the design and the threshold, not of the posterior at a single look. For this reason one of the routes the FDA draft describes, and this book’s default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, is to calibrate Bayesian success criteria by simulation to the type I error probability, and E20 Section 5.3 describes the same operating characteristics ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ; International Council for Harmonisation 2025 ) . cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.10.1 Looking does not change the posterior
text: type I error probability, and E20 Section 5.3 describes the same operating characteristics ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ; International Council for Harmonisation 2025 ) . Chapter 14 shows how. Having a valid posterior at every look does not make every look free. Looks cost in the currency of operating characteristics: a threshold chosen to be right at a single look must be raised, or the number of looks limited, if the design is to hold the type I error at 0.025 across the monitoring plan. Chapter 11 quantifies the price. What the likelihood principle removes is the conceptual objection that Bayesian inference “does not know about” the looks; what it does not remove is the regulator’s requirement, in practice, that it be shown that it does not matter. There is a debate, spanning decades, about what the likelihood principle implies for the way trials are run and judged ( Berger 1985 ; Edwards, Lindman, and Savage 1963 ) .

title: What a protocol has to say
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.11 What a protocol has to say
text: 6.11 What a protocol has to say Tip In the protocol A Bayesian primary analysis needs, at minimum, the following statements in the protocol or the statistical analysis plan. They follow from the definitions of this chapter and from the FDA draft’s emphasis on prespecification. The model: the sampling distribution of the endpoint given the parameter (for example, binomial with response probability \(p_j\) in arm \(j\) ; or \(\hat\theta \sim N(\theta, 4/d)\) for \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) ). The prior for every parameter, with its form and values (for example, \(p_j \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)\) for both arms), its effective sample size, and the reasoning behind it. The prior is specified before the data are unblinded. The quantity on which the decision is made, with its threshold (for example, \(\Pr(p_1 - p_0 > 0 \mid \text{data}) > 0.975\) , or the Pfizer-BioNTech rule \(\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\%) > 0.986\) at the final analysis and \(> 0.995\) at interims), so that the success criterion is explicit. The computation: whether the posterior is analytic or by Monte Carlo (and with how many draws, and with what seed and software), so that the result can be reproduced. The operating characteristics: type I error and power by simulation under the stated scenarios, referred to in the simulation report ( Chapter 14 ). A statement of how the traditional analysis (estimate, confidence interval, p-value) will be reported alongside, if the sponsor wants the Bayesian analysis to be read against it.

title: Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, phase 3 (C4591001)
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.12.1 Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, phase 3 (C4591001)
text: Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, phase 3 (C4591001) The phase 2/3 trial of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine is the cleanest large example of this chapter’s machinery. Its statistical analysis plan [ Pfizer Inc. ( 2022 ) , Section 7.1 and Appendix 2; the document at the cited ClinicalTrials.gov address is version 10, dated 7 October 2022, and is not an archived 2020 version] used a beta-binomial model, conditional on the total number of first COVID-19 cases \(s\) , of whom \(s_1\) occur in the vaccine arm. With equal allocation and equal follow-up, a case falls in the vaccine arm with probability \(p = (1 - \mathrm{VE})/(2 - \mathrm{VE})\) , where VE is the vaccine efficacy, one minus the ratio of incidence rates. Then \(s_1 \mid s \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(s, p)\) , and the prior is \(p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)\) . Its mean is \(0.4118\) , the value of \(p\) at VE \(= 30\%\) , so the prior is centered on the efficacy margin, and the plan calls it minimally informative and says it can be considered pessimistic. Its 95% interval for \(p\) is \((0.005, 0.964)\) , which is \((-26.2, 0.995)\) for VE written as a fraction, about \(-2{,}620\%\) to \(99.5\%\) : the lower limit corresponds to an incidence rate ratio of 27.2, a vaccine arm with 27 times the cases of the placebo arm, and the interval is nearly

The ESS of Section 6.4 is \(a + b = 1.7\) cases. title: REMAP-CAP: posterior probabilities of benefit as the reported result
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.12.2 REMAP-CAP: posterior probabilities of benefit as the reported result
text: REMAP-CAP: posterior probabilities of benefit as the reported result REMAP-CAP is a platform trial ( Chapter 20 ) whose primary analysis is a Bayesian cumulative logistic model for organ support-free days to day 21. The report on interleukin-6 receptor antagonists ( REMAP-CAP Investigators et al. 2021 ) states the rules as posterior probabilities, fixed in advance: efficacy if the posterior probability that the odds ratio exceeds 1 is above 99%, futility if the posterior probability that the odds ratio exceeds 1.2 is below 5%, and equivalence if the probability that the odds ratio between two non-control interventions lies between 0.83 and 1.2 exceeds 90%. Priors on the individual treatment effects were neutral. At an interim analysis in 2020, tocilizumab crossed the efficacy threshold with posterior probability \(99.75\%\) . The chronology and final estimates are in Chapter 20 . The lesson is the one of Section 6.5 at scale: the result is a posterior probability checked against a prespecified threshold, the stopping time is determined by when it crosses and not by a fixed sample size, and the reader is told, in the same units, how far above the threshold the evidence was. The posterior being valid at each look ( Section 6.10 ) is what lets the platform report while it continues.

title: Summary: what changed, what stayed
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.13 Summary: what changed, what stayed
text: 6.13 Summary: what changed, what stayed Starting from the traditional two-group comparison, the Bayesian version changed three things and left a fourth alone. The unknown becomes a distribution. The treatment effect is described by a prior, updated by data into a posterior, and statements are probabilities about the effect. The inputs gain a prior. The prior has to be chosen, prespecified and defended; it is worth a stated number of patients (its effective sample size). The outputs change meaning. The credible interval is a probability statement about the parameter, \(\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid y)\) is a probability that the treatment is better, and posterior predictive distributions say what future patients will do. The data’s role does not change. The likelihood is the same one the traditional trial uses, and with a flat prior and a large trial the numbers agree: \(\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid y) = 0.9855\) against \(1 - p = 0.9858\) here, and exactly \(1 - p\) in the normal-normal model. The regulator’s position, stated in ICH E9 and reaffirmed in the FDA draft and E20, is that the Bayesian approach is acceptable when the reasons for its use are clear and the conclusions are robust. Robust here is a technical word: the conclusion should survive a reasonable change of prior, and the design should have operating characteristics, demonstrated by simulation, that a

title: Summary: what changed, what stayed
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > 6.13 Summary: what changed, what stayed
text: when the reasons for its use are clear and the conclusions are robust. Robust here is a technical word: the conclusion should survive a reasonable change of prior, and the design should have operating characteristics, demonstrated by simulation, that a regulator can read in the language of error rates. Chapter 7 takes up the weighing of evidence, Chapter 8 the choice of priors, and Chapter 11 and Chapter 15 the use of the posterior and the predictive distribution in monitoring. Tip Try it in the lab Open module 01 of the companion lab, Prior and posterior . Before pressing “Toss 10,” predict where the posterior will peak after 7 heads and 3 tails starting from a flat prior and from the Beta(2,2) prior (the modes are 7/10 = 0.70 and 8/12 = 0.667; the means are 8/12 = 0.667 and 9/14 = 0.643, as in Section 6.3 ). Then load the “Newborn trial (real)” example and note how a single arm of 11 successes concentrates the posterior near 1 even from a flat start.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > Key points
text: Key points Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional probability: posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood. The diagnostic-test example, with a 27% positive predictive value from a 90% sensitive, 95% specific test at 2% prevalence, is the same logic as a trial posterior. Exchangeability, the judgment that the order of patients does not matter, replaces independence; de Finetti’s theorem turns it into a likelihood and a prior. It can fail. Randomization makes treatment assignment independent of prognosis; the response model separately assumes exchangeability within each arm or stratum. The Beta prior is conjugate to the binomial: the update adds responders and non-responders. The posterior mean is a weighted average of prior mean and sample proportion, and the prior’s effective sample size is \(a + b\) . With flat priors, \(\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid y) = 0.9855\) matches \(1 - p = 0.9858\) for the trial of 45/100 versus 30/100, and across simulated trials the two differ by at most 0.002. In the normal-normal model on \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) the match is exact. A Bayesian threshold of 0.975 with a flat prior is not a lower bar than a one-sided 0.025. A confidence interval describes a procedure and a credible interval describes a parameter. Predictive distributions, which add the uncertainty about the parameter to the sampling variability, are wider than plug-in predictions and are the basis

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 6: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior > Key points
text: bar than a one-sided 0.025. A confidence interval describes a procedure and a credible interval describes a parameter. Predictive distributions, which add the uncertainty about the parameter to the sampling variability, are wider than plug-in predictions and are the basis of predictive probability. The posterior at an interim look is the same function of the data whatever the stopping rule, but the type I error of a stopping rule is not; the first is a statement about this trial, the second about repeated trials. Regulators judge a Bayesian design by the second, which is why the FDA draft recommends prior prespecification and evaluated operating characteristics, with calibration to type I error as one of its three routes and this book’s default. A Beta(30, 70) prior is proposed for the control arm from a historical trial of 100 patients. What is its effective sample size, how much of the posterior mean would it contribute in a current trial with 50 control patients, and what would you ask the sponsor to show about the exchangeability of the historical and current patients? title: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7 Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities
text: A trial ends with a number, and the number has to be turned into a sentence: the drug works, the drug does not work, we cannot tell. Three numbers compete to play that role. The p-value is on the first page of nearly every clinical study report. The Bayes factor is the number a statistician reaches for when asked how strongly the data favor one hypothesis over another. The posterior probability of benefit is the number a physician wishes the p-value were, and it is the quantity the January 2026 FDA draft guidance on Bayesian methods puts in its success criterion. They answer three different questions, they can disagree sharply on the same data, and a protocol that names one of them has made a choice about what counts as evidence. This chapter lines them up on one example and one set of numbers. We start with the traditional quantity, the p-value, and say precisely what it is and what it is not. We then ask the question every sponsor and every regulator actually cares about, how often a “significant” result is a false alarm, and see that the answer depends on something the p-value does not contain. The Bayes factor and its built-in penalty for vague alternatives follow, with Lindley’s paradox as the cleanest demonstration that a fixed p-value does not mean a fixed

cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7 Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities
text: and see that the answer depends on something the p-value does not contain. The Bayes factor and its built-in penalty for vague alternatives follow, with Lindley’s paradox as the cleanest demonstration that a fixed p-value does not mean a fixed amount of evidence. A first look at the arithmetic of “how much evidence is enough” (the first two of the three deviation scales of Polson and Sokolov) comes next. The chapter closes on the criterion that regulators now write down for Bayesian trials, the posterior probability that the effect exceeds a threshold, and on how its two dials map onto the familiar one-sided 0.025. Important Regulatory anchor ICH E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (Step 4, February 1998). Section 1.2 and the Glossary acknowledge that the guideline is written mostly in frequentist language and do not exclude Bayesian approaches when their use is justified and the conclusions are robust. Section 5.5 sets out estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. Section 5.6 states that, when multiplicity is present, the usual frequentist approach “may necessitate an adjustment to the type I error.” Section 2.2.2 requires the primary variable to be defined in the protocol before the data are seen. title: What a p-value is
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.1 What a p-value is
text: 7.1 What a p-value is Chapter 4 built the p-value from a two-group comparison. Here is the definition again, stated with the care that the rest of the chapter needs. A trial has a null hypothesis \(H_0\) (the new treatment has no effect, \(\theta = 0\) ) and a test statistic \(T\) that is large when the data look unlike \(H_0\) in the direction of benefit. If the observed value is \(t_{\text{obs}}\) , then \[ p = \Pr\bigl(T \ge t_{\text{obs}} \mid H_0\bigr), \] computed over the repeated trials one could imagine running if \(H_0\) were true and the same design were repeated. For a one-sided z test of a treatment effect, \(T = Z_n = \hat\theta_n \sqrt{I_n}\) , where \(I_n\) is the Fisher information after \(n\) observations (one over the squared standard error of \(\hat\theta_n\) ), and \(p = 1 - \Phi(z_{\text{obs}})\) . The regulatory convention is a one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) , which corresponds to \(z_\alpha = 1.96\) and to the familiar two-sided 0.05 (this book uses one-sided 0.025 throughout unless it says otherwise). Section 4.5 discusses what the definition does and does not say. Three points from it matter here. The p-value is a statement about the data under \(H_0\) , not about \(H_0\) under the data. It depends on the experiment that would have been run, not only on the data in

title: What a p-value is
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.1 What a p-value is
text: say. Three points from it matter here. The p-value is a statement about the data under \(H_0\) , not about \(H_0\) under the data. It depends on the experiment that would have been run, not only on the data in hand (the 9 heads and 3 tails of that section have different p-values under different stopping plans; module 2 of the companion lab makes this concrete). And it measures surprise at the null without saying how well any alternative explains the data. None of this makes the p-value a bad tool. It is the basis of the type I error control that regulators require, and its reading as “how often would a trial of this design, run on an ineffective drug, look this good” is exactly the property a regulator wants to bound. The trouble starts when it is asked to answer a question it was not built for.

title: The ASA statement and the dirty dozen
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.1.1 The ASA statement and the dirty dozen
text: The ASA statement and the dirty dozen The ASA statement ( Wasserstein and Lazar 2016 ) and Goodman’s “dirty dozen” ( S. Goodman 2008 ) are summarized in Section 4.5 . Three of the twelve misreadings recur in every trial team and each matters for what follows. “p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.” False. The p-value is a probability of data given the null. The probability of the null given the data requires a prior probability for the null, and the p-value has none. The next section computes what the answer actually is. “A non-significant result means there is no effect.” False. EOLIA reported \(p = 0.09\) for 60-day mortality and was labeled “not significant,” yet a later Bayesian reanalysis put the probability that ECMO lowers mortality between 88% and 99%, depending on the prior (full account in Section 7.10 ). A p-value above 0.025 or 0.05 says the trial did not clear the bar. It does not say the treatment does nothing. “p = 0.05 in one trial and p = 0.001 in another means the second effect is bigger.” False. The p-value mixes the size of the effect with the size of the trial. A modest effect in a huge trial can have a tiny p-value, and a large effect in a small trial can

title: The ASA statement and the dirty dozen
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.1.1 The ASA statement and the dirty dozen
text: second effect is bigger.” False. The p-value mixes the size of the effect with the size of the trial. A modest effect in a huge trial can have a tiny p-value, and a large effect in a small trial can have a p-value above 0.05. The fix the ASA statement suggests, and that the regulatory documents already implement, is not to abolish the p-value but to surround it: a pre-specified primary analysis, an effect estimate with an interval, and a clear account of everything that was looked at.

title: The false positive risk
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.2 The false positive risk
text: 7.2 The false positive risk Suppose a sponsor tells you its phase 3 trial produced \(p = 0.02\) in a one-sided test. What is the probability that the drug does not work? The p-value cannot answer, but one more piece of information can: how often do drugs of this kind work to begin with? The calculation is the screening-test calculation that every clinician has done for a diagnostic test. A test with sensitivity 90% and false alarm rate 2.5% applied to a population where 1% have the disease will produce many more false positives than true positives, because the 99% without disease generate 0.025 times 99 false alarms for every 0.90 times 1 true detections. The trial is the test, the drug is the patient, and: sensitivity is the power \(1 - \beta\) of the trial, the chance of a significant result when the drug works; false alarm rate is the type I error \(\alpha\) ; prevalence is the prior probability \(\pi_a\) that the drug works , which is the fraction of drugs entering a trial of this kind that are in fact effective. Among all trials that end “significant,” the fraction in which the drug does not work is \[ \text{FPR} \;=\; \Pr(\text{no effect} \mid \text{significant}) \;=\; \frac{\alpha\,(1-\pi_a)}{\alpha\,(1-\pi_a) + (1-\beta)\,\pi_a}. \tag{7.1}\] This is Bayes’ theorem applied to the event “the trial was significant,” and

The type I error rate is \(\Pr(\text{significant} \mid \text{no effect})\) and is what a design controls. The false positive risk is \(\Pr(\text{no effect} \mid \text{significant})\) and is what a decision-maker wants. They are connected by the prior probability of an effect, and the Bayesian framework is the one that lets that prior enter the analysis openly instead of silently. title: The exact p-value and the Bayes factor
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3 The exact p-value and the Bayes factor
text: 7.3 The exact p-value and the Bayes factor The false positive risk above conditions on “significant at \(\alpha\) .” One can do better by conditioning on the actual data, and this requires comparing the null with a specific alternative. The Bayesian measure of the evidence in the data for one hypothesis against another is the Bayes factor . For a null \(H_0:\theta = 0\) and an alternative \(H_1\) under which \(\theta\) has a prior distribution \(\pi(\theta)\) , \[ \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid H_1)}{p(y \mid H_0)} \;=\; \frac{\int p(y \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}{p(y \mid \theta = 0)}, \] the ratio of the probabilities the two hypotheses assigned to the data that actually occurred. It updates prior odds into posterior odds: \[ \underbrace{\frac{\Pr(H_1 \mid y)}{\Pr(H_0 \mid y)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} \;=\; \mathrm{BF}_{10} \times \underbrace{\frac{\pi_a}{\pi_0}}_{\text{prior odds}}, \tag{7.2}\] where \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_a\) are the prior probabilities of the null and the alternative. The notation is the book’s (see Appendix A ); the sources in the Bayesian literature sometimes write the ratio the other way up, as \(\mathrm{BF}_{01}\) , and the two are reciprocals. Two things are worth noticing at once. The Bayes factor weighs the data against both hypotheses, which is what the p-value does not do. And it averages the likelihood under the alternative over the prior \(\pi(\theta)\) , rather than evaluating it at the best-fitting \(\hat\theta\) . This averaging is where the Bayes factor differs most from the likelihood ratio statistic familiar from frequentist testing, and it is where its penalty for vague alternatives comes from.

title: A Gaussian example with closed form
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3.1 A Gaussian example with closed form
text: A Gaussian example with closed form To keep the algebra short, work on the scale where the data reduce to the estimate \(\hat\theta_n\) with \(\hat\theta_n \mid \theta \sim N(\theta, 1/I_n)\) , so that \(Z_n = \hat\theta_n \sqrt{I_n}\) is the usual standardized statistic and \(I_n\) is the Fisher information after \(n\) observations (for a time-to-event endpoint with \(d\) events and \(\theta = -\log\mathrm{HR}\) , \(I_n \approx d/4\) ). Take the alternative to be \(\theta \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) , a prior centered at no effect with scale \(\tau\) that expresses how large an effect is plausible. Then the integral can be done exactly. With \(k = I_n \tau^2\) (the information in the data relative to the information in the prior), \[ \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; (1 + k)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left\{\tfrac12 Z_n^2 \,\frac{k}{1+k}\right\}, \qquad 2 \log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; Z_n^2 \,\frac{k}{1+k} \;-\; \log(1+k). \tag{7.3}\] This is the form given by Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026 ) , and it is the finite-sample version of the Schwarz criterion ( Schwarz 1978 ) . For large \(k\) the factor \(k/(1+k)\) tends to one and \[ 2 \log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;\approx\; \underbrace{Z_n^2}_{\text{fit}} \;-\; \underbrace{\log(1+I_n\tau^2)}_{L_n,\ \text{Ockham penalty}}. \tag{7.4}\] Read Equation 7.4 as a ledger. The first term is how well the best-fitting alternative explains the data, in standardized squared units, and it is the same quantity that the z test examines. The second term

cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3.1 A Gaussian example with closed form
text: \underbrace{\log(1+I_n\tau^2)}_{L_n,\ \text{Ockham penalty}}. \tag{7.4}\] Read Equation 7.4 as a ledger. The first term is how well the best-fitting alternative explains the data, in standardized squared units, and it is the same quantity that the z test examines. The second term is a charge for flexibility. An alternative that spreads its prior over a wide range of effects \(\theta\) gives most of that range to effects that the data rule out, so on average it predicts the data worse than a sharp alternative would. The more data we collect (the larger \(I_n\) ), the more sharply the data pin down \(\theta\) , and the larger the share of the prior that is wasted: the penalty grows like \(\log I_n\) . This is the Ockham penalty , the automatic, parameter-free version of “do not prefer a more complex hypothesis unless the data pay for it.” The practical content for a trial: with \(\tau = 0.25\) on the log hazard ratio scale and \(I_n = 400\) (about 1,600 events), the penalty is \(L_n = \log(26) = 3.26\) . The Bayes factor reaches 1 only when \(Z_n^2 \approx 3.26\) , that is \(|Z_n| \approx 1.8\) , and requires more than that for any substantial evidence. The p-value at \(|Z_n| = 1.8\) is 0.036 one-sided, which is not “significant” at 0.025 and yet is, on this measure, only just break-even

title: Lindley's paradox
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3.2 Lindley's paradox
text: Lindley’s paradox Lindley ( D. V. Lindley 1957 ) , following Jeffreys ( Jeffreys 1939 ) and Bartlett’s reply ( Bartlett 1957 ) , noticed that the penalty can turn a rejection of the null into evidence for the null (the Jeffreys-Lindley paradox). Consider a sequence of trials of increasing size, every one of which ends with the same two-sided p-value of exactly 0.01, so that \(|Z_n| = 2.576\) in every case. A frequentist reading says the evidence against the null is the same in each trial: significant at 1%. The Bayes factor says something else, because the Ockham penalty keeps growing while \(Z_n^2\) is stuck at 6.63. Show the R code z <- qnorm ( 1 - 0.005 ); tau <- 0.25 n <- c ( 10 , 100 , 1e3 , 1e4 , 1e5 , 1e6 ) lb <- bf10_normal (z, n * tau ^ 2 , log = TRUE ) knitr :: kable ( data.frame ( n = n, BF10 = exp (lb), ` P(H0 | data) ` = posterior_null (lb, 0.5 ), check.names = FALSE ), digits = c ( 0 , 2 , 3 )) Table 7.2: Lindley’s paradox. Every row has the same two-sided p-value, 0.01 (z = 2.576). Prior N(0, 0.25^2) on the effect under the alternative, unit standard deviation per observation, prior probability of the null 0.5.

Holding the two-sided p-value at 0.01 (and also at 0.05 and 0.001), the Bayes factor for the alternative first rises and then falls as the sample size grows, crossing below 1 for large n. The dashed line is BF = 1. How should a trialist react? There are two honest reactions and one dishonest one. The honest reactions are these. First, the paradox lives at sample sizes far larger than those of most confirmatory trials of a large effect, and with a vague prior ( \(\tau\) large) on a point null. It is a warning that a fixed p-value threshold cannot mean a fixed amount of evidence as the trial gets larger, which is why

title: Lindley's paradox
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3.2 Lindley's paradox
text: of a large effect, and with a vague prior ( \(\tau\) large) on a point null. It is a warning that a fixed p-value threshold cannot mean a fixed amount of evidence as the trial gets larger, which is why very large trials (cardiovascular outcome trials with tens of thousands of patients, platform trials with shared controls) sometimes find “significant” effects that are clinically trivial. The Bayesian remedy is a better question: instead of asking whether \(\theta\) is exactly zero, ask whether \(\theta\) exceeds a clinically relevant \(a\) . That is precisely the form of the FDA’s criterion, as the last section of this chapter shows. Second, the paradox is a reminder that the answer depends on the prior \(\tau\) under the alternative. A Bayes factor with \(\tau\) ten times larger needs a much larger \(Z_n\) to reach the same conclusion. This sensitivity is real, it is not hidden by the frequentist approach but simply left out of it, and it is the reason Chapter 8 treats prior choice and sensitivity analysis at length. The dishonest reaction is to pick \(\tau\) after seeing the data to give the result you want. A Bayes factor is as open to that abuse as a p-value is to choosing the test statistic after the fact, and the remedy is the same: pre-specify it in the protocol. Edwards, Lindman

title: Lindley's paradox
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.3.2 Lindley's paradox
text: to give the result you want. A Bayes factor is as open to that abuse as a p-value is to choosing the test statistic after the fact, and the remedy is the same: pre-specify it in the protocol. Edwards, Lindman and Savage ( Edwards, Lindman, and Savage 1963 ) gave lower bounds over all priors on the alternative, showing that a result significant at 5% is weak evidence against a point null at any sample size, and Berger and Sellke ( Berger and Sellke 1987 ) sharpened the point with lower bounds on the posterior probability of a point null over classes of priors, the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound used in the next section. Jeffreys, who developed the posterior-odds test of a point null in the 1930s ( Jeffreys 1935 ) and set it out in his book ( Jeffreys 1998 ) (the Oxford reprint of the third edition), wrote that the use of the p-value implies that “a hypothesis that may be true may be rejected because it has not predicted observable results that have not occurred”.

title: How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.4 How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value
text: 7.4 How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value The Bayes factor depends on the prior under the alternative. Can we say anything that does not? Yes, at the cost of being deliberately generous to the alternative. For any prior on the alternative, the Bayes factor against the null cannot be larger than what the most favorable choice produces. Sellke, Bayarri and Berger ( Sellke, Bayarri, and Berger 2001 ) showed that for a p-value \(p < 1/e\) and for a class of alternatives (the p-value is uniformly distributed under the null, and under the alternative the distribution of \(-\log p\) has a non-increasing hazard for \(Y = -\log p\) (their Section 3.1.3), of which the Beta \((\xi, 1)\) family of p-value densities is the leading example), the Bayes factor in favor of the null is at least \[ \mathrm{BF}_{01} \;\ge\; -e\, p \log p. \tag{7.5}\] This is a minimum Bayes factor , a bound on how strongly the data can favor the alternative within that class. The class matters: monotonicity of the p-value density alone is not enough, and the bound is not a statement about every prior. For \(Z \sim N(\theta, 1)\) with \(Z = 1.96\) and prior mass one half at each of \(\theta = \pm 1.96\) , the Bayes factor in favor of the null is about 0.29, below

Only at \(p = 0.001\) does the bound get to the neighbourhood of “strong evidence” (a Bayes factor of 53). This is the calculation behind the teal bar in module 2 of the companion lab (“the smallest chance that luck alone could still explain the result, given that p-value, assuming a 50:50 chance before the trial”). title: How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value

It is also an argument that has been made for tightening the default threshold for claims of new discoveries ( Benjamin et al. 2018 ) , a proposal that is controversial and does not apply to regulatory trials, where the one-sided 0.025 is set by decades of agency practice and by the substantial-evidence standard, not by a statistician’s preference. What the bound does not do is replace a design-specific calculation. It is generous to the alternative within its class (it asks which alternative would make the data look best for \(H_1\) ), so it understates what a reasonable analysis would find. In a trial, the prior under the alternative comes from the phase 2 data, the mechanism, and the effect size the trial was powered for, and Chapter 8 and Chapter 14 show how to build and defend it. The bound is a best case over a class of alternatives. A different route to the same kind of calibration fixes a Bayes factor threshold and asks which test reaches it most often. Johnson’s uniformly most powerful Bayesian tests ( Johnson 2013b ) choose, for a one-parameter exponential family such as a normal mean, the alternative that

title: How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.4 How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value
text: kind of calibration fixes a Bayes factor threshold and asks which test reaches it most often. Johnson’s uniformly most powerful Bayesian tests ( Johnson 2013b ) choose, for a one-parameter exponential family such as a normal mean, the alternative that maximizes the probability that the Bayes factor exceeds a stated threshold, and their link to classical uniformly most powerful tests gives an approximate calibration between p-values and Bayes factors. Johnson used it to argue for tighter standards of evidence ( Johnson 2013a ) , a proposal in the direction of Benjamin and colleagues’ 0.005 ( Benjamin et al. 2018 ) . Cornfield ( Cornfield 1966 ) put a prior probability on the null in a Bayesian sequential test for clinical trials, and Kass and Raftery ( Kass and Raftery 1995 ) give the scale on which such Bayes factors are usually read. Goodman’s two papers ( S. N. Goodman 1999a , 1999b ) explain to clinicians why a p-value is not the probability that the null is true and how a Bayes factor answers a different question. What the two bars of Section 7.5.1 add is that the threshold is not fixed: for a normal mixture alternative the Bayes factor bar grows with the information, so no single p-value cutoff corresponds to one Bayes factor as a trial grows.

title: One toll, three scales: how much evidence is enough?
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.5 One toll, three scales: how much evidence is enough?
text: 7.5 One toll, three scales: how much evidence is enough? The Ockham penalty in Equation 7.4 says that a Bayesian who uses a point null and a diffuse alternative has to see more than a one-sided z test’s \(Z_n^2 = 1.96^2 = 3.84\) before acting once the information is large (for a one-sided claim, with \(Z_n > 0\) ). The following is the first part of the framework in Polson and Sokolov’s working paper ( Polson and Sokolov 2026 ) ; the rest of it appears in later chapters, as flagged below. A reader may object that tuning a Bayesian rule until its type I error is 0.025 gives up the Bayesian position. Frequentist evaluation of Bayesian procedures has a long applied tradition. Rubin argued that the applied statistician should use Bayesian methods to build procedures and frequency calculations to judge them ( Rubin 1984 ) . Lewis and Berry applied exactly that program to clinical trials, judging Bayesian decision-theoretic designs by their classical operating characteristics ( Lewis and Berry 1994 ) , and Grieve’s “idle thoughts of a well-calibrated Bayesian” bring the argument to drug development and discuss how closely Bayesian procedures should match conventional frequentist targets ( Grieve 2016 ) . Dawid’s forecast-calibration result, that a coherent forecaster should expect to be well calibrated against the frequencies of the events forecast, concerns a

title: One toll, three scales: how much evidence is enough?
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.5 One toll, three scales: how much evidence is enough?
text: drug development and discuss how closely Bayesian procedures should match conventional frequentist targets ( Grieve 2016 ) . Dawid’s forecast-calibration result, that a coherent forecaster should expect to be well calibrated against the frequencies of the events forecast, concerns a different property than fixed-null type I error control ( Dawid 1982 ) . Evaluating a Bayesian procedure by its frequentist behavior is therefore Bayesian practice and not a compromise with the other school, and it is what the regulator asks for when the design is calibrated.

title: The two bars
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.5.1 The two bars
text: The two bars In plain terms: a fixed-level one-sided test acts when \(Z_n \ge z_\alpha\) , equivalently (for \(Z_n > 0\) ) when \(Z_n^2\) passes a constant bar, 3.84 at one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) , whatever the sample size. A Bayes rule that acts when the alternative is at least as probable as the null passes a bar that grows with the logarithm of the information, plus a constant that is positive when the null is favored at the outset. At small samples the Bayes bar is the lower one, at large samples it is the higher one, and whether a given trial is past the point where they cross depends on the prior scale. The comparison is for the specified uncalibrated point-null rule with a symmetric normal alternative. Figure 7.3 shows the two bars, and the note below derives them. Two rules, and what each charges: The fixed-level test acts when \(Z_n \ge z_\alpha\) , that is, when \(Z_n > 0\) and \(Z_n^2 \ge z_\alpha^2\) . The bar on \(Z_n^2\) is

Two rules, and what each charges: The fixed-level test acts when \(Z_n \ge z_\alpha\) , that is, when \(Z_n > 0\) and \(Z_n^2 \ge z_\alpha^2\) . The bar on \(Z_n^2\) is a constant: 3.84 at one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) , whatever the sample size. This is the traditional rule, calibrated to a type I error rate that does not depend on \(n\) . The Bayes rule acts when the posterior odds in favor of the alternative reach one, \(\pi_a \mathrm{BF}_{10} \ge \pi_0\) (act when the alternative is at least as probable as the null, which is optimal if wrongly acting and wrongly not acting cost the same). By Equation 7.2 this is \(\mathrm{BF}_{10} \ge \pi_0/\pi_a\) , and by Equation 7.4 it is, in the large-information approximation and with \(Z_n > 0\) for a one-sided claim, \[ Z_n^2 \;\ge\; L_n + C, \qquad L_n \sim \log n, \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_a}. \tag{7.6}\] The exact bar for the normal mixture of Equation 7.3 carries the factor \((1 + 1/k)\) : \(Z_n^2 \ge (1 + 1/k)\,(L_n + C)\) with \(k = I_n\tau^2\) . The bar of the Bayes rule is not constant. It grows with the logarithm of the sample size (more precisely, of the information \(I_n\tau^2\) ), plus a constant \(C\) that is zero if the null and
