text: \(k = I_n\tau^2\) . The bar of the Bayes rule is not constant. It grows with the logarithm of the sample size (more precisely, of the information \(I_n\tau^2\) ), plus a constant \(C\) that is zero if the null and the alternative are equally probable a priori, positive if the null is favored (the usual case for a drug that has to prove itself), and negative if the alternative is favored. Each bar is a price. The fixed-level test charges a flat \(z_\alpha^2\) . The Bayes rule charges \(\log n + C\) , which at small \(n\) is less than the flat price and at large \(n\) is more. Where do they cross? Set \(\log n + C = z_\alpha^2\) (asymptotically). With \(C = 0\) and \(\alpha = 0.025\) , \[ n^\ast \;=\; e^{z_\alpha^2} \;=\; e^{3.84} \;\approx\; 46. \tag{7.7}\] Here \(n\) is measured in units of the prior’s information, so that \(L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2) \approx \log n\) . The exact Gaussian expression of Equation 7.3 gives the crossing at \(I_n\tau^2 = 41.6\) , close to the asymptotic 46. In plain terms: once the data carry about forty to fifty times the information in the prior, the uncalibrated point-null Bayes rule asks for more than the fixed-level test does. Whether a given trial is past that point depends on the prior scale. For a

title: The two bars
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.5.1 The two bars
text: A recurring claim is that Bayesian trials “need less evidence.” Against a single unadjusted look at a fixed-level test, the opposite holds for the uncalibrated point-null rule once information times prior variance exceeds about 46 (exactly, about 41.6; a few dozen observations for a unit-information prior, far more at the prior scales used for hazard ratios): the Bayes rule with a point null charges more. A Bayesian bar calibrated to the same type I error is never lower at a single look without an informative prior. The gains of Bayesian adaptive designs come from elsewhere, namely monitoring, multiple arms and prior information, and each is costed later in the book ( Chapter 11 , Chapter 10 , Chapter 19 ). This is the thesis of the book and it is first visible in Equation 7.7 . A third toll exists, and it is the one that matters for monitoring. Both bars above are for a decision made once, at a pre-specified sample size. If the trial is looked at repeatedly and one wants the type I error to hold at every stopping time, the bar has to rise again. For the symmetric normal-mixture e-process of this chapter, comparing the threshold \(b = 1/\alpha\) with the baseline \(b = 1\) , the increase in the squared- \(Z\) bar is \(2\log(1/\alpha)(1 + 1/k)\) , which tends to

text: has to rise again. For the symmetric normal-mixture e-process of this chapter, comparing the threshold \(b = 1/\alpha\) with the baseline \(b = 1\) , the increase in the squared- \(Z\) bar is \(2\log(1/\alpha)(1 + 1/k)\) , which tends to the constant \(2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38\) at \(\alpha = 0.025\) as the information grows. This is the anytime-valid surcharge for this construction, and it comes from Ville’s inequality for test martingales. It is a large-information approximation for this normal mixture, not a universal minimum cost of sequential validity: other e-processes, such as those behind iterated-logarithm confidence sequences, behave differently. It is developed in Chapter 12 , and the sequential story, where the three tolls \(z_\alpha^2\) , \(\log n\) and \(\log n + 2\log(1/\alpha)\) become the three deviation scales and meet the group sequential boundaries (Pocock, O’Brien-Fleming, Lan-DeMets), is told in Chapter 11 . The Bayes factor of Equation 7.3 integrates the exponential likelihood ratio over the prior. A Laplace approximation of that integral gives the maximized log likelihood ratio, \(Z_n^2/2\) , minus the log of the ratio of the prior’s width to the posterior’s width, \(\tfrac12\log(1 + I_n\tau^2)\) . The posterior width shrinks like \(I_n^{-1/2}\) , so the ratio grows like \(I_n^{1/2}\) and its logarithm like \(\tfrac12 \log I_n\) . Doubling gives the \(L_n\) of Equation 7.4 . For the constant, the Bayes rule for a two-point decision with equal costs acts when the posterior probability of the alternative exceeds one half, that is, when \(\mathrm{BF}_{10}\,\pi_a/\pi_0 \ge 1\) . Taking logarithms, \(2\log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \ge 2\log(\pi_0/\pi_a)\) , and substituting Equation 7.4 gives Equation 7.6 . If the costs of the two errors differ, \(C\) absorbs their ratio as well. A regulator’s preference for protecting the public from false approvals can be written as a larger \(C\) . Setting \(b\) in “act when \(\mathrm{BF}_{10} \ge b\) ” to \(1/\alpha\) turns the Bayes factor into an e-value test and gives the anytime-valid bar, exactly \((1 + 1/k)(L_n + 2\log(1/\alpha))\) and approximately \(L_n + 2\log(1/\alpha)\) for large information, discussed in Chapter 12 . title: What this means for the protocol

text: What this means for the protocol A protocol written in the traditional style states a fixed-level test and a sample size computed from it. A protocol with a Bayes factor decision (rare in confirmatory trials, more common in early phase and in decision-theoretic designs) states the prior under the alternative, the prior odds or threshold, and the resulting bar. The table below compares the two on the same trial; the regulator’s question for either is the same one, namely what the operating characteristics are. Fixed-level z test Bayes factor rule Quantity compared with a bar \(Z_n\) against \(z_\alpha\) ( \(Z_n^2\) against \(z_\alpha^2\) when \(Z_n > 0\) ) \(\mathrm{BF}_{10}\) against \(\pi_0/\pi_a\) , or \(Z_n^2\) against \(L_n + C\) Bar depends on \(n\) ? No Yes, like \(\log n\) Needs a prior? No Yes: \(\tau\) and \(\pi_0/\pi_a\) Type I error \(\alpha\) , by construction Falls with \(n\) ; must be computed by simulation for the actual design Where it agrees One-sided p-value \(<0.025\) At the crossing \(n^\ast\) , where the two bars are equal What the regulator asks Is \(\alpha\) spent correctly? title: A test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6 A test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss
text: 7.6 A test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss The previous section priced evidence with a bar. This section asks what a bar is worth, and the answer ties the chapter back to the type I error and power of Chapter 4 . The frequentist ledger holds two numbers, the type I error \(\alpha\) and the power \(1-\beta_\theta\) at each effect \(\theta\) , each computed with the parameter held fixed. The Bayesian ledger holds one, the Bayes risk, which weighs the same two errors by how likely each state of the world is and by how much each mistake hurts. The two ledgers are not rivals: one is built from the other.

title: The Bayes risk of a test
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.1 The Bayes risk of a test
text: The Bayes risk of a test Let \(D(y) = 1\) declare the treatment effective. Let \(\pi_0 = \Pr(H_0)\) , let the effect have density \(g(\theta)\) under \(H_1\) , and let the loss be \(\ell_1\) for approving a useless drug and \(\ell_0\) for withholding a useful one (zero otherwise). The Bayes risk of \(D\) is its expected loss over both the parameter and the data, \[ r(D) \;=\; \pi_0\,\ell_1\,\alpha(D) \;+\; (1-\pi_0)\,\ell_0 \int \beta_\theta(D)\, g(\theta)\, d\theta . \tag{7.8}\] A frequentist who reports \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) has reported the ingredients of the risk, and the weights are what is missing: the prior probability of each state times the loss of the corresponding mistake. The rule that minimizes \(r(D)\) is found one data set at a time. For each \(y\) the contribution to the risk is linear in \(D(y) \in \{0, 1\}\) , so the optimal rule picks the action with the smaller coefficient, which gives \[ D^{B}(y) = \mathbf 1\{\mathrm{BF}_{10}(y) > b\}, \qquad b = \frac{\pi_0}{1-\pi_0}\cdot\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_0}, \tag{7.9}\] equivalently, reject when the posterior probability of \(H_0\) falls below \(\ell_0/(\ell_0 + \ell_1)\) . This is the rule for choosing between a point null and a symmetric alternative, with its threshold read as a loss ratio, and it uses only the data that occurred. It is two-sided model selection: the alternative \(N(0,\tau^2)\) puts mass on harmful effects, so \(\Pr(H_1\mid y)\) is

title: The Bayes risk of a test
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.1 The Bayes risk of a test
text: a point null and a symmetric alternative, with its threshold read as a loss ratio, and it uses only the data that occurred. It is two-sided model selection: the alternative \(N(0,\tau^2)\) puts mass on harmful effects, so \(\Pr(H_1\mid y)\) is not the benefit probability \(\Pr(\theta>a\mid y)\) of the FDA criterion in Equation 7.11 . A rule for approving on benefit needs hypotheses and losses that separate beneficial from harmful effects, and restricting this rule to \(Z_n>0\) does not preserve its optimality. The averaging over data that did not occur defines the risk it minimizes, but it is not needed to find the rule. The Neyman-Pearson lemma ( Neyman and Pearson 1933 ) is a statement about the same rules. Minimizing the type II error at a simple alternative \(\theta_1\) subject to \(\alpha(D) \le \alpha\) is the same as minimizing \(\beta_{\theta_1}(D) + \lambda\,\alpha(D)\) for some multiplier \(\lambda \ge 0\) , which is the Bayes risk with \(g\) a point mass, \((1-\pi_0)\ell_0 = 1\) and \(\pi_0 \ell_1 = \lambda\) . So every most powerful test is a Bayes rule for some prior odds and loss ratio, and the likelihood-ratio cutoff \(k_\alpha\) is the product in Equation 7.9 . A trialist who fixes \(\alpha\) has chosen this product without saying so. The useful question is how the implied choice behaves as the trial grows.

title: What a fixed level implies as information grows
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.2 What a fixed level implies as information grows
text: What a fixed level implies as information grows Take the normal model of Equation 7.3 , \(\theta \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) under \(H_1\) , with \(q = I_n\tau^2\) . The fixed-level test that acts when \(|Z_n| > z_{\mathrm{crit}}\) is exactly the Bayes rule \(\mathrm{BF}_{10} > b_n\) with \[ 2\log b_n \;=\; z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\frac{q}{1+q} - \log(1+q), \qquad\text{so}\qquad b_n \approx \frac{e^{z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2/2}}{\sqrt{q}} \to 0 . \tag{7.10}\] The implied threshold is simply the Bayes factor at the boundary, so the first column of Table 7.4 is both the Lindley paradox at \(Z = 1.96\) and the implied Bayes-factor threshold of the 5% test (a two-sided point-null quantity, not a one-sided benefit bar). A regulator that holds \(\alpha\) fixed behaves, as trials grow, as if the prior odds on the null or the harm of a false approval were shrinking toward zero. Here the prior is the unit-information prior, \(\tau = 1\) on the scale of one observation, so \(q = n\) ; the table of Section 7.3.2 used \(\tau = 0.25\) and a p-value of 0.01, and the pattern is the same. title: The type I error of the Bayes rule
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.3 The type I error of the Bayes rule
text: The type I error of the Bayes rule The converse question is what type I error the Bayes rule has. With equal odds and loss ( \(b = 1\) ), the exact bar on \(|Z_n|\) is \(\sqrt{(1 + 1/q)\log(1+q)}\) , the bar of Equation 7.6 with the factor of the technical note above, so the type I error is \(2\{1 - \Phi(\text{bar})\}\) . It exceeds 5% for small trials, passes 5% at the crossing \(q\) = 41.6 of Section 7.5.1 , and falls thereafter, roughly like \((q \log q)^{-1/2}\) in the large-information approximation. Table 7.5 gives the exact values, with the Bayes risk of the two rules at \(\pi_0 = 1/2\) and equal losses ( \(\ell_0 = \ell_1 = 1\) ). text: error rates tend to zero, the type I error by the display above and the type II error at each \(\theta \neq 0\) because the statistic grows like \(\sqrt{n}\,\theta\) while the bar grows like \(\sqrt{\log n}\) , so its risk tends to zero. A fixed bar spends a constant error forever, and by Lindley’s paradox the constant is spent on exactly the cases where the evidence favors the null. This is the point-null, two-sided calculation. The one-sided confirmatory rule of the protocol is a different decision problem, and deriving its Bayes rule needs hypotheses and losses that distinguish beneficial from harmful effects, which this section does not do.

title: Which error matters more
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.4 Which error matters more
text: Which error matters more The threshold-as-loss-ratio derivation and its table are in Section 1.6 ; here only the prior odds enter the new part. By Equation 7.9 , with equal prior odds, acting when \(\Pr(H_1 \mid y) > p^\star\) is optimal when a false approval is \(p^\star/(1-p^\star)\) times as costly as a false rejection, whatever the prior odds: with \(p^\star = \ell_1/(\ell_0+\ell_1)\) the prior odds are already inside the posterior, and they multiply only the Bayes-factor threshold \(b\) . Show the R code lr <- decide_loss_ratio ( pstar = c ( 0.975 , 0.99 , 0.995 )) knitr :: kable ( data.frame ( ` Threshold p* ` = lr $ pstar, ` Implied ratio l1/l0 ` = lr $ ratio, check.names = FALSE ), digits = c ( 3 , 0 )) Table 7.6: Posterior probability thresholds and the loss ratio they imply (false approval relative to false rejection). Threshold p* Implied ratio l1/l0 0.975 39 0.990 99 0.995 199 A threshold of 0.975 (which equals a one-sided 0.025 only under the flat-prior, normal, single-look conditions of Section 1.6 , and which is a threshold on the benefit probability of a continuous model, not on \(\Pr(H_1\mid y)\) in the point-null model, so the two 0.975 thresholds are not interchangeable) therefore says that approving a useless drug is 39 times worse than withholding a useful one,

title: Which error matters more
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.4 Which error matters more
text: on the benefit probability of a continuous model, not on \(\Pr(H_1\mid y)\) in the point-null model, so the two 0.975 thresholds are not interchangeable) therefore says that approving a useless drug is 39 times worse than withholding a useful one, 0.99 says 99, and 0.995 says 199. Writing the threshold as a loss ratio forces the question that a fixed \(\alpha\) hides: is a false approval in this indication really 100 or 200 times worse than a false rejection? The ratio is not a statistical quantity. In a refractory cancer with no effective therapy, delay costs months of life and a false approval of a drug that does little harm costs relatively little, so the ratio is small and the threshold can be lower. For a preventive drug taken for years by millions of healthy people, a false approval exposes a large population to side effects for no benefit while delay costs each person little, so the ratio is large and the threshold should be higher. In a pandemic vaccine the cost of delay is counted in deaths per week, and the ratio is small even though the population is large. Isakov, Lo and Montazerhodjat ( Isakov, Lo, and Montazerhodjat 2019 ) carry out this exercise across diseases with burden-of-disease data and find that the best threshold differs by disease, so that a single conventional

title: Which error matters more
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.4 Which error matters more
text: even though the population is large. Isakov, Lo and Montazerhodjat ( Isakov, Lo, and Montazerhodjat 2019 ) carry out this exercise across diseases with burden-of-disease data and find that the best threshold differs by disease, so that a single conventional \(\alpha\) cannot be the Bayes rule for all of them. A protocol that states its threshold with a loss ratio, and a reason, is more informative than one that states \(\alpha\) alone (the loss-ratio reading of a posterior threshold returns in Chapter 15 ).

title: The Jeffreys table, in terms of $q$
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.5 The Jeffreys table, in terms of $q$
text: The Jeffreys table, in terms of \(q\) The growth of the bar is old. Jeffreys ( Jeffreys 1939 ) derived it for a normal mean with the Cauchy prior he recommended on invariance grounds. To leading order in \(n\) the Bayes factor in favor of the null is \(K = \sqrt{\pi n/2}\,\exp(-t^2/2)\) , which falls through one at \(t_{\mathrm{crit}} = \sqrt{\log(\pi n/2)}\) . This is a large-information approximation, not an identity: evaluated exactly, the Cauchy Bayes factor at \(t_{\mathrm{crit}}\) is 1.30 at \(n = 10\) and 1.008 at \(n = 10^3\) . Table 7.7 restates the criterion in terms of \(q\) and sets it beside the exact bar of the normal-mixture rule of Section 7.5.1 , which is what the rest of the chapter uses. The Cauchy scale and the normal \(\tau\) are different priors (at \(q = 10\) the two bars in the table are approximately 1.66 and 1.62, the first being the asymptotic Cauchy threshold, whose exact crossing at \(n = 10\) is 1.83), and a prior concentrated on the small effects that cardiovascular trials target moves the same bar to much larger \(n\) : with \(\tau = 0.25\) the rows read at \(q = n/16\) , and the crossing with 1.96 arrives at the thousands of events found in Section 7.5.1 , not at \(n \approx 30\) . The statement that the fixed level is too lenient for every trial beyond a phase I cohort holds only for a unit-information prior. Second, the calculation prices a point null, and an exact zero effect is a convenience. Against an interval null of clinically negligible effects the dimensional penalties of the two continuous models can cancel, and the resulting bar depends on the interval and the priors chosen; no general growth rate is claimed here. title: Lindley information and the Ockham penalty
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.6.6 Lindley information and the Ockham penalty
text: Lindley information and the Ockham penalty Lindley ( Dennis V. Lindley 1956 ) defined the information in an experiment as the expected reduction in entropy from prior to posterior, the mutual information between \(\theta\) and the data. For a normal mean with prior variance \(\tau^2\) and data of precision \(n/\sigma^2\) it is \(\tfrac12\log(1 + q)\) , half of the Ockham penalty \(L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2)\) that sets the Bayes bar. The coincidence is not an accident: the Bayes factor charges the alternative the amount of information that an experiment of this size could deliver about \(\theta\) , and the bar rises like \(\log n\) because the information does. With \(\tau = 0.25\) and \(\sigma = 1\) a trial delivers 1.0, 1.9, 2.8, 3.8 bits at \(n = 50, 200, 800, 3200\) : each quadrupling of the trial adds about one bit. Information returns are logarithmic, so the evidence a larger trial must clear grows only slowly, and so does what it buys.

title: From p-values to posterior probabilities of benefit
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7 From p-values to posterior probabilities of benefit
text: 7.7 From p-values to posterior probabilities of benefit The Bayes factor compares two hypotheses. For most clinical purposes there is a more useful number: the posterior probability that the treatment effect is large enough to matter. Chapter 6 built the posterior distribution of \(\theta\) ; here the question is how to turn it into a go/no-go criterion that a regulator can accept.

title: The FDA's success criterion
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.1 The FDA's success criterion
text: The FDA’s success criterion The January 2026 FDA draft guidance on the use of Bayesian methodology ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) , section IV.A, describes the standard way a Bayesian trial defines success. It says that Bayesian success criteria are typically “based on the posterior probability that the true treatment effect size exceeds some threshold.” In the notation of the guidance and of this book, \[ \Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) \;>\; c, \tag{7.11}\] where \(\delta\) is the treatment effect, \(a\) is the threshold (a minimum clinically relevant benefit, or zero if any benefit counts) and \(c\) is the minimum posterior probability. The notation \(\delta\) is used when quoting the criterion; elsewhere the book writes \(\theta\) for the same quantity. Two dials, then. The threshold \(a\) says how big an effect counts. The probability \(c\) says how sure one must be that it is at least that big. For trials with an overall frequentist statistical analysis plan, the same guidance says the success criteria are “almost always” chosen so that the familywise type I error is no greater than 0.025, one-sided, and that “a and c can be chosen such that the overall FWER is controlled at a given level, typically 0.025 one-sided” (section IV.A.1). It also describes two other routes: direct interpretation of posterior probabilities (for example with borrowing, by agreement

title: The FDA's success criterion
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.1 The FDA's success criterion
text: that “a and c can be chosen such that the overall FWER is controlled at a given level, typically 0.025 one-sided” (section IV.A.1). It also describes two other routes: direct interpretation of posterior probabilities (for example with borrowing, by agreement with FDA) and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria (section IV.A.3). Section IV.A is thus clear that a Bayesian criterion is a rule whose operating characteristics are to be reported. Calibration to the one-sided 0.025 is one of FDA’s routes and this book’s default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing; it is not presented as FDA’s universal requirement.

title: The flat-prior case: where Bayes and the p-value agree
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.2 The flat-prior case: where Bayes and the p-value agree
text: The flat-prior case: where Bayes and the p-value agree The simplest instance connects the criterion to what the reader already knows. Let the estimate be \(\hat\theta \sim N(\theta, s^2)\) , with standard error \(s = 1/\sqrt{I_n}\) , and let the prior on \(\theta\) be flat. The posterior is \(N(\hat\theta, s^2)\) , so \[ \Pr(\theta > a \mid \hat\theta) \;=\; \Phi\!\left(\frac{\hat\theta - a}{s}\right). \] For the threshold \(a = 0\) , this is \(\Phi(Z_n)\) , which is exceeded by \(c = 0.975\) exactly when \(Z_n > 1.96\) , that is, exactly when the one-sided p-value is below 0.025. A flat-prior posterior probability of benefit is one minus the one-sided p-value. The two numbers differ in how they are read (probability about the effect, given the data; probability of the data, given no effect), but the posterior probability is one minus the one-sided p-value, so the two thresholds agree and a trial that succeeds by one succeeds by the other. This is a useful cross-check to keep in the SAP: whatever a Bayesian analysis with a very weak prior reports, it should be close to the frequentist analysis of the same trial. It is also why the passage of Chapter 6 on credible intervals matches the confidence interval of the CSR to the second decimal for large trials.

title: The mapping from $(a, c)$ to type I error
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.3 The mapping from $(a, c)$ to type I error
text: The mapping from \((a, c)\) to type I error With a flat prior, the criterion \(\Pr(\theta > a \mid \hat\theta) > c\) is equivalent to \(\hat\theta > a + z_c\, s\) , where \(z_c = \Phi^{-1}(c)\) . At \(\theta = 0\) (no effect) the probability that a trial meets the criterion is \[ \alpha(a, c) \;=\; 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{a}{s} + z_c\right). \tag{7.12}\] It follows that: With \(a = 0\) , \(\alpha = 1 - c\) . A criterion of \(c = 0.975\) gives \(\alpha = 0.025\) . A criterion of \(c = 0.95\) gives 0.05, one-sided. With \(a > 0\) , the type I error is smaller than \(1 - c\) , because clearing a positive threshold is harder. To keep \(\alpha = 0.025\) at \(\theta = 0\) one can lower \(c\) : the calibrating value is \(c = \Phi(z_{\alpha} - a/s)\) . Lowering \(c\) in this way controls the error under the null \(\theta \le 0\) , not under \(\theta \le a\) : with \(a = s = 0.1\) the calibrating \(c \approx 0.83\) gives about 17% rejection at \(\theta = a\) . The larger the threshold \(a\) is relative to the standard error, the lower \(c\) can be while the type I error stays at 0.025. When \(a\) is large compared with \(s\) one can end up at a \(c\) of 0.8 or

title: The mapping from $(a, c)$ to type I error
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.3 The mapping from $(a, c)$ to type I error
text: larger the threshold \(a\) is relative to the standard error, the lower \(c\) can be while the type I error stays at 0.025. When \(a\) is large compared with \(s\) one can end up at a \(c\) of 0.8 or so, a figure that looks lenient. This calibration reproduces the ordinary zero-null test: the rejection condition reduces to \(\hat\theta > z_\alpha s\) whatever \(a\) is, so it establishes superiority over zero, not benefit exceeding \(a\) . To support a claim that the effect exceeds \(a\) , calibrate at \(\theta = a\) ; in this flat-prior normal model that gives \(c = 0.975\) . FDA draft section IV.A.1 uses \(a = 0\) for calibrated superiority designs. The calibration depends on \(s\) , that is, on the sample size. A given pair \((a, c)\) gives a different \(\alpha\) in a trial with 200 patients than in one with 2,000. title: An informative prior changes the mapping
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.4 An informative prior changes the mapping
text: An informative prior changes the mapping A flat prior is the exception. The point of a Bayesian design is often to use prior information, or at least a skeptical prior that shrinks the estimate toward zero. With a prior \(\theta \sim N(0,\tau^2)\) the posterior is normal with mean \(w\hat\theta\) and variance \(w s^2\) , where \(w = \tau^2/(\tau^2 + s^2)\) is the weight on the data. The criterion becomes \(\hat\theta > (a + z_c\sqrt{w}\, s)/w\) , and a skeptical prior therefore raises the bar on \(\hat\theta\) at a given \(c\) : the trial must show a larger observed effect to convince a skeptic. The type I error at \(\theta = 0\) falls, and so does the power. title: An informative prior changes the mapping
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.4 An informative prior changes the mapping
text: it (0.79 and 0.59). Calibrating by lowering \(c\) (to 0.96 and 0.92) returns the type I error to 0.025. Once \(c\) is lowered to restore the type I error of 0.025, power returns to the flat-prior value of 0.85, and in this particular case the rule is exactly the flat-prior test, because a normal prior with a known variance and a one-sided criterion is equivalent to a z test with a different cut-off. The equivalence also holds for a normal prior with a shifted mean: once \(c\) is calibrated, the rejection region is again the same \(Z\) region. More generally, in this scalar normal model with known variance, any fixed prior that makes the posterior benefit probability strictly increasing in the estimate (any nondegenerate prior with mass on both sides of zero, mixtures included) yields, after threshold calibration, exactly the same rejection region as the \(Z\) test. More complex sampling models, nuisance parameters, and multi-arm or sequential decision rules require separate evaluation, by simulation, which is the subject of Chapter 14 . The consequence is important enough to state plainly. If the Bayesian criterion is calibrated to \(\alpha = 0.025\) and the prior is centered at no effect, then at a fixed sample size the trial has the same type I error and, to a first approximation, the same power as the traditional trial. The

title: An informative prior changes the mapping
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.4 An informative prior changes the mapping
text: calibrated to \(\alpha = 0.025\) and the prior is centered at no effect, then at a fixed sample size the trial has the same type I error and, to a first approximation, the same power as the traditional trial. The Bayesian version buys nothing at the single analysis. What it buys appears when the same posterior is used repeatedly, with multiple arms, or with an informative prior from earlier data, at which point the calibration is a simulation and the prior becomes a design element ( Chapter 8 , Chapter 19 ). If, on the other hand, an informative prior is used without calibration, the trial’s type I error can be higher or lower than 0.025 depending on the prior and the criterion (a prior \(N(0.01, 0.1^2)\) with \(s = 0.1\) and \(c = 0.975\) gives about 0.004), and a regulator will ask for the justification the FDA draft recommends in sections V.A and V.F (a pre-specified prior, and a demonstration that conclusions do not depend too strongly on it).

title: A worked comparison
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.7.5 A worked comparison
text: A worked comparison Consider a two-arm trial of a new therapy with a continuous outcome in which the estimated effect is 0.28 (in units of the outcome’s standard deviation) with standard error \(s = 0.10\) , so \(Z = 2.8\) and the one-sided p-value is 0.0026. Table 7.10 gives the summaries. Estimate 0.28, standard error 0.10. text: is the p-value in a different vocabulary, and the traditional design is the simpler thing to defend. The Bayesian criterion earns its place in the cases the later chapters take up, and its price, the extra specification and simulation burden, is paid in the currency regulators accept. Tip In the protocol A statistical analysis plan that uses a posterior-probability success criterion should state, before data are seen: the effect scale and the definition of \(\delta\) (for example, the log hazard ratio with benefit positive, or the risk difference); the threshold \(a\) and the probability \(c\) , with the clinical justification for \(a\) ; the prior distribution, with its source; the calibration: the simulation that shows the familywise type I error at \(\delta = 0\) (and at the least favorable point of the null) is no greater than 0.025 one-sided, with the number of simulated trials and the Monte Carlo error; the frequentist analysis that will be reported alongside (p-value and confidence interval), so that a reviewer can compare; a sensitivity analysis to the prior, including a weakly informative or flat prior, in line with FDA draft section V.F.

title: Reading the four quantities together
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.9 Reading the four quantities together
text: 7.9 Reading the four quantities together The four quantities of this chapter answer four different questions, and a clinician or reviewer who keeps the questions straight will rarely be misled. The p-value asks: if the treatment did nothing, how often would a trial like this look this good? It is the tool for controlling the rate of false approvals across a program, and it is what the type I error requirement is about. The false positive risk asks: among trials that look this good, how many are for drugs that do not work? It needs a prior probability that the drug works, and it explains why a fixed alpha is a different level of protection in different development settings. The Bayes factor asks: how much do the data favor a specific alternative over the null? It needs a prior under the alternative, it carries an Ockham penalty that grows with the information, and it is the quantity behind Lindley’s paradox. The posterior probability of benefit asks: how probable is it, given everything, that the effect is at least \(a\) ? It is the quantity a physician or a patient wants, it can be made to match the p-value exactly under a flat prior, and with an informative prior this book calibrates it by simulation, which is one of the draft’s three routes and the one

title: Reading the four quantities together
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.9 Reading the four quantities together
text: physician or a patient wants, it can be made to match the p-value exactly under a flat prior, and with an informative prior this book calibrates it by simulation, which is one of the draft’s three routes and the one a regulator will most readily recognize. A good SAP lets a reader recover all four from the same analysis. The p-value and the interval are what ICH E9 section 5.5 asks for. The posterior probability and its calibration are what the FDA draft and ICH E20 section 5.3 recommend reporting when the design is Bayesian. Where they disagree, the disagreement is information: a trial where the p-value is just under 0.025, the Bayes factor is barely above one, and the posterior probability of exceeding the clinically relevant threshold is 60% is a trial in which the regulator, the sponsor and the clinician should talk about what the evidence amounts to, not only about whether it met the criterion. title: In practice
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.10 In practice
text: 7.10 In practice Bayesian reanalysis of reported trials has a method literature. Harrell and Shih ( Harrell and Shih 2001 ) argued that decision makers need probabilities of actual interest, such as the probability of any benefit and of a clinically meaningful benefit; Zampieri and colleagues ( Zampieri et al. 2021 ) wrote a critical care tutorial, with a reanalysis of the ART trial; and Wijeysundera and colleagues ( Wijeysundera et al. 2009 ) applied Bayesian inference to contemporary randomized trials. Such reanalyses report the posterior probability of benefit, the posterior probability of a clinically meaningful benefit and the sensitivity to the prior, and they do not replace the prespecified analysis. Three published results show the chapter’s numbers at work. None of the Bayesian analyses below was a regulatory submission: two are post hoc reanalyses of trials already reported with a p-value, and the third is a survey of how often promising results are confirmed.

title: EOLIA: a p-value of 0.09 and its posterior probabilities
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.10.1 EOLIA: a p-value of 0.09 and its posterior probabilities
text: EOLIA: a p-value of 0.09 and its posterior probabilities EOLIA randomized 249 patients with very severe acute respiratory distress syndrome to early extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or conventional management and was stopped early for futility ( Combes et al. 2018 ) . Sixty-day mortality was 35% (44 of 124) with ECMO and 46% (57 of 125) with control, a relative risk of 0.76 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.04), \(p = 0.09\) . Thirty-five control patients (28%) crossed over to ECMO. By the convention of this chapter’s Section 7.1.1 the trial was “not significant.” Goligher and colleagues reanalyzed it post hoc, to show the effect of the prior ( Goligher et al. 2018 ) . The posterior probability that ECMO lowers 60-day mortality (relative risk below 1) was 96% under a minimally informative prior (RR 0.78, 95% credible interval 0.56 to 1.04), 99% under a moderately enthusiastic prior worth 264 patients at RR 0.78, 88% under a strongly skeptical prior worth 264 patients at RR 1.0 (RR 0.88, 0.71 to 1.09), and 99% under a prior from a downweighted meta-analysis of earlier studies. The skeptical prior is the weakest case and it still puts 88% on some benefit. The trial had been designed to detect a 20-point absolute reduction in mortality, and for that target the picture is different: the posterior probability of an absolute reduction

title: EOLIA: a p-value of 0.09 and its posterior probabilities
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.10.1 EOLIA: a p-value of 0.09 and its posterior probabilities
text: is the weakest case and it still puts 88% on some benefit. The trial had been designed to detect a 20-point absolute reduction in mortality, and for that target the picture is different: the posterior probability of an absolute reduction of at least 20 points was about 2% under the minimally informative prior. The lesson for this chapter is twofold. A flat-prior posterior probability is one minus a one-sided p-value (here about 0.96 for the observed RR of 0.76, up to the scale of the analysis), so a posterior of 88% to 99% is not a contradiction of \(p = 0.09\) but the same data read as a probability about the effect. And the choice of \(a\) matters: “any benefit” and “the benefit the trial was powered for” give very different answers from the same posterior, which is the point of the threshold \(a\) in Equation 7.11 . No regulatory action followed from the reanalysis.

title: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: a borderline trial under four priors
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.10.2 ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: a borderline trial under four priors
text: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: a borderline trial under four priors ANDROMEDA-SHOCK ( Hernández et al. 2019 ) , a trial of 424 patients with septic shock, missed its primary end point narrowly (two-sided \(p = 0.06\) ), and a post hoc reanalysis under four priors ( Zampieri et al. 2020 ) found the probability of benefit high under all of them; the trial and the reanalysis are told in full in Chapter 22 . The lesson is the one of Table 7.9 in a clinical setting: a result that sits just beyond the frequentist line ( \(p = 0.06\) two-sided, against 0.05, or equivalently 0.03 one-sided against 0.025) can be robust to the prior at a moderate \(c\) , and the reanalysis also shows where that robustness stops: a pessimistic prior, the analogue of the skeptical priors of that table, is what moves the conclusion ( Chapter 22 ). A sponsor who wants such a statement to count must specify the priors and \((a, c)\) before the data, as the FDA draft recommends (sections IV.A and V.A).

title: Zia and colleagues: false positive risk in practice
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > 7.10.3 Zia and colleagues: false positive risk in practice
text: Zia and colleagues: false positive risk in practice Zia and colleagues found that only 28% of phase III studies that repeated a regimen already tested in phase II were positive ( Zia et al. 2005 ) ; the full account is in Section 9.6.3 . A positive phase II result is the evidence that makes a phase III worthwhile, and yet fewer than a third of these confirmatory trials were positive. This is an empirical warning about predicting phase III results from phase II. It does not identify the fraction of ineffective treatments or an appropriate borrowing weight: a positive rate of 28% is produced, for example, by a development program in which half of the treatments are truly effective, average power is 53.5% and the type I error is 2.5%. The demand for adequate and well-controlled confirmation ( Chapter 3 ) is a response to this kind of attrition, and a Bayesian design that borrows a phase II result as a prior ( Chapter 19 ) has to justify its borrowing weight by other means.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 7: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities > Key points
text: Key points A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, it depends on the design that produced the data, and it carries no information about the alternative (ASA 2016; Goodman 2008). The false positive risk, \(\alpha(1-\pi_a)/[\alpha(1-\pi_a) + (1-\beta)\pi_a]\) , depends on the prior probability \(\pi_a\) that the drug works. At \(\pi_a = 0.1\) and 90% power, a result significant at one-sided 0.025 is wrong about one time in five. The Bayes factor weighs the data against both hypotheses and averages over the prior on the alternative, which creates an Ockham penalty of about \(\log n\) in \(2\log\mathrm{BF}\) . Lindley’s paradox is the consequence: a fixed p-value of 0.01 gives a Bayes factor that rises and then falls below one as \(n\) grows. Within the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger class of alternatives (a non-increasing hazard for \(Y = -\log p\) , not every prior), a two-sided p-value of 0.05 corresponds to a Bayes factor of at most about 2.5, and a posterior probability of the null of at least 29% from even prior odds. The bound is \(-e\,p\log p\) (Sellke, Bayarri and Berger 2001). The fixed-level test charges a flat \(z_\alpha^2 = 3.84\) . The Bayes rule charges \(\log n + C\) with \(C = 2\log(\pi_0/\pi_a)\) . They cross at about

text: even prior odds. The bound is \(-e\,p\log p\) (Sellke, Bayarri and Berger 2001). The fixed-level test charges a flat \(z_\alpha^2 = 3.84\) . The Bayes rule charges \(\log n + C\) with \(C = 2\log(\pi_0/\pi_a)\) . They cross at about \(n = e^{3.84} \approx 46\) prior-information units (that is, \(I_n\tau^2 \approx 46\) , exactly about 41.6; for a unit-information prior \(I_n\tau^2 = n\) ), after which the uncalibrated point-null Bayesian bar against a single unadjusted look is the higher one. For this normal-mixture construction the anytime-valid surcharge is \(2\log(1/\alpha)\) for large information and \(2\log(1/\alpha)(1 + 1/k)\) exactly; it is not a universal cost of sequential validity. It is the subject of Chapter 12 , and the sequential story of Chapter 11 . A Neyman-Pearson most powerful test between simple hypotheses has a Bayes-risk interpretation. In the symmetric normal example, the fixed-level two-sided test is a Bayes rule with an information-dependent Bayes-factor threshold that falls like \(1/\sqrt{q}\) as information grows. The exact Bayes rule has type I error that falls with \(n\) , and a posterior threshold of 0.975, 0.99 or 0.995 is a loss ratio of 39, 99 or 199 that the protocol should defend. The FDA draft’s success criterion is \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) . With a flat prior and \(a = 0\) , \(c = 0.975\) is the one-sided p-value

text: of 39, 99 or 199 that the protocol should defend. The FDA draft’s success criterion is \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) . With a flat prior and \(a = 0\) , \(c = 0.975\) is the one-sided p-value test at 0.025. A Bayesian criterion calibrated to the same type I error is not a lower bar at a single look. Its benefits come from monitoring, multiple arms and prior information, and each carries a price that later chapters itemize. How would you describe it to a clinical colleague, and what would change if the trial had been preceded by two positive phase 2 studies? What does “conservative” mean for a regulator, and what does it mean for a patient waiting for the drug? The minimum Bayes factor bound is generous to the alternative. title: Choosing and Defending Priors
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8 Choosing and Defending Priors
text: Every statistical analysis of a trial rests on assumptions that are not in the data, and the Bayesian analysis is distinguished mainly by the fact that it writes one of them down. That is also the objection to it. A sponsor who proposes a prior is proposing a number that a reviewer can attack, and a reviewer who has never been asked to attack the implicit assumptions of a power calculation may find the explicit ones easier to see. This chapter is about making the prior something a sponsor can state, justify, quantify and defend, in the form a regulator will ask for it. We begin with the traditional design, which has a prior of its own that rarely gets that name. We then ask where a prior comes from in a sponsor’s program, and why the apparently safe choice of a flat prior is often the least defensible one. We describe the three classical reference priors (skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative), the conditional means prior that lets a clinician specify a prior on the scale she can think on, and the effective sample size that says in patients how much a prior weighs. We close with prior-data conflict, sensitivity analysis and the tipping-point prior, and with what the FDA’s January 2026 draft says about all of it. title: The traditional design has no stated prior
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.1 The traditional design has no stated prior
text: 8.1 The traditional design has no stated prior Take the ordinary fixed-sample design of Chapter 4 . The protocol states a one-sided type I error of 0.025, a power of 90 percent, and a design alternative: a hazard ratio of 0.75, say. From these the sample size follows, and the protocol says nothing further about what the sponsor believes. In the protocol table of the working paper behind this book, the traditional column for the prior reads: “Not stated. The design alternative enters only through the power calculation.” ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) That sentence is accurate, and it hides something. The design alternative assigns no prior probability to any effect: it is a planning assumption. The power calculation evaluates the probability of success at one value of the treatment effect and treats that value as if it were known. For time-to-event data with 1:1 allocation, the standard deviation of the estimated log hazard ratio is approximately \(\sqrt{4/d}\) for \(d\) events, and with \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) the design needs \[ d = \frac{4(z_{\alpha} + z_{\beta})^2}{\theta_a^2} \tag{8.1}\] events ( Chapter 9 derives this and asks what it predicts). A hazard ratio of 0.75 gives \(\theta_a = 0.288\) and 508 events. The power calculation is conditional performance: the chance of success if the effect is exactly 0.288. It assigns no prior probability to that value,

It assigns no prior probability to that value, but it is silent about the rest of the sponsor’s uncertainty. Nobody believes the effect is exactly 0.288. The sponsor’s actual belief is a distribution, wide enough that the real hazard ratio might be 0.90 or 0.65. The program’s real uncertainty can be put back in. If the sponsor describes its uncertainty about \(\theta\) as a normal distribution centered at the design alternative with standard deviation \(s_0\) , the probability that the final z test rejects is no longer the nominal 90 percent. Table 8.1 computes it, using the package function prob_success . This prior-averaged performance is called assurance or Bayesian power ( O’Hagan, Stevens, and Campbell 2005 ) , and Chapter 9 develops it. Two consequences follow, and they organize the rest of the chapter. First, a Bayesian protocol is not adding uncertainty to a design that had none; it asks the sponsor to state the uncertainty about the effect that the conditional power calculation sets aside, and assurance averages power over it. Second, the regulator’s question about the Bayesian prior (“why this one, and how much does it matter?”) is matched by a fair question to the traditional design (what effect was assumed, and how sensitive is the conclusion to it?), and the Bayesian answer, a stated prior with a sensitivity analysis, is more transparent than the traditional one. The traditional analysis is not a bad choice for this reason. The Bayesian prior earns its place when the trial is small, when external information is genuinely available and relevant, when interim decisions must be made on little data, or when several subgroups, arms or doses must be estimated at once.

title: Where priors come from in a sponsor's program
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.2 Where priors come from in a sponsor's program
text: 8.2 Where priors come from in a sponsor’s program A prior is not a mood. In a drug development program it has an identifiable provenance, and the guidance asks the sponsor to document it. Four sources recur. Phase 2 data from the same program. The most natural source: a phase 2 trial of the same drug, in a similar population, on an endpoint that is the same or close. The estimate and its standard error give a normal prior on \(\theta\) or a beta prior on a response rate. This is also the source most likely to mislead, for a reason that is hardly specific to Bayesian analysis: programs advance when the phase 2 result looks good. We return to the selection problem below. The published literature and earlier programs. Trials of drugs of the same class, in the same disease, with the same control. A meta-analysis of such trials yields a distribution for the control response rate, which is how historical control information enters a modern design, and a distribution for effects in the class. Two cautions apply. A literature search is a sampling mechanism, and the prior should be built from a pre-specified search, not from the studies the sponsor happens to like. The FDA draft is explicit that the construction should guard against “preferential selection of favorable studies” (Section V.D.3). How much

text: mechanism, and the prior should be built from a pre-specified search, not from the studies the sponsor happens to like. The FDA draft is explicit that the construction should guard against “preferential selection of favorable studies” (Section V.D.3). How much weight a historical-trial prior should carry, and how the answer moves the posterior, is worked through for the GUSTO trials in Chapter 22 . Second, the populations, background therapy and endpoint definitions drift between decades, a problem we take up under borrowing in Chapter 19 . Expert elicitation. When data are thin, as in a rare disease or a new mechanism, the sponsor may elicit the beliefs of clinicians. Elicitation is a technique with a literature of its own, and its main finding is that experts are overconfident ( Garthwaite, Kadane, and O’Hagan 2005 ; O’Hagan et al. 2006 ) : intervals stated as 90 percent contain the truth far less often. Structured protocols exist to blunt this. The Sheffield Elicitation Framework (SHELF) ( Oakley and O’Hagan 2019 ; Gosling 2018 ) has experts give individual judgments on quantiles or probabilities of observable quantities, share and discuss the evidence, and then agree on a single distribution that a “rational impartial observer” would find reasonable; the facilitator fits a parametric family to the agreed judgments and shows the fit back to the group. The full treatment

text: and discuss the evidence, and then agree on a single distribution that a “rational impartial observer” would find reasonable; the facilitator fits a parametric family to the agreed judgments and shows the fit back to the group. The full treatment of the field is O’Hagan et al. ( 2006 ) . Three rules protect the clinician and the sponsor alike: elicit observables (a response rate in a defined group of patients) and not parameters (a log odds ratio); elicit tails as well as the middle, because the tails drive the posterior when data disagree; and document the dissenters, since a single “consensus” can hide a bimodal opinion that a mixture prior would represent honestly. Chaloner and colleagues elicited priors graphically from clinicians for a real trial ( Chaloner et al. 1993 ) , and Dallow, Best and Montague argue for formal elicitation as routine in drug development ( Dallow, Best, and Montague 2018 ) . Mechanistic and pharmacometric models. An exposure-response model or a disease-progression simulator can produce a distribution of the response at a given dose. The Statistics in Medicine manuscript on priors and predictive stopping ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) describes converting such output into the beta parameters of a conditional means prior by matching moments: if the simulator gives a mean \(\hat\mu\) and variance \(\hat v\) for the response rate, the

title: The phase 2 selection problem
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.2.1 The phase 2 selection problem
text: The phase 2 selection problem A phase 2 estimate that has been selected for being large is biased upward as an estimate of the true effect, because the program carried on only if the data looked good. A prior built naively from that estimate imports the bias into the confirmatory analysis. A small simulation makes the size of the problem concrete. The numbers below are illustrative and not drawn from any program: suppose the true log hazard ratio across the sponsor’s candidate drugs varies with mean 0.10 and standard deviation 0.10 (a typical true hazard ratio near 0.90), and that each drug gets a phase 2 trial with 100 events, so the estimate has standard error 0.20. Programs advance to phase 3 when the phase 2 estimate exceeds 0.20 (a hazard ratio below 0.82). Show the R code set.seed ( 2026 ); n <- 2e5 th <- rnorm (n, 0.10 , 0.10 ); est2 <- th + rnorm (n, 0 , sqrt ( 4 / 100 )); adv <- est2 > 0.20 About a third of drugs (0.33) advance. Among them the average phase 2 estimate corresponds to a hazard ratio of 0.71 while the average true effect corresponds to 0.86. A prior centered on the phase 2 estimate would be centered on an effect more than twice the size of the truth, on the

title: The phase 2 selection problem
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.2.1 The phase 2 selection problem
text: estimate corresponds to a hazard ratio of 0.71 while the average true effect corresponds to 0.86. A prior centered on the phase 2 estimate would be centered on an effect more than twice the size of the truth, on the log scale. This is the Bayesian form of the winner’s curse and of regression to the mean, and it is why the FDA draft warns that analyzing the external data further “risks overfitting to observed random highs” (Section VI). Three remedies are standard and all of them belong in the protocol. Discount the phase 2 information, by a factor or by inflating its variance, so that it counts for fewer patients than it enrolled. Center a prior on the distribution of true effects in the class, an estimate that the sponsor can often obtain from the pooled history of similar programs and not from its own favorable result. Or use the phase 2 data only through a skeptical prior of the kind described next, so that it cannot carry the confirmatory result on its own.

title: Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.3 Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors
text: 8.3 Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar ( 1994 ) proposed that a trial should be reported against a small set of reference priors, each standing for a recognizable audience, so that a reader can see which readers the data convince. The 1994 paper demonstrated the idea on actual trials and remains the clearest statement of it. The device grew out of Freedman and Spiegelhalter’s earlier work on eliciting clinical opinion for stopping rules ( L. S. Freedman and Spiegelhalter 1983 ) , was used in the CHART trials ( Parmar et al. 1994 ) and in the Lancet proposal for monitoring large trials ( Parmar et al. 2001 ) ; the later book Spiegelhalter, Abrams, and Myles ( 2004 ) is the standard reference. Freedman, Spiegelhalter and Parmar ( 1994 ) applied the same device to monitoring, the subject of Chapter 11 , where Freedman and Spiegelhalter compared Bayesian and group sequential monitoring ( Laurence S. Freedman and Spiegelhalter 1989 ) . For a treatment effect \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) (positive is benefit), with design alternative \(\theta_a\) , the three reference priors are the following. A noninformative (or reference) prior, such as a normal with a very large variance. It adds essentially no information, and for a normal likelihood the posterior is the likelihood: the posterior probability that \(\theta > 0\)

title: Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.3 Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors
text: priors are the following. A noninformative (or reference) prior, such as a normal with a very large variance. It adds essentially no information, and for a normal likelihood the posterior is the likelihood: the posterior probability that \(\theta > 0\) equals one minus the one-sided p-value. A skeptical prior, centered at zero with a spread chosen so that the prior probability that the effect reaches the design alternative is small: \(\theta \sim N(0, s^2)\) with \(s = \theta_a / 1.645\) , so that \(\Pr(\theta > \theta_a) = 0.05\) . It represents a colleague who thinks the drug does nothing, and who will concede only that it might work as well as the sponsor hoped, with probability one in twenty. An enthusiastic prior, centered at the design alternative with the same spread, so that the prior probability that the effect is zero or harmful is 0.05: \(\theta \sim N(\theta_a, s^2)\) . It represents the investigator who designed the trial. The enthusiastic prior is a calibration device and not an analysis prior. If a trial is positive even under the skeptical prior, the skeptic is convinced. If it is negative even under the enthusiastic prior, then even the investigator must accept that the drug is not delivering what it promised, which is the logic of a futility rule. The FDA draft states the position about skeptical priors

text: it is negative even under the enthusiastic prior, then even the investigator must accept that the drug is not delivering what it promised, which is the logic of a futility rule. The FDA draft states the position about skeptical priors in these terms: “Skeptical priors express skepticism about the presence of very large treatment effects.” The draft notes that they “have not been standard practice in drug development but could be considered”, in particular after failed related programs or where only an incremental gain is plausible, and that in adaptive designs they can serve to temper early stopping for efficacy in place of a more severe boundary (Section V.C). Under the draft’s other axis, a skeptical prior is a way to ask for more evidence without changing the threshold: a skeptic requires a larger observed effect to reach the same posterior probability, which is how a Bayesian design can reproduce the early conservatism of an O’Brien-Fleming boundary ( Chapter 11 ). The set is completed by a range of equivalence, a band of effects around zero that clinicians regard as no different from no effect. Freedman, Lowe and Macaskill ( L. S. Freedman, Lowe, and Macaskill 1984 ) stopped trials by reference to the opinion of clinicians about such a range, and the 1994 paper reports the posterior probability that the effect lies below the

cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.3 Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors
text: Freedman, Lowe and Macaskill ( L. S. Freedman, Lowe, and Macaskill 1984 ) stopped trials by reference to the opinion of clinicians about such a range, and the 1994 paper reports the posterior probability that the effect lies below the range, inside it and above it. This gives three decision regions in place of one threshold: the drug is favored when the posterior mass above the range is large, the control when the mass below is large, and practical equivalence when the mass inside is large. The middle region is the link to the rest of the book. A noninferiority test also uses an acceptable-loss boundary, but its margin requires a separate justification based on the active control’s established effect and the clinically acceptable loss ( Section 4.9 ). Some futility rules use a low posterior probability of exceeding a prespecified clinically relevant effect. Others use conditional power or predictive probability of final success ( Section 15.2 ). The threshold need not equal the design alternative. The same idea is now called a region of practical equivalence. Tutorials with worked examples of reference priors and of monitoring against them are Abrams, Ashby and Errington ( Abrams, Ashby, and Errington 1994 ) , Fayers, Ashby and Parmar ( Fayers, Ashby, and Parmar 1997 ) and the health technology assessment review of Spiegelhalter and colleagues ( Spiegelhalter

The skeptical and enthusiastic reference priors express informative positions about the treatment effect; the noninformative prior provides a baseline comparison. Where a prior is only meant to regularize a nuisance parameter, a weakly informative default is common: a half-normal or half-t prior on a between-trial standard deviation ( Gelman 2006 ) , and a heavy-tailed Student-t (Cauchy) prior on logistic regression coefficients ( Gelman et al. 2008 ) . A reviewer’s practical question about any of these defaults is the one the book asks of every prior: how many patients is it worth ( Section 8.6 ), and does the conclusion survive a change of scale? title: Why default flat priors fail on the scale that matters
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.4 Why default flat priors fail on the scale that matters
text: 8.4 Why default flat priors fail on the scale that matters The noninformative prior in the table was harmless because the likelihood for \(\theta\) was normal and the prior was flat on the same scale. It is not harmless in general, and the cases in which it fails are the ones in which a sponsor most needs the prior to behave: small trials, binary endpoints, regression models, and dose-response. The difficulty is that “noninformative” is a statement about one parameterization. A prior that is vague on a parameter is generally informative about every nonlinear function of it, and the treatment effect a trial is designed to estimate is nearly always a function of the parameters. The fullest statement is in the Statistics in Medicine manuscript on priors and predictive stopping ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) , whose treatment of this topic this section follows.

A prior that looks like “no opinion” about each response rate is, about the contrast, the opinion that the drug is very likely either dramatically effective or dramatically harmful. Treatment effects that reach a confirmatory trial are mostly modest ( Berry 2012 ; Sokolova, Sokolov, and Polson 2026 ) , so this is a prior that disagrees with the sponsor’s own experience. These priors permit clinically implausible differences, so their posterior influence and the stopping operating characteristics should be evaluated under the proposed design: with equal arm sizes the posterior mean difference is shrunk toward zero relative to the observed difference, and whether early stops for efficacy are in excess depends on the truth and the monitoring rule. Beta priors were used in trial analysis by Novick and Grizzle ( 1965 ) , whose convention reads \(\mathrm{Beta}(z + 1, m - z + 1)\) as \(m\) prior patients with \(z\) responders, the practical way to express a prior in patients, related to the conjugate prior-sample reading of Raiffa and Schlaifer ( Raiffa and Schlaifer 1961 ) ; Morita, Thall, and Müller ( 2008 ) give the general effective sample size. The opposite deliberate choice,

title: Flat priors on logistic coefficients
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.4.2 Flat priors on logistic coefficients
text: Flat priors on logistic coefficients The same issue arises with more force in regression. A logistic dose-response model, \(\mathrm{logit}\, p(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x - 30)\) , has coefficients on the log-odds scale, a scale on which most clinicians have no intuition. The common default is a vague normal prior on each coefficient, for example \(N(0, 10^2)\) . The vagueness is an illusion on the probability scale, because the inverse logit saturates: a coefficient on the log-odds scale with standard deviation 10 pushes almost all of the prior mass to the boundaries. Simulating the prior makes the point. Show the R code set.seed ( 2026 ); b0 <- rnorm ( 2e5 , 0 , 10 ); p_mid <- plogis (b0) # centre of the dose range, where x - 30 = 0 extreme <- mean (p_mid < 0.05 | p_mid > 0.95 ); flat_pct <- round ( 100 * extreme) For a patient at the center of the dose range, about 77 percent of the prior mass on the response probability lies below 0.05 or above 0.95. The prior says that the drug at that dose either almost always works or almost never does, which is not the “no information” the investigator meant. Sensible diffuse priors on the coefficient scale exist (the familiar recommendation of Gelman and colleagues ( Gelman et al. 2008 )

title: Flat priors on logistic coefficients
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.4.2 Flat priors on logistic coefficients
text: that dose either almost always works or almost never does, which is not the “no information” the investigator meant. Sensible diffuse priors on the coefficient scale exist (the familiar recommendation of Gelman and colleagues ( Gelman et al. 2008 ) is a Cauchy prior with scale 2.5 on coefficients of covariates standardized as they describe), but they are a decision to be defended with the same rigor as any other, and the correct way to defend it is to show what it implies on a scale the clinician understands. That is the idea of the next section.

title: The conditional means prior
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.5 The conditional means prior
text: 8.5 The conditional means prior Bedrick, Christensen and Johnson ( 1996 ) proposed to move the elicitation from the coefficient scale to the scale where beliefs already exist. The investigator specifies prior distributions for the response probability at several covariate values (dose levels, say), and the prior on the regression coefficients is whatever distribution those statements induce through the link function. A clinician cannot say what the log-odds slope of the dose-response curve is. She can say what she expects at 10 mg and at 50 mg. For a model with \(p\) coefficients, take \(p\) covariate vectors \(\tilde x_1, \dots, \tilde x_p\) that are linearly independent, so that the map from coefficients to the success probabilities at those points is invertible. Specify independent beta priors, \(\tilde m_i \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a_{1i}, a_{2i})\) , for the success probabilities \(\tilde m_i = F(\tilde x_i' \beta)\) , where \(F\) is the inverse link. The induced prior on the coefficients is \[ \pi(\beta) \propto \prod_{i=1}^{p} F(\tilde x_i' \beta)^{a_{1i} - 1}\,\bigl[1 - F(\tilde x_i' \beta)\bigr]^{a_{2i} - 1}\, f(\tilde x_i' \beta), \tag{8.2}\] where \(f = F'\) is the density associated with the link. ( Bedrick, Christensen, and Johnson 1996 ; Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) Note Technical note: why the conditional means prior is a data-augmentation prior Each factor in Equation 8.2 has the form of a binomial likelihood contribution for the success

( Bedrick, Christensen, and Johnson 1996 ; Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) Note Technical note: why the conditional means prior is a data-augmentation prior Each factor in Equation 8.2 has the form of a binomial likelihood contribution for the success probability at the design point \(	ilde x_i\) , with \(a_{1i} - 1\) successes and \(a_{2i} - 1\) failures. The conditional means prior is therefore equivalent to adding \(a_{1i} + a_{2i} - 2\) pseudo-observations at each of the \(p\) design points to the data, with the factor \(f(	ilde x_i' eta)\) playing the part of the Jacobian of the transformation from probabilities to coefficients. For the logistic link \(f = F(1 - F)\) , so the factors combine to \(F^{a_{1i}}(1 - F)^{a_{2i}}\) , which is exactly the likelihood of \(a_{1i}\) successes and \(a_{2i}\) failures. A conditional means prior on a logistic model is thus literally \(a_{1i} + a_{2i}\) pseudo-patients, and its weight in the analysis is countable. This is the property that makes the effective sample size of the next section exact for this prior. title: The conditional means prior
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.5 The conditional means prior
text: default prior puts nearly all of its mass at the extremes. Two features of this construction help in a protocol. First, the investigator can vary the means to test sensitivity to location, and the sample sizes \(\nu_i\) to test sensitivity to the amount of information, each in units he understands. Second, the induced prior differs between logit and probit links, which means that the same scientific belief gives different coefficient priors for different links without the investigator reasoning about the model ( Bedrick, Christensen, and Johnson 1996 ) . One limit is worth recording: independent beta statements at two doses do not enforce a monotone dose-response; if monotonicity is scientifically required, the elicitation must constrain the ordered probabilities or the induced slope. The slope probability reported above (3 percent negative) is the prior’s residual tolerance for a non-monotone response, and it is worth showing to the clinician. The method is not confined to dose-response models. With a covariate such as baseline severity, the design points are the typical patients at which a clinician has expectations (a mild and a severe patient, in a model with intercept and severity), and the same construction applies. Hanson, Branscum and Johnson ( 2014 ) extended the idea through informative \(g\) -priors for logistic regression.

title: How much does a prior weigh: effective sample size
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.6 How much does a prior weigh: effective sample size
text: 8.6 How much does a prior weigh: effective sample size A skeptical prior in the previous table was said to be worth 131 events. The idea that a prior has a weight in patients is old (it is the content of the Beta \((z+1, m-z+1)\) parameterization), and Morita, Thall and Müller ( 2008 ) made it precise. They define the effective sample size (ESS) of a parametric prior as the number of observations whose information about the parameter is equivalent to the prior’s, using a minimally informative reference prior as the baseline. The practical content for the common models is simple. For a response probability with a \(\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)\) prior the answer is the one Section 6.4 reached from the weighted-average form of the posterior mean, and the other definitions roughly agree with it: \[ \mathrm{ESS} = a + b. \tag{8.3}\] (The older convention of Novick and Grizzle, under which \(\mathrm{Beta}(z + 1, m - z + 1)\) stands for \(m = a + b - 2\) patients and a uniform prior is worth none, is discussed in Section 6.3 ; it differs by a constant 2, irrelevant for a prior worth 50 patients and not for one worth 3.) For a normal prior \(\theta \sim N(\mu_0, s_0^2)\) on the mean of observations with variance \(\sigma^2\) per observation, \[ \mathrm{ESS} = \frac{\sigma^2}{s_0^2}. \tag{8.4}\] For the

title: How much does a prior weigh: effective sample size
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.6 How much does a prior weigh: effective sample size
text: constant 2, irrelevant for a prior worth 50 patients and not for one worth 3.) For a normal prior \(\theta \sim N(\mu_0, s_0^2)\) on the mean of observations with variance \(\sigma^2\) per observation, \[ \mathrm{ESS} = \frac{\sigma^2}{s_0^2}. \tag{8.4}\] For the log hazard ratio with 1:1 allocation, each event carries variance 4, so \(\mathrm{ESS} = 4/s_0^2\) events, which is the package function ess_events used above. A skeptical prior with \(s_0 = 0.175\) is worth \(4/0.0306 = 131\) events, and the enthusiastic prior with the same spread is worth the same. If the trial plans 508 events, these priors carry about 26 percent as much information as the data. The working paper comparing Bayesian and standard design puts the guidance in a sentence: “A prior worth five patients in a trial of five hundred is a modelling choice; a prior worth two hundred is an assumption that needs defending.” ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) The point of reporting ESS is to turn the argument about the prior into an argument about patients. A reviewer may or may not accept that a phase 2 trial of 100 events deserves to count for 50 events in the confirmatory analysis, but both sides can see what they are disagreeing about. The conditional means prior of the previous section gives a prior ESS of \(\nu_i\) at each design point, here

The conditional means prior of the previous section gives a prior ESS of \(\nu_i\) at each design point, here 10 at each of two doses. A power prior on an external dataset of \(n_0\) patients, discounted by a factor \(a_0\) between 0 and 1, has an ESS of about \(a_0 n_0\) (plus the baseline prior’s own weight). Table 8.3 shows the pattern for a phase 2 trial of 100 patients with 30 responders, discounted at four levels; Chapter 19 returns to how \(a_0\) is chosen. title: Prior-data conflict and robust priors
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.7 Prior-data conflict and robust priors
text: 8.7 Prior-data conflict and robust priors Suppose the prior is informative and well justified, and the data turn out to disagree with it. A fully Bayesian analysis with a single normal prior will compromise between the two, weighted by their precisions, and it will do so however far apart they are . A skeptical prior with a standard deviation of 0.175 will drag a very large observed effect back toward the null by a fixed fraction, and an enthusiastic prior will drag an observed null result toward benefit. For a prior based on external information, such as a phase 2 trial or an earlier study in adults, the same arithmetic says that the posterior is pulled toward information that the data are telling us is irrelevant. The FDA draft recommends that sponsors examine prior-data conflict (Section V.D) and not assume it away. The standard defense, which this chapter only previews ( Chapter 19 develops it, with its connection to power priors and hierarchical models), is a robust mixture prior. The informative component is combined with a weakly informative component, with a prior weight on each. For example, the prior is \(0.8\, N(0.29, 0.10^2) + 0.2\, N(0, 1)\) : an 80 percent chance that the effect looks like the phase 2 estimate, and a 20 percent chance that nothing is known. After the data, the weights

title: Prior-data conflict and robust priors
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.7 Prior-data conflict and robust priors
text: For example, the prior is \(0.8\, N(0.29, 0.10^2) + 0.2\, N(0, 1)\) : an 80 percent chance that the effect looks like the phase 2 estimate, and a 20 percent chance that nothing is known. After the data, the weights update: the component that predicted the data better gains weight. If the data agree with the informative component, the posterior stays with it, and if they disagree, the weight shifts to the vague component and the posterior follows the data. Schmidli and colleagues ( 2014 ) developed this construction for historical controls, and it is the form the FDA draft calls a mixture prior. The FDA applied it in a real submission, the pediatric belimumab trial in lupus ( Section 8.13 ).
