title: Sensitivity analysis over the prior scale
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.8 Sensitivity analysis over the prior scale
text: 8.8 Sensitivity analysis over the prior scale The FDA draft asks that “sensitivity analyses should be planned that utilize a range of alternative reasonable choices for the prior distributions” (Section V.F), for instance by varying the strength of borrowing. The working paper comparing Bayesian and standard design says that it reports a sensitivity analysis for every Bayesian number ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) , and the protocol table calls for “a prespecified sensitivity analysis over the prior scale”. For a normal prior the natural one-parameter family is the prior standard deviation \(s_0\) at a fixed mean, because \(s_0\) sets the ESS through Equation 8.4 and spans the range from a dogmatic prior ( \(s_0 \to 0\) ) to a noninformative one ( \(s_0 \to \infty\) ). Show the R code pp_fun <- function (s, m = 0 ) { u <- normal_update (m, s, est, se_design); pnorm (u $ mean / u $ sd) } sg <- data.frame ( s = seq ( 0.04 , 1 , length.out = 300 )); sg $ pp <- pp_fun (sg $ s) ggplot (sg, aes (s, pp)) + geom_line ( colour = "#1B9E77" ) + geom_hline ( yintercept = 0.975 , linetype = 2 , colour = "grey40" ) + geom_hline ( yintercept = pnorm (est / se_design), linetype = 3 , colour = "grey40" ) +

title: Sensitivity analysis over the prior scale
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.8 Sensitivity analysis over the prior scale
text: axis gives the corresponding prior ESS in events. The dashed line is the 0.975 threshold. The curve in Figure 8.4 is flat to the right and falls only when the prior becomes strong. For prior standard deviations above about 0.15 (ESS up to about 180 events) the posterior probability of benefit stays above 0.98; it falls below the 0.975 threshold only when the skeptical prior is as tight as \(s_0 = 0.11\) , which is worth 328 events, about two thirds of the information in the trial. This shape is the typical answer when the data are decisive: the conclusion is robust to a wide family of priors and breaks only for priors that are themselves almost as informative as the trial. The multiplatform heparin trials pre-specified an enthusiastic prior as exactly this kind of check ( Section 8.13 ).

title: The tipping-point prior
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.8.1 The tipping-point prior
text: The tipping-point prior The sensitivity curve suggests a sharper way of reporting, borrowed from the handling of missing data: instead of asking what the conclusion is under a given prior, ask which prior would reverse it. A tipping-point prior is the least extreme prior in a stated family for which the success criterion is no longer met. In the family above, the tipping point is a standard deviation of 0.11, or an ESS of 328 events. A second family varies the prior mean at a fixed spread, which asks how pessimistic the skeptic must be to overturn the result. Holding the skeptical spread of 0.175, the posterior probability of benefit drops below 0.975 only if the prior mean is -0.109, a prior expectation of a hazard ratio of 1.12, which is to say a skeptic who believed that the drug was harmful on average before seeing the data. The tipping-point report is useful to the regulator because it replaces a debate about the right prior with a statement about which priors the regulator would have to hold to disagree with the sponsor, and a regulator can say plainly whether she holds one. A tipping point that lies in an incredible region (a skeptic who thought the drug harmful, a prior worth two thirds of the trial) supports the claim that the conclusion is driven by

title: The tipping-point prior
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.8.1 The tipping-point prior
text: can say plainly whether she holds one. A tipping point that lies in an incredible region (a skeptic who thought the drug harmful, a prior worth two thirds of the trial) supports the claim that the conclusion is driven by the data. A tipping point close to the sponsor’s own prior is a warning that the prior drives the answer, which is the case that point 6 of the next section addresses. The tipping-point analysis belongs in the statistical analysis plan, with the family and the success criterion written down before unblinding; a family chosen after seeing the data would be a way of looking for a prior that works.

title: What the FDA draft says
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.9 What the FDA draft says
text: 8.9 What the FDA draft says The FDA’s January 2026 draft guidance is the first FDA statement on the Bayesian method in drug trials in general, and its position on priors can be stated in six points. The text of the draft governs; the points below are a summary of Section IV.B and the section on priors. Pre-specification. “It is always critical for Bayesian analyses to have a prespecified prior” (Section IV.B), and the sponsor should pre-specify and justify the full details of the prior in the protocol. The prior used for analysis (the analysis prior) is distinguished from design (sampling) priors used only in planning simulations; the second may be skeptical or optimistic about the truth to explore performance, but only the first enters the inference. Calibration or direct use of the posterior. The draft describes three routes for the success criterion \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) : calibration to type I error, direct interpretation of posterior probabilities, and benefit-risk or decision-theoretic criteria. In a calibrated design, \(a\) and \(c\) are chosen by simulation so that the familywise type I error is at most 0.025 one-sided, and the prior is used as a modeling device whose choice affects power and not the error rate. In a non-calibrated design, in which the prior is meant to summarize real external information, the posterior probability

title: What the FDA draft says
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.9 What the FDA draft says
text: at most 0.025 one-sided, and the prior is used as a modeling device whose choice affects power and not the error rate. In a non-calibrated design, in which the prior is meant to summarize real external information, the posterior probability is read directly (a posterior probability of 0.98 means a 2 percent probability of ineffectiveness given the prior), and this is acceptable where the prior is specified so that it “accurately and comprehensively reflects the external data” (Section IV.A), by agreement with the Agency. Here the prior matters in the second sense: without calibration, “the accuracy of conclusions depends strongly on the choice of prior distribution” (Section IV.B.2). The third, decision-theoretic route chooses the threshold from stated losses ( Section 1.6 ). The calibration route is the subject of Chapter 14 . Noninformative and minimally informative priors. No single approach is universally preferred. They can still influence the posterior when data are sparse, and they are not invariant to transformation, so a prior that is flat on one scale must be checked on the scale of the estimand: the point of the beta and logistic examples above. They also serve as the reference against which ESS is reported. Skeptical priors. “Skeptical priors express skepticism about the presence of very large treatment effects.” They may be appropriate after failed related programs or where only an incremental

title: What the FDA draft says
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.9 What the FDA draft says
text: examples above. They also serve as the reference against which ESS is reported. Skeptical priors. “Skeptical priors express skepticism about the presence of very large treatment effects.” They may be appropriate after failed related programs or where only an incremental gain is plausible, and they can stand in for adjusting an early-stopping boundary. The same section also discusses enthusiastic priors. Informative priors need more. “Informative priors will generally need a greater amount of justification” (Section V.A), with strong justification for borrowing on the grounds of relevance and feasibility, most commonly in pediatrics and rare diseases. Details of prior construction (a pre-specified search, criteria against preferential selection of favorable studies, relevance of the estimand and population) are the substance of Chapter 19 . Quantify the influence. Report the prior mean and the ESS, over the plausible range of outcomes, and plan sensitivity analyses over alternative reasonable priors. The “when the prior drives the answer” scenario is the one in which a sponsor must show, by the sensitivity curve and the tipping point, that the conclusion survives or must justify the prior at the level of evidence that a regulator accepts for any other analytic assumption. The draft leaves several things open. It does not say how large an ESS is acceptable, how wide a family of sensitivity priors is enough, or how to resolve a disagreement

title: What the FDA draft says
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.9 What the FDA draft says
text: that a regulator accepts for any other analytic assumption. The draft leaves several things open. It does not say how large an ESS is acceptable, how wide a family of sensitivity priors is enough, or how to resolve a disagreement between a sponsor’s prior and the Agency’s. These are the points on which a sponsor should seek agreement in a formal meeting before the trial (the programs are in Chapter 3 and the practicalities in Chapter 23 ). The draft is also not binding, and a sponsor who relies on it should say in the briefing document that it does. ICH E20 in its Step 2 draft treats the prior in the same spirit, in Section 5.3: the Bayesian analysis combines a prior with the trial data, within the draft’s general expectation that adaptations and analysis methods are pre-specified and that the design’s performance is evaluated by simulation (see Chapter 14 ). As a Step 2 text, E20 was open for public consultation until 30 November 2025 and may change before final adoption.

title: The device precedent
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.9.1 The device precedent
text: The device precedent None of this is new at the Agency. The Center for Devices and Radiological Health issued its Bayesian guidance for medical device trials as a draft in 2006 and in final form in February 2010 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2010 ) , and several device approvals have rested on priors built from earlier studies, often a previous generation of the same device. The device guidance’s recipe is the one this chapter describes in different words: agree on the prior with the Agency before the trial, justify the exchangeability of the earlier data with the current trial, quantify how much the earlier data count, and show by simulation how the design performs when the prior is wrong. On the type I error it says (Section 4.8, “Assessing the operating characteristics of a Bayesian design”): “When using prior information, it may be appropriate to control type I error at a less stringent level than when no prior information is used,” and the degree of relaxation “is a case-by-case decision that depends on many factors, primarily the confidence we have in the prior information.” This parallels the distinction the 2026 drug draft draws between calibrated and non-calibrated designs. The device precedent shows that the regulatory machinery for an informative prior exists and works, and it shows the limits: devices are often iterations of a platform with a plausible exchangeability argument, an argument that is much harder for a new molecular entity.

title: Side by side: what changes in the protocol
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.10 Side by side: what changes in the protocol
text: 8.10 Side by side: what changes in the protocol Item Traditional design Bayesian design Prior information Implicit in the design alternative and the assumed variance or event rate Stated as a distribution, with source and justification Where the sponsor’s uncertainty appears Nowhere in the analysis; sometimes in an assurance calculation In the prior and in the sensitivity analysis How the effect of the assumption is reported Power at several alternatives Prior ESS; posterior under a skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative prior; tipping point Agreement with the regulator Design alternative and sample size Prior, success criterion, calibration, and sensitivity family When the traditional and Bayesian answers agree Flat prior and a normal likelihood: Pr(effect > 0) equals one minus the one-sided p-value Main regulatory question “Is the assumed effect realistic?” “Why this prior, how much does it weigh, and does it drive the answer?” What stays the same is the standard of evidence: the trial is still judged by whether the conclusion would survive an informed skeptic, and a Bayesian design for a confirmatory trial is calibrated to the same one-sided 0.025 when the prior is not meant to carry information. What changes is that the assumptions are written down and can be argued with.

title: Writing the prior into the protocol
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.11 Writing the prior into the protocol
text: 8.11 Writing the prior into the protocol Tip In the protocol A prior section of a protocol or statistical analysis plan should contain, at minimum: The analysis prior , by name and parameters, on the scale of the estimand, together with its implied distribution for the estimand (for example, the implied prior on the risk difference or the hazard ratio) so that a reviewer does not have to compute it. Its provenance : the data, search or elicitation exercise from which it was built, with the dates and the people involved, and the criteria for including or excluding sources, written before the data from the current trial are seen. Its effective sample size , as defined in Morita, Thall and Müller (2008), by formula for conjugate priors and by simulation for mixtures, over the plausible range of outcomes, and as a share of the planned sample size. The comparison priors : a noninformative prior (reference), a skeptical prior, and where useful an enthusiastic prior, with the posterior summaries under each. The sensitivity analysis : the family of priors (for example, standard deviation from the ESS-zero reference to twice the proposed ESS; mean over a stated range), the success criterion, and the tipping-point report. The robustness provision : if the prior is informative, the mixture or discounting rule applied under prior-data conflict, with its parameters, and

text: reference to twice the proposed ESS; mean over a stated range), the success criterion, and the tipping-point report. The robustness provision : if the prior is informative, the mixture or discounting rule applied under prior-data conflict, with its parameters, and the simulation that evaluated it. The success criterion and its calibration : whether \(a\) and \(c\) are calibrated to a familywise type I error of 0.025 one-sided by simulation, or the posterior probability is to be read directly (with the agreement with the Agency that supports it), or a benefit-risk or decision-theoretic criterion is used, with its losses.

title: What can go wrong
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.12 What can go wrong
text: 8.12 What can go wrong Four failures recur, and a sponsor can guard against each. The prior chosen after the data are seen. A prior that is fixed after unblinding is a free parameter, and an analysis plan that allows it is a plan that allows the conclusion to be selected. Pre-specification is not a formality (the first quotation in the regulatory anchor says “always critical”), and the sensitivity family and the tipping-point report are fixed in the same document. A single published estimate treated as a prior. One phase 2 result, selected for a good look, is the case simulated above. The cure is to discount, to center on a population of programs and not on the sponsor’s own estimate, or to cap the prior’s ESS at a level the sponsor is willing to defend. A flat prior mistaken for no prior. A flat prior is a choice and one that carries implicit commitments on every other scale. Compute what it implies about the estimand before claiming that it is neutral. In a large trial with a normal likelihood the issue disappears, and for small binary trials, dose-response and subgroup models it does not. A prior that matters presented as a prior that does not. A skeptical prior of ESS 131 in a trial of 508 events changes the posterior hazard ratio from 0.80 to 0.84. That is a prior that matters to the estimate, even if the conclusion survives. The report should say so, and let the reader judge.

title: In practice
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.13 In practice
text: 8.13 In practice Four trials show the prior at work: one where the regulator asked for a tipping-point analysis, one family of platform trials that fixed neutral priors in advance and tested an enthusiastic one, one reanalysis that shows the prior moving the conclusion, and one pivotal trial that chose a deliberately weak prior.

title: Pediatric belimumab in lupus: a tipping point over the borrowing weight
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.13.1 Pediatric belimumab in lupus: a tipping point over the borrowing weight
text: Pediatric belimumab in lupus: a tipping point over the borrowing weight The pediatric trial of intravenous belimumab in lupus (C1109, PLUTO) was not powered to stand on its own, so FDA requested a post hoc analysis that borrowed from the adult trials through a robust mixture prior with borrowing weight \(w\) ( Brunner et al. 2020 ; U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research 2026 ) . The sponsor was not asked to defend a single \(w\) : the posterior probability of efficacy was at least 97.5 percent whenever \(w\) was 0.55 or more, and the review division judged such a weight reasonable ( Pottackal et al. 2025 ) . The data, the mixture and the approval are told in Section 19.17.2 . The lesson is the tipping-point logic of Section 8.8.1 applied to the borrowing weight instead of the prior spread: the report names the weakest reliance on adult data under which the conclusion holds, and the argument moves from “what is the right weight” to “is a weight of 0.55 or more credible”. The FDA case study also stresses that the analysis was post hoc, and recommends that a future program agree and pre-specify the Bayesian approach early (pre-IND), which is the point of the regulatory anchor of this chapter. Chapter 19 returns to the mixture itself.

title: REMAP-CAP and the multiplatform heparin trials: neutral priors, enthusiastic sensitivity
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.13.2 REMAP-CAP and the multiplatform heparin trials: neutral priors, enthusiastic sensitivity
text: REMAP-CAP and the multiplatform heparin trials: neutral priors, enthusiastic sensitivity The REMAP-CAP platform fitted a Bayesian cumulative logistic model for organ support-free days, with neutral prior distributions for the individual treatment effects, and fixed its efficacy threshold (a posterior probability of an odds ratio above 1 exceeding 99 percent) before the data ( REMAP-CAP Investigators, Gordon, et al. 2021 ) . The tocilizumab results are in Section 6.12 . The point here is the choice of prior: it favored neither arm, so that the data had to do the work. The therapeutic heparin trials (ATTACC, ACTIV-4a and REMAP-CAP, run as a multiplatform trial) used the same style: weakly informative priors for the baseline probabilities, a hierarchical prior with the severe and moderate cohorts nested around an overall effect with a neutral mean, superiority at a posterior probability above 99 percent and futility at above 95 percent for an odds ratio below 1.2. The pre-specified sensitivity analysis used an enthusiastic prior with a mean odds ratio of 1.75 (95 percent credible interval 0.74 to 4.15, prior probability of superiority 90 percent), the enthusiastic reference prior of this chapter ( REMAP-CAP Investigators, ACTIV-4a Investigators, et al. 2021 ; ATTACC Investigators et al. 2021 ) . Enrollment in critically ill patients stopped for futility (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95 percent credible interval 0.67 to 1.03), and in non-critically

title: REMAP-CAP and the multiplatform heparin trials: neutral priors, enthusiastic sensitivity
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.13.2 REMAP-CAP and the multiplatform heparin trials: neutral priors, enthusiastic sensitivity
text: this chapter ( REMAP-CAP Investigators, ACTIV-4a Investigators, et al. 2021 ; ATTACC Investigators et al. 2021 ) . Enrollment in critically ill patients stopped for futility (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95 percent credible interval 0.67 to 1.03), and in non-critically ill patients the neutral-prior analysis gave a 98.6 percent posterior probability that therapeutic dosing increased organ support-free days (odds ratio 1.27, 1.03 to 1.58) ( ATTACC Investigators et al. 2021 ) . The lesson is the structure and not a single number. Neutral analysis priors, a calibration of the thresholds by simulation, and an enthusiastic prior as a stress test: a conclusion that holds with a skeptical-to-neutral analysis prior and is not overturned by the optimist is hard to attack. Chapter 20 treats the platform designs themselves.

title: EOLIA: how far the prior moves the conclusion
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.13.3 EOLIA: how far the prior moves the conclusion
text: EOLIA: how far the prior moves the conclusion EOLIA, whose design and p-value of 0.09 are described in Section 7.10 and whose full reanalysis is in Section 22.3 , is the standard real example of how far the prior can move a conclusion. In the post hoc reanalysis ( Goligher et al. 2018 ) the posterior probability of any mortality benefit ranged from 88 percent under a strongly skeptical prior to 99 percent under an enthusiastic or a published-study prior. The same reanalysis shows what the prior does not change. The probability that the absolute risk reduction reached the 20 points the trial was designed to detect stayed small under every prior (see Section 22.3 ). The lesson is the one of the sensitivity curve of this chapter: report the posterior probability of the clinically relevant effect (and not only of any benefit) under a skeptical, a neutral and an enthusiastic prior, and read the range, not a single value. The range 88 to 99 percent says that the answer about “some benefit” depends on who is asked, and the small probability of the large benefit says that the trial was not built for the effect size it assumed.

title: BNT162b2: a deliberately weak prior with a calibrated threshold
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > 8.13.4 BNT162b2: a deliberately weak prior with a calibrated threshold
text: BNT162b2: a deliberately weak prior with a calibrated threshold The pivotal Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine trial (analysis and numbers in Section 6.12 ) made the opposite choice: a deliberately weak prior with a threshold calibrated by simulation. Its \(\mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)\) prior on \(p = (1 - \mathrm{VE})/(2 - \mathrm{VE})\) , the probability that a case falls in the vaccine arm, has mean 0.4118 (the value at \(\mathrm{VE} = 30\) percent) and an ESS by Equation 8.3 of \(a + b = 1.7\) cases, against a final analysis planned at 164 cases. Success required a posterior probability of \(\mathrm{VE} > 30\) percent above 0.995 at an interim analysis and above 0.986 at the final one, with the thresholds set by simulation so that the overall one-sided type I error was 0.025 ( Pfizer Inc. 2022 ) . The lesson is the calibrated route of the FDA draft (point 2 of Section 8.9 ): the prior is a modeling device, small enough that no reviewer could say it carried the result, and the evidence standard sits in the threshold, whose frequentist behavior was checked in advance. The posterior calculation for this prior is in Section 6.12 .

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > Key points
text: Key points The traditional design conditions on a design alternative in the power calculation and states no uncertainty about it. A Bayesian protocol asks the sponsor to state that uncertainty as a prior, and assurance averages power over it. Priors come from phase 2 data, earlier programs and literature, structured expert elicitation (SHELF) and mechanistic models. Phase 2 estimates are inflated by selection: in the illustration, programs that advanced had a phase 2 hazard ratio of 0.71 and a true one of 0.86. Skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors are reference points that show which audiences the data convince. A skeptical prior with a 5 percent chance of the design effect is worth 131 events here, a quarter of a 508-event trial. “Flat” is a statement about one scale. Independent uniform or Jeffreys priors on two arms put 49 to 56 percent prior probability on a risk difference larger than 30 points, and N(0, 10^2) priors on logistic coefficients put 77 percent of mass on probabilities below 0.05 or above 0.95. The conditional means prior moves the elicitation to the probability scale, and it is a data-augmentation prior with countable pseudo-patients. Effective sample size reports the weight of a prior in patients: \(a + b\) for a beta, \(\sigma^2 / s_0^2\) for a normal, \(4/s_0^2\) events for a log hazard ratio. A prior worth 5 patients

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 8: Choosing and Defending Priors > Key points
text: data-augmentation prior with countable pseudo-patients. Effective sample size reports the weight of a prior in patients: \(a + b\) for a beta, \(\sigma^2 / s_0^2\) for a normal, \(4/s_0^2\) events for a log hazard ratio. A prior worth 5 patients in a trial of 500 is a modeling choice and one worth 200 is an assumption. A robust mixture prior defends against prior-data conflict by moving weight to a vague component when data disagree. It has its own price and is treated in Chapter 19 . Report a sensitivity analysis over the prior scale and a tipping point: the weakest prior in a stated family that reverses the conclusion. In practice: the belimumab pediatric analysis reported a tipping point over the borrowing weight (efficacy at least 97.5 percent once \(w \geq 0.55\) ), the multiplatform heparin trials stress-tested neutral priors with an enthusiastic one, EOLIA’s posterior probability of benefit ranged from 88 to 99 percent with the prior, and BNT162b2 used a Beta(0.700102, 1) prior worth 1.7 cases with calibrated thresholds. The FDA’s January 2026 draft recommends a pre-specified prior, distinguishes calibrated from non-calibrated success criteria, and asks for the ESS and sensitivity analyses. It is a draft; the 2010 device guidance is the final precedent. Note Discussion questions Your phase 3 protocol uses a hazard ratio of 0.75 for the sample size. The design

title: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9 Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size
text: Every protocol contains a sentence of the form “a sample size of N patients provides 90% power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.80 at a one-sided significance level of 0.025.” It is the most-read sentence in the statistical section, the one a finance officer uses to budget the trial, a regulator uses to judge whether the study is adequate, and a data monitoring committee uses to understand what the trial can and cannot show. It is also, as this chapter will argue, a sentence that hides a great deal. The number N is the output of a formula whose inputs are two error rates and a guess about the treatment effect, and the formula is silent about how the guess was made, how much the answer moves when the guess is wrong, and what the trial would look like if the sponsor believed something different about the drug before it started. This chapter does three things. First it presents the traditional calculation correctly and fairly: the formula, its binary, continuous and time-to-event versions, worked numbers, its sensitivity to the design alternative, and the power curve that shows what a fixed trial can detect. Second it presents the Bayesian reading of the same calculation. A conventional power calculation can be represented as assurance under a point-mass design prior, and averaging the power curve over an

title: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9 Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size
text: curve that shows what a fixed trial can detect. Second it presents the Bayesian reading of the same calculation. A conventional power calculation can be represented as assurance under a point-mass design prior, and averaging the power curve over an explicit prior gives a quantity called assurance (or probability of success) that answers the question the sponsor actually has. Third it presents a sample size equation derived by Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) from the Bayes decision rule, which replaces the constant \(z_\alpha\) in the textbook formula by a boundary that grows with the sample size. That equation contains a result that runs against the thesis of this book, stated here up front: a fixed-sample design built on the Bayes decision boundary (the moderate deviation scale) is larger than the textbook design, not smaller. The Bayesian saving in patients and time lies elsewhere, in the monitoring of the trial, and 11 and 21 show where. Important Regulatory anchor ICH E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (Step 4, 1998) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 ) , section 3.5, Sample Size. Requires that the number of subjects be determined by the primary objective, that the method of calculation and the assumptions behind it (variability, the two error rates, the size of the treatment difference) be given in the protocol, and encourages investigating

The regulation that defines an adequate and well-controlled investigation, and so what counts as substantial evidence under section 505(d) of the FD&C Act. It does not prescribe a sample size formula; it requires that the methods of analysis be adequate to assess the effect of the drug. A sample size justification is part of that adequacy. title: Two errors and one guess
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.1 Two errors and one guess
text: Two errors and one guess A trial that ends in a one-sided test can be wrong in two ways. It can declare a useless drug effective, a type I error, whose probability under the null hypothesis the protocol fixes at \(\alpha\) , conventionally 0.025 one-sided ( Chapter 4 explained why 0.025 and not 0.05). Or it can fail to declare an effective drug effective, a type II error, with probability \(\beta\) at a stated effect. The complement \(1-\beta\) is the power. The two errors are not symmetric in regulatory practice. Type I error control is a central regulatory design criterion, and calibration to one-sided 0.025 is this book’s default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing: the sponsor must demonstrate adequate control. Type II error is a business and ethical quantity: the sponsor chooses it, usually at 0.10 or 0.20, and bears the cost of a failed trial. A regulator will ask about it because an underpowered trial exposes patients to an experimental treatment without a realistic prospect of an answer, but power is not a condition of approval in the way that error control is. For a treatment effect \(\theta\) estimated by \(\hat\theta\) with standard error \(1/\sqrt{nI}\) , where \(n\) is the sample size and \(I\) the Fisher information per observation, the standardized statistic is \(Z = \hat\theta\sqrt{nI}\) . Under \(\theta = 0\) it is

title: Two errors and one guess
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.1 Two errors and one guess
text: For a treatment effect \(\theta\) estimated by \(\hat\theta\) with standard error \(1/\sqrt{nI}\) , where \(n\) is the sample size and \(I\) the Fisher information per observation, the standardized statistic is \(Z = \hat\theta\sqrt{nI}\) . Under \(\theta = 0\) it is standard normal, and the test rejects when \(Z > z_\alpha\) . Under a true effect \(\theta\) , \(Z\) is normal with mean \(\theta\sqrt{nI}\) and variance one, so \[ \text{Power}(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\theta\sqrt{nI} - z_\alpha\right). \tag{9.1}\] Setting this equal to \(1-\beta\) gives \(\theta\sqrt{nI} - z_\alpha = z_\beta\) , and solving for the sample size, \[ n = \frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2}{I\,\theta^2}. \tag{9.2}\] This is the formula the book writes as \(n = (z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2/\theta^2\) when \(I = 1\) . At \(\alpha = 0.025\) and power 90%, \(z_\alpha = 1.960\) and \(z_\beta = 1.282\) , so \((z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2 = 10.51\) . The numerator is the whole of the error specification. The denominator is the whole of the science: the effect \(\theta\) the trial is built to detect, on the scale of information. At 80% power the numerator is 7.85. A trial designed for 90% rather than 80% power therefore needs a third more patients (10.51 over 7.85 is 1.34), whatever the effect. Two features of Equation 9.2 deserve attention before any numbers. The sample size is inversely proportional to \(\theta^2\) , so halving the effect quadruples the sample size. And the

title: Two errors and one guess
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.1 Two errors and one guess
text: third more patients (10.51 over 7.85 is 1.34), whatever the effect. Two features of Equation 9.2 deserve attention before any numbers. The sample size is inversely proportional to \(\theta^2\) , so halving the effect quadruples the sample size. And the formula takes the effect as given. The guess about \(\theta\) is the one input the data of the trial have not yet informed, and it is the input to which the answer is most sensitive.

title: The same formula for three kinds of endpoint
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.2 The same formula for three kinds of endpoint
text: The same formula for three kinds of endpoint What changes between endpoints is only what \(I\theta^2\) means. Continuous endpoint. For a difference in means \(\Delta\) between two arms with common standard deviation \(\sigma\) and \(n\) patients per arm, the standard error of the difference is \(\sigma\sqrt{2/n}\) and \[ n_{\text{per arm}} = \frac{2\,\sigma^2 (z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2}{\Delta^2}. \tag{9.3}\] The standardized effect is \(\Delta/\sigma\) . This is the calculation behind the worked design of the book’s companion online lab (module 03, https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/03-errors-power.html) (an improvement of 3 points on a score with patient-to-patient standard deviation of 10 gives a standardized effect of 0.3): 10.51 times 4 over 0.09 is 467 patients in total at 90% power. Binary endpoint. For response probabilities \(p_0\) and \(p_1\) the variance of the difference in observed proportions is \(p_0(1-p_0)/n + p_1(1-p_1)/n\) and \[ n_{\text{per arm}} = \frac{(z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2\,\bigl[p_0(1-p_0) + p_1(1-p_1)\bigr]}{(p_1-p_0)^2}. \tag{9.4}\] The variance now depends on the unknown rates, so a second assumption, the control rate, enters the calculation alongside the effect. A trial that assumed a 30% control response rate and finds 40% has a different information per patient than the plan assumed, before any question of treatment effect arises. Equation 9.4 is an approximation. It uses the alternative variances in both the critical value and the power term, whereas software that uses a pooled variance under the null for the critical value gives a different

title: The same formula for three kinds of endpoint
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.2 The same formula for three kinds of endpoint
text: of treatment effect arises. Equation 9.4 is an approximation. It uses the alternative variances in both the critical value and the power term, whereas software that uses a pooled variance under the null for the critical value gives a different answer, and the difference need not be small when the rates are far apart. The two versions use the variance at different roles and neither is the exact one. Time-to-event endpoint. Here the information is carried by events, not patients. Schoenfeld ( Schoenfeld 1981 ) showed that for a logrank test with 1:1 allocation the statistic is approximately normal with mean \(\log(\mathrm{HR})\sqrt{d}/2\) , where \(d\) is the total number of events, so \(I = 1/4\) per event and \[ d = \frac{4\,(z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2}{\log(\mathrm{HR})^2}. \tag{9.5}\] With the book’s sign convention \(\theta = -\log\mathrm{HR}\) so that benefit is positive, this is Equation 9.2 with \(I = 1/4\) . Freedman’s ( Freedman 1982 ) formula, \(d = (z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2(1+\mathrm{HR})^2/(1-\mathrm{HR})^2\) , is the other version that software commonly prints, and it differs from Equation 9.5 in the second-order terms: at HR \(= 0.80\) , 90% power and one-sided \(\alpha = 0.025\) it gives 851 events against 844 for Schoenfeld’s, a difference of about one percent. The choice between them is not what drives a time-to-event design. The number of patients is then obtained from \(d\) by a second, separate calculation: how

title: The same formula for three kinds of endpoint
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.2 The same formula for three kinds of endpoint
text: it gives 851 events against 844 for Schoenfeld’s, a difference of about one percent. The choice between them is not what drives a time-to-event design. The number of patients is then obtained from \(d\) by a second, separate calculation: how many patients must be enrolled, and followed for how long, so that \(d\) events have occurred by the planned end of the trial. That second calculation depends on the control event rate, the accrual pattern, dropout and the follow-up time, and a trial that accrues slower than planned or has a lower event rate than assumed does not lose power through its enrollment but through its calendar. A time-to-event trial is complete when it has its events. title: Sensitivity to the design alternative
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.3 Sensitivity to the design alternative

A true effect of 70% of the design value leaves a power of about 62%. A trial sized for 90% power has 83% power if the true effect is 90% of the design alternative, 62% power at 70% of it, and 37% at half. The converse is equally striking and less discussed: if the drug is better than assumed, the trial is overpowered and ends later than it needed to. Both errors are expensive, and the traditional design has no means of correcting either once the first patient is enrolled, other than the sample size re-estimation and interim analyses of Chapter 11 . Design effect Information required 0.05 4203 0.10 1051 0.15 467 0.20 263 0.30 117 0.50 42 A halving of \(\theta\) from 0.20 to 0.10 takes the requirement from 263 to 1,051. A statistician who is asked “what effect should I design for” has an unusually consequential question on her hands, and E9 section 3.5 names two ways to answer it: the smallest effect that would be clinically relevant, or the effect the sponsor anticipates. Those are different numbers. A design for the minimal clinically important difference is conservative: it gives the trial the chosen power to detect superiority when the true effect equals that minimum. It does not establish that the effect exceeds the minimum, because the null being tested is still an effect of zero, and demonstrating benefit beyond a minimum requires a different success criterion. A design for the anticipated effect is optimistic and, if the anticipation is wrong, produces a failed trial. In

cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.3 Sensitivity to the design alternative
text: the null being tested is still an effect of zero, and demonstrating benefit beyond a minimum requires a different success criterion. A design for the anticipated effect is optimistic and, if the anticipation is wrong, produces a failed trial. In practice the sponsor picks something between, informed by phase 2, and that act of picking is a prior elicitation that the protocol never calls by that name. The price of getting it wrong is concrete: pivotal trials are expensive, and cost rises steeply with patients ( Section 9.6.1 ).

title: The power curve
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.4 The power curve
text: The power curve A single power number hides the shape. The power curve plots \(\text{Power}(\theta)\) for fixed \(n\) and \(\alpha\) over the whole range of effects. It equals \(\alpha\) at \(\theta = 0\) , rises through 50% at \(\theta = z_\alpha/\sqrt{nI}\) and passes the design value \(\theta_d\) at \(1-\beta\) . The middle curve is the design for \(\theta = 0.20\) at 90% power. Two things the curve shows that a single number does not. The trial has a threshold effect, the value at which power is 50%, and effects below it are more likely to be missed than

title: The power curve
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.4 The power curve
text: = 0.20\) at 90% power. Two things the curve shows that a single number does not. The trial has a threshold effect, the value at which power is 50%, and effects below it are more likely to be missed than found. That value is \(z_\alpha\sqrt{1/(nI)}\) , which for a design with 90% power at \(\theta_d\) is \(z_\alpha/(z_\alpha+z_\beta) = 60.5\%\) of the design effect: a trial with 90% power at a hazard ratio of 0.80 is, for an effect smaller than about a 13% hazard reduction, more likely than not to fail. And the curve is flat near the design point. Moving from 90% to 95% power at the design effect needs 24% more information, so the last points of power are bought at a steep price. One more observation concerns the left end of the curve. The probability that the trial reports a positive result for a drug that does nothing is \(\alpha\) . It does not depend on \(n\) . The protocol writer who increases the sample size buys power and nothing else; the type I error stays at 0.025 however large the trial, even if a trial of 20,000 patients would, for the same observed data, support a much more skeptical conclusion than a trial of 200. The moderate deviation analysis below challenges exactly this.

title: What the regulator sees, and what the sponsor can do wrong
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.5 What the regulator sees, and what the sponsor can do wrong
text: What the regulator sees, and what the sponsor can do wrong An E9 section 3.5 justification, as a regulator reads it, has five parts: the primary endpoint and estimand; the effect assumed and its source; the variability or event rate and its source; the error rates; and a sensitivity analysis. The common failures are well known to reviewers. The assumed effect is the observed effect from a small phase 2 trial, which is biased upward by selection (the drug was taken forward because it looked good). The variability is taken from the same small trial, with the uncertainty ignored. The assumed control event rate is taken from a historical cohort that no longer resembles the enrolled population. And the sponsor presents no sensitivity at all. The traditional calculation is correct as arithmetic. Its weakness is that it treats the inputs as known. One legitimate source of a smaller required sample is a prespecified covariate-adjusted analysis: a baseline covariate that explains a fraction \(R^2\) of the outcome variance lowers the required \(n\) by about the factor \(1 - R^2\) , as worked in Section 5.10 , and the sample size paragraph should say whether the calculation assumes the adjusted or the unadjusted analysis. Tip In the protocol A sample size paragraph that survives review names: the estimand and primary analysis; the design alternative and its provenance

title: What the regulator sees, and what the sponsor can do wrong
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.1.5 What the regulator sees, and what the sponsor can do wrong
text: and the sample size paragraph should say whether the calculation assumes the adjusted or the unadjusted analysis. Tip In the protocol A sample size paragraph that survives review names: the estimand and primary analysis; the design alternative and its provenance (minimal clinically important effect or anticipated effect, with the source study); the nuisance parameters (standard deviation, control rate, event rate) with their sources; \(\alpha\) one-sided and \(1-\beta\) ; the resulting \(n\) or number of events and the accrual and follow-up assumptions that deliver it; and a table of power for effects at 70%, 80%, 100% and 120% of the design alternative, together with the rule for what the trial does if the nuisance parameters turn out wrong (blinded re-estimation, in an adaptive protocol under E20).

title: Power is conditional
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.1 Power is conditional
text: Power is conditional Power is a conditional probability: it is the probability of a significant result given that the true effect equals \(\theta_d\) . The sponsor, the investors and the DMC are not conditioning on the truth. They want to know the probability that the trial succeeds, taking into account that they do not know the effect. A statement such as “90% power” is regularly heard in the boardroom as “90% chance of success”, which is a different claim. It would be the same claim only if the sponsor were certain that the effect equals the design value. The traditional literature responds to this by sensitivity analysis, as above. The Bayesian response is to make the uncertainty explicit and average. Let \(\pi(\theta)\) be a prior distribution over the effect, representing everything known before the trial, such as phase 2 results, mechanism and class experience. The probability that the trial will be successful is the average of the power curve under that prior, \[ \text{Assurance} = \int \text{Power}(\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta . \tag{9.6}\] O’Hagan, Stevens and Campbell ( O’Hagan, Stevens, and Campbell 2005 ) named this quantity assurance, and earlier versions go back to Spiegelhalter and Freedman ( Spiegelhalter and Freedman 1986 ) and Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Blackburn ( Spiegelhalter, Freedman, and Blackburn 1986 ) under the name predictive power, and to Brown and colleagues ( Brown et al.

title: Power is conditional
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.1 Power is conditional
text: earlier versions go back to Spiegelhalter and Freedman ( Spiegelhalter and Freedman 1986 ) and Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Blackburn ( Spiegelhalter, Freedman, and Blackburn 1986 ) under the name predictive power, and to Brown and colleagues ( Brown et al. 1987 ) under the name expected power. Kunzmann and colleagues ( Kunzmann et al. 2021 ) review the variants, including probability of success defined with a Bayesian rather than a frequentist final analysis. Chapter 15 uses the same logic at interim analyses, where the prior is updated by the data so far.

title: A closed form
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.2 A closed form
text: A closed form For a normal prior \(\theta \sim N(m, s^2)\) and the z test above, with standard error \(\mathrm{se} = 1/\sqrt{nI}\) of \(\hat\theta\) , the trial’s estimate is marginally normal with mean \(m\) and variance \(s^2 + \mathrm{se}^2\) . The test succeeds when \(\hat\theta > z_\alpha\,\mathrm{se}\) , so \[ \text{Assurance} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{m - z_\alpha\,\mathrm{se}}{\sqrt{s^2 + \mathrm{se}^2}}\right). \tag{9.7}\] Take a trial sized for \(\theta_d = 0.20\) at 90% power ( \(n = 263\) , \(\mathrm{se} = 0.0617\) ). Three sponsors with the same design have three beliefs. The first centers its prior at 0.20 with a standard deviation of 0.10, which is a sponsor that believes the design alternative but admits that it is uncertain by plus or minus half of itself. The second believes the drug is a bit worse, with prior mean 0.14 (70% of the design value) at the same standard deviation. The third is skeptical, with prior mean 0.10. With a point-mass prior (standard deviation 0.02 is close to a point) at the design value the assurance is about 0.89, near the 90% power the trial was sized for. As the sponsor becomes uncertain, assurance falls: at standard deviation 0.10 it is 0.75, and at 0.20 it is 0.65. This is not a flaw but a property of averaging. The power curve flattens as it approaches one, so the effects below \(\theta_d\) lose more power than the effects above gain. Uncertainty about the effect, even when it is symmetric around the design value, reduces the probability of success. And a skeptical sponsor, whose prior mean is 0.10 or 0.14, sees a

text: \(\theta_d\) lose more power than the effects above gain. Uncertainty about the effect, even when it is symmetric around the design value, reduces the probability of success. And a skeptical sponsor, whose prior mean is 0.10 or 0.14, sees a probability of success of 43% to 56% for the very same design, although the protocol says 90%. This is not a thought experiment: when chemotherapy regimens were taken unchanged from phase II into phase III, only 28% of the phase III trials were positive ( Zia et al. 2005 ) (see Section 9.6.3 ). The “90% power” in the protocol is a statement conditional on one value of \(\theta\) , and the assurance is the unconditional version. For a phase 3 trial with a program-level decision pending, assurance is the better planning quantity, and it can be computed in a spreadsheet. Spiegelhalter and Freedman’s argument, which is recognizable from the earliest days of Bayesian trial design, is that the traditional power calculation is already Bayesian in its inputs: the sponsor’s choice of \(\theta_d\) summarizes belief, but it summarizes it as a point mass and discards the uncertainty. title: What assurance is not
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.3 What assurance is not
text: What assurance is not Assurance is not a measure of evidence. It is a forecast, computed before the data, of the frequency with which a trial of this size will cross its pre-specified threshold. The threshold is still the frequentist one in the classical version above: \(z > z_\alpha\) with \(\alpha\) fixed at 0.025. A fully Bayesian version computes the probability that the posterior probability of benefit exceeds the threshold \(c\) in the FDA draft’s criterion \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , with the expectation taken over the design prior. This is sometimes called Bayesian assurance, and it separates the roles of two priors. The design prior (also called the sampling prior) describes what the sponsor believes about the effect and is used to forecast. The analysis prior is the one used in the final analysis, and it is the one that has to be pre-specified and defended to the regulator ( Chapter 8 ). A sponsor can be optimistic in the design prior and skeptical in the analysis prior; there is no inconsistency, and indeed that combination is a sound one. What the regulator will not accept is calibration of the Type I error under the design prior. Type I error is computed under the null, whatever the sponsor believes. The FDA draft ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) describes

title: What assurance is not
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.3 What assurance is not
text: the regulator will not accept is calibration of the Type I error under the design prior. Type I error is computed under the null, whatever the sponsor believes. The FDA draft ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) describes three routes (calibration, direct posterior, decision-theoretic), and this book’s default is calibration. Under the calibration route the operating characteristics reported are the type I error under the null scenarios (calibrated, typically to 0.025 one-sided), and power or probability of success under a range of alternative scenarios, shown with Monte Carlo error. Assurance is the average of the latter over the sponsor’s own prior, and it is a legitimate additional output, but it does not replace the scenario table. The other two routes justify the design differently (a direct posterior criterion, or a decision-theoretic one), but the draft still expects operating characteristics evaluated by simulation, and the draft recommends rather than requires.

title: A comparison
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.4 A comparison
text: A comparison Table 9.4: Power and assurance side by side. Traditional power Assurance Treats the effect as a single design value \(\theta_d\) uncertain, with prior \(\pi(\theta)\) Answers If the effect is \(\theta_d\) , how often does the test succeed? How often will the trial succeed, given what we believe? Inputs \(\alpha\) , \(\beta\) , \(\theta_d\) , nuisance parameters the same, plus a prior for \(\theta\) and its source Typical value the target, 80% or 90% lower, often 50% to 70% for a phase 3 sized on a phase 2 estimate Regulatory status required justification (E9 3.5) optional; a planning aid. The scenario table of operating characteristics is what is reported This is how assurance is used in sponsor practice, which is where a reader will meet it. Rufibach, Burger and Abt ( Rufibach, Burger, and Abt 2016 ) study the choice of prior for Bayesian predictive power used as a probability of success in drug development and make recommendations for its use, and Crisp and colleagues ( Crisp et al. 2018 ) report practical experience of adopting assurance as a framework for decisions in drug development. The usual pattern is a go or no-go decision on a phase 3 program: the prior is built from the phase 2 estimate and its uncertainty, often with a discount for the optimism of a selected result, elicited from

title: A comparison
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.4 A comparison
text: development. The usual pattern is a go or no-go decision on a phase 3 program: the prior is built from the phase 2 estimate and its uncertainty, often with a discount for the optimism of a selected result, elicited from the team where the data are thin, and the assurance is reported beside the design power. In the example above, a phase 2 estimate of 0.14 with standard deviation 0.10 (a 30% discount on the design effect of 0.20) turns a 90% power trial into one with assurance 56%. A phase 3 program with that number may still be worth running, but the decision is now explicit. Two cautions. Assurance is a planning quantity: it is not an error rate and it does not replace the scenario table of operating characteristics. And it is only as good as the prior, so the elicitation record and a sensitivity analysis to the discount belong with it.

title: Bayesian sample size criteria
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5 Bayesian sample size criteria
text: Bayesian sample size criteria Assurance is one of several ways to turn a prior into a sample size. Inoue, Berry and Parmigiani ( Inoue, Berry, and Parmigiani 2005 ) separate the Bayesian rules into three families and show how each relates to the power calculation. The first two are named by what they average. Most of these criteria involve two priors, the design prior that predicts the data and the analysis prior that turns the data into a posterior ( Wang and Gelfand ( 2002 ) call them the sampling prior and the fitting prior), and keeping the two apart (the distinction of Chapter 8 ) is the point of the distinction; the exception is the known-variance length criterion below, which needs no design prior. The taxonomy and the two-prior framing used here are this book’s presentation of that literature, not a development in Inoue and colleagues. Take a two-arm trial with outcome standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\) , an effect \(\theta\) with design prior \(N(0.3, 0.1^2)\) and a flat analysis prior. The next three criteria were introduced for binomial proportions by Joseph, Wolfson, and Berger ( 1995 ) and set out for means and proportions, with mixed Bayesian and likelihood versions, by Joseph, Berger, and Bélisle ( 1997 ) and, for normal means and their differences, by Joseph and Bélisle ( 1997 ) ;

title: Bayesian sample size criteria
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5 Bayesian sample size criteria
text: Berger ( 1995 ) and set out for means and proportions, with mixed Bayesian and likelihood versions, by Joseph, Berger, and Bélisle ( 1997 ) and, for normal means and their differences, by Joseph and Bélisle ( 1997 ) ; the CRAN packages SampleSizeProportions and SampleSizeMeans implement them, and Joseph and Bélisle ( 2019 ) extend them to a community of priors held by different stakeholders, sizing the trial so that skeptics and enthusiasts alike end with a narrow enough interval. Average length criterion (ALC). Choose \(n\) so that the posterior 95% interval has expected length at most \(\ell\) . With a flat analysis prior this is the familiar \(2 \times 1.96\sqrt{2\sigma^2/n} \le \ell\) , so \(n \ge 2(3.92\sigma/\ell)^2\) , which is 342 per arm for \(\ell = 0.3\) . It needs no design prior at all when the variance is known, and it sizes a trial for estimation, not for a decision. Average coverage criterion (ACC) and worst outcome criterion (WOC). Fix the length \(\ell\) of the interval, centered at the analysis posterior mean, and choose \(n\) so that its coverage under the design prior (the coverage actually delivered if the design prior were true) is at least a target, either on average over the data (ACC) or in the worst case over the central region of the data that contains 90% of the

title: Bayesian sample size criteria
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5 Bayesian sample size criteria
text: prior (the coverage actually delivered if the design prior were true) is at least a target, either on average over the data (ACC) or in the worst case over the central region of the data that contains 90% of the prior predictive probability (a modified WOC). This is the design-prior version of the criteria; in the formulation of Joseph and colleagues the coverage is the analysis-posterior mass, which with a flat analysis prior and known variance does not depend on the data, so that ACC and WOC coincide there. At \(\ell = 0.3\) the ACC is 0.87, 0.93 and 0.97 at 200, 300 and 400 per arm, and the WOC is lower, 0.68, 0.85 and 0.92, because it protects against the unlucky data and not the typical ones. When design and analysis priors coincide and the variance is known the two criteria agree. Posterior probability criterion. Choose \(n\) so that the preposterior probability of a convincing posterior, \(\Pr\{\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid X) > 0.975\}\) , reaches a target such as 0.8. With the design prior above and a flat analysis prior this is the assurance of the previous section, and it is 0.77, 0.86 and 0.91 at 200, 300 and 400 per arm. It first reaches 0.8 at 226 per arm. If the same informative prior is also the analysis prior, the probability is above

title: Bayesian sample size criteria
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5 Bayesian sample size criteria
text: of the previous section, and it is 0.77, 0.86 and 0.91 at 200, 300 and 400 per arm. It first reaches 0.8 at 226 per arm. If the same informative prior is also the analysis prior, the probability is above 0.99 already at 50 per arm, because the prior alone gives \(\Pr(\theta > 0) = \Phi(3) = 0.9987\) . The trial is then unnecessary for an analyst who holds that prior, which is the right conclusion for her and a warning against letting a sponsor’s design prior into a regulator’s analysis. The result that ties this to the first half of the chapter is that the power calculation is the posterior probability criterion with a point-mass design prior at the alternative and a flat analysis prior ( Inoue, Berry, and Parmigiani 2005 ) . A power calculation is a Bayesian sample size calculation with an unusually confident design prior. At \(\theta = 0.3\) a two-arm trial needs 234 per arm for 90% power (the criterion evaluates to 0.90 at that size), while the assurance at 234 per arm, which acknowledges the uncertainty about \(\theta\) , is 0.81. A decision-theoretic criterion, which chooses \(n\) to maximize expected utility net of the cost of sampling, is the third family; it is the one that asks how much information is worth buying, and it is the subject of

title: Bayesian sample size criteria
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5 Bayesian sample size criteria
text: is 0.81. A decision-theoretic criterion, which chooses \(n\) to maximize expected utility net of the cost of sampling, is the third family; it is the one that asks how much information is worth buying, and it is the subject of Section 9.5 . The Bayesian sample size literature is wider than these families. Adcock ( Adcock 1988 , 1997 ) gave early average-criterion treatments and a review of the field, Lindley ( Lindley 1997 ) set out the decision-theoretic choice of sample size, and Chaloner and Verdinelli ( Chaloner and Verdinelli 1995 ) review Bayesian experimental design more generally. Wang and Gelfand ( Wang and Gelfand 2002 ) made the simulation-based version practical. De Santis ( De Santis 2006 ) asks for sample sizes that remain adequate across a class of priors, and Brutti and De Santis ( Brutti and De Santis 2008 ) extend this to avoiding a range of equivalence. Gittins and Pezeshk ( Gittins and Pezeshk 2000 ) and Sahu and Smith ( Sahu and Smith 2006 ) mix Bayesian planning with a frequentist analysis, and Pezeshk ( Pezeshk 2003 ) reviews the field. Read by the question each answers, the coverage and length criteria size an estimate, the posterior probability criterion and assurance size a decision, the expected-utility criteria size a decision together with its cost, and the robust criteria protect

cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5 Bayesian sample size criteria
text: the field. Read by the question each answers, the coverage and length criteria size an estimate, the posterior probability criterion and assurance size a decision, the expected-utility criteria size a decision together with its cost, and the robust criteria protect against the choice of prior. For a confirmatory trial the regulator still asks for the operating characteristics of the final analysis, so these criteria serve planning and the calibrated error rates of Chapter 14 serve the claim.

title: A rare-disease example: lupus
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5.1 A rare-disease example: lupus
text: A rare-disease example: lupus Moore and Joseph ( A. D. Moore and Joseph 1999 ) make the case for estimation-based sample sizes in systemic lupus erythematosus, where trials are small because patients are few and follow-up is long. Their dichotomous example is progression to dialysis over five years in lupus nephritis, 50% on standard therapy and a hoped-for 25% on a new regimen. The textbook calculation with a two-sided 5% test and 90% power needs 77 patients per arm (the paper reports 77, from the normal approximation with rounded quantiles; power.prop.test gives the same after rounding up). That is a fair answer to the question it asks. The difficulty is that a 25-point reduction is a large effect, and a drug that delivers a more modest one, say 35% against 50%, needs 227 per arm, 454 in all, which may exceed the number of eligible patients in a registry of a rare disease. The alternative the paper recommends is to size the trial to estimate the difference to a stated accuracy. A total interval width of 0.3 (plus or minus 0.15) for a 95% interval gives 75 per arm by the frequentist formula, which is the paper’s 75. Its Bayesian counterparts take a Beta prior on each proportion, here worth four prior patients per arm and centered on the design values, and ask for the

title: A rare-disease example: lupus
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5.1 A rare-disease example: lupus
text: gives 75 per arm by the frequentist formula, which is the paper’s 75. Its Bayesian counterparts take a Beta prior on each proportion, here worth four prior patients per arm and centered on the design values, and ask for the same width on average (ALC), with average coverage of 95% (ACC), or with coverage of at least 95% for every possible dataset (WOC; restricting the guarantee to the central 90% of the prior predictive distribution, as in the previous section, gives the modified WOC). They were computed with Joseph and Bélisle’s package SampleSizeProportions ( Joseph, Bélisle, and du Berger 2023 ) , and the ACC is a Monte Carlo estimate with a fixed seed. The paper only mentions the Bayesian route and gives no Bayesian sample sizes, so these numbers have no published counterpart. They are smaller than the frequentist width calculation for the ALC and ACC, 55 and 57 per arm, for two reasons: the prior contributes a few patients’ worth of information, and the design prior averages \(p(1-p)\) over its support, which is below the value \(0.25\) that the plug-in formula uses at \(p = 0.5\) . The WOC, 81, is larger than the plug-in answer because it protects against unlucky data. The width is also the lever that matters: widening it to 0.4 (plus or minus 0.2) cuts the Bayesian sizes to

The width is also the lever that matters: widening it to 0.4 (plus or minus 0.2) cuts the Bayesian sizes to 33, 33 and 43 per arm for the modest scenario ( Table 9.5 ). It buys feasibility: a trial of 66 patients in all can be run where one of 454 cannot. It costs the guarantee of a decision. At that size the trial estimates the difference to within plus or minus 0.2, so if the true effect

title: A rare-disease example: lupus
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.2.5.1 A rare-disease example: lupus
text: trial of 66 patients in all can be run where one of 454 cannot. It costs the guarantee of a decision. At that size the trial estimates the difference to within plus or minus 0.2, so if the true effect is 15 points the interval will often include zero, and the trial is underpowered for a test of no difference. It is not underpowered for the question it was sized to answer, how large the benefit is, and an interval of that width, read with the prior in hand, is the evidence a small trial can honestly offer. The criteria also take their inputs from the design prior, so the sensitivity analysis recommended for the power calculation applies to them in the same way.

title: The fixed-n test has no memory of n
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.1 The fixed-n test has no memory of n
text: The fixed-n test has no memory of n In the textbook calculation the critical value \(z_\alpha\) is fixed. A trial of 200 patients and a trial of 20,000 patients both declare success at \(Z > 1.96\) . The consequences are known to every reader who has met a very large trial that reports a result with \(p = 0.04\) and a clinically trivial effect. A statistically significant result in a huge trial is weak evidence against the null when measured the Bayesian way: the Bayes factor in favor of the alternative at \(Z = 1.96\) shrinks as the sample size grows, which is Lindley’s paradox ( Chapter 7 ). A Bayesian decision maker who places a prior mass on the null and balances the costs of the two errors will use a critical value that increases with \(n\) . Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) , building on a result for the Bayes risk of a regular testing problem ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) , work out how fast. The Bayes-optimal boundary on the standardized scale is \[ t_{\text{crit}} = \sqrt{\log n + C}\,\bigl(1 + o(1)\bigr), \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0/\pi_a}{\pi(\theta_0)\sqrt{2\pi/I(\theta_0)}}, \tag{9.8}\] where \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_a\) are the prior probabilities of the null and the alternative and \(\pi(\theta_0)\) is the prior density of the effect at the null. For a unit-information prior

title: The fixed-n test has no memory of n
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.1 The fixed-n test has no memory of n
text: n + C}\,\bigl(1 + o(1)\bigr), \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0/\pi_a}{\pi(\theta_0)\sqrt{2\pi/I(\theta_0)}}, \tag{9.8}\] where \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_a\) are the prior probabilities of the null and the alternative and \(\pi(\theta_0)\) is the prior density of the effect at the null. For a unit-information prior the denominator is one and \(C = 2\log(\pi_0/\pi_a)\) ; with equal prior odds \(C = 0\) and the boundary is \(\sqrt{\log n}\) . This is called the moderate deviation scale because the boundary grows with \(n\) : it lies above the fixed value \(z_\alpha\) of the central limit regime and below the large-information approximation to the anytime-valid (large deviation) bar of the normal-mixture construction, \(\sqrt{\log n + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)}\) (an approximation for that construction, not a universal cost of anytime validity), and Chapter 11 sets the three scales side by side. Note Technical note: where the boundary comes from The Bayes rule rejects the null when the posterior probability of the alternative exceeds one half, after weighting by the prior probabilities. Compare the two marginal likelihoods. Under the null, the standardized statistic has the standard normal density \(\phi(t)\) . Under the alternative, with a prior \(\pi\) smooth at \(\theta_0\) , the marginal density of the data is, by Laplace’s method, proportional to \(\pi(\theta_0)/\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)}\) , because the prior mass that is compatible with the data has width of order \(1/\sqrt{nI}\) . The balance condition is

title: The fixed-n test has no memory of n
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.1 The fixed-n test has no memory of n
text: prior \(\pi\) smooth at \(\theta_0\) , the marginal density of the data is, by Laplace’s method, proportional to \(\pi(\theta_0)/\sqrt{nI(\theta_0)}\) , because the prior mass that is compatible with the data has width of order \(1/\sqrt{nI}\) . The balance condition is \[ \pi_0\,\phi(t_n) = \pi_a\,\frac{\pi(\theta_0)}{\sqrt{n\,I(\theta_0)}}, \] which equates a Gaussian density to an \(n^{-1/2}\) term. Taking logarithms, \(t_n^2/2 = \tfrac12\log n + \text{constant}\) , hence \(t_n^2 = \log n + C\) . The constant collects the prior odds and the prior density at the null. For a standard Cauchy prior on a unit-variance Gaussian mean the asymptotic approximation is \(t_{\text{crit}} = \sqrt{\log(\pi n/2)}\) , which is \(C = \log(\pi/2) = 0.452\) . The expression holds asymptotically; it is an approximation in \(n\) and the \(o(1)\) matters at small sample sizes. Two quick numbers fix ideas. The boundary with \(C = 0\) exceeds the textbook 1.96 for every \(n\) above 46 (since \(\sqrt{\log 46} = 1.96\) ). At \(n = 1000\) it is 2.63 and at \(n = 10{,}000\) it is 3.03. The induced type I error, which is no longer fixed, is exactly \(1-\Phi(t)\) one-sided and twice that two-sided; the Mills-ratio approximation \(2\phi(t)/t\) for the two-sided value is accurate only for large \(t\) , and the error falls like \((n\log n)^{-1/2}\) . This chapter reports the exact one-sided value, to match the one-sided 0.025 of the

title: The power function and the sample size equation
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.2 The power function and the sample size equation
text: The power function and the sample size equation The power of the moderate deviation rule against an effect \(\theta\) follows by the same normal approximation as before, with the fixed \(z_\alpha\) replaced by the boundary: \[ \text{Power}_n(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\sqrt{nI}\,\theta - \sqrt{\log n + C}\right) + o(1), \qquad \theta > 0 \text{ for the one-sided benefit rule}. \tag{9.9}\] Setting this equal to \(1-\beta\) gives the sample size equation \[ n\,I\,\theta^2 = \left(\sqrt{\log n + C} + z_\beta\right)^2 . \tag{9.10}\] Set it beside Equation 9.2 . The structure is identical, but \(z_\alpha\) has been replaced by \(\sqrt{\log n + C}\) , a quantity that depends on \(n\) itself. The equation is implicit, but only through a logarithm, and a fixed-point iteration converges in a handful of steps: compute the textbook \(n\) , put it into \(\sqrt{\log n + C}\) , recompute, and repeat. In the code the equation is solved with a root finder. A note on units, since the tables can otherwise confuse. In Equation 9.10 the quantity \(n\) is the sample size on the scale where one unit carries information \(I\) , so that \(nI\) is the total information. For a one-sample or paired standardized mean difference with \(I = 1\) , \(n\) is the number of patients. For a two-arm trial with 1:1 allocation and a standardized effect, the information is \(N/4\) , so the number of patients is \(N = 4n\) . For a logrank test there are two equivalent conventions: count in events with \(n = d\) and \(I

title: The power function and the sample size equation
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.2 The power function and the sample size equation
text: with 1:1 allocation and a standardized effect, the information is \(N/4\) , so the number of patients is \(N = 4n\) . For a logrank test there are two equivalent conventions: count in events with \(n = d\) and \(I = 1/4\) , or count in information units with \(n = d/4\) and \(I = 1\) . The boundary \(\log n + C\) must describe the same rule in both, so the constant moves with the unit: \(\log(d/4) + C_{\text{info}} = \log d + C_{\text{events}}\) , that is \(C_{\text{info}} = C_{\text{events}} + \log 4\) . Keeping \(C = 0\) while switching units changes the implied prior. The package function events_md() uses the information convention ( \(n = d/4\) , \(I = 1\) ), so its \(C = 0\) is the unit-information prior at equal prior odds on that scale, and \(C = 2\log(\pi_0/\pi_a)\) holds in that convention. The same numerical \(C = 0\) read in the events convention means \(C_{\text{info}} = \log 4 = 1.39\) , the constant of two-to-one odds in the information convention, and at a hazard ratio of 0.80 it calls for 1255 events rather than 1067. Any stated value of \(C\) must therefore name its unit. All tables below use the information convention, and the comparison with the textbook formula is made in the same units.

title: The surprising result
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.3 The surprising result
text: The surprising result Table 9.7 compares the textbook information requirement with the moderate deviation requirement. The textbook column uses the two-sided 5% convention, \(z = 1.96\) , because that is the convention of the comparison in POL; at one-sided 0.025 the critical value is the same. At \(\theta = 0.20\) the ratio is 1.30, so the moderate deviation fixed design is about 30% larger; at \(\theta = 0.10\) it is 1.52 and at \(\theta = 0.05\) it is 1.73. Only for large effects, at which the requirement is below 46 units and the boundary is below 1.96, does the ordering reverse. The reason is that the Bayes boundary is more demanding than 1.96 for any trial of moderate or large size: a test that demands \(Z > 2.42\) rather than \(Z > 1.96\) needs more information to reach 90% power. What the extra patients buy is in the last column. The one-sided type I error is no longer held at 2.5% at all sample sizes but falls as \(n\) grows: 0.79% at \(\theta = 0.20\) (the two-sided equivalent is twice that), 0.33% at \(\theta = 0.10\) and 0.14% at \(\theta = 0.05\) . title: The surprising result
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.3 The surprising result
text: but falls as \(n\) grows: 0.79% at \(\theta = 0.20\) (the two-sided equivalent is twice that), 0.33% at \(\theta = 0.10\) and 0.14% at \(\theta = 0.05\) . At a thousand units of information the induced one-sided error is 0.43% and at ten thousand 0.12%. POL’s reading is that a fixed error is the right error for no sample size in particular. Whether one accepts that reading or not, the arithmetic is clear: a design that maintains a lower error as information accumulates cannot be cheaper than one that does not.

title: The prior odds in the constant
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.4 The prior odds in the constant
text: rises from 342 to 400 and 454 information units, and the induced one-sided error falls from 0.79% to 0.33% and 0.14%. Skepticism is paid for in patients, at a rate the formula makes explicit. This is the property a protocol reviewer wants: the sponsor who claims the drug is a long shot is told how many more patients it will take, and the sponsor who claims equal prior odds is told what that claim is worth. It also shows what this approach does not do. It is not a method of getting out of a regulatory error-rate expectation. Where the sponsor takes the FDA draft’s calibration route, with a one-sided type I error of 0.025 verified by simulation, that target stays; the moderate deviation analysis is a design-stage theory of why a trial of a given size should be held to a stricter standard than the nominal one, and of the cost of holding it there.

title: Many parameters and many endpoints
cx: Chapter 9: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size > 9.3.5 Many parameters and many endpoints
text: Many parameters and many endpoints Two extensions carry over into design ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) . For a \(d\) -dimensional parameter, for instance a trial with \(d+1\) arms, the boundary is \(\sqrt{d\log n}\) , so at \(n = 1000\) the radius is 2.63 for one parameter, 3.72 for two and 4.55 for three. This is the moderate deviation form of the Schwarz penalty \(d\log n\) , a Bayesian counterpart of a multiplicity correction arrived at without reference to a family of tests ( Chapter 10 ). Both extensions are model-based approximations (a regular parametric model with \(d\) free parameters for the first, sparsity of the true signals for the second), and neither displayed expression by itself controls the familywise error rate across clinical claims. For \(p\) simultaneous endpoints or subgroups under sparsity the boundary is the universal threshold \(\sqrt{2\log p}\) , which is 3.03 at a hundred endpoints and 4.45 at twenty thousand, the latter being the scale of a genome-wide scan.
