cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.12.2 A posterior probability as the stopping rule: therapeutic heparin in Covid-19 (2021)
text: patients the trial was stopped when its prespecified criteria for superiority were met ( ATTACC Investigators et al. 2021 ) . Of 2244 randomized, 2219 were analyzed, the probability that the therapeutic dose increased organ support-free days was \(98.6\) percent, and the adjusted odds ratio was \(1.27\) (95% credible interval \(1.03\) to \(1.58\) ). The same rule gave opposite stops in two cohorts, and neither is a frequentist boundary. The comparison with this chapter is direct: the posterior is valid at any stopping time, but the operating characteristics of the rule (the chance of a false stop for benefit or futility) have to be shown by simulation, as in Chapter 14 . The group sequential alternative would have fixed the looks and the spending in advance.

title: A futility stop and its reanalysis: EOLIA (2018)
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.12.3 A futility stop and its reanalysis: EOLIA (2018)
text: A futility stop and its reanalysis: EOLIA (2018) EOLIA randomized 249 patients with very severe acute respiratory distress syndrome to early extracorporeal membrane oxygenation or conventional management ( Combes et al. 2018 ) . Sixty-day mortality was 35 percent (44 of 124) against 46 percent (57 of 125), a relative risk of \(0.76\) (95% confidence interval \(0.55\) to \(1.04\) ), \(P = 0.09\) . The trial was stopped for futility under a prespecified sequential design with a two-sided triangular test ( Whitehead and Stratton 1983 ) , the design of Section 11.4.1 . Goligher and colleagues ( Goligher et al. 2018 ) reanalyzed the trial post hoc to show the effect of the prior. The posterior probability of any mortality benefit (relative risk below 1) was 96 percent under a minimally informative prior, 99 percent under a moderately enthusiastic prior, 88 percent under a strongly skeptical prior, and 99 percent under a prior built from published studies. But the probability of the 20-point absolute reduction the trial was powered for was only 2 percent under the minimally informative prior and 4 percent under the meta-analytic prior. The lesson is that a frequentist futility stop and a Bayesian summary answer different questions. The first says the design target was unlikely to be reached. The second says benefit of some size is probable. Both can be true, and a decision maker needs both, which is the argument of Chapter 7 for reporting the posterior at several thresholds.

title: A stop for harm: the Women's Health Initiative (2002)
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > 11.12.4 A stop for harm: the Women's Health Initiative (2002)
text: A stop for harm: the Women’s Health Initiative (2002) The estrogen plus progestin trial of the Women’s Health Initiative, in healthy postmenopausal women, was stopped early for harm, on the recommendation of its data monitoring committee, and the principal results were published in JAMA in July 2002 ( Rossouw et al. 2002 ) . At the board’s recommendation on 31 May 2002, after a mean of 5.2 years of follow-up, the test statistic for invasive breast cancer had exceeded the stopping boundary for that adverse effect and the global index statistic supported risks exceeding benefits. The estimated hazard ratios (nominal 95% confidence intervals) were \(1.26\) ( \(1.00\) to \(1.59\) ) for invasive breast cancer (290 cases), \(1.29\) ( \(1.02\) to \(1.63\) ) for coronary heart disease (286 cases), \(1.41\) ( \(1.07\) to \(1.85\) ) for stroke, and \(1.15\) ( \(1.03\) to \(1.28\) ) for the global index, while total mortality was not affected ( \(0.98\) , \(0.82\) to \(1.18\) ). The nominal interval for breast cancer reaches \(1.00\) : the stop rested on the crossing of a sequential boundary, not on that interval. Safety and harm monitoring in a trial of this kind is not a formal alpha-controlled test of a single endpoint. The committee weighs a pattern of outcomes, and a stop for harm is a decision under uncertainty made with discretion, which is what the DMC section of this chapter describes. The charter, the guidance on DMCs and the stopping guidelines exist so that such a decision can be made by people who see unblinded data and are independent of the sponsor.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 11: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales > Key points
text: Key points Testing repeatedly at a fixed level is not a test: two equally spaced looks raise one-sided \(2.5\%\) to about 4.2 \(\%\) , ten to about 9.7 \(\%\) , and, with monitoring continued indefinitely, the fixed cutoff is eventually crossed with probability one (finite-horizon crossing probabilities remain below one). The Armitage-McPherson-Rowe recursion computes the exact inflation and every boundary in the traditional toolbox. O’Brien-Fleming boundaries ( \(4.05, 2.86, 2.34, 2.02\) for four looks) cost about 2 percent in sample size and keep the final bar near \(1.96\) . Pocock boundaries (about \(2.36\) throughout) stop earlier when the drug works and cost about 18 percent more patients if the trial runs to the end. Lan-DeMets spending fixes a function, not times: the boundaries follow the realized information fraction, provided the timing is not driven by the observed effect. Alpha is distributed, not consumed. Futility rules should be non-binding in confirmatory trials; power is computed as though they are obeyed. Binding rules buy back a little alpha at the price of validity if overridden. DMCs see unblinded data, recommend rather than decide, and treat boundaries as guidelines. Early-stopped estimates are biased upward. The posterior does not depend on the stopping rule, but the type I error does. A Bayesian monitoring rule can be perfectly calibrated under the prior and still reject a true null in about

text: guidelines. Early-stopped estimates are biased upward. The posterior does not depend on the stopping rule, but the type I error does. A Bayesian monitoring rule can be perfectly calibrated under the prior and still reject a true null in about 17.5% of trials: its frequentist error is computed by simulation ( Chapter 14 ). The Bayes sequential problem is solved by backward induction on a sufficient statistic. Wald’s SPRT is its two-point special case, with the large deviation ledger \(n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \log(1/\alpha)\) . The three tolls: \(Z_n \ge z_\alpha\) (fixed level), \(Z_n > 0\) and \(Z_n^2 \ge (1+1/q)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log b\}\) (Bayes, approximately \(\log n + C\) at large information) and the same with \(b = 1/\alpha\) and \(Z_n > 0\) (anytime valid for the normal mixture, approximately \(\log n + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)\) ). The Bayes-factor bar is above the unadjusted bar once \(I_n\tau^2 > 46\) ( \(n > 46\) for a unit-information prior), so the Bayesian saving is not against a single look. For the normal-mixture construction, against the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar, the approximate surcharge is \(7.38/10.51 \approx 70\%\) of a conventional trial asymptotically (a comparison of boundary terms, not an exact sample-size identity); calibration narrows it (SELECT reconstruction, among trials that declare efficacy: a median of 464 events for the calibrated Bayesian rule against 612 for the e-value rule, with powers 0.95

Note Discussion questions A sponsor proposes ten Bayesian looks, each stopping for efficacy if \(\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid \text{data}) > 0.975\) , and argues that the posterior “is not affected by looking”. What would you ask for before accepting the design, and what do the numbers in Table 11.1 and Table 11.4 suggest the answer will be? A cardiovascular trial plans an O’Brien-Fleming-type design with looks at 50 and 75 percent of events, and the second look takes place at 68 percent because event accrual was slow. What does a Lan-DeMets design do, what would a fixed-boundary design have to do, and what would you check about why the look moved? The DMC sees a crossing of the efficacy boundary at the first look, with a favorable trend on the primary endpoint and an unfavorable trend on all-cause mortality. Should the boundary be binding? How would the charter have to be written to give the committee the discretion it needs without compromising the type I error? title: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12 Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
text: A group sequential design is a promise made in advance. The protocol states how many looks there will be, at what information fractions, and which boundary applies at each; the type I error is then controlled because the analyst did exactly what the protocol said. Most of the time that is how a trial is run, and Chapter 11 showed that the machinery behind it is sound. But anyone who has sat on a data monitoring committee knows the promise is sometimes hard to keep. A competing trial reports early and the committee wants an extra look. A safety signal prompts an unscheduled unblinded review. The sponsor asks whether enrollment can be extended by 200 patients because the interim estimate is promising but the boundary was not crossed. Each of these is a look the protocol did not plan. For a classical fixed boundary schedule an unplanned look is outside the guarantee, although a spending-function design can accommodate a look whose timing does not depend on the accumulating comparative results. This chapter introduces a family of methods whose guarantee does not depend on the schedule. They are called anytime-valid, and the central object is the e-value: a nonnegative number that can be read as the outcome of a fair bet against the null hypothesis, and that can be updated as data arrive. The idea has

title: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12 Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
text: They are called anytime-valid, and the central object is the e-value: a nonnegative number that can be read as the outcome of a fair bet against the null hypothesis, and that can be updated as data arrive. The idea has a long history (Ville 1939 ( Ville 1939 ) , Wald’s sequential probability ratio test ( Wald 1945 ) , Robbins’s work on boundaries that hold for every sample size ( Robbins 1970 ) ) and a recent revival ( Shafer and Vovk 2019 ; Shafer 2021 ; Vovk and Wang 2021 ) . We follow the treatment of Sokolova and Sokolov ( A. O. Sokolova and Sokolov 2026 ) and the working papers of Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026c , 2026b ) . The chapter has a second purpose. The guarantee has a price in the construction studied here, and the price can be stated in one line: for the normal-mixture e-value, at large information the anytime-valid rule needs approximately \(2\log(1/\alpha)\) more units of squared evidence than a Bayesian rule at posterior odds of one, which at \(\alpha = 0.025\) is 7.38. title: What a group sequential design does not cover
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.1 What a group sequential design does not cover
text: 12.1 What a group sequential design does not cover In Chapter 11 a one-sided test at \(\alpha = 0.025\) was extended to \(K\) planned looks by spending the type I error over information fractions \(t_1 < \dots < t_K\) . The O’Brien-Fleming and Pocock boundaries and the Lan-DeMets spending functions are different ways to do the spending. All of them share three properties. The number and approximate timing of looks are fixed before the data are seen (or the spending function is fixed and the realized looks are allowed to vary within it). The boundary at each look is computed from that plan. And the type I error guarantee is a statement about the plan: if the trial had been run to the plan, the probability of ever crossing a boundary under the null is at most \(\alpha\) . Four situations leave the plan behind. An unplanned look. A Lan-DeMets spending function does accommodate looks at times that were not scheduled, provided the timing is not chosen on the basis of the observed effect. The question is whether the proviso holds: whether the request for the look used accumulating comparative results, and whether the spending or adaptation method remains valid for it. A look triggered by an interim signal in the trial’s own data does not satisfy it. An external publication. A different trial in

title: What a group sequential design does not cover
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.1 What a group sequential design does not cover
text: the look used accumulating comparative results, and whether the spending or adaptation method remains valid for it. A look triggered by an interim signal in the trial’s own data does not satisfy it. An external publication. A different trial in the same disease reads out. The committee wants to know whether the accumulating data are now so convincing that continuing is unethical, or so unpromising that it is pointless. Timing triggered entirely by independent external information need not depend on the trial’s own observed treatment effect, and a Lan-DeMets spending function can accommodate such an additional look; the adaptive-design guidance also discusses acceptable changes based solely on external information. What has to be checked is whether the committee’s request used accumulating comparative results, and whether the method keeps the error controlled if it did. Continuous review. Some DMCs review unblinded safety and efficacy data continuously, or at a frequency far greater than the number of looks in the charter. A boundary designed for four looks says nothing about the 40th. Extending the trial. The sample size was set from an assumed effect. At the interim the estimate is smaller, the trial is not futile, and the sponsor would like to continue to a larger sample. Doing so changes the sampling plan after the data were seen, which is precisely what the E20 and Adaptive Designs

None of this is a criticism of group sequential designs. If the schedule is known and will be kept, a group sequential design is the more powerful choice, and we will see the numbers below. title: The definition
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2.1 The definition
text: The definition An e-value for a null hypothesis \(H_0\) is a nonnegative random variable \(E\) whose expectation under every distribution in \(H_0\) is at most one, \[ \mathbb{E}_{H_0}[E] \le 1 . \] An observed e-value of 20 means that the data have multiplied by 20 an amount of evidence that is fair under the null. The name suggests the natural reading: \(E\) is the payoff of a bet. A gambler stakes one dollar against the null (that is, on the drug working), the null being the claim that the bet is fair. If the null is true, the gambler’s expected wealth afterwards is at most one dollar. If the gambler’s wealth ends at \(E = 20\) , that outcome was an event which, under the null, has probability at most \(1/20\) . This follows from Markov’s inequality, \[ \mathbb{P}_{H_0}(E \ge 1/\alpha) \le \alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{H_0}[E] \le \alpha . \] So the rule “reject \(H_0\) when \(E \ge 1/\alpha\) ” is a level- \(\alpha\) test. At \(\alpha = 0.025\) the threshold is \(E \ge 40\) . A fixed-sample e-value is nothing more than a new way of writing a test. The new thing is what happens when the data keep coming.

title: Test martingales and Ville's inequality
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2.2 Test martingales and Ville's inequality
text: Test martingales and Ville’s inequality Now let data arrive in a sequence, and let \(E_n\) be the gambler’s wealth after \(n\) observations, starting from \(E_0 = 1\) . Suppose each bet is fair under the null: given the past, the expected wealth after the next observation equals the wealth now. A nonnegative process with this property and \(E_0 = 1\) is called a test martingale ( Shafer et al. 2011 ) (if the expected wealth can only fall, it is a test supermartingale, and everything below holds for it too). Ville’s inequality, the mathematical heart of this chapter, says that such a process crosses a high level only rarely, and that this holds for the entire path, \[ \mathbb{P}_{H_0}\Bigl(\sup_{n} E_n \ge 1/\alpha\Bigr) \le \alpha . \] The word to notice is \(\sup\) . For a fixed \(n\) , Markov’s inequality gives the bound at that one time. Ville’s inequality gives the same bound for the supremum over all times, which is the probability that the wealth is ever above \(1/\alpha\) . The gambler is allowed to look at the wealth after every patient, to pause and resume, to stop for any reason, including a reason the protocol never considered, and the probability of ever declaring success under the null is still at most \(\alpha\) . This is what “anytime-valid” means. For likelihood ratios this bound

title: Test martingales and Ville's inequality
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2.2 Test martingales and Ville's inequality
text: and resume, to stop for any reason, including a reason the protocol never considered, and the probability of ever declaring success under the null is still at most \(\alpha\) . This is what “anytime-valid” means. For likelihood ratios this bound is the one Wald used for the error rates of his sequential probability ratio test ( Wald 1945 ) ; Ville’s version ( Ville 1939 ) covers any nonnegative martingale. Note Technical note: why Ville’s inequality holds Let \(T\) be the first time \(E_n \ge 1/\alpha\) (possibly infinite). The stopped process \(E_{n \wedge T}\) is again a nonnegative martingale, so \(\mathbb{E}[E_{n \wedge T}] = 1\) for every \(n\) . On the event \(\{T \le n\}\) the stopped wealth is at least \(1/\alpha\) , and it is nonnegative otherwise, so \[ 1 = \mathbb{E}[E_{n\wedge T}] \ge \frac{1}{\alpha}\,\mathbb{P}(T \le n). \] Hence \(\mathbb{P}(T \le n) \le \alpha\) for every \(n\) , and letting \(n \to \infty\) gives \(\mathbb{P}(T < \infty) \le \alpha\) . The argument is Markov’s inequality applied at the stopping time, with the martingale property supplying the identity \(\mathbb{E}[E_{n \wedge T}] = 1\) . Note what is not used: the distribution of the data, the number of looks, and the reason for stopping. The same argument works for a test supermartingale, for which one has \(\mathbb{E}[E_{n \wedge T}] \le 1\) .

title: A betting martingale for a binary endpoint
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2.3 A betting martingale for a binary endpoint
text: A betting martingale for a binary endpoint Take the two-arm binary trial of Sokolova and Sokolov ( A. O. Sokolova and Sokolov 2026 ) : patients are enrolled in matched pairs, one to treatment and one to control, and for pair \(i\) let \(D_i = Y_{T,i} - Y_{C,i}\) , which equals \(+1\) if only the treated patient responded, \(-1\) if only the control patient responded, and \(0\) otherwise. Under the null that the response probabilities are equal, \(p_T = p_C = p\) for any common value \(p\) , we have \(\mathbb{P}(D = +1) = \mathbb{P}(D = -1)\) , so \(\mathbb{E}[D] = 0\) . Choose a betting fraction \(\lambda \in (0, 1)\) and let \[ E_n = \prod_{i=1}^{n} (1 + \lambda D_i). \] Then \(\mathbb{E}[1 + \lambda D_i] = 1\) under the null whatever \(p\) is, so \(E_n\) is a test martingale for the composite null “the two arms have the same response probability”. The nuisance parameter \(p\) never needs to be estimated. In the book’s companion online lab (module 08, https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/08-e-values.html) the paths of this process under the null and under an alternative can be drawn directly. title: How big a bet? The growth rate
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2.4 How big a bet? The growth rate
text: How big a bet? The growth rate A bet that is fair under the null can still be a good or a bad bet under the alternative. If \(\lambda\) is small, wealth grows slowly; if it is large, the wealth wobbles and can collapse. For the binary design above the expected log-growth per pair under the alternative is \[ g(\lambda) = \mathbb{P}(D = +1)\log(1+\lambda) + \mathbb{P}(D = -1)\log(1-\lambda), \] and the expected number of pairs to reach \(1/\alpha\) is roughly \(\log(1/\alpha)/g(\lambda)\) , which is Wald’s identity from the sequential probability ratio test. In the 45 versus 30 percent design of Sokolova and Sokolov the best fraction is \(\lambda^\ast = 0.312\) with \(g = 0.0238\) nats per pair, giving an expected crossing near 155 pairs ( A. O. Sokolova and Sokolov 2026 ) . The trade-off is sharp: in their simulations a fraction of 0.10 gives power 0.119, 0.31 gives 0.723 and 0.50 gives 0.589 at 200 pairs. This is the e-value analogue of choosing a design effect size, and it has the same protocol implication: the bet is chosen in advance from the effect one hopes to detect, and an unrealistic choice costs power, not validity. The validity holds for every \(\lambda\) .

title: Cornfield and the betting odds of 1966
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.2.5 Cornfield and the betting odds of 1966
text: Cornfield and the betting odds of 1966 The idea is older than the vocabulary. Cornfield ( 1966a , 1969 ) proposed what he called relative betting odds as a sequential stopping criterion: the likelihood ratio of the alternative to the null, accumulated as the data arrive and averaged over a prior on the alternative. His companion argument was that the stopping rule should not change the strength of the evidence ( Cornfield 1966b ) . For a simple null the betting odds are a test martingale in the sense of this chapter, so Ville’s inequality bounds the probability that they ever cross a high level, a guarantee that does not need his argument. His proposal lost to alpha spending for a reason that is not statistical. Betting odds require a declared prior on the alternative, and the reviewer has to accept it. The mixture e-value of this chapter makes the same trade, and the regulatory conversation about registering the prior ( Chapter 3 ) is the modern version of that objection. Shafer and colleagues ( Shafer et al. 2011 ) connect test martingales, Bayes factors and \(p\) -values. Vovk and Wang ( Vovk and Wang 2021 ) develop calibration and combination rules for e-values.

title: Likelihood ratios
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.3.1 Likelihood ratios
text: Likelihood ratios When the null and the alternative are each a single distribution, the likelihood ratio \(\prod_i q(Y_i)/p_0(Y_i)\) is a test martingale: under \(p_0\) the expected ratio of densities is \(\int (q/p_0)p_0 = 1\) . This is Wald’s SPRT statistic, and for a simple alternative it is the best possible bet in the sense of growth. Its limitation is that it requires committing to one alternative. A bet on a hazard ratio of 0.70 pays badly if the truth is 0.90.

title: Mixtures
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.3.2 Mixtures
text: Mixtures The standard remedy is to average over alternatives. If \(L_n(\theta) = \prod_i p_\theta(Y_i)/p_0(Y_i)\) is a likelihood-ratio martingale for each \(\theta\) in the alternative, then for any mixing distribution \(H\) \[ E_n = \int L_n(\theta)\,dH(\theta) \] is again a test martingale, because an average of martingales with unit start is a martingale with unit start. For the Gaussian trial of Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026c ) , let \(X_i \sim N(\theta, 1)\) denote the standardized treatment-minus-control difference for pair \(i\) , \(S_n = \sum_{i\le n} X_i\) , and \(H_0:\theta \le 0\) . Mixing \(\exp(gS_n - ng^2/2)\) over a half-normal distribution for \(g\) with scale \(\rho\) gives, with \(A_n = n + \rho^{-2}\) , the closed form \[ E_n^{+} = \frac{2}{\rho\sqrt{A_n}}\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{S_n^2}{2A_n}\Bigr)\,\Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{A_n}}\Bigr). \tag{12.1}\] For \(\theta < 0\) each integrand is a supermartingale (a martingale at \(\theta = 0\) ), so Ville’s inequality holds for the whole composite null. A mirror process, obtained by replacing \(S_n\) with \(-S_n\) , monitors the opposite one-sided null and can be used for futility. The scale \(\rho\) plays the role of a prior standard deviation on the effect: it states how large an effect the bet is hedged against. It is a design parameter and not a nuisance. In the authors’ sweep the integrated Bayes risk of the e-value rule changes by only a few percent across \(\rho\) from 0.10 to 0.32, so the choice matters less than the choice of threshold.

title: E-processes
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.3.3 E-processes
text: E-processes Not every sequential statistic is a martingale. Often what one has is a process \(E_n\) that is dominated, under every null distribution, by some test martingale: an e-process. The definitions of this section are enough for the trials in this book, and the distinction matters mainly because it allows e-values to be built for composite nulls and with covariates in cases where no exact martingale exists. For the reader the working rule is the same: if \(\sup_n E_n \ge 1/\alpha\) has probability at most \(\alpha\) under every null, the process can be monitored continuously.

title: From e-values to p-values and confidence sequences
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.4 From e-values to p-values and confidence sequences
text: 12.4 From e-values to p-values and confidence sequences A regulator reads a p-value and a confidence interval. An e-process supplies both, in a form that survives continuous monitoring. The always-valid p-value after \(n\) observations is \[ p_n = \min\Bigl(1, \frac{1}{\max_{m\le n} E_m}\Bigr). \] It is nonincreasing in \(n\) , it can only improve as evidence accrues, and \(\mathbb{P}_{H_0}(\inf_n p_n \le \alpha) \le \alpha\) : the probability that the always-valid p-value is ever below \(\alpha\) is at most \(\alpha\) . For a fixed-sample e-value the same relation, \(p = \min(1, 1/E)\) (with \(p = 1\) when \(E = 0\) ), is a valid but conservative p-value by Markov’s inequality, and the conservatism is part of what is paid. A running maximum of 15.3 gives \(p = 0.065\) , a running maximum of 45.8 gives \(0.022\) . These are the numbers from the reanalysis of the Novick and Grizzle ulcer trial in Sokolova and Sokolov ( A. O. Sokolova and Sokolov 2026 ) , where the e-value of surgery A versus B is 15.3 and A versus C is 45.8 (these are the e-values of that paper’s dataset, not computed from the ulcer data table of Chapter 10 , and the patient order is simulated because the original order is not recorded; this is an illustration and not a valid test of that trial). A confidence sequence

title: From e-values to p-values and confidence sequences
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.4 From e-values to p-values and confidence sequences
text: dataset, not computed from the ulcer data table of Chapter 10 , and the patient order is simulated because the original order is not recorded; this is an illustration and not a valid test of that trial). A confidence sequence is the interval analogue. It is a sequence of intervals \(C_n\) such that \(\mathbb{P}(\theta \in C_n \text{ for all } n) \ge 1-\alpha\) , constructed by inverting the e-process over null values, and the idea goes back to the confidence sequences of Darling and Robbins ( Darling and Robbins 1967 ; Robbins 1970 ) , studied further by Lai ( Lai 1976 ) , and its group sequential counterpart in clinical trials is the repeated confidence interval of Jennison and Turnbull ( Jennison and Turnbull 1984 ) . A confidence sequence is wider than a fixed-sample confidence interval at the same \(n\) , and it can be read at any time, including at the time the DMC stopped the trial. The estimation principle in the Adaptive Designs guidance, that estimates be “sufficiently reliable”, is what the confidence sequence is for.

title: The surcharge: what validity at every stopping time costs
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.5 The surcharge: what validity at every stopping time costs
text: 12.5 The surcharge: what validity at every stopping time costs The exact tolls and their derivation are in Chapter 11 ( Equation 11.8 , Table 11.6 ); this section only identifies the construction and the comparison baseline. The e-process rule at level \(\alpha\) is the symmetric normal-mixture Bayes factor with \(b = 1/\alpha\) , with \(q = I_n\tau^2\) : the log of the symmetric normal-mixture e-value is \(\tfrac12\{qZ_n^2/(1+q) - \log(1+q)\}\) , so for a one-sided claim ( \(Z_n > 0\) ) it acts when \(Z_n^2 \ge (1+1/q)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log(1/\alpha)\}\) , which exceeds the Bayes bar at \(b = 1\) by \(2\log(1/\alpha)(1+1/q)\) , approximately \(2\log 40 = 7.38\) at large information. The half-normal mixture of Equation 12.1 has the exact log e-value \(\log 2 + \tfrac12\{qZ_n^2/(1+q) - \log(1+q)\} + \log\Phi\bigl(Z_n\sqrt{q/(1+q)}\bigr)\) ; at large information the correction reduces to \(\log 2\) , which lowers the bar by about \(2\log 2 = 1.39\) . The baseline is the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar (posterior odds of one). The resulting figure of about seventy percent of a conventional trial ( Equation 11.11 ) compares boundary terms asymptotically and is not an exact sample-size identity, and it is a cost of this construction, not of anytime validity in general (iterated-logarithm boundaries ( Robbins 1970 ) behave differently). Calibration narrows it, as the SELECT comparison below shows. The figure is also not a statement that a sponsor who adopts an e-value design will run a trial 70 percent longer than a fixed design: stopping early at a large effect is built into the e-value design.

title: E-values and Bayes factors
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.6 E-values and Bayes factors
text: 12.6 E-values and Bayes factors The mixture e-value ( Equation 12.1 ) looks like a Bayes factor, and it is one: it is the ratio of the marginal likelihood under a half-normal prior on the effect to the likelihood at the null value. The two ideas share their statistic and differ in how the statistic is read. A Bayes factor \(\mathrm{BF}_{10}\) is read as a measure of evidence , on the scale of Jeffreys’s table, or combined with prior odds to give a posterior probability. For a simple null, \(\mathbb{E}_{H_0}[\mathrm{BF}_{10}] = 1\) , so a Bayes factor is an e-value ( Shafer et al. 2011 ; Shafer and Vovk 2019 ) . An e-value is read as a test statistic with a guaranteed error rate : reject when it exceeds \(1/\alpha\) . The calibration is fixed by Markov’s and Ville’s inequalities and does not need a prior. So the same number, say 40, is “strong evidence” on a Jeffreys scale and “a level 0.025 test” on the e-value scale. That is the sense in which the difference is one of calibration and not of statistic. A Bayes factor of 3 is a Bayes factor and an e-value of 3; it supports the alternative, but rejecting at 3 has a frequentist type I error as high as \(1/3\) . The Bayesian reading is not wrong, it

title: E-values and Bayes factors
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.6 E-values and Bayes factors
text: A Bayes factor of 3 is a Bayes factor and an e-value of 3; it supports the alternative, but rejecting at 3 has a frequentist type I error as high as \(1/3\) . The Bayesian reading is not wrong, it answers a different question, and Chapter 7 discussed which. Two caveats. With a composite null, a Bayes factor with a prior on the null parameter is not an e-value in general, because its expectation is only an average under the null prior. And most e-values are not Bayes factors: the betting martingale of the binary trial multiplies \(1 + \lambda D_i\) , which is a likelihood ratio against no particular prior. The e-value framework is wider than Bayes factors, and the Bayes factor is the particular e-value that is calibrated for the prior used to mix it. Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) push the observation further. Their theory companion shows that the loss-optimal rejection boundary on the standardized scale grows like \(\sqrt{\log n}\) (the moderate deviation scale), that the \(1/\alpha\) rule is a fixed worst-case bound on a different (large deviation) scale, and that the Bayes factor is the e-variable calibrated at the first of these. The practical content is the next section: the statistic can be the same and the threshold different, and the threshold is where most of the

title: Power and stopping time: e-value, Bayesian and group sequential designs

text: 12.7 Power and stopping time: e-value, Bayesian and group sequential designs There are two comparisons, one on a binary endpoint ( A. O. Sokolova and Sokolov 2026 ) and one on a time-to-event endpoint that reconstructs the SELECT trial of semaglutide ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) . They produce different power orderings, and the difference is instructive. For SELECT there is one set of numbers in this book, those of the full reconstruction in Table 12.2 .

title: Time-to-event design: the SELECT reconstruction
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.7.2 Time-to-event design: the SELECT reconstruction
text: Time-to-event design: the SELECT reconstruction Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) reconstruct SELECT, the cardiovascular outcomes trial of semaglutide ( Lincoff et al. 2023 ) , as a counterfactual: a Gaussian approximation in event time with a true hazard ratio held at the observed 0.80 (SELECT itself was designed for 0.83, at 90% power, with 1,225 planned events and one superiority interim at two thirds of them ( Ryan et al. 2020 ) ), a normal prior of scale \(\tau = 0.25\) on the log hazard ratio, and a trial that ends at 1,270 events. Three rules are compared at a nominal 2.5 percent type I error under their own monitoring (the O’Brien-Fleming boundary and the Bayesian threshold are calibrated to it, and the e-value rule is bounded by it through Ville’s inequality, with a lower realized rate): a four-look O’Brien-Fleming design at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of the events; the e-value mixture (the symmetric normal mixture, whose bar exceeds the Bayes bar by about the surcharge \(2\log 40 = 7.38\) ), continuous, \(E \ge 40\) ; and the continuous Bayesian posterior rule with a threshold raised until the type I error is 2.5 percent. title: Why the orderings differ
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.7.3 Why the orderings differ
text: Why the orderings differ The two comparisons give power orderings that appear to contradict each other. In the SELECT-like trial the calibrated Bayesian rule has more power than the e-value rule (94.7 against 83.1 percent in Table 12.2 ). In the binary trial it has less (68.8 against 72.3 percent). Both can hold, and the following are the plausible contributors, which neither Sokolova and Sokolov nor Polson and Sokolov isolates. Prior scale relative to the effect. In SELECT the effect (a hazard ratio of 0.80) is of a plausible size relative to a prior with \(\tau = 0.25\) , so the calibrated Bayesian bar (the \(Z\) bar implied by \(p^\ast\) , which is above the uncalibrated \(\sqrt{L_n}\) ) is low relative to the realized \(Z_n\) (about 4 at the end). In the binary design the effect is modest relative to the information, and the Bayes bar is not much below the e-value bar. Conservatism of the e-value. The e-value rule’s realized type I error is 0.58 percent in the SELECT design and 1.2 percent in the binary design, against a nominal 2.5. Some of the lost power is spent on that unused budget, and the amount depends on the design. The endpoint. Time-to-event data accumulate on an information scale where \(L_n\) is modest ( \(3.0\) at 1,270 events with \(\tau = 0.25\) ) and slowly

title: Why the orderings differ
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.7.3 Why the orderings differ
text: lost power is spent on that unused budget, and the amount depends on the design. The endpoint. Time-to-event data accumulate on an information scale where \(L_n\) is modest ( \(3.0\) at 1,270 events with \(\tau = 0.25\) ) and slowly growing, while the binary trial is small and its likelihood ratio has a different shape. Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) conclude that the robust finding across both studies concerns stopping time, not power, and that the direction of the power difference should be checked for the design at hand. We agree. In the language of Chapter 14 , this is a statement that the operating characteristics have to be simulated for the specific design, and no theory replaces that report.

title: What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.8 What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
text: 12.8 What a Bayes-risk comparison adds The comparison so far is by type I error, power and stopping time, which are the currency of regulators. A different comparison asks what each rule costs in patients, and the working paper of Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026c ) makes it for a stylized mortality-type problem. Each pair is \(N(\theta, 1)\) with a prior \(\theta \sim N(0, 0.15^2)\) , at most 1,000 pairs, a post-trial population of \(M = 20{,}000\) patients, and a loss equal to \(M|\theta|\) if the wrong terminal decision is made, plus \(|\theta|\) per enrolled pair. The effect \(\theta\) is a standardized effect, which is not an absolute mortality-risk difference, so the losses below are in illustrative loss units, not literal deaths; reading them as deaths would need a mortality scale and a conversion from the standardized effect. Relative reductions within the stipulated loss model are meaningful as they stand. The Bayes-optimal rule is computed by backward induction on the sufficient statistic \((n, S_n)\) ( Chapter 15 ). The e-value rule is \(E_n^{+} \ge 40\) with the mirror process for futility. We report their numbers, which we have not re-run. Neither rule dominates. The risk functions cross. For marginally harmful treatments ( \(\theta \in [-0.05, -0.015]\) ) the e-value rule has the lower expected loss, because its bar of 40 almost never

title: What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.8 What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
text: report their numbers, which we have not re-run. Neither rule dominates. The risk functions cross. For marginally harmful treatments ( \(\theta \in [-0.05, -0.015]\) ) the e-value rule has the lower expected loss, because its bar of 40 almost never approves a harmful drug (approval probability at most 0.006, against 0.333 for the Bayes rule at \(\theta = -0.015\) ). For beneficial treatments the Bayes rule is far better: at \(\theta = 0.07\) the e-value rule approves 32.7 percent of the time against 98.2 percent, runs on average 849 pairs against 412, and has an expected loss of 1,001 against 55 loss units. The e-value rule is underpowered for effects of that size in a trial of 1,000 pairs. Integrated Bayes risk. Averaged over the prior, the Bayes rule has an expected loss of 53.4 loss units and the e-value rule 237.6, a reduction of 77.5 percent (Monte Carlo standard errors 1.0 and 3.1). The reduction stays between 71 and 82 percent for horizons from 500 to 2,000 pairs, and widens as the stakes rise: 73.1 percent at \(M = 10^4\) and 84.4 percent at \(M = 10^5\) . This is by construction, since the Bayes rule minimizes this criterion. It does not say that the Bayes rule is better by the criterion of a regulator. Where the gap comes from. The gap decomposes into

title: What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.8 What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
text: \(M = 10^5\) . This is by construction, since the Bayes rule minimizes this criterion. It does not say that the Bayes rule is better by the criterion of a regulator. Where the gap comes from. The gap decomposes into two parts. A rule that monitors the same e-process but stops at the loss-optimal threshold ( \(E^{+} \ge 3.5\) ) instead of \(E^{+} \ge 40\) has Bayes risk 118.3, so recalibrating the threshold closes 119.3 of the 184.2 loss-unit gap (64.8 percent), and the remaining 35.2 percent is the value of the sampling-cost-aware continuation region. In the words of the authors, the e-process statistic is sound; it is the \(1/\alpha\) calibration that carries most of the loss. A caveat on the hybrid rule. The working paper recommends the loss-tuned rule as a default for a sponsor unwilling to give up validity. That recommendation needs care. By Ville’s inequality a threshold of 3.5 bounds the type I error by \(1/3.5 \approx 0.29\) , so the tuned rule does not keep the 2.5 percent guarantee at its tuned threshold; what it keeps is the validity of the always-valid p-value computed from the same process, which can still be reported even if the trial is stopped on a different, loss-based criterion. A rule that keeps both the 2.5 percent guarantee and the loss-based stopping is the open problem

title: What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.8 What a Bayes-risk comparison adds
text: always-valid p-value computed from the same process, which can still be reported even if the trial is stopped on a different, loss-based criterion. A rule that keeps both the 2.5 percent guarantee and the loss-based stopping is the open problem the authors identify: a monitoring rule that is anytime-valid and calibrated to the moderate deviation scale at its realized stopping time. The same paper makes a large-scale comparison, e-BH against empirical Bayes in 2,000 simultaneous tests with 5 percent signals: the e-BH procedure has a false discovery rate of 0.002 and power 0.174, while an empirical-Bayes rule that targets an FDR of 0.10 has FDR 0.098 and power 0.317. It is not a trial-level comparison and we note it only as a statement of the same pattern, robustness paid for in efficiency (see Chapter 10 for the multiplicity machinery the reader will meet in a trial).

title: When should a sponsor pay the surcharge?
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.9 When should a sponsor pay the surcharge?
text: 12.9 When should a sponsor pay the surcharge? The design question is not Bayesian against frequentist in the abstract, but whether the trial needs validity at stopping times the protocol cannot anticipate ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) . If it does, the surcharge \(2\log(1/\alpha)\) is the price, worth about seventy percent of a conventional trial by Equation 11.11 against the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar (the realized gap to a calibrated Bayesian rule is smaller, 612 against 464 events among SELECT-reconstruction trials that declare efficacy), and it belongs in the sample size justification as an explicit line and not as a footnote about anytime validity. The advice of Polson and Sokolov is to itemize the toll before choosing the paradigm. A practical test has five questions. Is the monitoring schedule under the sponsor’s control and will it be kept? If the DMC charter fixes the looks and the committee will not deviate, a classical group sequential design is the more powerful choice (86 against 72 percent in the binary example), and the sponsor should not pay the surcharge. Is a continuously monitored or open-ended decision part of the design? Platform trials with continuous or frequent interim reviews, adaptive enrichment with open-ended expansion, and trials whose end is defined by a data-driven event are the natural cases for an anytime-valid design. In Chapter 20 the reader will

title: When should a sponsor pay the surcharge?
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.9 When should a sponsor pay the surcharge?
text: of the design? Platform trials with continuous or frequent interim reviews, adaptive enrichment with open-ended expansion, and trials whose end is defined by a data-driven event are the natural cases for an anytime-valid design. In Chapter 20 the reader will see that arm-level decisions in a platform repeat the same question many times. Can the sponsor foresee the plausible unplanned looks? If an external readout, a safety review or an extension is likely, a classical design can, in part, accommodate it by pre-specification (a spending function, a pre-specified sample size re-estimation). If the sponsor cannot enumerate them, the e-value design is insurance. Is there a reason to expect off-schedule looks that the protocol cannot list? An e-process protects against optional stopping, whatever the schedule, under its assumptions. It does not repair bias from unblinding, altered endpoint assessment, selective data collection or invalid model changes, so confidentiality and conduct safeguards are as necessary for an e-process design as for a group sequential one. A sponsor whose DMC has a history of ad hoc looks may still judge that a guarantee that does not depend on the look schedule is worth the price. Can the sponsor live with the power cost? The cost is real. In the binary example the e-value rule lost 14 points of power to a group sequential design that knew its schedule, and

title: When should a sponsor pay the surcharge?
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.9 When should a sponsor pay the surcharge?
text: look schedule is worth the price. Can the sponsor live with the power cost? The cost is real. In the binary example the e-value rule lost 14 points of power to a group sequential design that knew its schedule, and in the Bayes-risk comparison the e-value rule is far behind for modest effects. Restoring it means a larger horizon or a better process while keeping the efficacy threshold at 40. A loss-based stopping decision, such as the threshold of 3.5 in the Bayes-risk comparison, does not itself establish efficacy at 0.025, and reporting the e-process p-value beside it does not restore that guarantee for the decision. If the answers to the first and third questions are yes, do not pay. If the answers to the second and fourth are yes, pay and say so in the sample size section. If the answers are mixed, the middle route is a protocol that keeps a group sequential or Bayesian design as the primary analysis, with an e-process monitored in parallel as an always-valid ledger. Sokolova and Sokolov suggest exactly that: run the e-process alongside a Bayesian rule and report the e-value, its always-valid p-value and a confidence sequence as a frequentist evidential record of the trial ( A. O. Sokolova and Sokolov 2026 ) . The primary analysis is not displaced, and the ledger answers the inevitable

title: When should a sponsor pay the surcharge?

text: and report the e-value, its always-valid p-value and a confidence sequence as a frequentist evidential record of the trial ( A. O. Sokolova and Sokolov 2026 ) . There is also a Bayesian answer to optional stopping that does not concede the point: posterior and predictive probabilities condition on the data actually observed, so a Bayesian analysis is coherent regardless of when or why the data were examined, and the stopping rule does not enter the posterior ( A. Sokolova, Sokolov, and Polson 2026 ) . That is true of the posterior. It is not true of a decision rule that has been calibrated to type I error under a stated monitoring scheme, which is the route this book takes as its default for confirmatory designs without borrowing (one of the routes the FDA draft describes), and the calibration is the part that does not survive a deviation. The Bayesian rule of the SELECT comparison holds 2.5 percent under the scheme it was calibrated to and some other number under another scheme. The two paradigms make different promises, and the comparison of the SELECT table is a comparison under the Bayesian’s assumptions. The e-value rule trades some of the efficiency for a promise that does not need that

title: Many subgroups at once: a negative result for the mixture e-value
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.9.1 Many subgroups at once: a negative result for the mixture e-value
text: Many subgroups at once: a negative result for the mixture e-value An e-value looks attractive when the analysis choices cannot be enumerated, as in the garden of forking paths of Section 10.3 , because a mixture over a prespecified family of \(K\) candidate analyses is a valid e-value for the global null that all candidate subgroup effects are nonpositive. Rejecting it does not establish efficacy in a selected subgroup, and subgroup-specific claims need an appropriate multiplicity procedure. When \(K\) is known, declared and fixed, the comparison is with the Sidak-corrected maximum, and the answer is mixed. We simulate \(K = 20\) standardized statistics with equicorrelation \(\varrho\) , and compare the naive rule (report the largest, test at 0.025), the Sidak maximum, and the equal-weight mixture e-value \(\bar e = K^{-1} \sum_k 2(1+\lambda^2)^{-1/2} \exp\{\lambda^2 Z_k^2 / (2(1+\lambda^2))\}\,\mathbb{1}\{Z_k > 0\}\) with \(\lambda^2 = 9\) at the threshold \(1/\alpha\) . The indicator makes the mixture a positive-direction (one-sided) e-value, so that the maximum and the mixture test the same alternative, a positive effect in at least one subgroup; the squared symmetric form would also spend power on negative effects. Power is compared at thresholds recalibrated to realized size 0.025. Show the R code mk <- bayestrials :: decide_max_of_k_sim ( K = 20 , nsim = 2e5 , seed = 7 , direction = "positive" ) sz <- mk

The mixture e-value at its nominal threshold is very conservative, with realized size at most 0.0012 against a nominal 0.025, because Markov’s inequality is loose for a single look. Recalibrating to matched size removes that penalty. With no correlation and several true effects the positive-direction mixture is at least as powerful as Sidak (0.80 against 0.69 for five effects at \(\varrho = 0\) ), because it pools evidence across the true effects, while for a single effect the two tie (0.51 against 0.51). Under correlation \(\varrho = 0.5\) the maximum wins in every scenario, by 0.05 to 0.12. The reading is therefore narrow: the mixture is competitive when several subgroups carry effects and the statistics are nearly independent, and loses when they are correlated. title: Many subgroups at once: a negative result for the mixture e-value
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.9.1 Many subgroups at once: a negative result for the mixture e-value
text: competitive when several subgroups carry effects and the statistics are nearly independent, and loses when they are correlated. What this licenses is limited. It does not say mixture e-values dominate multiplicity corrections, nor that they are dominated, and the simulation covers one fixed look at known \(K\) and a few configurations. The mixture displayed here is a fixed-look e-value: it has no time index and no prespecified construction for further analyses, so its guarantee holds at the single look at which it is computed. Applying its constant threshold repeatedly to standardized cumulative data would cross under the null with probability one eventually. Validity under continued monitoring, or continuation into a second cohort, would need component e-processes with prespecified weights and a proof of their joint monitoring guarantee, which is not shown here. The Sidak guarantee also needs \(K\) declared and fixed. The guarantee is never free, and what a mixture buys beyond the maximum is a way to weight prespecified analyses, not an answer to unlisted ones.

title: What the regulator will ask
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.10 What the regulator will ask
text: 12.10 What the regulator will ask No guidance names e-values, so the sponsor is arguing from principle. The principle is available and it is the one the Adaptive Designs guidance and E20 state: the chance of erroneous conclusions should be adequately controlled, the design should be completely prespecified, and the trial’s integrity should be maintained. An e-value design satisfies the first under its assumptions: the type I error is at most \(\alpha\) for every stopping time, which is stronger than the guidance asks. That protection is against optional stopping; it does not repair bias from unblinding, altered endpoint assessment, selective data collection or invalid model changes. It satisfies the second in a particular way: what is prespecified is the e-process, the mixing distribution (or betting fraction), the threshold and the horizon, and not the look schedule. On the third, it removes the statistical consequence of an off-schedule look but not the need for the same confidentiality and conduct safeguards that a group sequential design requires. What will not be familiar to the reviewer is the machinery, so the submission has to carry what a standard SAP would not: a statement of the null hypothesis as a composite null for which the process is a test supermartingale, the proof (or a reference) that the process is one, the choice of \(\rho\) or \(\lambda\) with its justification

text: SAP would not: a statement of the null hypothesis as a composite null for which the process is a test supermartingale, the proof (or a reference) that the process is one, the choice of \(\rho\) or \(\lambda\) with its justification from the target effect, a simulation report showing type I error and power over the scenarios of interest (the same report as Chapter 14 , with the difference that the type I error is expected to be below nominal and the report should say by how much), and the always-valid p-value and confidence sequence in the format of the CSR. The FDA’s CID paired meeting program and the Type B and C meetings described in Chapter 3 are the forum. A sponsor should also expect the question “why not a spending function?”, and the answer is the five-question test above, not a general preference. The null hypothesis is rejected, and the trial may stop for efficacy, at the first interim review at which \(E_n^{+} \ge 40\) .

title: In practice
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.11 In practice
text: 12.11 In practice No trial has yet been run on an e-process as its primary analysis, and no regulator has said anything about the method. What real trials do offer is the situation the chapter is about: a monitoring schedule that was fixed in advance, and the question of what would have happened had it not been.

title: BNT162b2: several interim looks on a schedule fixed in the SAP
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > 12.11.1 BNT162b2: several interim looks on a schedule fixed in the SAP
text: BNT162b2: several interim looks on a schedule fixed in the SAP The phase 3 trial of the Pfizer and BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine (Protocol C4591001, NCT04368728) is a clear example of a Bayesian design with several interim looks, prespecified before the relevant unblinded analyses ( Pfizer Inc. 2022 ) . The linked document is a later amended version of the SAP (version 10, dated 7 October 2022), so it documents the rules but does not by itself establish their chronology. The model, prior, thresholds and the clinical result are in Section 21.5 , and the worked posterior computation is in Chapter 6 . What matters here is the schedule: the final analysis was planned at 164 primary cases, with interim looks planned at 32, 62, 92 and 120 cases and posterior thresholds of 0.995 at an interim analysis and 0.986 at the final one, calibrated to an overall one-sided type I error of 2.5 percent. According to the SAP the look at 32 cases was not performed; the remaining three looks and the thresholds were unchanged, and the SAP states that the overall type I error stays at 0.025. The lesson for this chapter is about what the design needed and what it did not. The number of looks and the threshold at each were fixed before the first case, so the group sequential-type guarantee held

The number of looks and the threshold at each were fixed before the first case, so the group sequential-type guarantee held and a method that is valid at every stopping time was not needed; a sponsor in this position should not pay the surcharge. The case supports prespecified decision rules. It does not show that an unlisted case count necessarily breaks validity: FDA’s statistical review (section 6.1.9) reports that the first interim analysis actually performed was at 94 cases and the final analysis at 170, not at exactly the listed 92 and 164, which is the ordinary operational overrun between a planned trigger and the realized data cut. Distinguishing planned triggers from exact analysis counts matters: whether an analysis at a realized count differing from the plan stays within the type I error guarantee depends on whether the thresholds were defined on the planned counts or adjusted to the realized information, and that is a rule the SAP must state. The thresholds of 0.995 and 0.986 are a bar calibrated for the planned looks (four interim looks plus the final analysis), and the SAP’s own handling of the dropped first look (the thresholds were kept) can only lower the type I error, since removing a look

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > Key points
text: Key points A classical group sequential design controls the type I error as a property of its plan. Unplanned looks that depend on the accumulating comparative results, data-dependent looks under a fixed boundary schedule, continuous DMC review and extensions of the trial are outside that plan, while independent external triggers such as a publication can be accommodated if the monitoring rule is valid at arbitrary times, as an e-value rule is. For each the question is whether the request used accumulating comparative results and whether the spending or adaptation method remains valid. An e-value is a nonnegative statistic with expectation at most one under the null. A test martingale is a nonnegative process starting at one whose next value has conditional expectation equal to its current value under every null distribution (replacing equality by an upper bound gives a test supermartingale), and Ville’s inequality bounds the probability that it ever exceeds \(1/\alpha\) by \(\alpha\) , for every stopping time. Likelihood ratios and mixtures of them are test martingales. The always-valid p-value is \(1/\max E_m\) and a confidence sequence is the matching interval. The same statistic is a Bayes factor (read as evidence) or an e-value (read with the threshold \(1/\alpha\) as a level- \(\alpha\) test). The difference is calibration, not statistic. For the normal-mixture e-value, the approximate price of validity at every stopping time is

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 12: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values > Key points
text: is a Bayes factor (read as evidence) or an e-value (read with the threshold \(1/\alpha\) as a level- \(\alpha\) test). The difference is calibration, not statistic. For the normal-mixture e-value, the approximate price of validity at every stopping time is the surcharge \(2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38\) in squared standardized evidence (exactly \(7.38(1+1/q)\) ), about 70 percent of a conventional trial against the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar, as a comparison of boundary terms; it is not a universal cost of anytime validity. Calibration narrows it (SELECT reconstruction, among trials that declare efficacy: 464 events for the calibrated Bayesian rule, 612 for the e-value rule). The Bayes-factor bar is itself above a single unadjusted look once \(I_n\tau^2 > 46\) asymptotically. The orderings are design-dependent: group sequential with a known schedule has the most power at full information; the calibrated Bayesian rule stops first; the e-value rule is conservative. The power ordering of Bayes and e-value reversed between the two studies’ designs, and the stopping-time ordering did not. No FDA or ICH guidance names e-values as of November 2026. The argument is the type I error control principle of the Adaptive Designs guidance and E20, made in a CID-type interaction. title: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13 Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring
text: Efficacy questions arrive one at a time and are asked of a trial built to answer them. Safety questions arrive by the thousand, are asked of data collected for another purpose, and are answered too late if they wait for statistical significance. A trial is sized for its efficacy endpoint, so the rare adverse event that matters most is usually the one the trial is least able to detect. After approval the same drug is taken by millions of people, and the signal arrives as a trickle of spontaneous reports. This asymmetry makes safety the part of drug evaluation where continuous, cumulative reasoning is most natural, and where Bayesian shrinkage has been in routine regulatory use the longest. The chapter has four parts. The first is the case that defined the field, the withdrawal of rofecoxib, read as a cumulative analysis with a traditional and a Bayesian account of what could have been said, and when. The second compares two ways of monitoring continuously, the posterior probability and the Bayes factor read as an e-value, and connects to Chapter 12 . The third is the empirical Bayes shrinkage used to screen spontaneous reports. The fourth is the monitoring of toxicity inside a trial, with a Bayesian stopping boundary, its exact operating characteristics, and a Pocock-type repeated test as the traditional counterpart. The lifecycle setting is

title: Rofecoxib: a cumulative signal
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.1 Rofecoxib: a cumulative signal
text: 13.1 Rofecoxib: a cumulative signal Rofecoxib, sold as Vioxx, was a selective inhibitor of cyclooxygenase 2 approved in 1999 for arthritis and pain. It was designed to relieve pain with less gastrointestinal bleeding than traditional nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and it was prescribed to tens of millions of patients. The VIGOR trial randomized 8076 patients with rheumatoid arthritis to rofecoxib 50 mg daily or naproxen 500 mg twice daily. It did show fewer confirmed upper gastrointestinal events on rofecoxib (2.1 against 4.5 per 100 patient-years), but myocardial infarction was reported in 0.4 percent of the rofecoxib patients and 0.1 percent of the naproxen patients, roughly a fourfold difference ( Bombardier et al. 2000 ) . The difference was attributed at the time to a protective effect of naproxen, not to harm from rofecoxib. A 2005 editorial expression of concern from the journal concerned cardiovascular events that had not been reported in the published paper ( Curfman, Morrissey, and Drazen 2005 ) . Merck withdrew the drug on 30 September 2004, after the placebo-controlled APPROVe trial in 2586 patients with a history of colorectal adenoma showed confirmed thrombotic events in 46 of 1287 rofecoxib patients (1.50 per 100 patient-years) against 26 of 1299 on placebo (0.78 per 100 patient-years), a rate ratio of 1.92 (95% CI 1.19 to 3.11), with the curves separating after about 18 months ( Bresalier et al. 2005 ) .

title: What the traditional analysis said
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.1.1 What the traditional analysis said
text: What the traditional analysis said Later in 2004, Jüni and colleagues published a cumulative meta-analysis of the randomized trials, adding one trial at a time in the order of completion ( Jüni et al. 2004 ) . By the end of 2000 the trials had accumulated 52 myocardial infarctions among 20,742 patients, with a pooled relative risk of 2.30 (95% CI 1.22 to 4.33, \(p = 0.010\) ). A year later, with 64 events among 21,432 patients, it was 2.24 (1.24 to 4.02, \(p = 0.007\) ). The relative risk was tested for heterogeneity by type of control group ( \(p = 0.41\) ) and by duration of treatment ( \(p = 0.82\) ). Neither test detected heterogeneity. Observational studies put the cardioprotective effect of naproxen at a relative risk of 0.86 (0.75 to 0.99), far too small to explain VIGOR. The authors concluded that the drug should have been withdrawn several years earlier. The traditional reading is a significance test applied to a pooled estimate: by the end of 2000 the interval excluded 1. This is a fair account of the evidence, and it is the account a regulator can defend. Its weakness for decision making is in what it leaves out. A \(p\) -value of 0.010 does not say how large the harm probably was, how probable a harm of clinical importance was, or what to do while the evidence was still accumulating.

title: What a Bayesian reading adds

title: From inference to decision
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.1.3 From inference to decision
text: From inference to decision The posterior probability does not by itself say what to do. The decision turns on the size of the risk and on what the drug offered in return. Let the baseline risk of myocardial infarction in the arthritis population be \(r_0\) per year, let rofecoxib multiply it by \(RR\) , and let the gastrointestinal benefit relative to a traditional NSAID be a reduction of \(g\) serious bleeding events per patient-year, each with a disutility \(d_G\) relative to the disutility \(d_M\) of a myocardial infarction. Rofecoxib is preferred for a patient when \[ g\, d_G > r_0 (\mathbb{E}[RR] - 1)\, d_M. \tag{13.1}\] Whether the inequality holds depends on inputs this book does not supply from sources: the baseline risk \(r_0\) , the gastrointestinal benefit \(g\) against the relevant comparator (a traditional NSAID with or without a proton pump inhibitor changes \(g\) ), and the disutilities. For a patient at high risk of bleeding and low cardiovascular risk it may hold; for others it may not, and the answer should be shown over a range of inputs (Exercise 2 gives one). What the cumulative evidence supplies is the term \(\mathbb{E}[RR]\) . Under every prior in Table 13.1 the posterior mean at the end of 2000 is at least 1.28, so the right-hand side was positive and not small, and a patient-level benefit-risk analysis of the kind above was warranted well before the withdrawal. This is a book-level illustration with stated inputs, not a regulatory benefit-risk analysis, which would use the full evidence on both sides and patient-level risk.

title: The naproxen hypothesis as a model comparison
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.1.4 The naproxen hypothesis as a model comparison
text: The naproxen hypothesis as a model comparison The two explanations of VIGOR, harm from rofecoxib or protection from naproxen, are competing models, and Bayesian model comparison asks how well each predicts all the data. The naproxen model predicts an elevated relative risk only against naproxen; the harm model predicts it against every comparator, including placebo. Jüni and colleagues found no evidence that the relative risk differed by control group. We have not computed the Bayes factor between the two models, which would need the trial-level data, but its direction is clear: every placebo-controlled trial that showed a raised rate counted for harm and nothing for protection by naproxen. A frequentist analysis can compare comparator-specific effects with a meta-regression or an interaction test, as Jüni and colleagues did, and a significant interaction would favor the naproxen explanation. What posterior model probabilities add is a weight for each explanation that accounts for how well each predicts all the data at once, including the penalty for the flexibility of the rival, where a nonsignificant interaction test only fails to reject one of them. Explaining away an unwelcome signal with a plausible rival is how safety signals are most often lost, and writing the rival down as a model with its own predictions is the remedy.

title: Monitoring continuously: posterior probability and e-value
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.2 Monitoring continuously: posterior probability and e-value
text: 13.2 Monitoring continuously: posterior probability and e-value A safety monitor looks at the data whenever it changes. A test applied at each look inflates the false alarm rate with the number of looks ( Section 12.1 ), and group sequential boundaries ( Chapter 11 ) presume a schedule and a maximum sample size that pharmacovigilance does not have. Two statistics survive continuous looking, and they answer different questions. The first is the posterior probability. It is coherent under any stopping rule, because the likelihood principle holds: the posterior after a hundred looks is the posterior after the last one, however the looks were chosen. Its frequentist false alarm rate is not controlled, and Chapter 12 says why that matters when the regulator’s question is about error under the null. The second is the Bayes factor read as an e-value ( Section 12.6 ). The Bayes factor of an alternative against \(RR = 1\) , computed with a fixed prior under the alternative, is a nonnegative martingale under the null, so Ville’s inequality ( Ville 1939 ) gives \[ \Pr\left(\sup_t \mathrm{BF}_t \geq 1/\alpha \mid RR = 1\right) \leq \alpha. \tag{13.2}\] Safety monitoring asks about harm, so the null is \(RR \leq 1\) and the alternative is a harmful relative risk. Take the alternative \(\log RR \sim N(0, 0.5^2)\) restricted to positive values, with density \(2N(\theta; 0,

Take the alternative \(\log RR \sim N(0, 0.5^2)\) restricted to positive values, with density \(2N(\theta; 0, 0.5^2)\) on \(\theta > 0\) . The likelihood ratio of any single \(\theta > 0\) against \(\theta = 0\) has expectation at most one under every \(\theta \leq 0\) , so the mixture is an e-value for the whole composite null and Equation 13.2 holds for it. (A two-sided Bayes factor with the unrestricted \(N(0, 0.5^2)\) alternative also alarms when the risk is protective, so its bound is for the wrong null.) Acting when the harm-only Bayes factor first reaches twenty gives a false alarm probability below 5 percent however often one looks. For rofecoxib at the end of 2000, with posterior mean \(m\) and variance \(v\) of \(\log RR\) under the \(N(0, 0.5^2)\) prior, \[ \mathrm{BF} = 2\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{m}{\sqrt{v}}\right)\frac{N(0.833;\, 0,\, 0.323^2 + 0.5^2)}{N(0.833;\, 0,\, 0.323^2)} = 11.2, \] where the second ratio is the two-sided Bayes factor 5.7. The value is substantial but short of the anytime-valid threshold of 20. The conclusion is different from the one a posterior probability gives, and not contradictory. title: Signals in spontaneous reports
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.3 Signals in spontaneous reports
text: 13.3 Signals in spontaneous reports Most rare adverse effects are first noticed in spontaneous reports, not in trials. The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and the WHO’s VigiBase together hold tens of millions of reports. The data are a large sparse table of counts \(n_{ij}\) of reports that mention drug \(i\) and event \(j\) , with an expected count \(E_{ij}\) computed from the margins under independence. Reports come from two streams, voluntary submissions by clinicians and patients and mandatory reports from manufacturers, but neither gives exposure denominators and ascertainment is incomplete, so the table cannot give incidence; it can only say which pairs are reported more than the margins predict ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) . That is disproportionality.

title: The traditional measure
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.3.1 The traditional measure
text: The traditional measure The simplest statistics are the relative reporting ratio \(n_{ij}/E_{ij}\) and its cousins, the proportional reporting ratio ( Evans, Waller, and Davis 2001 ) and the reporting odds ratio ( Puijenbroek et al. 2002 ; Rothman, Lanes, and Sacks 2004 ) , with a confidence interval and a screening rule. Evans and colleagues ( Evans, Waller, and Davis 2001 ) flagged a pair when the proportional reporting ratio is at least 2, the chi-square statistic at least 4 and there are at least three reports, and a common variant asks for a lower confidence bound above 1 with at least three reports. They are simple, transparent and still used, and the EMA guideline names them ( European Medicines Agency 2017 ) . Their weakness is at the sparse end. For a rare pair the ratio is dominated by noise: one report against an expected count of 0.05 gives a ratio of twenty, and a table with millions of cells will contain many such pairs by chance alone.

title: The gamma-Poisson shrinker
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.3.2 The gamma-Poisson shrinker
text: The gamma-Poisson shrinker DuMouchel proposed the gamma-Poisson shrinker, the empirical Bayes method behind the FDA’s data mining of its reports database ( DuMouchel 1999 ; Szarfman, Machado, and O’Neill 2002 ) . Each pair has a true reporting ratio \(\lambda_{ij}\) , with \(n_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{ij} E_{ij})\) , and the \(\lambda_{ij}\) are drawn from a mixture of two gamma distributions, \[ \lambda \sim P\, \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_1, \beta_1) + (1 - P)\, \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_2, \beta_2), \tag{13.3}\] whose five parameters are estimated from the whole table by maximum marginal likelihood. The marginal distribution of \(n\) given \(E\) under each component is negative binomial, and the posterior of \(\lambda\) is again a two-component gamma mixture: component \(k\) becomes \(\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_k + n, \beta_k + E)\) , with weights proportional to the prior weight times the negative binomial likelihood. Signals are ranked by the empirical Bayes geometric mean, \(\mathrm{EBGM} = \exp(\mathbb{E}[\log \lambda \mid n])\) , and screened on its fifth percentile, EB05. The other main Bayesian disproportionality tool is the information component of the Bayesian confidence propagation neural network, which underlies the WHO’s VigiBase screening ( Bate et al. 1998 ) , and Madigan and colleagues ( Madigan et al. 2011 ) and Zorych and colleagues ( Zorych et al. 2013 ) extend Bayesian pharmacovigilance to longitudinal databases. Berry and Berry apply the hierarchical idea one level up, borrowing strength across adverse event categories within a trial, which is the within-trial version of the same remedy for multiplicity ( Berry and Berry 2004 ) . Two cautions belong with any use of the method. A high EB05 is a hypothesis for clinical and pharmacoepidemiologic assessment, not evidence of causation, since reporting is influenced by publicity, indication and the reporter (EMA says this in the guideline). And the Bayesian machinery protects against noise in rare cells, not against bias in the reporting mechanism. Neither the expected count nor the shrinkage can correct for a cause of reporting that is not in the margins.

title: Toxicity monitoring inside a trial
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.4 Toxicity monitoring inside a trial
text: 13.4 Toxicity monitoring inside a trial The rofecoxib analysis is retrospective and the shrinker is post-market. Inside a trial the question is prospective: given a toxicity that the protocol defines, when should enrollment pause? This is the case in which the Bayesian rule is simple, and in which it has a precise traditional counterpart.

title: The traditional counterpart
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.4.1 The traditional counterpart
text: The traditional counterpart The traditional trial would apply a repeated exact binomial test of \(H_0: q \le \bar q\) after every five patients, up to 40, where \(\bar q = 0.2\) is the acceptable toxicity rate. A Pocock-type version uses the same nominal level \(a\) at every look: pause at look \(n\) if \(\Pr(X_n \ge x \mid \bar q) \le a\) ( Pocock 1977 gives the normal-theory version for efficacy) . The nominal level is then chosen so that the probability of ever stopping at \(q = \bar q\) is a stated overall level. We use two calibrations. The first matches the overall stopping probability at \(q = \bar q\) of the Bayesian rule introduced next, and the second uses a conventional overall level of 0.05.

title: The Bayesian rule
cx: Chapter 13: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring > 13.4.2 The Bayesian rule
text: The Bayesian rule Bayesian monitoring of toxicity in single-arm trials goes back to Thall, Simon and Estey ( Thall, Simon, and Estey 1995 , 1996 ) , and Ivanova, Qaqish and Schell ( Ivanova, Qaqish, and Schell 2005 ) treat continuous toxicity monitoring in phase II trials; the rule below is a simple member of that family. Let the toxicity rate \(q\) in the single-arm study have a Beta( \(a_0\) , \(b_0\) ) prior, with \(a_0 = 0.5\) and \(b_0 = 2.5\) , a prior mean of 1/6 below the acceptable rate with the weight of three patients. After \(x\) toxicities in \(n\) patients the posterior is Beta( \(a_0 + x\) , \(b_0 + n - x\) ). The Bayesian rule, at the same looks: after every five patients, pause if \[ \Pr(q > \bar q \mid x, n) > \kappa, \qquad \kappa = 0.75. \tag{13.4}\] Because the posterior probability is increasing in \(x\) at fixed \(n\) , the rule is a table of counts, one stopping count per look, which is how it goes into a protocol and a DMC charter. Table 13.4 gives it next to the traditional counterpart above. The Bayesian rule does not escape the repeated-testing arithmetic; it chooses a point on it, with a threshold, 0.75, that is a statement about how much risk of a false pause the investigators will accept.
