title: The exact beta-binomial computation
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.2.3 The exact beta-binomial computation
text: The exact beta-binomial computation For a binary endpoint no normal approximation is needed. Suppose \(n\) of the planned \(N\) patients are observed, with \(s\) responders, and the prior on the response probability is \(\mathrm{Beta}(a_0,b_0)\) . The posterior is \(\mathrm{Beta}(a_0+s, b_0+n-s)\) , and the number of responders \(X\) among the \(m = N-n\) remaining patients has the beta-binomial predictive distribution \[ \Pr(X = x \mid s, n) = \binom{m}{x}\frac{B(a_0+s+x,\; b_0+n-s+m-x)}{B(a_0+s,\; b_0+n-s)}, \qquad x = 0,\dots,m, \tag{15.3}\] with \(B(\cdot,\cdot)\) the beta function. Each value of \(x\) completes a data set of \(N\) patients, to which the final success criterion can be applied directly, so the predictive probability is the sum of the beta-binomial probabilities of the \(x\) for which the criterion is met: \[ \mathrm{PP}(s, n) = \sum_{x=0}^{m} \Pr(X=x \mid s,n)\; \mathbf{1}\{\Pr(p > p_0 \mid s+x,\, N) > \eta\}. \tag{15.4}\] There is no integration and no simulation. The same construction for two arms takes a double sum over the future counts in each arm, with the posterior probability of superiority computed for each pair by adaptive numerical integration on the rank scale, cached across states ( pp_two_arm in bayestrials ); the predictive sum itself is exact. title: A time-to-event example
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.2.4 A time-to-event example
text: A time-to-event example The normal-case formulas apply directly to an event-driven trial, where total information is \(D/4\) for \(D\) events (so the information fraction is \(D/D_{\max}\) ) and the log hazard ratio has variance about \(4/D\) . The worked example, with the predictive probability and the conditional power under the design effect and under the current trend side by side for four interim states, is in Section 18.4 . The three summaries condition on different things (a fixed design effect, a fixed current estimate, and a posterior that averages over the effect), and which is more useful depends on how much the interim estimate is trusted against the design assumption; none is wrong, and the table there shows where they differ. The same logic applies when the interim is combined with an earlier trial. In a continuous-endpoint program (an invented example), a skeptical posterior from phase 2 of mean 0.20 and standard deviation 0.115 is combined with a half-information interim of a pivotal trial (300 patients per arm at the interim, 600 per arm at the final analysis) that reports \(\hat\theta_1 = 0.15\) with standard error \(\sqrt{2/300}\) . Show the R code w <- c ( 1 / 0.115 ^ 2 , 300 / 2 ) # precisions: phase 2 posterior, interim data m2 <- sum (w * c ( 0.20 , 0.15 )) /

text: error \(\sqrt{2/300}\) . Show the R code w <- c ( 1 / 0.115 ^ 2 , 300 / 2 ) # precisions: phase 2 posterior, interim data m2 <- sum (w * c ( 0.20 , 0.15 )) / sum (w); s2 <- 1 / sqrt ( sum (w)) # final estimate = (theta1 + theta2)/2, need z >= 2.02 at SE sqrt(2/600) thr <- 2 * 2.02 * sqrt ( 2 / 600 ) - 0.15 # required value of the second-half estimate pp_prog <- pnorm ((m2 - thr) / sqrt (s2 ^ 2 + 2 / 300 )) The combined posterior has mean 0.167 and standard deviation 0.067, and the predictive probability of crossing the final boundary of 2.02 is 0.79, high enough to continue. An interim estimate near zero would have started a futility discussion, and the predictive probability, not the conditional power at the design effect, would have been the quantity to discuss. The regulator analyzes the pivotal trial on its own data, so the type I error is controlled by that analysis; the sponsor deciding whether to continue may use everything it knows. These are different decisions, and they can use different priors.

title: The traditional phase 2 design, and where Bayesian monitoring started
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.3 The traditional phase 2 design, and where Bayesian monitoring started
text: 15.3 The traditional phase 2 design, and where Bayesian monitoring started The single-arm phase 2 trial is a widely used early efficacy design in oncology, and its traditional form is older than the predictive probability designs that follow. A response rate \(p\) is judged against an uninteresting rate \(p_0\) and a target rate \(p_1\) . Gehan ( 1961 ) proposed a first stage that stops when there are no responses, and Fleming ( 1982 ) a one-sample multiple testing procedure with early stopping. The design most protocols use is the two-stage design of Simon ( 1989 ) : enroll \(n_1\) patients and stop for futility if at most \(r_1\) respond; otherwise enroll to a total of \(n\) and declare the drug promising if more than \(r\) respond. Among the pairs of stages that meet the stated type I error and power, the optimal design is the one with the smallest expected sample size under \(p_0\) . Both error rates are exact binomial sums, so the design is computed, not simulated. text: designs came in two steps. Herson ( 1979 ) proposed stopping on the predictive probability of a positive final result. Thall and Simon ( 1994 ) monitored on the posterior probability that the response rate exceeds a target and chose the thresholds by their frequentist operating characteristics; Thall, Simon, and Estey ( 1995 ) extended the idea to several outcomes, and Heitjan ( 1997 ) , Tan and Machin ( 2002 ) and the BOP2 design of Zhou, Lee, and Yuan ( 2017 ) are later versions. title: Predictive probability monitoring for phase 2
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.4 Predictive probability monitoring for phase 2
text: 15.4 Predictive probability monitoring for phase 2 Lee and Liu ( 2008 ) turned the predictive probability of success into a two-threshold monitoring design for phase 2 with a printed stopping table. Related treatments include Johns and Andersen ( 1999 ) (phase 2 and 3), Dmitrienko and Wang ( 2006 ) (normal and time-to-event endpoints, with the link to conditional power) and Saville et al. ( 2014 ) (practical interim use). The idea is the same as the predictive probability futility rule of Section 15.2 , written in the units a phase 2 clinician uses: after each cohort, compute the predictive probability that the trial will end in success. Stop for futility if it is below a lower threshold \(\eta_L\) , stop for efficacy if it is above an upper threshold \(\eta_U\) , and otherwise continue. At the maximum sample size the trial declares success if the posterior probability criterion \(\Pr(p > p_0 \mid \text{data}) > \eta\) is met. Because the rule is a function of \((n, s)\) only, the decision for every possible interim outcome can be tabulated before the trial begins and printed in the protocol. Real trials use the same logic: the BNT162b2 trial planned to stop for futility if the predictive probability of success fell to 5% or less, and the DAWN stroke trial used predictive probability for both futility and

title: Predictive probability monitoring for phase 2
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.4 Predictive probability monitoring for phase 2
text: there are three or fewer, and after 30 if there are seven or fewer; it stops for success after 10 with six or more responders, after 20 with nine or more, and after 30 with twelve or more. The operating characteristics follow from exact enumeration of all paths, not from simulation: the probability of declaring success is 0.048 under the null rate (compared with 0.043 for the fixed design) and 0.867 at \(p = 0.40\) (0.871 for the fixed design), with an expected sample size of about 27 patients under either, against 40 for the fixed design. Three observations. First, power is essentially unchanged and the sample size falls by roughly a third. Second, the expected sample size is almost the same under the null and the alternative (26.6 and 27.2), because efficacy stops under the alternative offset futility stops under the null. Third, the type I error is not guaranteed to stay at the fixed-design value once efficacy stopping is allowed: with looks every five patients the null success probability rises to 0.057 (power 0.862, expected \(N\) 22.6 to 23.2), above 0.043, so the thresholds have to be recalibrated by exact enumeration or simulation ( Chapter 14 ). Phase 2 trials often accept a type I error of 0.05 to 0.10 by design; a confirmatory trial targets 0.025 one-sided.

title: What the predictive probability design is, and is not
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.4.1 What the predictive probability design is, and is not
text: What the predictive probability design is, and is not Predictive probability monitoring is a Bayesian way of computing a stopping boundary and a frequentist way of judging it. The decisions are made on a Bayesian quantity. The design is accepted or rejected on its operating characteristics under simulated truth. For a trial that adapts only by stopping, the realized design is a group sequential design with an unusual, data-driven boundary shape, and its probability of success under any true \(p\) is exact. This is how the FDA Bayesian draft expects a Bayesian design to be defended, and it is why the draft’s demand for pre-specified thresholds and simulation is no obstacle: the table above is the pre-specification. The approximation of Marion et al. ( 2025 ) shows that the exact calculation can be avoided in normal-approximation settings. If \(q_n\) is the current posterior probability of superiority, \(r\) the information fraction and \(\eta\) the final threshold, then \[ \mathrm{PP} \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(q_n) - \Phi^{-1}(\eta)\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{1-r}}\right), \tag{15.5}\] which needs only the current posterior probability and the information fraction. The approximation assumes a Gaussian posterior and test statistic, and with a flat prior \(r\) is the share of the final information accrued, \(I_n/I_N\) . With an informative normal prior of precision \(J_0\) the fraction for the posterior-threshold formula is \((J_0 + I_n)/(J_0 + I_N)\) rather than \(I_n/I_N\) , and with

title: What the predictive probability design is, and is not
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.4.1 What the predictive probability design is, and is not
text: a flat prior \(r\) is the share of the final information accrued, \(I_n/I_N\) . With an informative normal prior of precision \(J_0\) the fraction for the posterior-threshold formula is \((J_0 + I_n)/(J_0 + I_N)\) rather than \(I_n/I_N\) , and with longitudinal outcomes \(r\) is the fraction of final information carried by the observed data, not the fraction of patients enrolled ( Marion et al. 2025 ) . In the binary example of the working paper by Polson and Sokolov (cited below as SIM) ( Polson and Sokolov 2026 ) , with ten looks, thresholds 0.95 and 0.05 and final threshold 0.975, the approximation and the exact computation differ by 0.013 in mean absolute error across all interim states, and at most 9.0% of states receive different monitoring actions. Run through the full trial, the two give null success probabilities of 0.042 and 0.041, powers of 0.932 and 0.928, and expected sample sizes of 48.2 and 47.6 per arm. The approximation is good enough for planning, but the numbers also show that it is a design component to validate rather than an identity: where the final decision depends on a fine threshold, use the exact calculation.

title: The economic threshold $PP^*$
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.4.2 The economic threshold $PP^*$
text: The economic threshold \(PP^*\) The thresholds 0.05 and 0.95 are conventions. A decision-theoretic reading ties the futility threshold to money. Suppose a false go costs \(c_3\) , the expected cost of a failed phase 3, and a missed active drug forfeits \(V\) , its expected net value if developed. Continuing from the interim costs the remaining patients, \(m c_2\) , and \(\rho\) is the probability that phase 3 succeeds given a phase 2 success. The myopic rule continues if \(\mathrm{PP}\,[\rho V - (1-\rho) c_3] > m c_2\) , so the continuation threshold is \[ \mathrm{PP}^* = \frac{m c_2}{\rho V - (1-\rho) c_3}, \tag{15.6}\] which is small when the drug is valuable and the remaining phase 2 is cheap. The numbers below are invented for teaching, not taken from a real program. title: The Goldilocks design: two predictive probabilities
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.5 The Goldilocks design: two predictive probabilities
text: 15.5 The Goldilocks design: two predictive probabilities Phase 2 monitoring asks one question: will the trial succeed at its maximum size? A confirmatory trial with a long follow-up asks two, and the Goldilocks sample size design of Broglio, Connor, and Berry ( 2014 ) separates them ( Section 14.7 introduces it as a design chosen by simulation; this section gives the construction). The trial has a maximum sample size \(N_{\max}\) per arm and enrolls continuously. Because the primary endpoint is observed after a delay (say at week 12), at an interim look some enrolled patients have outcomes and some are still pending . At each look the design computes two predictive probabilities, both for the final success criterion, say \(\Pr(p_1 - p_0 > 0 \mid \text{data}) > 0.975\) : \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) : the probability of success if enrollment stops now and the pending patients are followed to complete their outcomes. Only the pending outcomes are unknown. \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max}\) : the probability of success if the trial continues to the maximum sample size, where every patient not yet observed (pending or not yet enrolled) is unknown. The decisions are: stop enrolling for expected success if \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) is high (the trial has already answered the question, and the pending patients will confirm it); stop for futility if \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max}\) is low (even the full sample is unlikely to succeed); otherwise,

title: The Goldilocks design: two predictive probabilities
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.5 The Goldilocks design: two predictive probabilities
text: are: stop enrolling for expected success if \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) is high (the trial has already answered the question, and the pending patients will confirm it); stop for futility if \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max}\) is low (even the full sample is unlikely to succeed); otherwise, keep enrolling. The “not too big, not too small” name refers to the sample size that the data pick, between the two limits. The two probabilities are different questions with different thresholds, and the design adjusts the sample size to both. The full design of Broglio and colleagues, as summarized in Section 14.7 , also has an immediate-success rule that declares success without following the pending patients when \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) passes a higher threshold; this chapter includes only the stop-enrollment rule above. With 30 of 50 against 15 of 50 the posterior probability of superiority is already 0.999, \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) is 0.999, and the design stops enrolling; completion is predicted to meet the success criterion with probability about 0.999, although unfavorable pending outcomes could reverse the decision. The modest lead (24 against 15, posterior probability 0.966) is not yet there: \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) is 0.545, \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max}\) is 0.735, and the design keeps enrolling. The narrow lead of 22 against 19 gives \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max} = 0.133\) , above the futility floor of 0.05, so the trial continues but is in trouble. Equal rates at 18 of 50 give \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max} = 0.022\) and the design stops for futility. Two cautions, both of the kind a regulator raises. The thresholds (0.95 and 0.05 here are illustrative) must be calibrated by simulation so that the overall type I error is controlled ( Section 14.4 shows this for the four-look example of Chapter 14 , where the flat posterior threshold of 0.975 becomes \(c = 0.9907\) ), and the look frequency and the delay length change the calibration. And stopping enrollment when

title: The Goldilocks design: two predictive probabilities
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.5 The Goldilocks design: two predictive probabilities
text: ( Section 14.4 shows this for the four-look example of Chapter 14 , where the flat posterior threshold of 0.975 becomes \(c = 0.9907\) ), and the look frequency and the delay length change the calibration. And stopping enrollment when the predictive probability of success is high is an efficacy decision: it spends type I error just as a group sequential efficacy boundary does ( Chapter 14 ). The same two questions run through the DAWN stroke trial ( Section 15.10 ); I-SPY 2 uses a single predictive probability, that of success in a follow-on phase 3 trial. The Goldilocks design replaces three separate traditional elements (an interim efficacy boundary, a futility boundary, and a sample size re-estimation) with one pre-specified rule, and its operating characteristics are what justify it. It also has a price: the sample size is random, so budgets and supply have to be planned for the maximum and the expected sample size reported alongside it.

title: Backward induction: the Bayes-optimal stopping rule
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6 Backward induction: the Bayes-optimal stopping rule
text: 15.6 Backward induction: the Bayes-optimal stopping rule Predictive probability monitoring is a rule with thresholds that the designer chooses and calibrates. A natural question is whether a best rule exists, for a stated loss. For a sequential decision problem with a finite horizon the answer is yes, and it can be found by working backward from the end. The method is backward induction , or dynamic programming ( Bellman 1957 ) . Sequential analysis itself goes back to Wald ( 1947 ) , and Bayes sequential solutions by backward induction to Arrow, Blackwell, and Girshick ( 1949 ) . Anscombe ( 1963 ) and Colton ( 1963 ) cast the trial as a Bayesian decision problem over a patient horizon, and Berry and Ho ( 1988 ) derived clinical-trial stopping boundaries by backward induction; Lewis and Berry ( 1994 ) evaluated such designs by their frequentist operating characteristics, the stance of this book. Later work includes Carlin, Kadane, and Gelfand ( 1998 ) , Cheng and Shen ( 2005 ) and P. Müller et al. ( 2007 ) for sequential trials with a sufficient statistic; Brockwell and Kadane ( 2003 ) gave a gridding method for the normal model and Jiang, Lee, and Müller ( 2013 ) combined it with response-adaptive randomization. The presentation below follows SIM ( Polson and Sokolov 2026 ) .

title: The decision problem
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6.1 The decision problem
text: The decision problem A two-arm trial with binary outcomes enrolls one pair of patients at a time, one per arm, up to a maximum of \(T\) pairs. After \(k\) pairs, the trial can stop and declare a winner, or pay a cost \(\kappa\) for one more pair . A stopping loss records the consequences of the terminal decision, and the continuation cost records the consequences of waiting. Two stopping losses are useful. The utility version stops for treatment when the posterior mean effect \(\hat\theta_k\) is positive and for control otherwise, with stopping value \(h_k = -\max(0, \hat\theta_k)\) , the negative of the expected benefit of the chosen arm. It has no separate cost for a false positive, so it is a decision rule for patient benefit, not an evidence rule, and it is deliberately aggressive under the null. The classification version fixes the losses \(L_{\mathrm{FP}}\) for declaring superiority when it is absent and \(L_{\mathrm{FN}}\) for failing to declare it when it is present. With \(q_k = \Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid \text{data}_k)\) , \(\gamma = L_{\mathrm{FP}}/(L_{\mathrm{FP}}+L_{\mathrm{FN}})\) and \(\kappa\) the cost per pair normalized by \(L_{\mathrm{FP}}+L_{\mathrm{FN}}\) , the Bayes stopping loss and action are \[ h_k = \min\{\gamma(1-q_k),\ (1-\gamma) q_k\}, \qquad \text{declare superiority if } q_k > \gamma. \tag{15.7}\] A loss ratio of \(L_{\mathrm{FP}} : L_{\mathrm{FN}} = 39 : 1\) gives \(\gamma = 0.975\) , which is

title: The decision problem
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6.1 The decision problem
text: the Bayes stopping loss and action are \[ h_k = \min\{\gamma(1-q_k),\ (1-\gamma) q_k\}, \qquad \text{declare superiority if } q_k > \gamma. \tag{15.7}\] A loss ratio of \(L_{\mathrm{FP}} : L_{\mathrm{FN}} = 39 : 1\) gives \(\gamma = 0.975\) , which is the Bayesian reading of one-sided 0.025: a false positive is 39 times worse than a false negative. This ratio is illustrative; the elicitation of the real ratio is the part of the design that belongs to clinicians, sponsors and regulators, not to the statistician.

title: The sufficient-statistic reduction
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6.2 The sufficient-statistic reduction
text: The sufficient-statistic reduction The data history up to pair \(k\) is a sequence of \(4^k\) possible outcome patterns. The posterior depends on the history only through the success counts \((s_1, s_0)\) and \(k\) , because the beta-binomial model has sufficient statistics. With the prior \(\mathrm{Beta}(a_{0i}, b_{0i})\) in arm \(i\) , the predictive probability of the next outcome in that arm is \[ \tilde p_i(s_i, k) = \frac{a_{0i} + s_i}{a_{0i} + b_{0i} + k}, \tag{15.8}\] so the future depends on the past only through \((s_1, s_0, k)\) . This is the sufficient-statistic reduction : the decision tree, which grows exponentially, collapses to a lattice with \((k+1)^2\) states at stage \(k\) , and the trial’s whole future is a function of where on the lattice it stands. With \(V_k(s_1, s_0)\) the minimum expected loss from state \((s_1, s_0)\) at stage \(k\) onward, the Bellman equation is \[ V_k(s_1,s_0) = \min\Big\{ h_k(s_1,s_0),\ \kappa + \sum_{y_1,y_0\in\{0,1\}} \Pr(y_1,y_0 \mid s_1,s_0,k)\, V_{k+1}(s_1+y_1,\, s_0+y_0) \Big\}, \tag{15.9}\] for \(0 \le k < T\) , with \(V_T = h_T\) at the horizon (the trial is forced to decide). The first term is the loss from stopping now. The second is the cost of one more pair plus the expected loss at the next stage, averaged over the four outcomes of the next pair with the predictive probabilities of Equation 15.8 . The minimum of

title: The sufficient-statistic reduction
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6.2 The sufficient-statistic reduction
text: from stopping now. The second is the cost of one more pair plus the expected loss at the next stage, averaged over the four outcomes of the next pair with the predictive probabilities of Equation 15.8 . The minimum of the two is the best that can be done from here, and the argument that achieves it is the optimal action. One computes \(V_T\) first, then \(V_{T-1}\) from it, and so on back to \(V_0\) : backward induction. Note Technical note: why the optimal policy is a function of the lattice state, and its cost Proposition (SIM, Appendix). For fixed prior parameters and horizon \(T\) , the optimal policy at stage \(k\) is a function of \((s_1, s_0, k)\) only, and the recursion in Equation 15.9 evaluates \(\sum_{k=0}^{T}(k+1)^2 = (T+1)(T+2)(2T+3)/6 = O(T^3)\) states, each in constant time. Proof sketch. By conjugacy the posterior at stage \(k\) is \(\mathrm{Beta}(a_{0i} + s_i, b_{0i} + k - s_i)\) in each arm, so \((s_1, s_0, k)\) is a Markov sufficient state for the future. The one-step predictive probabilities of Equation 15.8 depend on no other feature of the history, so the continuation value is a function of the state, and so is the minimum over the two actions. Each update is the arithmetic of four lookups of \(V_{k+1}\) . Summing the number of states over stages gives the cubic

text: so the continuation value is a function of the state, and so is the minimum over the two actions. Each update is the arithmetic of four lookups of \(V_{k+1}\) . Summing the number of states over stages gives the cubic count. For \(T = 200\) pairs, about 2.7 million states. \(\square\) For normal data with known variance the same argument holds with the posterior mean as the scalar state, and the lattice is replaced by a grid of the posterior mean; Brockwell and Kadane ( 2003 ) used 12,000 grid points on \([-6, 6]\) . The result is exact for the binary endpoint: no simulation, no approximation, no quadrature. The only approximation in the classification version is numerical, the computation of \(q_k\) for each state, which is a one-dimensional integral that bayestrials evaluates by the same adaptive rank-scale integration, with caching. The classification-loss version is implemented in backward_induction of the bayestrials package, together with an exact forward propagation ( forward_oc ) that returns the probability of declaring superiority and the expected sample size under any true pair \((p_1, p_0)\) . title: The sufficient-statistic reduction

text: proportions among continuation states at each stage (a projection: the full policy is indexed by the pair of success counts, and states with the same difference can have different actions). Continuation states lie within the shaded envelope between the two edges; the action at a particular point requires both success counts. Above the upper edge the trial stops for treatment, below the lower edge for control. Figure 15.2 shows the familiar funnel. Early in the trial a large observed difference is needed to stop for treatment (0.8 after 10 pairs, 0.55 after 20, 0.4 after 30, 0.28 after 50), because a few patients say little; the trial stops for control once the observed difference falls to about 0 after 30 pairs. The region closes as \(k\) approaches the horizon, because the trial is forced to decide at \(T\) whatever happens. The optimal rule has the shape of a group sequential boundary, with efficacy and futility stopping, but it is derived from a loss and a cost, not from an error-spending function. The projection onto the observed difference is only a summary: the full policy is indexed by \((s_1, s_0, k)\) , and states with the same difference can have different decisions.

title: What backward induction does and does not do
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6.3 What backward induction does and does not do
text: What backward induction does and does not do Three honest limits. First, a Bayes-optimal rule is optimal for the stated loss under the stated prior , and the loss ratio and cost are inputs somebody has to choose. A decision-theoretic submission should justify its loss function, prior, success criterion, and operating characteristics. For the error-calibrated approach used in this book, the route from one to the other is the calibration above: choose \(\gamma\) and \(\kappa\) , compute the policy, simulate (or enumerate) its operating characteristics under the full range of scenarios, and adjust until they meet the protocol targets. The decision-theoretic framing is a way of generating a good design; the frequentist operating characteristics are how it is judged ( Chapter 14 ). Second, the utility-only version shows what happens when a loss does not penalize false positives. In SIM’s calculation, with \(\kappa = 0.0005\) and a maximum of 100 per arm, utility-only backward induction declares treatment better with probability 0.513 under the null (Monte Carlo standard error 0.005) and 0.98 at the large effect, with an expected sample size of only 14.4 per arm. It is a good rule for choosing the arm that gives patients the best outcomes, and a useless rule for a confirmatory claim: its “null error” is a treatment-choice probability, not a type I error. The classification version, with \(\gamma

title: What backward induction does and does not do
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6.3 What backward induction does and does not do
text: It is a good rule for choosing the arm that gives patients the best outcomes, and a useless rule for a confirmatory claim: its “null error” is a treatment-choice probability, not a type I error. The classification version, with \(\gamma = 0.975\) , has a null declaration probability of 0.026, and its expected sample size at the large effect is 54.3 per arm with power 0.903. The loss function is the design. Third, the lattice assumes that outcomes are observed before the next decision, balanced allocation, and no pending patients. Delayed outcomes enlarge the state to include the pending counts, which is the setting of the Goldilocks design above, and response-adaptive allocation adds the allocation decision to the action set ( Chapter 16 ). Those extensions are what make exact dynamic programming harder; the sufficient-statistic reduction is what makes it feasible at all.

title: A single-arm example
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.6.4 A single-arm example
text: A single-arm example The two-arm lattice above has a one-arm counterpart that can be printed as a table. A single-arm trial enrolls patients one at a time, up to 60, with a Beta(3, 7) prior on the response rate \(p\) , centered at a standard-of-care rate \(p_0 = 0.3\) . Each patient costs \(c = 0.002\) in utility units. When the trial stops at \(n\) patients with \(x\) responders it adopts the drug if the posterior mean exceeds \(p_0\) , earning \(M(\hat p - p_0)\) with \(M = 10\) standing for the population of future patients, and abandons it otherwise. With \(\hat p_n = (3 + x)/(10 + n)\) , the value \(V_n(x)\) of state \((n, x)\) satisfies \[ V_n(x) = \max\Bigl\{\max\bigl(M(\hat p_n - p_0),\, 0\bigr),\ -c + \hat p_n V_{n+1}(x+1) + (1-\hat p_n) V_{n+1}(x)\Bigr\}, \tag{15.10}\] solved backward from \(V_{60}\) . This is an invented teaching example with no regulatory standing: it has no type I error target. The operating characteristics, computed exactly by forward propagation, are small where the stakes are large and large only where the two actions are nearly equivalent: at \(p = 0.2\) the drug is adopted with probability 0.053 after 24.8 patients on average, at the boundary \(p = 0.3\) with probability 0.50 after 32.3, and at \(p = 0.45\) with probability 0.976 after 19.1. This is the general shape of Bayes sequential designs. The same caveat applies as above: the loss and the cost are inputs, and a regulator reviews the operating characteristics (or, under the other routes of the FDA draft, the posterior or benefit-risk criterion), not the loss.

The rows are different specifications , with different objectives and monitoring schedules, so the table is a description of each and not a ranking of methods. The traditional group sequential design, fixed at one sample size and efficacy-only, cuts the expected sample size from 100 to 64.8 per arm at this large effect with simulated power unchanged at 0.96: the Bayesian predictive designs are not the first to stop early. That comparator is an approximate O’Brien-Fleming-shaped rule with boundary \(\Phi^{-1}(0.975)\sqrt{5/j}\) , not recalibrated for discrete data, and its realized null rejection probability is 0.033 against 0.028 for the fixed Wald test, so the comparison is not calibrated and no claim of a costless saving in power follows. The predictive probability and classification-loss designs go further because they also stop for futility, at a cost in power (0.93 and 0.90 against 0.96) that the calibration can trade back. And the utility-only rule shows that the objective changes everything: a rule that stops after 14 patients per arm and is right 98% of the time at the large effect is also wrong half the time under the null. The honest reading of Table 15.12 is that backward induction does not “beat” group sequential monitoring. It chooses a rule for a stated loss, and the rule, once calibrated to the same operating characteristics, is in the family of the others. title: Side by side: what changes in the protocol
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.8 Side by side: what changes in the protocol
text: prior, simulated type I error and power, expected \(N\) , sensitivity to prior and delay What stays the same The final test criterion, the type I error target (0.025 one-sided), the pre-specification, the walled-off DMC The two approaches agree numerically in simple cases: with a flat prior and a large trial, the predictive probability of success at an interim is a function of the same \(Z_t\) and \(t\) as conditional power under the current trend, and the flat-prior posterior probability of benefit at the end is approximately one minus the one-sided \(p\) -value ( Chapter 7 ). What the Bayesian design adds is the language, the prior, the forward-looking quantity that clinicians understand, and the framework for optimization. What it does not add is a lower bar. When is the traditional design the better choice? A single interim for futility with a non-binding rule is simple, well understood by every DMC and regulator, and needs no prior and no simulation beyond the standard group sequential software. If the DMC will take its decision on clinical grounds, the extra machinery of a predictive probability rule has no one to use it. Where the decision is not a single stop-or-go but a sequence (several looks, a pending-outcome structure, a platform with many arms), the predictive design earns its complexity. Where the decision is not a single stop-or-go but a sequence (several looks, a pending-outcome structure, a platform with many arms), the predictive design earns its complexity. Tip In the protocol A predictive monitoring section should state, before any outcome data are seen: The final success criterion in full (for example, \(\Pr(p_1 - p_0 > 0 \mid \text{data}) > 0.975\) at \(N_{\max}\) ) and the prior used to compute the predictive probability, including its justification. The look schedule (information fractions or patient numbers) and the quantity used at each look. The thresholds for futility and for efficacy, and whether the futility threshold is binding. State that the DMC may recommend continuation against a non-binding futility threshold without affecting the final analysis. The method of computation (exact beta-binomial, or the normal approximation of Equation 15.5 , with its validation). The handling of pending outcomes , if any: whether \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) and \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max}\) are both used, and how patients enrolled but not yet observed enter the computation. A pointer to the simulation report : scenarios (null, design alternative, several in-between and adverse), type I error, power, expected and maximum sample size, probability of each stopping reason, and sensitivity to the prior and to delays.

title: Regulatory reading of the chapter's designs
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.9 Regulatory reading of the chapter's designs
text: 15.9 Regulatory reading of the chapter’s designs The position on each tool follows from two requirements: pre-specification and operating characteristics. A futility rule is the lowest-risk adaptation, provided it is pre-specified and interim access to comparative data is controlled (ICH E9 4.5; FDA 2019), and non-binding is the safe default; the new element in a Bayesian version is the prior inside the predictive probability, which has to be defended. Sample size re-estimation divides into blinded (low risk) and unblinded (needs type I error control by design and a prespecified algorithm); E20 says “the number and complexity of adaptations should generally be limited” in confirmatory trials (section 3.2, PDF p9) and requires a “clear and compelling justification” (PDF p8), which a promising zone or Goldilocks design in a pivotal trial must supply. A predictive probability rule inside a design under the January 2026 FDA draft is a stopping rule and needs the report of any adaptive decision rule: simulated type I error and power, expected sample size, prior sensitivity. No guidance mentions backward induction. A decision-theoretic submission should justify its loss function and prior (the FDA draft discusses expected-loss criteria in Section IV.A.3), and document the resulting policy as a table of boundaries for every \((s_1, s_0, k)\) with its operating characteristics. A Bayes-optimal rule is submitted as a pre-specified table and justified by those characteristics, and a novel rule in a pivotal trial is a subject for the CID paired meeting program ( Chapter 3 , Chapter 23 ).

title: In practice
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.10 In practice
text: 15.10 In practice Five trials show the chapter’s quantities at work: one that stopped on a posterior probability of futility, I-SPY 2 with two arms judged on predictive probability, one stroke trial and one vaccine trial with predictive stopping rules written into the analysis plan, and one platform arm that stopped for limited efficacy.

title: CALGB 49907: futility stopping in practice
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.10.1 CALGB 49907: futility stopping in practice
text: CALGB 49907: futility stopping in practice CALGB 49907 compared capecitabine with standard adjuvant chemotherapy in women aged 65 or older with early-stage breast cancer ( Muss et al. 2009 ) . The design planned up to 1,800 patients, with a Bayesian monitoring rule on the noninferiority comparison and noninformative priors. At the first interim, after 600 patients, the posterior probability that capecitabine would fail the noninferiority criterion was 96%, over the pre-specified 80% futility boundary. Enrollment stopped at 633 patients, 65% fewer than the planned maximum. After further follow-up the hazard ratio was 2.09 (95% CI 1.38 to 3.17), confirming the superiority of standard chemotherapy ( Muss et al. 2009 ) . Berry ( 2025 ) describes it as, to his knowledge, the first fully Bayesian randomized trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine . The case illustrates the value of futility stopping where the new drug is worse , not just no better: the trial spent 633 patients, not 1,800, to learn that capecitabine was inferior in this population. It also illustrates something regulators look for: the criterion was a probability statement with a pre-specified boundary, and the boundary was crossed by the data, not chosen after the fact. Note that the quantity reported at the interim is a posterior probability of failing noninferiority, and the design as described in the primary report did not stop on a conditional power value.

title: I-SPY 2: predictive probability as the graduation criterion
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.10.2 I-SPY 2: predictive probability as the graduation criterion
text: I-SPY 2: predictive probability as the graduation criterion The original I-SPY 2 trial in neoadjuvant breast cancer ( Barker et al. 2009 ; Berry 2015 ) tested multiple agents against a shared control. Its decision criteria are written in predictive probability. An agent graduated in a biomarker signature when its Bayesian predictive probability of success in an equally randomized 300-patient phase 3 trial reached at least 85%; it was dropped for futility when that probability fell below 10% in every one of the ten signatures ( Berry 2025 ; Park et al. 2016 ) . This is the Goldilocks logic applied to a platform: the question at each interim is not whether the data already show benefit, but whether a specific follow-on trial would succeed, and the follow-on trial is part of the definition. Two arms show how the rule behaves. Neratinib (127 randomized, 115 evaluable, against 78 evaluable concurrent controls) graduated only in the HER2-positive, hormone-receptor-negative signature, with an estimated pathologic complete response rate of 56% against 33% for the control and a final predictive probability of phase 3 success of 79%, below the 85% threshold ( Park et al. 2016 ) . The drop was anticipated: graduation is declared on interim predictions that use imaging, and the probability is recomputed once all pathology is in, which is why the authors set the threshold

title: I-SPY 2: predictive probability as the graduation criterion
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.10.2 I-SPY 2: predictive probability as the graduation criterion
text: 85% threshold ( Park et al. 2016 ) . The drop was anticipated: graduation is declared on interim predictions that use imaging, and the probability is recomputed once all pathology is in, which is why the authors set the threshold high at 85%. Pembrolizumab with chemotherapy (69 patients against 181 controls) reached the threshold in all three signatures it was tested in and randomization was halted; the final predictive probabilities were 98.5% (HER2-negative), 99.6% (hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative) and 83.4% (triple negative) ( Nanda et al. 2020 ) . The triple-negative value is also under 85%, and the arm still counts as graduated. The lesson is that a predictive probability threshold is a decision rule on partially observed outcomes, and its realized value at the end can fall below the nominal one. A protocol that sets the threshold should say which data enter the calculation and how the final recomputation is treated. The platform structure, the shared control and the arm-level multiplicity are treated in Chapter 20 , and the allocation rule in Section 16.9 .

title: DAWN: predictive probability for expected success and futility
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.10.3 DAWN: predictive probability for expected success and futility
text: DAWN: predictive probability for expected success and futility DAWN tested thrombectomy with the Trevo device in acute ischemic stroke 6 to 24 hours after onset in patients with a mismatch between clinical deficit and infarct core ( Jovin et al. 2017 ) . Its statistical analysis plan ( Stryker Neurovascular 2017 ) makes predictive probability the stopping quantity. From 200 randomized patients, with at least 100 since the last enrichment, the trial stops for expected success if the predictive probability of success exceeds 95% at 200 and 250 patients, 90% at 300 and 350, 85% at 400, and 80% at 450 and 500. It stops for futility if the predictive probability of success, under any enrichment possibility, at the maximum sample size is under 10%. The thresholds fall as the sample grows, so an early stop needs more certainty than a late one. The final success criterion and its adjustment for enrichment are in Section 14.11 . This is the Goldilocks structure of Section 15.5 with a schedule of thresholds, and it shows what a regulator reads in such a design: not the decision theory but the table of looks and thresholds and the simulation that calibrates the final criterion.

title: BNT162b2: a futility rule in a vaccine efficacy trial
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.10.4 BNT162b2: a futility rule in a vaccine efficacy trial
text: BNT162b2: a futility rule in a vaccine efficacy trial The pivotal phase 2/3 trial of the Pfizer and BioNTech vaccine declared efficacy on a posterior probability with calibrated thresholds (the model and prior are in Chapter 6 , the thresholds and their calibration in Section 14.11 ), and added a futility rule that is predictive: stop if the posterior predictive probability of success at the final analysis is 5% or less, with non-binding boundaries (for example, 27.8% observed efficacy at 62 cases and 38.6% at 92 cases). The first interim analysis planned at 32 cases was not performed, the thresholds were unchanged and the type I error stayed at 2.5% ( Pfizer Inc. 2022 ) . The lesson is the one of the section on futility rules: a predictive futility boundary that is non-binding costs nothing in type I error, and a sponsor can pre-specify it as a table of case splits that a monitoring committee can read without a computer.

title: GBM AGILE: predictive power as the futility quantity
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.10.5 GBM AGILE: predictive power as the futility quantity
text: GBM AGILE: predictive power as the futility quantity GBM AGILE is a Bayesian adaptive platform for glioblastoma with a screening stage and a confirmatory stage ( Alexander et al. 2018 ) . The first arm to finish was regorafenib, equally randomized against control in newly diagnosed MGMT-unmethylated (temozolomide plus radiotherapy control) and recurrent (lomustine control) disease. Efficacy would be declared at a Bayesian probability of benefit (hazard ratio below 1) of at least 98%. Analyses ran monthly, and the arm stopped enrolling for limited efficacy when the Bayesian predictive power was below 25% in all signatures ( Wen et al. 2026 ) . It did: the median hazard ratios were 1.05, 1.07 and 1.07 (newly diagnosed, recurrent, all) with probabilities of benefit of 0.421, 0.312 and 0.296, and the drug had more toxicity than control ( Wen et al. 2026 ) . An erratum to the regorafenib report has been published ( Wen, Berry, et al. 2026 ) . The stopping rule needed no unblinded judgment: the threshold was in the design and the data crossed it. The lesson for this chapter is the choice of threshold. A 25% limit on predictive power is far more aggressive than the 5% or 10% limits above, and the loss in power that it causes has to be paid for in the simulation report.

title: Summary
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > 15.11 Summary
text: 15.11 Summary Conditional power, predictive probability, the Lee-Liu design, the Goldilocks design and the backward induction policy are one idea at increasing ambition: conditional power fixes the effect, predictive probability averages over it, and backward induction derives the rule from a loss. All are judged by the operating characteristics of Chapter 14 . Tip Try it in the lab Open module 09 (Adaptive Bayesian) at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/09-adaptive-bayesian.html . Before moving the sampling-cost control, predict what happens to the expected sample size and to the probability that the rule says “better” when the drug does nothing; then check. The module’s CALGB 49907 example (a planned 1,800 patients, stopped at 633) is the case of this chapter. Then open the simulator at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/14-simulator.html (the full version is 14-studio.html ) and set a futility threshold on predictive probability: predict how much the expected sample size falls under the null, then run it.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > Key points
text: Key points Conditional power depends on an assumed effect: under the design alternative it is optimistic after a poor interim, under the current trend it is pessimistic. Report which, and do not mix them. Predictive probability of success is conditional power averaged over the posterior of the effect. It needs a prior, and the prior has to be pre-specified and stress-tested. For binary endpoints the predictive probability is exact: a beta-binomial sum over the future responder counts, with no integration or simulation. Futility stopping cannot inflate the type I error, and a non-binding rule keeps the final test valid even if the DMC does not follow it. Efficacy stopping spends error and requires calibration. Lee and Liu’s predictive probability design tabulates, before the trial, the responder counts that stop for futility or success at each look, and its operating characteristics can be computed exactly. In the worked example, three looks cut the expected sample size from 40 to about 27 with power 0.867 against 0.871. The Goldilocks design uses two predictive probabilities: success if enrollment stops now ( \(\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}\) ) and success at the maximum size ( \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max}\) ). Stopping accrual for expected success spends type I error. Backward induction gives the optimal stopping rule for a stated loss and cost per patient. The sufficient-statistic reduction makes it exact and cheap for binary endpoints: \(O(T^3)\)

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 15: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping > Key points
text: size ( \(\mathrm{PP}_{\max}\) ). Stopping accrual for expected success spends type I error. Backward induction gives the optimal stopping rule for a stated loss and cost per patient. The sufficient-statistic reduction makes it exact and cheap for binary endpoints: \(O(T^3)\) states. The optimal rule is only as good as its loss. A utility-only rule chooses the better arm quickly and says “better” half the time under the null; it is not a confirmatory rule. In the 60-pair example, at the target alternative the classification version uses about 24% fewer patients on average, with power 0.790 rather than 0.806; the null rejection probabilities both round to 0.024. Regulators judge all of these by simulated or exact operating characteristics under a pre-specified design (E20 section 5, FDA Bayesian draft), not by the elegance of the decision theory. title: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16 Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits
text: In 1933 William Thompson asked a question that every clinician has felt at the bedside: if the first patients treated with a new drug seem to do better than those on the old one, why should the next patient be assigned by a coin flip? His answer was to let the odds shift toward the treatment that is looking better, and his motive was ethical, to spare patients from being “sacrificed” to the inferior treatment. The idea is called response-adaptive randomization (RAR), and in the language of operations research it is a multi-armed bandit problem. It is the most intuitive of the adaptive features in this book and the most contested. It is contested because it asks a randomized trial to do two jobs at once. A trial has to produce a comparison that a regulator will accept as substantial evidence, and that comparison is cleanest when allocation is fixed and balanced. A bandit has to maximize the benefit to the patients inside the study, and that is best done by abandoning the losing arm as soon as it is identifiable. The two objectives pull in opposite directions, and the history of RAR, from the ECMO trial of 1985 to the critiques of the 2010s, is a history of finding out how far. This chapter follows the book’s rule and starts with the traditional design:

text: in opposite directions, and the history of RAR, from the ECMO trial of 1985 to the critiques of the 2010s, is a history of finding out how far. This chapter follows the book’s rule and starts with the traditional design: fixed allocation, usually 1:1, and the reasons it is the default. It then develops the bandit view, including the surprising fact (due to Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) ) that the logarithm that governs the Bayes sequential boundary also governs the regret of an optimal bandit policy. It tells the ECMO story, the one case every trialist knows. It then gives the critiques their due, simulates the failure that matters most in practice (drift in the patient population over calendar time), and shows what fixes it. It ends with the multi-arm setting, where RAR earns its place, and with what the regulators say. title: The traditional default: fixed allocation
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.1 The traditional default: fixed allocation
text: 16.1 The traditional default: fixed allocation A traditional two-arm trial fixes the allocation ratio in the protocol and keeps it for the whole study. Almost always the ratio is 1:1, implemented by permuted blocks, perhaps stratified by site or a prognostic factor ( Chapter 5 ). The sample size comes from the power formula of Chapter 9 , and the analysis is the test of Chapter 4 . This is the design that RAR must beat, so it is worth saying exactly why it is hard to beat.

title: Why 1:1
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.1.1 Why 1:1
text: Why 1:1 For a comparison of two means or two proportions with the same variance in each arm, the standard error of the estimated difference is proportional to \(\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_0}\) . For a fixed total \(n = n_0 + n_1\) this is smallest when \(n_0 = n_1\) . If the ratio is \(r = n_1/n_0\) , the information about the treatment effect is proportional to \(4r/(1+r)^2\) of its 1:1 value, and the sample size needed for the same power is inflated by the reciprocal. Table 16.1 gives the numbers. Show the R code r <- c ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 9 ); eff <- 4 * r / ( 1 + r) ^ 2 kable ( data.frame ( Ratio = paste0 (r, ":1" ), Efficiency = round (eff, 3 ), ` Inflation of n ` = round ( 1 / eff, 3 ), ` Share on the larger arm ` = pct (r / ( 1 + r)), check.names = FALSE )) Table 16.1: Cost of unequal fixed allocation. Efficiency is the information relative to 1:1 for the same total n. Inflation is the factor by which the total sample size must grow to keep the power of a 1:1 design. Ratio Efficiency Inflation of n Share on the larger arm 1:1 1.000 1.000 50% 2:1 0.889 1.125 67%

text: total n. Inflation is the factor by which the total sample size must grow to keep the power of a 1:1 design. Ratio Efficiency Inflation of n Share on the larger arm 1:1 1.000 1.000 50% 2:1 0.889 1.125 67% 3:1 0.750 1.333 75% 4:1 0.640 1.562 80% 9:1 0.360 2.778 90% A 2:1 ratio costs 12.5 percent more patients. A 3:1 ratio costs a third more, and 9:1 costs almost three times as many. These are not small prices, and they are paid whatever the data show. When the outcome is binary the variances differ between the arms, and the optimal (Neyman) allocation puts more patients on the arm with the larger variance. For a control response of 0.30 and a treatment response of 0.45 the optimal share on the treatment arm is only 52 percent, so the textbook gain from Neyman allocation is negligible in the range where trials are run. Equal allocation is close to optimal for the questions trials usually ask. Three other reasons keep 1:1 the default, and none is about the variance formula. The first is simplicity of the protocol and the analysis. Allocation is a pre-specified schedule independent of the outcomes, so every patient’s assignment is, in the words of ICH E9, a deliberate element of chance, and the randomization distribution of the test statistic is exactly known.

title: Why 1:1
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.1.1 Why 1:1
text: protocol and the analysis. Allocation is a pre-specified schedule independent of the outcomes, so every patient’s assignment is, in the words of ICH E9, a deliberate element of chance, and the randomization distribution of the test statistic is exactly known. The type I error of the test of Chapter 4 is a property of the design, not of a model for how patients enter. The second is balance in calendar time. With permuted blocks, each arm receives, within one block, the same number of patients, so any change in the patient mix, the standard of care, the assay or the site mix during enrollment hits both arms equally. Time is the covariate nobody records and everybody has. Fixed allocation makes it harmless by construction. This property is the one RAR gives up, and the simulations below show what that costs. The third is the absence of a statistical contract with the data. A fixed design says nothing about what the interim results may be. The data monitoring committee can look at them ( Chapter 11 ), but allocation does not react, so the trial cannot amplify a lucky early streak.

title: Unequal fixed allocation and when it is justified
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.1.2 Unequal fixed allocation and when it is justified
text: Unequal fixed allocation and when it is justified There are good reasons to depart from 1:1, and regulators accept them when stated in advance. A sponsor may want more patients on the experimental arm to collect safety exposure, a rare-disease trial may find enrollment on the experimental arm easier when the odds of getting it are 2:1, and a shared control in a multi-arm trial should be larger than each experimental arm. For \(k\) experimental arms and one shared control, Dunnett’s classical result ( Dunnett 1955 ) is that the control arm should be about \(\sqrt{k}\) times as large as each treatment arm, to minimize the variance of the \(k\) comparisons with control. Table 16.2 shows how far this is from equal allocation. Show the R code k <- c ( 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 8 ) kable ( data.frame ( k = k, ` Equal allocation ` = pct ( 1 / (k + 1 ), 1 ), ` Dunnett sqrt(k) rule ` = pct ( sqrt (k) / (k + sqrt (k)), 1 ), check.names = FALSE )) Table 16.2: Share of patients on the control arm under equal allocation and under Dunnett’s square root rule, for k experimental arms. k Equal allocation Dunnett sqrt(k) rule 2 33.3% 41.4% 3 25.0% 36.6% 4 20.0% 33.3% 5 16.7% 30.9% 8

The FDA master protocols draft makes the same point in its own words (control allocated more than each drug arm), and the EMA draft acknowledges the sqrt(k) rule as more efficient for fixed designs while noting that it is not always suitable when arms enter and leave. These are fixed ratios. A fixed control share protects control accrual but does not establish regulatory acceptability of adaptive experimental allocation, because the ratio of each experimental arm to control still moves when the experimental allocation does. The question the rest of the chapter asks is what, if anything, is gained by letting the ratios among the experimental arms move with the data.

title: Exploring and exploiting
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.1 Exploring and exploiting
text: Exploring and exploiting Suppose two treatments have unknown success probabilities \(p_0\) and \(p_1\) and patients arrive one at a time. Each assignment does two things. It treats the patient (the reward, a success or a failure), and it teaches us about the arm (information that improves later assignments). Assigning the arm that currently looks better exploits what we know. Assigning the other arm explores. A trial that explores too little may lock onto the wrong arm. A trial that explores too much wastes patients on the arm it already suspects is worse. This is the multi-armed bandit problem, named for a row of slot machines with unknown payout rates, and it was posed in medicine before it was named anywhere. Thompson ( Thompson 1933 ) proposed that the next patient be assigned to arm 1 with probability equal to the current posterior probability that arm 1 is better, \(\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid \text{data})\) . Robbins ( Robbins 1952 ) formulated the sequential allocation problem for two populations with unknown distributions, together with its reward-shortfall criterion (regret, the shortfall of the reward actually obtained against the reward of always giving the best arm); Lai and Robbins ( Lai and Robbins 1985 ) established the logarithmic lower bound (below). Clinical-trial versions of the problem are traced in Section 1.9 and Section 15.6 . Gittins ( Gittins and

text: reward of always giving the best arm); Lai and Robbins ( Lai and Robbins 1985 ) established the logarithmic lower bound (below). Clinical-trial versions of the problem are traced in Section 1.9 and Section 15.6 . Gittins ( Gittins and Jones 1974 ; Gittins 1979 ) showed that when future patients are discounted geometrically, the optimal policy is an index policy, and Berry and Fristedt ( Berry and Fristedt 1985 ) gave the definitive Bayesian account. Villar, Bowden and Wason ( Villar, Bowden, and Wason 2015 ) review the use of these models in trial design and are frank about the obstacles, which the simulations of this chapter quantify. The allocation rules in the clinical literature came by three routes. The first is the urn: Zelen ( 1969 ) proposed the play-the-winner rule, and randomized versions followed ( Wei and Durham ( 1978 ) ; the ECMO trial in Section 16.3 ). The second is target allocation: Rosenberger and Lachin ( 1993 ) reviewed response-adaptive designs, Rosenberger et al. ( 2001 ) derived allocation proportions that minimize the expected number of treatment failures for a fixed power, and the doubly adaptive biased coin design ( Eisele 1994 ; Hu and Zhang 2004 ; Hu and Rosenberger 2006 ) is the usual frequentist way to reach a stated allocation target with controlled variability. The Bayesian bandit

title: Thompson sampling in four lines
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.2 Thompson sampling in four lines
text: Thompson sampling in four lines With a Beta prior on each success probability, the posterior after \(s\) successes and \(f\) failures is \(\mathrm{Beta}(1+s, 1+f)\) ( Chapter 6 ). Thompson sampling draws one value from each arm’s posterior and assigns the patient to the arm with the largest draw. For two arms, the probability that arm 1 is chosen is exactly \(\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid \text{data})\) . Show the R code set.seed ( 1 ) prob_better <- function (s1, f1, s0, f0, M = 2e5 ) mean ( rbeta (M, s1 + 1 , f1 + 1 ) > rbeta (M, s0 + 1 , f0 + 1 )) # uniform priors # after 20 patients: 7 of 10 respond on the new arm, 4 of 10 on control early <- prob_better ( 7 , 3 , 4 , 6 ) # after 200 patients with the same observed rates, the posterior is far more concentrated late <- prob_better ( 70 , 30 , 40 , 60 ) kable ( data.frame ( Stage = c ( "After 20 patients" , "After 200 patients" ), ` P(new arm better) ` = round ( c (early, late), 3 ), check.names = FALSE )) Stage P(new arm better) After 20 patients 0.901 After 200 patients 1.000 Early in a trial the allocation probability is close to one half and

title: The Bellman equation
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.3 The Bellman equation
text: The Bellman equation A trial is a reinforcement-learning problem in the sense that its state is the posterior. Let \(\pi_t\) be the posterior over the arms’ success probabilities \(p_k\) after \(t\) patients and \(m\) the number of patients still to be treated. The best policy solves \[ V(\pi_t, m) = \max\Bigl\{ \underbrace{m \max_k \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k]}_{\text{stop and treat}},\; \max_k \Bigl( \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k] + \mathrm{E}\bigl[ V(\pi_{t+1}, m-1) \mid \pi_t, \text{arm } k \bigr] \Bigr) \Bigr\}, \tag{16.1}\] where the first term stops the trial and gives every remaining patient the arm that currently looks best, and the second assigns the next patient to arm \(k\) , collects the expected response, and moves to the updated posterior by Bayes’ theorem. Reinforcement learning calls this a belief-state Markov decision process, and statisticians have called it a Bayesian sequential design since the 1950s ( Chapter 11 ). The two literatures solve the same equation. It is solvable exactly only for small problems, which is why the rest of this section looks at its two famous approximations: the Gittins index for the discounted infinite horizon, and Thompson sampling.

title: The Gittins index
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.4 The Gittins index
text: The Gittins index The Gittins index ( Gittins and Jones 1974 ) is the exact solution to a cleaner problem. Each arm has a state (for a binary outcome, the counts of successes and failures). Future rewards are discounted by a factor \(\gamma < 1\) per patient. The index of an arm in state \(s\) is the highest achievable ratio of expected discounted reward to expected discounted time, over the stopping times \(\tau\) at which one might abandon the arm, \[ G(s) = \sup_{\tau > 0} \frac{\mathrm{E}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \gamma^t r_t \mid s\bigr]}{\mathrm{E}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \gamma^t \mid s\bigr]}, \tag{16.2}\] or, equivalently, the constant payoff per patient at which a decision maker would be exactly indifferent between continuing with that arm and retiring to a sure thing paying that constant forever ( Whittle 1980 ) . The optimal policy is to give each patient the arm with the highest index. The remarkable part is that each arm’s index depends only on that arm’s own history, so a problem with many arms is solved by tabulating one-arm indices. It is exact for an infinite, discounted horizon, whereas a trial has a fixed number of patients and a finite horizon problem has no index solution. Practical designs therefore use approximations, with Thompson sampling the most common. And the objective is the reward to patients in the trial, which, as we see below, is not the objective of a confirmatory comparison.

title: Regret and the Lai-Robbins bound
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.5 Regret and the Lai-Robbins bound
text: Regret and the Lai-Robbins bound Regret measures how much a policy loses against an oracle that knows the best arm. For a two-arm trial the regret after \(T\) patients is the expected number of patients on the inferior arm times the gap in response probabilities. Equal randomization puts half the patients on the inferior arm, so its regret grows linearly in \(T\) . The question is how much better any policy can do. Lai and Robbins ( Lai and Robbins 1985 ) answered it. For any policy that is uniformly good in the sense of Lai and Robbins ( 1985 ) (expected regret of order \(o(T^a)\) for every \(a > 0\) and every parameter value; the bound holds for single-parameter families under regularity conditions), the expected number of patients on an inferior arm \(i\) satisfies \[ \liminf_{T\to\infty} \frac{\mathbb{E}[N_i(T)]}{\log T} \;\ge\; \frac{1}{\mathrm{KL}(p_i, p^\ast)}, \tag{16.3}\] where \(\mathrm{KL}(p_i, p^\ast)\) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the response distribution of the inferior arm and that of the best arm. In words: a good policy cannot avoid giving the inferior arm a number of patients that grows like the logarithm of the horizon, and the constant is the reciprocal of how distinguishable the arms are. The regret of the best possible policy is logarithmic, not linear. For response probabilities 0.30 and 0.45 the divergence is 0.047 and the bound is about

The Lai-Robbins bound is asymptotic (a liminf as \(T\) grows), so finite-horizon counts can sit below the plotted slope, as Thompson sampling does at \(t = 5{,}000\) (about 90 patients against about 181 from \(\log T/\mathrm{KL}\) ). Note Technical note: why the bound is logarithmic To tell an inferior arm from the best arm at error probability \(\epsilon\) , a policy needs about \(\log(1/\epsilon)/\mathrm{KL}\) observations on that arm, because \(\mathrm{KL}\) is the rate at which log likelihood ratio evidence accumulates per observation. A policy that must be uniformly efficient for every possible truth cannot let the error probability on this question fall slower than polynomially in the horizon \(T\) , since a mistaken commitment costs a number of patients linear in \(T\) . Setting \(\epsilon \approx 1/T\) gives \(\log T/\mathrm{KL}\) observations on the inferior arm, which is Equation 16.3 . The logarithm is the price of a bar that tightens with the horizon, and the argument of the next section is that the same price appears in sequential testing.

title: The same logarithm
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.6 The same logarithm
text: The same logarithm Polson and Sokolov ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) observe that the scale in Equation 16.3 is the scale of the Bayes sequential boundary of Chapter 11 and the moderate deviation sample size equation of Chapter 9 . We give the argument as they make it and mark which parts are exact and which are an analogy. For contiguous alternatives (a small standardized effect \(\theta\) ) the Kullback-Leibler divergence is \(\mathrm{KL} \approx \theta^2/2\) . The moderate deviation relation for a test that balances the two errors is \(n\theta^2 \asymp \log n\) , which in terms of divergence is \(n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \tfrac12 \log n\) . For asymptotically optimal policies, the Lai-Robbins bound is attained in order, \(\mathbb{E}[N_i(T)]\,\mathrm{KL}_i \sim \log T\) ; the theorem itself supplies only the lower bound. These are the same relation with the horizon \(T\) in place of the sample size \(n\) , up to a factor of two. The number of patients a bandit policy must waste on an inferior arm is the number of observations the Bayes rule needs to distinguish that arm at the moderate deviation scale. The frequentist bandit algorithm makes the same point from the other side. UCB1 adds the bonus \(\sqrt{2\log t / N_i}\) , which comes from a Hoeffding bound for rewards in \([0,1]\) whose error probability shrinks polynomially in \(t\) (as \(t^{-4}\)

text: The frequentist bandit algorithm makes the same point from the other side. UCB1 adds the bonus \(\sqrt{2\log t / N_i}\) , which comes from a Hoeffding bound for rewards in \([0,1]\) whose error probability shrinks polynomially in \(t\) (as \(t^{-4}\) in the analysis of Auer and coauthors). So UCB’s confidence level also decays with the horizon, and its bonus grows like \(\sqrt{\log t}\) , the same order as the Bayes bar \(\sqrt{\log T}\) . The constants are not comparable in general, because the UCB radius is on the response scale and a testing boundary is on the standardized scale, so they depend on the variance proxy. title: An analogy that does not transfer as design advice
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.7 An analogy that does not transfer as design advice
text: An analogy that does not transfer as design advice Polson and Sokolov are explicit that the analogy is exact at the level of the deviation scale and misleading at the level of the objective, and that a recommendation of Thompson sampling for confirmatory trials on the strength of the first would be wrong. Regret is a loss in the trial. Power is a property of the final decision. Optimizing the first damages the second, and the next sections show it. As mathematics, the analogy shows that this particular normal-mixture construction shares a logarithmic scale with optimal bandit regret. As design advice it does not transfer to a trial whose conclusion will govern treatment for a population far larger than the trial. The place where it does transfer is early-phase work, where the population inheriting the decision is the next trial, and that is where the utility-based designs of Chapter 17 put it. Note If it works for Amazon: Thompson sampling on the web Hill and colleagues ( Hill et al. 2017 ) describe how Amazon used Thompson sampling to choose among the very many layouts of a web page, searching a combinatorial space of page elements in real time. They report that after a single week of online optimization the chosen layout lifted purchases by about 21 percent over the median layout. The comparison with

title: An analogy that does not transfer as design advice
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.2.7 An analogy that does not transfer as design advice
text: of a web page, searching a combinatorial space of page elements in real time. They report that after a single week of online optimization the chosen layout lifted purchases by about 21 percent over the median layout. The comparison with a trial is instructive and the transfer is limited. A click is observed in seconds, the experiment never really ends, and the visitors after the experiment matter as much as the visitors in it, so in-experiment reward is close to the right objective. A confirmatory trial has delayed outcomes, a population of future patients that may outnumber those enrolled a thousand to one, and a regulator who must trust the final estimate. That is the argument of the analogy section above and of Section 16.4 .

title: What was done
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3.1 What was done
text: What was done Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a form of heart-lung bypass. In the early 1980s, Bartlett and colleagues were convinced that it saved newborns with persistent pulmonary hypertension and a very high predicted mortality, and that randomizing such infants to conventional medical therapy (CMT) was close to unethical. Their trial ( Bartlett et al. 1985 ) used a randomized play-the-winner rule ( Wei and Durham 1978 ) , the randomized form of Zelen’s play-the-winner rule ( Zelen 1969 ) . In its simplest form the rule is an urn: start with one ball for each treatment, draw a ball to assign each patient, and after each outcome add a ball for the treatment that succeeded (or for the other treatment after a failure). As the urn drifted toward ECMO, one infant was assigned to CMT and died, and the other eleven were assigned to ECMO and all survived. The final tally was 11 of 11 on ECMO and 0 of 1 on CMT, with intracerebral hemorrhage in 1 of the 11 ECMO infants ( Bartlett et al. 1985 ) . A Fisher exact test of 11 of 11 against 0 of 1 gives a one-sided \(p = 1/12 = 0.083\) , and Ware and Epstein ( Ware and Epstein 1985 ) commented on the trial in the same journal.

title: The controversy
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3.2 The controversy
text: The controversy Ware ( Ware 1989 ) used the trial as a case study of the difficulties of investigating therapies of potentially great benefit. The difficulty is specific. The conclusion that ECMO works rests on twelve infants, and the comparison with control rests on one death. A reader who accepts the trial does so largely because they already believe ECMO works and because the historical mortality of such infants was dreadful, and a reader who does not believe it can reasonably say that the trial did not provide the evidence. The design that was meant to reconcile ethics with science had allocated the information away from the comparison. The ethics of randomizing in such a case is treated as a problem of statistical inference by Royall ( 1991 ) , who describes the randomized trial as a scientific and ethical dilemma and notes that statisticians have tended to emphasize only one side of it. The Bayesian reading, as discussed by Kass and Greenhouse in their commentary ( Kass and Greenhouse 1989 ) and by Berry on the ethics ( Berry 1989 ) , is more forgiving in one respect: the posterior depends on the data observed and not on the rule that produced them. With uniform priors the posteriors are \(\mathrm{Beta}(12,1)\) for ECMO and \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,2)\) for CMT, and the posterior probability that ECMO is better

title: The Harvard two-stage trial
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3.3 The Harvard two-stage trial
text: The Harvard two-stage trial The comment on the Michigan trial was that it could not settle the question, and the Harvard group (Boston Children’s Hospital) designed a second trial with that in mind ( O’Rourke et al. 1989 ) . In the first phase infants were randomized between ECMO and CMT until a fourth death had occurred in one arm. That happened on the CMT arm: 9 of 9 ECMO infants survived against 6 of 10 on CMT. In the second phase the next 20 infants all received ECMO and 19 survived, so that overall 28 of 29 ECMO infants survived against 6 of 10 on CMT. The trial report is O’Rourke et al. ( O’Rourke et al. 1989 ) ; the analysis that made it a teaching case is Ware’s ( Ware 1989 ) . The first phase alone has a one-sided Fisher \(p\) of 0.054, just short of the conventional bar, and the data from the second phase cannot be used in a randomized comparison because they were not randomized.

title: The UK collaborative trial
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3.4 The UK collaborative trial
text: The UK collaborative trial The question was settled by a conventional randomized trial in the United Kingdom ( UK Collaborative ECMO Trial Group 1996 ) . It enrolled 185 infants in 55 hospitals from 1993 to 1995 and compared referral to one of five ECMO centers with continued conventional care. It was stopped early on the advice of the data monitoring committee. Thirty of 93 infants allocated to ECMO died against 54 of 92 allocated to conventional care, a relative risk of 0.55 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.77, \(p = 0.0005\) ), or about one extra survivor for every three to four infants allocated to ECMO. (Only 84% of those allocated to ECMO received it, so this is an intention-to-treat comparison of a referral policy.)
