title: What the rule did to the information
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3.6 What the rule did to the information
text: What the rule did to the information The design question is cleaner than the argument about whether ECMO works. Under a randomized play-the-winner rule, how many patients end up on the control arm, and how much power does the trial have? The simulation below runs the urn with 12 infants and true survival 0.80 on ECMO and 0.20 on CMT, the extreme scenario the SIM paper uses as a stress test ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) , and compares it with a fixed 6:6 trial analyzed by a one-sided Fisher exact test at level 0.025. Show the R code u <- rar_ecmo_urn ( reps = 20000 , n = 12 , p = c ( 0.2 , 0.8 ), m = 2000 , seed = 14 ) Play-the-winner puts on average about 3.7 of the 12 infants on CMT, and in about 11 percent of trials at most one, which is the situation in which a comparison is essentially impossible. Its power is 0.15, against 0.29 for a fixed 6:6 split, and neither is a trial anyone would call adequate (twelve patients is not a sample size at which any test can detect even a large effect with confidence, and the true advantage assumed here is huge). The point of the numbers is the direction. The rule gave more infants the treatment the investigators believed in, and it did so at the cost of the information the trial was meant to produce. That is the pattern of every RAR design: the benefit is in-trial reward, the price is terminal information.

title: The aftermath and what it means for design
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3.7 The aftermath and what it means for design
text: The aftermath and what it means for design A frequentist re-expression of the same logic appears in the later EOLIA trial of ECMO for adult ARDS ( Combes et al. 2018 ) , whose primary analysis gave \(p = 0.09\) . A Bayesian reanalysis reported 88 to 99 percent posterior probability that ECMO reduces mortality, depending on the prior ( Goligher et al. 2018 ) . As the SIM paper puts it, this is a model-dependent re-expression of evidence, not a resolution. The SIM paper also treats the ECMO data as a prior-sensitivity stress test for a backward-induction stopping design ( Chapter 15 ), with a \(\mathrm{Beta}(4,16)\) prior for CMT and a \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) prior for ECMO. That analysis is explicitly not a reconstruction of the play-the-winner trial and not a proposed design: it asks what a pre-specified Bayesian rule would have concluded and how fast, and it finds that with an extreme generating effect and an asymmetric historical prior the rule stops after a handful of patients per arm. Its warning is the one to carry forward. Extreme early data and an informative prior can make a rule stop almost immediately, and a protocol must show, by simulation, that this is the behavior it wants ( Chapter 14 ). The lessons of ECMO for RAR are three. A rule that reacts to a few early

title: The aftermath and what it means for design
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.3.7 The aftermath and what it means for design
text: make a rule stop almost immediately, and a protocol must show, by simulation, that this is the behavior it wants ( Chapter 14 ). The lessons of ECMO for RAR are three. A rule that reacts to a few early outcomes can move allocation sharply on very little evidence. The treatment that looks best early is not always best, and an urn that has drifted toward it will take a long time to correct the error. And the argument over whether the evidence was adequate is an argument about the comparison, which was thin because the design starved it.

title: The case against, in two arms
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.4.1 The case against, in two arms
text: The case against, in two arms By the 2010s the experience with Bayesian adaptive randomization in oncology produced a set of published criticisms that the practitioners of RAR now regard as the fair statement of its costs. Korn and Freidlin ( Korn and Freidlin 2011 ) argued that in two-arm trials outcome-adaptive randomization offers little over equal allocation, while its costs in efficiency and logistics are real. Thall, Fox and Wathen ( P. Thall, Fox, and Wathen 2015 ) collected the scientific and ethical objections, among them lower power for a given sample size, highly variable arm sizes, a non-trivial chance of putting more patients on the inferior arm than equal allocation would have, and sensitivity to time trends, and they questioned whether the ethical gain that motivates RAR survives these defects. Hey and Kimmelman ( 2015 ) argue that the ethical advantage claimed for outcome-adaptive allocation does not survive scrutiny in two-armed or early-phase studies. The summaries here follow the papers’ main arguments and are not exhaustive. Wathen and Thall ( Wathen and Thall 2017 ) followed with a simulation study of multi-arm trials, and Proschan and Evans ( Proschan and Evans 2020 ) titled their review as advice: resist the temptation. The balanced review of Robertson and coauthors ( Robertson et al. 2023 ) separates the myths from the practical considerations and arrives at guidance that this chapter follows: use a burn-in, restrict extreme allocation, model time trends, and justify the ethical claim explicitly.

title: The case for, and the replies
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.4.2 The case for, and the replies
text: The case for, and the replies The critiques have replies, and a fair account gives them. Berry and Eick ( 1995 ) analyzed adaptive assignment against balanced randomization as a decision problem whose objective is to treat as many patients, in and out of the trial, as effectively as possible. Randomization is satisfactory when the disease is at least moderately common, and adaptive procedures can play a role when a substantial proportion of all patients with the disease are in the trial. That is the premise the later simulations test, and, on our reading, the two-arm trials of the critique are mostly settings with a large population outside the trial. Villar, Robertson, and Rosenberger ( 2020 ) is a reply to the review of Proschan and Evans, and Villar, Bowden, and Wason ( 2018 ) propose response-adaptive designs for binary responses that keep patient benefit while being robust to time trends. Lee, Chen, and Yin ( 2012 ) revisited the usefulness of outcome-adaptive randomization, and Wason and Trippa ( 2014 ) compared Bayesian adaptive randomization with multi-stage designs for multi-arm trials, which puts the cost of RAR against alternatives that also drop arms early. On our reading the case is weakest in a two-arm confirmatory trial with a large outside population, and strongest with several arms and a small population ( Section 16.6 ), provided

title: The case for, and the replies
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.4.2 The case for, and the replies
text: of RAR against alternatives that also drop arms early. On our reading the case is weakest in a two-arm confirmatory trial with a large outside population, and strongest with several arms and a small population ( Section 16.6 ), provided the ethical claim is made explicitly and the design guards against drift ( Section 16.5 ). This is not a point of agreement: P. Thall, Fox, and Wathen ( 2015 ) and Wathen and Thall ( 2017 ) argue that the problems persist with several arms.

title: Reproducing the critique
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.4.3 Reproducing the critique
text: Reproducing the critique We simulate the two-arm trial of the Polson and Sokolov example: 400 patients, response 0.30 on control and 0.45 on the experimental arm, binary outcome observed immediately, outcomes analyzed by a one-sided pooled \(z\) test of two proportions at \(\alpha = 0.025\) . Three allocation rules are compared. Equal 1:1 is the traditional design, here simple randomization with probability one half (permuted blocks would give exact balance within periods). Thompson uses the posterior probability that the experimental arm is better, recomputed after every batch of 20 patients. Capped Thompson adds a burn-in of the first 25 percent of patients at 1:1 and then bounds the allocation probability between 0.10 and 0.90 (the bounds are enforced exactly, with the probabilities still summing to one). The simulator is rar_simulate() in the package, wrapped by rar_two_arm() . We report the number of responders in the trial, the share of patients on the better arm, the number of patients on the inferior arm, the standard deviation of the number of patients on the better arm (how variable the design is from trial to trial), and power. The number of patients on the better arm has a standard deviation of about 41 from trial to trial, against 10 for equal allocation, which is the variability Thall and colleagues describe. In this scenario the effect is large, the outcome is immediate and the posterior converges quickly, and the costs that remain are power and variability. title: Reproducing the critique
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.4.3 Reproducing the critique
text: the trade is what Polson and Sokolov describe: for a 400-patient trial whose conclusion will govern treatment of many more patients, the loss of 14 to 26 points of power is not a trade a sponsor should accept in a confirmatory setting. Note Technical note: why power falls For a binary outcome the variance of the estimated difference is approximately \(p_1(1-p_1)/n_1 + p_0(1-p_0)/n_0\) , where \(n_1\) and \(n_0\) are the realized arm sizes. When allocation is driven by the data, \(n_0\) falls quickly once arm 1 looks better and the term \(p_0(1-p_0)/n_0\) dominates, so the standard error is much larger than that of the 1:1 design at the same total \(n\) . With 87 percent of 400 patients on the better arm, \(n_0 \approx 52\) and the standard error is about 1.4 times the 1:1 value. In addition \(n_0\) is random and correlated with the outcomes, which is why the nominal \(z\) test is no longer exactly standard normal under the null: the simulation below finds a type I error of about 0.049 for Thompson sampling, almost twice the nominal 0.025, even with no drift.

title: The mechanism
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.5.1 The mechanism
text: The mechanism RAR reacts to accumulating data, which means it reacts to chance. Under the null hypothesis, if the experimental arm happens to look better in the early patients, RAR sends it more of the later patients. Outcome-adaptive allocation can invalidate the naive analysis even without drift (the no-drift Thompson analysis above has type I error near 0.049 against a nominal 0.025). Changes in the patient population add confounding with calendar time. Suppose the background response rate rises during enrollment, because the standard of care improves, the site mix changes, a referral pattern shifts, or a variant changes. The arm that benefited from early luck now receives more of the later, healthier patients, and it looks better still. The bias runs through allocation alone. Nothing about the treatment has changed, and the comparison of response rates is confounded with calendar time. This is the central practical objection to RAR in confirmatory trials, and it is the property that fixed allocation with permuted blocks was designed to defeat. The FDA draft on master protocols and the EMA draft both refer to the same mechanism: changes in the allocation probability over time introduce time-varying selection bias, so comparisons should use concurrent controls and the analysis can be hard to adjust.

title: Simulation
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.5.2 Simulation
text: Simulation We simulate a null trial (response 0.30 in both arms) in which the response probability of every patient rises linearly from \(0.30 - d/2\) at the first patient to \(0.30 + d/2\) at the last, with drift \(d\) from 0 to 0.30. In the larger values this is a very large change in the patient mix across enrollment; the range is chosen to show the shape of the effect and not to describe a typical trial. Two analyses are applied to each trial. The naive analysis is the pooled \(z\) test. The stratified analysis divides enrollment into four consecutive periods, forms the difference in response rates within each period, and combines them with Mantel-Haenszel-type weights. Type I error is the probability that the experimental arm is declared better at one-sided level 0.025. Rule d = 0 naive d = 0 stratified d = 0.2 naive d = 0.2 stratified Equal 1:1 0.025 0.025 0.026 0.026 Thompson 0.049 0.053 0.196 0.052 Capped Thompson 0.029 0.032 0.138 0.031 The pattern is clear. Under equal allocation, drift is harmless: the type I error stays at its nominal level even for a 30-point drift, because allocation does not depend on the outcomes, so each period contributes equally to both arms in expectation. Under Thompson sampling, the naive test has a type I error that climbs with the drift, from 0.049 with none to 0.196 at \(d = 0.2\) and 0.295 at \(d = 0.3\) , many times the nominal level. Capped Thompson reduces the problem (0.029 with no drift, 0.138 at \(d = 0.2\) ) but does not remove it. A trial that drifts by 20 points has roughly a one-in-seven chance of declaring a useless drug effective under capped Thompson, and roughly one in five under plain Thompson.

title: The fixes
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.5.3 The fixes
text: The fixes Three fixes are standard, and they should be pre-specified as a package. Stratify the analysis by enrollment period. If allocation probabilities are fixed within each period and the analysis compares arms only within a period, then the allocation within a period is independent of the outcomes in that period and each stratum is a valid comparison. The type I error stops growing with the drift, as the dashed lines show: 0.047 to 0.053 for Thompson (about twice nominal), 0.028 to 0.032 for capped Thompson. The remaining excess for plain Thompson (about 0.05, not 0.025) comes from allocation updating within a period and from small-count behavior of the \(z\) test, and is removed by calibrating the critical value by simulation ( Chapter 14 ). The price is power. In the no-drift table of the previous section, the stratified analysis has power 49% under Thompson and 64% under capped Thompson (the corresponding naive figures are 61% and 73%), because comparing within periods discards the information in between-period contrasts when allocation is unbalanced across them. Pre-specified adjustment for calendar time as a covariate in a regression model is the continuous counterpart, with the same trade. Burn-in and a cap. Start with a period of fixed 1:1 allocation, and keep the allocation probability away from 0 and 1. A burn-in prevents the first handful of outcomes from

title: The fixes
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.5.3 The fixes
text: model is the continuous counterpart, with the same trade. Burn-in and a cap. Start with a period of fixed 1:1 allocation, and keep the allocation probability away from 0 and 1. A burn-in prevents the first handful of outcomes from steering the whole trial, as the urn in ECMO did. A cap guarantees that every arm keeps contributing concurrent data, which is what makes later calendar-time adjustment possible. The cap reduced the type I error from 0.196 to 0.138 at \(d = 0.2\) in the table above, which is helpful but not sufficient alone. Keep the control allocation fixed. Hold the control arm at a pre-specified share, and let only the experimental arms trade patients. The comparison of each experimental arm with the control then rests on a control stream that is balanced in time. This keeps the control stream balanced in time and is the fix with the best operating characteristics in the multi-arm simulation below. It does not by itself make the design acceptable to regulators: the FDA master protocols draft describes a larger fixed control allocation as appropriate, but the ratio of each experimental arm to control still changes with the data, and the EMA draft recommends fixed ratios for every comparison of interest. In a two-arm trial there is nothing left to adapt once the control is fixed, which is the

title: The fixes
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.5.3 The fixes
text: each experimental arm to control still changes with the data, and the EMA draft recommends fixed ratios for every comparison of interest. In a two-arm trial there is nothing left to adapt once the control is fixed, which is the honest reason that two-arm RAR is hard to defend. A fourth route is to model the time trend instead of designing around it. The platform-trial literature smooths the control rate across calendar periods and borrows from non-concurrent controls with discounting, the Bayesian time machine of Saville et al. ( 2022 ) , which is developed in Chapter 20 . For multi-arm binary trials, Villar, Bowden, and Wason ( 2018 ) studied protected control allocation and found approximately nominal error under the time trends examined. They also assessed randomization-based inference and regression adjustment. The protocol should prespecify the allocation rule and analysis method, and simulations should assess plausible drift and any time-model misspecification. Tip In the protocol: pre-specifying a response-adaptive randomization rule If a protocol includes RAR, the statistical analysis plan should state, before the first patient is enrolled: the allocation rule in full (for Thompson-type rules, the formula, the tuning exponent if any, and the update frequency); the burn-in size and the lower and upper bound on each arm’s allocation probability; the share of patients on the control arm and whether it is fixed; the

title: The fixes
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.5.3 The fixes
text: rules, the formula, the tuning exponent if any, and the update frequency); the burn-in size and the lower and upper bound on each arm’s allocation probability; the share of patients on the control arm and whether it is fixed; the primary analysis, including how enrollment period or calendar time enters it, and the estimand (ICH E9(R1)); the simulation report: type I error under the null and under pre-specified drift scenarios (a monotone drift of at least 10 and up to 20 percentage points in the control response is a reasonable starting range), power, expected patients per arm, and the distribution of the allocation, not only its mean; how the allocation algorithm is shielded: who runs it, who sees the allocation probabilities, and how the sponsor’s blinding is preserved (the DMC charter of Chapter 23 ).

title: The multi-arm case
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.6.1 The multi-arm case
text: The multi-arm case The strongest argument for RAR is not the two-arm trial but the trial with several experimental arms (doses, regimens, or drugs) and a shared control. Two things differ. First, there are many inferior arms, so equal allocation wastes a larger share of the trial (75 percent of patients are on arms other than the best one in a four-arm trial with one best). Second, the comparison that matters, best arm against control, can be protected by fixing the control share while the experimental arms compete for the rest. This is the setting of I-SPY 2 ( Barker et al. 2009 ) and REMAP-CAP ( Angus et al. 2020 ) (both in Section 16.9 below, with BATTLE) and the one in which the review of Robertson and coauthors ( Robertson et al. 2023 ) finds the best case for RAR. Wathen and Thall ( Wathen and Thall 2017 ) study the multi-arm setting by simulation. We simulate a four-arm trial: a control at 0.30 and three experimental arms at 0.30, 0.40 and 0.50, 600 patients, with the same batch size of 20. The four rules are equal allocation, Thompson sampling with allocation proportional to the posterior probability that each arm is best (the multi-arm form of Thompson’s rule, which generalizes to arbitrary exponents as in Thall and Wathen ( P. F. Thall and

Two caveats keep the result honest. The power reported is for the best arm. The 0.40 arm

title: The multi-arm case
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.6.1 The multi-arm case
text: design that moves that sample to the contender, while the control comparison stays balanced in time, spends it on the question being asked. Two caveats keep the result honest. The power reported is for the best arm. The 0.40 arm gets less data under the adaptive rule than under equal allocation and its comparison with control has lower power, so if the question is to estimate every dose, equal allocation is the better design. And the result depends on the effect being large enough, and the endpoint fast enough, for the allocation to converge in the trial. With a delayed endpoint, the allocation moves on information that is months old, and the gain shrinks. A simulation that mimics the real lag between enrollment and outcome is a required part of the design report.

title: Dunnett-type and fixed control allocation
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.6.2 Dunnett-type and fixed control allocation
text: Dunnett-type and fixed control allocation The fixed control share in the fourth row is 1/4, the share equal allocation would give. The Dunnett sqrt(k) share for three experimental arms is 36.6 percent ( Table 16.2 ). A protocol that wants the best control comparison in a fixed design should use the latter, and a protocol with RAR among the experimental arms can choose any fixed share it can defend. The regulatory text asks for the choice to be justified and the ratio to be held fixed, and says nothing that requires either number. The extra control patients increase the power for every comparison with control and cost experimental-arm allocation, a trade the simulation report should show.

title: Where RAR fits
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.6.3 Where RAR fits
text: Where RAR fits The conditions under which a case for RAR can be made are those the simulations suggest and the literature endorses ( Robertson et al. 2023 ) . There are several experimental arms, so there is a lot to be saved from visibly inferior arms. The primary endpoint is observed quickly relative to the enrollment period, so allocation has something to learn from. The trial is large enough for the allocation to converge, and small enough in population that the in-trial benefit matters (a rare serious disease, an early-phase screening trial). The control share is fixed and concurrent controls are used. And the trial’s regulatory role is exploratory or seamless-with-confirmation, not the single confirmatory comparison of record. The platform designs of Chapter 20 and the dose-finding designs of Chapter 17 are where these conditions are most often met. Where they are not (two arms, a slow endpoint, a confirmatory objective) the traditional design wins, and a sponsor that chooses RAR anyway owes the regulator a simulation that shows what it buys.

title: What the regulators say
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.7 What the regulators say
text: 16.7 What the regulators say The regulatory texts agree on the principle and differ on strictness. The principle is that RAR is an adaptive design feature and so falls under the general requirements for adaptive designs: prospective planning, control of the false positive rate, reliable estimation, and integrity of the trial. The differences are in how much the text expects a sponsor to justify it. FDA, Adaptive Designs (2019). Changes to allocation fall within its definition of an adaptive design (anchor above; Chapter 3 ). The drift simulation above illustrates its warning that adaptive features can inflate the type I error probability, and it expects the analysis, not only the allocation, to be pre-specified, since an analysis that ignores how patients were assigned can be biased. It does not forbid RAR. It places the burden of proof on the sponsor. ICH E20 (draft, June 2025). For RAR in confirmatory trials the “clear and compelling justification” is the argument of Section 16.6 : why the adaptive design is better than a fixed one for this question, shown by simulation under realistic drift and delay. For a two-arm confirmatory trial, Table 16.8 and Table 16.9 are what a reviewer would produce to ask for the justification. FDA Bayesian draft (January 2026). Nothing in the Bayesian label relaxes the above. This chapter takes calibration by simulation as the

Nothing in the Bayesian label relaxes the above. This chapter takes calibration by simulation as the default (anchor above). A Bayesian design with RAR is a design with a Bayesian analysis and a data-dependent allocation, and the calibration by simulation ( Chapter 14 ) must include the allocation rule and the drift scenarios. A Bayesian analysis does not by itself solve the confounding of calendar time with arm in a drifting trial. The posterior is conditional on the data, which is why a Bayesian can say that the stopping rule is ignorable, but the model for those data must contain the drift for the posterior to be right. FDA master protocols (revised draft, June 2026). Its worked examples of ratio changes are fixed schemes in which the ratio changes as drugs enter or leave a platform, not changes driven by outcome data, so it does not address outcome-driven allocation there. It asks that the primary analysis use only concurrently eligible controls. EMA, draft reflection paper on confirmatory platform trials (October 2026). title: What the regulators say
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.7 What the regulators say
text: EMA, draft reflection paper on confirmatory platform trials (October 2026). The EMA text is the strictest: it reasons that changes in allocation probability over time can cause time-varying bias that is difficult to adjust for, and concludes that response-adaptive randomization is not supported in confirmatory platform trials. It is a draft. A sponsor with a global program should assume that RAR in the confirmatory trial of record will be queried in Europe. The draft’s conclusion concerns confirmatory platform trials; exploratory and seamless-stage uses still need case-specific justification and agency discussion. What changes is where the burden lies. Some designs, conventional or adaptive, permit analytic or exact recursive evaluation of their operating characteristics; designs with data-driven allocation generally require simulation. Both conventional and Bayesian designs require justification of the complete procedure, including the analysis, the multiplicity handling, the estimation and the operations. For the adaptive trial of this chapter the operating characteristics are known from the simulation report, so the sponsor must make the case, scenario by scenario.

title: Practical guidance
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.8 Practical guidance
text: 16.8 Practical guidance For a confirmatory two-arm trial, use fixed allocation. The simulations of this chapter and the critiques of Korn and Freidlin and of Thall and colleagues point the same way: at best a small gain to in-trial patients, a loss of power, and a new route to type I error inflation. If ethics requires protecting patients inside the trial, use a group sequential design with a futility and efficacy boundary ( Chapter 11 and Chapter 15 ), which achieves much of the saving without touching allocation. SHINE ( Section 16.9 ) paired a group sequential design with limited adaptive allocation. For a multi-arm trial or a platform, decide whether to adapt among experimental arms, and if so, fix the control share, include a burn-in, cap the allocation probabilities, analyze with concurrent controls, adjust for calendar time, and report type I error under drift, together with the power for each experimental arm and not only the best. Chapter 20 develops the platform setting, including how arms enter and leave. Chapter 17 develops the early-phase use, where Thall’s utility-based designs are the strongest case for RAR because the objective there is to choose a dose for the next trial. For a rare disease, where equal allocation means half of a handful of patients on an arm that may be inferior, a Bayesian design with RAR

For a rare disease, where equal allocation means half of a handful of patients on an arm that may be inferior, a Bayesian design with RAR can be the least bad option and may be the only one the community will accept. The same safeguards apply, and so does the warning from ECMO: the more extreme the allocation, the less information the trial produces about the comparison that regulators will have to judge.

title: In practice: four trials
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.9 In practice: four trials
text: 16.9 In practice: four trials The trials below use adaptive allocation, or sit next to it, in settings where the chapter’s conditions are partly met. The facts are from the primary reports cited in each subsection.

title: I-SPY 2
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.9.1 I-SPY 2
text: I-SPY 2 I-SPY 2 is a neoadjuvant breast cancer platform with ten prospectively defined biomarker signatures (all patients, HR+, HR-, HER2+, HER2-, MammaPrint high-2, and the four HER2 by HR combinations). Patients are classified into eight mutually exclusive subtypes defined by HR, HER2 and MammaPrint status for adaptive randomization, and efficacy and graduation are assessed in the ten overlapping signatures. The allocation probability of each experimental arm follows its current Bayesian probability of success in the subtype, so arms that look better receive more patients, while a fixed share of patients goes to control ( Park et al. 2016 ; Nanda et al. 2020 ) . No experimental arm exceeds 120 patients, and the model is a covariate-adjusted logistic regression on pathologic complete response (pCR) ( Park et al. 2016 ) . The graduation and futility rules, which are written in predictive probability, and the neratinib and pembrolizumab results are in Section 15.10 . The lesson for this chapter is the multi-arm one of Section 16.6 . Adaptation among experimental arms, with a concurrent control, serves a screening purpose, and the platform pays for it with a conservative graduation bar and a later confirmatory trial.

title: REMAP-CAP
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.9.2 REMAP-CAP
text: REMAP-CAP REMAP-CAP ( Angus et al. 2020 ) is a platform in which several domains of treatment are randomized at once, and its protocol allows response-adaptive updating of allocation within a domain. What is documented are the Bayesian stopping triggers in the interleukin-6 receptor antagonist domain ( REMAP-CAP Investigators et al. 2021 ) : efficacy if the posterior probability of an odds ratio above 1 against control exceeds 99 percent, futility if the probability of an odds ratio above 1.2 is below 5 percent, with neutral priors and a hierarchical model that nests tocilizumab and sarilumab under an overall IL-6 effect. At the interim analysis of 28 October 2020, tocilizumab met the efficacy criterion (posterior probability 99.75 percent, odds ratio 1.87, 95 percent credible interval 1.20 to 2.76), and assignment to control closed on 19 November. The final adjusted odds ratio on organ-support-free days was 1.64 (1.25 to 2.14) for tocilizumab. Here the adaptation is in the stopping rule, a posterior probability, and the report was made while the platform kept running. The lesson is the one the drift simulation teaches: the analysis adjusts for 2-week time epochs, site and age, which is the calendar-time adjustment that adaptive allocation requires.

title: BATTLE
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.9.3 BATTLE
text: BATTLE BATTLE ( Kim et al. 2011 ; the design is in Zhou et al. 2008 ) was a biopsy-mandated trial of pretreated advanced non-small cell lung cancer with about 255 patients and four treatments (erlotinib, vandetanib, erlotinib plus bexarotene, sorafenib). After an initial period of equal randomization, a Bayesian probit model moved allocation toward the treatments performing better within biomarker groups. It is described as the first completed biomarker-based, adaptively randomized trial in this disease. An earlier Bayesian adaptive randomization design for recurrent glioblastoma, evaluated retrospectively on four phase 2 trials, is Trippa et al. ( 2012 ) . The lesson is the caution of Section 16.6 and Section 16.5 : allocation among treatments inside small biomarker strata moves on little data, so the burn-in, the cap and an analysis that respects calendar time matter more, not less.

title: SHINE and its Bayesian re-analysis
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > 16.9.4 SHINE and its Bayesian re-analysis
text: SHINE and its Bayesian re-analysis SHINE (NCT01369069) compared intensive with standard glucose control for 72 hours in acute ischemic stroke with hyperglycemia. Its design combined group sequential stopping with response-adaptive randomization, and it was not a Bayesian trial. It found no significant difference in favorable 90-day outcome, and severe hypoglycemia occurred in 15 of 581 patients (2.6 percent) on intensive treatment ( Johnston et al. 2019 ) . A later paper compared the Bayesian adaptive design developed in the ADAPT-IT project with the frequentist design that was used, in a retrospective comparison ( Broglio et al. 2022 ) . The lesson is regulatory in tone: a confirmatory-scale trial can combine a classical error-controlled stopping rule with limited adaptation of allocation, which is the conservative end of what Section 16.7 describes, and a Bayesian alternative is judged against it by simulation and not by assertion. Tip Try it in the lab Open Module 9, https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/09-adaptive-bayesian.html , and go to “Send more patients to the winner” (control 30 percent, new drug 50 percent). Before running a trial, predict how many more successes Thompson sampling will give than the 80 expected from an equal split of 200 patients, then run ten more trials and check. Then open the Studio, https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/14-studio.html , switch the allocation from fixed to adaptive and add a drifting scenario: read the operating-characteristics table for power and type I error. The lab shows the gain in successes, and the book and the Studio show the price.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > Key points
text: Key points Fixed 1:1 allocation is the default because it maximizes power for a given total, makes the randomization distribution exact, and balances calendar time within blocks. Unequal fixed ratios cost 12.5 percent more patients at 2:1 and a third more at 3:1. Allocation is a bandit problem. Thompson sampling assigns each patient to an arm with probability equal to its posterior probability of being best. The Gittins index solves the discounted infinite-horizon problem exactly, and the Lai-Robbins bound says the best possible regret grows like \(\log T\) . The logarithm that governs bandit regret is the same logarithm that governs the Bayes sequential boundary: \(n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \tfrac12\log n\) against \(\mathbb{E}[N_i]\,\mathrm{KL}_i \sim \log T\) for asymptotically optimal policies (Polson and Sokolov). Repeated marginal tests at an unchanged cutoff fail in both. The analogy is exact for the scale and does not transfer as design advice, because regret is a loss in the trial and confirmatory power is a property of the final decision. In a two-arm trial of 400 patients (0.30 against 0.45), Thompson sampling adds about 22 responders and cuts power from about 88% to about 61%, with much larger variation in the arm sizes. Drift in the response rate over enrollment breaks RAR. With a 20-point drift the type I error of the naive test is about 0.196 under Thompson sampling and 0.138

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 16: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits > Key points
text: to about 61%, with much larger variation in the arm sizes. Drift in the response rate over enrollment breaks RAR. With a 20-point drift the type I error of the naive test is about 0.196 under Thompson sampling and 0.138 under capped Thompson against 0.025 nominal, and it is unaffected under equal allocation. Stratifying the analysis by enrollment period removes the effect of drift (capped Thompson about 0.031; plain Thompson stays near 0.05 until the critical value is calibrated by simulation), at a cost in power. In a multi-arm trial with a fixed control share, a burn-in and a cap, RAR gave about 24 more responders, about half of the patients on the best arm, and higher power for the best arm than equal allocation, reported for the period-stratified analysis (93% against 87%) with its type I error under drift (1.4%); the naive analysis of the same design has type I error 3.4% and its power is not claimable. ECMO illustrates the cost of aggressive allocation: play-the-winner moved nearly all infants to one arm and starved the comparison that the trial existed to make. Regulators accept RAR as an adaptive feature subject to FDA 2019 and E20 (clear and compelling justification, limited adaptations), expect simulation including time trends, and describe a larger fixed control share as appropriate (which protects control accrual but does not by

text: accept RAR as an adaptive feature subject to FDA 2019 and E20 (clear and compelling justification, limited adaptations), expect simulation including time trends, and describe a larger fixed control share as appropriate (which protects control accrual but does not by itself establish acceptability of adaptive allocation among experimental arms). The EMA draft of October 2026 recommends fixed allocation ratios and concludes that response-adaptive randomization is not supported in confirmatory platform trials. Note Discussion questions A sponsor proposes 2:1 allocation to the experimental arm in a two-arm confirmatory trial because “patients prefer it”. What does the 2:1 design cost in sample size for the same power, and is that cost the same as the cost of a data-driven shift to 2:1 halfway through enrollment? Which of the two does the FDA 2019 guidance treat as an adaptive design? In the drift simulation, equal allocation has the right type I error at any drift and Thompson sampling does not. Explain in words why blocking in calendar time protects the first and why data-dependent allocation exposes the second. What would you add to the SAP to defend a Thompson design against this objection? In the four-arm simulation, the adaptive design with a fixed control has higher power for the best arm than equal allocation, while in the two-arm simulation every adaptive rule has lower power. What is different?

title: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17 Dose Finding and Dose Optimization
text: Every drug that reaches a confirmatory trial has already been given a dose, and that dose was chosen on very little data. A first-in-human trial may enroll twelve to thirty patients, and the dose that comes out of it is carried into trials of hundreds or thousands. If the dose is too high, patients are harmed and the product may be approved at a dose that later has to be reduced. If it is too low, an effective drug is lost. The statistical problem is small in sample size and large in consequence, which is where a Bayesian design has its clearest case: the data are scarce, the decisions are sequential, and the regulator has long expected, and in its August 2024 oncology guidance restated, that the dose be chosen on more than the highest tolerable level. This chapter starts with the design most clinicians have actually run, the 3+3, and simulates it so that its operating characteristics are on the table rather than in folklore. It then introduces the model-based and model-assisted designs one at a time (the continual reassessment method, the Bayesian optimal interval design, escalation with overdose control), each as a change to the same trial and judged on the same scenarios. It moves from toxicity-only designs to designs that weigh efficacy against toxicity, which is where the regulatory conversation has gone,

It moves from toxicity-only designs to designs that weigh efficacy against toxicity, which is where the regulatory conversation has gone, and it ends with seamless designs that carry the dose decision into the confirmatory stage, a comparison of the designs, and five real development programs. Chapter 14 supplies the general simulation discipline used here, and Chapter 16 treats response-adaptive randomization, which dose-finding designs resemble but do not copy. title: What a phase 1 trial in oncology is for
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.1.1 What a phase 1 trial in oncology is for
text: What a phase 1 trial in oncology is for A phase 1 trial of a cytotoxic cancer drug answers a narrow question. Doses of the drug are fixed in advance on an ascending ladder, say six levels. Patients are enrolled in small cohorts. At each dose, a patient either does or does not experience a dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), a prespecified adverse event within a prespecified window, usually the first cycle. The goal is to find the maximum tolerated dose (MTD), the highest dose whose DLT probability is acceptable. The acceptable level is a target toxicity rate , commonly 0.20 to 0.33. This chapter uses \(\Gamma = 0.25\) for the target and writes \(p_d\) for the true DLT probability at dose level \(d\) . The reasoning behind the aim is old. For cytotoxic drugs, both efficacy and toxicity were expected to increase with dose, so the highest tolerable dose was expected to be the most active one.

title: The rule
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.1.2 The rule
text: The rule The 3+3 design is the rule-based method that grew out of this setting, and it is still the most commonly used phase 1 design ( Le Tourneau, Lee, and Siu 2009 ) . It has no model. A dose-escalation rule, with no probability anywhere in it, tells the investigator what to do. Treat three patients at the current dose. If none of the three has a DLT, move to the next higher dose. If one of the three has a DLT, treat three more at the same dose. If at most one of the six has a DLT, move up. If two or more of the six have a DLT, stop. If two or more of the first three have a DLT, stop. When the trial stops at dose \(d\) , the MTD is declared to be the dose below, \(d-1\) . If it stops at the lowest dose, no dose is declared tolerable. If the highest dose is cleared by rule 2 or 3, it is recommended. This is the variant simulated here. It has no step in which three or more additional patients are treated at the dose below the stopping dose to confirm it, and variants that add one (to have at least six patients at the declared MTD) will select somewhat differently. The up-and-down idea behind the rule goes

title: The rule
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.1.2 The rule
text: additional patients are treated at the dose below the stopping dose to confirm it, and variants that add one (to have at least six patients at the declared MTD) will select somewhat differently. The up-and-down idea behind the rule goes back to Dixon and Mood ( 1948 ) , and Storer ( 1989 ) formalized and analyzed the traditional algorithm-based designs and proposed alternatives. The accelerated titration designs of Simon et al. ( 1997 ) initially used single-patient cohorts, reverting to conventional cohorts after one DLT or two grade 2 toxicities, with the assessment period depending on the variant. Their simulations showed fewer patients treated at low doses. The 3+3 design is attractive for good reasons. It is easy to explain to a clinical team and an ethics committee. Nobody needs software. It never escalates after seeing two DLTs in a cohort.

title: Operating characteristics, by simulation
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.1.3 Operating characteristics, by simulation
text: Operating characteristics, by simulation The rule has no stated target toxicity rate. We can, however, ask what target it implies and what it does in practice. Operating characteristics are the currency of this book, and for the 3+3 they are most easily found by simulation (exact enumeration of the rule is also possible ( Reiner, Paoletti, and O’Quigley 1999 ; Y. Lin and Shih 2001 ) ), which is a few lines of code (the package functions dose_three_plus_three() and dose_simulate() do the work, and the rule itself is a short function). We use the three scenarios with six dose levels shown in Table 17.1 . In each, the true DLT probabilities are fixed, and the true MTD is the highest dose with \(p_d \le 0.25\) . In scenario A the MTD is dose 3. In scenario B toxicity is low until late and the MTD is dose 5. In scenario C the MTD is dose 2. We run 2,000 simulated trials per design and scenario (the 3+3 check below uses 5,000 trials in scenario A alone). title: What six patients can tell you
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.1.4 What six patients can tell you
text: What six patients can tell you Most of the cost of the 3+3 is not in the rule but in the information it leaves behind. A trial that ends with one DLT in six patients at the recommended dose is described in the protocol as showing a “tolerable” dose. The thinness of what a 3+3 trial learns has been shown by exact enumeration of the rule ( Reiner, Paoletti, and O’Quigley 1999 ; Y. Lin and Shih 2001 ) and in comparison with the CRM ( Iasonos et al. 2008 ) , and is discussed in our working paper ( Polson and Sokolov 2026b ) ; the arithmetic below is a Bayesian version of the same point. Take the prior on the DLT probability to be Beta(0.25, 0.75) (a weakly informative prior with prior mean 0.25 and the weight of one prior patient). One DLT in six patients gives a Beta(1.25, 5.75) posterior. The same trial that is reported as having “found” a dose with a one-in-six observed DLT rate is compatible, at that level, with a DLT rate that is half. A frequentist exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval for one in six is wider still (roughly 0.004 to 0.64), so the problem is the sample size and not the Bayesian treatment of it. The designs below do not repair this by magic. They do three things: they use every patient treated at every dose (the 3+3 forgets all previous doses when it moves), they state the target toxicity rate, and they let the sample size be chosen deliberately instead of by the stopping rule.

title: What stays the same
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.1.5 What stays the same
text: What stays the same A fair summary of the 3+3: it is simple, transparent and safe in the sense that few patients are exposed to high doses, at the price of a low chance of finding the MTD and a poor estimate of the DLT rate at the dose it recommends. For a trial of a drug with a well-understood toxicity profile and a small number of doses, a team may reasonably choose it. Simulation makes the consequences of choosing the 3+3 explicit and supports the design justification, because the simulation above is exactly the evidence on which it should be judged.

title: The Bayesian version: model-based and model-assisted designs
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2 The Bayesian version: model-based and model-assisted designs
text: 17.2 The Bayesian version: model-based and model-assisted designs Chapter 6 updated a belief about a probability with data. A dose-finding design is that same update, repeated after every cohort and used to choose the next dose. The Bayesian designs differ from the 3+3 in two ways. They name a target toxicity rate \(\Gamma\) . And they assume that the DLT probability increases with dose, so information at one dose informs the neighboring ones. They differ from one another in how much of that structure they use.

title: The continual reassessment method
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.1 The continual reassessment method
text: The continual reassessment method The continual reassessment method (CRM) of O’Quigley, Pepe and Fisher ( O’Quigley, Pepe, and Fisher 1990 ) was the first Bayesian design in phase 1 and remains the reference model-based design. In its simplest form it posits a one-parameter curve through \(K\) doses, \[ p_d(a) = \pi_d^{\exp(a)}, \qquad d = 1, \dots, K, \] where \(\pi_1 < \dots < \pi_K\) is a prespecified skeleton (a set of guessed DLT probabilities, one per dose) and \(a\) is an unknown parameter with a prior, here \(a \sim N(0, 1.34)\) . After each cohort, the posterior of \(a\) is computed from the data at all doses, and the next cohort is given the dose whose posterior mean DLT probability is closest to \(\Gamma\) . Two safety rules are standard: no skipping a dose when escalating, and a stopping rule if the lowest dose is judged too toxic. The original proposal treats one patient at a time; the version in use adds cohorts, no skipping of untried doses and a start at the lowest dose ( Goodman, Zahurak, and Piantadosi 1995 ) . The likelihood version ( O’Quigley and Shen 1996 ) and the book of Cheung ( 2011 ) popularized the power working model used here, and Garrett-Mayer ( 2006 ) is a tutorial. The consequence for the protocol is that the sponsor now

title: The continual reassessment method
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.1 The continual reassessment method
text: version ( O’Quigley and Shen 1996 ) and the book of Cheung ( 2011 ) popularized the power working model used here, and Garrett-Mayer ( 2006 ) is a tutorial. The consequence for the protocol is that the sponsor now writes down a skeleton and a prior, which the 3+3 never needed. The skeleton is not the truth; it is a shape. The design uses the data to move the whole curve up or down. In our simulation the skeleton (0.05, 0.12, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70) is close to the truth in scenario A (it differs only at dose 2) and wrong in scenarios B and C; a real simulation report should include scenarios in which the skeleton is badly wrong. Note Technical note: the CRM posterior With \(y_d\) DLTs among \(n_d\) patients at dose \(d\) , the likelihood of \(a\) is \(\prod_d p_d(a)^{y_d}\{1-p_d(a)\}^{n_d - y_d}\) . The posterior \(\pi(a \mid y) \propto \pi(a) \prod_d p_d(a)^{y_d}\{1-p_d(a)\}^{n_d-y_d}\) is one-dimensional, so it is computed on a grid of a few hundred points (as dose_crm() does) and the posterior mean of each \(p_d(a)\) is a weighted sum over the grid. No MCMC is needed. The one-parameter form is deliberately rigid: it is well-behaved with few patients because it cannot fit anything but a monotone curve. Richer two-parameter logistic models, such as the Bayesian logistic regression model used with

title: The continual reassessment method
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.1 The continual reassessment method
text: the grid. No MCMC is needed. The one-parameter form is deliberately rigid: it is well-behaved with few patients because it cannot fit anything but a monotone curve. Richer two-parameter logistic models, such as the Bayesian logistic regression model used with escalation with overdose control ( Neuenschwander, Branson, and Gsponer 2008 ) , estimate the slope too and need informative priors to behave. The chapter’s code uses dose_crm() from the book’s package bayestrials , which is written for teaching and for the simulations here. For production work the maintained CRAN packages are the tools to use: dfcrm and trialr for CRM and related Bayesian designs, and BOIN for the Bayesian optimal interval designs below (the boundaries computed by dose_boin_bounds() agree with BOIN::get.boundary ). A sponsor’s statistical analysis plan should name the software and version that generated the simulation report.

title: The Bayesian optimal interval design
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.2 The Bayesian optimal interval design
text: The Bayesian optimal interval design The Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN) design of Liu and Yuan ( Liu and Yuan 2015 ) is a model-assisted design. It is derived from a Bayesian argument, but at the bedside it is a table. For each dose, the observed DLT rate \(\hat p_d = y_d/n_d\) is compared with two fixed boundaries. If \(\hat p_d \le \lambda_e\) , escalate; if \(\hat p_d \ge \lambda_d\) , de-escalate; otherwise stay. The boundaries are chosen to minimize the probability of a wrong decision between three simple hypotheses: the dose is at the target, it is below the target toxicity rate, at \(0.6\,\Gamma\) , or it is overly toxic at \(1.4\,\Gamma\) . The boundaries do not depend on the dose or on the number of patients treated. text: ]] * n - 1e-9 ), check.names = FALSE ), align = "ccc" ) Patients Escalate if DLTs at most De-escalate if DLTs at least 3 0 1 6 1 2 9 1 3 With cohorts of three, this rule says escalate on zero DLTs and de-escalate on one or more, which is more cautious than the 3+3 in the first cohort. A dose is eliminated, together with all higher ones, if the posterior probability that its DLT rate exceeds \(\Gamma\) exceeds 0.95 (with a uniform prior and at least three patients treated). At the end, the MTD is chosen as the dose whose isotonically smoothed DLT rate is closest to \(\Gamma\) . The smoothing follows the reference implementation ( BOIN::select.mtd ): isotonic regression with inverse posterior-variance weights, and, when two doses are equally close with rates below the target, the higher one. The practical appeal is that the protocol contains the same kind of table as the 3+3: a grid of numbers of DLTs and numbers of patients. A clinician needs no software on the day. The statistician has the operating characteristics, by simulation, in the design report. title: The other interval designs: mTPI, mTPI-2 and Keyboard
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.3 The other interval designs: mTPI, mTPI-2 and Keyboard
text: The other interval designs: mTPI, mTPI-2 and Keyboard BOIN is not the only design whose decisions are printed as a table. The toxicity probability interval designs divide the DLT-rate axis into an underdosing interval, an equivalence interval around the target and an overdosing interval. The first version is Ji, Li, and Bekele ( 2007 ) , and its modified form (mTPI) ( Ji et al. 2010 ) computes the posterior probability mass of each interval divided by the interval’s width and moves toward the interval with the largest value. The mTPI-2 design ( Guo et al. 2017 ) changes how the intervals are formed, in response to a weakness of mTPI that its authors frame as an Ockham’s razor problem. The Keyboard design ( Yan, Mandrekar, and Yuan 2017 ) lays equal-width keys, each as wide as the target interval, over the DLT-rate axis, and recommends the move toward the key with the highest posterior probability. As with BOIN, the protocol carries a table of decisions by number of DLTs and number treated, and the logic can be checked by hand. Which to choose is an empirical question, and the evidence is simulation. Horton, Wages, and Conaway ( 2017 ) compared the CRM, mTPI and BOIN on the percentage of correct selection of the true MTD, patient allocation near it and an accuracy index, and

Horton, Wages, and Conaway ( 2017 ) compared the CRM, mTPI and BOIN on the percentage of correct selection of the true MTD, patient allocation near it and an accuracy index, and Zhou, Yuan, and Nie ( 2018 ) compared several newer phase 1 designs on accuracy, safety and reliability. Those are comparisons in stated scenarios at stated sample sizes, like the comparison of this chapter, and the lesson is the same as for CRM and BOIN: the protocol should report the chosen design’s own operating characteristics in scenarios that include a badly placed target.

title: Comparing the designs

text: Comparing the designs Back to Table 17.2 . With 30 patients in cohorts of three, CRM selects the true MTD in about 52 to 71 percent of trials and BOIN in about 52 to 69 percent, against 36 to 41 percent for the 3+3. CRM and BOIN also make fewer under-selection errors, which is where the 3+3 loses most. But the table is honest in the other direction too. CRM and BOIN treat 30 patients, the 3+3 about 10 to 19. They therefore treat more patients at toxic doses in absolute terms (about 5 to 6 for CRM and BOIN against about 3 for the 3+3 in scenarios A and C) and see more DLTs. title: Escalation with overdose control
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.5 Escalation with overdose control
text: Escalation with overdose control Escalation with overdose control (EWOC) ( Babb, Rogatko, and Zacks 1998 ) changes the criterion for the next dose. Instead of the dose whose estimated DLT rate is closest to \(\Gamma\) , EWOC chooses the highest dose for which the posterior probability of overdosing (exceeding the MTD) does not exceed a feasibility bound \(\eta\) (several doses may satisfy the constraint), often starting at 0.25 and raised as the trial proceeds. A dose that has some chance of being too toxic is therefore not the one most likely to be chosen. This builds a patient-safety constraint into the decision itself, which is one reason EWOC was an early attempt to give ethical control a formal expression. The Bayesian logistic regression model (BLRM) of Neuenschwander, Branson, and Gsponer ( 2008 ) applies the same overdose-control idea to interval probabilities of the DLT rate under a two-parameter logistic model with informative priors, and with either design the dose-escalation decisions then rest on a posterior that depends strongly on the prior, which the FDA draft on Bayesian methodology says should be justified and subjected to sensitivity analysis (see Chapter 8 ).

title: A worked escalation decision with the logistic model

text: A worked escalation decision with the logistic model To see what the posterior looks like at a decision point, take doses of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 mg with reference dose 8 mg, and the two-parameter logistic model \(\mathrm{logit}\,p(d) = \log\alpha + \beta \log(d/8)\) with \(\beta = e^{\log\beta}\) . The prior is \(\log\alpha \sim N(\mathrm{logit}\,0.25, 2^2)\) , which centers the toxicity rate at the reference dose on the target of 0.25 with wide uncertainty, and \(\log\beta \sim N(0, 1)\) . Four cohorts have been treated: 0 of 3 DLTs at 1 mg, 0 of 3 at 2 mg, 1 of 3 at 4 mg and 1 of 6 at 8 mg. Each dose is classified by its true DLT rate: underdosing below 0.16, target from 0.16 to 0.33, overdosing at 0.33 or above. title: Protocol language
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.2.7 Protocol language
text: Protocol language Tip In the protocol: a model-based dose-escalation design State the target toxicity rate \(\Gamma\) and the DLT definition and window. State the dose ladder, the starting dose, the cohort size and the maximum sample size. For CRM, give the skeleton and the prior on its parameter, with the reason for each. For BOIN, give the escalation and de-escalation boundaries and the elimination rule. State the no-skipping rule and the stopping rule for an overly toxic lowest dose. Attach a simulation report with at least five scenarios (including a flat-toxic scenario and one where the MTD is the top dose) with the probability of correct selection, the probability of overdose selection, the number of patients at doses above the target, and the sensitivity of each to the skeleton or prior. Specify who can override the design’s recommendation (usually a safety review committee) and in what circumstances, for example when late toxicities, or toxicities after the DLT window, appear. See Chapter 23 for the general protocol table.

title: Why the MTD is a poor target for modern agents
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.1 Why the MTD is a poor target for modern agents
text: Why the MTD is a poor target for modern agents The MTD paradigm assumes that more is better until it hurts. That was a reasonable working belief for cytotoxic chemotherapy, and it was written into the designs above, which look only at toxicity. It is a poor assumption for targeted therapies, immunotherapies and antibody-drug conjugates. For such agents the dose-response curve for efficacy may reach a plateau well below the MTD, a drug may be taken for months or years rather than for a few cycles, and chronic low-grade toxicity may lead to dose reductions and discontinuations that cannot be seen in a short DLT window. A dose chosen as the MTD can then be both more toxic and no more effective than a lower one. The FDA’s stated concern is that choosing the dose this way can leave patients on doses with more toxicity and no more benefit than a lower dose ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024 ) . The rationale for the initiative is set out by FDA authors in Shah et al. ( 2021 ) , and the statistical principles, with a review of FDA initial approvals of small molecules and antibody-drug conjugates in 2019 to 2021, in Fourie Zirkelbach et al. ( 2022 ) .

title: What the FDA guidance asks
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.2 What the FDA guidance asks
text: What the FDA guidance asks The final guidance of August 2024 (docket FDA-2022-D-2827, Oncology Center of Excellence with CDER and CBER) has a stated scope. The guidance does not address first-in-human starting-dose selection. It does not specifically address dosage optimization for radiopharmaceuticals, cellular and gene therapies, oncolytic viruses, microbiota or cancer vaccines, or pediatric development, although some recommendations may apply to these settings. Developed through Project Optimus, launched in 2021 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021 , 2024 ) , the guidance recommends that sponsors of oncology products take a dose selection approach different from that of the 3+3. In paraphrase, and the guidance should be consulted for the precise wording, it recommends the following. Doses to be taken to registrational trials should be chosen on a broader basis than the MTD alone: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, exposure-response for efficacy and safety, and clinical safety, tolerability and activity, including late and low-grade toxicities. Dose-ranging in the clinic should compare several dosages, and where feasible with randomization, rather than rely on a single-arm escalation to one dose. The comparison is intended to characterize the dose-response and dose-toxicity relationships, not to establish superiority or noninferiority of one dose over another at registrational error rates. Model-based and model-informed methods, including Bayesian ones, are expected to be useful in this process, and sponsors should discuss the design with FDA early.

title: What the FDA guidance asks
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.2 What the FDA guidance asks
text: relationships, not to establish superiority or noninferiority of one dose over another at registrational error rates. Model-based and model-informed methods, including Bayesian ones, are expected to be useful in this process, and sponsors should discuss the design with FDA early. The guidance does not require a specific design, and neither does it exclude the 3+3. Dose selection should be explained in the context of the intended population and the treatment’s schedule. ICH E4 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 1994 ) already established these principles: the dose-response relationship should be characterized during development, several dose-response designs (including Bayesian and pharmacometric methods) are discussed, prospective randomized multidose studies are recommended, and the highest tolerated dose need not be optimal even in life-threatening disease. The August 2024 guidance gives them a focused application to contemporary oncology dosage optimization. For the exposure-response models that support the choice, ICH M15 ( International Council for Harmonisation 2026 ) is the framework. A sponsor who uses a model to select between two doses has to state the question of interest and the context of use, and assess how much weight the model carries in the decision and how costly a wrong decision would be.

title: A Bayesian formulation: utility
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.3 A Bayesian formulation: utility
text: A Bayesian formulation: utility A Bayesian can state the dose problem directly. Let \(\pi_E(x)\) be the probability of a favorable efficacy outcome at dose \(x\) and \(\pi_T(x)\) the probability of a toxicity. Elicit a utility for each of the four joint outcomes, as in the utility-based designs described in our working paper ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) : efficacy without toxicity is the best, no efficacy and toxicity the worst, with efficacy and toxicity together somewhere in between. The expected utility of a dose is the average of these utilities under the posterior. A design chooses the dose that maximizes it, among those that are acceptable : meeting a minimum efficacy and a maximum toxicity bound at a stated posterior probability. title: EffTox and phase 1/2 designs
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.4 EffTox and phase 1/2 designs
text: EffTox and phase 1/2 designs The EffTox design of Thall and Cook ( Thall and Cook 2004 ) formalizes this. It models efficacy and toxicity probabilities as functions of dose, with a quadratic logistic form for efficacy so that the dose-efficacy curve can turn down, a monotone logistic form for toxicity, and a copula for the association between the two outcomes in the same patient ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) . Rather than ask for utilities for four outcomes, the original EffTox design elicits a trade-off contour in the plane of \((\pi_T, \pi_E)\) : the investigator names several pairs of efficacy and toxicity probabilities that are equally desirable. A dose is acceptable if its posterior probabilities satisfy the minimum efficacy and maximum toxicity constraints, and the next cohort receives the acceptable dose with the highest desirability. Early phase 1/2 designs of this kind are described in Thall and Russell ( 1998 ) . Later work extends the utility approach to ordinal efficacy and toxicity outcomes and combinations of agents, including the utility-based combination design of Houede and colleagues ( Houédé et al. 2010 ) and an adaptive-randomization version for bivariate ordinal outcomes ( Thall et al. 2015 ) . Book-length treatments are Yuan, Nguyen, and Thall ( 2016 ) and Thall ( 2024 ) . Three things are different from the toxicity-only designs. The

title: EffTox and phase 1/2 designs
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.4 EffTox and phase 1/2 designs
text: and an adaptive-randomization version for bivariate ordinal outcomes ( Thall et al. 2015 ) . Book-length treatments are Yuan, Nguyen, and Thall ( 2016 ) and Thall ( 2024 ) . Three things are different from the toxicity-only designs. The trial needs a probabilistic model for efficacy , so it needs an efficacy endpoint that can be observed quickly enough to be used during the trial (a response, a biomarker, a PD measure). Early efficacy readouts that are only surrogate for the clinical endpoint bring a surrogacy question into the dose decision. The designs need larger samples, usually 40 to a few hundred. And the elicitation of the contour or utility is an extra step that must be defended. In return the trial can state what it says about the dose-response, and the dose that it picks is accompanied by a distribution of efficacy and toxicity at that dose.

title: Late-onset toxicity and utility-based interval designs
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.5 Late-onset toxicity and utility-based interval designs
text: Late-onset toxicity and utility-based interval designs The phase 1/2 designs above need the outcome of each cohort before the next one is dosed, which is the logistic problem of late-onset toxicity. The time-to-event CRM of Cheung and Chappell ( 2000 ) incorporates incomplete follow-up from patients without an observed DLT, commonly using the fraction of the observation window completed, while observed DLTs contribute full event information, so that enrollment need not pause while earlier patients are followed. Yuan et al. ( 2018 ) built the same idea into the interval design: TITE-BOIN allows real-time dose assignment for new patients while some enrolled patients’ toxicity data are still pending, and so addresses both late-onset toxicity, which is common for targeted agents and immunotherapy, and rapid accrual. For the efficacy-toxicity trade-off, BOIN12 of R. Lin et al. ( 2020 ) targets the optimal biologic dose that optimizes the risk-benefit trade-off, for agents whose efficacy does not necessarily increase with dose, and is built to be simple enough that its decision rules can be tabulated in the protocol as BOIN’s are. In the setting of Figure 17.2 , where efficacy plateaus below the MTD, for the illustrative true curves the MTD is dose 5 and expected utility is highest at dose 4. Yuan, Zhou, and Liu ( 2024 ) review the design strategies for dose-optimization trials and the practical considerations in planning them, including the randomized comparison the FDA guidance recommends.

title: Randomized dose comparison, and what a regulator will ask
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.3.6 Randomized dose comparison, and what a regulator will ask
text: Randomized dose comparison, and what a regulator will ask The guidance recommends comparing dosages directly, and a randomized comparison of two or three candidate doses after the escalation phase is the common implementation. The trial need not be powered for formal superiority or noninferiority between doses at registrational error rates. Its size should support sufficiently precise assessments of safety and antitumor activity at each dosage, and the doses are not expected to differ by much in efficacy, which is why the evidence is expected to include PK/PD, safety and tolerability, and modeling. A Bayesian formulation is to compute the posterior probability that each dose’s efficacy is within a prespecified margin of the best dose and the posterior probability that its tolerability is better, and to select the lowest dose that meets both, with simulated operating characteristics. The chapter on simulation ( Chapter 14 ) describes the report. For a design of this kind a reviewer is likely to ask the following. What are the operating characteristics for choosing a dose that is not the one that maximizes efficacy: the probability of selecting a dose that is too low or too toxic under each scenario? How were the utility, trade-off contour or margins elicited, and what changes if they are altered? What priors were used for the efficacy and toxicity models, and how much do they affect the dose choice? How are late toxicities and dose reductions after cycle 1 handled in the dose decision? What is the role of the exposure-response model ( Section 17.3 ) and how was its risk assessed under M15?

title: Dose-response estimation outside oncology: MCP-Mod
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.4 Dose-response estimation outside oncology: MCP-Mod
text: 17.4 Dose-response estimation outside oncology: MCP-Mod Most of this chapter concerns oncology, where the dose question is how much toxicity to accept. Most other programs run a phase 2 dose-ranging study whose question is the shape of the dose-response curve and which dose to take to phase 3. The traditional method that regulators know best here is MCP-Mod, which combines a multiple comparison step with a modeling step ( Bretz, Pinheiro, and Branson 2005 ; Pinheiro et al. 2014 ) . It is on FDA’s fit-for-purpose list with a determination of 26 May 2016 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025 ) , and it is the dose-finding method on that list that belongs to the frequentist tradition. The method has two steps. First, before the data, the protocol names a candidate set of dose-response shapes (for example linear, Emax, exponential and umbrella) with guessed parameters, and from each shape computes the contrast of the dose means that has the most power if that shape is true. The test of “no dose-response” is the maximum of these contrast statistics, and its critical value comes from their joint (multivariate normal or \(t\) ) distribution, so the familywise type I error over the candidate shapes is held at one-sided 0.025 when there is no dose-response at all. Second, if the test finds a signal, the models that

Second, if the test finds a signal, the models that passed are fitted, and the dose-response curve and a target dose (for example the smallest dose with a clinically relevant effect) are estimated, by selecting a model or by averaging. The test detects a non-flat dose-response in the directions of the candidates, not benefit at some dose. A declining truth can still trigger a contrast when the candidates allow declines, which is why the candidates are chosen as benefit shapes ( Bretz, Pinheiro, and Branson 2005 ) ; with the candidates here a harmful linear decline signals in only 0.015 of trials. The price is that the candidate set is a pre-specified list, and a truth outside it loses power; this is the dose-response counterpart of the skeleton choice for the CRM. The Bayesian designs in this chapter allocate and decide adaptively: ASTIN ( Grieve and Krams 2005 ; Krams et al. 2003 ) and the Bayesian dose selection in the lecanemab and AWARD-5 examples ( Section 17.8 ). title: Adaptive enrichment and subgroup-specific doses
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.5 Adaptive enrichment and subgroup-specific doses
text: 17.5 Adaptive enrichment and subgroup-specific doses When benefit, or the best dose, differs by a biomarker-defined subgroup, broad enrollment can dilute the effect estimates, and a single dose may be wrong for part of the population. An enrichment design starts with broad enrollment and restricts to responsive subgroups as data accumulate ( Polson and Sokolov 2026a ) . At each interim analysis, subgroup-specific posterior probabilities of benefit, \(\Pr(\theta_g > 0 \mid \text{data})\) for subgroup \(g\) , map to one of three actions: continue broadly, restrict enrollment to the promising subgroups, or stop. The thresholds that govern these actions are calibrated by simulation, which is exactly the procedure the FDA draft Bayesian guidance asks for ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . The multiplicity cost is real: subgroup-by-interim looks multiply the number of opportunities for a chance finding, and Chapter 10 describes the shrinkage and error-control tools that apply. Hierarchical models that borrow strength across subgroups ( Chapter 19 ) are the Bayesian answer to the same problem. For a dose-finding trial the usual practice is to treat the dose-selection and the enrichment decisions separately unless the trial is built for both.

title: Phase 2/3
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.6.1 Phase 2/3
text: Phase 2/3 A conventional program has a phase 2 dose-finding trial, a gap in which the sponsor analyzes the data, writes a new protocol and opens new sites, and a phase 3 trial. A seamless phase 2/3 design merges the two. A first stage compares several doses or regimens with a control and selects one or two on interim data, and a second stage continues into confirmation under a prespecified rule. The statistical machinery is older than the guidance: Thall, Simon, and Ellenberg ( 1988 ) proposed two-stage designs that select among treatments and then test, Stallard and Todd ( 2003 ) gave sequential phase III designs that select the most promising treatment at the first interim analysis, and Bretz et al. ( 2009 ) review confirmatory adaptive designs, including combined phase II/III studies with treatment selection at an interim. The common structure is selection at the interim followed by a pre-specified final test that accounts for the selection. In an inferentially seamless design, data from the first stage for the selected dose are used in the final test, so the analysis has to account for the fact that the dose was selected because it looked good. In an operationally seamless design, the stages run under a single protocol but the final analysis uses second-stage data only. The motivation is the elimination of the “dead

title: Phase 2/3
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.6.1 Phase 2/3
text: for the fact that the dose was selected because it looked good. In an operationally seamless design, the stages run under a single protocol but the final analysis uses second-stage data only. The motivation is the elimination of the “dead time” between phases, and the use of the trial’s own data to choose a dose rather than committing to a weak one. The price is complexity in the design, a need for a pre-specified selection rule, and the inferential adjustment. FDA’s adaptive design guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019 ) expects the selection rule, the control of the type I error probability, and the firewall that protects the unblinded interim data to be written down in advance, and treats seamless designs under the same principles as other adaptive designs. A simulation study of the inferentially seamless case in which one arm is selected at the end of the first stage found that pooling the two stages and using an adjusted final alpha, as in a group sequential design, does better than analyzing the second stage alone at full alpha, and slightly better than a combination test. It also found that putting roughly 30 to 50 percent of the patients in the first stage is close to optimal across a range of dose-response shapes ( L. R. Berry et al. 2024 ) . Two

Berry et al. 2024 ) . Two cautions apply to sizing. The power calculated for the arm that is eventually selected overstates the power of the design, because the first stage sometimes advances the wrong arm, so the true power must be found by simulating the selection. And when the first-stage endpoint is delayed, the patients enrolled while it matures belong to the cost of the first stage and the planned split should count them. The two best-documented cases of Bayesian dose finding that continues into later stages, dulaglutide (AWARD-5) and lecanemab, are described in Section 17.8 .
