text: model-dependent answer if the skeleton or prior is poor Utility elicitation, surrogate efficacy endpoint, larger sample What stays the same is that a dose-escalation design is a decision rule fixed before the first patient and judged by its operating characteristics, and that safety oversight by a committee with the power to override stays in place for every design. What changes is that the rule can use all the data, that the question can be about the benefit-risk trade-off, and that the evidence offered to the regulator is a simulation report and a model assessment, not an appeal to convention.

title: How often are model-based designs used, and does it matter?
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.1 How often are model-based designs used, and does it matter?
text: How often are model-based designs used, and does it matter? The 3+3 survives mostly out of habit. Model-based designs were used in 1.6 percent of phase 1 trials published from 1991 to 2006 and in 6.4 percent of those published from 2012 to 2014, according to the figures reported by Love et al. ( 2017 ) (who cite an earlier survey for them). Their review and survey of investigators named the barriers: a lack of training, investigators’ preference for the 3+3, and limited design resources available before a trial is funded. Rogatko et al. ( 2007 ) is the earlier paper that documented the gap between published methods and the designs that trials used. The other side of the record is reassuring on safety: a review of 53 completed phase 1 cancer trials published from 2003 to 2013 that used the CRM or a variant concluded that the model-guided escalation was safe and generalizable ( Iasonos and O’Quigley 2014 ) . The most direct evidence of what the 3+3 costs is a re-analysis. Silva et al. ( 2021 ) sampled 60 published dose-finding trials, took the 22 that had used the 3+3, and re-applied the CRM and BOIN to the published data, at target toxicity rates of 0.25 and 0.30 and without the expansion cohorts. The model-based designs recommended a different dose from the published

title: How often are model-based designs used, and does it matter?
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.1 How often are model-based designs used, and does it matter?
text: the 22 that had used the 3+3, and re-applied the CRM and BOIN to the published data, at target toxicity rates of 0.25 and 0.30 and without the expansion cohorts. The model-based designs recommended a different dose from the published MTD in a number of trials, treated fewer patients at suboptimal doses and escalated faster. Lesson. The reanalysis shows that alternative designs can recommend different doses. Because the true MTDs were unknown and some outcomes were simulated, it does not establish their real-world correct-selection probabilities. The obstacle to adoption is not statistical but organizational, and a protocol that offers a one-page table (BOIN) removes part of it.

title: BOIN and FDA's fit-for-purpose determination
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.2 BOIN and FDA's fit-for-purpose determination
text: BOIN and FDA’s fit-for-purpose determination The BOIN design of Liu and Yuan ( 2015 ) is the one model-assisted design for which FDA has issued a determination: the Drug Development Tools Fit-for-Purpose list records a determination for BOIN dose finding dated 10 December 2021 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025 ) . What was reviewed was the method for a stated context of use (phase 1 dose finding with a toxicity endpoint). Lesson. The regulator’s acceptance attaches to a method and a context of use, and a sponsor still has to supply its own simulations and a protocol-specific justification. Chapter 3 places the fit-for-purpose initiative among FDA’s other tools.

title: Sotorasib and the dose that was not optimized
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.3 Sotorasib and the dose that was not optimized
text: Sotorasib and the dose that was not optimized Sotorasib, a KRAS G12C inhibitor for non-small-cell lung cancer, is the case most often cited for Project Optimus. The pivotal single-arm trial ( Skoulidis et al. 2021 ) used the 960 mg dose, and the accelerated approval of May 2021 came with a postmarketing requirement to compare that dose with a lower one. The randomized comparison of 960 mg and 240 mg was run only after approval. Lesson. This is the situation the August 2024 guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024 ) was written for: a dose chosen without a randomized comparison of lower doses, with the evidence for a lower dose collected only after approval. The cost of the dose question is then borne by patients and by a postmarketing study, rather than by a randomized comparison in phase 1/2.

title: Dulaglutide (AWARD-5): seamless dose finding
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.4 Dulaglutide (AWARD-5): seamless dose finding
text: Dulaglutide (AWARD-5): seamless dose finding The best-documented example of a Bayesian seamless dose-finding design is the AWARD-5 trial of dulaglutide in type 2 diabetes, which started in 2008 with seven doses and two controls ( Geiger et al. 2012 ; D. A. Berry 2025 ) . Stage 1 used response-adaptive randomization with interim analyses every two weeks, scored by a composite clinical utility index combining HbA1c, weight, heart rate and blood pressure. Longitudinal modeling predicted the 12-month outcome from early data, so that doses could be chosen before anyone reached the primary endpoint. The algorithm selected two non-adjacent doses (0.75 and 1.50 mg) at the earliest permitted time and the trial moved to stage 2, fixed randomization against the controls. The dose-finding results are reported in Skrivanek et al. ( 2014 ) , and the design in Geiger et al. ( 2012 ) . The data monitoring board could depart from the algorithm only on safety, and did so: in April 2009 randomization to the 3.0 mg dose was stopped on its recommendation after increases in heart rate and concerns about pancreatic safety ( European Medicines Agency 2014 ) . Both doses were approved by FDA in 2014. By Berry’s estimate the seamless design saved at least a year compared with separate phase 2 and phase 3 trials ( D. A. Berry 2025 ) .

This is a utility-based design in the sense of the previous section, and it shows the pattern of regulation that has to be in place: a prespecified algorithm, an agreed role for the DMC, and a simulated operating-characteristics report. A sponsor of such a design today would seek agreement with the regulator in advance, by the routes described in Chapter 3 .

title: Lecanemab: Bayesian dose finding in phase 2b
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.5 Lecanemab: Bayesian dose finding in phase 2b
text: Lecanemab: Bayesian dose finding in phase 2b Study 201 of lecanemab in early Alzheimer’s disease was a Bayesian phase 2b trial with five dose regimens and placebo, with response-adaptive allocation and interim analyses beginning after 196 patients and every 50 patients thereafter ( Swanson et al. 2021 ; D. A. Berry 2025 ) . It identified 10 mg/kg biweekly as the estimated 90 percent effective dose (the dose achieving 90 percent of the modeled maximum effect). The trial did not meet its prespecified 12-month primary success criterion: the posterior probability of at least a 25 percent reduction in decline was 0.64, short of the required 0.80 ( D. A. Berry et al. 2023 ) . The prespecified 18-month clinical and biomarker results were part of the broader evidence package, and the selected regimen was carried into the subsequent phase 3 program. Lesson. The case shows two things relevant to a dose-optimization protocol. A design can fail its primary criterion and still produce the right dose, which is why the protocol should say in advance how the dose-selection evidence will be read in that event. And a prespecified Bayesian criterion that is not met is a result, to be reported as one.

title: ASTIN: a Bayesian adaptive dose-response trial in stroke
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > 17.8.6 ASTIN: a Bayesian adaptive dose-response trial in stroke
text: ASTIN: a Bayesian adaptive dose-response trial in stroke Note ASTIN (Krams et al. 2003) The Acute Stroke Therapy by Inhibition of Neutrophils (ASTIN) trial was a Bayesian adaptive dose-response study of a neutrophil inhibitor in acute ischemic stroke ( Krams et al. 2003 ) . Rather than assign patients to a few fixed doses, it modeled the dose-response curve over a wide dose range with a smoothing model, so that the response at each dose borrowed strength from its neighbors, and used the accumulating posterior to choose the doses of later patients, to target the dose giving close to the maximum effect, and to stop early for efficacy or futility under prespecified rules. The trial stopped for futility at an interim analysis. The design paper is Grieve and Krams ( 2005 ) . The point for this chapter is that the dose-finding model, the allocation rule and the stopping rule were all specified in advance and evaluated by simulation, as the 2026 FDA draft expects for a Bayesian design. We keep the description general: the exact dynamic linear model and allocation criterion should be taken from the original papers, not from this summary. Tip Try it in the lab The open simulator at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/14-studio.html lets you set doses, adaptive allocation and scenarios and read off operating characteristics tables. Before opening it, predict how a design that updates after every cohort should behave when the true dose-response is flat across the top two doses, then change the true curves in the scenarios of this chapter ( dose_scenarios() ) and check your prediction.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > Key points
text: Key points The 3+3 is simple and exposes few patients to toxic doses, but in our simulations it selects the true MTD in only about 36 to 41 percent of trials, and under-selection is its most common selection error in these scenarios. Its operating characteristics can be obtained by exact enumeration or simulation, and they should be reported. One DLT in six patients with a Beta(0.25, 0.75) prior leaves a 95 percent posterior interval for the DLT probability of 0.01 to 0.51. Small phase 1 trials identify a dose much less precisely than their rule suggests (see Reiner, Paoletti, and O’Quigley ( 1999 ) and Polson and Sokolov ( 2026b ) ). CRM and BOIN name a target toxicity rate and use the data from all doses. In our scenarios, with 30 patients, they select the true MTD more often than the 3+3, at the price of more patients, and a design must be compared at a stated sample size. BOIN is listed in FDA’s fit-for-purpose initiative (determination of 10 December 2021) for a defined context of use ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2025 ) . The MTD is the wrong target for many modern agents. The August 2024 FDA guidance recommends choosing the dosage on pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, safety and efficacy evidence, preferably with a randomized comparison of several dosages ( U.S. Food and

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 17: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization > Key points
text: ) . The MTD is the wrong target for many modern agents. The August 2024 FDA guidance recommends choosing the dosage on pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, safety and efficacy evidence, preferably with a randomized comparison of several dosages ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2024 ) . Utility-based and EffTox designs make the benefit-risk trade-off explicit. The price is an elicited utility or contour, an efficacy model and endpoint, and a larger sample, all of which a regulator will ask about. Seamless phase 2/3 designs remove the gap between dose selection and confirmation, and require a prespecified selection rule, type I error control that accounts for the selection, and simulated operating characteristics. The AWARD-5 trial ( Section 17.8 ) is the documented precedent. Exposure-response models that support a dose choice fall under ICH M15: state the context of use and assess model influence and the consequence of a wrong decision ( International Council for Harmonisation 2026 ) . title: Time-to-Event Endpoints
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18 Time-to-Event Endpoints
text: Most confirmatory trials in cardiology and oncology are event driven. The primary endpoint is the time to death, progression or a major adverse cardiovascular event, the analysis is a log-rank test or a Cox model, and the trial ends not at a fixed sample size but when a target number of events has accrued. SELECT and REWIND ( Chapter 21 ) are both of this kind: SELECT planned 1,225 events and observed 1,270, REWIND observed 1,257. A trial of 17,604 patients is, statistically, a trial of about 1,270 events. The Bayesian treatment of these trials is simpler than its reputation. For the decisions that matter (whether to stop at an interim analysis, how confident to be in a hazard ratio, whether a promising interim justifies more events) almost everything follows from two facts: the information about a log hazard ratio is proportional to the number of events, and the information about a single hazard is a gamma posterior. The chapter starts with the traditional analysis (log-rank test, Cox model, Schoenfeld’s event formula), then works through both facts with numbers, then turns to the case that breaks the first fact, non-proportional hazards. Important Regulatory anchor No FDA or ICH document is devoted to the Bayesian analysis of time-to-event data, and, as far as we are aware, none is devoted to non-proportional hazards or to restricted mean

text: breaks the first fact, non-proportional hazards. Important Regulatory anchor No FDA or ICH document is devoted to the Bayesian analysis of time-to-event data, and, as far as we are aware, none is devoted to non-proportional hazards or to restricted mean survival time. The following documents set the frame; Chapter 3 gives each one’s status. ICH E9(R1), Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis (Step 4, November 2019) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2019 ) . For a time-to-event endpoint the estimand must name the population, the variable (time to first event, or a composite), the handling of intercurrent events such as treatment discontinuation, rescue therapy or death before the non-fatal event, and the summary measure. A hazard ratio is one summary measure; the difference in restricted mean survival time or in survival probability at a landmark time are others. The choice is made before the trial, not after the curves are seen. ICH E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials (1998) ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 ) . Section 3.5 on sample size and section 4.5 on interim analysis apply unchanged to event-driven trials: the number of events, and the assumptions behind it, must be stated in the protocol, and the interim plan must be fixed in advance. FDA, Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft guidance, January 2026) (

A draft, which recommends and does not require. Its success criteria are posterior probabilities of the form \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , and nothing in it is specific to time-to-event data. For a trial with a frequentist statistical analysis plan, the operating characteristics of a Bayesian rule on the hazard ratio are calibrated as in Chapter 14 . FDA, Clinical Trial Endpoints for the Approval of Cancer Drugs and Biologics (final guidance, December 2018) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018 ) . Discusses overall survival, progression-free survival and related endpoints and the biases of each. It is the document sponsors most often cite for oncology time-to-event endpoints; it does not prescribe a method for non-proportional hazards.

title: The traditional analysis
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.1 The traditional analysis
text: 18.1 The traditional analysis Let \(T\) be the event time and \(S(t) = \Pr(T > t)\) the survival function. The hazard is \(h(t) = \lim_{\delta \to 0}\Pr(t \le T < t + \delta \mid T \ge t)/\delta\) , and the cumulative hazard is \(H(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,du\) , so that \(S(t) = e^{-H(t)}\) . Patients still event-free at the data cutoff, or lost to follow-up, are censored: their event time is only known to exceed the last contact. The Kaplan-Meier estimate of \(S(t)\) ( Kaplan and Meier 1958 ) handles censoring without a model, and it is the curve every trial report draws. The treatment comparison has two standard forms. The log-rank test ( Mantel 1966 ; Peto and Peto 1972 ) compares, at each event time, the observed number of events in the treated arm with the number expected if the two arms shared one hazard, and sums the differences. It is the score test of a proportional hazards model. The Cox model ( Cox 1972 ) writes \(h(t \mid z) = h_0(t)e^{-\theta z}\) for a treatment indicator \(z\) , leaves the baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\) unspecified, and estimates \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) (positive when treatment reduces the hazard, the book’s benefit-positive convention) from the partial likelihood ( Cox 1975 ) . Under 1:1 allocation the variance of \(\hat\theta\) is approximately \[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) \approx \frac{4}{D},

text: \(h_0(t)\) unspecified, and estimates \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) (positive when treatment reduces the hazard, the book’s benefit-positive convention) from the partial likelihood ( Cox 1975 ) . Under 1:1 allocation the variance of \(\hat\theta\) is approximately \[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) \approx \frac{4}{D}, \tag{18.1}\] where \(D\) is the total number of events ( D. Schoenfeld 1981 ; D. A. Schoenfeld 1983 ) . The approximation is accurate when the hazard ratio is not far from one. It carries the whole of the design: the number of patients enters only through the events they produce, which is why an event-driven trial fixes \(D\) and lets the sample size, the accrual period and the follow-up be chosen to deliver it. When randomization was stratified, the log-rank test and the Cox model should be stratified on the same factors (a stratified log-rank test, or a Cox model with a baseline hazard per stratum), and prognostic baseline covariates can be added for precision, with the caveat that the hazard ratio is non-collapsible and so changes meaning when covariates are added; Section 5.10 sets out the conditional and marginal estimands and the regulatory guidance. Inverting Equation 18.1 gives the sample size formula of Chapter 9 . To detect a hazard ratio \(\mathrm{HR}\) with one-sided level \(\alpha\) and power \(1-\beta\) , the trial needs \[ D = \frac{4\,(z_{\alpha} + z_{\beta})^2}{(\log \mathrm{HR})^2} \tag{18.2}\] events. A cardiovascular outcomes trial hoping for a hazard ratio of 0.90 needs 3,787 events, and so tens of thousands of patients followed for years. Oncology trials, with larger effects and higher event rates, need hundreds. Two cautions belong with the traditional analysis, and a Bayesian analysis inherits both. First, a single hazard ratio is a clean summary under proportional hazards. When the hazard ratio changes over time, the ordinary Cox estimate is a weighted average whose weights depend on the censoring pattern and on follow-up ( Struthers and Kalbfleisch 1986 ) , so that the same drug can yield different hazard ratios in different trials ( Section 18.5 ). Time-specific or explicitly defined average hazard ratios remain possible, but they need careful definition and interpretation. Second, the information in Equation 18.1 is the number of events of the primary endpoint as

text: requires. To be 95 percent sure that a 20 percent reduction in hazard is at least a 10 percent reduction, a trial needs about 800 events: with 800 events the probability is 0.95, with 400 it is 0.88. The same calculation run backwards translates a prior into events. To make the posterior standard deviation of \(\theta\) equal to \(s\) the trial needs \(D = 4/s^2\) events, and a prior of standard deviation \(s_0\) on the log hazard ratio contributes \(4/s_0^2\) effective events. A prior with \(s_0 = 0.2\) is worth 100 events. This exchange rate is the cleanest way to explain prior borrowing ( Chapter 19 ) to a clinical team: “the historical trials contribute as much as 100 events in this trial” is a statement a clinician can accept or reject, where “a normal prior with standard deviation 0.2” is not.

text: row.names = FALSE ) Table 18.3: Posterior for a constant hazard and for the exponential median survival, 60 events in 400 patient-years, Gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior. Quantity Posterior mean 2.5% 97.5% Hazard (per year) 0.150 0.114 0.190 Median survival (years) 4.699 3.643 6.054 The posterior mean hazard is 0.15 per year, with 95 percent interval 0.114 to 0.19. The median survival under the exponential model is \(\log 2/\lambda\) . Its posterior mean is 4.7 years, not the plug-in \(\log 2/0.15 = 4.62\) : the median is a reciprocal of the hazard, so averaging it is not the same as transforming the average. The interval, 3.6 to 6.1 years, is asymmetric for the same reason. The Bayesian computation transforms the posterior directly and so gets the asymmetry right without the delta method. A constant hazard is rarely realistic over years of follow-up. Dividing time into intervals \(I_1, \dots, I_K\) with constant hazard \(\lambda_k\) in each, the likelihood factors into independent gamma terms, one per interval, with \(d_k\) events and \(T_k\) exposure. A hierarchical prior that ties neighboring hazards together, for example a random walk on \(\log\lambda_k\) , smooths the hazard and lets sparse late intervals borrow from earlier ones. title: The gamma posterior for a hazard
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.3 The gamma posterior for a hazard
text: smooths the hazard and lets sparse late intervals borrow from earlier ones. The piecewise exponential model ( Holford 1976 ; Breslow 1974 ) , with a gamma-process prior for the cumulative hazard as the nonparametric Bayes extension ( Kalbfleisch 1978 ) , underlies most Bayesian analyses of time-to-event data (see Ibrahim, Chen, and Sinha ( 2001 ) ), and with a proportional hazards term \(\lambda_k e^{-\theta z}\) it approaches the Cox model as the intervals become finer. Two further Bayesian survival models are worth knowing. The power prior reviewed in Ibrahim et al. ( 2015 ) is not limited to binary data: its discounting of the historical likelihood ( Section 19.4 ) extends to a survival likelihood. When the historical data may not be exchangeable with the current trial, Murray and colleagues give a semiparametric commensurate model for time-to-event data from two possibly non-exchangeable sources, designed to attenuate bias and increase efficiency, and illustrated with post-market surveillance of stents in dialysis patients ( Murray et al. 2014 ) . Chen and colleagues develop a Bayesian promotion-time cure model, distinct from the mixture model illustrated in Section 18.5 .

title: Predictive probability in an event-driven trial
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.4 Predictive probability in an event-driven trial
text: 18.4 Predictive probability in an event-driven trial Chapter 15 developed conditional power and predictive probability for a generic standardized statistic. For an event-driven trial the information scale is the event count, and the formulas become explicit. Suppose a trial is designed for \(D_{\max} = 600\) events and succeeds if the final one-sided \(z\) statistic for \(\theta > 0\) exceeds 1.96. At an interim analysis with \(D_1\) events the estimate is \(\hat\theta_1\) . The remaining \(D_2 = D_{\max} - D_1\) events contribute an independent estimate \(\hat\theta_2 \sim N(\theta, 4/D_2)\) , and the final estimate is the information-weighted average \(\hat\theta = (D_1\hat\theta_1 + D_2\hat\theta_2)/D_{\max}\) . Under a flat prior the posterior of \(\theta\) is \(N(\hat\theta_1, 4/D_1)\) , so the predictive distribution of \(\hat\theta_2\) is \(N(\hat\theta_1, 4/D_2 + 4/D_1)\) and the final estimate is normal with mean \(\hat\theta_1\) and variance \((D_2/D_{\max})^2(4/D_2 + 4/D_1)\) . The predictive probability of success is a single normal probability. The calculation has a history in time-to-event monitoring. Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar proposed skeptical and enthusiastic priors on the log hazard ratio for exactly this purpose ( Spiegelhalter, Freedman, and Parmar 1994 ) , and the CHART radiotherapy trials were the worked example of Bayesian design and monitoring in practice ( Parmar et al. 1994 ) . Two frequentist summaries are often reported instead. Conditional power under the design assumption plugs in the hazard

Events D1 Observed HR Interim z PP CP, design CP, trend 300 0.75 2.49 0.94 0.95 0.99 300 0.85 1.41 0.51 0.72 0.52 300 0.95 0.44 0.09 0.35 0.03 450 0.88 1.36 0.25 0.42 0.22 The three numbers can tell different stories. In the third row, conditional power under the design assumption is 0.35, which might persuade a data monitoring committee to continue. But halfway through, the observed hazard ratio is 0.95, whose approximate 95 percent interval (0.76 to 1.19) includes the design value of 0.8 as well as no effect, so the data neither confirm nor exclude the design assumption. Conditional power under the trend, 0.03, conditions on the interim estimate as if it were the true effect, although half the events are still to come. The predictive probability, 0.09, averages over the posterior of the hazard ratio, so it reflects both the interim estimate and its uncertainty. The three differ in what they condition on, and a committee should see all three. (A predictive probability under a flat prior is itself pessimistic when the design effect was supported by earlier trials; the flat prior is the conservative end, and Chapter 15 shows the effect of a design-alternative prior.) The second row, a promising but uncertain interim, is the situation in which adaptive designs propose to increase \(D_{\max}\) . The predictive probability makes the trade-off visible. Increasing \(D_{\max}\) to 900 raises the predictive probability of success from 0.51 to 0.63 at a cost of 300 more events. Whether that is worth it depends on the value of approval and on what the extra events cost, the question of the value of the extra information, and not on a rule that conditional power lies in a “promising zone”. Any such change must be pre-specified and its type I error consequences controlled, as the FDA adaptive design guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019 ) (final, November 2019) recommends; the calculation above is a decision aid, not a license to adapt.

title: Non-proportional hazards
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5 Non-proportional hazards
text: 18.5 Non-proportional hazards Immunotherapy trials have taught oncologists that hazards need not be proportional ( Alexander, Schoenfeld, and Trippa 2018 ) . A treatment that engages the immune system may do nothing for months and then produce durable responses in a minority of patients. The survival curves overlap or cross early and separate late, and a single hazard ratio misdescribes both phases. The consequences for the traditional analysis are concrete: the log-rank test loses power when the effect is delayed, because the early events, which carry weight in the test, are uninformative about the treatment; and the Cox hazard ratio becomes a quantity that depends on how long the trial runs ( Hernán 2010 ) . Figure 18.1 shows three scenarios built from the same control arm, a constant hazard of 0.15 per year (median survival 4.6 years). Treatment either cuts the hazard by 40 percent from the start (proportional), cuts it by 40 percent only after a delay of one year, or cures 20 percent of patients and leaves the rest at the control hazard. title: Non-proportional hazards
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5 Non-proportional hazards
text: Bayesian responses are in common use. The first is a piecewise treatment effect, \(\theta_k = -\log\mathrm{HR}_k\) in interval \(k\) , with a hierarchical prior that lets the effect change over time but shrinks it toward a common value. It is the piecewise exponential model of Section 18.3 with a treatment effect in each interval, and its posterior answers the clinical question “when does the benefit begin?” directly. The second is a mixture cure model ( Boag 1949 ; Berkson and Gage 1952 ) , in which a fraction \(\pi\) of treated patients are effectively cured and the rest follow the control hazard, \(S_1(t) = \pi + (1-\pi)S_0(t)\) (in the Berkson-Gage model the uncured patients have a survival function of their own, and following the control hazard is a special case; Chen, Ibrahim, and Sinha ( 1999 ) give a Bayesian promotion-time (non-mixture) cure model with a surviving fraction). The posterior for \(\pi\) is the quantity a patient cares about, but it is identifiable only if follow-up is long enough for the curve to plateau; with immature data it is dominated by the prior, which has to be stated. The third is to change the estimand to the restricted mean survival time up to a horizon \(\tau\) , \[ \mathrm{RMST}(\tau) = \int_0^\tau S(t)\,dt, \tag{18.3}\] whose posterior is computed from draws of the survival curve. The difference

The difference in RMST is the average event-free time gained within \(\tau\) , in months or years, which is the unit in which patients and payers think, and it does not require proportional hazards ( Royston and Parmar 2011 , 2013 ; Uno et al. 2014 ) . The idea of a restricted mean life is older than these papers ( Irwin 1949 ; Karrison 1987 ) . It does require a horizon, and the choice of \(\tau\) is part of the estimand and must be fixed in the protocol. title: Power loss under a delayed effect
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5.1 Power loss under a delayed effect
text: Power loss under a delayed effect How much does the log-rank test lose? The simulation below compares a trial of 300 patients per arm followed for five years, with the control hazard 0.15 per year, under a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 and under a delayed effect with no benefit for two years and a hazard ratio of 0.583 afterward. The two scenarios are matched so that the treated survival at five years is the same, 0.57, so they describe the same final benefit reached by different paths. Show the R code set.seed ( 1507 ) rpwexp <- function (n, rates, breaks) { # inversion for a piecewise exponential e <- rexp (n); H <- c ( 0 , cumsum (rates[ - length (rates)] * diff (breaks))) k <- findInterval (e, H); breaks[k] + (e - H[k]) / rates[k] } sim_power <- function (rates1, breaks1, n = 300 , tau = 5 , R = 2000 ) { rej <- numeric (R); ev <- numeric (R) for (r in seq_len (R)) { t0 <- rexp (n, 0.15 ); t1 <- rpwexp (n, rates1, breaks1) time <- pmin ( c (t0, t1), tau); status <- as.integer ( c (t0, t1) <= tau) grp <- rep ( 0 : 1 , each = n) lr <- survival :: survdiff (survival :: Surv (time, status) ~ grp) z

Scenario Power Mean.events Proportional, HR 0.75 0.68 287 Delayed 2 years, then HR 0.583 0.55 287 The simulated power is 0.68 under the constant hazard ratio and 0.55 under the delayed effect, with a similar number of events, although the five-year survival difference is the same. The Schoenfeld calculation of Table 18.1 , which assumes a single hazard ratio, would not have warned about the difference. Two responses are used in practice: a weighted log-rank test (Fleming-Harrington weights ( Harrington and Fleming 1982 ; Fleming and Harrington 1991 ) ) that gives more weight to late events, and a design that states the delayed-effect model, with its simulation, in the protocol. Either choice is made before the trial; choosing the weights after seeing the curves invalidates the type I error. The next subsection shows what the weighted tests recover.

title: Tests built for a delayed effect
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.5.2 Tests built for a delayed effect
text: Tests built for a delayed effect The Fleming-Harrington weighted log-rank test multiplies the contribution of each event time by a weight \(S(t)^\rho\{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma\) , where \(S\) is the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate ( Harrington and Fleming 1982 ; Fleming and Harrington 1991 ) . The choice \(\rho = \gamma = 0\) is the ordinary log-rank test, and \((\rho, \gamma) = (0, 1)\) puts the weight on late events, where a delayed effect shows. A test that is best for one shape of effect can be poor for another, so the combination test takes the largest of several standardized weighted statistics, usually the four with \(\rho, \gamma \in \{0, 1\}\) , and refers it to the multivariate normal distribution implied by their correlation ( Lee 2007 ; Lin et al. 2020 ) . This is the MaxCombo test. Table 18.7 repeats the simulation of Table 18.6 with the weighted test and the MaxCombo test, and adds a null scenario to check the level. text: rates are 0.024, 0.022 and 0.021 against the nominal 0.025. Two cautions go with the table. First, these tests are tests of identical survival curves, and the weighted tests can reject when early harm and late benefit cancel in the average, so that a significant result does not by itself mean that patients on average did better; the modestly weighted tests of Magirr and Burman were proposed to control the risk of declaring a uniformly inferior drug superior ( Magirr and Burman 2019 ) . Second, the choice among them is a design decision with regulatory weight: the cross-pharma working group’s straw-man guidance ( Roychoudhury et al. 2021 ) treats the choice of test and the plausible non-proportional scenarios as something to settle, with simulation, at the design stage. Restricted mean survival time, the other main alternative, has an empirical record: in 54 oncology trials whose individual patient data were reconstructed from the published curves, the hazard ratio gave on average a larger treatment effect than the ratio of restricted mean survival times (average ratio 1.11, with substantial variation between trials), and the authors recommend that restricted mean survival time be reported routinely ( Trinquart et al. 2016 ) . The rule of this chapter is the same for every alternative: the primary test, its weights or horizon, and the simulation under the delayed-effect scenario

title: Regulation and practice
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.6 Regulation and practice
text: 18.6 Regulation and practice Four points follow from the guidance landscape. First, the estimand comes first. Under ICH E9(R1) ( International Council for Harmonisation 2019 ) the hazard ratio, the RMST difference and the survival difference at a landmark time are different estimands, and a Bayesian analysis reports the posterior of the one the protocol names. The five strategies for intercurrent events of Chapter 5 apply: for time to a non-fatal event in the presence of death, the usual choice is a composite (death counts as an event) or a competing-risks treatment, and each leads to a different model. Second, what exists on non-proportional hazards is thin. We are not aware of an FDA or ICH guidance that sets a required method for non-proportional hazards or for RMST; the closest thing to a consensus document is the straw-man guidance of the cross-pharma working group discussed above ( Roychoudhury et al. 2021 ) , which is industry and academic guidance and not regulatory text. The oncology endpoints guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018 ) discusses the endpoints and their biases, and the practice of FDA reviewers, which can be read in public review documents, is to accept pre-specified alternatives to the log-rank test as sensitivity analyses and to scrutinize post hoc ones. The summary of a drug’s effect on the product label is still

title: Regulation and practice
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > 18.6 Regulation and practice
text: FDA reviewers, which can be read in public review documents, is to accept pre-specified alternatives to the log-rank test as sensitivity analyses and to scrutinize post hoc ones. The summary of a drug’s effect on the product label is still usually a hazard ratio. This is an area where agreement with the agency at a pre-submission meeting, on the primary analysis and on the sensitivity analyses, matters more than the choice among statistical methods. Third, the Bayesian elements map onto the existing framework. An informative prior on the log hazard ratio is judged as in Chapter 8 and Chapter 19 , and its worth in events is stated as in Section 18.2 . The book’s default for a confirmatory adaptive design without borrowing is a Bayesian success criterion calibrated to the type I error by simulation, with the event-time process (accrual, censoring, the NPH model) inside the simulation. The FDA draft Bayesian guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) describes this as one of three routes, the others being direct interpretation of posterior probabilities (for example with borrowing, by agreement with FDA) and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria. The predictive probability of Section 18.4 is a monitoring aid and enters the formal rules only as a pre-specified futility or sample-size criterion. Fourth, the event count itself is a design element. The final analysis is

text: decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria. The predictive probability of Section 18.4 is a monitoring aid and enters the formal rules only as a pre-specified futility or sample-size criterion. Fourth, the event count itself is a design element. The final analysis is triggered by the event count, so the data monitoring committee and the sponsor must agree on how events are adjudicated and counted, and the timing rule for an interim analysis must be prespecified, whether by a number of events or by calendar date. If the analysis occurs at an information fraction other than the target, or events overrun the plan, the actual information fraction has to be handled by a prespecified method (for example an alpha-spending function evaluated at the observed fraction).

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 18: Time-to-Event Endpoints > Key points
text: Key points The information about a log hazard ratio is one quarter of the number of events, \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) \approx 4/D\) under 1:1 allocation. Event-driven trials fix \(D\) , and the Schoenfeld formula \(D = 4(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2/(\log\mathrm{HR})^2\) is the sample size formula of Chapter 9 in event units. A prior with standard deviation \(s_0\) on the log hazard ratio is worth \(4/s_0^2\) events. A prior of standard deviation 0.2 is worth 100 events. To be 95 percent sure that an observed hazard ratio of 0.8 is below 0.9, a trial needs about 800 events (probability 0.95). For a constant hazard the posterior is gamma, and posterior summaries of the median survival come from transforming draws. In the worked example the posterior mean median is 4.7 years, not the plug-in 4.62. Conditional power under the design assumption and under the trend condition on different fixed effects; predictive probability averages over the posterior of the effect: in the worked row with an observed hazard ratio of 0.95 at half the events the three values are 0.35, 0.03 and 0.09. Under non-proportional hazards a single Cox hazard ratio can depend on censoring and follow-up, so the estimand needs explicit definition. The log-rank test loses power under a delayed effect (simulated 0.55 against 0.68 for a constant hazard ratio), and the RMST difference and the cure fraction are alternatives, each requiring pre-specification. No FDA or ICH document, to our knowledge, prescribes a method for non-proportional hazards or RMST. ICH E9(R1) requires that whatever summary measure is chosen be defined as an estimand before the trial.

title: Borrowing Information
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19 Borrowing Information
text: A sponsor planning a trial of a new drug in a rare disease already knows something about the control arm. Earlier trials enrolled similar patients, a registry holds their outcomes, and a pediatric program can lean on what is known in adults. Using that knowledge looks like plain common sense, and there is a cost argument too: every patient who does not have to be randomized to control is a patient who can be treated, or a trial that can finish sooner. This chapter is about how to use such information, how regulators judge it, and what it costs when the borrowed information turns out to be wrong. Of the four mechanisms by which Bayesian designs save patients (monitoring, multiple arms, shrinkage, and prior information), borrowing is the one with the sharpest trade. Done well, it recovers precision that a small trial cannot supply. Done badly, it can introduce substantial bias into a small current trial, whose data may be insufficient to reveal the mismatch, and it does so under the sponsor’s own prior. The central message of the chapter is that borrowing is not free, that the price is measurable by simulation, and that the regulator will ask to see that price before agreeing to the design. title: What the traditional design does with prior data
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.1 What the traditional design does with prior data
text: 19.1 What the traditional design does with prior data A traditional trial uses prior data heavily, but only before the trial starts. Phase 2 results and earlier studies of the control treatment set the design alternative (the effect size the trial is powered to detect), the assumed control response rate or event rate, the variance, the dropout rate, and therefore the sample size. In the notation of Chapter 9 , the sample size is a function of \(\theta\) and of nuisance parameters, and all of them come from earlier data. A sponsor who assumed a 30% control response rate because three earlier trials averaged 30% has used those trials fully. Then the data are set aside. In a conventional standalone randomized-trial analysis, the analysis of the new trial uses only the new trial. The earlier studies appear in the introduction of the protocol and in the clinical overview, and nowhere in the p-value or the confidence interval. This is the usual convention, and it has a reason. The frequentist guarantee, a one-sided type I error of 0.025 at every parameter value in the null hypothesis, is a statement about repeated use of the same procedure on the same kind of data. If last year’s data entered this year’s test statistic, the guarantee would depend on how last year’s data happen to relate to this year’s

title: What the traditional design does with prior data
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.1 What the traditional design does with prior data
text: is a statement about repeated use of the same procedure on the same kind of data. If last year’s data entered this year’s test statistic, the guarantee would depend on how last year’s data happen to relate to this year’s patients, and nothing in the protocol controls that. Frequentist methods can incorporate historical information under explicit assumptions (the margin synthesis later in this chapter is one, and FDA’s 2016 noninferiority guidance describes a frequentist synthesis method that combines the historical and current estimates and their uncertainties ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016 ) ), but the guarantee then holds only under those assumptions. The rule has a cost that is easy to see in a small trial. If the control arm must be as large as the treatment arm, half of a scarce population is randomized to a comparator whose behavior is, to a good approximation, already known. In a pediatric rare-disease program the number of eligible children may not support a trial of conventional size at all. The traditional design answers this with a smaller trial and a looser level of evidence, a larger effect size in the alternative, or a single-arm design. The single-arm design is where the question of external information becomes unavoidable.

title: External and historical controls: the traditional objections
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.2 External and historical controls: the traditional objections
text: 19.2 External and historical controls: the traditional objections In a single-arm trial all patients receive the new treatment, and the effect is judged by comparing the observed outcome with what is expected without it. The expectation comes from somewhere: a published control arm, a registry, a set of earlier trials, a cohort of patients treated in routine care. ICH E10 calls this the externally controlled trial, including the historical control, and lists it among the five kinds of control group ( International Council for Harmonisation 2000 ) . The guideline’s stance is cautious. Because treatment assignment between the trial and the external control is not randomized, and the external controls may also be nonconcurrent, differences between the groups can arise from sources other than the treatment, and the design is regarded as suitable only where the effect of treatment is large relative to the variability of the natural course of the disease. FDA’s substantial-evidence reasoning is the same: “Because of the lack of randomized treatment assignment”, differences between groups are a concern (see Chapter 3 for the sources). Pocock (1976) gave the classic list of conditions under which a historical control group can be combined with a randomized one ( Pocock 1976 ) . In paraphrase, the historical controls should have: received exactly the treatment now given to the concurrent controls; been part of a

title: External and historical controls: the traditional objections
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.2 External and historical controls: the traditional objections
text: conditions under which a historical control group can be combined with a randomized one ( Pocock 1976 ) . In paraphrase, the historical controls should have: received exactly the treatment now given to the concurrent controls; been part of a recent study with the same protocol, so that eligibility and the evaluation of outcome are the same; been treated at the same institutions or by the same investigators, so far as possible; had the same distribution of important prognostic factors; and shown no unexplained differences in outcome from the concurrent controls. These criteria are still the working checklist. They are demanding, because the situations in which a sponsor wants historical data are exactly the ones in which standard of care, diagnostic criteria, supportive care and patient selection have drifted since the older study. Three mechanisms make an external control misleading. First, selection : patients who enter a trial are not the same as patients in a registry, because trial entry requires being well enough to travel, to consent and to meet eligibility, and investigators choose whom to offer a new drug. Second, time : outcomes of untreated and standard-treated patients move over time as care improves and as diagnosis happens earlier, so a control from five years ago may be worse than a control today. Third, measurement : endpoints assessed in routine care (a response

text: of untreated and standard-treated patients move over time as care improves and as diagnosis happens earlier, so a control from five years ago may be worse than a control today. Third, measurement : endpoints assessed in routine care (a response recorded in a chart) are not assessed as in a trial (a central radiology read at scheduled visits). Each of these gives a bias, not a variance, so a larger external sample does not help. The regulatory response has been to give external controls a structure rather than to ban them. FDA’s draft guidance on externally controlled trials was issued in February 2023 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023a ) . It asks for a pre-specified protocol and analysis plan, a justification of why a concurrent randomized control is not feasible, careful choice of the data source, and an assessment of whether the external group is comparable on the prognostic factors and on how outcomes were measured. In 2025 the UK MHRA published a draft guideline on external control arms built from real-world data, and the EMA published a concept paper (draft in July 2025, adopted in May 2026) announcing a reflection paper on the same topic ( Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency 2025 ; European Medicines Agency 2026 ) . Both are drafts or plans, not binding, and both repeat the same

Both are drafts or plans, not binding, and both repeat the same two planning considerations: pre-specification before the external data are examined, and demonstration that the data are fit for the purpose. None of these documents describes a statistical method as the answer. They describe a design discipline in which the statistical method sits. Two final guidances of 2023 sit beside the draft and are summarized in the regulatory anchor at the start of the chapter: the real-world data and evidence guidance points to the externally controlled trials draft for external-control designs ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023b ) , and the rare-diseases guidance reserves external controls for specific circumstances ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023c ) . Both recommend and do not require. The DIA working group’s roadmap for historical controls gives a checklist for judging the quality and comparability of a historical source ( Ghadessi et al. 2020 ) . The Bayesian methods in the rest of this chapter should be read with that background. They are a way of deciding how much to rely on external data once a regulator has accepted that the data are admissible. They do not make inadmissible data admissible.

title: Bayesian borrowing: the idea
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.3 Bayesian borrowing: the idea
text: 19.3 Bayesian borrowing: the idea Let \(p_c\) be the response rate on control in the current trial, and suppose historical data \(y_h\) from \(n_h\) control patients are available. Treating the two sources as the same population and pooling gives a posterior that is a Beta distribution with the historical successes and failures added to the current ones. In Chapter 8 the prior was measured in patients: a Beta \((a,b)\) prior has an effective sample size of \(a+b\) . Borrowing the whole historical control arm is a prior with effective sample size \(n_h\) . If the historical data are right, the current control arm is effectively enlarged by \(n_h\) patients. If they are wrong, the posterior is anchored on the wrong rate. The methods below differ in what they assume about the relationship between \(p_c\) and the historical rate \(p_h\) : \(p_c = p_h\) exactly (full pooling). \(p_c\) is close to \(p_h\) , and a single number says how close (power prior with a fixed discount, static borrowing). \(p_c\) and \(p_h\) are draws from a common distribution whose spread is estimated (hierarchical models, meta-analytic-predictive priors). \(p_c\) is either like \(p_h\) or unrelated to it, and the data decide which (mixture priors, robust MAP). How close \(p_c\) is to \(p_h\) is itself a parameter that is updated by comparing the two datasets (commensurate priors, normalized power priors).

How close \(p_c\) is to \(p_h\) is itself a parameter that is updated by comparing the two datasets (commensurate priors, normalized power priors). Methods 1 and 2 are static : the amount of borrowing is fixed before the trial. Methods 3 to 5 are dynamic : the amount of borrowing depends on how well the current data agree with the historical data. FDA’s draft guidance uses exactly this split and says that dynamic methods “borrow less when the data are less similar and more when the data are more similar” ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . The distinction between exchangeable and non-exchangeable sources is the Bayesian analogue of Pocock’s checklist. Real programs illustrate both kinds: the OPTIMIZER device approval used a fixed 30% weight on an earlier study ( Section 19.17.3 ), and the REBYOTA phase 3 trial used a hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study ( Section 19.17.1 ). Borrowing methods have a lineage, and these approaches make different assumptions about historical comparability. Table 19.1 lists it so that the names used in the rest of the chapter can be placed. title: Exchangeability and hierarchical models
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.3.1 Exchangeability and hierarchical models
text: Exchangeability and hierarchical models Two groups of patients are exchangeable if, before seeing any data, we would not be surprised by relabeling them: nothing we know distinguishes the response rate of one group from that of the other. Exchangeability does not say the rates are equal. It says their joint prior is symmetric. We model the group rates as conditionally independent draws from a common distribution with unknown parameters, which is the hierarchical model. This is a modeling assumption; de Finetti’s representation ( Chapter 6 ) motivates it when exchangeability extends to an infinite sequence. For \(K\) groups with response rates \(p_1,\ldots,p_K\) , a standard hierarchical model for binary data is \[ y_k \mid p_k \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_k,p_k),\qquad \mathrm{logit}\,p_k \mid \mu,\tau_b \sim N(\mu,\tau_b^2),\qquad (\mu,\tau_b)\sim \pi(\mu,\tau_b). \tag{19.1}\] The between-group standard deviation \(\tau_b\) controls borrowing. When \(\tau_b\) is near zero the groups are close to identical and each group’s estimate is pulled towards the common mean. When \(\tau_b\) is large the groups are nearly independent and each keeps its own data. The key feature is that \(\tau_b\) is estimated from the data: if the groups disagree, the posterior for \(\tau_b\) moves up and borrowing falls. For a normal outcome with group effects \(\theta_k\) , the posterior mean of group \(k\) is, approximately, a weighted average, \[ \mathbb{E}[\theta_k \mid y] \approx \lambda_k \bar\theta + (1-\lambda_k)\hat\theta_k,\qquad \lambda_k = \frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\tau_b^2}, \tag{19.2}\]

title: Exchangeability and hierarchical models
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.3.1 Exchangeability and hierarchical models
text: for \(\tau_b\) moves up and borrowing falls. For a normal outcome with group effects \(\theta_k\) , the posterior mean of group \(k\) is, approximately, a weighted average, \[ \mathbb{E}[\theta_k \mid y] \approx \lambda_k \bar\theta + (1-\lambda_k)\hat\theta_k,\qquad \lambda_k = \frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\tau_b^2}, \tag{19.2}\] where \(\sigma_k^2\) is the sampling variance of the group’s own estimate \(\hat\theta_k\) and \(\bar\theta\) is the precision-weighted overall mean. A small group has large \(\sigma_k^2\) and so is shrunk more. This is the same shrinkage that Chapter 10 used for several endpoints and Stein’s normal-means result (1956) shows that carefully chosen shrinkage estimators can reduce total squared error under its assumptions ( Stein 1956 ) . Whether shrinkage improves estimation in the hierarchical binomial model above has to be assessed under plausible heterogeneity, because the theorem does not cover estimated heterogeneity or arbitrary shrinkage rules. The same structure is used in multicenter trials, where the groups are centers. Polson and Sokolov ( 2026 ) fit a hierarchical logistic-normal model to the eight-center topical-cream trial of Skene and Wakefield, with a bivariate normal on the pair of center-specific log odds for the two arms, so that centers borrow strength on both arms and on their difference ( Skene and Wakefield 1990 ) . Individual centers had 5 to 37 patients per arm, so single-center estimates were imprecise, and the model improves them without discarding center-level variation.

text: centers borrow strength on both arms and on their difference ( Skene and Wakefield 1990 ) . Individual centers had 5 to 37 patients per arm, so single-center estimates were imprecise, and the model improves them without discarding center-level variation. Two warnings. First, shrinkage lowers total error only under conditions, and not the error of every group: under the normal model with known variances and three or more means, Stein’s result is that shrinkage lowers the total squared-error risk, but an individual group can be estimated worse, and a group that really is different usually is, compared with its own estimate. This is the price of borrowing in one sentence. Second, with few groups \(\tau_b\) is poorly estimated, and the answer depends on its prior. With four historical trials, a half-normal prior with scale 0.5 on \(\tau_b\) and one with scale 1.0 can give quite different degrees of borrowing, and the sensitivity analysis should show it. The FDA draft’s insistence on sensitivity analyses over “a range of alternative reasonable choices for the prior” is aimed at precisely this point ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) .

title: Power priors and their normalized version
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.4 Power priors and their normalized version
text: 19.4 Power priors and their normalized version The power prior of Ibrahim and Chen (2000) is the most direct way to down-weight historical data ( Ibrahim and Chen 2000 ; Ibrahim et al. 2015 ) . Given a vague initial prior \(\pi_0(\theta)\) and historical data \(D_h\) with likelihood \(L(\theta\mid D_h)\) , the power prior is \[ \pi(\theta \mid D_h, a_0) \propto L(\theta \mid D_h)^{a_0}\,\pi_0(\theta),\qquad 0\le a_0\le 1. \tag{19.3}\] Setting \(a_0=0\) discards the historical data and \(a_0=1\) pools them fully. For a binomial response with \(y_h\) successes in \(n_h\) patients and a Beta \((1,1)\) initial prior, the power prior is Beta \((1+a_0y_h,\,1+a_0(n_h-y_h))\) , so its effective sample size is \(a_0 n_h+2\) and one can read \(a_0\) as the fraction of the historical patients that count. With \(n_h=100\) and \(a_0=0.3\) , the historical arm counts as about 30 patients. If \(a_0\) is fixed in advance, the method is static. It is easy to describe and easy to simulate, and the regulator can see the borrowing in one number. It also has a feature that surprises people: the power prior discounts the precision of the historical data but does not move their center . Historical data that say 30% are still a prior centered near 30%, only a weaker one. With a Beta \((1,1)\) initial prior and \(a_0=0.3\) the prior is Beta \((10,22)\) , centered at 0.3125, with

The power prior at \(a_0=0.3\) adds the equivalent of 32 patients to the 30 current controls (ESS \(a_0 n_h+2\) ), and the posterior narrows to a standard deviation of 0.06 and moves from 0.41 towards the historical 0.30, to 0.35. The narrowing is the gain, and the shift is the risk: the current data say 40% and the posterior is pulled down by an amount the trial cannot verify. The larger the gap between the historical and the current rate, the more the borrowed bars mislead, and Table 19.3 (and the drift scenarios in Section 19.8 ) put numbers on what that costs in type I error. A natural improvement is to treat \(a_0\) as unknown with its own prior, so that the data choose it. This runs into a technical difficulty: the prior in Equation 19.3 as written has a normalizing constant that depends on \(a_0\) , and ignoring it makes the posterior favor small \(a_0\) in a way that has nothing to do with agreement between the datasets. The normalized power prior divides by the constant, \[ \pi(\theta, a_0 \mid D_h) = \frac{L(\theta\mid D_h)^{a_0}\,\pi_0(\theta)}{\int L(\theta\mid D_h)^{a_0}\,\pi_0(\theta)\,d\theta}\;\pi(a_0), \tag{19.4}\] and then the marginal posterior of \(a_0\) increases

title: Power priors and their normalized version
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.4 Power priors and their normalized version
text: in a way that has nothing to do with agreement between the datasets. The normalized power prior divides by the constant, \[ \pi(\theta, a_0 \mid D_h) = \frac{L(\theta\mid D_h)^{a_0}\,\pi_0(\theta)}{\int L(\theta\mid D_h)^{a_0}\,\pi_0(\theta)\,d\theta}\;\pi(a_0), \tag{19.4}\] and then the marginal posterior of \(a_0\) increases when the current data resemble the historical data and decreases when they do not. The normalized power prior is due to Duan, Ye, and Smith ( 2006 ) and Neuenschwander, Branson, and Spiegelhalter ( 2009 ) , and M.-H. Chen and Ibrahim ( 2006 ) relate it to hierarchical models. For FDA a fixed \(a_0\) is a static method, and a random \(a_0\) updated by the data is a dynamic one (the draft also lists supervised power priors, a term we do not use again). The cost of dynamic methods is more parameters to specify, including the prior on \(a_0\) , and an operating characteristic that has to be simulated.

cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.4.1 A rare-disease trial: choosing $a_0$ by the marginal likelihood
text: A rare-disease trial: choosing \(a_0\) by the marginal likelihood A fixed \(a_0\) is a judgment. The data can say something about it, and the simplest way to see how is a small example. Consider a rare metabolic disease. A natural-history study of 40 patients on standard care found 12 responders by a functional criterion (30%). The new trial randomizes 25 patients to the treatment and 15 to standard care, a 5:3 allocation (hypothetical, like the rest of this example) chosen to limit the number of patients on a comparator of doubtful benefit, and observes 14 of 25 responses on treatment and 6 of 15 on control. With uniform priors and no borrowing, the posterior probability that the treatment rate exceeds the control rate is 0.83, an inconclusive result by the 0.975 standard. Table 19.2 shows what the power prior adds. It does not remove the need for the drift simulation of Section 19.8 , because a regulator will ask what the design concludes if the true control rate is 45%, not 30%. title: Commensurate priors
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.5 Commensurate priors
text: 19.5 Commensurate priors Hobbs, Carlin, Mandrekar and Sargent (2011) put the question of agreement into a parameter of its own ( Hobbs et al. 2011 ) (the paper treats Gaussian data, and the extension to generalized linear models, the case the binary examples of this chapter need, is in Hobbs, Sargent, and Carlin ( 2012 ) ). Write \(\eta_c\) for the current parameter and \(\eta_h\) for the historical one (for binary data, the logits \(\eta_c=\operatorname{logit}p_c\) and \(\eta_h=\operatorname{logit}p_h\) , so that the normal prior is placed on the logit scale). The commensurate prior says \[ \eta_c \mid \eta_h, \tau_c \sim N(\eta_h,\; 1/\tau_c), \tag{19.6}\] where the commensurability parameter \(\tau_c\) is a precision, with its own prior, typically a spike-and-slab or a discrete mixture that allows a large value (near agreement) and a small value (near independence). Large posterior \(\tau_c\) means the current data support the claim that the two parameters are close, and the historical data count heavily. Small posterior \(\tau_c\) means they do not, and the historical data are down-weighted. In this form the method looks like a hierarchical model with two groups, but there is an important difference in how the historical group is used. In the two-stage version the historical posterior is held fixed and the direction of borrowing is one way, which is the way a regulator thinks about an earlier trial that

title: Commensurate priors
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.5 Commensurate priors
text: an important difference in how the historical group is used. In the two-stage version the historical posterior is held fixed and the direction of borrowing is one way, which is the way a regulator thinks about an earlier trial that has already been reported. In the fully Bayesian joint model, information flows both ways through the commensurability parameter. Hobbs and colleagues also give a version in which the commensurate model sits on a power prior, so that the two ideas, discounting and agreement, are combined. In applications there is a practical issue the original paper discusses: a method that learns agreement from a small current control arm has little to learn from, and so in a small trial the commensurate prior behaves much like a static one with weights fixed by the prior on \(\tau_c\) .

title: Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.6 Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures
text: 19.6 Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures Often there is not one historical control arm but several, from different trials. The meta-analytic-predictive (MAP) prior of Neuenschwander and colleagues (2010) does a random-effects meta-analysis of the historical control rates, using the hierarchical model of Equation 19.1 , and then takes the predictive distribution of the control parameter in a new trial as the prior ( Neuenschwander et al. 2010 ) . The predictive distribution is wider than the meta-analytic mean because it includes the between-trial variation \(\tau_b\) : even if the historical trials were estimated without error, a new trial’s control rate would differ from their average by about \(\tau_b\) . This is the logic of an exchangeable new trial, and it is the reason a MAP prior does not become more informative than the heterogeneity warrants however many historical patients there are. Figure 19.2 shows this with four illustrative historical control arms (80, 100, 70 and 150 patients, 400 in total). The calculation is a normal-normal random-effects model on the logit scale, with a half-normal prior with scale 0.5 on \(\tau_b\) , and the predictive distribution is converted to a Beta prior by matching mean and variance. cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.6 Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures
text: 0.471), with posterior mean \(\tau_b\) of 0.18, and its Beta approximation is Beta(18.8, 38.2). The MAP prior is worth about 57 patients, although 400 patients contributed. The pooled analysis, which ignores between-trial variation, would claim a prior effective sample size of 402 (the 400 historical patients plus the 2 patients of the Beta(1, 1) reference prior). The difference is the between-trial variation, and it is the most important number a regulator can ask for, since it quantifies how much a new trial’s control arm can be expected to differ from the old ones. A MAP prior is still an exchangeability assumption: it assumes that the new control rate is another draw from the same distribution as the historical ones. If the new trial differs systematically, because standard of care changed or the population is different, the MAP prior is confidently wrong. Schmidli and colleagues (2014) proposed protecting against this with a robust MAP prior, a mixture of the MAP prior and a vague prior ( Schmidli et al. 2014 ) : \[ \pi_{\text{rob}}(\theta) = w\,\pi_{\text{MAP}}(\theta) + (1-w)\,\pi_{\text{vague}}(\theta). \tag{19.7}\] The conjugate update of a mixture is a mixture of conjugate updates, with the weights multiplied by the marginal likelihood of the current data under each component. If the current control data look like the MAP prior, the weight stays on the informative component. If they do

cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.6 Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures
text: a mixture of conjugate updates, with the weights multiplied by the marginal likelihood of the current data under each component. If the current control data look like the MAP prior, the weight stays on the informative component. If they do not, the weight moves to the vague component and the posterior reverts to the current data ( Schmidli et al. 2014 ) . The weight \(1-w\) on the vague component is a choice made at the design stage; values of 0.1 to 0.5 are our working range, not a figure taken from the literature on robust priors. The mixture weight after the data are in plays the role of the commensurability parameter in the previous section, and it is the quantity to report: it says how much of the final answer comes from outside the trial. For production use, the R package RBesT (on CRAN) fits MAP priors by MCMC, approximates them by mixtures of conjugate distributions, and computes robust versions and operating characteristics ( Weber et al. 2021 ) ; the chunks in this chapter use a simpler normal-normal approximation from bayestrials so that every step is visible. The belimumab pediatric analysis ( Section 19.17.2 ) is the clearest regulatory example of a robust mixture prior. title: Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.6 Meta-analytic-predictive priors and robust mixtures
text: every step is visible. The belimumab pediatric analysis ( Section 19.17.2 ) is the clearest regulatory example of a robust mixture prior. Note Technical note: why robust mixtures learn agreement slowly Let the informative component be Beta \((a,b)\) and the vague one Beta \((1,1)\) , with prior weights \(w\) and \(1-w\) . After \(y\) successes in \(n\) current control patients, the posterior weight on the informative component is proportional to \(w\,B(a+y,b+n-y)/B(a,b)\) , against \((1-w)\,B(1+y,1+n-y)\) . The ratio of the two marginal likelihoods is a Bayes factor between a sharp and a diffuse prior. For small \(n\) it takes a large discrepancy to change the Bayes factor by much, because both components assign comparable marginal likelihood to a wide range of \(y\) . The weight starts to move only when \(\hat\theta\) is more than a couple of standard errors, \(\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)/n}\) , from the informative component’s mean. In a control arm of 30 patients the standard error is about 0.08, so a true rate 0.10 above the historical rate is within two standard errors and the weight barely moves. This is not a defect of the method. It is the statement that 30 patients cannot tell 30% from 40%, and therefore that dynamic borrowing in a small trial offers weak protection against moderate drift. The simulation below shows the consequence.

title: How much does the borrowed information weigh? Effective sample size and conflict
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.7 How much does the borrowed information weigh? Effective sample size and conflict
text: 19.7 How much does the borrowed information weigh? Effective sample size and conflict Chapter 8 defined the effective sample size of a prior, and its best known definition is that of Morita, Thall and Mueller ( Morita, Thall, and Müller 2008 ) . Definitions differ and give different numbers for the same prior, so a request for the “ESS” should be answered with the definition stated. For borrowing it is the central summary, and FDA asks for it: the draft guidance defines ESS as “a measure of the information in a probability distribution in terms of the equivalent number of patients in the target population”, asks that it be reported across the plausible range of outcomes, with its maximum and its mean, and asks for the ratio of prior ESS to trial size ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . For a static prior the ESS is a number. For a dynamic prior it is a function of the observed current data: the ESS is high when the current control agrees with the historical one and falls when it does not. For a robust mixture there is no unique patient-equivalent ESS. A simple convention, used here, is the component-weighted ESS: the posterior weight on each component times that component’s ESS (102 for the informative Beta \((31,71)\) , 2 for the vague Beta \((1,1)\)

Other conventions give different numbers. Figure 19.3 shows it for the example used in the rest of the chapter: a historical control arm of 100 patients with 30 responders, and a current control arm of 30 patients, with a robust prior that puts weight 0.8 on the historical-data Beta \((31,71)\) and 0.2 on Beta \((1,1)\) . text: () Figure 19.3: Dynamic (component-weighted) effective sample size of the robust prior as a function of the number of responders in the current control arm of 30. The historical control is 30/100. At the historical rate (9 of 30) the weight on the historical component is 0.94 and the borrowed ESS is about 96. At 12 of 30, which is an observed rate ten percentage points above the historical one, the weight is still 0.91. At 15 of 30 it is 0.69, and at 18 of 30 it has fallen to 0.18. The method protects against a gross conflict and does very little against a moderate one. Prior-data conflict is the general name for this problem: the current data are unlikely under the prior. Two practical diagnostics are used. The first is a prior predictive check: compute the probability, under the prior, of data at least as extreme as the observed control data (a Box p-value), and report it. The second is the weight on the vague component or the posterior of \(a_0\) or \(\tau_c\) . Neither detects conflict that the current data are too small to see. The FDA draft asks sponsors to explore prior-data conflict in the design simulations, including a scenario with no effect in the target population ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) .

title: What borrowing costs: type I error and power under drift
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.8 What borrowing costs: type I error and power under drift
text: 19.8 What borrowing costs: type I error and power under drift Now the central calculation. Take a two-arm trial with a binary endpoint, with 60 patients on the new treatment and 30 on control (2:1 randomization, so that a smaller concurrent control arm is accepted in return for borrowing). The historical control arm has 100 patients and 30 responders. The decision rule is the one the FDA draft uses, \(\Pr(\delta>0 \mid \text{data}) > c\) with \(\delta=p_1-p_0\) and \(c=0.975\) , with a Beta \((1,1)\) prior on the treatment arm. The control arm gets one of four priors: No borrowing : Beta \((1,1)\) . Full pooling : Beta \((31,71)\) , the historical arm added as if it were current. Power prior , \(a_0=0.3\) : Beta \((10,22)\) . Robust MAP-type mixture : 0.8 Beta \((31,71)\) + 0.2 Beta \((1,1)\) , with weights updated by the data. We then ask what happens when the true control rate in the current trial is not the historical 30% but \(0.30+d\) , for drift \(d\) between \(-0.15\) and \(+0.20\) . For type I error the true treatment rate equals the true control rate. For power the true treatment effect is 0.20 above the control rate. The calculation is exact: the number of responders in each arm is binomial, the decision is a function of the two counts, and the rejection probability is

text: rate, full pooling raises power from 0.43 to 0.79 with the same 90 patients, and the type I error is below 0.025 (it is conservative because the decision threshold has not been recalibrated for the borrowed information). The saving is real: it would take a no-borrowing trial with roughly 170 control patients, rather than 30, to match this power (computed with the same exact enumeration and 60 treated patients). The power prior at \(a_0=0.3\) and the robust prior sit in between. With drift upward, borrowing inflates the type I error, and the inflation is large. If the true control rate is 40% instead of 30%, the Bayesian rule that was conservative at \(d=0\) rejects a true null 14.6% of the time under full pooling, 5.4% under the power prior and 8.9% under the robust prior. At a 20 point drift, full pooling rejects 52% of the time. Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic: the rule “is the treatment rate above the posterior control rate” is correctly computed, and the posterior control rate is anchored at the wrong value. The false positive arises because the historical control appears worse than the treatment, which is exactly the signature of a successful drug. Without borrowing the type I error does not move. The first column is nearly flat, between 0.016 and 0.023 for every drift. This is the

title: What borrowing costs: type I error and power under drift

text: control appears worse than the treatment, which is exactly the signature of a successful drug. Without borrowing the type I error does not move. The first column is nearly flat, between 0.016 and 0.023 for every drift. This is the property the traditional design buys by discarding prior data: validity does not depend on any assumption about the past. The same drift that inflates type I error gives spurious power. The columns for full pooling and the power prior at \(d=+0.10\) show power of 0.97 and 0.83, but this is a mixture of a real effect and an artifact, and a sponsor cannot tell which from the trial. Conversely, at \(d=-0.15\) (the current control rate is 15 points lower than history) full pooling loses power, falling from 0.79 at no drift to 0.18, against 0.51 without borrowing: the posterior control rate is pulled up towards the old 30%, which hides a real treatment effect. Drift in one direction costs type I error and drift in the other costs power. Neither is controlled by the trial. The robust prior is not a cure. At a ten point drift it still has a type I error of 0.089, higher than the power prior’s 0.054, and only at a twenty point drift (0.147 against 0.171) does it start to protect.
