text: point drift it still has a type I error of 0.089, higher than the power prior’s 0.054, and only at a twenty point drift (0.147 against 0.171) does it start to protect. Viele and colleagues compared pooling, power priors and hierarchical borrowing in simulations of this kind and found, as here, that the gain from borrowing is lost or reversed when the current control rate drifts, and that dynamic methods protect only in part ( Viele et al. 2014 ) . Galwey argues that, unless a strong assumption is made about the degree of discounting, dynamic borrowing may give little or no gain over using the current data alone, and recommends comparing the consequences of a range of assumptions ( Galwey 2017 ) ; for a control arm of 30 this agrees with the technical note above. When there is a single historical study, as in the example here, Röver and Friede treat the discount as shrinkage estimation in a Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of two studies, and illustrate it with a trial and a clinical registry in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease ( Röver and Friede 2020 ) .

title: What the regulator does with this
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.8.1 What the regulator does with this
text: What the regulator does with this In the settings studied by Kopp-Schneider and colleagues, borrowing cannot improve power over an optimal current-data test while preserving strict conditional type I error control given the historical data ( Kopp-Schneider, Calderazzo, and Wiesenfarth 2020 ) . Recalibration can restore control, but may remove the gain. So the claim “type I error at most 0.025 over every drift” is available only for a recalibrated rule, and for the uncalibrated rules above inflation at some drift is unavoidable: a rule that is conservative when the historical rate is right gives up something when it is wrong. The FDA draft recognizes this. For designs with borrowing, “this default success criterion may not be applicable or appropriate”, and the sponsor should agree an alternative with the Agency ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . The draft says that it does not recommend using type I error inflation as the measure of how much has been borrowed , because it regards that as philosophically inconsistent with having chosen to borrow, and observes that dynamic methods already reduce borrowing near the null ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . What it asks for instead: the ESS of the prior and the ratio of prior ESS to the trial’s size, over the range of plausible data; simulations of prior-data conflict, including

title: Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.10 Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
text: 19.10 Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A Pediatric trials are the setting where borrowing is most often justified, because enrollment is small and withholding treatment from children is difficult ethically. The ICH E11A guideline on pediatric extrapolation, adopted at Step 4 in August 2024, sets out a general approach ( International Council for Harmonisation 2024 ) . It asks for a pediatric extrapolation plan with three parts: an assessment of how similar the disease, the drug’s pharmacology and the response to treatment are in the source (adult) and target (pediatric) populations, using whatever is known about the mechanism; a description of the gaps and uncertainties; and a plan for the data to be generated in children, which can range from PK and safety only (full extrapolation of efficacy) to a reduced efficacy trial to a full one. The more similar the populations, the less pediatric data are needed. Bayesian borrowing is one of the quantitative tools that the guideline allows for the middle case, in which adult data are used to inform the pediatric efficacy analysis, and the guideline emphasizes that the same evidence-based judgment of similarity should come first and the statistics second. The intravenous belimumab program in pediatric lupus, analyzed with a robust mixture prior and a tipping-point analysis over the borrowing weight, is described in Section 19.17.2 . The FDA framework for extrapolating

title: Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.10 Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
text: similarity should come first and the statistics second. The intravenous belimumab program in pediatric lupus, analyzed with a robust mixture prior and a tipping-point analysis over the borrowing weight, is described in Section 19.17.2 . The FDA framework for extrapolating adult data to children is described by Dunne et al. ( 2011 ) , and Bayesian modeling for it by Gamalo‐Siebers et al. ( 2017 ) . For rare diseases generally, FDA’s final guidance of December 2023 says that Bayesian methods may inform pediatric investigations through incorporation of adult data ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023c ) . The FDA Bayesian draft gives pediatric extrapolation as a core use of an informative prior and names empagliflozin and linagliptin in pediatric type 2 diabetes as examples where Bayesian analyses were supportive ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . It draws two practical points. First, undiscounted adult data would often overwhelm a small pediatric sample, so a prior centered on the adult effect with an inflated variance, representing the possibility that children respond differently, is often more reasonable than pooling. Second, the sources can be related in several ways: equal relevance (adolescents enrolled with adults), exchangeability (a hierarchical model across age strata after adjusting for known effect modifiers), a bias parameter (the pediatric effect equals the adult effect plus an unknown shift), and functional

title: Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.10 Pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A
text: be related in several ways: equal relevance (adolescents enrolled with adults), exchangeability (a hierarchical model across age strata after adjusting for known effect modifiers), a bias parameter (the pediatric effect equals the adult effect plus an unknown shift), and functional dependence (a pharmacometric model predicting the pediatric effect from adult data and exposure). The bias-parameter form is the one that fits the discount most naturally: if the pediatric effect is \(\theta_p=\theta_a+b\) with \(b\sim N(0,\omega^2)\) , then the adult data enter the pediatric prior with variance \(\sigma_a^2+\omega^2\) , and the sponsor’s judgment of pediatric similarity is the number \(\omega\) . With a large \(\omega\) the adult data contribute little. With \(\omega=0\) they are pooled. The protocol, in effect, writes down \(\omega\) and defends it with the pharmacology. The design consequence is the same as in the simulation above. Drift in this setting is “the pediatric effect is not the adult effect”, and its plausible range is a clinical judgment about physiology, not a statistical estimate. The simulation of conflict should therefore cover scenarios in which children respond less well than adults, including no effect, and say what the pediatric trial would conclude. A numerical example shows the bias-parameter form with a mixture prior. Let \(\theta_A\) be the adult log odds ratio, estimated as \(-0.5\) with standard error \(0.08\) , and let \(\theta_P\) be the pediatric effect.

title: Noninferiority with borrowed information
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.11 Noninferiority with borrowed information
text: 19.11 Noninferiority with borrowed information A noninferiority trial is a borrowing problem from the start. Its margin comes from the control’s effect in earlier placebo-controlled trials, and its validity rests on the constancy assumption that this effect still holds ( Section 4.9 ; FDA 2016 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2016 ) ; ICH E10 ( International Council for Harmonisation 2000 ) ). The traditional analysis uses the historical data once to fix a margin and then treats the margin as known. The Bayesian analysis can state the same thing as a model. Take a difference in event rates \(\theta=p_N-p_C\) (new minus control, events bad), noninferior if \(\theta<M\) . Suppose a trial estimates \(\hat\theta=0.01\) with standard error \(0.015\) and the margin is \(M=0.04\) . The upper limit of the two-sided 95% interval is \(0.01+1.96\times0.015=\) 0.0394, just under the margin, so the traditional test succeeds. Table 19.4 gives the posterior probability of noninferiority under three priors. Skeptical prior: N(M, 0.02^2). Enthusiastic prior: N(0, 0.01^2). Flat: improper uniform. Prior Posterior mean Pr(theta < M) Flat 0.010 0.977 Skeptical, N(M, 0.02^2) 0.021 0.945 Enthusiastic, N(0, 0.01^2) 0.003 >0.999 Under the flat prior the posterior probability is one minus the one-sided p-value, 0.977, as it must be ( Section 4.10 ). The skeptical prior, centered at the margin, is the natural regulatory prior for noninferiority: it represents a reviewer who thinks the new drug is as likely to be unacceptably worse as acceptably close. Under it the probability is 0.945, below the 0.975 that the traditional test implicitly demands. The prior is doing visible work, and the reviewer and the sponsor can argue about its standard deviation instead of about a p-value.

title: Margin synthesis
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.11.1 Margin synthesis
text: Margin synthesis Regulatory practice preserves a fraction \(f\) of the control’s effect against placebo, \(\delta_{CP}\) , estimated from the historical trials as \(N(d,s_{CP}^2)\) . The fixed-margin approach takes the lower 95% limit of \(\delta_{CP}\) , multiplies by \(1-f\) (the loss of effect that is allowed), and uses the result as the margin \(M_2\) . The synthesis alternative asks directly for the posterior probability that the new drug retains at least the fraction \(f\) , \[ \Pr\bigl(\theta_{NC}<(1-f)\,\delta_{CP}\mid\text{data}\bigr), \tag{19.9}\] with \(\theta_{NC}\) the new-minus-control difference (events bad). The network meta-analytic-predictive approach of Schmidli, Wandel and Neuenschwander is the hierarchical-model counterpart: it combines the historical trials with data on the active control and on placebo, together with the noninferiority trial, in a network meta-analysis, and predicts the effect of the test treatment against placebo in the noninferiority trial while carrying the between-trial variability of all parameters ( Schmidli, Wandel, and Neuenschwander 2013 ) . Prior-data conflict can be handled by a robust mixture, as in Section 19.6 . The synthesis method is usually credited to Rothmann et al. ( 2003 ) , with an earlier method for comparison to placebo in active-control trials in Hasselblad and Kong ( 2001 ) , its preservation-of-effect interpretation and error properties are in Snapinn and Jiang ( 2008 ) , a Bayesian formulation is in Simon ( 1999 ) , and the constancy

title: Margin synthesis
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.11.1 Margin synthesis
text: placebo in active-control trials in Hasselblad and Kong ( 2001 ) , its preservation-of-effect interpretation and error properties are in Snapinn and Jiang ( 2008 ) , a Bayesian formulation is in Simon ( 1999 ) , and the constancy assumption is discussed by Fleming ( 2008 ) . The fixed-margin approach reduces the historical estimate to a single conservative number, the lower confidence limit, and so builds in a deliberate conservatism; the synthesis carries the full uncertainty of the historical estimate into the comparison. Both rest on the constancy assumption, and the synthesis makes it visible: if care has improved since the historical trials and the control’s effect has shrunk, discounting by a power prior with \(a_0<1\) would only widen the distribution of \(\delta_{CP}\) and leave its center where it was. A shrunken effect has to be modeled directly, for example by shifting or scaling the center of \(\delta_{CP}\) by an attenuation or bias parameter with its own prior, and the retained fraction should be assessed over a range of plausible downward shifts. The fixed margin is half the lower 95% limit, 0.03, tighter than the 0.04 above, and the trial with \(\hat\theta=0.01\) and standard error 0.015 (upper limit 0.039) does not meet it. The synthesis probability of retaining at least half of the effect is 0.987. The two answers differ because the fixed margin spends all of the historical uncertainty at its worst limit and then asks the current trial to clear that limit at 0.025, which is two conservative operations stacked. The synthesis is not automatically more lenient: for a trial with \(\hat\theta=0.04\) the probability of retaining half the effect is only 0.71. Whether a regulator will accept a synthesis rule in place of a fixed margin, and with what threshold, is a question for the protocol and for early discussion with the agency; the 2016 guidance describes both approaches.

text: 19.12 Indirect comparison through a common comparator: the tirzepatide chain The question a guideline committee asks of SURPASS-CVOT is how much tirzepatide lowers cardiovascular risk compared with no incretin therapy at all. No trial answers it directly: SURPASS-CVOT compared tirzepatide with dulaglutide, and REWIND compared dulaglutide with placebo ( Nicholls et al. 2025 ; Gerstein et al. 2019 ) . The answer has to be assembled, and on the log scale the effects add, \[ \log\mathrm{HR}_{T:P}=\log\mathrm{HR}_{T:D}+\log\mathrm{HR}_{D:P}, \tag{19.10}\] with variances adding if the two estimates are independent. SURPASS-CVOT gave a hazard ratio of 0.92 (95.3% CI 0.83 to 1.01) and REWIND 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.99). title: Borrowing across subgroups: basket trials
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.13 Borrowing across subgroups: basket trials
text: 19.13 Borrowing across subgroups: basket trials A basket trial tests one therapy in several tumor types or biomarker-defined subgroups that share a molecular target. Each basket is small, and the question is which baskets respond. The traditional design runs a separate single-arm test in each basket, with a multiplicity adjustment across them ( Chapter 10 ). The Bayesian design puts the baskets in a hierarchical model, Equation 19.1 , so that responses in one basket inform the others. Thall and colleagues (2003) proposed the hierarchical model for phase II trials in diseases with multiple subtypes, and Berry and colleagues (2013) applied it to oncology subpopulations, reporting designs that need fewer patients per subgroup than independent analyses at the same type I error under their scenarios ( Thall et al. 2003 ; Berry et al. 2013 ) . In Polson and Sokolov ( 2026 ) the quoted figure is 4 to 7 patients per group fewer than independent analyses. It comes from the scenarios that Berry and colleagues chose themselves, so it shows what the method can achieve and not what it will achieve in a given trial. The next chunk shows the mechanism with ten baskets of 30 patients each. In the first scenario nine baskets have 12 responders (40%) and one has 3 (10%). In the second all ten have 12. Code: hierarchical shrinkage

Code: hierarchical shrinkage across ten baskets a <- borrow_basket_posterior ( c ( rep ( 12 , 9 ), 3 ), rep ( 30 , 10 )) b <- borrow_basket_posterior ( rep ( 12 , 10 ), rep ( 30 , 10 )) In the all-equal scenario the model estimates a small \(\tau_b\) and every basket’s estimate stays at its observed 40%. The estimate is close to the observed rate because nothing disagrees, and the posterior interval for each basket is narrower than it would be alone. In the outlier scenario, the observed heterogeneity pushes \(\tau_b\) up, so that the nine typical baskets are pulled down from 40% to about 38% by the outlier and the outlier is pulled up from 10% to about 29%. The outlier is moved a lot because it has only 30 patients and the model, informed by nine similar baskets, regards a rate of 10% as probably a low draw. If the outlier is in fact a non-responding tumor type, the model has overstated its response rate by almost three-fold, which is the “estimated worse” warning of the earlier section. The treatment effect in

If the outlier is in fact a non-responding tumor type, the model has overstated its response rate by almost three-fold, which is the “estimated worse” warning of the earlier section. The treatment effect in a basket that really does not respond is overestimated, and a decision rule such as \(\Pr(p_k>0.2\mid y)>c\) will, for some true rates, reject more often than it would with independent analyses. The inflation is again the price, and the same remedy applies: calibrate the threshold by simulation, over scenarios in which some baskets respond and others do not, and report the false positive rate for the non-responding baskets in each. FDA’s draft guidance lists basket trials under borrowing across similar diseases or subtypes, and recommends that the sponsor justify exchangeability and to model known effect modifiers, such as biomarker status, explicitly ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . Chapter 20 returns to the master-protocol setting, and Chapter 10 treats the shrinkage idea for endpoints. Several variants are worth knowing. The calibrated Bayesian hierarchical model (CBHM) of Chu and Yuan ( 2018a ) sets the amount of shrinkage as a function of the heterogeneity seen in the data, so that baskets that agree borrow more. The Bayesian latent subgroup design (BLAST) of Chu and Yuan ( 2018b ) assigns each cancer type to a

cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.13 Borrowing across subgroups: basket trials
text: the amount of shrinkage as a function of the heterogeneity seen in the data, so that baskets that agree borrow more. The Bayesian latent subgroup design (BLAST) of Chu and Yuan ( 2018b ) assigns each cancer type to a latent sensitive or insensitive subgroup and jointly models the binary response and a longitudinal biomarker, so that a non-responding tumor type is not averaged with responding ones. The exchangeability-nonexchangeability model (EXNEX) of Neuenschwander et al. ( 2016 ) gives each basket a prior probability of belonging to the common group, much as the robust prior does for a single historical control. Other designs monitor exchangeability as data accrue ( Hobbs and Landin 2018 ) or estimate which baskets are exchangeable ( Kaizer, Koopmeiners, and Hobbs 2018 ) , and Simon et al. ( 2016 ) give a Bayesian basket design. All fit the same template: the amount of borrowing is a parameter, and the operating characteristics under heterogeneity, above all the false positive rate when some baskets do not respond, have to be simulated.

title: When borrowing failed: the NSCLC case study
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.14 When borrowing failed: the NSCLC case study
text: 19.14 When borrowing failed: the NSCLC case study A sponsor deciding whether a fixed-weight power prior is enough can look at a case study that tested it. Struebing and colleagues (2024) built a matched real-world external control arm in first-line non-small cell lung cancer, augmented it with historical-trial data through a fixed-weight power prior, and compared the result with the survival result of the randomized trial whose control arm it replaced ( Struebing et al. 2024 ) . The result was a negative one: the augmented external control did not reproduce the randomized result. The lesson is the one in the simulation, from a real dataset. A power prior with a fixed discount lowers the weight of the historical data but does not change their center. Discounting does not remove differences between the sources, and if real-world patients differ from trial patients in prognostic factors that matching did not capture, the augmented control stays biased. The study is one case and should not be generalized beyond what it shows, but it is the right example to put in front of a team that proposes to replace a concurrent control with a matched external one: matching on measured covariates removes only the measured bias.

title: Prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.15 Prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins
text: 19.15 Prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins There is a way of using external data that does not borrow outcomes of the control arm and therefore carries no bias risk of this kind. Prognostic covariate adjustment (PROCOVA) builds a prognostic model of the control-arm outcome from external data, such as historical trial data, and then uses each trial participant’s predicted outcome (their “digital twin” prediction under control) as a baseline covariate in the analysis of the randomized trial. The treatment effect is still estimated by comparing the randomized arms, so the analysis remains valid, and the covariate absorbs variation in the outcome, so the variance falls. The EMA’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use adopted a qualification opinion for the method in September 2022, for phase 2 and 3 trials with continuous outcomes ( European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2022 ) . The key regulatory feature, as with the covariate adjustment guidance of FDA, is that the model is fixed before the trial starts: with an independently developed, pre-specified score and appropriate analysis and variance estimation, PROCOVA can preserve asymptotic type I error control despite poor prediction, whereas small trials need suitable finite-sample inference ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023d ; European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2022 ) . Precision gains

title: Prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.15 Prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins
text: preserve asymptotic type I error control despite poor prediction, whereas small trials need suitable finite-sample inference ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2023d ; European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) 2022 ) . Precision gains depend on prognostic performance. What the sponsor gains is variance reduction, which can be converted into a smaller sample size, up to the limit the qualification opinion sets; no assumption about the stability of the control arm over time is made. The contrast to take away is that PROCOVA uses external data to sharpen a randomized comparison, whereas borrowing uses them to replace part of it ( Ross et al. 2024 ) . This is why the method is often the first one to propose to a regulator who is wary of external controls. It gives up less (the randomized control stays) and so buys less than a full borrowing design, but what it buys carries no assumption about drift. It is a special case of the covariate adjustment of Section 5.10 , with a single prognostic score as the covariate, and the guidance of FDA and EMA on prespecification and the estimand applies to it.

title: Putting it together: a decision guide
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.16 Putting it together: a decision guide
text: 19.16 Putting it together: a decision guide The chapter’s methods fall on a line from no use of external information to full reliance on it. A practical ordering for a team choosing among them: Is a concurrent randomized control feasible? If yes, and the question is the effect of the drug in the current population, use it at full size, or use PROCOVA-type adjustment to raise precision without borrowing. This is the traditional design and it is hard to beat. If the concurrent control must be small, is there a randomized source for the same control treatment in the same population? If so, a pre-specified dynamic borrowing design (robust MAP or commensurate) is defensible, as in REBYOTA ( Section 19.17.1 ). Report the ESS, the conflict simulations and a sensitivity analysis without borrowing. If the only sources are non-randomized (registries, real-world data, historical single-arm series)? Follow the FDA external-controls draft: pre-specify, demonstrate comparability, quantify what is borrowed, and treat the result as supportive unless the effect is large and the natural history is predictable (ICH E10). Expect the NSCLC lesson to apply. Pediatric? Begin with the E11A extrapolation plan. Write the similarity judgment as a number ( \(\omega\) , \(a_0\) , \(w\) ), defend it, and simulate the case in which it is wrong. Subgroups of a disease or baskets? A hierarchical model is natural. Justify exchangeability across baskets, include known effect modifiers, and simulate scenarios with some baskets not responding.

title: In practice
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17 In practice
text: 19.17 In practice Three regulatory cases show what borrowing buys and what it risks. Two more appear earlier in the chapter: the NSCLC external-control study ( Section 19.14 ), where a matched real-world control with a fixed-weight power prior failed to reproduce a randomized result, and the EMA qualification of PROCOVA ( Section 19.15 ), which uses external data to sharpen a randomized comparison without borrowing outcomes.

title: REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17.1 REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study
text: REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study REBYOTA (RBX2660, fecal microbiota, live-jslm) prevents recurrence of Clostridioides difficile infection after antibiotics, and was approved on 30 November 2022. The sponsor first planned two phase 3 trials of about 300 patients each. After FDA’s July 2013 enforcement discretion on fecal microbiota transplantation made enrollment difficult, it proposed a single phase 3 trial (study 2017-01, PUNCH CD3) plus a Bayesian integration of the earlier phase 2b study 2014-01. FDA wrote that the studies “are generally exchangeable” but not identical, and accepted a Bayesian hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing, in which the extent of borrowing depends on how similar the effect is in both the active and placebo arms ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research 2022 ) . The January 2026 FDA draft guidance cites this as its example of borrowing from a previous trial of the same drug ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . The success criteria are the interesting part. The sponsor set two thresholds on the posterior probability of superiority as analogues of a one-sided type I error of 0.025 (one adequate and well-controlled trial) and one-sided 0.00125 (a substitute for two trials), each without borrowing. After adjusting for the information fraction actually reached, they were 0.9750338 and 0.9993275. The modified intention-to-treat result was an estimated

title: REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17.1 REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study
text: I error of 0.025 (one adequate and well-controlled trial) and one-sided 0.00125 (a substitute for two trials), each without borrowing. After adjusting for the information fraction actually reached, they were 0.9750338 and 0.9993275. The modified intention-to-treat result was an estimated success rate of 0.71 on RBX2660 against 0.57 on placebo (difference 0.13, computed from unrounded estimates, 95% credible interval 0.02 to 0.24), with posterior probability of superiority 0.991. That met the one-trial threshold and missed the two-trial threshold ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research 2022 ) . The lesson is about data alignment, not about the model. During the review FDA requested a refined analysis that aligned the success definition, the assessment period (9 weeks in 2014-01 against 8 weeks in 2017-01) and the analysis populations of the old study to those of the new one, so as to improve exchangeability. The sponsor’s primary analysis had also used non-final 2014-01 data, from which six randomized but undosed subjects had been wrongly excluded. Both the specified analysis and the refined one reached the same conclusion. The briefing document gives no borrowing weight or ESS, so the amount borrowed cannot be read from it. For a sponsor, the checklist of Section 19.16 applies: same product, randomized source, pre-specified model, and alignment of definitions before the data are analyzed.

title: Belimumab in pediatric lupus: a robust mixture and a tipping point
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17.2 Belimumab in pediatric lupus: a robust mixture and a tipping point
text: Belimumab in pediatric lupus: a robust mixture and a tipping point The pediatric trial of intravenous belimumab in systemic lupus erythematosus (C1109, PLUTO) randomized 93 children (92 in the analysis below). At week 52 the SRI-4 response was 28 of 53 (52.8%) on belimumab and 17 of 39 (43.6%) on placebo, an observed difference of 9.2 points with an odds ratio of 1.5 (95% CI 0.6 to 3.5) ( Brunner et al. 2020 ; U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research 2026 ) . That interval is far too wide to stand alone. FDA recommended a post hoc Bayesian analysis that borrowed from two adult trials (C1056 and C1057) with the same SRI-4 endpoint and the same 10 mg/kg dose ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research 2026 ) . The prior was a robust mixture of the form of Equation 19.7 : an informative component built from the adult placebo and 10 mg/kg arms, and a minimally informative component, with borrowing weight \(w\) . Instead of fixing one value of \(w\) , the analysis was a tipping-point analysis. The posterior probability of efficacy reached at least 97.5% whenever \(w\) was 0.55 or more, and the review division judged such a weight reasonable given a similar disease course, similar pharmacokinetics and similar baseline characteristics ( U.S.

The posterior probability of efficacy reached at least 97.5% whenever \(w\) was 0.55 or more, and the review division judged such a weight reasonable given a similar disease course, similar pharmacokinetics and similar baseline characteristics ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research 2026 ) . The case study stresses that the analysis was post hoc and that future programs should pre-specify it, with the discussion starting before the IND. The tipping-point analysis is the practical answer to the question “what weight should we use?”. It reports the smallest amount of borrowing that supports the conclusion and leaves the judgment of its plausibility to the clinical and pharmacological evidence, which is the role of \(\omega\) in the pediatric section above.

title: OPTIMIZER Smart: what a fixed 30% weight buys
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > 19.17.3 OPTIMIZER Smart: what a fixed 30% weight buys
text: OPTIMIZER Smart: what a fixed 30% weight buys The OPTIMIZER Smart System (cardiac contractility modulation, Impulse Dynamics, PMA P180036) was reviewed by an FDA device panel on 4 December 2018 and approved on 21 March 2019 for heart failure patients in NYHA class III with ejection fraction 25 to 45%. The pivotal trial FIX-HF-5C randomized 160 patients 1:1 and was analyzed with a Bayesian model that included “30% fixed borrowing” of data from the 229 patients with ejection fraction above 25% in the earlier FIX-HF-5 study. The primary endpoint was the change in peak VO2 at 24 weeks, and success required a posterior probability above 0.975 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Devices and Radiological Health 2019 ) . Table 13 of the summary of safety and effectiveness gives the result under four ways of handling missing data. With borrowing the posterior probability was between 0.977 and 0.989 in all four, so the success criterion was met. FIX-HF-5C alone gave 0.957 and 0.960 under two of the imputation models, 0.916 for the complete-case analysis and 0.911 with last observation carried forward, below 0.975 in each ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Devices and Radiological Health 2019 ) . The success of the device therefore depended on the borrowed 30%, and this is the clearest illustration in the book of both sides

The success of the device therefore depended on the borrowed 30%, and this is the clearest illustration in the book of both sides of borrowing. The borrowed information was worth a decision, which is the gain of the simulation above. It also carries the risk of the same simulation: if the earlier study overstated the effect, the conclusion rests on that overstatement. The FDA device guidance expects the sponsor to show simulated operating characteristics under such discrepancies ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2010 ) , and the fixed weight is the device analogue of the power prior with \(a_0=0.3\) used in our example.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > Key points
text: Key points A conventional standalone randomized-trial analysis uses prior data to choose the alternative, the control rate and the sample size, and then ignores them in the analysis. This is why its type I error does not depend on the past. External and historical controls are regarded with caution by ICH E10 and by FDA, MHRA and EMA because of selection, time trends and measurement differences. Pocock’s 1976 criteria are still the checklist. FDA’s externally controlled trials draft (February 2023), the MHRA draft and the EMA concept paper (2025, adopted May 2026) ask for pre-specification and fitness for purpose. Bayesian methods choose how much to borrow: fixed discount (power prior), estimated heterogeneity (hierarchical model, MAP prior), estimated agreement (commensurate, normalized power prior), or a mixture with a vague component (robust MAP). Static methods fix the borrowing in advance; dynamic ones let the data adjust it. Effective sample size is the summary of how much of the answer comes from outside the trial. A MAP prior built from 400 historical patients can be worth about 57 patients once between-trial variation is counted. Borrowing buys power when the historical rate is right (0.43 to 0.79 in the example) and inflates type I error when it is wrong (0.023 without borrowing, 0.146 with full pooling, 0.054 with the power prior and 0.089 with the robust prior at a

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > Key points
text: the historical rate is right (0.43 to 0.79 in the example) and inflates type I error when it is wrong (0.023 without borrowing, 0.146 with full pooling, 0.054 with the power prior and 0.089 with the robust prior at a ten point drift). A control arm of 30 cannot detect a ten point drift well enough for a dynamic method to protect against it. FDA’s January 2026 draft asks for the prior ESS, simulations of prior-data conflict (including no effect), and sensitivity analyses. It does not recommend using type I error inflation to measure the amount of borrowing. REBYOTA is the template of a good case: a randomized phase 2b source for the same product, a pre-specified hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing, a posterior of 0.991 that met the one-trial threshold (0.975) but not the two-trial one (0.99933), and a data-alignment fix from FDA. In OPTIMIZER the success criterion (0.975) was met with a fixed 30% borrowing (0.977 to 0.989) and missed without it (0.911 to 0.960). Belimumab in children was supported by a robust mixture prior with a tipping point at borrowing weight 0.55. ICH E11A (August 2024) puts the similarity judgment first in pediatric extrapolation, and Bayesian borrowing second. Basket trials use hierarchical models to borrow across tumor types, at the price of over-estimating the response in baskets that do not respond. In

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 19: Borrowing Information > Key points
text: ICH E11A (August 2024) puts the similarity judgment first in pediatric extrapolation, and Bayesian borrowing second. Basket trials use hierarchical models to borrow across tumor types, at the price of over-estimating the response in baskets that do not respond. In an NSCLC case study, a matched real-world control augmented with a fixed-weight power prior did not reproduce the randomized result. PROCOVA uses external data without borrowing outcomes, so the randomized comparison and its type I error are unchanged, and the gain is variance reduction. Note Discussion questions A sponsor proposes a 2:1 trial with a control arm of 30, borrowing from a historical control of 100 patients with a robust prior. What drift would you want the simulation to cover, who should decide the range, and what type I error at the edge would you accept for a serious but non-life-threatening condition? For a condition with no approved therapy? The FDA draft recommends against using type I error inflation as the measure of how much a design borrows, yet asks for conflict simulations that include a no-effect scenario. How are these two positions consistent? Where would you draw the line between a legitimate price of borrowing and an unacceptable one? A MAP prior from four trials has an ESS of 57 while the pooled analysis would give 400. Which of those two numbers would you

text: would you draw the line between a legitimate price of borrowing and an unacceptable one? A MAP prior from four trials has an ESS of 57 while the pooled analysis would give 400. Which of those two numbers would you put in the protocol, and what does the difference tell a clinician about how much a new control arm should be expected to differ from the old ones? In the pediatric setting, the similarity judgment \(\omega\) is a clinical, not a statistical, number. Who should supply it, when should it be fixed, and what should the sponsor do if the pediatric interim data suggest it was too optimistic? In a basket trial, nine tumor types respond and one does not. The hierarchical model reports the non-responding type at 29% against an observed 10%. What decision rule and what calibration would you propose so that a regulator would not label the basket “responding” on the strength of the other nine? title: Master Protocols and Platform Trials
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20 Master Protocols and Platform Trials
text: A conventional program builds a trial, answers one question, and takes the trial down. The site contracts, the database, the randomization system, the monitoring board and the regulatory file are all rebuilt for the next drug. A master protocol keeps that machinery standing and lets questions pass through it. The idea is not new, and it is not Bayesian. The UK prostate cancer platform STAMPEDE opened in 2005 with frequentist stopping rules and is still the clearest demonstration that a shared control arm and a standing infrastructure pay for themselves. What the Bayesian designs added is a different toolkit for the arms that nobody had planned yet: a decision rule per arm, calibrated by simulation, and hierarchical models that share information. Both frameworks can accommodate new arms and share information. They differ in their inferential machinery and decision rules, and both need a justified hypothesis family and demonstrated operating characteristics. This chapter follows the order the rest of the book uses. It starts with the traditional answer to “we have five drugs to test”, which is five separate two-arm trials, and measures what is wasted. It then describes the frequentist multi-arm multi-stage platform (STAMPEDE), the shared-control arithmetic that all platforms inherit, the problem of non-concurrent controls and calendar drift, and the multiplicity rules that differ between FDA and EMA. Only then does it turn to

title: Separate trials, and what they cost
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.1 Separate trials, and what they cost
text: 20.1 Separate trials, and what they cost Suppose a sponsor, or a network, has \(k\) experimental treatments for the same disease. The textbook plan runs \(k\) two-arm trials. Each has its own protocol and its own control group of \(m\) patients, so the program randomizes \(2km\) patients, half of them to a control arm that answers one question each. The plan is correct, easy to audit, and it is what regulators have approved drugs on for decades. Each trial has its own type I error rate and its own power, and nothing in one trial can contaminate another. Its cost is the control arm. A trial of five drugs at 80 patients per arm randomizes 800 patients, 400 of them to the same standard of care measured five times. In the separate-trials plan, 400 participants receive standard of care, measured five times, so that five separate questions could each have an isolated comparison. The sponsor pays for it in time as well, since each trial must be started, sited and closed separately. A platform answers the same \(k\) questions with one control group of size \(m\) . Each drug-versus-control comparison has the same precision as before, because its variance depends only on the two arms it uses, and the program enrolls \((k+1)m\) patients rather than \(2km\) . The saving is \[ 1 - \frac{k+1}{2k} =

Each drug-versus-control comparison has the same precision as before, because its variance depends only on the two arms it uses, and the program enrolls \((k+1)m\) patients rather than \(2km\) . The saving is \[ 1 - \frac{k+1}{2k} = \frac{k-1}{2k}, \tag{20.1}\] which is 25% for two drugs, 37.5% for four and 40% for five, approaching one half as \(k\) grows ( Polson and Sokolov 2026 ) . Saville and Berry simulated whole development programs and found the same direction on a larger scale: platform designs found beneficial treatments with fewer patients, fewer patient failures, less time and a greater probability of success than a traditional two-arm strategy ( Benjamin R. Saville and Berry 2016 ) . These are simulations under stated assumptions, not trial results. The saving falls on control assignments. Whether that reduces exposure to an inferior treatment depends on the experimental treatments’ actual effects. Real platforms add arms later, which creates the control problem discussed below. Second, it treats the \(k\) questions as separate. title: Definitions: master protocol, basket, umbrella, platform
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.2 Definitions: master protocol, basket, umbrella, platform
text: 20.2 Definitions: master protocol, basket, umbrella, platform The terms and the taxonomy were set out by Woodcock and LaVange ( 2017 ) , and the platform trial was presented to clinicians in S. M. Berry, Connor, and Lewis ( 2015 ) . FDA’s June 2026 draft defines the terms as follows. A master protocol is “a protocol designed with multiple substudies, which may have different objectives and involve coordinated efforts to evaluate one or more drugs” (Section I, printed pages 1 to 2). The three kinds it names are: Umbrella. “a trial designed to evaluate multiple drugs concurrently for a single disease or condition.” Basket. “a trial designed to evaluate a drug for multiple diseases, conditions, or disease subtypes.” Platform. “evaluate multiple drugs for one or more diseases, conditions, or disease subtypes in an ongoing manner, with drugs entering or leaving the platform.” The three differ in what is held fixed. A basket fixes the drug and varies the population, as in the tissue-agnostic approvals built on a molecular marker. An umbrella fixes the disease and varies the drug, often assigning patients to arms by biomarker. A platform fixes the disease and the infrastructure and lets the drugs change over time. In practice the terms overlap: I-SPY 2 is a platform with biomarker-defined signatures, and many baskets are platforms for one drug family. The Adaptive

title: Definitions: master protocol, basket, umbrella, platform

text: biomarker. A platform fixes the disease and the infrastructure and lets the drugs change over time. In practice the terms overlap: I-SPY 2 is a platform with biomarker-defined signatures, and many baskets are platforms for one drug family. The Adaptive Platform Trials Coalition uses adaptive platform trial for a platform whose adaptations (dropping or graduating arms, response-adaptive randomization, sample-size changes) follow decision rules fixed in advance ( Coalition et al. 2019 ) . The EC/EMA/HMA question-and-answer document defines a platform trial as a shared framework in which several investigational products enter and leave at different times under pre-specified decision rules, possibly in different diseases ( European Commission and European Medicines Agency and Heads of Medicines Agencies 2022 ) . Early reviews of how often the three designs were used, and with what mix of features, are J. J. H. Park et al. ( 2019 ) and Meyer et al. ( 2020 ) . Basket designs and the borrowing that makes them efficient belong to Chapter 19 and are not treated further here. The treatment-specific part of a platform sits in a module attached to the master protocol. It is called an intervention-specific appendix, sub-protocol, substudy appendix or, in REMAP-CAP, a domain-specific appendix. The master protocol holds what is common: eligibility, endpoints, schedule of assessments, the randomization system, the statistical framework and the governance. The module

title: The frequentist platform: multi-arm multi-stage designs
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.3 The frequentist platform: multi-arm multi-stage designs
text: 20.3 The frequentist platform: multi-arm multi-stage designs The platform with the longest record is frequentist. STAMPEDE (Systemic Therapy in Advancing or Metastatic Prostate Cancer: Evaluation of Drug Efficacy) was designed at the MRC Clinical Trials Unit at UCL as a multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) trial. The first patient was randomized in October 2005 to one of six arms, a control on standard hormone therapy and five research arms, with allocation 2:1:1:1:1:1, so that the control received twice the share of each research arm ( Mahesh K. B. Parmar et al. 2017 ) . The MAMS design for time-to-event outcomes, with stopping for lack of benefit on an intermediate outcome, was introduced by Royston, Parmar, and Qian ( 2003 ) , with stopping guidelines in Royston et al. ( 2011 ) ; Stallard and Todd ( 2003 ) gave a sequential treatment-selection design and Wason and Jaki ( 2012 ) optimal designs. The design follows the logic of a group sequential trial ( Chapter 11 ) with one change: at each interim look every research arm is compared with the control, and arms that fail a pre-specified bar are dropped while the others continue ( Sydes et al. 2009 ) . Three features of the design carry over to every platform. Intermediate outcome first. The final outcome in STAMPEDE is overall survival, which takes years. The early

cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.3 The frequentist platform: multi-arm multi-stage designs
text: bar are dropped while the others continue ( Sydes et al. 2009 ) . Three features of the design carry over to every platform. Intermediate outcome first. The final outcome in STAMPEDE is overall survival, which takes years. The early stages use failure-free survival as an intermediate outcome, with a hazard-ratio cut-off at each stage that is lenient early and tighter later, so that arms with no sign of benefit leave the trial at a fraction of the cost. In STAMPEDE the early stages are therefore futility gates on an intermediate outcome, failure-free survival, ahead of the definitive outcome, overall survival. The intermediate outcome need not be a validated surrogate, and a MAMS design can instead use the same endpoint at successive stages ( Sydes et al. 2009 ) . General MAMS methods calibrate the stopping boundaries through the joint distribution of the test statistics across stages and arms, so as to control a chosen error rate such as the pairwise or familywise rate for the comparisons in a family ( Magirr, Jaki, and Whitehead 2012 ) . Which error family is required depends on the claims the trial intends to make. STAMPEDE’s own strategy was comparison-level testing: each research arm is compared with the control at its own level, and its investigators report a familywise error rate of 6.75% for the three original comparisons

title: Shared-control arithmetic
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.4 Shared-control arithmetic
text: 20.4 Shared-control arithmetic Suppose every experimental arm \(j = 1, \dots, k\) has \(n\) patients, the control has \(n_0 = r n\) patients, and outcomes have unit variance. The estimate of the effect of arm \(j\) is the difference of arm mean and control mean. Its variance is \[ \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_j) = \frac{1}{n} + \frac{1}{n_0} = \frac{1}{n}\left(1 + \frac{1}{r}\right), \tag{20.2}\] and it depends on \(r\) and on \(n\) , with \(N = (k + r) n\) the total enrollment. Fixing \(N\) and minimizing the variance over the split gives Dunnett’s rule: the best allocation puts \(\sqrt{k}\) patients on the control for every patient on an experimental arm, \(r = \sqrt{k}\) ( Dunnett 1955 ) . Equal allocation \(r = 1\) is optimal only for \(k = 1\) . The test statistics for two arms are correlated, because both subtract the same noisy control mean. With \(n_0 = r n\) the correlation between the \(z\) statistics of two arms is \(1/(1 + r)\) : 0.5 under equal allocation, and \(1/(1+\sqrt{k})\) under the square-root rule, which is 0.33 for four arms. Those are gains in precision at a fixed total sample size, which equals the same power with about 10 to 15% fewer patients. The control arm is larger than each experimental arm but is still a smaller share of the whole than in \(k\) separate trials. With four arms and \(r = 2\) , 2 patients in 6 are on control, compared with 1 in 2 in a two-arm trial, so the chance that a given participant gets the control falls even though the control arm is the largest. FDA’s draft asks for the same thing in words: with a shared control, the master protocol should consider allocating “more participants to the control arm than each individual drug arm” (PDF p. 9), and the EMA draft gives the square-root rule as one example ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ; European Medicines Agency 2026 ) . Both texts are drafts. The statistical content is old and exact, and the protocol should state the allocation ratio and the reason for it. In practice the ratio is a design parameter that moves. When arms enter and leave, the number of arms open at a given time changes, so a platform fixes either a constant ratio per open arm

title: Shared-control arithmetic
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.4 Shared-control arithmetic
text: the reason for it. In practice the ratio is a design parameter that moves. When arms enter and leave, the number of arms open at a given time changes, so a platform fixes either a constant ratio per open arm or a constant control fraction. I-SPY 2 and GBM AGILE hold a fixed fraction of patients on control per subtype (20% in both ( Nanda et al. 2020 ; Alexander et al. 2018 ) ), and let the rest be allocated according to performance. For confirmatory platforms, the October 2026 EMA draft recommends maintaining each treatment-to-control allocation ratio and does not support response-adaptive randomization (Section 3.2.1). Sponsors proposing it should address this position explicitly ( European Medicines Agency 2026 ) .

title: The number of false positives
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.4.1 The number of false positives
text: The number of false positives Every analysis of \(k\) arms against one control makes \(k\) tests. If each test is run at one-sided level 0.025 and all arms are null, the expected number of false positives is \(0.025k\) , regardless of the correlation between tests. The correlation changes the distribution of that count. With a shared control, a control sample that happens to be unlucky low will make several arms look good together, and a lucky control will make none look good. In the four-arm illustration below, the probability of at least one false positive falls below the independent-trials value and the probability of two or more rises above it. That comparison of count tails is specific to the illustration, and the general statement is only the \(k\alpha\) expectation. The result is a lesson for how a platform is judged. A design that reports only “the probability of at least one false positive is below the independent-trial value” is correct and leaves out the thing a sponsor with five programs would worry about, which is that when the control is unusually good or bad, several programs are misjudged together. FDA’s draft makes this point when it says that a larger control allocation reduces the risk that a poorly or unusually well-performing control arm yields several correlated erroneous findings, and EMA notes that bringing the probability of multiple false positives down by tightening each arm’s level would require thresholds more stringent than Bonferroni, so more control participants is the more efficient remedy ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ; European Medicines Agency 2026 ) . The simulation report required by Chapter 14 should therefore show the distribution of the number of errors across arms and not only the familywise rate. text: ) . The simulation report required by Chapter 14 should therefore show the distribution of the number of errors across arms and not only the familywise rate. Note Technical note: why the mean is unchanged Each test statistic \(Z_j\) is marginally standard normal under the null, whatever the allocation, so \(\mathbb{P}(Z_j > z_\alpha) = \alpha\) and by linearity of expectation \(\mathbb{E}[\#\text{false positives}] = k\alpha\) . The correlation \(\rho = 1/(1+r)\) affects only the joint tail probabilities. For two arms, \(\mathbb{P}(Z_1 > z_\alpha, Z_2 > z_\alpha)\) is larger than \(\alpha^2\) for any \(\rho > 0\) , which is why the count of two or more rises in the four-arm illustration. The expectation calculation holds for any number of arms and any correlation, but the shape of the count distribution does not, so the distribution should be computed for the design at hand. The code simulates the arm means directly: a common control mean with variance \(1/n_0\) , and \(k\) independent arm means with variance \(1/n\) .

title: Concurrent and non-concurrent controls
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.5 Concurrent and non-concurrent controls
text: 20.5 Concurrent and non-concurrent controls A platform that runs for years faces a question that separate trials never face: which control patients may be compared with a given arm? Concurrent controls are those randomized while the arm was open. Non-concurrent controls were randomized before it opened. They are tempting because they are free patients, and they are dangerous because of drift. Over a platform’s life the standard of care, the mix of patients, the sites and the conduct of the trial change, so an arm that opens late is compared with controls treated under different conditions ( Dodd, Freidlin, and Korn 2021 ) .

title: Regulatory position
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.5.1 Regulatory position
text: Regulatory position FDA’s June 2026 draft is the stricter of the two. It asks that the primary comparison for a drug use only concurrently eligible controls: those who met that drug’s eligibility criteria and could have been randomized to it but were randomized to control instead (PDF p. 11, “only concurrently eligible control participants”). Controls enrolled earlier, and controls enrolled at the same time who could not have received the drug (a kidney-toxic drug excludes some patients, or a site offers only some arms), are left out of the primary analysis. The draft says that using non-concurrent data can bias the estimate and change the type I and type II error probabilities even when the analysis tries to model a time trend, and that the shared control keeps most of its efficiency gain when only concurrent controls are used. A sponsor who wants to use non-concurrent data should justify this in advance, weigh the amount of data against the calendar gap, pre-specify the method, and run sensitivity analyses that give the non-concurrent data less weight or none ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ) . The EMA draft reflection paper defines concurrent controls as those with a positive probability of being randomized to the arm of interest, states a strong preference for them, and says that non-concurrent controls are usually not acceptable for the

title: Regulatory position
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.5.1 Regulatory position
text: . The EMA draft reflection paper defines concurrent controls as those with a positive probability of being randomized to the arm of interest, states a strong preference for them, and says that non-concurrent controls are usually not acceptable for the primary analysis of the primary endpoint, though they may support supplementary analyses or rarely observed secondary endpoints ( European Medicines Agency 2026 ) . Both documents are drafts. They agree on the default and differ in how much room they leave for model-based exceptions.

title: How big is the bias? A simulation

The simulation below makes the arithmetic explicit. text: all controls 2.4 8.1 drift 2 pts/yr, B null time-adjusted 0.0 2.8 drift 2 pts/yr, B +10 pts concurrent 10.1 53.0 drift 2 pts/yr, B +10 pts all controls 12.4 85.8 drift 2 pts/yr, B +10 pts time-adjusted 10.1 59.4 With no drift ( Table 20.4 ), pooling all controls costs nothing and the three methods agree. With a 2-point-per-year drift and no true effect, the concurrent comparison is unbiased and rejects at about the nominal 2.5% (2.9% in 4,000 simulations), while pooling all controls produces a bias of 2.4 percentage points and a one-sided type I error of 8.1%, more than three times the nominal level. The platform’s own control arm turns into a source of false positives. When arm B has a true effect of 10 points, pooling “improves” power from 53% to 86%, and the improvement is partly spurious: the estimate is 12.4 points rather than 10. The calendar-time adjustment does what it was designed to do under this smooth, linear drift: no bias, nominal type I error, and slightly higher power than the concurrent-only analysis (59% against 53%), because the non-concurrent controls are used to estimate the slope. That result depends on the model being right. FDA’s draft warns that modeling does not guarantee error control, and the time-machine simulation below shows a related failure when history breaks.

title: The Bayesian time machine
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.5.3 The Bayesian time machine
text: The Bayesian time machine A less rigid alternative to a linear term lets the control rate drift as a random walk across calendar periods and estimates the control rate in the current period by borrowing from the neighboring periods, with a smoothing parameter \(\sigma_s\) that controls how fast the rate is allowed to change. This is the idea behind the time machine of Saville and colleagues, used in I-SPY 2, proposed for GBM AGILE and Precision Promise, and cited as such in FDA’s Bayesian draft ( Benjamin R. Saville et al. 2022 ; U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) . Small \(\sigma_s\) pools almost everything, large \(\sigma_s\) is nearly the concurrent-only estimate. The code below is an illustrative first-order Gaussian smoother over period-level control rates, fitted from the simulated data only (the period variances are estimated from the observed rates, not taken from the truth). It is not the published second-order model, so its results illustrate the trade-off and do not establish the robustness of the published method. It is run two ways: with \(\sigma_s\) learned from the data by restricted maximum likelihood (REML), and with \(\sigma_s\) fixed at three values for illustration. The simulation ( Table 20.5 ) estimates the control success rate in the current period under three histories of the true rate: constant, linear drift of 2 points per period, and

That value of \(\sigma_s\) was fixed with knowledge of the scenarios, which a real protocol does not have. Two points follow for the protocol. First, a time machine involves a smoothing choice, and whether it is learned from a few periods or fixed in advance, it depends on how the standard of care can change, which is a clinical judgment to be made before the data. Second, in all three illustrated histories the loosest fixed smoother ( \(\sigma_s = 0.10\) ) has a lower rmse than the concurrent-only analysis (3.9, 4.1 and 4.3 against 4.5, 4.8 and 4.8 points). Three scenarios do not establish that it is better for other histories (an abrupt drift, for example), the value was fixed with knowledge of the scenarios, and smoothing introduces bias that has to be checked: borrowing gains precision when history is stable and gives it back when history breaks. The simulation report of Chapter 14 therefore has to include scenarios with a step change,

The simulation studies and reviews of non-concurrent controls that examine this trade-off are Lee and Wason ( 2020 ) , Roig et al. ( 2022 ) , Roig et al. ( 2023 ) and Jiang et al. ( 2023 ) , and the R package ncc implements the analyses ( Krotka et al. 2023 ) . FDA’s Bayesian draft adds that the relevance of borrowed data depends on recency and on changes in standard of care, which is the same point in different words (see Chapter 19 and Chapter 16 ).

title: Multiplicity across arms
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6 Multiplicity across arms
text: 20.6 Multiplicity across arms A traditional trial with several treatment arms and one control usually controls the familywise error rate at 0.025, through Bonferroni, Holm, or Dunnett’s step-down procedure, because a regulator who approves a drug on one of several comparisons must know how many chances the sponsor had ( Chapter 10 ). A platform raises the question of what the family is. Five unrelated drugs from five sponsors that happen to share a control group would never be put in a common family in separate trials, and their arrival in the same protocol does not change their clinical independence.

title: FDA
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6.1 FDA
text: FDA The FDA draft says so directly: FDA “generally does not recommend the use of multiplicity adjustments to strongly control the probability of making at least one type I error across the multiple comparisons of different drugs” (Section H, PDF pp. 18 to 19). The reason it gives is the one of the previous section: “the expected total number of type I errors is the same regardless of whether these comparisons are made in independent trials or in a single trial” (PDF p. 19). The unit of control is the drug, with its own level, not the platform. Collignon and colleagues similarly argue that sharing a control arm does not itself call for an additional multiplicity adjustment across substudies investigating different drugs, while recognizing the possibility of multiple false positive regulatory decisions ( Collignon et al. 2020 ) . The draft keeps the adjustment where the comparisons answer one question: several doses or formulations of one drug, the components of a combination, or several endpoints for one drug. In those cases the sponsor should define the family arm by arm and defend the definition before the data are seen. Doses of one drug compared with a shared control, for example, are one family with \(d\) comparisons, and the usual tools of Chapter 10 apply: Bonferroni, Holm, a graphical procedure, or the Dunnett critical value, which uses the correlation of the shared-control statistics and is less conservative than Bonferroni.

title: EMA
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6.2 EMA
text: EMA The EMA draft is more cautious about the same fact. It notes that the shared control makes errors correlated, that the probability of at least one false positive may fall while the probability of several rises, and that tightening each arm’s level to hold down the chance of multiple false positives would require thresholds stricter than Bonferroni ( European Medicines Agency 2026 ) . It treats the choice of family as a design decision to be made in advance and argued, and it offers alternatives such as larger control groups. The comparison with FDA is subtle. Both reject a blanket adjustment across unrelated arms, and both want the sponsor to define the families. EMA’s draft puts more weight on the arms that share a regulatory submission or a sponsor, and on the distribution of the number of errors, which is the quantity the earlier simulation computed. For a program whose arms are all developed by one sponsor for one eventual label, a regulator in either jurisdiction may regard the arms as a single family; this needs a conversation, and Chapter 23 describes how to have it.

title: Bayesian error control across arms
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6.3 Bayesian error control across arms
text: Bayesian error control across arms A Bayesian platform does not remove the question, it moves it. Each arm has a success criterion of the form \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) ( Chapter 7 ). For confirmatory adaptive comparisons without borrowing, this book uses simulation-calibrated criteria, and the same calibration can be extended to a familywise rate over a defined family if the regulator asks for one. FDA’s draft also discusses direct posterior interpretation and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria; the proposed route should be discussed with FDA. FDA’s Bayesian draft specifies that the sponsor describe how the success criteria map to error control, and the simulation report shows it by arm and by family ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) . The Bayesian framework also offers a natural route to sharing information across arms, shrinkage, which frequentist analyses can reach as well through hierarchical or empirical-Bayes estimation with its own calibration. If arms in the same platform are modeled as exchangeable, with each arm’s effect drawn from a common distribution with between-arm variance \(\tau_b^2\) and sampling variance \(v\) , each estimate keeps weight \(w = \tau_b^2/(\tau_b^2 + v)\) on its own data and is pulled toward the common mean with weight \(1-w\) , and its posterior variance falls from \(v\) to \(v w\) , an information multiple of \(1/w\) ( Polson and

title: Bayesian error control across arms
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.6.3 Bayesian error control across arms
text: weight \(w = \tau_b^2/(\tau_b^2 + v)\) on its own data and is pulled toward the common mean with weight \(1-w\) , and its posterior variance falls from \(v\) to \(v w\) , an information multiple of \(1/w\) ( Polson and Sokolov 2026 ) . The reverse is also a cost: the multiple is an upper bound that treats the common mean as known, and an arm whose effect is far from its neighbors is shrunk toward them. That information is paid for by an assumption: that the arms are exchangeable. Between unrelated drugs that assumption is hard to defend, and FDA’s Bayesian draft asks that a model borrowing across substudies justify exchangeability and include known effect modifiers, such as biomarker status, as covariates rather than treating the groups as interchangeable ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) . Shrinkage across arms is therefore most defensible for arms from one drug class, doses of one drug, or the same drug in related subgroups, which is the territory of Chapter 19 . It is not a substitute for the multiplicity decision across unrelated drugs, and the protocol should not present it as one.

title: Bayesian platforms
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7 Bayesian platforms
text: 20.7 Bayesian platforms The Bayesian platforms differ from STAMPEDE in what they do at each interim look and in how they treat information shared across arms.

title: I-SPY 2: graduation by predictive probability
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.1 I-SPY 2: graduation by predictive probability
text: I-SPY 2: graduation by predictive probability I-SPY 2 is a platform for neoadjuvant breast cancer that has enrolled since 2010 and was later reconfigured as I-SPY 2.2 ( J. W. Park et al. 2016 ; D. A. Berry 2025 ) . The primary endpoint of each arm was pathologic complete response (pCR) at surgery, with tumor volume measured by MRI during treatment used to predict pCR for patients still in follow-up. Patients were classified into biomarker subtypes by hormone receptor status, HER2 status and a genomic profile, and each therapy was evaluated in each of up to ten signatures , the subtype combinations that might become a regulatory indication ( Barker et al. 2009 ; Wang and Yee 2019 ) . An arm graduated in a signature when its Bayesian predictive probability of success in a hypothetical 300-patient, equally randomized phase 3 trial against the same control, with pCR as endpoint, reached 85%; it was dropped for futility if that probability fell below 10% in all ten signatures, and no arm took more than 120 patients ( J. W. Park et al. 2016 ) . The decision is made from phase 2 data, so it answers the question a sponsor asks at a go/no-go meeting. It differs from a posterior probability of benefit, which asks whether the effect is positive and says nothing about the

title: I-SPY 2: graduation by predictive probability
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.1 I-SPY 2: graduation by predictive probability
text: The decision is made from phase 2 data, so it answers the question a sponsor asks at a go/no-go meeting. It differs from a posterior probability of benefit, which asks whether the effect is positive and says nothing about the size and power of the trial that would follow. The simulation below ( Table 20.7 ) shows the difference with four phase 2 results, 50 patients per arm in the signature, and a phase 3 with 150 per arm tested at one-sided 0.025. text: can see at the start what phase 2 result would be enough. Predictive probabilities are developed in Chapter 15 . Three further features of I-SPY 2 are relevant. Randomization was response adaptive within a signature, with a fixed share held on control (20% ( Nanda et al. 2020 ) ), the remainder going to arms that looked better ( J. W. Park et al. 2016 ) . A control cohort for each signature accumulated over the years, with a time machine used to smooth the control response over time. And the platform also tested combination regimens as experimental arms against the shared control. The graduation results of the first two graduates, neratinib and pembrolizumab, and why their final predictive probabilities fell after all pathology was in, are told in Section 15.10 . Because allocation adapts toward responsive subtypes, the raw difference should not be read as the treatment effect, and a design that allocates by subtype responsiveness needs a model that adjusts for it; Chapter 16 describes the mechanism and the critiques. I-SPY 2 is a phase 2 screening platform. A graduation is a decision to run a phase 3, and it carries a false positive rate that was calibrated by simulation to be acceptable for a screening stage ( Chapter 14 ). title: GBM AGILE: a registration platform
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.2 GBM AGILE: a registration platform
text: GBM AGILE: a registration platform GBM AGILE (Adaptive Global Innovative Learning Environment, NCT03970447) is a Bayesian response-adaptive platform in glioblastoma designed with registration in mind, which I-SPY 2 was not ( Alexander et al. 2018 ) . An antecedent is the Bayesian adaptive randomized design for recurrent glioblastoma of Trippa et al. ( 2012 ) . It uses a seamless phase 2/3 structure: in stage 1 each arm is randomized adaptively against a shared control (temozolomide in newly diagnosed disease, lomustine in recurrent), with allocation in proportion to the posterior probability of a hazard ratio below a benchmark and arms evaluated monthly; an arm that clears the stage 1 bar graduates to stage 2 with fixed randomization to confirm the finding for registration ( Alexander et al. 2018 ) . In the first completed arm, regorafenib, efficacy required a Bayesian probability of benefit (hazard ratio below 1) of at least 98%, and enrollment stopped for limited efficacy when the Bayesian predictive power fell below 25% in all signatures ( Wen et al. 2026 ) . The published report has since been corrected by an erratum ( Wen, Berry, et al. 2026 ) . Patients are classified into signatures based on newly diagnosed versus recurrent disease and MGMT methylation status, and 20% of each subtype’s patients are assigned to control ( Alexander et al. 2018 )

title: GBM AGILE: a registration platform
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.2 GBM AGILE: a registration platform
text: ( Wen, Berry, et al. 2026 ) . Patients are classified into signatures based on newly diagnosed versus recurrent disease and MGMT methylation status, and 20% of each subtype’s patients are assigned to control ( Alexander et al. 2018 ) . The 98% is the kind of number the FDA Bayesian draft discusses under calibration to type I error: the threshold is set by simulation so that the false positive rate over the design’s scenarios is acceptable, not by a view about the prior, and the simulation report is part of the submission ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) . GBM AGILE is also the example FDA’s Bayesian draft names for the time machine: the shared control over the years has to be used carefully when standard of care changes. The platform’s own registry record lists 17 arm entries ( ClinicalTrials.gov 2026 ) , including regorafenib, paxalisib and VAL-083, with several arms (VT1021, troriluzole, ADI-PEG 20, tinostamustine) running dose-finding and enhanced safety management phases before the main arm. That reflects an amendment pattern worth copying: a safety lead-in as part of the arm’s appendix, with its own go/no-go rule, ahead of the efficacy comparison.

title: REMAP-CAP: domains, response-adaptive randomization, and an embedded design
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.3 REMAP-CAP: domains, response-adaptive randomization, and an embedded design
text: REMAP-CAP: domains, response-adaptive randomization, and an embedded design REMAP-CAP (Randomized, Embedded, Multifactorial Adaptive Platform trial for Community-Acquired Pneumonia) is a platform designed before the pandemic it became known for ( Angus et al. 2020 ) . After the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, an EU-funded network built the infrastructure, which began enrolling in April 2016 according to its ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT02735707) and carried a dormant pandemic stratum that was activated for COVID-19. Its design has four features that distinguish it from the oncology platforms. Multifactorial. The platform is organized by domains , each a set of alternative interventions for one aspect of care: corticosteroids, antivirals, immune modulators, anticoagulation, antibiotic strategy, ventilation. A patient is randomized in every domain for which he or she is eligible, so a single patient can contribute to several comparisons, and the domains are analyzed together in a model that includes the interactions that were prespecified. Each domain has its own appendix and its own statistical analysis plan, which means the master protocol is stable while the domains come and go. Embedded. The trial runs inside routine care and uses routinely collected data where it can, which keeps the burden per patient low enough for ICUs under pandemic load. Ordinal primary endpoint. For the pandemic stratum the primary endpoint was organ-support-free days to day 21, an ordinal scale with death as the worst

title: REMAP-CAP: domains, response-adaptive randomization, and an embedded design
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.3 REMAP-CAP: domains, response-adaptive randomization, and an embedded design
text: where it can, which keeps the burden per patient low enough for ICUs under pandemic load. Ordinal primary endpoint. For the pandemic stratum the primary endpoint was organ-support-free days to day 21, an ordinal scale with death as the worst outcome, analyzed with a Bayesian proportional-odds model ( REMAP-CAP Investigators, Gordon, et al. 2021 ) . Response-adaptive randomization and decision rules. Allocation within a domain is updated at pre-specified intervals to favor arms with a higher posterior probability of being best, and the domain stops when a pre-specified trigger is crossed. In the IL-6 domain the triggers were: superiority if the posterior probability of being best exceeded 99%; efficacy if the probability that the odds ratio against control exceeded 1 was above 99%; futility if the probability that the odds ratio exceeded 1.2 was below 5%; and equivalence of two non-control arms if the probability of an odds ratio between 0.83 and 1.2 exceeded 90% ( REMAP-CAP Investigators, Gordon, et al. 2021 ; Angus et al. 2020 ) . The platform declared that interleukin-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab and sarilumab) improved outcomes, including survival, in critically ill patients with COVID-19 ( REMAP-CAP Investigators, Gordon, et al. 2021 ) . Note that a platform with this structure can declare a domain complete and move on without waiting for the others, which is the property the sponsors of
