Note that a platform with this structure can declare a domain complete and move on without waiting for the others, which is the property the sponsors of separate trials have to give up. The domains share a hierarchical structure in one sense: the pandemic and non-pandemic strata, and subgroups within a domain, can be modeled with partial pooling. This is borrowing in the sense of Chapter 19 , and the conditions under which it is acceptable are the same.

title: The COVID anticoagulation multiplatform
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.4 The COVID anticoagulation multiplatform
text: The COVID anticoagulation multiplatform Three independently funded Bayesian platforms (REMAP-CAP, ATTACC in Canada, and ACTIV-4a in the United States) asked the same question early in the pandemic: therapeutic-dose against prophylactic-dose anticoagulation in COVID-19. Separate reports would have invited conflicting results and a post hoc meta-analysis. The three teams instead harmonized their protocols and statistical analysis plans before the data were in, and combined patient-level data in a Bayesian hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing across severity strata ( ATTACC Investigators et al. 2021 ; REMAP-CAP Investigators, ACTIV-4a Investigators, et al. 2021 ) . The stopping rule was superiority at a posterior probability above 99% or futility at above 95% for an odds ratio below 1.2, applied separately in each severity cohort. In critically ill patients enrollment stopped for futility (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CrI 0.67 to 1.03, futility probability 99.9%); in non-critically ill patients therapeutic dosing increased organ-support-free days (odds ratio 1.27, 95% CrI 1.03 to 1.58, probability of benefit 98.6%) ( REMAP-CAP Investigators, ACTIV-4a Investigators, et al. 2021 ; ATTACC Investigators et al. 2021 ) . The severity strata had been specified in advance, so the finding was not a post hoc subgroup. The anticoagulation project is an unusual use of the platform idea. The shared object was a pre-agreed analysis, not a shared control group, and the platforms are the data sources for a single multi-site analysis. It shows what is possible when the sponsors agree on the estimand in advance, and it is the nearest thing the field has to a meta-analysis designed before the data exist.

title: Pragmatic pandemic platforms: RECOVERY and PANORAMIC
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.7.5 Pragmatic pandemic platforms: RECOVERY and PANORAMIC
text: Pragmatic pandemic platforms: RECOVERY and PANORAMIC Not every pandemic platform was an elaborate Bayesian adaptive design. RECOVERY (Randomized Evaluation of COVID-19 Therapy) was a large, pragmatic and open-label platform in hospitalized patients, analyzed with frequentist methods, with deliberately little data collected beyond what the health service already records and 28-day mortality as the primary outcome. Its first major result was that dexamethasone reduced 28-day mortality overall (rate ratio 0.83, a reduction of about a sixth), by more among patients on invasive mechanical ventilation (0.64), and not at all among those who needed no oxygen ( RECOVERY Collaborative Group et al. 2021 ) . PANORAMIC took the pragmatic approach into UK primary care and analyzed its primary outcome with Bayesian logistic regression using weakly informative Cauchy priors. Its molnupiravir comparison randomized 25,783 participants between December 2021 and April 2022 to molnupiravir plus usual care or usual care alone (the platform’s total of 26,411 includes other comparisons), and hospitalization or death within 28 days in about 1% of each group (adjusted odds ratio 1.06), a clear negative result from a platform that could enroll that many community patients in under five months ( Butler et al. 2023 ) . The two trials show that simplicity and volume can do the work that a more elaborate adaptive design does elsewhere, and that a platform’s value comes first from its infrastructure and its speed.

title: Traditional against Bayesian platforms: what differs

text: across arms or strata with a justified exchangeability argument ( Chapter 19 ) What the regulator asks the MAMS calculation and the stopping boundaries the simulation report, prior and borrowing justification, time-trend handling Where they agree for a normal likelihood with known standard error, a flat prior and a single final look, the posterior probability of benefit equals one minus the one-sided p-value, and the corresponding thresholds agree the same (for binary outcomes the correspondence is approximate) The traditional design is the better choice when the arms are known, the intermediate outcome is trusted, and the sponsor wants the simplest possible regulatory conversation. A Bayesian platform can earn its complexity when the outcome can be modeled longitudinally, or when information can be shared across strata with a defensible exchangeability argument. Frequentist platforms also accommodate added arms, and for confirmatory use the EMA draft does not support response-adaptive randomization, so the allocation rule is a point to settle with the regulator.

title: Governance, firewalls and the monitoring board
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.8 Governance, firewalls and the monitoring board
text: 20.8 Governance, firewalls and the monitoring board A platform survives its first arm only if the governance is built for arms that are not yet known. Typically a single data monitoring committee (DMC) oversees all arms, an independent statistical center runs the unblinded interim analyses and feeds the allocation algorithm, and a separate committee approves applications for new arms. The arrangement serves one aim: no sponsor sees how a competitor’s arm is performing. Under a Bayesian response-adaptive design, in which allocation probabilities depend on accumulating results, the allocation proportions themselves leak information, so the sponsor-facing report should show enrollment counts only when they cannot be inverted into outcomes. A burn-in period of equal allocation before adaptation begins, with the statistical center and not the sponsor holding the algorithm, is the usual safeguard ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ; European Commission and European Medicines Agency and Heads of Medicines Agencies 2022 ) . Several other elements of governance have regulatory consequences. Who is the sponsor. A master protocol needs a sponsor responsible for the platform (the “master protocol sponsor” of FDA’s draft) and, for each arm, an arm sponsor who owns the drug and its safety reporting. In the US, when all substudies sit under one master IND, FDA’s draft recommends that a new substudy be submitted at least 30 days before it begins

text: each arm, an arm sponsor who owns the drug and its safety reporting. In the US, when all substudies sit under one master IND, FDA’s draft recommends that a new substudy be submitted at least 30 days before it begins and that the regulatory project manager is notified at least 48 hours before the amendment is submitted ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ) . In the EU, a new arm is a substantial modification of the authorization, and since a change to one sub-protocol can force changes to others, each sub-protocol states how far it depends on the rest ( European Commission and European Medicines Agency and Heads of Medicines Agencies 2022 ) . STAMPEDE’s experience was that each new comparison was a substantial amendment, and that drug supply could set the pace. Simulating before opening. Analytical error-rate and power calculations are available for some platform designs with added arms. Platforms combining staggered entry, allocation changes and adaptive decisions generally need simulation to assess their full operating characteristics ( Choodari-Oskooei et al. 2020 ; Meyer et al. 2025 ) , and the simulation report of Chapter 14 is the vehicle. Meyer and colleagues draw lessons on why and how platform trials should be simulated from the EU-PEARL consortium. What the firewall protects. The sponsor of one arm should not see another arm’s data,

text: report of Chapter 14 is the vehicle. Meyer and colleagues draw lessons on why and how platform trials should be simulated from the EU-PEARL consortium. What the firewall protects. The sponsor of one arm should not see another arm’s data, the control arm’s results, or the platform’s allocation algorithm in a way that would let it infer them. The DMC sees everything. The master protocol’s governance section should state who sees what, and the confidentiality agreements for arm sponsors should say so. Rules fixed before data. The DMC charter should list the decision rules for each arm (stopping for efficacy, futility, graduation) and state that the DMC can override them for safety but not for convenience. The decision rules and the allocation algorithm are changed only by protocol amendment, with the simulation report updated accordingly. Operating characteristics must be re-established when anything that affects them changes ( Chapter 14 ); a late-arriving arm changes the correlation structure and the allocation ratio, and the previous simulation may no longer apply. title: EPAD: a platform that never opened an arm
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > 20.9 EPAD: a platform that never opened an arm
text: 20.9 EPAD: a platform that never opened an arm The European Prevention of Alzheimer’s Dementia program (EPAD) is the standard example of a platform that did not work. A 64-million-euro, five-year IMI-funded project, it built a 2,000-participant readiness cohort with detailed pre-characterization (amyloid status, cognitive baselines and longitudinal follow-up) to reduce the very high screen-failure rates of Alzheimer’s prevention trials ( Ritchie et al. 2016 ; Saunders et al. 2022 ) . It never enrolled a single treatment arm. In the project’s own post-mortem, two obstacles were decisive: owners of candidate interventions were reluctant to hand sponsorship of a critical asset to a university-run platform, and the stakeholders could not agree on a legal framework that suited every party ( Saunders et al. 2022 ) . When the five-year term ended in 2020, the treatment platform had never opened and the pandemic had made funding harder. The cohort data and biobank outlived the project. The lesson is organizational, not statistical: nothing in EPAD’s statistical design was at fault, and the sample-size, borrowing and decision rules were never tested. Platforms need three things before a first arm. A legal framework that arm sponsors will sign, because they are handing control of an asset to a shared structure. A funding model that does not depend on the commercial pipeline the platform is meant to serve; the Healey ALS Platform Trial is the contrast ( Quintana et al. 2023 ) . And a governance structure that answers the question “who decides?” before the first arm’s sponsor asks it.

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > Key points
text: Key points A platform shares control patients: \(k\) comparisons need \((k+1)m\) patients rather than \(2km\) , a saving of \((k-1)/(2k)\) , with the same precision per comparison. Five drugs at 80 per arm need 480 patients, not 800. The best allocation puts \(\sqrt{k}\) patients on the control for each patient on an arm (Dunnett). FDA recommends more patients on the control than on any single arm, and the EMA draft cites the square-root rule. A shared control keeps the expected number of false positives at \(k\alpha\) but makes them correlated: in the four-arm illustration the chance of at least one falls and the chance of several rises. Report the distribution of the number of errors. Non-concurrent controls carry drift. In the simulation, pooling them under a 2-point-per-year drift raised the one-sided type I error from about 2.5% to 8.1%. FDA asks for concurrently eligible controls for the primary analysis, and EMA generally rejects non-concurrent controls for the primary endpoint. Time-trend models and time-machine smoothers recover power when history is stable and lose it, or bias, when it breaks. In our three illustrated histories the loosest fixed smoother had a lower rmse than the concurrent-only analysis, but three scenarios do not show it is better for other histories (an abrupt drift, for example), and the smoothing bias must be checked. FDA generally does not recommend multiplicity

title: Key points
cx: Chapter 20: Master Protocols and Platform Trials > Key points
text: fixed smoother had a lower rmse than the concurrent-only analysis, but three scenarios do not show it is better for other histories (an abrupt drift, for example), and the smoothing bias must be checked. FDA generally does not recommend multiplicity adjustment across unrelated drugs in a master protocol, and expects the sponsor to define families (doses, combinations, endpoints of one drug) in advance. Hierarchical shrinkage across arms needs a defensible exchangeability argument. STAMPEDE shows a frequentist MAMS platform works. I-SPY 2 graduates arms by predictive probability, GBM AGILE adds a seamless registration stage, and REMAP-CAP combines domains, ordinal outcomes and adaptive allocation. The anticoagulation multiplatform pre-agreed one analysis across three platforms. For confirmatory platforms the EMA draft does not support response-adaptive randomization. Governance decides whether a platform opens: EPAD had the cohort and the design and never enrolled an arm. title: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21 Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials
text: The earlier chapters argued in general terms: that a Bayesian rule monitored continuously can reach the same conclusion as a fixed design with fewer events, that the saving comes from the monitoring and not from a lower bar, and that every gain has a price. This chapter tests the argument on five trials that were actually run, and it keeps the argument honest by choosing them to differ. SELECT is the favorable case: a large effect, cleanly estimated, in a trial big enough for the asymptotics to apply. REWIND is the unfavorable case: an effect half as large on the log scale, which barely cleared its threshold and in which the scheduled design wins. SURPASS-CVOT is an active-comparator case with a noninferiority margin, where the lesson is what the margin and a transportability assumption allow a Bayesian reading to say. TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 is a different kind of case: a trial with two prespecified design features, a biomarker-guided treatment duration and baseline tau strata, that a Bayesian analysis could be proposed to handle differently. BNT162b2, the last case, is a trial that was Bayesian in its confirmatory analysis as well as in its design, and that led to an emergency use authorization and a biologics license. Each case follows the same order, in line with the rule of this book that the traditional design comes first.

Each case follows the same order, in line with the rule of this book that the traditional design comes first. We say what the trial did and how it was monitored; we then reconstruct the Bayesian alternative on the trial’s own published numbers; and we close with what a data monitoring committee (DMC) and a regulator would have had to accept in order to act on it. Everything in the SELECT and REWIND reconstructions and in the stratum illustration for TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 is a counterfactual, and we say so each time it matters. BNT162b2 is the exception: its Bayesian analysis was the trial’s actual analysis. No sponsor ran these trials the way we simulate them, and nothing here is a claim that any of them should have stopped early. The reconstructions are a way of pricing the design choices in units that a sponsor, a payer and a regulator can all read: events, patients, years, quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and money. The others are direct interpretation of posterior probabilities, for example with borrowing and by agreement with FDA, and decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criteria (Section IV.A.3). Calibration is this book’s default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, and the route this chapter follows; it is one of FDA’s routes and not its universal requirement, and a draft recommends and does not require. The prior must be prespecified (Sections IV.B and V). FDA, Demonstrating Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness (revised draft, June 2026): the statutory standard of adequate and well-controlled investigations, and the conditions under which one trial with confirmatory evidence can suffice. Cardiovascular outcomes trials are usually the only large trial a sponsor has, which makes this the standard in play. title: The trial as conducted
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.1.1 The trial as conducted
text: The trial as conducted SELECT randomized 17,604 adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease, without diabetes, to weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, at 804 sites in 41 countries, enrolling from 2018 to 2021 ( Lincoff et al. 2023 ) . The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke, analyzed as time to first event. It occurred in 569 of 8,803 patients on semaglutide and 701 of 8,801 on placebo: 1,270 events in all, hazard ratio 0.80 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.72 to 0.90, and \(p < 0.001\) . Mean follow-up was 39.8 months. This is the traditional trial in its standard form: an event-driven design with a single primary hypothesis, a Cox model for the hazard ratio, an independent DMC, and a final analysis at which the type I error is spent. SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 (a 17 percent reduction) with 90 percent power at one-sided 0.025, which calls for 1,225 planned events, and it planned one superiority interim analysis at two thirds of the planned events (about 817) followed by the final analysis, with the group sequential design accounted for in the final test ( Ryan et al. 2020 ) . The textbook formula at the design hazard ratio gives about 1,211 events, close to the

The textbook formula at the design hazard ratio gives about 1,211 events, close to the plan. The observed hazard ratio of 0.80 was more favorable than the design alternative. The four-look O’Brien-Fleming design below is a separate hypothetical comparator, and SELECT’s actual two-look design is carried through every comparison as a fourth rule. The reconstruction asks a different question from the one the sponsor faced: if the true hazard ratio were 0.80 and the trial’s information as observed, what would each monitoring scheme, each held to the same one-sided error of 2.5 percent, have needed? In information time the trial is a clean object. With \(d = 1{,}270\) events, the standard error of the log hazard ratio is approximately \(2/\sqrt{d}\) , because each event carries about \(1/4\) of a unit of Fisher information under 1:1 allocation (this is the standard approximation for a log-rank or Cox analysis, and it is why \(I_n = d/4\) throughout this chapter). The log hazard ratio is \(\theta = -\log(0.80) = 0.2231\) in the book’s sign convention, so that benefit is positive, and the final standardized score is \(Z = 3.98\) . title: Three monitoring schemes and SELECT's own design, one error rate
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.1.2 Three monitoring schemes and SELECT's own design, one error rate
text: Three monitoring schemes and SELECT’s own design, one error rate A speed comparison means nothing unless the rules carry the same type I error under the monitoring each actually uses, and this is where naive comparisons fail. We compare three rules and add SELECT’s actual design as a comparator. Group sequential, O’Brien-Fleming. Four equally spaced looks at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of the events, with the O’Brien-Fleming boundaries on the \(Z\) scale of 4.049, 2.863, 2.337 and 2.024 (see Chapter 11 ; the working paper printed 4.05, 2.87, 2.34 and 2.03 from a rounded constant; the reconstruction uses the exact values above). It can act only at a scheduled look. This is the design most event-driven outcomes trials use today, and it is the one a regulator will expect to see first. Bayesian posterior probability, monitored on a fine event grid. Stop for benefit when \(\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid \text{data}) \ge p^\ast\) , with a normal prior on the log hazard ratio centered at zero with scale \(\tau = 0.25\) (a prior 95 percent interval for the hazard ratio of 0.61 to 1.63, a skeptical prior in the sense of Chapter 8 ), and \(p^\ast\) chosen so that the one-sided type I error is 2.5 percent when the rule is evaluated at every second event from 4 to 1,270. text: What the saving would be worth in calendar time and exposure From here to the end of the chapter every conversion of events into time, exposure, QALYs or money is a modeled counterfactual: it combines the simulated stopping distribution with an accrual model and with assumptions about what would have happened to patients after a decision. Note Technical note: why the e-value rule is slow here The e-value rule uses the same normal prior scale \(\tau\) and the same score \(S\) as the Bayesian rule, with \(I_n = d/4\) events-based information and \(A = I_n + 1/\tau^2\) . The simulated Bayesian rule acts when \(\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid \text{data}) = \Phi(S/\sqrt{A}) \ge p^\ast\) , which on the scale \(Z = S/\sqrt{I_n}\) is \(Z \ge \sqrt{1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2)}\, z_{p^\ast}\) with \(z_{p^\ast} = \Phi^{-1}(p^\ast)\) , or \(Z^2 \ge (1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2))\, z_{p^\ast}^2\) with \(Z > 0\) . The e-value rule acts when the mixture likelihood ratio \(E_n\) reaches \(1/\alpha\) , which on the same scale is \(Z^2 \ge (1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2))\,[\log(1 + I_n\tau^2) + 2\log(1/\alpha)]\) with \(Z > 0\) . At \(\tau = 0.25\) and \(p^\ast = 0.9952\) the Bayes bar is \(Z^2 \ge 7.6\) at 464 events and 7.0 at 1,270, and the e-value bar is 10.8 and 10.9, so the e-value rule asks for 3.2 more units of \(Z^2\) at 464 events and 3.9 more at 1,270. The constant \(2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38\) at \(\alpha = 0.025\) is, for this normal-mixture construction and in the large-information approximation, the surcharge of the e-value bar over the uncalibrated Bayes-factor rule at posterior odds 1, \(Z^2 \ge \log(1 +

The constant \(2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38\) at \(\alpha = 0.025\) is, for this normal-mixture construction and in the large-information approximation, the surcharge of the e-value bar over the uncalibrated Bayes-factor rule at posterior odds 1, \(Z^2 \ge \log(1 + I_n\tau^2)\) , of Chapter 11 and Chapter 12 ; the exact surcharge is \(7.38\,(1 + 1/(I_n\tau^2))\) . It is not a universal cost of anytime validity, since other e-processes behave differently. It is also not the surcharge over the calibrated posterior-probability rule simulated here, whose bar \(p^\ast\) was itself raised by simulation to pay for monitoring on the grid. The e-value rule’s realized type I error of about 0.6 percent against a budget of 2.5 percent is the visible form of the remaining difference: it is paying for protection at stopping times this trial never used. In this construction the surcharge is a constant in the large-information approximation, and its relative cost falls only as \(1/\log I_n\) ; see Chapter 12 .

title: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.1.5 What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
text: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept The reconstruction is only useful if the Bayesian rule could have been proposed, accepted and run. Walk through the four principles of the FDA adaptive-designs guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019a ) and the success-criterion language of the Bayesian draft ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) . Error control. This is met by construction in the reconstruction, on the event grid and to the 1,270-event horizon, because \(p^\ast\) was found by simulation so that the one-sided familywise type I error under the monitoring plan is 2.5 percent. That fixes the rejection proportion in the calibration sample, not the population error, so a protocol would report the Monte Carlo uncertainty (about 0.0008 at 40,000 paths), validate the threshold on independent null simulations as above, and repeat both across nuisance scenarios. The draft describes calibration as one of three routes, and for a design with a frequentist analysis plan and no borrowing it is the usual one. The weakness is that the calibration holds under a specific monitoring plan. A rule calibrated to a fine grid is conservative for a DMC that meets twice a year, because any subset of the grid inherits the bound. A rule calibrated to meetings twice a year is anti-conservative if the committee also looks ad hoc,

title: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.1.5 What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
text: to a fine grid is conservative for a DMC that meets twice a year, because any subset of the grid inherits the bound. A rule calibrated to meetings twice a year is anti-conservative if the committee also looks ad hoc, for example after a safety signal. A DMC that cannot commit to a schedule can calibrate to a dense grid at the cost of a higher threshold, but monitoring off the grid or beyond the horizon needs recalibration, and a trial that cannot bound its looks should use a fixed design, a spending function or an anytime-valid rule. Reliable estimation. A trial that stops at the conditional median of 464 events yields a hazard ratio estimate that is biased away from the null on average, as is true of trials that stop early for efficacy, and the confidence interval is wider than the interval from 1,270 events by about \(\sqrt{1270/464} = 1.65\) . The Bayesian posterior shrinks the estimate towards the prior, which is a correction in the right direction but not a free one. The trial’s other jobs would also suffer: the key secondary endpoints, the safety database for an agent intended for long-term use, and the subgroup results a label depends on all need events and patient-years, not just a primary endpoint that crossed a bar. For a drug intended for chronic use

text: endpoints, the safety database for an agent intended for long-term use, and the subgroup results a label depends on all need events and patient-years, not just a primary endpoint that crossed a bar. For a drug intended for chronic use by people without diabetes, a regulator may well prefer the longer exposure. This is a real cost and the reason the calendar saving in this chapter should not be read as a recommendation. Prespecification. The prior scale, the threshold, the monitoring schedule and the stopping rule would all have to be written into the protocol and the statistical analysis plan, prospectively. E9 requires interim analyses to be planned and described in the protocol (Section 4.5) and permits justified amendments before unblinded access to comparative data, with their statistical consequences addressed ( International Council for Harmonisation 1998 ) . The simulation report that supports them is the operating-characteristics evidence the FDA asks for ( Chapter 14 ). Trial integrity. The DMC would have been shown a posterior probability and a threshold instead of a boundary. The sponsor would remain blind to the interim comparisons, as it does under a group sequential plan. Nothing about the Bayesian rule changes the firewall; what changes is the number the committee reads. The regulator’s question about the prior is the one a group sequential design never faces. Here it is

text: does under a group sequential plan. Nothing about the Bayesian rule changes the firewall; what changes is the number the committee reads. The regulator’s question about the prior is the one a group sequential design never faces. Here it is answered the way the draft asks: the prior is skeptical, it is prespecified, and its influence on the decision is bounded by the calibration, since a different \(\tau\) changes \(p^\ast\) and leaves the simulated type I error unchanged (see Chapter 8 ). A regulator who accepts that the final decision rule is “reject when the calibrated posterior probability exceeds \(p^\ast\) ” is accepting a test with simulated size and power, which is also what it accepts from an O’Brien-Fleming design. In the language of the substantial-evidence draft ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ) , the evidence in either case is a single well-controlled trial whose persuasiveness comes from its effect size and its error control, and a hazard ratio of 0.80 with a final score near 4 is persuasive under any of the rules.

title: The trial as conducted
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.2.1 The trial as conducted
text: The trial as conducted REWIND randomized 9,901 patients with type 2 diabetes to weekly dulaglutide or placebo, enrolling from August 2011 to August 2013 with a median follow-up of 5.4 years, and reported in 2019 ( Gerstein et al. 2019 ) . The primary composite cardiovascular outcome occurred in 594 of 4,949 on dulaglutide and 663 of 4,952 on placebo, so 1,257 events, with a hazard ratio of 0.88, a 95 percent interval from 0.79 to 0.99, and \(p = 0.026\) . REWIND ran in the regulatory setting of the 2008 diabetes guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2008 ) , which asked sponsors of new glucose-lowering drugs to show that the drug did not raise cardiovascular risk beyond a prespecified margin on the hazard ratio. That is the historical context, but REWIND itself was designed to demonstrate cardiovascular superiority, with 90 percent power, and not merely to exclude the 2008 margin ( Gerstein et al. 2019 ) . A reconstruction that asks about stopping for benefit is therefore as natural for REWIND as for SELECT, and the contrast below is about the size of the effect and not about the purpose of the trial. The information content is almost identical to SELECT, 1,257 events against 1,270. The effect is half the size on the log scale, 0.128 against 0.223, so the final standardized

title: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.2.3 What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
text: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept The honest conclusion for REWIND is that the scheduled design was the right choice, and a Bayesian statistician advising the sponsor would have said so if the expected effect was a hazard ratio near 0.88. Four things follow for a protocol. First, the reconstruction does not rescue the argument for continuous monitoring in a marginal trial, and it should not be offered to a regulator as if it did. The regulator’s concern with a glucose-lowering drug would also include the one stated in the 2008 guidance: precision at the upper bound of the interval, which is a property of the full trial and cannot be got from half of it. Second, the same Bayesian machinery is useful for a different purpose in such a trial. A posterior distribution for the hazard ratio from the final data, with a skeptical prior, answers the question the 2008 guidance asks (is the upper bound of the effect on cardiovascular risk below the margin?) in the units of the margin. This does not change when the trial can stop; it changes how the result is reported ( Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 ). Third, the contrast between SELECT and REWIND is itself the finding. The saving from continuous Bayesian monitoring grows with the size of the effect relative

title: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.2.3 What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
text: stop; it changes how the result is reported ( Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 ). Third, the contrast between SELECT and REWIND is itself the finding. The saving from continuous Bayesian monitoring grows with the size of the effect relative to the precision, which a sponsor knows only roughly in advance. The assurance calculation of Chapter 9 is the tool for deciding which design to pick before the trial: the average of the probability of success over a prior on the effect. A prior that puts most of its mass on hazard ratios near 0.80 favors continuous monitoring; a prior centered at 0.90 does not. Fourth, the reconstruction conditions on the observed effect. For REWIND this is a hazard ratio of 0.88 that barely cleared the bar. Had the true effect been closer to 0.90 the trial would more likely have failed, and the reconstruction would show fewer simulated trials declaring efficacy at a true hazard ratio of 0.90. Assessing early futility would require an additional prespecified rule and a separate operating-characteristics calculation ( Chapter 15 ).

title: SURPASS-CVOT: an active comparator and a noninferiority margin
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.3 SURPASS-CVOT: an active comparator and a noninferiority margin
text: 21.3 SURPASS-CVOT: an active comparator and a noninferiority margin The preceding two cases compared a drug with placebo. SURPASS-CVOT compared two active drugs, which changes the question ( Nicholls et al. 2025 ) . It randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, double blind and 1:1, to weekly tirzepatide (up to 15 mg) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg, the dose that REWIND had shown to reduce cardiovascular events. After 134 exclusions for ineligibility the modified intention-to-treat population was 13,165 (6,586 on tirzepatide and 6,579 on dulaglutide). The primary outcome was the first of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke, and the primary hypothesis was noninferiority: the upper limit of the 95.3 percent confidence interval for the hazard ratio had to lie below 1.05, and superiority could be claimed if the upper limit was below 1.00. The traditional logic of the noninferiority test, a margin fixed in advance and a one-sided bound on the interval, is the one set out in Chapter 4 . The primary outcome occurred in 801 patients (12.2 percent) on tirzepatide and 862 (13.1 percent) on dulaglutide, a hazard ratio of 0.92 with a 95.3 percent confidence interval from 0.83 to 1.01. Noninferiority was established ( \(p = 0.003\) ) and superiority was not ( \(p = 0.09\) ). We omit the secondary and component hazard ratios, which

The trial “failed” to show superiority because the upper limit of 1.01 sat just above 1.00, yet the probability that the hazard ratio is below one is 0.95. These are not competing statements: the frequentist \(p = 0.09\) is the chance, if the hazard ratio were exactly one, of data at least this extreme in either direction, and the posterior probability is a statement about the hazard ratio given the data and a flat prior. Neither is wrong, and a decision-maker needs the second to weigh a benefit against a cost. The probability of a reduction of at least 10 percent is only 0.33, which is the honest size of the uncertainty about how much better tirzepatide is. As with REWIND, the posterior under a skeptical prior would be pulled toward one, and for a trial of this size the flat-prior numbers are the upper end of what the data support. Tirzepatide was never tested against placebo for cardiovascular outcomes in this trial, and the missing comparison can be filled by an indirect chain through dulaglutide, shown in the last row of Table 21.7 (0.81, interval 0.70 to 0.94). title: The trial as conducted
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.4.1 The trial as conducted
text: The trial as conducted TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 randomized 1,736 participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease to donanemab or placebo, with efficacy measured at 18 months (76 weeks), and reported a 35 percent slowing of decline on its integrated Alzheimer’s Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) in the prespecified low and medium tau population of 1,182 participants, and a 22 percent slowing in the combined population of 1,736 ( Sims et al. 2023 ) . The primary analysis was prespecified for two populations, the tau-defined one and the combined one, and the trial therefore had to choose how to spend its type I error between them. The order of testing is given in the publication and its supplement ( Sims et al. 2023 ) . This is a traditional design in the sense of this book: a fixed duration, a prespecified primary analysis with a multiplicity procedure across populations, and a single final analysis. It differs from a textbook parallel-group trial in two respects. Both are prespecified design features, and neither is Bayesian as conducted; a Bayesian analysis could be proposed for the second.

title: Two prespecified design features
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.4.2 Two prespecified design features
text: Two prespecified design features The first is that treatment duration was guided by a biomarker. Participants completed their course of donanemab once they reached a prespecified level of amyloid plaque clearance, and the report gives 52 percent of the low and medium tau participants as having reached the clearance criterion by one year, among those with a PET assessment at that visit ( Sims et al. 2023 ) . This is a stopping rule applied to each participant rather than to the trial, driven by an intermediate biomarker. It is a prespecified biomarker-guided treatment strategy, and it does not require Bayesian inference. It is related to individualized dosing in the patient-specific dose-finding designs reviewed in Chapter 17 , and because it depends only on each participant’s own biomarker and not on accumulating comparative results, it is a treatment strategy and not a trial adaptation in the sense of the FDA guidance. It is also a rule that a fixed-duration comparison cannot evaluate on its own: the trial estimates the effect of the strategy “stop when cleared” against placebo, not the effect of a fixed dose and duration, and the estimand has to say so (ICH E9(R1), Chapter 5 ). The second is baseline tau stratification. The trial reports a 35 percent effect in one stratum and a 22 percent effect in the combined population. Tau

title: Two prespecified design features
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.4.2 Two prespecified design features
text: and duration, and the estimand has to say so (ICH E9(R1), Chapter 5 ). The second is baseline tau stratification. The trial reports a 35 percent effect in one stratum and a 22 percent effect in the combined population. Tau status is measured at baseline, and the strata do not change in response to accumulating results, so this is baseline stratification and not an adaptive feature. The standard apparatus requires that the populations and the order of testing be designated before the data arrive, and the designation then governs the claim. A prespecified hierarchical model ( Chapter 19 , Chapter 10 ) could estimate effects in both disjoint strata with borrowing between them. Population claims and their success criteria would still require prespecification and an evaluation of false-positive risks. The sizes of the two strata, 1,182 participants in the low and medium tau stratum and 552 in the high tau stratum as reported, do not by themselves establish that borrowing would be large; that depends on the between-stratum variance, as the illustration below shows. The arithmetic of that shrinkage is simple enough to show. Suppose the two strata have estimated effects with standard errors proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\) , and the between-stratum standard deviation \(\tau_b\) of the true effect is the quantity the data cannot tell us much about. The weight on the stratum’s own estimate

title: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.4.3 What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
text: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept Which analysis a regulator prefers is not a question we can settle. The trial as conducted had to choose a primary population and a multiplicity procedure, and it did, in a way the FDA could review against the substantial-evidence standard. A hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the two strata would be a proposed alternative, not a description of what the trial did, and would need three things the draft guidance asks of any borrowing: a prespecified model, a stated rationale for exchangeability of the strata, and a simulation of its type I error across the scenarios in which the effect is present in one stratum only ( Chapter 19 ). Those scenarios are the ones that matter, because a hierarchical model that shrinks a null stratum towards a positive pooled effect will raise the false-positive rate for that stratum. The regulatory cost is a longer simulation report and a more demanding conversation about the prior on the between-stratum variance. For the biomarker-guided duration, the regulator’s concern is the estimand and the integrity of blinding (the blind has to survive the switch when a participant stops active treatment after clearance, which is a matter of masking procedure and not of the analysis). Neither is Bayesian or frequentist. They are the design properties that made a prespecified

title: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.4.3 What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept
text: blind has to survive the switch when a participant stops active treatment after clearance, which is a matter of masking procedure and not of the analysis). Neither is Bayesian or frequentist. They are the design properties that made a prespecified biomarker-guided feature acceptable to the FDA in this case. The lesson is different from SELECT’s. In SELECT, a Bayesian monitoring rule would change when the trial stops. In TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2, the traditional apparatus handled two prespecified features, and the trial shows that regulators accept them when they are specified in advance. A hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the strata would not make the trial more or less adaptive. It would express the stratum analysis through one model in place of a testing hierarchy, at the price of the prespecification and simulation described above.

title: The trial as conducted
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.5.1 The trial as conducted
text: The trial as conducted The phase 2/3 trial of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine (Protocol C4591001, Pfizer and BioNTech) began in July 2020 and reported the efficacy of the vaccine in preventing COVID-19 ( Polack et al. 2020 ) . Its statistical analysis plan, posted on ClinicalTrials.gov, makes the primary analysis Bayesian ( Pfizer Inc. 2022 ) . This case differs from the other four in kind: the Bayesian rule is not a counterfactual reconstruction but the decision rule the trial itself used, and it supported a regulatory action. The beta-binomial model of Chapter 6 is the whole of the machinery.

title: The Bayesian element
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.5.2 The Bayesian element
text: The Bayesian element The conjugate beta-binomial model, with prior Beta(0.700102, 1) on the vaccine share of cases, the transformation to VE and the posterior arithmetic, is worked in full in Section 6.12 . The plan calls the prior minimally informative and says it can be considered pessimistic. The case-specific points are the success criterion, \(\Pr(\mathrm{VE} \ge 30\% \mid \text{data})\) , which must exceed 0.995 at an interim analysis and 0.986 at the final analysis, with the thresholds calibrated so that the overall one-sided type I error is 2.5 percent (Section 7.1 of the plan; the calibration is the kind of simulation of Chapter 14 ). Two primary objectives, VE in participants with no evidence of prior infection and VE in all participants, were evaluated in sequence. The final analysis was planned at 164 first primary cases, with interim looks and a futility rule based on the predictive probability of success, nonbinding, of 5 percent or less. Two features set it apart from SELECT’s reconstruction. The bar is on VE of 30 percent, a margin of clinical relevance, and not on zero, so the criterion is the \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) of the FDA draft with \(a\) different from zero. And the model is conjugate, so each look is a closed-form calculation with no simulation of the posterior itself, only of the operating

title: What happened and what the regulator did
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.5.3 What happened and what the regulator did
text: What happened and what the regulator did The published analysis counted 8 cases in the vaccine group and 162 in the placebo group, a vaccine efficacy of 95.0 percent with a 95 percent credible interval of 90.3 to 97.6 percent ( Polack et al. 2020 ) . Our calculation ( Section 6.12 ), with the surveillance-time ratio of 2.222 to 2.214 reported in the FDA briefing document, gives 90.3 to 97.6 percent against the published 90.3 to 97.6 (the counts of 8 and 162 are exact), and a posterior probability of VE above 30 percent that is indistinguishable from one (1), far above 0.986. FDA issued an emergency use authorization on 11 December 2020 for individuals 16 years of age and older ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021a ) , and approved the biologics license application (Comirnaty) on 23 August 2021, again for those 16 and older ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2021b ) .

title: The lesson for this chapter
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.5.4 The lesson for this chapter
text: The lesson for this chapter Where the SELECT and REWIND reconstructions are counterfactuals, BNT162b2 shows the regulatory path already traveled: a minimally informative prior, a margin, calibration to 0.025 one-sided, and a protocol that fixed the thresholds before the first case. One caution. The plan on ClinicalTrials.gov is a sponsor document with several amendments. The efficacy boundaries tabulated in the plan, written as case splits, reproduce from the stated prior: at the final analysis of 164 cases, 53 vaccine cases is the largest count with \(\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\% \mid \text{data}) > 0.986\) (53 gives 0.990, 54 gives 0.985). The backing for a rule of this kind comes from Chapter 6 for the model and Chapter 14 for the calibration.

title: What the saving is worth
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6 What the saving is worth
text: 21.6 What the saving is worth A claim that a design decides at 486 events (the all-trial median; 464 among trials that declare efficacy) rather than 1,270 is not yet an argument that anyone outside the field will weigh. This section converts it into five currencies. Every conversion is a modeled counterfactual, and the conversions differ in how many assumptions they stack. They use the expected stopping point over all simulated trials, so that trials which never cross, and therefore save nothing, are counted.

title: Trial cost
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.2 Trial cost
text: Trial cost Moore and colleagues reviewed the pivotal trials of 59 novel agents approved by the FDA in 2015 and 2016 ( Moore et al. 2018 ) . The median estimated cost of a pivotal trial was $19.0 million, the costliest single trial in the review was about $347 million, and the mean estimated cost of the five cardiovascular pivotal trials was $157.2 million (their Table 2). SELECT, with 17,604 patients at 804 sites in 41 countries and about five years of follow-up, is far larger than the typical trial in that review, and we have no published cost for it. We therefore take the cited cardiovascular mean of $157 million as the base case and $350 million and $600 million as scenarios for a larger trial, not as estimates of the cost of any particular trial. The saving is not proportional to the whole budget. Variable costs, which are site payments, patient visits, monitoring, laboratory work and drug supply, scale with person-time; fixed costs, which are protocol development, startup, regulatory work and the final analysis, do not. With 56.5 percent of the person-time avoided on average, the modeled saving is that share of the variable share. title: Label revenue brought forward
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.4 Label revenue brought forward
text: Label revenue brought forward The largest sum in the accounting is commercial, and it rests on the least. Patent expiry is fixed, so a cardiovascular indication reached earlier adds the same number of years of protected, label-driven sales. Novo Nordisk reported global Wegovy sales of DKK 58.2 billion for 2024 ( Novo Nordisk A/S 2025 ) . The share of sales that the cardiovascular label drives is not public, and we assume 10 to 25 percent. At an assumed 6.9 DKK per dollar the 2024 sales are about $8.4 billion, and brought forward by the all-trial median saving of 2.2 years the label-driven revenue is $1.8 billion to $4.6 billion. This is a modeled counterfactual of revenue, not profit, and an upper bound: approval, reimbursement and uptake would not all have moved forward by the full statistical acceleration, for the reasons given for the population bound above, and the sales level, the label share and the exchange rate are assumptions. REWIND gives the same arithmetic only conditionally. Trulicity (dulaglutide) had revenue of $4.13 billion in 2019 ( Eli Lilly and Company 2022 ) , and the FDA approved its cardiovascular indication on 21 February 2020 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2020 ) . title: Label revenue brought forward
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.4 Label revenue brought forward
text: the FDA approved its cardiovascular indication on 21 February 2020 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2020 ) . In the reconstruction the Bayesian rule acts in only 49 percent of simulated REWIND trials, so the all-trial median saving is zero, because fewer than half of the simulated trials cross. The unconditional expected saving can still be positive: the mean decision falls at 973 of 1,257 events, so on average 23 percent of the events and person time would come after it. The revenue figures below describe the conditional median among trials that cross, and multiplying the crossing probability by a conditional median would not give an expected revenue (that needs the calendar saving averaged over all paths, which the summary output does not keep). Conditional on its acting, the median decision falls at 680 of 1,257 events. Under an accrual model with an assumed 24 months of linear enrollment and the 85 months between the registered start and primary completion dates ( ClinicalTrials.gov 2026j ) , that is month 51, or 2.8 years before the read-out. With an assumed 10 to 20 percent of 2019 sales attributable to the label, the revenue brought forward would be $1.2 billion to $2.3 billion, but only in the trials in which the rule acts, and the scheduled design acts more often there. Two caveats from the earlier

title: Label revenue brought forward
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.6.4 Label revenue brought forward
text: 2019 sales attributable to the label, the revenue brought forward would be $1.2 billion to $2.3 billion, but only in the trials in which the rule acts, and the scheduled design acts more often there. Two caveats from the earlier sections apply to every currency in this section. Among trials stopping early for efficacy, naive estimates tend to exaggerate benefit. Skeptical priors may reduce this bias; bias and interval coverage should be evaluated for the specified estimator and stopping rule. And a regulator would want safety follow-up to continue after an efficacy decision, which recovers only part of the cost saving.

Traditional (what the trials did) Bayesian reconstruction What the regulator will ask Monitoring Event-driven; DMC reviews at scheduled looks, boundaries from a spending function (SELECT: one interim at two thirds of the planned events) Monitoring of a posterior probability on a fine event grid The monitoring plan, written in advance (E9 4.5) Decision rule Test statistic crosses a boundary \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > p^\ast\) Calibration of \(p^\ast\) to 0.025 one-sided by simulation, with Monte Carlo error Type I error Spent by alpha spending Calibrated by simulation under the plan Simulation report, scenarios, Monte Carlo error Prior None Skeptical normal on the log hazard ratio Prespecified, with sensitivity to \(\tau\) Where it wins Marginal effects, fixed looks (REWIND) Large effects, DMC that can commit to a plan (SELECT) Evidence the choice was made before the data What does not change Randomization, blinding, endpoint, firewall, intention-to-treat estimand Same Same Where the two agree numerically: with a flat prior, the posterior probability of benefit equals one minus the one-sided \(p\) value, so a single-look Bayesian rule with threshold \(c\) is the fixed one-sided test at level \(1 - c\) .

title: Trials running now
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.8 Trials running now
text: are asked to do. All are randomized and masked. Several cardiovascular outcomes trials are event driven; AHEAD and TRIUMPH-3 assess their primary outcomes at specified follow-up times. Each is built to stand alone as substantial evidence, and a sibling trial’s result does not automatically change the analysis plan. Justified amendments based solely on external information may be acceptable while comparative interim results remain protected ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2019b ) . For the proposed Bayesian designs, the borrowing and updating procedures, including any incorporation of future sibling results, should be prespecified. The Bayesian changes in the last column are therefore proposals with a price: each borrowed prior must be fixed before the data, discounted and justified, and each design with it simulated for its operating characteristics under a plan the regulator has seen ( Chapter 19 , Chapter 14 ). Where we write that a Bayesian rule could stop sooner, the size of the gain depends on an effect size that is not yet known, and the SELECT reconstruction above is not a forecast for any of these trials.

title: Retatrutide in TRIUMPH-3
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.8.1 Retatrutide in TRIUMPH-3
text: Retatrutide in TRIUMPH-3 Lilly’s announcement reports 44 five-component events (all-cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure event or coronary revascularization) on pooled retatrutide against 52 on placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.82 with a 95 percent interval from 0.55 to 1.22, in prespecified analyses of a trial whose registered primary outcome was weight ( Eli Lilly and Company 2026 ) . The three-component MACE hazard ratio in the same announcement was 1.12 (0.64 to 1.96). A frequentist reading of the five-component interval says that benefit is not established, and that is a correct statement about the interval. A Bayesian reading adds what the interval does not say, and shows how much of it depends on the prior. The interval gives the log hazard ratio \(\log 0.82\) with standard error \((\log 1.22 - \log 0.55)/3.92\) . For a class prior we use SELECT, with a hazard ratio of 0.80 and interval 0.72 to 0.90 ( Lincoff et al. 2023 ) , discounted by inflating its variance (doubling it for half weight, quadrupling it for quarter weight), and for contrast a skeptical normal prior with standard deviation 0.15 and a flat prior ( Section 22.1 ). title: What a Lp(a)HORIZON result does to OCEAN(a)
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.8.2 What a Lp(a)HORIZON result does to OCEAN(a)
text: What a Lp(a)HORIZON result does to OCEAN(a) When an analyst moves the probability that a related trial succeeds from \(p_0\) to \(p_1\) after a sibling reads out, the analyst has implicitly applied a Bayes factor, the ratio of the posterior odds to the prior odds: \[B = \frac{p_1/(1 - p_1)}{p_0/(1 - p_0)}.\] We could not confirm a published analyst estimate of the probability of success of OCEAN(a)-Outcomes after the Lp(a)HORIZON announcement of 4 September 2026, so we use an illustrative move from 50 to 20 percent, which is not a finding about any analyst. On that illustration \(B = 0.25\) : the analyst treats the Lp(a)HORIZON result as 4 times as likely if olpasiran fails as if it succeeds. A fall from 50 percent to 40, 30 or 10 percent implies factors of 0.67, 0.43 and 0.11. On the flat-prior normal approximation to the log hazard ratio, the posterior probability that the hazard ratio is below 0.90 is 0.023, below 0.85 0.002 and below 0.80 0.0001, so a 10 percent or larger benefit is largely ruled out for pelacarsen at its depth of lowering. If the benefit of Lp(a) lowering is proportional to the absolute reduction, a drug that lowers it further should be judged against a different benchmark and the factor should be closer to 1. A hierarchical model with the depth of lowering as a covariate makes that assumption explicit and lets the data weigh it, which one revised probability does not.

title: Limits of the reconstruction
cx: Chapter 21: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials > 21.9 Limits of the reconstruction
text: 21.9 Limits of the reconstruction The numbers above are order-of-magnitude arguments, and a reader should know exactly where they would break. The counterfactual is not the trial. The Bayesian rule is evaluated on simulated paths with the observed hazard ratio. Nobody observed a SELECT that stopped at 486 events, and the conditional medians describe only the paths that crossed, which are the lucky ones. Calibration is under a known grid and horizon. A threshold of 0.9952 is calibrated for evaluation at every second event up to 1,270 events, not for literally continuous monitoring. Any subset of that grid, including unscheduled meetings at event counts on it, inherits the error bound, because the maximum over a subset cannot exceed the maximum over the grid. Monitoring off the grid or beyond the horizon needs additional justification and a recalibration, and the calibration is a property of the plan and not of the number. The error rates are estimates. A type I error read from 40,000 paths has a Monte Carlo standard error of about 0.0008, and the calibrated threshold should be validated on independent null simulations and across nuisance scenarios. The information model is approximate. The calculation assumes a Gaussian score process with \(I_n = d/4\) , proportional hazards and 1:1 allocation, which is accurate to two digits for the final analysis and approximate for early looks.

title: Key points

text: Key points Using a common nominal one-sided bound of 2.5 percent (the Bayesian rule is calibrated to it by simulation, the four-look design by its boundaries, and the e-value rule is controlled by its bound through Ville’s inequality), a Bayesian rule monitored on a fine event grid stops, among simulated trials that declare efficacy, at a median of 464 events on SELECT’s data, against 612 for an e-value rule and 952 for a four-look O’Brien-Fleming design. Over all trials, counting those that never cross at the 1,270-event read-out, the medians are 486, 714 and 952, with power 95, 83 and 98 percent and realized type I errors of 2.5, 0.58 and 2.55 percent. SELECT’s actual two-look design (one interim at two thirds of 1,225 planned events) stops at a median of 817 with power 97 percent and realized type I error 2.5 percent; the trial reported at 1,270. This is a reconstruction that uses the trial’s observed hazard ratio and is not a power calculation. An uncalibrated posterior threshold of 0.975 on the same grid has a type I error of about 12 percent. Any claim of speed has to come with the error it was calibrated to, and with the power. title: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22 Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials
text: A published trial gives a likelihood, not a conclusion. The conclusion depends on the prior the reader brings and on the loss attached to acting wrongly, and a trial that ends with \(p = 0.09\) or \(p = 0.06\) can support action, inaction, or a new trial depending on both. This chapter reanalyses four trials from their published summaries. In each case the same three steps recur. First, reduce the report to an approximately normal likelihood for a log relative risk, a log hazard ratio or a risk difference. Second, combine it with a small family of priors chosen to represent defensible positions. Third, report posterior probabilities of effects large enough to matter, not only the probability that the effect is nonzero. Each trial reported a prespecified primary analysis at a prespecified level, and it did its job: GUSTO, EOLIA and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK each answered the question the protocol asked. The designs differ: EOLIA, for example, was a group sequential trial with a triangular boundary, which matters for the futility discussion below. A reanalysis asks a different question, and the last section of this chapter says what it can and cannot claim. Every number below is computed from the counts or intervals quoted, with the reanalysis_ functions of the bayestrials package (one per trial, plus the general reanalysis_normal() and the hierarchical reanalysis_hier() ). Where published Bayesian

Where published Bayesian reanalyses exist, we compare with them. Our numbers differ from theirs because we use normal approximations on the stated effect scale for each trial and because our priors are simple stand-ins for theirs. Important Regulatory anchor FDA, Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft guidance, January 2026) ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) . The draft recommends that the prior be prespecified and justified in the protocol, that sensitivity to the prior be examined, and describes a posterior probability criterion as one way to define success; skeptical priors are one option for particular circumstances, not a requirement (Sections IV.A, V.A, V.C and V.F). All of this concerns a trial designed to be analyzed this way. It says nothing that turns a post hoc reanalysis of a finished trial into evidence of effectiveness. A draft, not binding. ICH E9 (1998), sections 3.4 and 5.1. Analysis methods are fixed before the data are unblinded, and the primary analysis is the prespecified one. A reanalysis is a secondary or exploratory analysis in this sense. See Chapter 3 .

title: The normal approximation and its posterior
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.1 The normal approximation and its posterior
text: 22.1 The normal approximation and its posterior Let \(\hat\theta\) be the estimate on the log scale and \(s\) its standard error. A reported interval \((\ell, u)\) at 95 percent gives \[ s = \frac{\log u - \log \ell}{2 \times 1.96}. \tag{22.1}\] With a normal prior \(\theta \sim N(m_0, s_0^2)\) , the posterior is normal with precision equal to the sum of the precisions and mean equal to the precision-weighted average, \[ \frac{1}{s_1^2} = \frac{1}{s^2} + \frac{1}{s_0^2}, \qquad m_1 = s_1^2\left(\frac{\hat\theta}{s^2} + \frac{m_0}{s_0^2}\right). \tag{22.2}\] Write \(\theta = -\log RR\) (or minus the log hazard ratio), so that positive means benefit, as in the code. For a benefit threshold \(\theta^\ast\) (for example \(\theta^\ast = -\log 0.8\) for a twenty percent relative reduction), \(\Pr(\theta > \theta^\ast \mid \text{data}) = \Phi((m_1 - \theta^\ast)/s_1)\) . The prior is worth \(s^2/s_0^2\) trials of the present size: a prior with \(s_0 = s\) counts as much as the trial itself (this is the effective sample size of Chapter 8 ). Ratios are reported back on their natural scale. Spiegelhalter, Freedman, and Parmar ( 1994 ) proposed a standard family of priors for this exercise, and we use versions of them. Elicited skeptical priors for stopping rules have an earlier statement in Freedman and Spiegelhalter ( 1983 ) , and the CHART trials were the worked example ( Parmar et al. 1994 )

title: The normal approximation and its posterior
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.1 The normal approximation and its posterior
text: this exercise, and we use versions of them. Elicited skeptical priors for stopping rules have an earlier statement in Freedman and Spiegelhalter ( 1983 ) , and the CHART trials were the worked example ( Parmar et al. 1994 ) . A skeptical prior is centered at no effect with enough spread that a large benefit is unlikely a priori. An enthusiastic prior is centered at the effect the trial was designed to detect. A reference prior is flat. A positive trial is convincing when it persuades the skeptic, and a negative trial is convincing when it discourages the enthusiast. Section 8.3 discusses the three families and Section 8.8 the sensitivity analysis over the prior scale.

title: The trial and its traditional analysis
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.2.1 The trial and its traditional analysis
text: The trial and its traditional analysis GUSTO ( GUSTO Investigators 1993 ) randomized 41,021 patients with acute myocardial infarction to four strategies: streptokinase with subcutaneous heparin, streptokinase with intravenous heparin, accelerated tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) with intravenous heparin, and a combination. Thirty-day mortality was 6.3 percent on accelerated tPA and 7.2 and 7.4 percent on the two streptokinase-only arms, about 7.3 percent pooled. The prespecified comparison of tPA with the two streptokinase arms gave a 14 percent relative reduction in mortality (95 percent interval 5.9 to 21.3 percent), \(p = 0.001\) . The frequentist conclusion was that tPA was superior, with an absolute benefit of one percentage point, or ten lives per thousand treated, at a substantially higher drug cost.

title: The Bayesian question
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.2.2 The Bayesian question
text: The Bayesian question Brophy and Joseph ( 1995 ) asked what a cardiologist should have believed given the two earlier megatrials that compared the agents, GISSI-2 and ISIS-3, with 2,411 deaths among 24,118 patients on tPA and 2,384 among 24,176 on streptokinase between them (their Table 1). They gave the earlier trials weights of 100, 50 and 10 percent, took one percentage point of absolute mortality as the smallest clinically superior difference, and concluded that the clinical superiority of tPA “remains uncertain”. They put the prior on each arm’s mortality rate, a beta distribution built from that arm’s earlier deaths and survivors, and with GUSTO’s data the probability that tPA lowers mortality was 0.17, 0.44 and 0.98 at the three weights and 0.9995 with GUSTO alone (their Table 2). In the counts Brophy and Joseph used, GUSTO had 652 deaths among 10,343 patients on accelerated tPA and 1,473 among 20,173 on the two streptokinase arms combined. text: then absorbs the difference between trials into the difference between agents, the mechanism of Simpson’s paradox, and at full weight the arm model makes tPA probably worse although no trial found it so. For these trials, borrowing within-trial treatment contrasts avoids pooling dissimilar baseline mortality rates. An arm-level model would need trial-specific baseline risks and justified borrowing between trials ( Chapter 19 ). The table still separates two questions: whether there is any benefit, and whether it is large enough to matter. A test against zero addresses the first, and an interval or a test against the one-point threshold addresses the second; the posterior probabilities read both directly, conditional on the prior. On the difference scale, that tPA lowers mortality at all is very probable under every weight: the probability is at least 0.968. That it lowers mortality by a full percentage point, enough to justify its price, is a coin toss (0.50) with no prior information, 0.33 at weight 0.1, and unlikely once the earlier trials count at half weight or more. Brophy and Joseph’s conclusion, that clinical superiority remains uncertain, holds in both models; their low probabilities of any benefit come from the arm-wise pooling. The decision to pay for tPA turns on the second question and on the price of a life year.

title: The trial and its traditional analysis
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.3.1 The trial and its traditional analysis
text: The trial and its traditional analysis EOLIA ( Combes et al. 2018 ) randomized 249 patients with very severe acute respiratory distress syndrome to early venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or to conventional lung-protective ventilation, with rescue ECMO allowed in the control arm. Sixty-day mortality was 35 percent (44 of 124) with ECMO and 46 percent (57 of 125) in the control arm, a relative risk of 0.76 with 95 percent interval 0.55 to 1.04 and \(p = 0.09\) . Thirty-five control patients (28 percent) crossed over to ECMO, and 20 of them died. The trial was widely reported as negative. The design was group sequential with a two-triangle boundary, with analyses after every 60 randomized participants and a maximum of 331, and the trial stopped for futility at the fourth interim analysis ( Combes et al. 2018 , Methods) . 1

title: The Bayesian analysis
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.3.2 The Bayesian analysis
text: The Bayesian analysis Goligher et al. ( 2018 ) carried out the published Bayesian reanalysis. Under a minimally informative prior they reported a posterior relative risk of 0.78 (95 percent credible interval 0.56 to 1.04), a posterior probability of any mortality reduction of 96 percent, of a relative risk below 0.67 of 18 percent, and of an absolute risk reduction of at least 2 percentage points of 92 percent. Across their other priors (moderately enthusiastic, strongly skeptical, and one built from earlier studies) the probability of benefit ranged from 88 to 99 percent. Our own calculation uses the counts, so \(\log \widehat{RR} = \log(0.355/0.456) =\) -0.251 with \(s^2 = 1/44 - 1/124 + 1/57 - 1/125 =\) 0.0242, \(s =\) 0.156. The counts give a relative risk of 0.778, a little different from the published 0.76, which is adjusted. The priors are normal on the log relative risk and every one is stated in Table 22.2 . Goligher’s own figure for two points, under their minimally informative prior, is 92 percent. The two agree closely even though the models differ, which is itself a robustness statement. The lesson is about what the trial ruled out. EOLIA did not rule out the effect it was designed to find: it made that effect less likely (0.17 under the flat prior), but not unlikely. What it established is that some benefit is probable under the four priors examined (the probability of benefit runs from 0.87 to 0.99). A hospital deciding whether to maintain an ECMO program for severe ARDS faces a decision with a large upside and a known cost, and for that decision a probability of about 0.9 that the treatment helps is a strong argument. A nonsignificant result is nonrejection of the null, not evidence of no effect, and the interval from 0.55 to 1.04 already said as much. text: 22.4 ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: the same pattern with a hazard ratio ANDROMEDA-SHOCK ( Hernández et al. 2019 ) randomized 424 adults with septic shock in 28 intensive care units to an 8-hour resuscitation targeting normalization of capillary refill time or targeting serum lactate. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 34.9 percent (74 of 212) in the capillary refill arm and 43.4 percent (92 of 212) in the lactate arm, a hazard ratio of 0.75 with 95 percent interval 0.55 to 1.02 and \(p = 0.06\) . The reported interval gives \(\log \widehat{HR} =\) -0.288 and \(s =\) 0.158. Zampieri et al. ( 2020 ) published the Bayesian reanalysis with four priors (optimistic, neutral, null and pessimistic) and found a posterior probability of benefit at 28 days above 90 percent under all of them. Their model was on the odds-ratio scale, with priors on the odds ratio. Ours is on the hazard-ratio scale, so the rows below illustrate the same logic and are not a replication of their table. It centers the prior at a hazard ratio of 1.1, an instantaneous hazard ten percent higher, which is not a ten percent higher probability of death, and its posterior probability of benefit is 0.79. A sufficiently concentrated prior centered at no effect also lowers the posterior probability of benefit, so the table shows how much prior skepticism the result tolerates. There is also a decision argument that no p value captures. Capillary refill time is measured with a finger and a stopwatch, and lactate needs a laboratory. If the two strategies were equally effective, the cheaper and faster one would be preferred. A strategy that is cheaper, at least as safe, and probably better need not clear \(p < 0.05\) to be adopted. Whether it should be adopted is a question of expected net benefit, and we do not compute it here: that needs a utility function, a measured cost difference and a mapping from the hazard ratio to absolute mortality, none of which the posterior probabilities in Table 22.4 supply. The argument is conditional: if the strategies are equally safe and capillary refill is cheaper, adoption is favored to the extent that the posterior makes a loss in survival improbable, and Chapter 1 shows how to put numbers on that.

text: familiar source of false findings, and the frequentist instinct is to distrust them unless an interaction test is significant ( Section 10.3 ). The Bayesian instinct is to shrink them toward a common mean by an amount the data choose ( Section 10.4 ). Let \(\theta_j = -\log RR_j\) be the benefit-positive effect in stratum \(j\) , with \(\hat\theta_j \sim N(\theta_j, s_j^2)\) and \(\theta_j \sim N(\mu, \tau_b^2)\) . With a flat prior on \(\mu\) and a prior on \(\tau_b\) , the marginal likelihood of \(\tau_b\) is \[ p(\tau_b \mid \hat\theta) \propto p(\tau_b)\, V_\mu(\tau_b)^{1/2} \prod_j (s_j^2 + \tau_b^2)^{-1/2} \exp\left\{-\frac{(\hat\theta_j - \hat\mu(\tau_b))^2}{2(s_j^2+\tau_b^2)}\right\}, \tag{22.3}\] where \(\hat\mu(\tau_b)\) is the precision-weighted mean and \(V_\mu(\tau_b)\) its variance. The conditional posterior mean of each \(\theta_j\) is \((1 - B_j)\hat\theta_j + B_j \hat\mu\) with \(B_j = s_j^2/(s_j^2 + \tau_b^2)\) . With only three strata, the data say little about \(\tau_b\) and its posterior is sensitive to the prior placed on it. We use a uniform prior on \(\tau_b\) over \((0, 1]\) on the log scale. Under that prior the posterior median of \(\tau_b\) is 0.41 and the posterior mean is 0.45. The mean is the less stable summary: moving the upper bound from 1 to 3 changes the median to 0.52 and the mean to 0.73, because with three groups the posterior has a heavy right tail that the truncation point controls. The
