cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.5 RECOVERY: subgroups and shrinkage
text: is the less stable summary: moving the upper bound from 1 to 3 changes the median to 0.52 and the mean to 0.73, because with three groups the posterior has a heavy right tail that the truncation point controls. The shrinkage factors are small in either case, and the shrunk estimates in Table 22.5 barely move (0.64 to 0.66, 1.19 to 1.13). That is the right answer. Shrinkage is not a rule that every subgroup be pulled to the mean. It is a rule that the data decide how much to pull, and here the pattern of benefit rising with severity is both large and biologically expected, because the inflammatory phase of Covid-19 is where a corticosteroid should help. The decision implication is the one clinicians drew: treat patients on oxygen or ventilation, and do not treat patients without oxygen. In our model the posterior probability of harm (rate ratio above 1) in the no-oxygen stratum is 0.81, and even if one discounts the point estimate, no benefit is plausible enough to justify exposure. This probability, like the shrunk estimates, comes from our model, not from RECOVERY. Published Bayesian reanalyses of other RECOVERY comparisons exist for comparison, for example of tocilizumab (a preprint) ( Albuquerque et al. 2021 ) .

title: What the four reanalyses share
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.6 What the four reanalyses share
text: 22.6 What the four reanalyses share Four patterns recur. Existence and magnitude are separate questions. In GUSTO some benefit was very probable and its magnitude was the open question. In EOLIA and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK the primary test did not reject the null, which is nonrejection and not evidence of absence, and the intervals (0.55 to 1.04 and 0.55 to 1.02) already showed that sizeable benefits were compatible with the data. Frequentist intervals describe the uncertainty about magnitude, and tests can target a clinically meaningful threshold instead of zero. A posterior adds direct probability statements at chosen thresholds, conditional on the prior, and the comparison with the estimate, interval and threshold test is the useful one. The priors are arguments, not confessions. Each prior in the tables represents a position someone in the field actually held or could defend. Displaying the posterior under each is how a Bayesian report shows readers where they stand, and it is far more informative than a single interval. A stopping rule can stop a trial despite a high probability of some benefit. EOLIA stopped for futility at its fourth analysis, after 240 patients, when the lower boundary of its triangular design was crossed ( Combes et al. 2018 ) . 2 A boundary rule and a predictive-probability rule can both do this, depending on the final success criterion each is built

title: What the four reanalyses share
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.6 What the four reanalyses share
text: 240 patients, when the lower boundary of its triangular design was crossed ( Combes et al. 2018 ) . 2 A boundary rule and a predictive-probability rule can both do this, depending on the final success criterion each is built around, because each asks whether that criterion is likely to be met, which is not the same as whether the treatment works. Decisions need utilities. In each case the action depends on more than the posterior: on the cost of tPA, the burden of ECMO, the convenience of capillary refill and the harm of steroids in early disease. The reanalyses supply the probabilities, and a utility turns them into choices ( Chapter 1 ).

title: Prespecification
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.1 Prespecification
text: Prespecification The trials above were designed, powered and analyzed as frequentist trials. Their prespecified analysis is the one the protocol and statistical analysis plan fixed, and for EOLIA, ANDROMEDA-SHOCK and GUSTO that analysis was fixed before the data were seen. A Bayesian reanalysis is done after the results are known, by people who know them. Even with the best intentions, the choice of priors, thresholds and scale is made in the light of the answer. That does not make it wrong, and Goligher and Zampieri both chose their priors in a documented way. It does mean the reanalysis is exploratory in ICH E9’s sense, and that the honest report lists every prior tried and not only the favorable ones. The tables above follow that rule: each row is shown, including the pessimistic prior that gives the weakest result.

title: Prior choice
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.2 Prior choice
text: Prior choice The posterior is as defensible as the prior. A flat prior on the log scale is not neutral on the absolute scale ( Section 8.4 ), a skeptical prior centered at no effect is a belief and not an absence of belief, and a prior built from earlier trials, as Brophy and Joseph did for GUSTO, depends on how much weight they get and on whether the populations are exchangeable ( Chapter 19 ). The recommended practice is the one the FDA draft asks of a prospective design: state each prior’s mean and standard deviation, show the posterior across a range of them, and say which readers each prior represents. The weight table for GUSTO and the four priors for EOLIA do that. A reanalysis that reports one prior, chosen after the data, does not.

title: The regulator's view
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.3 The regulator's view
text: The regulator’s view The FDA Bayesian draft ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026 ) is written for a trial that is designed to be Bayesian. It asks for a prespecified prior, a success criterion of the form \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , simulation of operating characteristics, and, for trials with an overall frequentist analysis plan, familywise type I error control at 0.025 one-sided. It allows direct interpretation of the posterior probability and decision-theoretic criteria. It does not describe a post hoc reanalysis as substantial evidence, and nothing in it says a posterior probability of 0.9 computed after a negative primary analysis converts that analysis into a positive one. In this book’s reading (not the draft’s words), a reanalysis is useful input to a sponsor planning the next trial, to a guideline committee weighing a decision, and to a hospital choosing a practice, and it is not a substitute for the prespecified analysis in a regulatory submission. It is a draft, not binding, and the substantial-evidence standard is in the statute ( Chapter 3 ).

title: A reanalysis is not a new trial
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.4 A reanalysis is not a new trial
text: A reanalysis is not a new trial A reanalysis uses the data once more. It cannot add patients, cannot repair a design flaw such as open-label assessment or crossover, and cannot change the probability that the original trial would have rejected a null effect. What it can do is change the question from “did the trial cross its threshold?” to “what should we believe now, and what should we do?”. The honest consequence is that a strongly positive posterior after a negative trial is a reason to run a confirmatory trial designed around the effect sizes the reanalysis found plausible, with the priors written in the protocol. EOLIA’s reanalysis and the later ECMO literature are a reminder of this: the posterior pointed to probable benefit, and the decision to adopt rested on clinical judgment and further evidence, not on the posterior alone. RECOVERY shows the other side: a trial so large that its prespecified analysis was decisive, where shrinkage of subgroups changes the numbers but not the practice.

title: What critics say
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.5 What critics say
text: What critics say Reanalyzing a trial after the result is known has a literature of its own, with supporters and critics, and the cases above sit inside it. An early instance is the debate over extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in newborns, in which Ware described the trials and Kass and Greenhouse commented from a Bayesian perspective ( Ware 1989 ; Kass and Greenhouse 1989 ) . EOLIA put the same question to adults ( Section 16.3 ), and its Bayesian reanalysis ( Goligher et al. 2018 ) was published beside an editorial asking whether clinicians should embrace their inner Bayesian ( Lewis and Angus 2018 ) . Systematic programs followed. Wijeysundera and colleagues reanalyzed 88 randomized trials from four general medical journals and concluded that Bayesian and frequentist analyses complement each other and that trial reports should include both ( Wijeysundera et al. 2009 ) . Diamond and Kaul used Bayesian approaches to interpret clinical megatrials ( Diamond and Kaul 2004 ) , Quintana, Viele and Lewis describe how prior information is used to interpret trial results ( Quintana, Viele, and Lewis 2017 ) , and Ryan and colleagues showed what a simple Bayesian analysis of the OPTIMISE trial of hemodynamic therapy in major gastrointestinal surgery adds to the traditional one ( Ryan et al. 2019 ) . The case for these reanalyses is that they

title: What critics say
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.5 What critics say
text: Ryan and colleagues showed what a simple Bayesian analysis of the OPTIMISE trial of hemodynamic therapy in major gastrointestinal surgery adds to the traditional one ( Ryan et al. 2019 ) . The case for these reanalyses is that they state probabilities at clinically meaningful thresholds, and that showing the posterior under several priors makes the dependence on the prior visible, in the spirit of the acknowledgment of multiple perspectives that Gelman and Hennig propose as a virtue of statistical work ( Gelman and Hennig 2017 ) . The criticism we cite is a commentary by de Grooth and Cremer, “Bayes and the Evidence Base: Reanalyzing Trials Using Many Priors Does Not Contribute to Consensus” ( Grooth and Cremer 2024 ) . It recommends testing whether a result would persuade a reasonable adversary and assessing bias and generalizability separately. That connects to the skeptical-prior analyses above, in which the skeptical prior stands in for the adversary, and to a point that we make in our own words, that a table of many priors invites each reader to pick the row that agrees with what he or she already believed, so the table can sharpen a disagreement instead of resolving it. Two further objections follow from the structure of a reanalysis and are not attributed to any source. First, the priors are chosen after the result

title: What critics say
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.5 What critics say
text: or she already believed, so the table can sharpen a disagreement instead of resolving it. Two further objections follow from the structure of a reanalysis and are not attributed to any source. First, the priors are chosen after the result is known. Second, which trials are reanalyzed is itself a choice that nobody prespecified. A cardiology example shows both the power and the risk. Brophy reanalyzed the EXCEL trial of stenting against bypass surgery for left main disease: EXCEL’s prespecified three-year analysis established noninferiority against a 4.2 percentage point margin ( Stone et al. 2016 ) . Applying that original margin to the five-year results, Brophy observed that noninferiority was no longer established by this comparison, and his Bayesian reanalysis estimated a 95 percent probability of more composite events with stenting, so the headline moved with the question asked. Adding three other trials found by a stated search as informative priors lowered the probability of any excess mortality with stenting from 99 to 85 percent, which shows how much depends on which trials enter, and it is the stated search rule that makes that choice auditable ( Brophy 2020 ) . Our reading is that each side is right about something different. A reanalysis is informative as a way of seeing what the data can and cannot support, and weak as evidence when the priors

title: What critics say
cx: Chapter 22: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials > 22.7.5 What critics say
text: auditable ( Brophy 2020 ) . Our reading is that each side is right about something different. A reanalysis is informative as a way of seeing what the data can and cannot support, and weak as evidence when the priors and the trials were chosen after the fact. The rule that follows extends the one stated above: write the reanalysis down before looking, with the priors fixed and the trials chosen by a stated rule, report every prior tried, and treat the result as input to the next trial and not as a verdict on the last one. Note Key points A published trial yields a likelihood, and a conclusion needs a prior and a loss. Use an approximately normal likelihood on the stated effect scale, such as a risk difference or a log ratio, then show the posterior under a family of stated priors. GUSTO: with the prior on the risk difference, that tPA helps is very probable under every weight, but whether it helps by a full percentage point depends on how much weight the earlier trials get. Brophy and Joseph’s priors on each arm’s rate pool baseline risks across trials and make any benefit look doubtful. Borrowing within-trial treatment contrasts avoids that, and an arm-level model would need trial-specific baseline risks and justified borrowing between trials. text: each arm’s rate pool baseline risks across trials and make any benefit look doubtful. Borrowing within-trial treatment contrasts avoids that, and an arm-level model would need trial-specific baseline risks and justified borrowing between trials. EOLIA and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: a missed threshold at \(p = 0.09\) or \(0.06\) left a high posterior probability of benefit under most priors. Our hazard-ratio rows for ANDROMEDA-SHOCK are not a replication of Zampieri et al.’s odds-ratio analysis. RECOVERY: hierarchical shrinkage leaves strongly supported subgroup effects nearly unchanged and pulls a weak one only a little. The posterior of the between-stratum SD depends on its prior, so state the prior and report the median. A reanalysis is exploratory, prior choices are made after the data, and it cannot replace the prespecified analysis or serve as a new trial. Report every prior tried, and use the result to design the next trial.

title: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23 Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators
text: A design is only as good as the document that fixes it. The earlier chapters argued that a trial is a decision, that a regulator approves on evidence meeting a legal standard, and that Bayesian adaptive designs reach that standard sooner by monitoring, by handling several arms together, and by using prior information, not by lowering the bar. All of that is worth nothing to a sponsor until it has been turned into sentences in a protocol, a statistical analysis plan, a simulation report and a data monitoring committee charter, and until a regulator has read those sentences and not objected. The practical question is which sentences change. A sponsor who has written a dozen group sequential protocols knows what the document looks like. A Bayesian protocol shares most of its sections with that document and differs in a handful, and the handful is where reviewers will spend their time. The chapter walks through the protocol section by section, traditional version first, then the Bayesian version, with model sentences in “In the protocol” callouts that a sponsor can adapt. It then covers the statistical analysis plan and the simulation report, the structured protocol formats now in use, the data monitoring committee and its firewalls, the sequence of meetings with FDA and the parallel routes at EMA, the standard of substantial evidence and where Bayesian evidence

title: Traditional first
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.1 Traditional first
text: Traditional first A traditional confirmatory protocol states a null hypothesis and a one-sided type I error of 0.025 (two-sided 0.05 divided by two, as everywhere in this book). It fixes a sample size, or for a time-to-event endpoint a number of events, from a power formula at a design alternative, and fixes the allocation, usually one to one. If there are interim analyses it schedules them, names the boundary family and the alpha spending function, and says that unscheduled looks are protocol deviations. It handles multiple comparisons by a stated procedure, Bonferroni, Holm, a gatekeeping sequence or a graphical scheme ( Chapter 10 ). It lists safety stopping rules, often informally. It names the primary analysis population and, since E9(R1), the estimand. The final report carries a point estimate, a confidence interval and an adjusted \(p\) -value. Each of these has a regulatory basis: ICH E9 on prespecification of interim analyses and on multiplicity, E9(R1) on estimands, the 2019 adaptive designs guidance on anything that departs from a fixed design. The Bayesian protocol keeps the skeleton and changes the parts that depend on how evidence is summarized and how the trial may change as data accumulate.

title: The prior
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.3 The prior
text: The prior The prior is the section with no traditional counterpart, and the one FDA’s draft recommends prespecifying and justifying in the protocol; this book treats prespecification as essential design practice. The Bayesian draft calls it “always critical” that a Bayesian analysis have a prespecified prior, asks that the full details be fixed and justified in the protocol, and, where the prior is informative or borrows external data, asks for strong justification, a description of each source including excluded ones, the discounting method, how prior-data conflict will be handled, and the ESS and other influence metrics ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026d ) . Chapter 8 and Chapter 19 give the methods. For the protocol, three habits matter. State the ESS, the number of patients the prior is worth, in the sense of Morita, Thall, and Müller ( 2008 ) . A prior worth five patients in a trial of five hundred is a modeling choice, and one worth two hundred is an assumption that needs defending. Distinguish the analysis prior (used to compute the posterior that decides success) from design priors (used only in simulation to explore scenarios, including pessimistic ones). And plan a sensitivity analysis, naming the alternative priors in advance. title: The success criterion and its calibration
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.4 The success criterion and its calibration
text: The success criterion and its calibration The Bayesian draft describes the usual form of the criterion as based on the posterior probability that the true effect exceeds a threshold, \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , where \(a\) is the minimum benefit and \(c\) the minimum probability. It asks the sponsor to justify both \(a\) and \(c\) , to give criteria for each primary and key secondary estimand, and, if the design is calibrated, to provide simulation evidence that the familywise error rate is controlled ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026d ) . The draft also recognizes that calibration to 0.025 “may not be applicable or appropriate” in some cases, for instance with borrowing, and describes two other routes, in which success rests on a direct interpretation of the posterior or on a decision-theoretic or benefit-risk criterion (Section IV.A.3) if sponsor and FDA agree in advance. A sponsor who wants that route has to ask for it, in a meeting, with a reason. The BNT162b2 statistical analysis plan is a worked example: posterior thresholds of 0.995 at the interim analyses and 0.986 at the final analysis, chosen so that the overall one-sided type I error is 2.5% (see “In practice” below). Tip In the protocol: success criterion and calibration “The trial will be declared successful for the primary estimand if, at the final

cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.4 The success criterion and its calibration
text: the final analysis, chosen so that the overall one-sided type I error is 2.5% (see “In practice” below). Tip In the protocol: success criterion and calibration “The trial will be declared successful for the primary estimand if, at the final analysis or at an interim analysis specified in Section [x], \(\Pr(\theta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , with \(a =\) [value, with clinical rationale] and \(c =\) [value]. The threshold \(c\) at each analysis was calibrated by simulation so that the probability of declaring success under the null hypothesis \(\theta = 0\) , across all analyses in the schedule and under the stated enrollment and dropout assumptions, does not exceed 0.025 one-sided. Simulation details are in the simulation report (version [x], dated [date]); the code and seeds are provided. If the number or timing of analyses departs from the schedule, the thresholds will be recomputed as described in Section [y] only if the change is demonstrably independent of comparative interim results, follows a prespecified rule whose timing mechanism was simulated, or is handled by a prespecified conditional-error method.”

title: Interim schedule and decision rules
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.5 Interim schedule and decision rules
text: Interim schedule and decision rules E9 says that interim analyses “should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol”, and E20 repeats the point for adaptations in general. A Bayesian posterior is formally unaffected by how many times it is computed, and that is a property of the posterior, not of the decision rule. A rule that stops when a posterior probability crosses a threshold has operating characteristics that do depend on when and how often it is evaluated ( Chapter 11 ). The protocol therefore does not say “continuous monitoring”. It says when looks occur, by information fraction or calendar rule, who sees them, what decisions are possible at each (stop for efficacy, stop for futility, continue, change allocation, drop an arm), and what happens if a look is missed or added. A look added after an external publication is a deviation from the simulated design, and the protocol should say what will be done about it, which is acceptable to handle by recalibration only if the change was demonstrably independent of comparative interim results, followed a prespecified rule whose timing mechanism was simulated, or is handled by a valid conditional-error approach; keeping the sponsor blinded does not by itself establish independence, and treating a schedule shaped by interim results as fixed ignores the selection mechanism ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration

The DAWN stroke trial wrote its whole predictive-probability stopping schedule into the SAP (see “In practice” below). The DMC will be informed of the following rules, and the sponsor will not see unblinded comparisons: stop for efficacy if (a) exceeds [ \(c_k\) ]; stop for futility if (b) is below [value]; otherwise continue. The DMC may recommend stopping for safety or any other reason at any time under the charter, independent of these rules. title: Adaptive randomization
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.6 Adaptive randomization
text: Adaptive randomization If the design uses response-adaptive randomization, the rule belongs in the protocol, and so do its limits. Chapter 16 covers why a reviewer’s first questions concern time trends, bias in the estimate, and whether the control arm retains enough participants. EMA’s October 2026 draft reflection paper on confirmatory platform trials does not support response-adaptive randomization in that setting ( European Medicines Agency 2026 ) (a draft, and its position on this point is a reason to ask EMA early). FDA’s Adaptive Designs guidance does not forbid it but asks that the chance of erroneous conclusions be controlled and the estimates be reliable. Adaptive randomization has a long Bayesian pedigree in dose finding and elsewhere ( Thall et al. 2015 ) . Many Bayesian protocols therefore use a restricted rule: a fixed burn-in at equal allocation, a floor on each arm’s probability, a cap on any change in allocation between updates, and analysis stratified by allocation period. Tip In the protocol: adaptive randomization rule “After a burn-in of [number] participants randomized 1:1, allocation to each experimental arm will be updated every [number] participants in proportion to the posterior probability that the arm is best, raised to the power [value], subject to a minimum of [percentage] of participants per arm and a maximum change of [percentage points] between updates. The control arm will receive at

title: Adaptive randomization
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.6 Adaptive randomization
text: proportion to the posterior probability that the arm is best, raised to the power [value], subject to a minimum of [percentage] of participants per arm and a maximum change of [percentage points] between updates. The control arm will receive at least [percentage] of participants. The primary analysis will adjust for calendar period [method]. The operating characteristics of the rule, including bias of the effect estimate and the probability of allocating more than [x] participants to an inferior arm, are in Section [z] of the simulation report.”

title: Safety rules
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.7 Safety rules
text: Safety rules Traditional protocols often leave safety stopping to the DMC’s judgment, with a guideline. A Bayesian protocol can state it as a posterior probability, which is more transparent and, more usefully, can be simulated: what is the probability that a safe arm is stopped, and that a harmful arm is not? The safety rule sits outside the efficacy error budget, so the protocol should say what its own false-stop rate is, and who may override it. Tip In the protocol: safety rules “An arm will be suspended and referred to the DMC if, at any safety review, \(\Pr(\text{[event rate]} > [\text{limit}] \mid \text{data}) > 0.90\) under the prior in Section [x]. Reviews take place after every [number] participants per arm. By simulation, the probability of suspending an arm whose true event rate equals [acceptable rate] is [value], and the probability of suspending an arm whose true rate equals [unacceptable rate] within [number] participants is [value]. The rule is a trigger for DMC review, not an automatic stopping rule.”

title: The estimand
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.1.8 The estimand
text: The estimand Nothing about the estimand is different in a Bayesian trial, and that is the point. E9(R1) defines an estimand as “a precise description of the treatment effect reflecting the clinical question posed by a given clinical trial objective” and requires that “the targets of estimation are to be defined in advance of a clinical trial” ( International Council for Harmonisation 2019 ) . It has five attributes: the treatment, the population, the variable, the strategy for each intercurrent event, and the population-level summary. The posterior is a summary of the data about a parameter, and the parameter is the estimand. The common error is to build a Bayesian model for a convenient analysis, a model on the observed outcome ignoring discontinuation, and then describe it afterwards in estimand language. The protocol should do it in the other order. Tip In the protocol: the estimand “The primary estimand is the [summary, for example hazard ratio] of [variable] at [time] for participants with [condition], comparing [treatment] with [control], under a treatment policy strategy for [intercurrent event 1] and a [hypothetical, composite, while on treatment] strategy for [intercurrent event 2]. The Bayesian model in Section [x] targets this estimand: the parameter \(\theta\) is [definition]; the likelihood handles [intercurrent event] by [method]. Sensitivity analyses address [list].”

title: The statistical analysis plan and the simulation report
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.2 The statistical analysis plan and the simulation report
text: 23.2 The statistical analysis plan and the simulation report The SAP is finalized before unblinding, and for a Bayesian design it carries the detail the protocol should not: the exact model, the likelihood, the parameterization of the prior, the computation (software, sampler, chains, burn-in, convergence diagnostics, seeds), the handling of missing data and intercurrent events in the model, the full set of success criteria at each analysis, and the plan for sensitivity analyses. The Bayesian draft asks for all of this “as early as possible” and says that FDA does not require any particular software ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026d ) . It asks that reproducibility be built in at the results stage as well: software versions, documented code and the seeds used to initialize chains. For the primary analysis it also fixes the baseline covariates for adjustment, the stratification factors that enter the model, the handling of missing covariate values and whether the estimand is conditional or marginal, as set out in Section 5.10 . The simulation report is a separate document, and for a Bayesian or complex adaptive design it is the central one. It is what replaces, for the reviewer, the closed form power calculation. Chapter 14 describes how to design the simulation and what to report; choosing a design by simulation has a longer history in Bayesian decision theory

title: The statistical analysis plan and the simulation report
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.2 The statistical analysis plan and the simulation report
text: the central one. It is what replaces, for the reviewer, the closed form power calculation. Chapter 14 describes how to design the simulation and what to report; choosing a design by simulation has a longer history in Bayesian decision theory ( Müller and Parmigiani 1995 ) . For the protocol, what matters is the contents a regulator will look for, assembled from the Bayesian draft, the Adaptive Designs guidance and E20 Section 5: The design as simulated, with every rule of the protocol, in enough detail to be reproduced, including enrollment rate, delay in observing the endpoint, dropout and any operational assumptions. The scenarios: the null (global null where there are several arms), the design alternative, a range of plausible effects, effects smaller than planned, prior-data conflict scenarios, and, for several arms, configurations such as one effective arm or a non-monotone dose response. The draft asks that scenarios be “pre-specified, comprehensive, and plausible”. The operating characteristics under each scenario: probability of success (type I error under the null, power under the alternative), expected and maximum sample size, probability of stopping at each look, bias, mean squared error, interval coverage, and for adaptive randomization the allocation distribution. For a non-calibrated design the draft asks for Bayesian power, expected bias, interval width and mean squared error. Monte Carlo error: the number of simulated trials and the resulting

text: squared error, interval coverage, and for adaptive randomization the allocation distribution. For a non-calibrated design the draft asks for Bayesian power, expected bias, interval width and mean squared error. Monte Carlo error: the number of simulated trials and the resulting precision on each reported probability. A type I error of 0.024 estimated from a thousand runs is not evidence that it is below 0.025. Comparison with a simpler design. The draft asks for it for complex designs, and the question it answers is whether the complexity buys anything. Sensitivity of the operating characteristics to the prior and to model misspecification. The code, the seeds and the software environment. The calibration that the SAP and the simulation report both reference can be a few lines of R. title: The statistical analysis plan and the simulation report

text: validation across its prespecified nuisance grid (event rate, dropout, accrual). The power is 0.815, and the expected total sample size is 264 under the alternative against a maximum of 400. The same simulation gives the bias of the observed difference among trials that stop early for success, 0.062 under the alternative, which is the number the simulation report must show for the early-stopping reasons given in Chapter 21 . The scenario grid, the futility rules ( oc_with_futility ) and the prior (the prior argument) are added the same way. A sponsor that has done the calibration of Chapter 14 can write this report from its outputs. The report is versioned, and the protocol references a version by date, so that the design that was simulated is demonstrably the design that was run. A final point about the SAP. The temptation in an adaptive design is to leave details to be fixed at an interim. E20 says the opposite: the number and complexity of adaptations in a confirmatory trial should generally be limited, and everything that drives a decision is prespecified. A Bayesian SAP that defers the prior or the success threshold to a later version has not prespecified the design.

title: Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.3 Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
text: 23.3 Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025 Two standards shape the document itself, and neither is specific to Bayesian designs. ICH M11, the Clinical Electronic Structured Harmonised Protocol (CeSHarP), reached Step 4 in November 2025 and comes with a harmonized template and a technical specification, so that protocols present the same information in the same place and can be exchanged in a format acceptable to regulators ( International Council for Harmonisation 2025b ) . SPIRIT 2025 is a checklist of minimum items a protocol of a randomized trial should address ( Chan et al. 2025 ) . The reporting counterpart for adaptive trials is the CONSORT 2010 adaptive-designs extension (ACE) ( Dimairo et al. 2020 ) . The practical consequence is a mapping problem. M11 has sections where the design and statistics go, and a Bayesian design has components (prior, simulation-based calibration, predictive probability rules) that the template does not name. The sponsor should place them where a reviewer would look for the traditional counterpart: the prior with the statistical hypotheses and analysis methods, the decision rules with the interim analysis section, the operating characteristics with the sample size justification, and the detailed model and computation in the SAP, which the protocol references. The test of a good mapping is that a reviewer who has read only the protocol knows that the design is

title: Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.3 Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
text: characteristics with the sample size justification, and the detailed model and computation in the SAP, which the protocol references. The test of a good mapping is that a reviewer who has read only the protocol knows that the design is Bayesian, what the success criterion is, and where the simulation report is. A protocol that mentions “Bayesian methods” only in an appendix invites the first review question to be “where is the prior”. Several reporting guidelines sit around the protocol, and none of them is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial. SPIRIT 2013 ( Chan et al. 2013 ) is the antecedent of SPIRIT 2025, CONSORT 2025 ( Hopewell et al. 2025 ) is the reporting guideline for the results of a randomized trial, ACE, which extends CONSORT 2010 and predates CONSORT 2025, adds items on the pre-specified adaptations, and a guideline on the content of statistical analysis plans lists what the SAP should contain ( Gamble et al. 2017 ) . Only a few guidelines are written for Bayesian analyses, and they are author guidelines: the seven-item ROBUST checklist for reporting a Bayesian analysis of a clinical study ( Sung et al. 2005 ) , the Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines (BARG) ( Kruschke 2021 ) , and a consensus checklist for clinicians who read a trial analyzed by Bayesian methods ( Ferreira et

title: Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.3 Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025
text: analysis of a clinical study ( Sung et al. 2005 ) , the Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines (BARG) ( Kruschke 2021 ) , and a consensus checklist for clinicians who read a trial analyzed by Bayesian methods ( Ferreira et al. 2020 ) . The items a Bayesian trial adds to the generic lists are the same ones this chapter has put in the protocol: the prior and its source, the success criterion with its threshold and calibration, the interim schedule and the simulation report, the software and seeds, and the sensitivity analyses to the prior. A report that gives each of them where the generic checklist asks for its traditional counterpart satisfies the intent of all of these lists.

title: The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.4 The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
text: 23.4 The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what Adaptive trials add a requirement that fixed trials mostly avoid: someone must see unblinded comparative data during the trial in order to apply the adaptation rules, and the sponsor must not. The Adaptive Designs guidance lists trial integrity as one of its four principles, and the integrity concern is that knowledge of interim results, or even of what decision was made, can change the behavior of investigators, patients and sponsor staff, and so bias the trial. The practice is by now standard, and the DMC guidance of 2006 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2006 ) remains the starting document (FDA issued a draft revision in February 2024). What a Bayesian adaptive design adds is that the DMC charter must spell out the rules in more detail, because more of the design is executed at interim. A workable arrangement has four parties. The independent statistical center (or an unblinded statistician walled off from the sponsor’s team) holds the randomization code, runs the interim analyses, computes posterior and predictive probabilities, and reports to the DMC. It is also the place where an adaptive randomization update is computed and passed to the randomization system. The DMC reviews the unblinded reports, applies or overrides the rules, and makes recommendations to the sponsor. The charter states that the prespecified

title: The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.4 The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
text: is also the place where an adaptive randomization update is computed and passed to the randomization system. The DMC reviews the unblinded reports, applies or overrides the rules, and makes recommendations to the sponsor. The charter states that the prespecified rules are guides and that the committee keeps its judgment on safety, so that nothing in the Bayesian machinery turns the DMC into a rule executor. The sponsor’s blinded team receives from the DMC only what the charter allows: typically a recommendation to continue, stop or modify, and for a modification, the minimum information needed to implement it. For response-adaptive randomization, the allocation ratios themselves can reveal results, so the charter says who knows the current ratios and how site staff are kept from inferring a trend. Regulators may, under the charter, see more than the sponsor, and the sponsor should expect that a regulator reviewing a submission will want to see the interim reports, the minutes of the closed sessions, and the log of who had access. Tip In the protocol: DMC and firewall “An independent DMC, whose membership and charter are described in Appendix [x], will review unblinded data at each analysis in Section [y]. The independent statistical center will compute all decision quantities; no member of the sponsor’s study team, the investigators or the CRO’s blinded team will have access to unblinded

title: The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.4 The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
text: Appendix [x], will review unblinded data at each analysis in Section [y]. The independent statistical center will compute all decision quantities; no member of the sponsor’s study team, the investigators or the CRO’s blinded team will have access to unblinded comparative results or to the current allocation ratios, except [named roles and what they see]. Access to the unblinded system is logged. The DMC charter specifies the prespecified rules, the DMC’s authority to depart from them for safety or other reasons with documentation, the meeting schedule, the content of closed and open reports, and the communication path to the sponsor. A copy of the simulation report is available to the DMC.” What does a Bayesian design change about who sees what? Two things. First, the DMC should receive the simulation report, or a summary, so that its members know what the rules were designed to do and how often they are expected to trigger. A DMC that is asked to apply a posterior probability rule it does not understand will either follow it blindly or ignore it, and neither is acceptable. Second, firewalls in a platform trial are more complex, since arms enter and leave, and a sponsor of one arm should not see data of competing arms. Chapter 20 describes the structure, and one independent statistical center with one DMC over all arms is

title: The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.4 The data monitoring committee, firewalls, and who sees what
text: platform trial are more complex, since arms enter and leave, and a sponsor of one arm should not see data of competing arms. Chapter 20 describes the structure, and one independent statistical center with one DMC over all arms is a possible arrangement. FDA permits an independent external DMC or another appropriate independent entity, and the EMA reflection paper discusses separate analysis or study teams for different interventions, so the proposed structure has to protect independence and confidentiality across arms ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026c ; European Medicines Agency 2026 ) .

title: The interaction timeline with FDA
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.5 The interaction timeline with FDA
text: 23.5 The interaction timeline with FDA A regulator should never meet a Bayesian design for the first time in the submission. The Bayesian draft says that for complex designs the sponsor should request a meeting before the trial starts, and the substantial evidence draft says that a single-trial plan should be discussed with FDA before the single trial is started. The sequence below is the one a sponsor with a Bayesian confirmatory design should plan around. Meeting types and timelines are from the PDUFA formal meetings guidance of August 2026 ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026b ) ; the program descriptions are from FDA’s program pages and the CID guidance ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2020 ) , which a sponsor should reread before applying, since program details change with each PDUFA cycle. Table 23.2: Where a Bayesian design is raised with FDA. Pre-IND Type B meeting The development plan and, where a Bayesian phase 1 or 2 design is proposed, the design and the safety rules. Phase 2 design Type C or Type B;

In calendar days from receipt of the request, FDA’s response time is 14 for Type A, 21 for Type B, 14 for an end-of-phase Type B, 21 for Type C, 14 for Type D and 21 for INTERACT. Scheduling the meeting, or delivering a written response only (WRO), is 30 days for Type A, 60 for Type B, 70 for an end-of-phase meeting, 75 for Type C and 50 for Type D (Tables 1 and 2 of the guidance; the guidance says when the meeting is scheduled relative to the request, and the times in force should be checked against the guidance in effect). A sponsor planning a protocol should count backwards: an end-of-phase meeting requested in January is a spring meeting, and the simulation report has to be ready before the briefing package is due, which is earlier. The meeting is an opportunity to get written FDA feedback on the design, and the format of a written response only is often enough for a narrow question such as whether the proposed prior is acceptable. FDA’s Complex Innovative Trial Design program was established under the PDUFA VI commitments, and continued under PDUFA VII, to give sponsors extra interaction on designs whose operating characteristics cannot be derived in closed form, which in practice means Bayesian designs and complex adaptive designs ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.c ) . The December 2020 guidance describes how to interact with FDA on such designs ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2020 ) . As the program page describes it, the program now runs under PDUFA VII for fiscal years 2023 to 2027 and is run by CDER and CBER. Requests are due on the last day of each quarter (31 March, 30 June, 30 September, 31 December), FDA notifies sponsors within 45 days, and it selects one or two proposals per quarter, up to eight a year. A granted request receives an initial meeting and a follow-up meeting on the same proposal, the second approximately 90 days after FDA receives the briefing materials, which is when the simulation work is done and a reviewer can say something concrete. The sponsor needs a pre-IND or IND number, the trial cannot be first in human, and there must be enough clinical information to inform the proposed design. Before

The sponsor needs a pre-IND or IND number, the trial cannot be first in human, and there must be enough clinical information to inform the proposed design. Before the first meeting the sponsor and FDA agree which information FDA may publish in a public case study, which is how the January 2026 draft can name examples. To apply, a sponsor submits a request that describes the product and the development program, the proposed design and why it needs the program (what is complex about it), the planned use in an application, the simulation plan, and why the design is better for this product than a conventional alternative. A selection is not an agreement on the design, and the program is not a substitute for the regular Type B and C meetings. MIDD paired meetings. The Model-Informed Drug Development Paired Meeting Program offers a similar structure for modeling and simulation in a specific program ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.e ) . A Bayesian design with a pharmacometric component, such as exposure-response modeling to support dose selection or a prior built from a model, may fit here as well as at CID. The ICH M15 guideline on model-informed drug development (Step 4 in January 2026, International Council for Harmonisation ( 2026 ) )

The ICH M15 guideline on model-informed drug development (Step 4 in January 2026, International Council for Harmonisation ( 2026 ) ) frames the discussion in terms of question of interest, context of use, model influence, consequence of a wrong decision and model risk. A Bayesian trial whose prior or analysis depends on a model can use that vocabulary: the more the model decides, and the worse the consequences of a wrong decision, the more evaluation the regulator will want. CPIM. Critical Path Innovation Meetings are nonbinding and not tied to a product, and are aimed at discussing emerging methods and technologies ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.d ) . A sponsor who has developed a method, for example a way to build a prior from historical data in a specific disease area, can seek FDA’s informal views before any product depends on it. FDA describes CPIM discussions as non-regulatory, product-independent and nonbinding on both FDA and the requester, and says they do not substitute for pre-IND, IND, NDA or BLA meetings. Special Protocol Assessment. An SPA is a request for FDA’s written agreement on the design, endpoints and statistical analysis of certain trials, including trials intended to form the primary basis of an efficacy claim,

text: pre-IND, IND, NDA or BLA meetings. Special Protocol Assessment. An SPA is a request for FDA’s written agreement on the design, endpoints and statistical analysis of certain trials, including trials intended to form the primary basis of an efficacy claim, whatever their phase ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018 ) . The current guidance is the April 2018 revision. If FDA agrees, the agreement is documented, and FDA will not change its position on the agreed critical design elements unless a substantial scientific issue essential to determining safety or effectiveness is identified after the trial begins and the sponsor is notified (the statute also allows changes by agreement with the sponsor). An SPA resubmission after FDA comments is reviewed on a 45-day goal. It is worth considering for a Bayesian confirmatory trial, because it gets the prior, the criterion and the calibration agreed in writing before the data are seen. It is also demanding: FDA will not agree to what it has not seen, so the SAP and the simulation report must be complete, and the process will expose any design that cannot be defended. A sponsor should read the guidance on what happens if the sponsor changes the design afterwards. An SPA does not guarantee approval, or even that FDA will file the application: the agreement is about the design and not the

title: The interaction timeline with FDA
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.5 The interaction timeline with FDA
text: defended. A sponsor should read the guidance on what happens if the sponsor changes the design afterwards. An SPA does not guarantee approval, or even that FDA will file the application: the agreement is about the design and not the result. What to send. The Bayesian draft’s Section VIII is a ready list of what FDA wants in a pre-trial package: the prior and its justification; for informative priors the sources, including those excluded; the success criteria and the justification of \(a\) and \(c\) ; simulation evidence of familywise error control if calibrated, or Bayesian power and related metrics if not; the full simulation report with code; the computational details; and a comparison with simpler designs ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026d ) . A briefing package structured around that list makes the meeting short. What to ask. Meetings are won by specific questions. “Is a Bayesian design acceptable?” gets a vague answer. “Does FDA agree that the success criterion \(\Pr(\theta > 0.1 \mid \text{data}) > 0.985\) , calibrated to a one-sided familywise error of 0.025 under the scenarios in Table [x], is acceptable for the primary estimand?” gets a yes, a no with reasons, or a request for more simulation. Good questions name the prior, the criterion, the scenario grid, the interim schedule, the borrowing (if any) and the evidence package.

title: EMA and other regulators
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.6 EMA and other regulators
text: 23.6 EMA and other regulators At EMA the corresponding route is scientific advice from the CHMP, with the Scientific Advice Working Party, and for novel methods a qualification procedure or the Innovation Task Force; in the EU the Complex Clinical Trials Q&A of the Commission, EMA and the Heads of Medicines Agencies discusses Bayesian methods and recommends early dialogue ( European Commission and European Medicines Agency and Heads of Medicines Agencies 2022 ) . The Q&A asks sponsors to justify the use of Bayesian methods and to document priors. The 2007 reflection paper on adaptive designs is more conservative than the FDA’s guidance; ICH E20 is a Step 2 draft, and until it is final the 2019 guidance is FDA’s current final guidance. The October 2026 draft reflection paper on confirmatory platform trials takes a cautious position on response-adaptive randomization and non-concurrent controls ( European Medicines Agency 2026 ) . The practical advice is that a global development should plan for both agencies, request advice from EMA in parallel, and raise the points where the agencies may differ (adaptive randomization, borrowing from non-concurrent controls) in both. Where agencies differ, the protocol follows the stricter reading unless advice says otherwise. The structured protocol format, ICH M11, is harmonized, which helps. Details of the programs, with their dates and links, are in Appendix B .

title: Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.7 Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
text: 23.7 Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits The legal standard is in FD&C Act section 505(d), and 21 CFR 314.126 defines the adequate and well-controlled investigation. The statute speaks of “adequate and well-controlled investigations”, and for decades the working interpretation was two trials, each significant at two-sided 0.05, which is one-sided 0.025 each. The book’s companion online lab (module 11, https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/11-substantial-evidence.html) shows what that rule means arithmetically: a useless drug wins one trial in 40, and wins two independent trials about one time in 1,600 (one-sided 0.025 squared). Two trials are a strong filter, and a costly one. FDA’s revised draft guidance of June 2026 describes when one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence can satisfy the standard ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026a ) . A draft, not final, and not binding. It says that such an approach “will involve a highly persuasive trial or a source of strong confirmatory evidence” (Section IV.A). Among the factors it weighs: the seriousness of the disease and the unmet need, and “whether it is ethical and practicable to conduct more than one adequate and well-controlled trial”. Confirmatory evidence need not be another trial. The draft allows mechanistic evidence of the drug’s treatment effect in a particular disease as confirmatory evidence in appropriate cases. And it says that the plan “should

title: Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.7 Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
text: than one adequate and well-controlled trial”. Confirmatory evidence need not be another trial. The draft allows mechanistic evidence of the drug’s treatment effect in a particular disease as confirmatory evidence in appropriate cases. And it says that the plan “should be discussed with FDA prior to initiating the single trial”. The 2026 text revises the 2019 draft of the same name. Where does Bayesian evidence fit? Three places, and they need to be kept apart. First, a Bayesian trial can be one of the two trials, or the one trial. If its success criterion is calibrated to a familywise one-sided error of 0.025, it meets the default frequentist bar, and a reviewer treats it as a trial with a different analysis. This is the cleanest case, and nothing in the substantial evidence standard requires a \(p\) -value. Second, a Bayesian analysis can combine the one trial with other evidence in a formal way. A prior built from earlier data, a borrowing model from an adult trial for a pediatric population, or a hierarchical model across related populations is a way to represent the confirmatory evidence. FDA’s Bayesian draft discusses borrowing, and the REBYOTA program, where a prior phase 2 trial informed the phase 3 analysis, is the example it gives ( Chapter 19 ; the “In practice” section below shows how its two success thresholds

title: Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.7 Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
text: FDA’s Bayesian draft discusses borrowing, and the REBYOTA program, where a prior phase 2 trial informed the phase 3 analysis, is the example it gives ( Chapter 19 ; the “In practice” section below shows how its two success thresholds map onto one trial and two trials). The draft warns that a prior that is too informative “risks overwhelming the data collected in the target population”, that dynamic discounting should borrow less when the data are less similar, and that type I error inflation is a poor measure of borrowing, so the sponsor must propose and justify other metrics such as the ESS. Here the Bayesian method does what the substantial evidence draft asks to be done informally. It does not remove the need for the persuasion: the judgment of whether the other evidence is relevant and strong remains with FDA. Third, a Bayesian posterior probability can be offered as the measure of persuasiveness. A trial whose posterior probability of benefit is 0.9999 under a skeptical prior is “highly persuasive” in a way that a trial with \(p = 0.024\) is not. The draft does not say that a particular posterior probability makes a trial highly persuasive, and a sponsor should not claim so. The honest position is that the measure of how persuasive a single trial is can be stated on the posterior scale,

title: Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.7 Substantial evidence: two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits
text: not say that a particular posterior probability makes a trial highly persuasive, and a sponsor should not claim so. The honest position is that the measure of how persuasive a single trial is can be stated on the posterior scale, as it can be stated on the \(p\) -value scale or as predictive probability of replication, and the reviewer decides. Module 11 of the companion lab makes this concrete: a trial that barely wins repeats only about half the time if its observed effect is the true effect, so a single marginal win is not persuasive on any scale. And the substantial evidence standard is not lowered by a fast review: expedited programs speed the review of serious conditions and do not lower the proof. A final caution, from Chapter 21 and Chapter 7 : among single trials that stop early for efficacy under a calibrated Bayesian rule, the observed effect estimate is biased away from the null on average, and the sponsor should show the bias in the simulation report and report estimates that account for it where possible. A highly persuasive single trial is persuasive about the existence of an effect, and its estimate may still need shrinkage.

title: In practice
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.8 In practice
text: 23.8 In practice Five documents show how sponsors wrote Bayesian rules into protocols and SAPs and what regulators did with them. Two are SAPs, one is an FDA briefing document, one an FDA case study, and one the FDA’s own January 2026 list of design examples.

title: BNT162b2: thresholds calibrated to 2.5%
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.8.1 BNT162b2: thresholds calibrated to 2.5%
text: BNT162b2: thresholds calibrated to 2.5% The vaccine trial’s SAP wrote a beta-binomial success criterion with posterior thresholds of 0.995 at the interim analyses and 0.986 at the final analysis, calibrated so that the overall one-sided type I error was 2.5% ( Pfizer Inc. 2022 ) . The full case, with the prior, the arithmetic and the regulatory outcome, is in Section 21.5 . FDA’s announcements contain no statement on the Bayesian criterion, so the lesson is about the sponsor’s side: a prior with its numbers stated, a calibrated threshold, a nonbinding futility rule and a changed look schedule (the first interim analysis was not performed) handled by saying what remained fixed. The binomial model assumes equal surveillance time in the two arms, an approximation that FDA’s briefing document adjusts with the surveillance-time ratio.

title: DAWN: enrichment and a predictive-probability schedule
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.8.2 DAWN: enrichment and a predictive-probability schedule
text: DAWN: enrichment and a predictive-probability schedule DAWN’s SAP is the most complete Bayesian adaptive design among this chapter’s sources: every threshold, every look, the enrichment rule and its irreversibility, and the predictive-probability stopping bounds were fixed before unblinding, with the type I error a simulation output ( Stryker Neurovascular 2017 ; Jovin et al. 2017 ) . The design is discussed in Chapter 15 and Chapter 14 .

title: REBYOTA: the data alignment and the one-trial threshold
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.8.3 REBYOTA: the data alignment and the one-trial threshold
text: REBYOTA: the data alignment and the one-trial threshold The protocol lesson is that success thresholds can be written in the language of the substantial evidence standard (analogues of a one-sided 0.025 for one trial and 0.00125 for a substitute for two), and that exchangeability is something the reviewer tests in the data alignment. The full case is in Section 19.17.1 .

title: Belimumab in children: a post hoc Bayesian analysis requested by FDA
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.8.4 Belimumab in children: a post hoc Bayesian analysis requested by FDA
text: Belimumab in children: a post hoc Bayesian analysis requested by FDA The protocol lesson is that when a borrowing weight cannot be justified in advance, a tipping-point table is a defensible fallback, and it is a post hoc one. FDA’s case study recommends early consultation, ideally at a pre-IND meeting, and discussion of the detailed analysis plan before the clinical investigation begins ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research 2026 ) . The full case is in Section 19.17.2 .

title: The January 2026 draft's named CID examples
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.8.5 The January 2026 draft's named CID examples
text: The January 2026 draft’s named CID examples Two of the examples in FDA’s Bayesian draft come from the CID program, whose case studies are published ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2026d ) . A pediatric multiple sclerosis study is a randomized, double-blind, Bayesian group sequential non-inferiority trial against an approved active control, with one interim analysis for efficacy, using a robust meta-analytic-predictive prior from a completed pediatric trial and several adult trials, and FDA lists the first use of an active-controlled non-inferiority design in this setting, the borrowing, and model-based extrapolation from adults as the innovative features ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.b ) . An epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (EMAS) study is a placebo-controlled trial that borrows from related epilepsy populations through a hierarchical model, with sample size updated at unblinded interim analyses by Goldilocks predictive probabilities ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, n.d.a ) . Both are proposals discussed in the program, not approvals, and the case studies say so by calling them proposed. The lesson for this chapter is what the CID route produced: a published description of a design FDA found worth discussing, which a sponsor can cite in its own briefing package.

title: What the Bayesian design does not buy
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.9 What the Bayesian design does not buy
text: 23.9 What the Bayesian design does not buy A protocol chapter should say what the design cannot do, because sponsors who believe otherwise write the wrong protocol. There are four limits, taken from the working paper ( Polson and Sokolov 2026 ) and stated plainly. The saving is not against a single unadjusted analysis at a fixed level. The Bayes-factor bar is below the unadjusted \(z_\alpha^2\) only at small information: it exceeds it once \(I_n\tau^2\) passes about 41.6 for the exact normal-mixture boundary (for a unit-information prior, \(n > 41.6\) ; Chapter 11 ). In the SELECT reconstruction an unadjusted single look crosses at 309 events on the mean path, earlier than the calibrated Bayesian rule’s mean-path crossing near 600 events (conditional median stopping point 464). The unadjusted single look is not available to anyone who intends to look more than once, and the Bayesian gain is against the repeatedly monitored trial with the right error control, not against the fixed single look. Against a single analysis, the calibrated Bayesian bar is never lower unless an informative prior or borrowing is used. The surcharge the Bayesian rule avoids buys a real guarantee. An e-value rule holds its level at every stopping time, including ones the protocol never contemplated: a look inserted after an external publication, an early stop ordered for reasons outside the trial, continuous

title: What the Bayesian design does not buy
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.9 What the Bayesian design does not buy
text: Bayesian rule avoids buys a real guarantee. An e-value rule holds its level at every stopping time, including ones the protocol never contemplated: a look inserted after an external publication, an early stop ordered for reasons outside the trial, continuous unblinded inspection by a committee. A calibrated Bayesian rule holds 2.5 percent under the scheme to which it was calibrated, and under another scheme it holds something else. A sponsor who cannot commit to a monitoring plan should read Chapter 12 before choosing. The calibration requires knowing the monitoring plan and the horizon. That is exactly the knowledge the anytime valid construction is built to do without. The two paradigms make different promises. In protocol terms: the Bayesian design is credible only if the schedule is fixed, the horizon is stated, and deviations trigger a recalibration that is independent of interim results. The power ordering is not universal. In the SELECT reconstruction the calibrated Bayesian rule had higher power than the e-value rule, 94.7 against 83.1 percent. In a two arm binary endpoint design reported by Sokolova and Sokolov ( 2026 ) the order is reversed, 68.8 against 72.3 percent, with the Bayesian rule stopping slightly earlier. The comparison depends on prior scale, endpoint and monitoring grid. The robust finding concerns stopping time, not power, and the direction of the power difference should be checked

title: What the Bayesian design does not buy
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.9 What the Bayesian design does not buy
text: reversed, 68.8 against 72.3 percent, with the Bayesian rule stopping slightly earlier. The comparison depends on prior scale, endpoint and monitoring grid. The robust finding concerns stopping time, not power, and the direction of the power difference should be checked by simulation for the design at hand. Two further statements belong with these, from the case studies. The traditional scheduled design wins in some settings: the REWIND comparison in Chapter 21 is one, a single look with a sponsor that has no interest in early stopping. And no design, Bayesian or otherwise, removes the need for an adequate and well-controlled trial. A Bayesian design with a poor control, a bad endpoint or an unblinded outcome assessment is still a poor trial.

title: Checklists
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.10 Checklists
text: 23.10 Checklists For the sponsor , before the end-of-phase 2 meeting and again before the protocol is final: The estimand is written per E9(R1), with intercurrent event strategies, and the model targets it. The prior is stated in full, with ESS, source of any external data (including excluded sources), design priors for simulation, and named sensitivity analyses. The success criterion gives \(a\) and \(c\) with their clinical rationale, for each primary and key secondary estimand and at each interim analysis. Calibration is by simulation to familywise one-sided error 0.025, or the sponsor has asked FDA in advance to accept a different standard and said why. The interim schedule is fixed, with information fractions or calendar rules, and the operating characteristics were simulated on that schedule. The protocol says what happens if the schedule is missed. The simulation report is complete (scenarios, Monte Carlo error, comparison with a simpler design, code, seeds, software) and the protocol cites its version. Adaptive randomization, if used, has burn-in, floors, caps, time-trend handling and a bias assessment. Safety rules are stated as posterior statements with simulated false-stop and missed-harm rates, and the DMC retains its judgment. The DMC charter, firewall and access log are in place, and the DMC has seen the simulation summary. For multiple arms or endpoints, familywise error control is shown where the guidance expects it, or

title: Checklists
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.10 Checklists
text: and the DMC retains its judgment. The DMC charter, firewall and access log are in place, and the DMC has seen the simulation summary. For multiple arms or endpoints, familywise error control is shown where the guidance expects it, or the departure is explained. The computation is documented: software, sampler settings, convergence diagnostics, seeds, non-convergence plan. The evidence plan is clear: two trials, or one trial plus confirmatory evidence, and FDA has been asked about it before the trial starts. The meeting plan is dated: which meeting, which request type, which package, which questions. The protocol is mapped into the M11 template and SPIRIT items, with the Bayesian components placed where a reviewer would look. For the reviewer , reading a Bayesian submission: Is the prior prespecified, and could the data have changed it? Is the ESS reported and reasonable relative to the trial size? Is each informative component justified by relevant, complete evidence, including skeptical evidence and excluded sources, and what happens under prior-data conflict? What is the success criterion, and is it calibrated to the standard that applies? If not, was a different standard agreed? Do the simulated scenarios include the null, plausible smaller effects, and prior-data conflict, and does the Monte Carlo error support the reported rates? Was the simulated design the design that was run, in schedule, sample size, randomization and

text: standard agreed? Do the simulated scenarios include the null, plausible smaller effects, and prior-data conflict, and does the Monte Carlo error support the reported rates? Was the simulated design the design that was run, in schedule, sample size, randomization and analysis? Does the estimate at an early stop show the bias that stopping early implies, and does the report address it? Were firewalls maintained, and does the access log show it? How much does the conclusion depend on the prior, and does the report show a range of priors? For one trial plus confirmatory evidence: is the trial highly persuasive on the stated scale, and is the other evidence relevant to the population and endpoint? Is the whole analysis reproducible from the code and seeds supplied?

title: What to take away
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.11 What to take away
text: 23.11 What to take away Two pieces of advice are distinctive to this book and worth stating once. Clinicians and payers should ask what prior was used and how many patients it was worth, and should read a posterior probability as conditional on the model and the prior. Sponsors, regulators and statisticians should decide early whether the trial needs validity at stopping times the protocol cannot anticipate, and should report the realized type I error of whatever rule is used, with power beside it and stopping times as distributions. The key points below summarize the chapter.

title: Open questions
cx: Chapter 23: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators > 23.11.1 Open questions
text: Open questions Several questions remain open. The e-value price is exact for mixture e-values built on the same statistic as the Bayes factor, as an extra squared-standardized gap of \(2\log(1/\alpha)(1+1/q)\) , whose constant large-information approximation is \(2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38\) at \(\alpha = 0.025\) ( Chapter 11 ). For betting e-processes with adaptively chosen bets the analogous quantity depends on the strategy and we have no general expression. The calibration of a posterior rule to a frequentist error under continuous monitoring, which this book did numerically, has no asymptotic characterization here. A posterior-probability cutoff cannot itself diverge, so any such result would concern a transformed boundary, such as the implied standardized boundary, over a stated monitoring horizon, and we do not state one. Finally, the utility-based designs of Thall and Cook ( 2004 ) and Houédé et al. ( 2010 ) have operating characteristics that have not been compared with the conventional apparatus on the deviation-scale ledger of Chapter 11 , and doing so would show whether the phase 1 and 2 savings have the same source as the confirmatory ones. text: check. Note Key points A Bayesian protocol keeps the estimand, the randomization and the prespecification of a traditional one. It changes the objective, the prior, the sample size (a maximum), the interim rules, the multiplicity handling, the safety rules and, above all, how operating characteristics are shown. The prior should be prespecified and stated with its effective sample size, with named sensitivity analyses and design priors for simulation. The success criterion is \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) , calibrated by default in this book to one-sided familywise error 0.025. FDA’s draft also describes direct interpretation and decision-theoretic routes; a different standard, for instance with borrowing, should be agreed with FDA in advance. The simulation report is the central deliverable: scenarios, operating characteristics, Monte Carlo error, comparison with a simpler design, code and seeds. The DMC charter and firewall are part of the design, and the DMC should see the simulation summary. Raise the design early: pre-IND, Type B end of phase 2, the CID and MIDD paired meetings for complex designs, CPIM for methods, SPA for agreement on the phase 3 protocol, and EMA scientific advice in parallel. One adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence can meet the standard under the June 2026 draft, if highly persuasive or strongly confirmed, and it should be discussed with FDA before the trial starts. title: Notation
cx: Chapter A: Notation > A Notation
text: This appendix fixes the meaning of every symbol the book uses, defines the abbreviations, and gives short definitions of the key terms. Each symbol has one meaning throughout. Where a chapter needs a local symbol, it defines it on the spot and does not reuse one from this table.

title: Symbols
cx: Chapter A: Notation > A.1 Symbols
text: A.1 Symbols Symbol Meaning \(\theta\) Treatment effect (generic). For time-to-event outcomes \(\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}\) , so that benefit is positive. \(\delta\) Treatment effect in the FDA draft’s success criterion \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c\) . Used only when quoting that criterion; elsewhere the book writes \(\theta\) . \(a\) , \(c\) The minimum clinically relevant effect and the posterior probability threshold in that criterion. \(b\) Threshold on the Bayes factor (or on the e-value, \(b = 1/\alpha\) ), distinct from the posterior probability threshold \(c\) . \(p_j\) Response probability in arm \(j\) . The index \(j = 0\) is the control arm. \(n\) , \(n_j\) Sample size in patients or, for time-to-event outcomes, the number of events. \(n_j\) is the size of arm \(j\) . \(I\) Fisher information per patient (or per event). The total information is \(nI\) . \(Z_n\) Standardized test statistic after \(n\) observations. \(y\) , \(y_{1:n}\) , \(Y\) Observed data, the first \(n\) observations, and the corresponding random variable. \(\pi(\theta)\) Prior density of \(\theta\) . \(\pi(\theta \mid y)\) Posterior density of \(\theta\) given the data. \(p(y \mid \theta)\) Likelihood of the data, read as a function of \(\theta\) . \(\pi_0\) , \(\pi_a\) Prior probabilities of the null and of the alternative hypothesis. \(\alpha\) One-sided type I error rate, 0.025 unless stated otherwise. \(\beta\) Type II error rate. Power is \(1-\beta\)
