title: Abbreviations
cx: Chapter A: Notation > A.3 Abbreviations
text: A.3 Abbreviations Abbreviation Meaning BLA Biologics License Application. BOIN Bayesian optimal interval design for dose finding. CID Complex innovative trial design. Also the name of the FDA paired meeting program for such designs. CPIM Critical Path Innovation Meetings, an FDA program for nonbinding, product-independent discussion of methods. CRM Continual reassessment method, a model-based dose-finding design. CSR Clinical study report. DDT Drug development tool, as in the FDA qualification programs. DMC Data monitoring committee. EMA European Medicines Agency. ESS Effective sample size of a prior, the number of patients’ worth of information it carries. FDA United States Food and Drug Administration. FWER Familywise error rate, the probability of at least one false positive among a family of hypotheses. HMA Heads of Medicines Agencies. HR Hazard ratio. ICH International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use. IND Investigational New Drug application. IRT Interactive response technology, the system that randomizes patients and assigns drug supply. ITT Intention to treat, analysis of all randomized patients in the arms to which they were assigned. MAMS Multi-arm multi-stage design. MAP Meta-analytic-predictive prior, built from historical trials. MHRA Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (United Kingdom). MIDD Model-informed drug development. NDA New Drug Application. OC Operating characteristics of a design, such as type I error, power and expected sample size. PDUFA Prescription Drug User Fee Act, the statute and commitment letters under which FDA programs such as CID are run. QALY Quality-adjusted life year. RAR Response-adaptive randomization. SAP Statistical analysis plan. SPA Special protocol assessment, an agreement with FDA on a protocol’s design and analysis.

title: Key terms
cx: Chapter A: Notation > A.4 Key terms
text: A.4 Key terms Assurance. The probability of trial success averaged over a prior for the true effect, as opposed to power, which is computed at one assumed effect ( Chapter 9 ). Concurrent control. Control patients randomized during the same period as the patients on a given experimental arm. Control patients enrolled before that arm joined a platform trial are non-concurrent ( Chapter 20 ). Effective sample size. The number of patients whose data would carry the same information as the prior distribution ( Chapter 8 ). E-value. A nonnegative statistic whose expectation under the null is at most one. A running product of nonnegative factors forms a test supermartingale when each factor has conditional expectation at most one given the preceding data under every null distribution, and then, by Ville’s inequality, it allows valid decisions at any stopping time ( Chapter 12 ). Estimand. The precise description of the treatment effect to be estimated: the treatment condition, the population, the variable, how intercurrent events are handled, and the population-level summary (ICH E9(R1), Chapter 5 ). Intercurrent event. An event after treatment starts that affects the interpretation or existence of the measurements, such as discontinuation, rescue medication or death. Operating characteristics. The frequentist behavior of a design under stated scenarios, usually by simulation: type I error, power, expected sample size, bias ( Chapter 14 ).

title: Key terms
cx: Chapter A: Notation > A.4 Key terms
text: the interpretation or existence of the measurements, such as discontinuation, rescue medication or death. Operating characteristics. The frequentist behavior of a design under stated scenarios, usually by simulation: type I error, power, expected sample size, bias ( Chapter 14 ). Predictive probability. The probability, given the data so far, that a trial will meet its success criterion at the planned end, averaging over the unseen future data ( Chapter 15 ). Posterior probability of benefit. \(\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data})\) , the quantity compared with the threshold \(c\) in the FDA Bayesian draft ( Chapter 7 ).

title: Regulatory Documents and Programs
cx: Chapter B: Regulatory Documents and Programs > B Regulatory Documents and Programs
text: This appendix lists, in one place, each regulatory document and program the book relies on. Status is as of November 2026. A draft guidance is not binding: it proposes recommendations that may change before they are finalized, and it does not represent finalized agency thinking. Final FDA guidances also generally contain nonbinding recommendations. Dates are those printed on the document. Where this book has not confirmed an official address, the entry says “URL: see issuer website”. text: B.2 Products and trials named in FDA’s January 2026 Bayesian draft guidance Section III of the January 2026 draft guidance (printed pages 3 to 5) lists situations where Bayesian methods have been used and names the following products and trials. This list is of what the draft names, not an assessment of each case. Where the book has read a primary FDA document on a case, that source is given. REBYOTA (RBX2660), phase 3 trial. Borrowing from a previous phase 2 placebo-controlled study of the same product (Section III.A). The draft says the Bayesian analysis supported effectiveness and that REBYOTA was approved in 2022. The FDA briefing document for the advisory committee meeting of 22 September 2022 describes the hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing and its two success thresholds ( U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research 2022 ) . GBM AGILE (NCT03970447) and Precision Promise (NCT04229004). Oncology platform trials that augment the concurrent control with external or nonconcurrent control data, using Bayesian models for temporal shifts (Section III.B). A pediatric multiple sclerosis non-inferiority study run through the CID program, with a prespecified Bayesian analysis that borrows historical active-comparator data (Section III.B, revisited in Section V). It is described in an FDA CID case study ( https://www.fda.gov/media/172313/download ). Empagliflozin and linagliptin in pediatric type 2 diabetes. Supportive Bayesian analyses in supplements,

title: FDA programs

text: B.3 FDA programs Complex Innovative Trial Design (CID) Meeting Program. Active, a PDUFA commitment. title: Software and Code
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C Software and Code
text: All numerical results in the book are produced by R code that the reader can run. Nearly all of the computation lives in a companion R package, bayestrials , and the chapters call it in short chunks and draw the figures with ggplot2. This appendix describes how to install the package, how it is organized, a worked example, how to reproduce the results, the companion online lab, and the established software that practitioners use for trial design.

title: Installation
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.1 Installation
text: C.1 Installation The book was built with R 4.5.2. The package declares R 4.1 as its minimum version; it is version 0.1.0, it exports 203 functions, it passes R CMD check , and its tests run under testthat. The source is in the bayestrials/ directory of the book repository. From a clone of the repository it installs with R CMD INSTALL bayestrials or, directly from its GitHub repository ( https://github.com/VadimSokolov/bayestrials ), with the line below. remotes :: install_github ( "VadimSokolov/bayestrials" ) The chapters also use ggplot2 for figures, and the package imports only stats and parallel , with mvtnorm and the other packages it can use listed under Suggests. Quarto renders the book through knitr, and each chapter begins with a hidden setup chunk that loads bayestrials and ggplot2 .

title: How the package is organized
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.2 How the package is organized
text: C.2 How the package is organized Functions are named in snake_case, and the prefix tells the reader which part of the book the function belongs to. Arguments follow one convention throughout (see Section A.2 ): alpha is the one-sided type I error, theta an effect, p0 and p1 response rates, n a number of patients or events, nsim the number of simulated trials, and seed an optional random seed. Functions return numbers, named vectors, data frames or named lists. They never print or plot. Table C.1: Function families of bayestrials . title: A worked example
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.3 A worked example
text: C.3 A worked example The example calibrates a two-arm Bayesian design with three looks, at 100, 200 and 300 patients per arm and a control response rate of 0.30. The success rule is that the posterior probability of superiority exceeds a threshold \(c\) at any look. oc_calibrate chooses the smallest \(c\) that keeps the type I error at 0.025 under the null, and then the same threshold is applied to the alternative of a response rate of 0.45. Show the R code library (bayestrials) looks <- c ( 100 , 200 , 300 ) sim0 <- oc_simulate ( p0 = 0.3 , p1 = 0.3 , looks = looks, nsim = 20000 , seed = 1 ) c_star <- oc_calibrate (sim0, alpha = 0.025 ) sim0v <- oc_simulate ( p0 = 0.3 , p1 = 0.3 , looks = looks, nsim = 20000 , seed = 3 ) sim1 <- oc_simulate ( p0 = 0.3 , p1 = 0.45 , looks = looks, nsim = 20000 , seed = 2 ) oc0 <- oc_summarize (sim0, c_star); oc0v <- oc_summarize (sim0v, c_star); oc1 <- oc_summarize (sim1, c_star) The script gives a calibrated threshold of \(c =\) 0.989. The rejection proportion in the calibration run, 0.0246, is the calibration target and not an error assessment. On a fresh null run with another seed the type I error

title: A worked example
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.3 A worked example
text: c_star) The script gives a calibrated threshold of \(c =\) 0.989. The rejection proportion in the calibration run, 0.0246, is the calibration target and not an error assessment. On a fresh null run with another seed the type I error is 0.0234 and the expected total sample size is 594 (the maximum is 600). Under the alternative the power is 0.943 and the expected total sample size is 346, because the trial stops early at the first look that crosses the threshold. These numbers are Monte Carlo estimates from 20,000 trials; the seed makes them repeatable and a different seed gives values that differ in the third decimal place. A full validation would repeat the fresh null run across the prespecified nuisance grid. Chapter 14 explains how to report the Monte Carlo error.

title: Reproducibility
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.4 Reproducibility
text: C.4 Reproducibility Every simulation either calls set.seed() in the chunk or passes seed = to the package function, so the seed is visible next to the result. Functions draw random numbers from R’s global generator after the seed is set, so a chunk is repeatable but its results depend on the order of the random calls inside it. Monte Carlo results are reported with their Monte Carlo error ( Chapter 14 ). Quarto’s freeze mechanism ( freeze: auto in _quarto.yml ) stores the computed output of each chapter, so a rebuild reuses stored results unless the source of that chapter has changed, and the slow simulation chunks are also knitr-cached with the cache keyed to a checksum of the installed package. To regenerate a result after the package changes, reinstall it, delete the chapter’s directory under _freeze/ and its knitr cache directory, and render the chapter again. The R version and the installed package versions can be recorded with sessionInfo() , and the authors recommend that a reader who needs exact reproduction record them for their own protocol.

title: The companion lab
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.5 The companion lab
text: C.5 The companion lab An interactive tutorial accompanies the book at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/ . It runs in the browser and has modules that match the chapters, where the reader predicts an outcome and then checks it. The Bayesian trial simulator at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/14-simulator.html lets the reader set a design (arms, prior, thresholds, interim looks) and see simulated operating characteristics, in the spirit of the simulation report discussed in Chapter 14 . The full open simulator at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/14-studio.html is a free tool in the style of commercial design software such as FACTS: it handles several doses, adaptive allocation, scenarios and operating characteristics tables, and is the place to explore a design before writing code. Chapters that have a matching module end with a “Try it in the lab” callout. An online encyclopedia built on this volume, at https://vsokolov.org/bayesian_trials_lab/encyclopedia/ , has entries for the methods, trials, regulatory documents and people in the book, each linked to the section that treats it.

title: Established trial-design software
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text: C.6 Established trial-design software The following tools are in wide use. The descriptions are brief and cover only the purpose of each tool; consult each tool’s documentation for current features and versions. The R packages below are on CRAN, except bcrm, which CRAN archived on 8 May 2026. On the machine where the book was built, rpact 4.4.0, gsDesign 3.11.0, BOIN 2.7.2, brms 2.23.0 and rstan 2.32.7 were installed; the other tools were not checked. rpact (R package). Confirmatory adaptive design: group sequential designs, sample size reassessment and combination tests, with simulation. gsDesign (R package). Group sequential design, including spending functions and boundaries, and power and sample size calculation. A reader can compare its boundaries with gs_boundary and gs_spending_boundary ( Chapter 11 ). RBesT (R package). Bayesian evidence synthesis tools: construction of meta-analytic-predictive priors, robustification, and operating characteristics for designs that use historical data. Relevant to Chapter 19 . SampleSizeProportions and SampleSizeMeans (R packages, by Joseph and Bélisle). Bayesian sample size criteria (ALC, ACC, WOC) for proportions and means. The lupus example of Section 9.2.5.1 uses SampleSizeProportions 1.1.3. BOIN (R package). Design and simulation of Bayesian optimal interval phase I dose-finding trials. Relevant to Chapter 17 . trialr (R package). Bayesian clinical trial designs fitted with Stan, including dose-finding and phase II designs. adaptr (R package). Simulation of Bayesian adaptive multi-arm trials, with response-adaptive randomization,

title: Established trial-design software
cx: Chapter C: Software and Code > C.6 Established trial-design software
text: Bayesian optimal interval phase I dose-finding trials. Relevant to Chapter 17 . trialr (R package). Bayesian clinical trial designs fitted with Stan, including dose-finding and phase II designs. adaptr (R package). Simulation of Bayesian adaptive multi-arm trials, with response-adaptive randomization, early stopping and calibration of the stopping rules, summarized as operating characteristics. It is the closest open R counterpart to the simulation part of bayestrials for multi-arm designs. bcrm (R package; archived on CRAN on 8 May 2026, so it no longer installs from CRAN by default). Bayesian continual reassessment method for dose finding. Relevant to Chapter 17 . Stan and brms. Stan is a probabilistic programming language for Bayesian inference by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. brms is an R package that fits multilevel models through Stan with a formula interface. Both are used to fit analysis models when conjugate formulas are not available. FACTS (Berry Consultants). Commercial software for designing and simulating Bayesian adaptive trials, including dose finding, response-adaptive randomization and platform designs. Simulation output of this kind is what regulators ask for in a CID meeting ( Chapter 3 ). East Horizon (Cytel). Commercial software for the design, simulation and monitoring of fixed, group sequential and adaptive trials. It belongs to the same family as the East product line from the same company.
